Kirschner, of Charlottenburg, (contributions to the index of passages), Pastor Köhler, of Augst, Dr. Liebmann, of Kuczkow, Posen, Prof. Th. Nöldeke, of Strassburg, Pastor S. Preiswerk junior, of Bâle, Dr. Schwarz, of Leipzig, and Prof. B. Stade, of Giessen (died in 1906). Special mention must be made of the abundant help received from three old friends of this book, Prof. P. Haupt, of Baltimore, Prof. Knudtzon, of Kristiania, and Prof. H. Strack, of Berlin, and also, in connexion with the present edition, Prof. H. Hyvernat, of the University of Washington, who has rendered great service especially in the correction and enlargement of the indexes. I take this opportunity of thanking them all again sincerely. And I am no less grateful also to my dear colleague Prof. C. Steuernagel for the unwearying care with which he has helped me from beginning to end in correcting the proof-sheets. 

Among material changes introduced into this edition may be mentioned the abolition of the term {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ medium}} ({{GHGpar|10|d}}). 
In this I have adopted, not without hesitation, the views of Sievers. I find it, however, quite impossible to follow him in rejecting all distinctions of quantity in the vowels. It is no doubt possible that such matters may in the ''spoken'' language have worn a very different appearance, and especially that in the period of nearly a thousand years, over which the Old Testament writings extend, very great variations may have taken place. Our duty, however, is to represent the language in the form in which it has been handed down to us by the Masoretes; and that this form involves a distinction between unchangeable, tone-long, and short vowels, admits in my opinion of no doubt. The discussion of any 
earlier stage of development belongs not to Hebrew grammar but to comparative Semitic philology. 

The same answer may be made to Beer's desire ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ThLZ.|Theologische Literaturzeitung, ed. by E. Schürer. Lpz. 1876 ff.}}}} 1904,<section end=from_the_german_preface/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

11.text:
col. 314 f.) for an 'historical Hebrew grammar describing the actual growth of the language on a basis of comparative philology, as it may still be traced within the narrow limits of the Old Testament'. Such material as is available for the purpose ought indeed to be honestly set forth in the new editions of Gesenius; but Beer seems to me to appraise such material much too highly when he refers to it as necessitating an 'historical grammar'. In my opinion these historical differences have for the most part been obliterated by the harmonizing activity of the Masoretes.
E. KAUTZSCH.
Halle,
''July'', 1909.

Rem.—Line 1 probably began with {{GHGheb|text=תם}}, cf. {{GHGpar|145|o}}, since there is hardly room for {{GHGheb|text=תַּמָּה}}. Line 2. The reading {{GHGheb|text=להנקב}} is supported by the fact that a trace of the top of the {{GHGheb|text=ק}} is visible; cf Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, i. 53. The next word was probably, as {{nowrap|P. Haupt}} suggests, {{GHGheb|text=וישמע}}, the imperf. consec. Qal or Nipḥʿal. Line 3. {{GHGheb|text=זדה}}, not found in the Old Testament, most probably means a ''cleft'', ''crack'', but the etymology and consequently the pronunciation of it [{{GHGheb|text=זִדָּה}}?] are still doubtful.

{{larger|HEBREW GRAMMAR}}
INTRODUCTION
{{GHGpar-heading|1|The Semitic Languages in General}} {{fs|90%|B. Stade, {{GHGcite|title=Lehrb. der hebr. Gramm.}}, Lpz. 1879, § 2 ff.; E. König, {{GHGcite|title=Hist.-krit. Lehrgeb. der hebr. Spr.}}, i. Lpz. 1881, § 3; H. Strack, {{GHGcite|title=Einl. in das A.T.}}, 6th ed., Munich, 1906, p. 231 ff. (a good bibliography of all the Semitic dialects); Th. Nöldeke, article 'Semitic Languages', in the 9th ed. of the {{GHGcite|title=Encycl. Brit.}} ({{GHGcite|title=Die semit. Sprachen}}, 2nd ed., Lpz. 1899), and {{GHGcite|title=Beitr. sur sem. Sprachwiss.}}, Strassb., 1904; W. Wright, {{GHGcite|title=Lectures on the Comparative Grammar of the Semitic Languages}}, Cambr. 1890; H. Reckendorf, 'Zur Karakteristik der sem. Sprachen,' in the {{GHGcite|title=Actes du Xme Congrès internat. des Orientalistes}} (at Geneva in 1894), iii. 1 ff., Leiden, 1896; O. E. Lindberg, {{GHGcite|title=Vergl. Gramm. der sem. Sprachen}}, i A: {{GHGcite|title=Konsonantismus}}, Gothenburg, 1897; H. Zimmern, {{GHGcite|title=Vergl. Gramm. der sem. Sprachen}}, Berlin, 1898 ; E. König, {{GHGcite|title=Hebräisch und Semitisch: Prolegomena und Grundlinien einer Gesch. der sem. Sprachen}}, &c., Berlin, 1901; C. Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Semitische Sprachwissenschaft}}, Lpz. 1906, {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss der vergl. Gramm. der sem. Sprachen}}, vol. i (Laut- und Formenlehre), parts 1-5, Berlin, 1907 f. and his {{GHGcite|title=Kurzgef. vergleichende Gramm.}} (Porta Ling. Or.) Berlin, 1908.—The material contained in inscriptions has been in process of collection since 1881 in the Paris {{GHGcite|title=Corpus Inscriptionum Semiticarum}}. To this the best introductions are M. Lidzbarski's {{GHGcite|title=Handbuch der Nordsem. Epigraphik}}, Weimar, 1898, in 2 parts (text and plates), and his {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris zur sem. Epigraphik}} (5 parts published), Giessen, 1900 f. [G. A. Cooke, {{GHGcite|title=Handbook of North-Semitic Inscriptions}}, Oxford, 1903].}} {{GHGmargin-letter|1|a}} 1. The Hebrew language is one branch of a great family of languages in Western Asia which was indigenous in Palestine, Phoenicia, Syria, Mesopotamia, Babylonia, Assyria, and Arabia, that is to say, in the countries extending from the Mediterranean to the other side of the Euphrates and Tigris, and from the mountains of Armenia to the southern coast of Arabia. In early times, however, it spread from Arabia over Abyssinia, and by means of Phoenician colonies over many islands and sea-boards of the Mediterranean, as for instance to the Carthaginian coast. No comprehensive designation is found in early times for the languages and nations of this family; the name {{GHGterm|Semites}} or {{GHGterm|Semitic''First used by Schlözer in Eichhorn's {{GHGcite|title=Repertorium für bibl. u. morgenl. Literatur}}, 1781, p. 16 1.'' languages}} (based upon the fact that according to {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=21 ff.}} almost all nations speaking these languages are descended from Shem) is, however, now generally accepted, and has accordingly been retained here.From Shem are derived ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=21 ff.}}) the Aramaean and Arab families as well as the Hebrews, but not the Canaanites (Phoenicians), who are traced back to Ham ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=6.15 ff.|hidebook=vv}}), although their language belongs decidedly to what is now called Semitic. The language of the Babylonians and Assyrians also was long ago shown to be Semitic, just as Aššur ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=22}}) is included among the sons of Shem.

26.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Kathleen.wright5" /></noinclude><section begin="par1" />{{GHGmargin-letter|1|b}}
2. The better known Semitic languages may be subdivided<ref>For conjectures as to the gradual divergence of the dialects (first the Babylonian, then Canaanite, including Hebrew, lastly Aramaic and Arabic) from primitive Semitic, see Zimmern, {{GHGcite|title=KAT.}}<sup>3</sup>, ii. p. 644 ff.</ref> as follows:—

1. The South Semitic or Arabic branch. To this belong, besides the classical literary language of the Arabs and the modern vulgar Arabic, the older southern Arabic preserved in the Sabaean inscriptions (less correctly called Himyaritic), and its offshoot, the Geʿez or Ethiopic, in Abyssinia. 

II. The Middle Semitic or Canaanitish branch. To this belongs the Hebrew of the Old Testament with its descendants, the New Hebrew, as found especially in the Mishna (see below, {{GHGpar|3|a}}), and Rabbinic; also Phoenician, with Punic (in Carthage and its colonies), and the various remains of Canaanitish dialects preserved in names of places and persons, and in the inscription of Mêšaʿ, king of Moab.

{{GHGmargin-letter|1|c}}
III. The North Semitic or Aramaic branch. The subdivisions of this are—(1) The Eastern Aramaic or Syriac, the literary language of the Christian Syrians. The religious books of the Mandaeans (Nasoraeans, Sabians, also called the disciples of St. John) represent a very debased offshoot of this. A Jewish modification of Syriac is to be seen in the language of the Babylonian Talmud. (2) The Western or Palestinian Aramaic, incorrectly called also 'Chaldee'.<ref>In a wider sense all Jewish Aramaic is sometimes called 'Chaldee'.</ref> This latter dialect is represented in the Old Testament by two words in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=47}}, by the verse {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=11}}, and the sections {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=2|verse=4}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=4|verse=8}} to {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=6|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=7|verse=12–26}} as well as by a number of non-Jewish inscriptions and Jewish papyri (see below, under {{GHGmargin-letter-fmt|m}}), but especially by a considerable section of Jewish literature (Targums, Palestinian Gemara, &c.). To the same branch belongs also the Samaritan, with its admixture of Hebrew forms, and, except for the rather Arabic colouring of the proper names, the idiom of the Nabataean inscriptions 
in the Sinaitic peninsula, in the East of Palestine, &c.

{{fs|90%|For further particulars about the remains of Western Aramaic (including those in the New Test., in the Palmyrene and Egyptian Aramaic inscriptions) see Kautzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Biblisch-Aramäischen}}, Lpz. 1884, p. 6 ff.}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|1|d}}
IV. The East Semitic branch, the language of the Assyrio-Babylonian cuneiform inscriptions, the third line of the Achaemenian inscriptions. 

{{fs|90%|On the importance of Assyrian for Hebrew philology especially from a lexicographical point of view cf. Friedr. Delitzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Prolegomena eines neuen}}}}<section end="par1" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

27.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Kathleen.wright5" /></noinclude><section begin="par1" />{{GHGcite|title=hebr.-aram. Wörterbuchs zum A.T.}}, Lpz. 1886; P. Haupt, 'Assyrian Phonology, &c.,' in {{GHGcite|title=Hebraica}}, Chicago, Jan. 1885, vol. i. 3; Delitzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Assyrische Grammatik}}, 2nd ed., Berlin, 1906. 

If the above division into four branches be reduced to two principal groups, No. 1, as South Semitic, will be contrasted with the three North Semitic branches.<ref>{{GHGcite|title=Hommel, Grundriss der Geogr. und Gesch. des alten Orients}}, Munich, 1904, p. 75 ff., prefers to distinguish them as Eastern and Western Semitic branches. Their geographical position, however, is of less importance than the genealogical relation of the various groups of dialects, as rightly pointed out by A. Jeremias in {{GHGcite|title=Th.LZ.}} 1906, col. 291.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|1|e}}
{{fs|90%|All these languages stand to one another in much the same relation as those of the Germanic family (Gothic, Old Norse, Danish, Swedish; High and Low German in their earlier and later dialects), or as the Slavonic languages (Lithuanian, Lettish; Old Slavonic, Serbian, Russian; Polish, Bohemian). They are now either wholly extinct, as the Phoenician and Assyrian, or preserved only in a debased form, as Neo-Syriac among Syrian Christians and Jews in Mesopotamia and Kurdistan, Ethiopic (Geʿez) in the later Abyssinian dialects (Tigre, Tigriña, Amharic), and Hebrew among some modern Jews, except in so far as they attempt a purely literary reproduction of the language of the Old Testament. Arabic alone has not only occupied to this day its original abode in Arabia proper, but has also forced its way in all directions into the domain of other languages.}}

{{fs|90%|The Semitic family of languages is bounded on the East and North by another of still wider extent, which reaches from India to the western limits of Europe, and is called Indo-Germanic<ref>First by Klaproth in {{GHGcite|title=Asia Polyglotta}}, Paris, 1823; cf. Leo Meyer in {{GHGcite|title=Nachrichien d. Gött. Gesellschaft}}, 1901, p. 454.</ref> since it comprises, in the most varied ramifications, the Indian (Sanskrit), Old and New Persian, Greek, Latin, Slavonic, as well as Gothic and the other Germanic languages. With the Old Egyptian language, of which Coptic is a descendant, as well as with the languages of north-western Africa, the Semitic had from the earliest times much in common, especially in grammatical structure; but on the other hand there are fundamental differences between them, especially from a lexicographical point of view; see Erman, 'Das Verhältnis des Aegyptischen zu den semitischen Sprachen,' in the {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xlvi, 1892, p. 93 ff., and Brockelmann, Grundriss, i. 3.}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|1|f}}
3. ''The grammatical structure'' of the Semitic family of languages, as compared with that of other languages, especially the Indo-Germanic, exhibits numerous peculiarities which collectively constitute its distinctive character, although many of them are found singly in other languages. These are—(''a'') among the consonants, which in fact form the substance of these languages, occur peculiar gutturals of different grades; the vowels are subject, within the same consonantal framework, to great changes in order to express various modifications of the same stem-meaning; (''b'') the word-stems are almost invariably triliteral, i.e. composed of three consonants; (c) the verb is restricted to two tense-forms, with a peculiarly regulated use; (d) the noun has only two genders (masc. and fem.); and peculiar expedients are adopted for the purpose of indicating the case-relations; (e) the<section end="par1" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

28.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Kathleen.wright5" /></noinclude><section begin=par1/>oblique cases of the personal pronoun, as well as all the possessive pronouns and the pronominal object of the verb, are denoted by forms appended directly to the governing word (suffixes); (''f'') the almost complete absence of compounds both in the noun (with the exception of many proper names) and in the verb; (''g'') great simplicity in the expression of syntactical relations, e.g. the small number of particles, and the prevalence of simple co-ordination of clauses without periodic structure. Classical Arabic and Syriac, however, form a not unimportant exception as regards the last-mentioned point.

{{GHGmargin-letter|1|g}}
4. From a lexicographical point of view also the vocabulary of the Semites differs essentially from that of the Indo-Germanic languages, although there is apparently more agreement here than in the grammar. A considerable number of Semitic roots and stems agree in sound with synonyms in the Indo-Germanic family. But apart from expressions actually borrowed (see below, under {{GHGmargin-letter-fmt|i}}), the real similarity may be reduced to imitative words (onomatopoetica), and to those in which one and the same idea is represented by similar sounds in consequence of a formative instinct common to the most varied families of language. Neither of these proves any ''historic'' or ''generic'' relation, for which an agreement in grammatical structure would also be necessary. 

Comp. Friedr. Delitzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Studien über indogermanisch-semitische Wurzelverwandtschaft}}, Lpz. 1873; {{GHGcite|title=Nöldechen, Semit. Glossen zu Fick und Curtius}}, Magdeb. 1876 f.; McCurdy, {{GHGcite|title=Aryo-Semitic Speech}}, Andover, U. S. A., 1881. The phonetic relations have been thoroughly investigated by {{nowrap|H. Möller}} in {{GHGcite|title=Semitisch und Indogermanisch}}, Teil i, {{GHGcite|title=Konsotianten}}, Copenhagen and Lpz. 1907, a work which has evoked considerable criticism.

{{GHGmargin-letter|1|h}}
As onomatopoetic words, or as stem-sounds of a similar character, we may compare, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לָקַק}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָחַךְ}} {{polytonic|λείχω}}, {{lang|la|text=''lingo''}}, Skt. {{lang|sa|text=''lih''}}, Eng. {{GHGtranslate|to lick}}, Fr. {{lang|fr|text=''lécher''}}, Germ. {{lang|de|text=''lecken''}}; {{GHGheb|text=גָּלַל}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=אָגַל}}, {{GHGheb|text=עָגַל}}) {{polytonic|κυλίω}}, {{lang|la|text=''volvo''}}, Germ. {{lang|de|text=''quellen''}}, {{lang|de|text=''wallen''}}, Eng. {{GHGtranslate|to well}}; {{GHGheb|text=גָּרַד}}, {{GHGheb|text=חָרַט}}, {{GHGheb|text=חָרַת}} {{polytonic|χαράττω}}, Pers. {{lang|fa|text=''khârîdan''}}, Ital. {{lang|it|text=''grattare''}}, Fr. {{lang|fr|text=''gratter''}}, Eng. {{GHGtranslate|to grate}}, {{GHGtranslate|to scratch}}, Germ. {{lang|de|text=''kratzen''}}; {{GHGheb|text=פָּרַק|translate=frango|en=to break}}, Germ. {{lang|de|text=''brechen''}}, &c.; Reuss, {{GHGcite|title=Gesch. der hl. Schriften A.T.'s}}, Braunschw. 1881, p. 38, draws attention moreover to the Semitic equivalents for {{GHGtranslate|earth}}, {{GHGtranslate|six}}, {{GHGtranslate|seven}}, {{GHGtranslate|horn}}, {{GHGtranslate|to sound}}, {{GHGtranslate|to measure}}, {{GHGtranslate|to mix}}, {{GHGtranslate|to smell}}, {{GHGtranslate|to place}}, {{GHGtranslate|clear}}, {{GHGtranslate|to kneel}}, {{GHGtranslate|raven}}, {{GHGtranslate|goat}}, {{GHGtranslate|ox}}, &c. An example of a somewhat different kind is {{GHGpron|am}}, {{GHGpron|ham (sam)}}, {{GHGpron|gam}}, {{GHGpron|kam}}, in the sense of the German {{lang|de|text=''samt''}}, {{lang|de|text=''zusammen''}}, {{GHGtranslate|together}}; in Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=אָמַם}} (whence {{GHGheb|text=אֻמָּה|translate=people}}, properly {{GHGtranslate|assembly}}), {{GHGheb|text=עִם}} ({{GHGtranslate|with}}) {{lang|de|text=''samt''}}, {{GHGheb|text=גַּם|translate=also}}, {{GHGtranslate|moreover}}, Arab. {{GHGheb|text=גּמע}}<ref>{{GHGcritic|In Arabic script: {{lang|ar|text=جمع}}.}}</ref> {{GHGtranslate|to collect}}; Pers. {{lang|fa|text=''ham''}}, {{lang|fa|text=''hamah''}} ({{GHGtranslate|at the same time}}); Skt. {{lang|sa|text=''samâ''}} (with), Gk. {{polytonic|ἅμα}} ({{polytonic|ἅμφω}}), {{polytonic|ὁμός}}, {{polytonic|ὁμόῦ}} ({{polytonic|ὅμιλος}}, {{polytonic|ὅμαδος}}), and harder {{polytonic|ἅμφω}}, Lat. {{lang|la|text=''cum''}}, {{lang|la|text=''cumulus''}}, {{lang|la|text=''cunctus''}}; with the corresponding sibilant Skt. {{lang|sa|text=''sam''}}, Gk. {{polytonic|σύν}}, {{polytonic|ξύν}}, {{polytonic|ξυνός}} = {{polytonic|κοινός}}, Goth. {{lang|got|text=''sama''}}, Germ. {{lang|de|text=''samt''}}, {{lang|de|text=''sammeln''}}; but many of these instances are doubtful. 

{{GHGmargin-letter|1|i}}
Essentially different from this internal connexion is the occurrence of the same words in different languages, where one language has borrowed directly from the other. Such loan-words are—
<section end=par1/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

29.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Kathleen.wright5" /></noinclude><section begin="par1" />(a) In Hebrew: some names of objects which were originally indigenous in Babylonia and Assyria (see a comprehensive list of Assyrio-Babylonian loan-words in the Hebrew and Aramaic of the Old Testament in Zimmern and Winckler, {{GHGcite|title=KAT.}}<sup>3</sup> ii. p. 648 ff.), in Egypt, Persia, or India, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יְאֹר}} (also in the plural) {{GHGtranslate|river}}, from Egyptian {{lang|egy|text=''yoor''}}, generally as the name of the Nile (late Egypt. {{lang|egy|text=''yaro''}}, Assyr. {{lang|akk|text=''yaruʾu''}}), although it is possible that a pure Semitic {{GHGheb|text=יאר}} has been confounded with the Egyptian name of the Nile (so Zimmern); {{GHGheb|text=אָ֫חוּ}} (Egyptian) Nile-reed (see Lieblein, 'Mots égyptiens dans la Bible,' in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|PSBA.|Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archæology. London, 1879 ff.}}}} 1898, p. 202 f.); {{GHGheb|text=פַּרְדֵּס}} (in Zend {{lang|ira|text=pairidaêza}}, circumvallation = {{polytonic|παράδειδος}}) {{GHGtranslate|pleasure-garden}}, {{GHGtranslate|park}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֲדַרְכּוֹן|translate=daric}}, Persian gold coin; {{GHGheb|text=תֻּכִּיִּים|translate=peacocks}}, perhaps from the Malabar {{lang|mal|text=''tôgai''}} or {{lang|mal|text=''tôghai''}}. Some of these words are also found in Greek, as {{GHGheb|text=כַּרְפַּס}} (Pers. {{lang|ira|karbâs}}, Skt. {{lang|san|karpâsa}}) cotton, {{polytonic|κάρπασος}}, {{GHGtranslate|carbasus}}. On the other hand it is doubtful if {{GHGheb|text=קוֹף}} corresponds to the Greek {{polytonic|κῆπος}}, {{polytonic|κῆβος}}, Skt. {{lang|san|''kapi''}}, ape. 

(b) In Greek, &c.: some originally Semitic names of Asiatic products and articles of commerce, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בּוּץ}} {{polytonic|βύσσος}}, {{GHGtranslate|byssus}}; {{GHGheb|text=לְבֹנָה}}, {{polytonic|λίβανος}}, {{polytonic|λιβανωτός}}, {{GHGtranslate|incense}}; {{GHGheb|text=קָנֶה}} {{polytonic|κάνη}}, {{polytonic|κάννα}}, {{GHGtranslate|canna}}, cane; {{GHGheb|text=כַּמֹּן}} {{polytonic|κύμινον}}, {{GHGtranslate|cuminum}}, cumin; {{GHGheb|text=קְצִיעָה}} {{polytonic|κασσία}}, {{GHGtranslate|cassia}}; {{GHGheb|text=גָּמָל}} {{polytonic|κάμηλος}}, {{GHGtranslate|camelus|en=camel}}; {{GHGheb|text=עֵֽרָּבוֹן}}<ref>{{GHGcritic|It is unclear why this word is spelled here with a Dagesh in ר and with a Mèthĕg.|Amire80}}</ref> {{polytonic|ἀρραβών}}, {{GHGtranslate|arrhabo}}, {{GHGtranslate|arrha}}, pledge. Such transitions have perhaps been brought about chiefly by Phoenician trade. Cf. A. Müller, 'Semitische Lehnworte im älteren Griechisch,' in Bezzenberger's {{GHGcite|title=Beitrage zur Kunde der Indo-germ. Sprachen}}, Göttingen, 1877, vol. i. p. 273 ff.; E. Ries, {{GHGcite|title=Quae res et vocabula a gentibus semiticis in Graeciam pervenerint}}, Breslau, 1890; Muss-Arnolt, 'Semitic words in Greek and Latin,' in the {{GHGcite|title=Transactions of the American Philological Association}}, xxiii. p. 35 ff.; H. Lewy, {{GHGcite|title=Die semitischen Fremdwörter im Griech.}}, Berlin, 1895; {{GHGcite|title=J. H. Bondi, Dem hebr.-phöniz. Sprachzweige angehör. Lehnworter in hieroglyph, m. hieratischen Texten}}, Lpz. 1886. 

{{GHGmargin-letter|1|k}}
5. No system of writing is ever so perfect as to be able to reproduce the sounds of a language in all their various shades, and the ''writing of the Semites'' has one striking fundamental defect, viz. that only the consonants (which indeed form the substance of the language) are written as real letters,<ref>So also originally the Ethiopic writing, which afterwards represented the vowels by small appendages to the consonants, or by some other change in their form. On the Assyrio-Babylonian cuneiform writing, which likewise indicates the vowels, see the next note, ad fin.</ref> whilst of the vowels only the longer are indicated by certain representative consonants (see below, {{GHGpar|7}}). It was only later that special small marks (points or strokes below or above the consonants) were invented to represent to the eye all the vowel-sounds (see {{GHGpar|8}}). These are, however, superfluous for the practised reader, and are therefore often wholly omitted in Semitic manuscripts and printed texts. Semitic writing, moreover, almost invariably proceeds from right to left.<ref>The Sabaean (Himyaritic) writing runs occasionally from left to right, and even alternately in both directions ({{GHGterm|boustrophedon}}), but as a rule from right to left. In Ethiopic writing the direction from left to right has become the rule; some few old inscriptions exhibit, however, the opposite direction. The cuneiform writing also runs from left to right, but this is undoubtedly borrowed from a non-Semitic people. Cf. {{GHGpar|5|d}}, note 3.</ref>
<section end="par1" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

30.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Kathleen.wright5" /></noinclude><section begin=par1/>With the exception of the Assyrio-Babylonian (cuneiform), all varieties of Semitic writing, although differing widely in some respects, are derived from one and the same original alphabet, represented on extant monuments most faithfully by the characters used on the stele of Mêšaʿ, king of Moab (see below, {{GHGpar|2|d}}), and in the ''old'' Phoenician inscriptions, of which the bronze bowls from a temple of Baal ({{GHGcite|title=CIS.}} i. 22 ff. and Plate IV) are somewhat earlier than Mêšaʿ. The old Hebrew writing, as it appears on the oldest monument, the Siloam inscription (see below, {{GHGpar|2|d}}), exhibits essentially the same character. The old Greek, and indirectly all European alphabets, are descended from the old Phoenician writing (see {{GHGpar|5|i}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|1|l}}
{{fs|90%|See the Table of Alphabets at the beginning of the Grammar, which shows the relations of the older varieties of Semitic writing to one another and especially the origin of the present Hebrew characters from their primitive forms. For a more complete view, see Gesenius' {{GHGcite|title=Scripturae linguaeque Phoeniciae monumenta}}, Lips. 1837, 4to, pt. i. p. 15 ff., and pt. iii. tab. 1-5. From numerous monuments since discovered, our knowledge of the Semitic characters, especially the Phoenician, has become considerably enlarged and more accurate. Cf. the all but exhaustive bibliography (from 1616 to 1896) in Lidzbarski's {{GHGcite|title=Handbuch der Nordsemitischen Epigraphik}}, i. p. 4 ff., and on the origin of the Semitic alphabet, ibid., p. I73ff., and {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}} (see the heading of {{GHGpar|1|a}} above), i. pp. 109 ff., 142, 261 ff., and his 'Altsemitische Texte', pt. i, {{GHGcite|title=Kanaanäische Inschriften}} (Moabite, Old-Hebrew, Phoenician, Punic), Giessen, 1907.—On the origin and development of the ''Hebrew'' characters and the best tables of alphabets, see {{GHGpar|5|a}}, last note, and especially {{GHGpar|5|e}}.}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|1|m}}
6. As regards the relative ''age'' of the Semitic languages, the oldest literary remains of them are to be found in the Assyrio-Babylonian (cuneiform) inscriptions,<ref>According to Hilprecht, {{GHGcite|title=The Babylonian Expedition of the University of Pennsylvania}}, i. p. ii ff., the inscriptions found at Nippur embrace the period from about 4000 to 450 b. c.</ref> with which are to be classed the earliest Hebrew fragments occurring in the old Testament (see {{GHGpar|2}}).

The earliest non-Jewish Aramaic inscriptions known to us are that of {{GHGheb|text=זכר}} king of Hamath (early eighth cent. {{smaller|B.C.}}), on which see Nöldeke, {{GHGcite|title=ZA.}} 1908, p. 376, and that found at Teima, in N. Arabia, in 1880, probably of the fifth cent. {{smaller|B.C.}}, cf. E. Littmann in the {{GHGcite|title=Monist}}, xiv. 4 [and Cooke, ''op. cit.'', p. 195]. The monuments of Kalammus of Samʾal, in the reign of Shalmanezer II, 859-829 {{smaller|B.C.}} (cf. A. Šanda, {{GHGcite|title=Die Aramäer}}, Lpz. 1902, p. 26), and those found in 1888-1891 at Zenjîrlî in N. Syria, including the Hadad inscription of thirty-four lines (early eighth cent. {{smaller|B.C.}}) and the Panammu inscription (740 {{smaller|B.C.}}), are not in pure Aramaic. The Jewish-Aramaic writings begin about the time of Cyrus (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=6|verse=3 ff.}}), specially important being the papyri from Assuan ed. by Sayce and Cowley, London, 1906 (and in a cheaper form by Staerk, Bonn, 1907), which are precisely dated from 471 to 411 {{smaller|B.C.}}, and three others of 407 {{smaller|B.C.}} ed. by Sachau, Berlin, 1907.
<section end=par1/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

31.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Innotata" /></noinclude><section begin=par1/>Monuments of the ''Arabic'' branch first appear in the earliest centuries {{smaller|A.D.}} (Sabaean inscriptions, Ethiopic translation of the Bible in the fourth or fifth century, North-Arabic literature from the sixth century {{smaller|A.D.}}).

It is, however, another question which of these languages has adhered longest and most faithfully to the original character of the Semitic, and which consequently represents to us the earliest phase of its development. For the more or less rapid transformation of the sounds and forms of a language, as spoken by nations and races, is dependent on causes quite distinct from the growth of a literature, and the organic structure of a language is often considerably impaired even before it has developed a literature, especially by early contact with people of a different language. Thus in the Semitic group, the Aramaic dialects exhibit the earliest and greatest decay, next to them the Hebrew-Canaanitish, and in its own way the Assyrian. Arabic, owing to the seclusion of the desert tribes, was the longest to retain the original fullness and purity of the sounds and forms of words.<ref>Even now the language of some of the Bèdawîs much purer and more archaic than that of the town Arabs. It must, however, be admitted that the former exalted estimate of the primitiveness of Arabic has been moderated in many respects by the most recent school of Semitic philology. Much apparently original is to be regarded with Nöldeke ({{GHGcite|title=Die semit. Spr.}}, p. 5 [={{GHGcite|title=Encycl. Brit.}}, ed. 9, art. {{Small-caps|Semitic Languages}}, p. 642]) only as a modification of the original. The assertion that the Arabs exhibit Semitic characteristics in their purest form, should, according to Nöldeke, be rather that ‘the inhabitants of the desert lands of Arabia, under the influence of the extraordinarily monotonous scenery and of a life continually the same amid continual change, have developed most exclusively some of the principal traits of the Semitic race’.</ref> Even here, however, there appeared, through the revolutionary influence of Islam, an ever-increasing decay, until Arabic at length reached the stage at which we find Hebrew in the Old Testament.

{{GHGmargin-letter|1|n}}
{{Font-size90%/s}}Hence the phenomenon, that in its grammatical structure the ancient Hebrew agrees more with the modern than with the ancient Arabic, and that the latter, although it only appears as a written language at a later period, has yet in many respects preserved a more complete structure and a more original vowel system than the other Semitic languages, cf. Nöldeke, ‘Das klassische Arabisch und die arabischen Dialekte,’ in {{GHGcite|title=Beiträge zur semitischen Sprachwissenschaft}}, p. 1 ff. It thus occupies amongst them a position similar to that which Sanskrit holds among the Indo-Germanic languages, or Gothic in the narrower circle of the Germanic. But even the toughest organism of a language often deteriorates, at least in single forms and derivatives, while on the contrary, in the midst of what is otherwise universal decay, there still remains here and there something original and archaic; and this is the case with the Semitic languages.

Fuller proof of the above statements belongs to the comparative Grammar of the Semitic languages. It follows, however, from what has been said: (1) that the Hebrew language, as found in the sacred literature of the Jews, has, in respect<section end=par1/><noinclude>{{Font-size90%/e}}
{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

32.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Kathleen.wright5" />{{Font-size90%/s}}</noinclude><section begin="par1" />to its organic structure, already suffered more considerable losses than the Arabic, which appears much later on the historical horizon; (2) that, notwithstanding this fact, we cannot at once and in all points concede priority to the latter; (3) that it is a mistake to consider with some that the Aramaic, on account of its simplicity (which is only due to the decay of its organic structure), is the oldest form of Semitic speech.{{Font-size90%/e}}
<section end="par1" />
<section begin="par2" />{{GHGpar-heading|2|Sketch of the History of the Hebrew Language}}

See Gesenius, {{GHGcite|title=Gesch. der hebr. Sprache u. Schrift}}, Lpz. 1815, §§ 5–18; Th. Nöldeke’s art., ‘Sprache, hebräische,’ in Schenkel’s {{GHGcite|title=Bibel-Lexikon}}, Bd. v, Lpz. 1875; F. Buhl, ‘Hebräische Sprache,’ in Hauck’s {{GHGcite|title=Realencycl. für prot. Theol. und Kirche}}, vii (1899), p. 506 ff.; A. Cowley, ‘Hebrew Language and Literature,’ in the forthcoming ed. of the {{GHGcite|title=Encycl. Brit.}}; W. R. Smith in the {{GHGcite|title=Encycl. Bibl.}}, ii. London, 1901, p. 1984 ff.; A. Lukyn Williams, ‘Hebrew,’ in Hastings’ {{GHGcite|title=Dict. of the Bible}}, ii. p. 325 ff., Edinb. 1899.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|a}}
'''1.''' The name {{GHGterm|Hebrew Language}} usually denotes the language of the sacred writings of the Israelites which form the canon of the {{GHGterm|Old Testament}}. It is also called {{GHGterm|Ancient Hebrew}} in contradistinction to the New Hebrew of Jewish writings of the post-biblical period ({{GHGpar|3|a}}). The name Hebrew language ({{GHGheb|text=לָשׁוֹן עִבְרִית}} {{polytonic|γλῶσσα τῶν Ἑβραίων}}, {{polytonic|ἑβραϊστί}}) does not occur in the Old Testament itself. Instead of it we find in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=19|verse=18}} the term ''language of Canaan'',<ref>That Hebrew in its present form was actually developed in Canaan appears from such facts as the use of ''yām'' (sea) for the west, ''nègeb'' (properly ''dryness'', afterwards as a proper name for the south of Palestine) for the south.</ref> and {{GHGheb|text=יְהוּדִית}} ''in the Jews’ language'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=18|verse=26.28}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=36|verse=11.13}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=13|verse=24}}. In the last-cited passage it already agrees with the later (post-exilic) usage, which gradually extended the name ''Jews, Jewish'' to the whole nation, as in Haggai, Nehemiah, and the book of Esther.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|b}}
The distinction between the names ''Hebrew'' ({{GHGheb|text=עִבְרִים}} {{polytonic|Ἑβραῖοι}}) and ''Israelites'' ({{GHGheb|text=בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל}}) is that the latter was rather a national name of honour, with also a religious significance, employed by the people themselves, while the former appears as the less significant name by which the nation was known amongst foreigners. Hence in the Old Testament ''Hebrews'' are only spoken of either when the name is employed by themselves as contrasted with foreigners ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=6 f.}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=18|hidebook=1}} &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=1|verse=9}}) or when it is put in the mouth of those who are not Israelites ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=14.17}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=12|hidebook=1}} &c.) or, finally, when it is used in opposition to other nations ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=13}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=32|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=11.13}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=1|hidebook=1}}). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=13|verse=3.7}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=21|hidebook=1}} the text is clearly corrupt. In the Greek and Latin authors, as well as in Josephus, the name {{polytonic|Ἑβραῖοι}}, Hebraei,<ref>The Graeco-Roman form of the name is not directly derived from the Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=עִבְרִי}}, but from the Palestinian Aramaic ''ʿebrāyā'', ‘''the'' Hebrew.’</ref> &c., alone occurs. Of the many explanations of the gentilic {{GHGheb|text=עִבְרִי}}, the derivation from {{GHGheb|text=עֵבֶר|translate=a country on the other side}} with the derivative suffix {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}} ({{GHGpar|86|h}}) appears to be the only one philologically possible. The name accordingly denoted the Israelites as being those who inhabited the ''ʿeber'', i.e. the district on the other side of the Jordan (or according to others the Euphrates), and would therefore originally be only appropriate when used by the nations on this side of the Jordan or Euphrates. We must, then, suppose that after the crossing of the river in question it had been retained by the Abrahamidae as an old-established name, and within certain limits
<section end="par2" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

33.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="2" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par2" />(see above) had become naturalized among them. In referring this name to the patronymic Eber, the Hebrew genealogists have assigned to it a much more comprehensive signification. For since in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=21}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=24|verse=24}} does not apply) Shem is called the ''father of all the children of Eber'', and to the latter there also belonged according to {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=14 ff.}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=25 ff.|hidebook=1}} Aramean and Arab races, the name, afterwards restricted in the form of the gentilic ''ʿibrî'' exclusively to the Israelites, must have originally included a considerably larger group of countries and nations. The etymological significance of the name must in that case not be insisted upon.<ref>We may also leave out of account the linguistically possible identification of the ʿIbriyyîm with the Ḫabiri who appear in the Tell-el-Amarna letters (about 1400 {{smaller|B.C.}}) as freebooters and mercenaries in Palestine and its neighbourhood.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|c}}
The term {{polytonic|ἑβραϊστί}} is first used, to denote the old Hebrew, in the prologue to Jesus the son of Sirach (about 130 {{smaller|B.C.}}), and in the New Testament, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Rv|chapter=9|verse=11}}. On the other hand it serves in {{GHGbible-ref|book=John|chapter=5|verse=2|actualbook=John}}<!-- "Jn" is printed, but elsewhere "Jn" refers to Jonah. This will be fixed using a new bible-ref template. -->, {{GHGbible-ref|book=John|chapter=19|verse=13.17|hidebook=1}} perhaps also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=John|chapter=19|verse=20|hidebook=1}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Rv|chapter=16|verse=16}} to denote what was then the (Aramaic) vernacular of Palestine as opposed to the Greek. The meaning of the expression {{polytonic|ἑβραῒς διάλεκτος}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Acts|chapter=21|verse=40}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Acts|chapter=22|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Acts|chapter=26|verse=14|hidebook=1}} is doubtful (cf. Kautzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Bibl.-Aram.}}, p. 19 f.). Josephus also uses the term ''Hebrew'' both of the old Hebrew and of the Aramaic vernacular of his time.

The Hebrew language is first called the ''sacred language'' in the Jewish-Aramaic versions of the Old Testament, as being the language of the sacred books in opposition to the ''lingua profana'', i.e. the Aramaic vulgar tongue.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|d}}
'''2.''' With the exception of the Old Testament (and apart from the Phoenician inscriptions; see below, {{GHGpar|2|f|nonumber=1}}–{{GHGpar|2|h|nonumber=1}}), only very few remains of old Hebrew or old Canaanitish literature have been preserved. Of the latter—(1) an inscription, unfortunately much injured, of thirty-four lines, which was found in the ancient territory of the tribe of Reuben, about twelve miles to the east of the Dead Sea, among the ruins of the city of Dîbôn (now Dîbân), inhabited in earlier times by the Gadites, afterwards by the Moabites. In it the Moabite king Mêšaʿ (about 850 {{smaller|B.C.}}) recounts his battles with Israel (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=4 ff.}}), his buildings, and other matters.<ref>This monument, unique of its kind, was first seen in August, 1868, on the spot, by the German missionary F. A. Klein. It was afterwards broken into pieces by the Arabs, so that only an incomplete copy of the inscription could be made. Most of the fragments are now in the Louvre in Paris. For the history of the discovery and for the earlier literature relating to the stone, see Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Nordsemitische Epigraphik}}, i. pp. 103 f., 415 f., and in the bibliography (under Me), p. 39 ff. The useful reproduction and translation of the inscription by Smend and Socin (Freiburg in Baden, 1886) was afterwards revised and improved by Nordlander, {{GHGcite|title=Die Inschrift des Königs Mesa von Moab}}, Lpz. 1896; by Socin and Holzinger, ‘Zur Mesainschrift’ ({{GHGcite|title=Berichte der K. Sächsischen Gesell. d. Wiss.}}, Dec. 1897); and by Lidzbarski, ‘Eine Nachprüfung der Mesainschrift’ ({{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, i. 1, p. 1 ff.; text in his {{GHGcite|title=Altsemitischs Texte}}, pt. 1, Giessen, 1907); J. Halévy, {{GHGcite|title=Revue Sémitique}}, 1900, pp. 236 ff., 289 ff., 1901, p. 297 ff.; M. J. Lagrange, {{GHGcite|title=Revue biblique internationale}}, 1901, p. 522 ff.; F. Prätorius in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1905, p. 33 ff., 1906, p. 402. Its genuineness was attacked by A. Löwy, {{GHGcite|title=Die Echtheit der Moabit. Inschr. im Louvre}} (Wien, 1903), and G. Jahn in {{GHGcite|title=Das Buch Daniel}}, Lpz. 1904, p. 122 ff. (also in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1905, p. 723 ff.), but without justification, as shown by E. König in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1905, pp. 233 ff. and 743 ff. [Cf. also Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Notes on the Hebrew Text of the Books of Samuel}}, Oxford, 1890, p. lxxxv ff.; Cooke, ''op. cit.'', p. 1 ff.]</ref> Of old Hebrew: (2) an inscription<section end="par2" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

34.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Kathleen.wright5" /></noinclude><section begin="par2"/>of six lines (probably of the eighth century {{smaller|B.C.}}<ref>Of this inscription—unfortunately not dated, but linguistically and palaeographically very important—referring to the boring of the tunnel, a facsimile is given at the beginning of this grammar. See also Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Nordsemitische Epigraphik}}, i. 105, 163, 439 (bibliography, p. 56 ff.; facsimile, vol. ii, plate xxi, 1); on the new drawing of it by Socin ({{GHGcite|title=ZDPV}}. xxii. p. 61 ff. and separately published at Freiburg i. B. 1899), see Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, i. 53 ff. and 310 f. (text in {{GHGcite|title=Altsemit. Texte}}, p. 9 f.). Against the view of A. Fischer ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1902, p. 800 f.) that the six lines are the continuation of an inscription which was never executed, see Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, ii. 71. The inscription was removed in 1890, and broken into six or seven pieces in the process. It has since been well restored, and is now in the Imperial Museum at Constantinople. If, as can hardly be doubted, the name {{GHGheb|text=שִׁלֹּחַ}} (i.e. ''emissio'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=6}} refers to the discharge of water from the Virgin’s Spring, through the tunnel (so Stade, {{GHGcite|title=Gesch. Isr.}} i. 594), then the latter, and consequently the inscription, was already in existence about 736 {{smaller|B.C.}} [Cf. Cooke, ''op. cit.'', p. 15 ff.]</ref>) discovered in June, 1880, in the tunnel between the Virgin’s Spring and the Pool of Siloam at Jerusalem; (3) about forty engraved seal-stones, some of them pre-exilic but bearing little except proper names﻿﻿﻿<ref>M. A. Levy, {{GHGcite|title=Siegel u. Gemmen, &c.}}, Bresl. 1869, p. 33 ff.; Stade, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1897, p. 501 ff. (four old-Semitic seals published in 1896); Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Handbuch}}, i. 169 f.; {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, i. 10 ff.; W. Nowack, {{GHGcite|title=Lehrb. d. hebr. Archäol}}. (Freib. 1894), i. 262 f.; I. Benzinger, {{GHGcite|title=Hebr. Archäol}}.<sup>2</sup> (Tübingen, 1907), pp. 80, 225 ff., which includes the beautiful seal inscribed {{GHGheb|text=לשמע עבד ירבעם}} from the castle-hill of Megiddo, found in 1904; [Cooke, p. 362].</ref>﻿; (4) coins of the Maccabaean prince Simon (from ‘the 2nd year of deliverance’, 140 and 139 {{smaller|B.C.}}) and his successors,<ref>De Saulcy, {{GHGcite|title=Numismatique de la Terre Sainte}}, Par. 1874; M. A. Levy, {{GHGcite|title=Gesch. der jüd. Münzen}}, Breslau, 1862; Madden, {{GHGcite|title=The Coins of the Jews}}, Lond. 1881; Reinach, {{GHGcite|title=Les monnaies juives}}, Paris, 1888.—Cf. the literature in Schörer’s {{GHGcite|title=Gesch. des jüd.Volkes im Zeitalter J. C.}}<sup>3</sup>, Lpz. 1901, i. p. 20 ff.; [Cooke, p. 352 ff.].</ref>﻿ and the coinage of the revolts in the times of Vespasian and Hadrian.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|e}}
'''3.''' In the whole series of the ancient Hebrew writings, as found in the Old Testament and also in non-biblical monuments (see above, {{GHGpar|2|d|nonumber=1}}), the language (to judge from its consonantal formation) remains, as regards its general character, and apart from slight changes in form and differences of style (see {{GHGpar|2|k|nonumber=1}} to {{GHGpar|2|w|nonumber=1}}), at about the same stage of development. In this form, it may at an early time have been fixed as a literary language, and the fact that the books contained in the Old Testament were handed down as ''sacred'' writings, must have contributed to this constant uniformity.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|f}}
To this old Hebrew, the language of the Canaanitish or Phoenician<ref>{{GHGheb|text=כְּנַעַן}}, {{GHGheb|text=כְּנַֽעֲנִי}} is the native name, common both to the Canaanitish tribes in Palestine and to those which dwelt at the foot of the Lebanon and on the Syrian coast, whom we call Phoenicians, while they called themselves {{GHGheb|text=כנען}} on their coins. The people of Carthage also called themselves so.</ref> stocks came the nearest of all the Semitic languages, as is evident partly from the many Canaanitish names of persons and places with a Hebrew form and meaning which occur in the Old Testament (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק}}, {{GHGheb|text=קִרְיַת סֵפֶר}}, &c.;<section end="par2"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

35.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Kathleen.wright5" /></noinclude><section begin="par2" />on ‘Canaanite glosses’<ref>Cf. inter alia: ''aparu'', also ''ḫaparu'' (Assyr. ''epru, ipru'') = {{GHGheb|text=עָפָר}}; ''ḫullu'' = {{GHGheb|text=עֹל}} (with hard {{GHGheb|text=ע}}; cf. {{GHGpar|6|c}}, and Assyr. ''ḫumri'' = {{GHGheb|text=עָמְרִי}}, ''ḫazzatu'' = {{GHGheb|text=עֶזָּה}}); ''iazkur'' = {{GHGheb|text=יִזְכֹּר}}, ''zuruḫu'' = {{GHGheb|text=זרוֹעַ}}, ''abadat'' = {{GHGheb|text=אָֽבְדָה}}, ''šaḫri'' = {{GHGheb|text=שַעַר}}, ''gate''; ''baṭnu'' = {{GHGheb|text=בֶּטֶן}}, ''belly''; ''kilūbi'' = {{GHGheb|text=כְּלוּב}}, ''net''; ''ṣaduk'' = {{GHGheb|text=צָדֹק}} ({{GHGheb|text=צַדִּיק}}), &c. [Cf. Böhl, {{GHGcite|title=Die Sprache d. Amarnabriefe}}, Lpz. 1909.]</ref> to Assyrian words in the cuneiform tablets of Tell-el-Amarna [about 1400 {{smaller|B.C.}}] cf. H. Winckler, ‘{{GHGcite|title=Die Thontafeln von Tell-el-Amarna}},’ in {{GHGcite|title=Keilinschr. Bibliothek}}, vol. v, Berlin, 1896 f. [transcription and translation]; J. A. Knudtzon, {{GHGcite|title=Die El-Amarna-Tafeln}}, Lpz. 1907 f.; H. Zimmern, {{GHGcite|title=ZA}}. 1891, p. 154 ff. and {{GHGcite|title=KAT}}.<sup>3</sup>, p. 651 ff.), and partly from the numerous remains of the Phoenician and Punic languages.

The latter we find in their peculiar writing ({{GHGpar|1|k}}, {{GHGpar|1|l|nonumber=1}}) in a great number of inscriptions and on coins, copies of which have been collected by Gesenius, Judas, Bourgade, Davis, de Vogüé, Levy, P. Schröder, v. Maltzan, Euting, but especially in Part I of the {{GHGcite|title=Corpus Inscriptionum Semiticarum}}, Paris, 1881 ff. Among the inscriptions but few public documents are found, e.g. two lists of fees for sacrifices; by far the most are epitaphs or votive tablets. Of special importance is the inscription on the sarcophagus of King Ešmûnazar of Sidon, found in 1855, now in the Louvre; see the bibliography in Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Nordsem. Epigr.}}, i. 23 ff.; on the inscription, i. 97 ff., 141 f., 417, ii. plate iv, 2; [Cooke, p. 30 ff.]. To these may be added isolated words in Greek and Latin authors, and the Punic texts in Plautus, {{GHGcite|title=Poenulus}} 5, 1–3 (best treated by Gildemeister in Ritschl’s edition of Plautus, Lips. 1884, tom. ii, fasc. 5). From the monuments we learn the native orthography, from the Greek and Latin transcriptions the pronunciation and vocalization; the two together give a tolerably distinct idea of the language and its relation to Hebrew.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|g}}
Phoenician (Punic) words occurring in inscriptions are, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אל|translate=God}}, {{GHGheb|text=אדם|translate=man}}, {{GHGheb|text=בן|translate=son}}, {{GHGheb|text=בת|translate=daughter}}, {{GHGheb|text=מלך|translate=king}}, {{GHGheb|text=עבד|translate=servant}}, {{GHGheb|text=כהן|translate=priest}}, {{GHGheb|text=זבח|translate=sacrifice}}, {{GHGheb|text=בעל|translate=lord}}, {{GHGheb|text=שמש|translate=sun}}, {{GHGheb|text=ארץ|translate=land}}, {{GHGheb|text=ים|translate=sea}}, {{GHGheb|text=אבן|translate=stone}}, {{GHGheb|text=כסף|translate=silver}}, {{GHGheb|text=ברזל|translate=iron}}, {{GHGheb|text=שמן|translate=oil}}, {{GHGheb|text=עת|translate=time}}, {{GHGheb|text=קבר|translate=grave}}, {{GHGheb|text=מצבת|translate=monument}}, {{GHGheb|text=מקם|translate=place}}, {{GHGheb|text=משכב|translate=bed}}, {{GHGheb|text=כל|translate=all}}, {{GHGheb|text=אחד|translate=one}}, {{GHGheb|text=שנים|translate=two}}, {{GHGheb|text=שלש|translate=three}}, {{GHGheb|text=ארבע|translate=four}}, {{GHGheb|text=חמש|translate=five}}, {{GHGheb|text=שש|translate=six}}, {{GHGheb|text=שבע|translate=seven}}, {{GHGheb|text=עשר|translate=ten}}, {{GHGheb|text=כן}} (=Hebr. {{GHGheb|text=היה}}) {{GHGtranslate|to be}}, {{GHGheb|text=שמע|translate=to hear}}, {{GHGheb|text=פתח|translate=to open}}, {{GHGheb|text=נדר|translate=to vow}}, {{GHGheb|text=ברך|translate=to bless}}, {{GHGheb|text=בקש|translate=to seek}}, &c. Proper names: {{GHGheb|text=צדן|translate=Sidon}}, {{GHGheb|text=צר|translate=Tyre}}, {{GHGheb|text=חנא|translate=Hanno}}, {{GHGheb|text=חנבעל|translate=Hannibal}}, &c. See the complete vocabulary in Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Nordsem. Epigr.}}, i. 204 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|h}}
Variations from Hebrew in Phoenician orthography and inflection are, e.g. the almost invariable omission of the vowel letters ({{GHGpar|7|b}}), as {{GHGheb|text=בת}} for {{GHGheb|text=בית|translate=house}}, {{GHGheb|text=קל}} for {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל|translate=voice}}, {{GHGheb|text=צדן}} for {{GHGheb|text=צִידוֹן}}, {{GHGheb|text=כהנם}} for {{GHGheb|text=כֹּֽהֲנִים|translate=priests}}, {{GHGheb|text=אלנם}} (in Plaut. ''alonim'') ''gods'' ; the fem., even in the absolute state, ending in {{GHGheb|text=ת}} (''ath'') ({{GHGpar|80|b}}) as well as {{GHGheb|text=א}} (''ô''), the relative {{GHGheb|text=אש}} (Hebr. {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}), &c. The differences in pronunciation are more remarkable, especially in Punic, where the {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} was regularly pronounced as ''û'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שֹׁפֵט|pron=sûfēṭ}} (judge), {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלשׁ|pron=sālûs}} (three), {{GHGheb|text=רש|pron=rûs}} = {{GHGheb|text=רֹאשׁ|translate=head}}; ''i'' and ''e'' often as the obscure dull sound of ''y'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הִנֶּנּוּ|pron=ynnynnu}} ({{GHGtranslate|''ecce eum''|en=here we are}}), {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} ({{GHGheb|text=אית}}) ''yth;'' the {{GHGheb|text=ע}} as ''o'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מעקר|translate=Mocar}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=מַֽעֲכָה}} LXX, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=24}} {{polytonic|Μωχά}}). See the collection of the grammatical peculiarities in Gesenius, {{GHGcite|title=Monuments Phoenicia}}, p. 430 ff.; Paul Schröder, {{GHGcite|title=Die phöniz. Sprache}}, Halle, 1869; B. Stade, ‘Erneute Pröfung des zwischen dem Phönic. und Hebr. bestehenden Verwandtschaftsgrades,’ in the {{GHGcite|title=Morgenländ. Forschungen}}, Lpz. 1875, p. 169 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|i}}
'''4.''' As the Hebrew writing on monuments and coins mentioned in {{GHGpar|2|d||nonumber=1}} consists only of consonants, so also the writers of the Old<section end="par2" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

36.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Kathleen.wright5" /></noinclude><section begin=par2/>Testament books used merely the consonant-signs ({{GHGpar|1|k}}), and even now the written scrolls of the Law used in the synagogues must not, according to ancient custom, contain anything more. The present pronunciation of this consonantal text, its vocalization and accentuation, rest on the tradition of the Jewish schools, as it was finally fixed by the system of punctuation ({{GHGpar|7|h}}) introduced by Jewish scholars about the seventh century {{smaller|A.D.}}; cf. {{GHGpar|3|b}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|k}}
An earlier stage in the development of the Canaanitish-Hebrew language, i.e. a form of it anterior to the written documents now extant, when it must have stood nearer to the common language of the united Semitic family, can still be discerned in its principal features:—(1) from many archaisms preserved in the traditional texts, especially in the names of persons and places dating from earlier times, as well as in isolated forms chiefly occurring in poetic style; (2) in general by an ''a posteriori'' conclusion from traditional forms, so far as according to the laws and analogies of phonetic change they clearly point to an older phase of the language; and (3) by comparison with the kindred languages, especially Arabic, in which this earlier stage of the language has been frequently preserved even down to later times ({{GHGpar|1|m}}, {{GHGpar|1|n|nonumber=1}}). In numerous instances in examining linguistic phenomena, the same—and consequently so much the more certain—result is attained by each of these three methods.

Although the systematic investigation of the linguistic development indicated above belongs to comparative Semitic philology, it is nevertheless indispensable for the scientific treatment of Hebrew to refer to the ground-forms<ref>Whether these can be described simply as ‘primitive Semitic’ is a question which may be left undecided here.</ref> so far as they can be ascertained and to compare the corresponding forms in Arabic. Even elementary grammar which treats of the forms of the language occurring in the Old Testament frequently requires, for their explanation, a reference to these ground-forms.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|l}}
'''5.''' Even in the language of the Old Testament, notwithstanding its general uniformity, there is noticeable a certain progress from an earlier to a later stage. Two periods, though with some reservations, may be distinguished: the ''first'', down to the end of the Babylonian exile; and the ''second'', after the exile.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|m}}
To the former belongs, apart from isolated traces of a later revision, the larger half of the Old Testament books, viz. (''a'') of the prose and historical writings, a large part of the Pentateuch and of Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings; (''b'') of the poetical, perhaps<section end=par2/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

37.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Kathleen.wright5" /></noinclude><section begin=par2/>a part of the Psalms and Proverbs; (''c'') the writings of the earlier prophets (apart from various later additions) in the following chronological order: Amos, Hosea, Isaiah I, Micah, Nahum, Zephaniah, Habakkuk, Obadiah (?), Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah II (ch. 40–55).

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|n}}
The beginning of this period, and consequently of Hebrew literature generally, is undoubtedly to be placed as early as the time of Moses, although the Pentateuch in its present form, in which very different strata may be still clearly recognized, is to be regarded as a gradual production of the centuries after Moses. Certain linguistic peculiarities of the Pentateuch, which it was once customary to regard as archaisms, such as the epicene use of {{GHGheb|text=נַעַר|translate=boy, youth}}, for {{GHGheb|text=נַֽעֲרָה|translate=girl}}, and {{GHGheb|text=הוא}} for {{GHGheb|text=היא}}, are merely to be attributed to a later redactor; cf. {{GHGpar|17|c}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|o}}
The linguistic character of the various strata of the Pentateuch has been examined by Ryssel, {{GHGcite|title=De Elohistae Pentateuchici sermone}}, Lpz. 1878; König, {{GHGcite|title=De criticae sacrae argumento e linguae legibus repetito}}, Lpz. 1879 (analysis of {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1}}–{{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|hidebook=1}}); F. Giesebrecht, ‘Der Sprachgebr. des hexateuchischen Elohisten,’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1881, p. 177 ff., partly modified by Driver in the {{GHGcite|title=Journal of Philology}}, vol. xi. p. 201 ff.; Kräutlein, {{GHGcite|title=Die sprachl. Verschiedenheiten in den Hexateuchquellen}}, Lpz. 1908.—Abundant matter is afforded also by Holzinger, {{GHGcite|title=Einleitung in den Hexateuct}}, Freib. 1893; Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Introduction to the Literature of the Old Testament}}<sup>8</sup>, Edinburgh, 1908; Strack, {{GHGcite|title=Einleitung ins A.T.}}<sup>6</sup>, Munich, 1906; König, {{GHGcite|title=Einleitung in das A.T.}}, Bonn, 1893.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|p}}
'''6.''' Even in the writings of this first period, which embraces about 600 years, we meet, as might be expected, with considerable differences in linguistic form and style, which are due partly to differences in the time and place of composition, and partly to the individuality and talent of the authors. Thus Isaiah, for example, writes quite differently from the later Jeremiah, but also differently from his contemporary Micah. Amongst the historical books of this period, the texts borrowed from earlier sources have a linguistic colouring perceptibly different from those derived from later sources, or passages which belong to the latest redactor himself. Yet the structure of the language, and, apart from isolated cases, even the vocabulary and phraseology, are on the whole the same, especially in the prose books.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|q}}
But the ''poetic language'' is in many ways distinguished from prose, not only by a ''rhythm'' due to more strictly balanced (parallel) members and definite metres (see {{GHGpar|2|r|nonumber=1}}), but also by peculiar ''words'' and ''meanings, inflexions'' and ''syntactical constructions'' which it uses in addition to those usual in prose. This distinction, however, does not go far as, for example, in Greek. Many of these poetic peculiarities occur in the kindred languages, especially in Aramaic, as the ordinary modes of expression, and probably are to be regarded largely as archaisms which poetry retained. Some perhaps, also, are<section end=par2/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

38.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par2 />embellishments which the Hebrew poets who knew Aramaic adopted into their language.<ref>That already in Isaiah’s time (second half of the eighth century {{smaller|B.C.}}) educated Hebrews, or at least officers of state, understood Aramaic, while the common people in Jerusalem did not, is evident from {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=18|verse=26}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=36|verse=11}}).</ref>

The prophets, at least the earlier, in language and rhythm are to be regarded almost entirely as poets, except that with them the sentences are often more extended, and the parallelism is less regular and balanced than is the case with the poets properly so called. The language of the later prophets, on the contrary, approaches nearer to prose.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|r}}
On the ''rhythm'' of Hebrew poetry, see besides the Commentaries on the poetical books and Introductions to the O.T., J. Ley, {{GHGcite|title=Grundzüge des Rhythmus, &c}}., Halle, 1875; {{GHGcite|title=Leitfaden der Metrik der hebr. Poesie}}, Halle, 1887; ‘Die metr. Beschaffenheit des B. Hiob,’ in {{GHGcite|title=Theol. Stud. u. Krit}}., 1895, iv, 1897, i; Grimme, ‘Abriss der bibl.-hebr. Metrik,’ {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1896, p. 529 ff., 1897, p. 683 ff.; {{GHGcite|title=Psalmenprobleme &c}}., Freiburg (Switzerland), 1902 (on which see Beer in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ThLZ.|Theologische Literaturzeitung, ed. by E. Schürer. Lpz. 1876 ff.}}}} 1903, no. 11); ‘Gedanken über hebr. Metrik,’ in Altschüler’s {{GHGcite|title=Vierteljahrschrift}}, i (1903), 1 ff.; Döller, {{GHGcite|title=Rhythmus, Metrik u. Strophik in d. bibl.-hebr. Poesie}}, Paderborn, 1899; Schloegl, {{GHGcite|title=De re metrics veterum Hebraeorum disputatio}}, Vindobonae, 1899 (on the same lines as Grimme); but especially Ed. Sievers, {{GHGcite|title=Metrische Studien}} : i {{GHGcite|title=Studien zur hebr. Metrik}}, pt. 1 {{GHGcite|title=Untersuchungen}}, pt. 2 {{GHGcite|title=Textproben}}, Lpz. 1901: ii {{GHGcite|title=Die hebr. Genesis}}, 1 {{GHGcite|title=Texte}}, 2 {{GHGcite|title=Zur Quellenscheidung u. Textkritik}}, Lpz. 1904 f.: iii {{GHGcite|title=Samuel}}, Lpz. 1907; {{GHGcite|title=Amos metrisch bearbeitet}} (with H. Guthe), Lpz. 1907; and his {{GHGcite|title=Alttest. Miszellen}} (1 Is 24–27, 2 Jena, 3 Deutero-Zechariah, 4 Malachi, 5 Hosea, 6 Joel, 7 Obadiah, 8 Zephaniah, 9 Haggai, 10 Micah), Lpz. 1904–7.—As a guide to Sievers’ system (with some criticism of his principles) see Baumann, ‘Die Metrik u. das A.T.;,’ in the {{GHGcite|title=Theol. Rundschau}}, viii (1905), 41 ff.; W. H. Cobb, {{GHGcite|title=A criticism of systems of Hebrew Metre}}, Oxford, 1905; Cornill, {{GHGcite|title=Einleitung ins A.T}}.<sup>5</sup>, Tübingen, 1905, p. 11 ff.; Rothstein, {{GHGcite|title=Zeitschr. für d. ev. Rel.-Unterricht}}, 1907, p. 188 ff. and his {{GHGcite|title=Grundzüge des hebr. Rhythmus}}, Lpz. 1909 (also separately {{GHGcite|title=Psalmentexte u. der Text des Hohen Liedes}}, Lpz. 1909); W. R. Arnold, ‘The rhythms of the ancient Heb.,’ in {{GHGcite|title=O.T. and Semitic Studies in memory of W. R. Harper}}, i. 165 ff., Chicago, 1907, according to whom the number of syllables between the beats is only limited by the physiological possibilities of phonetics; C.v. Orelli, ‘Zur Metrik der alttest. Prophetenschriften,’ in his {{GHGcite|title=Kommentar zu den kl. Propheten}}<sup>3</sup>, p. 236 ff., Munich, 1908.—In full agreement with Sievers is Baethgen, {{GHGcite|title=Psalmen}}<sup>3</sup>, p. xxvi ff., Göttingen, 1904. [Cf. Budde in {{GHGcite|title=DB}}. iv. 3 ff.; Duhm in {{GHGcite|title=EB}}. iii. 3793 ff.]

Of all views of this matter, the only one generally accepted as sound was at first Ley’s and Budde’s discovery of the Qina- or Lamentation-Verse ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1882, 5 ff.; 1891, 234 ff.; 1892, 31 ff.). On their predecessors, Lowth, de Wette, Ewald, see Löhr, {{GHGcite|title=Klagelied}}<sup>2</sup>, p. 9. This verse, called by Duhm ‘long verse’, by Sievers simply ‘five-syllabled’ (Fünfer), consists of two members, the second at least one beat shorter than the other. That a regular repetition of an equal number of syllables in ''arsis'' and ''thesis'' was observed by other poets, had been established by Ley, Duhm, Gunkel, Grimme, and others, especially Zimmern, who cites a Babylonian hymn in which the members are actually marked ({{GHGcite|title=ZA}}. x. 1 ff., xii. 382 ff.; cf. also Delitzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Das babyl. Weltschöpfungsepos}}, Lpz. 1896, pp. 60 ff.). Recently, however, E. Sievers, the recognized authority on metre in other branches of literature, has indicated, in the works mentioned above, a number of fresh facts and views, which have frequently been confirmed by the conclusions of Ley and others. The most important are as follows:—

Hebrew poetry, as distinguished from the quantitative Classical and Arabic<section end=par2 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

39.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par2 />and the syllabic Syriac verse, is {{GHGterm|accentual}}. The number of unstressed syllables between the beats ({{GHGterm|ictus}}) is, however, not arbitrary, but the scheme of the verse is based on an irregular anapaest which may undergo rhythmical modifications (e.g. resolving the ictus into two syllables, or lengthening the arsis so as to give a double accent) and contraction, e.g. of the first two syllables. The foot always concludes with the ictus, so that toneless endings, due to change of pronunciation or corruption of the text, are to be disregarded, although as a rule the ictus coincides with the Hebrew word-accent. The metrical scheme consists of combinations of feet in {{GHGterm|series}} (of 2, 3 or 4), and of these again in {{GHGterm|periods}}—double threes, very frequently, double fours in narrative, fives in Lamentations (see above) and very often elsewhere, and sevens. Sievers regards the last two metres as catalectic double threes and fours. Connected sections do not always maintain the same metre throughout, but often exhibit a mixture of metres.

It can no longer be doubted that in the analysis of purely poetical passages, this system often finds ready confirmation and leads to textual and literary results, such as the elimination of glosses. There are, however, various difficulties in carrying out the scheme consistently and extending it to the prophetical writings and still more to narrative: (1) not infrequently the required number of feet is only obtained by sacrificing the clearly marked parallelism, or the grammatical connexion (e.g. of the construct state with its genitive), and sometimes even by means of doubtful emendations; (2) the whole system assumes a correct transmission of the text and its pronunciation, for neither of which is there the least guarantee. To sum up, our conclusion at present is that for poetry proper some assured and final results have been already obtained, and others may be expected, from the principles laid down by Sievers, although, considering the way in which the text has been transmitted, a ''faultless'' arrangement of metres cannot be expected. Convincing proof of the ''consistent'' use of the same metrical schemes in the prophets, and ''a fortiori'' in narrative, can hardly be brought forward.

The great work of D. H. Müller, {{GHGcite|title=Die Propheten in ihrer ursprüngl. Form}} (2 vols., Vienna, 1896; cf. his {{GHGcite|title=Strophenbau u. Respension}}, ibid. 1898, and {{GHGcite|title=Komposition u. Strophenbau}}, ibid. 1907), is a study of the most important monuments of early Semitic poetry from the point of view of strophic structure and the use of the refrain, i.e. the repetition of the same or similar phrases or words in corresponding positions in different strophes.

The arrangement of certain poetical passages in verse-form required by early scribal rules ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=1–19}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=1–43}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=1–10}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=23|verse=1–7|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=136|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=31|verse=10–31}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=16|verse=8–36}}: cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=12|verse=9–24}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=2–8}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=9|verse=7–10}}) has nothing to do with the question of metre in the above sense.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|s}}
Words are used in poetry, for which others are customary in prose, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֱנוֹשׁ|translate=man}} = {{GHGheb|text=אָדָם}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֹרַח|translate=path}} = {{GHGheb|text=דֶּרֶךְ}}; {{GHGheb|text=מִלָּה|translate=word}} = {{GHGheb|text=דָּבָר}}; {{GHGheb|text=חָזָה|translate=to see}} = {{GHGheb|text=רָאָה}}; {{GHGheb|text=אָתָה|translate=to come}} = {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹא}}.

To the poetic ''meanings of words'' belongs the use of certain poetic ''epithets'' as substantives; thus, for example, {{GHGheb|text=אביר}} (only in constr, st. {{GHGheb|text=אֲבִיר}}) ''the strong one'' for ''God''; {{GHGheb|text=אַבִּיר|translate=the strong one}} for ''bull, horse''; {{GHGheb|text=לְבָנָה|translate=alba|en=white (f.)}} for {{GHGtranslate|luna|en=moon}}; {{GHGheb|text=צַר|translate=enemy}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֹיֵב}}.

Of word-forms, we may note, e.g. the longer forms of prepositions of place ({{GHGpar|103|n}}) {{GHGheb|text=עֲלֵי}} = {{GHGheb|text=עַל}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֵי}} = {{GHGheb|text=אֶל}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֲדֵי}} = {{GHGheb|text=עַד}}; the endings {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} in the noun ({{GHGpar|90}}); the pronominal suffixes {{GHGheb|text=מוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ָ֫מוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ֫מוֹ}} for {{GHGheb|text=ם}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ֵם}} ({{GHGpar|58}}); the plural ending {{GHGheb|text=־ִין}} for {{GHGheb|text=־ִים}} ({{GHGpar|87|e}}). To the {{GHGterm|syntax}} belongs the far more sparing use of the article, of the relative pronoun, of the accusative particle {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}}; the construct state even before prepositions; the shortened imperfect with the same meaning as the ordinary form ({{GHGpar|109|i}}); the wider governing power of prepositions; and in general a forcible brevity of expression.
<section end=par2 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

40.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par2 />{{GHGmargin-letter|2|t}}
'''7.''' The ''second'' period of the Hebrew language and literature, after the return from the exile until the Maccabees (about 160 {{smaller|B.C.}}), is chiefly distinguished by a constantly closer approximation of the language to the kindred western Aramaic dialect. This is due to the influence of the Aramaeans, who lived in close contact with the recent and thinly-populated colony in Jerusalem, and whose dialect was already of importance as being the official language of the western half of the Persian empire. Nevertheless the supplanting of Hebrew by Aramaic proceeded only very gradually. Writings intended for popular use, such as the Hebrew original of Jesus the son of Sirach and the book of Daniel, not only show that Hebrew about 170 {{smaller|B.C.}} was still in use as a literary language, but also that it was still at least understood by the people.<ref>The extensive use of Hebrew in the popular religious literature which is partly preserved to us in the Midrašim, the Mišna, and the Liturgy, indicates, moreover, that Hebrew was widely understood much later than this. Cf. M. H. Segal, ‘Mišnaic Hebrew and its relations to Biblical Hebrew and Aramaic,’ in {{GHGcite|title=J.Q.R.}}, 1908, p. 647 ff. (also separately).</ref> When it had finally ceased to exist as a living language, it was still preserved as the ''language of the Schools''—not to mention the numerous Hebraisms introduced into the Aramaic spoken by the Jews.

For particulars, see Kautzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Bibl.-Aram.}}, pp. 1–6. We may conveniently regard the relation of the languages which co-existed in this later period as similar to that of the High and Low German in North Germany, or to that of the High German and the common dialects in the south and in Switzerland. Even amongst the more educated, the common dialect prevails orally, whilst the High German serves essentially as the literary and cultured language, and is at least understood by all classes of the people. Wholly untenable is the notion, based on an erroneous interpretation of {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=8|verse=8}}, that the Jews immediately after the exile had completely forgotten the Hebrew language, and therefore needed a translation of the Holy Scriptures.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|u}}
The Old Testament writings belonging to this second period, in all of which the Aramaic colouring appears in various degrees, are: certain parts of the Pentateuch and of Joshua, Ruth, the books of Ezra, Nehemiah, Chronicles, Esther; the prophetical books of Haggai, Zechariah, Isaiah III (56–66), Malachi, Joel, Jonah, Daniel; of the poetical books, a large part of Proverbs, Job, Song of Songs, Ecclesiastes, and most of the Psalms. As literary compositions, these books are sometimes far inferior to those of the first period, although work was still produced which in purity of language and aesthetic value falls little short of the writings of the golden age.

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|v}}
''Later words'' (Aramaisms) are, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַחְוָה|translate=declaration}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָנַס|translate=compel}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּר|translate=son}}, {{GHGheb|text=גִּיר|translate=chalk}}, {{GHGheb|text=זְמָן}} = {{GHGheb|text=עֵת|translate=time}}, {{GHGheb|text=זָקַף|translate=raise up}}, {{GHGheb|text=חסד}} Pi. {{GHGtranslate|reproach}}, {{GHGheb|text=טלל}} Pi. {{GHGtranslate|roof over}},<section end=par2 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

41.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude>
<section begin="par2" />{{GHGheb|text=טָעָה|translate=stray}}, {{GHGheb|text=כֵּף|translate=rock}}, {{GHGheb|text=מלך|translate=advise}}, {{GHGheb|text=סוֹף}} = {{GHGheb|text=קֵץ|translate=end}}, {{GHGheb|text=קִבֵּל}} = {{GHGheb|text=לָקַח|translate=take}}, {{GHGheb|text=רָעַע}} = {{GHGheb|text=רָצַץ|translate=break}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָׂגָא|translate=be many}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלַט}} = {{GHGheb|text=מָלַךְ|translate=rule}}, {{GHGheb|text=תָּקֵף}} = {{GHGheb|text=אָמֵץ|translate=be strong}}.—Later ''meanings'' are, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָמַר}} (to say) {{GHGtranslate|to command}}; {{GHGheb|text=עָנָה}} (to answer) {{GHGtranslate|to begin speaking}}.—''Orthographical'' and ''grammatical'' peculiarities are, the frequent {{GHGterm|scriptio plena|en=full writing}} of {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} and {{GHGheb|text={{GHGvowel-holder|ִי}}}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=דָּוִיד}}<ref>{{GHGheb|text=דָּוִיד}} in the Minor Prophets throughout ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=3|verse=5}}, &c.) is due merely to a caprice of the Masoretes.</ref> (elsewhere {{GHGheb|text=דָּוִד}}), even {{GHGheb|text=קוֹדֶש}} for {{GHGheb|text=קֹדֶש}}, {{GHGheb|text=רוֹב}} for {{GHGheb|text=רֹב}}; the interchange of {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=־ָא}} final; the more frequent use of substantives in {{GHGheb|text=וֹן}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ָן}}, {{GHGheb|text=וּת}} &c. Cf. {{nowrap|Dav. Strauss}}, {{GHGcite|title=Sprachl. Studien zu d. hebr. Sirachfragmenten}}, Zürich, 1900, p. 19 ff.; for the Psalms Cheyne, {{GHGcite|title=Origin of the Psalter}}, p. 461 ff., and especially Giesebrecht in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1881, p. 276 ff.; in general, Kautzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Die Aramaismen im {{nowrap|A.T.}}}} (i, Lexikal. Teil), Halle, 1902.

But all the peculiarities of these later writers are not Aramaisms. Several do not occur in Aramaic and must have belonged at an earlier period to the Hebrew vernacular, especially it would seem in northern Palestine. There certain parts of Judges, amongst others, may have originated, as is indicated, e.g. by {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ{{זונג}}ּ}}, a common form in Phoenician (as well as {{GHGheb|text=אשׁ}}), for {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} ({{GHGpar|36}}), which afterwards recurs in Jonah, Lamentations, the Song of Songs, the later Psalms, and Ecclesiastes. 

{{GHGmargin-letter|2|w}}
Rem. I. Of dialectical varieties in the old Hebrew language, only one express mention occurs in the O.T. ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=12|verse=6}}), according to which the Ephraimites in certain cases pronounced the {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}} as {{GHGheb|text=ס}}. (Cf. Marquart in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1888, p. 151 ff.) Whether in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=13|verse=24}} by the ''speech of Ashdod'' a Hebrew, or a (wholly different) Philistine dialect is intended, cannot be determined. On the other hand, many peculiarities in the North Palestinian books (Judges and Hosea) are probably to be regarded as differences in dialect, and so also some anomalies in the Moabite inscription of Mêšaʿ (see above, {{GHGpar|2|d|nonumber=1}}). On later developments see {{nowrap|L. Metman}}, {{GHGcite|title=Die hebr. Sprache, ihre Geschichte u. lexikal. Enticickelung seit Abschluss des Kanons u. ihr Bau in d. Gegenwart}}, Jerusalem, 1906. 

2. It is evident that, in the extant remains of old Hebrew literature,<ref>According to the calculation of the Dutch scholar Leusden, the O.T. contains 5,642 different Hebrew and Aramaic words; according to rabbinical calculations, 79,856 altogether in the Pentateuch. Cf. also {{nowrap|E. Nestle}}, {{GHGcite|title=ZAW}}, 1906, p. 283; {{nowrap|H. Strack}}, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1907, p. 69 ff.; Blau, 'Neue masoret. Studien,' in {{GHGcite|title=JQR.}} xvi. 357 ff., treats of the number of letters and words, and the ve se- division in the O.T.</ref> the entire store of the ancient language is not preserved. The canonical books of the Old Testament formed certainly only a fraction of the whole Hebrew national literature.
<section end="par2" />
<section begin="par3" />{{GHGpar-heading|3|Grammatical Treatment of the Hebrew Language}}

Gesenius, {{GHGcite|title=Gesch. der hebr. Sprache}}, §§ 19-39; Oehler's article, 'Hebr. Sprache,' in Schmid's {{GHGcite|title=Encykl. des ges. Erziehungs- u. Unterrichtswesens}}, vol. iii. p. 346 ff. (in the 2nd ed. revised by Nestle, p. 314 ff.). Cf. also the literature cited above in the headings of §§ 1 and 2; also Böttcher, {{GHGcite|title=Lehrb. der hebr. Spr.}}, i. Lpz. 1866, p. 30 ff.; {{nowrap|L. Geiger}}, {{GHGcite|title=Das Studium der Hebr. Spr. in Deutschl. vom Ende des XV. bis zur Mitte des XVI. Jahrh.}}, Breslau, 1870; {{nowrap|B. Pick}}, 'The Study of the Hebrew Language among Jews and Christians,' in {{GHGcite|title=Bibliotheca Sacra}}, 1884, p. 450 ff., and 1885, p. 470 ff.; {{nowrap|W. Bacher}}, article 'Grammar' in the {{GHGcite|title=Jew. Encyclopaedia}}, vol. vi, New York and London, 1904. Cf. also the note on {{GHGmargin-letter-fmt|d}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|3|a}}
1. At the time when the old Hebrew language was gradually 
becoming extinct, and the formation of the O.T. canon was
<section end="par3" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

42.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par3 />approaching completion, the Jews began to explain and critically revise their sacred text, and sometimes to translate it into the vernacular languages which in various countries had become current among them. The oldest {{GHGterm|translation}} is the Greek of the ''Seventy'' (more correctly ''Seventy-two'') Interpreters (LXX), which was begun with the Pentateuch at Alexandria under Ptolemy Philadelphus, but only completed later. It was the work of various authors, some of whom had a living knowledge of the original, and was intended for the use of Greek-speaking Jews, especially in Alexandria.
