Somewhat later the Aramaic translations, or Targums ({{GHGheb|text=תַּרְגּוּמִים}} i.e. ''interpretations''), were formed by successive recensions made in Palestine and Babylonia. The ''explanations'', derived in part from alleged tradition, refer almost exclusively to civil and ritual law and dogmatic theology, and are no more scientific in character than much of the textual tradition of that period. Both kinds of tradition are preserved in the ''Talmud'', the first part of which, the {{GHGterm|Mišna}}, was finally brought to its present form towards the end of the second century; of the remainder, the {{GHGterm|Gemāra}}, one recension (the ''Jerusalem'' or ''Palestinian Gem.'') about the middle of the fourth century, the other (the ''Babylonian Gem.'') about the middle of the sixth century {{smaller|A.D.}} The Mišna forms the beginning of the New-Hebrew literature; the language of the Gemaras is for the most part Aramaic. 

{{GHGmargin-letter|3|b}}
'''2'''. To the interval between the completion of the Talmud and the earliest grammatical writers, belong mainly the vocalization and accentuation of the hitherto unpointed text of the O.T., according to the pronunciation traditional in the Synagogues and Schools ({{GHGpar|7|h}}, {{GHGpar|7|i|nonumber=1}}), as well as the greater part of the collection of critical notes which bears the name of Masōra ({{GHGheb|text=מָֽסוֹרָה|translate=traditio|en=tradition}}?).<ref>On the name Masora (or Massora, as e.g. {{nowrap|E. König}}, {{GHGcite|title=Einleitung in das A.T.}}, p. 38 ff.; {{GHGcite|title=Lehrgeb. d. hebr. Sprache}}, ii. 358 ff.), and the great difficulty of satisfactorily explaining it, cf. De Lagarde, {{GHGcite|title=Mitleilungen}}, i. 91 ff. W. Bacher's derivation of the expression (in {{GHGcite|title=JQR.}} 1891, p. 785 ff.; so also C. Levias in the {{GHGcite|title=Hebrew Union College Annual}}, Cincinnati, 1904, p. 147 ff.) from {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=20|verse=37}} ({{GHGheb|text=מָסֹרֶת הַבְּרִית}}; {{GHGheb|text=מסרה}}, i.e. {{GHGheb|text=מֽוֹסֵרָה}}, being an equally legitimate form) is rightly rejected by König, l. c. The correctness of the form {{GHGheb|text=מָֽסֹרָה}} (by the side of the equally well-attested form {{GHGheb|text=מַסֹּרֶת}}) does not seem to us to be invalidated by his arguments, nor by Blau's proposal to read {{GHGheb|text=מְסוֹרֶת}} ({{GHGcite|title=JQR.}} xii. 241). The remark of Levias (l.c.) deserves notice, that with the earlier Masoretes 
{{GHGheb|text=מסורת}} is equivalent to orthography, i.e. {{GHGterm|plene-}} and {{GHGterm|defective}} writing, and only later came to mean {{GHGtranslate|traditio|en=tradition}}.—G. Wildboer, in ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1909, p. 74, contends that as {{GHGheb|text=מסר|translate=to hand on}} is not found in the O.T., it must be a late denominative in this sense.</ref> From this the text which has since been transmitted with rigid uniformity by the MSS.,<section end=par3 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

43.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par3 />and is still the received text of the O.T., has obtained the name of the Masoretic Text.

{{GHGmargin-letter|3|c}}
E. F. K. Rosenmüller already ({{GHGcite|title=Handbuch für d. Liter. der bibl. Kritik u. Exegese}}, 1797, i. 247; {{GHGcite|title=Vorrede zur Stereotyp-Ausg. des A.T.}}, Lpz. 1834) maintained that our O.T. text was derived from Codices belonging to a single recension. J. G. Sommer (cf. Cornill, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1892, p. 309), Olshausen (since 1853), and especially De Lagarde ({{GHGcite|title=Proverbien}}, 1863, p. 1 ff.), have even made it probable that the original Masoretic text was derived from a single standard manuscript. Cf., however, E. König in {{GHGcite|title=Ztschr. f. kirchl. Wiss.}}, 1887, p. 279 f., and especially his {{GHGcite|title=Einleitung ins A.T.}}, p. 88 ff. Moreover a great many facts, which will be noticed in their proper places, indicate that the Masora itself is by no means uniform but shows clear traces of different schools and opinions; cf. H. Strack in {{GHGcite|title=Semitic Studies in memory of... Kohut}}, Berlin, 1897, p. 563 ff. An excellent foundation for the history of the Masora and the settlement of the masoretic tradition was laid by Joh. Buxtorf in his {{GHGcite|title=Tiberias seu Commentarius Masorethicus}}, first published at Basel in 1620 as an appendix to the Rabbinical Bible of 1618 f. For more recent work see Geiger, {{GHGcite|title=Jüdische Ztschr.}}, iii. 78 ff., followed by Harris in {{GHGcite|title=JQR.}} i. 128 ff., 243 ff.; S. Frensdorff. {{GHGcite|title=Ochla W’ochla}}, Hanover, 1864; and his {{GHGcite|title=Massor. Wörterb.}}, part i, Hanover and Lpz. 1876; and Ch. D. Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=The Massora compiled from Manuscripts, &c.}}, 3 vols., Lond. 1880 ff., and {{GHGcite|title=Introduction to the Massoretico-critical edition of the Hebr. Bible}}, Lond. 1897 (his text, reprinted from that of Jacob b. Ḥayyîm [Venice, 1524–5] with variants from MSS. and the earliest editions, was published in 2 vols. at London in 1894, 2nd ed. 1906; a revised edition is in progress); H. Hyvernat, ‘La langue et le langage de la Massore’ (as a mixture of New-Hebrew and Aramaic), in the {{GHGcite|title=Revue biblique}}, Oct. 1903, p. 529 ff. and B: ‘Lexique massorétique,’ ''ibid.'', Oct. 1904, p. 521 ff., 1905, p. 481 ff., and p. 515 ff. In the use of the Massora for the critical construction of the Text, useful work has been done especially by S. Baer, in the editions of the several books (only Exod.-Deut. have still to appear), edited from 1869 conjointly with Fr. Delitzsch, and since 1891 by Baer alone. Cf. also {{GHGpar|7|h}}.

The various readings of the Q<sup>e</sup>rê (see {{GHGpar|17}}) form one of the oldest and most important parts of the Masora. The punctuation of the Text, however, is not to be confounded with the compilation of the Masora. The former was settled at an earlier period, and is the result of a much more exhaustive labour than the Masora, which was not completed till a considerably later time.

{{GHGmargin-letter|3|d}}
'''3.''' It was not until about the beginning of the tenth century that the Jews, following the example of the Arabs, began their grammatical compilations. Of the numerous grammatical and lexicographical works of R. Saʿadya,<ref>On his independent attitude towards the Masoretic punctuation, see Delitzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Comm. zu den Psalmen}}<sup>4</sup>, p. 39.</ref> beyond fragments in the commentary on the Sepher Yeṣira (ed. Mayer-Lambert, pp. 42, 47, 75, &c.), only the explanation in Arabic of the seventy (more correctly ninety) {{GHGterm|hapax legomena}} in the O.T. has been preserved. Written likewise in Arabic, but frequently translated into Hebrew, were the still extant works of the grammarians R. Yehuda Ḥayyûǵ (also called Abu Zakarya Yaḥya, about the year 1000) and R. Yona (Ahu ʾl-Walîd Merwân ibn Ǵanâḥ, about 1030). By the aid of these earlier labours, Abraham ben Ezra (commonly called Aben Ezra, ob. 1167) and R. David Qimḥi (ob. c. 1235) especially gained a classical reputation by their Hebrew grammatical writings.
<section end=par3 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

44.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par3 />From these earliest grammarians are derived many principles of arrangement and technical terms, some of which are still retained, e.g. the naming of the conjugations and weak verbs according to the paradigm of {{GHGheb|text=פעל}}, certain {{GHGterm|voces memoriales}}, as {{GHGheb|text=בְּגַדְכְּפַת}} and the like.<ref>On the oldest Hebrew grammarians, see Strack and Siegfried, {{GHGcite|title=Lehrb. d. neuhebr. Spr. u. Liter.}}, Carlsr. 1884, p. 107 ff., and the prefaces to the Hebrew Lexicons of Gesenius and Fürst; Berliner, {{GHGcite|title=Beiträge zur hebr. Gramm. im Talmud u. Midrasch}}, Berlin, 1879; Baer and Strack, {{GHGcite|title=Die Dikduke ha-t<sup>e</sup>amim des Ahron ben Moscheh ben Ascher u. andere alte grammatisch-massorethische Lehrstücke}}, Lpz. 1879, and P. Kahle’s criticisms in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} lv. 170, n. 2; Ewald and Dukes, {{GHGcite|title=Beiträge z. Gesch. der ältesten Auslegung u. Spracherklärung des A.T.}}, Stuttg. 1844, 3 vols.; Hupfeld, {{GHGcite|title=De rei grammaticae apud Judaeos initiis antiquissimisque scriptoribus}}, Hal. 1846; W. Bacher, ‘Die Anfänge der hebr. Gr.,’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1895, 1 ff. and 335 ff.; and {{GHGcite|title=Die hebr. Sprachwissenschaft vom ''10.'' bis zum ''16.'' Jahrh.}}, Trier, 1892.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|3|e}}
'''4.''' The father of Hebrew philology among Christians was John Reuchlin (ob. 1522),<ref>A strong impulse was naturally given to these studies by the introduction of printing—the Psalter in 1477, the Bologna Pentateuch in 1482, the Soncino O.T. complete in 1488: see the description of the twenty-four earliest editions (down to 1528) in Ginsburg’s {{GHGcite|title=Introduction}}, p. 779 ff.</ref> to whom Greek literature also is so much indebted. Like the grammarians who succeeded him, till the time of John Buxtorf the elder (ob. 1629), he still adhered almost entirely to Jewish tradition. From the middle of the seventeenth century the field of investigation gradually widened, and the study of the kindred languages, chiefly through the leaders of the Dutch school, Albert Schultens (ob. 1750) and N. W. Schröder (ob. 1798), became of fruitful service to Hebrew grammar.

{{GHGmargin-letter|3|f}}
'''5.''' In the nineteenth century<ref>Of the literature or the subject down to the year 1850, see a tolerably full account in Steinschneider’s {{GHGcite|title=Bibliogr. Handb. f. hebr. Sprachkunde}}, Lpz. 1859.</ref> the advances in Hebrew philology are especially connected with the names of W. Gesenius (born at Nordhausen, Feb. 3, 1786; from the year 1810 Professor at Halle, where he died Oct. 23, 1842), who above all things aimed at the comprehensive observation and lucid presentation of the actually occurring linguistic phenomena; H. Ewald (ob. 1875, at Göttingen; {{GHGcite|title=Krit. Gramm. der Hebr. Spr.}}, Lpz. 1827; {{GHGcite|title=Ausführl. Lehrb. d. hebr. Spr.}}, 8th ed., Gött. 1870), who chiefly aimed at referring linguistic forms to general laws and rationally explaining the latter; J. Olshausen (ob. 1882, at Berlin; {{GHGcite|title=Lehrb. der hebr. Sprache}}, Brunswick, 1861) who attempted a consistent explanation of the existing condition of the language, from the presupposed primitive Semitic forms, preserved according to him notably in old Arabic. F. Böttcher ({{GHGcite|title=Ausführl. Lehrb. d. hebr. Spr.}} ed. by F.Mühlau, 2 vols., Lpz. 1866–8) endeavoured to present an exhaustive synopsis of the linguistic phenomena, as well as to give an explanation of them from the sphere of Hebrew<section end=par3 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

45.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par3 />alone. B. Stade, on the other hand ({{GHGcite|title=Lehrb. der hebr. Gr.}}, pt. i. Lpz. 1879), adopted a strictly scientific method in endeavouring to reduce the systems of Ewald and Olshausen to a more fundamental unity. E. König<ref>{{GHGcite|title=Historisch-krit. Lehrgeb. der hebr. Sprache mit steter Beziehung auf Qimchi und die anderen Autoritäten}}: I, ‘Lehre von der Schrift, der Aussprache, dem Pron. u. dem Verbum,’ Lpz. 1881; II. 1, ‘Abschluss der speziellen Formenlehre u. generelle Formenl.,’ 1895; ii. 2, ‘Historisch-kompar. Syntax d. hebr. Spr.,’ 1897.</ref> in his very thorough researches into the phonology and accidence starts generally from the position reached by the early Jewish grammarians (in his second part ‘with comparative reference to the Semitic languages in general’) and instead of adopting the usual dogmatic method, takes pains to re-open the discussion of disputed grammatical questions. The syntax König has ‘endeavoured to treat in several respects in such a way as to show its affinity to the common Semitic syntax’.—Among the works of Jewish scholars, special attention may be called to the grammar by S. D. Luzzatto written in Italian (Padua, 1853–69).

The chief requirements for one who is treating the grammar of an ancient language are—(1) that he should ''observe'' as fully and accurately as possible the existing linguistic phenomena and ''describe'' them, after showing their organic connexion (the empirical and historico-critical element); (2) that he should try to ''explain'' these facts, partly by comparing them with one another and by the analogy of the sister languages, partly from the general laws of philology (the logical element).

{{GHGmargin-letter|3|g}}
Such observation has more and more led to the belief that the original text of the O.T. has suffered to a much greater extent than former scholars were inclined to admit, in spite of the number of variants in parallel passages: {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=2 ff.}} = {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=4|verse=1 ff.}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=36}}-{{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=39|hidebook=1}} = {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=18|verse=13}}–{{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=20|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=52}} = {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=24|verse=18}}–{{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=25|verse=30|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=22}} = {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=14}} = {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=53}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=40|verse=14 ff.}} = {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=70}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=108}} = {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=57|verse=8 ff.}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=60|verse=7 ff.|hidebook=1}}. Cf. also the parallels between the Chronicles and the older historical books, and F. Vodel, {{GHGcite|title=Die konsonant. Varianten in den doppelt überlief. poet. Stücken d. masoret. Textes}}, Lpz. 1905. As to the extent and causes of the corruption of the Masoretic text, the newly discovered fragments of the Hebrew Ecclesiasticus are very instructive; cf. Smend, {{GHGcite|title=Gött. gel. Anz.}}, 1906, p. 763.

The causes of ''unintentional'' corruption in the great majority of cases are:—Interchange of similar letters, which has sometimes taken place in the early ‘Phoenician’ writing; transposition or omission of<section end=par3 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

46.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par3 />single letters, words, or even whole sentences, which are then often added in the margin and thence brought back into the text in the wrong place; such omission is generally due to homoioteleuton (cf. Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, p. 171 ff.), i.e. the scribe’s eye wanders from the place to a subsequent word of the same or similar form. Other causes are dittography, i.e. erroneous repetition of letters, words, and even sentences; its opposite, haplography; and lastly wrong division of words (cf. Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, p. 158 ff.), since at a certain period in the transmission of the text the words were not separated.<ref>This {{GHGterm|scriptio continua}} is also found in Phoenician inscriptions. The inscription of Mêšaʿ always divides the words by a point (and so the Siloam inscription; see the facsimile at the beginning of this grammar), and frequently marks the close of a sentence by a stroke.</ref>—''Intentional'' changes are due to corrections for the sake of decency or of dogma, and to the insertion of glosses, some of them very early.

Advance in grammar is therefore closely dependent on progress in {{GHGterm|textual criticism}}. The systematic pursuit of the latter has only begun in recent years: cf. especially Doorninck on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1}}–{{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|hidebook=1}}, Leid. 1879; Wellhausen, {{GHGcite|title=Text der Bb. Sam.}}, Gött. 1871; Cornill, {{GHGcite|title=Ezechiel}}, Lpz. 1886; Klostermann, {{GHGcite|title=Bb. Sam. u. d. Kön.}}, Nördl. 1887; Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Notes on the Hebr. text of the Books of Sam.}}, Oxf. 1890; Klostermann, {{GHGcite|title=Deuterojesaja}}, Munich, 1893; Oort, {{GHGcite|title=Textus hebr. emendationes}}, Lugd. 1900; Burney on {{GHGcite|title=Kings}}, Oxf. 1903; the commentaries of Marti and Nowack; the {{GHGcite|title=Internat. Crit. Comm.}}; Kautzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Die heil. Schriften des A.T.}}<sup>2</sup>, 1909–10. A critical edition of the O.T. with full textual notes, and indicating the different documents by colours, is being published in a handsome form by P. Haupt in {{GHGcite|title=The Sacred Books of the Old Test.}}, Lpz. and Baltimore, 1893 ff. (sixteen parts have appeared: Exod., Deut., Minor Prophets, and Megilloth are still to come); Kittel, {{GHGcite|title=Biblia hebraica}}<sup>2</sup>, 1909, Masoretic text from Jacob b. Ḥayyim (see {{GHGpar|3|c|nonumber=1}}), with a valuable selection of variants from the versions, and emendations.<section end=par3 />
<section begin=par4 />{{GHGpar-heading|4|Division and Arrangement of the Grammar}}

The division and arrangement of Hebrew grammar follow the three constituent parts of every language, viz. (1) articulate ''sounds'' represented by ''letters'', and united to form ''syllables'', (2) ''words'', and (3) ''sentences''.

The first part (the elements) comprises accordingly the treatment of ''sounds'' and their representation in writing. It describes the nature and relations of the sounds of the language, teaches the pronunciation<section end=par4 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

47.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par4 />of the written signs (orthoepy), and the established mode of writing (orthography). It then treats of the sounds as combined in syllables and words, and specifies the laws and conditions under which this combination takes place.

The second part (etymology) treats of words in their character as parts of speech, and comprises: (1) the principles of the {{GHGterm|formation of words}}, or of the derivation of the different parts of speech from the roots or from one another; (2) the principles of {{GHGterm|inflexion}}, i.e. of the various forms which the words assume according to their relation to other words and to the sentence.

The third part (syntax, or the arrangement of words): (1) shows how the word-formations and inflexions occurring in the language are used to express different shades of ideas, and how other ideas, for which the language has not coined any forms, are expressed by periphrasis; (2) states the laws according to which the parts of speech are combined in sentences (the principles of the sentence, or syntax in the stricter sense of the term).<section end=par4 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

48.text:
FIRST PART ELEMENTARY PRINCIPLES OR THE SOUNDS AND CHARACTERS CHAPTER I THE INDIVIDUAL SOUNDS AND CHARACTERS
{{GHGpar-heading|5|The Consonants: their Forms and Names}}
(Cf. the Table of Alphabets.)
Among the abundant literature on the subject, special attention is directed to: A. Berliner, {{GHGcite|title=Beitrage zurhebr. Gramm.}}, Berlin, 1879, p. 15 ff., on the names, forms, and pronunciation of the consonants in Talmud and Midrash; H. Strack, {{GHGcite|title=Schreibkunst u. Schrift bei d. Hebräern, PRE.}}3, Lpz. 1906, p. 766 ff.; Benzinger, {{GHGcite|title=Hebr. Archäologie}}2, Tübingen, 1907, p. 172 ff.; Nowack, {{GHGcite|title=Lehrbicch d. hebr. Archäologie}}2, Freiburg, 1894, i. 279 ff.; Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Handbuch d. nordsem. Epigraphik}}, Weimar, 1898, i. I73ff.; also his art. 'Hebrew Alphabet,' in the {{GHGcite|title=Jewish Encyclopaedia}}, i, 1901, p. 439 ff. (cf. his {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, i. 316 ff.); and 'Die Namen der Alphabetbuchstaben', in {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, ii. 125 ff.; Kenyon, art. 'Writing,' in the {{GHGcite|title=Dictionary of the Bible}}, iv. Edinb. 1902, p. 944 ff.; Nöldeke, 'Die semit. Buchstabennamen,' in {{GHGcite|title=Beitr. sur semit. Sprachwiss.}}, Strassb. 1904, p. 124 ff.; F. Praetorius, {{GHGcite|title=Ueber den Ursprung des kanaan. Alphabets}}, Berlin, 1906; H. Grimme, 'Zur Genesis des semit. Alphabets,' in {{GHGcite|title=ZA}}. xx. 1907, p. 49 ff.; R. Stübe, {{GHGcite|title=Grundlinien su einer Entwickelungsgesch, d. Schrift}}, Munich, 1907; Jermain, {{GHGcite|title=In the path of the Alphabet}}, Fort Wayne, 1907.—L. Blau, {{GHGcite|title=Studien zum althebr. Buchwesen, &c.}}, Strassb. 1902; and his 'Ueber d. Einfluss d. althebr. Buchwesens auf d. Originale', &c., in {{GHGcite|title=Festschr. zu Ehren A. Berliners}}, Frkf. 1903. The best tables of alphabets are those of J. Euting in G. Bickell's {{GHGcite|title=Outlines of Heb. Gram.}}, transl. by S. I. Curtiss, Lpz. 1877; in Pt. vii of the {{GHGcite|title=Oriental Series}} of the Palaeographical Soc., London, 1882; and, the fullest of all, in Chwolson's {{GHGcite|title=Corpus inscr. Hebr.}}, Petersburg, 1882; also Lidzbarski's in the {{GHGcite|title=Jewish Encycl.}}, see above. {{GHGmargin-letter|5|a}} 1. The Hebrew letters now in use, in which both the manuscripts of the O.T. are written and our editions of the Bible are printed, commonly called the {{GHGterm|square character}} ({{GHGheb|text=כְּתָב מְרֻבָּע}}), also the {{GHGterm|Assyrian character}} ({{GHGheb|text=כְּ׳ אַשּׁוּרִי}}),The name {{GHGheb|text=אַשּׁוּר}} (Assyria) is here used in the widest sense, to include the countries on the Mediterranean inhabited by Aramaean; cf. Stade in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1882, p. 292 f. On some other names for Old Hebrew writing, cf. G. Hoffmann, ibid. 1881, p. 334 ff.; Buhl, {{GHGcite|title=Canon and Text of the O.T.}} (transl. by J. Macpherson), Edinb. 1893, p. 200. are not those originally employed. {{GHGterm|Old Hebrew}} (or {{GHGterm|Old Canaanitish}}It is tacitly assumed here that this was the mother of ''all'' Semitic alphabets. In {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1909, p. 189 ff., however, Prätorius has shown good grounds for believing that the South Semitic alphabet is derived not from the Mêšaʿ character, or from some kindred and hardly older script, but from some unknown and ''much'' earlier form of writing.) writing, as it was used on

49.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par5 />public monuments in the beginning of the ninth and in the second half of the eighth century {{smaller|B.C.}}, is to be seen in the inscription of Mêšaʿ, as well as in that of Siloam. The characters on the Maccabaean coins of the second century {{smaller|B.C.}}, and also on ancient gems, still bear much resemblance to this (cf. {{GHGpar|2|d}}). With the Old Hebrew writing the Phoenician is nearly identical (see {{GHGpar|1|k}}, {{GHGpar|2|f}}, and the Table of Alphabets). From the analogy of the history of other kinds of writing, it may be assumed that out of and along with this monumental character, a less antique and in some ways more convenient, rounded style was early developed, for use on softer materials, skins, bark, papyrus, and the like. This the Samaritans retained after their separation from the Jews, while the Jews gradually<ref>On the effect of the transitional mixture of earlier and later forms on the constitution of the text, see R. Kittel, {{GHGcite|title=Ueber d. Notwendigk. d. Herausg. einer neuen hebr. Bibel}}, Lpz. 1901, p. 20 ff.—L. Blau, ‘Wie lange stand die althebr. Schrift bet den Juden im Gebrauch?’ in {{GHGcite|title=Kaufmanngedenkbuch}}, Breslau, 1900, p. 44 ff.</ref> (between the sixth and the fourth century) exchanged it for an Aramaic character. From this gradually arose (from about the fourth to the middle of the third century) what is called the {{GHGterm|square character}}, which consequently bears great resemblance to the extant forms of Aramaic writing, such as the Egyptian-Aramaic, the Nabatean and especially the Palmyrene. Of Hebrew inscriptions in the older square character, that of ʿArâq al-Emîr (15½ miles north-east of the mouth of the Jordan) probably belongs to 183 {{smaller|B.C.}}<ref>Not 176, as formerly held. Driver and Lidzbarski now read {{GHGheb|text=ערביה}}, correctly, not {{GHGheb|text=טוביה}}.</ref>

The Jewish sarcophagus-inscriptions of the time of Christ, found in Jerusalem in 1905, almost without exception exhibit a pure square character. This altered little in the course of centuries, so that the age of a Hebrew MS. cannot easily be determined from the style of the writing. The oldest known biblical fragment is the Nash papyrus (found in 1902), containing the ten commandments and the beginning of {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=6|verse=4 f.}}, of the end of the first or beginning of the second century {{smaller|A.D.}}; cf. N. Peters, {{GHGcite|title=Die älteste Abschr. der 10 Gebote}}, Freibg. i. B. 1905. Of actual MSS. of the Bible the oldest is probably one of 820–850 {{smaller|A.D.}} described by Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, p. 469 ff., at the head of his sixty principal MSS.; next in age is the codex of Moses ben Asher at Cairo (897 {{smaller|A.D.}}, cf. the art. ‘Scribes’ in the {{GHGcite|title=Jew. Encycl.}} xi and Gottheil in {{GHGcite|title=JQR.}} 1905, p. 32). The date (916 {{smaller|A.D.}}) of the Codex prophetarum Babylon. Petropol. (see {{GHGpar|8|g}}, note) is quite certain.—In the synagogue-rolls a distinction is drawn between the Tam-character (said to be so called from Rabbi Tam, grandson of R. Yiṣḥāqî, in the twelfth century) with its straight strokes, square corners and ‘tittles’ (tāgîn), in German and Polish MSS., and the ''foreign'' character with rounded letters and tittles in Spanish MSS. See further E. König, {{GHGcite|title=Einl. in das A.T.}}, Bonn, 1893, p. 16 ff.

7.text:
TRANSLATOR'S PREFACE
The translation of the twenty-sixth German edition of this grammar, originally prepared by the Rev. G. W. Collins and revised by me, was published in 1898. Since that date a twenty-seventh German edition has appeared; and Prof. Kautzsch was already engaged on a twenty-eighth in 1908 when the English translation was becoming exhausted. He sent me the sheets as they were printed off, and I began revising the former translation in order to produce it as soon as possible after the completion of the German. The whole of the English has been carefully compared with the new edition, and, it is hoped, improved in many points, while Prof. Kautzsch's own corrections and additions have of course been incorporated. As before, the plan and arrangement of the original have been strictly followed, so that the references for sections and paragraphs correspond exactly in German and English. Dr. Driver has again most generously given up time, in the midst of other engagements, to reading the sheets, and has made numerous suggestions. To him also are chiefly due the enlargement of the index of subjects, some expansions in the new index of Hebrew words, and some additions to the index of passages, whereby we hope to have made the book more serviceable to students. I have also to thank my young friend, Mr. Godfrey R. Driver, of Winchester College, for some welcome help in correcting proofs of the Hebrew index and the index of passages. {{GHGheb|text=בן חכם ישמח אב}}. Many corrections have been sent to me by scholars who have used the former English edition, especially the Rev. W. E. Blomfield, the Rev. S. Holmes, Mr. P. Wilson, Prof. Witton Davies, Mr. G. H. Skipwith, and an unknown correspondent

8.text:
at West Croydon. These, as well as suggestions in reviews, have all been considered, and where possible, utilized. I am also much indebted to the Press-readers for the great care which they have bestowed on the work. Finally, I must pay an affectionate tribute to the memory of Prof. Kautzsch, who died in the spring of this year, shortly after finishing the last sheets of the twenty-eighth edition. For more than thirty years he was indefatigable in improving the successive editions of the Grammar. The German translation of the Old Testament first published by him in 1894, with the co-operation of other scholars, under the title {{GHGcite|title=Die Heilige Schrift des A Ts}}, and now (1910) in the third and much enlarged edition, is a valuable work which has been widely appreciated: the {{GHGcite|title=Apocryphen und Pseudepigraphen des A Ts}}, edited by him in 1900, is another important work: besides which he published his {{GHGcite|title=Grammatik des Biblisch-Aramäischen}} in 1884, two useful brochures {{GHGcite|title=Bibelwissenschaft und Religionsunterricht}} in 1900, and {{GHGcite|title=Die bleibende Bedeutung des A Ts}} in 1903, six popular lectures on {{GHGcite|title=Die Poesie und die poetischen Bücher des A Ts}} in 1902, his article 'Religion of Israel' in Hastings' {{GHGcite|title=Dictionary of the Bible}}, v. (1904), pp. 612-734, not to mention minor publications. His death is a serious loss to Biblical scholarship, while to me and to many others it is the loss of a most kindly friend, remarkable alike for his simple piety and his enthusiasm for learning.
A. C.
{{Small-caps|Magdalen College, Oxford,}}
''Sept''. 1910.

100.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par21" />{{GHGheb|text=פ‍}}, even at the beginning of a syllable, by {{polytonic|χ}} and {{polytonic|φ}}; {{polytonic|Χερούβ}}, {{polytonic|Χαλδαῖοι}}, {{polytonic|Φαρφάρ}}, &c.—The forms {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽדְכֹד}} (after {{GHGheb|text=וְשַׂמְתִּ֫י}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=54|verse=12}}, and {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽלְכֵל}} (after {{GHGheb|text=וְנִלְאֵ֫יתִי}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=9}} are doubly anomalous.

{{GHGmargin-letter|21|e}}
(2) In the middle of words after {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ quiescens}}, i.e. at the beginning of a syllable immediately after a vowelless consonant,<ref>The exceptions {{GHGheb|text=יָקְתְאֵל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=38}} (see ''Minḥat shay'', on this passage), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=14|verse=7}}, and {{GHGheb|text=יָקְדְעָם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=56}} may perhaps be due to the character of the {{GHGheb|text=ק}}.</ref> e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יִרְפָּא|pron=yirpā}} ({{GHGtranslate|he heals}}), {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתֶּם|translate=ye have killed}}; but after {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רְפָא}} ''r<sup>e</sup>phā'' (''heal thou''), {{GHGheb|text=כָּֽבְדָה|translate=she was heavy}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|21|f}}
On {{GHGheb|text=קָטַלְתְּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּשְׁבְּ}} and similar forms, see {{GHGpar|10|i}}.

Whether {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} be vocal and consequently causes the aspiration of a following {{GHGterm|tenuis}}, depends upon the origin of the particular form. It is almost always vocal

(''a'') When it has arisen from the weakening of a strong vowel, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רִדְפוּ|translate=pursue ye}} (not {{GHGheb|text=רִדְפּוּ}}) from {{GHGheb|text=רְדֹף}}; {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכֵי}} (not {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכֵּי}}), because originally {{GHGpron|mălăkhê}}, but {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכִּי}} from the ground-form {{GHGpron|malk}}.

(''b'') With the {{GHGheb|text=כ‍}} of the pronominal suffixes of the 2nd pers. {{GHGheb|text=־ְךָ}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ְכֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ְכֶן}}, since Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile is characteristic of these forms (see {{GHGpar|58|f}}; {{GHGpar|91|b}}).

Rem. Forms like {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלַ֫חַתְּ|translate=thou ''(fem.)'' hast sent}}, in which we should expect an aspirated {{GHGheb|text=ת}} after the vowel, cf. {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּ֫חַדְּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=9}}, have arisen from {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלַחְתְּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=יִחְדְּ}}, &c.; Pathaḥ being here simply a helping vowel has no influence on the tenuis; cf. {{GHGpar|28|e}}.
<section end="par21" />
<section begin="par22" />{{GHGpar-heading|22|Peculiarities of the Gutturals}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|22|a}}
The four gutturals {{GHGheb|text=ח}}, {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, {{GHGheb|text=ע}}, {{GHGheb|text=א}}, in consequence of their peculiar pronunciation, have special characteristics, but {{GHGheb|text=א}}, as the weakest of these sounds, and sometimes also {{GHGheb|text=ע}} (which elsewhere as one of the harder gutturals is the opposite of {{GHGheb|text=א}}), differ in several respects from the stronger {{GHGheb|text=ה}} and {{GHGheb|text=ח}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|22|b}}
'''1.''' They do not admit of {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}, since, in consequence of a gradual weakening of the pronunciation (see below, note 2), the strengthening of the gutturals was hardly audible to the Masoretes. But a distinction must be drawn between (''a'') the complete omission of the strengthening, and (''b'') the mere {{GHGterm|echo}} of it, commonly called {{GHGterm|half}} doubling, but better, {{GHGterm|virtual}} strengthening.

{{GHGmargin-letter|22|c}}
In the former case, the short vowel before the guttural would stand in an open syllable, and must accordingly be lengthened or modified.<ref>Cf. ''terra'' and the French ''terre'', the German ''Rolle'' and the French ''rôle''; German ''drollig'' and French ''drôle''. The omission of the strengthening shows a deterioration of the language. Arabic still admits of the strengthening of gutturals in all cases.</ref><section end="par22" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

51.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="BlobcatsAreCool" /></noinclude><section begin="par5" />{{GHGmargin-letter|5|c}}
'''3.''' As the Table shows, five letters have a special form at the end of the word. They are called final letters, and were combined by the Jewish grammarians in the mnemonic word {{GHGheb|text=כַּמְנֶפֶץ}} {{GHGpron|Kamnèphäṣ}}, or better, with A. Müller and Stade, {{GHGheb|text=כַּמְנַפֵּץ}} i.e. {{GHGtranslate|as the breaker in pieces}}.<ref>In the Talmud, disregarding the alphabetical order, {{GHGheb|text=מִן־צֹֽפְךָ|translate=of thy watcher}}, i.e. {{GHGtranslate|prophet}}. See the discussions of this mnemonic word by Nestle, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1907, p. 119 ff., König, Bacher (who would read {{GHGheb|text=מִן־צֹפַיִךְ}} = proceeding {{GHGtranslate|from thy prophets}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=52|verse=8}}), Krauss, Marmorstein, ibid. p. 278 ff. All the twenty-two letters, together with the five final forms, occur in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=3|verse=8}}.</ref> Of these, {{GHGheb|text=ך}}, {{GHGheb|text=ן}}, {{GHGheb|text=ף}}, {{GHGheb|text=ץ}} are distinguished from the common form by the shaft being drawn straight down, while in the usual form it is bent round towards the left.<ref>Chwolson, {{GHGcite|title=Corpus Inscr. Hebr.}}, col. 68, rightly observes that the more original forms of these letters are preserved in the {{GHGterm|literae finales}}. Instances of them go back to the time of Christ.</ref> In the case of {{GHGheb|text=ם}} the letter is completely closed.

{{GHGmargin-letter|5|d}}
'''4.''' Hebrew is read and written from right to left.<ref>The same was originally the practice in Greek, which only adopted the opposite direction exclusively about 400 {{smaller|B.C.}} On the {{GHGterm|boustrophēdon}} writing (alternately in each direction) in early Greek, early Sabaean, and in the Safa-inscriptions of the first three centuries {{smaller|A.D.}}, cf. Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, i. 116 f.</ref> Words must not be divided at the end of the lines;<ref>This does not apply to early inscriptions or seals. Cf. Mêšaʿ, II. 1–5, 7, 8, &c., Siloam 2, 3, 5, where the division of words appears to be customary.</ref> but, in order that no empty space may be left, in MSS. and printed texts, certain letters suitable for the purpose are dilated at the end or in the middle of the line. In our printed texts these {{GHGterm|literae dilatabiles}} are the five following: {{nowrap|{{GHGheb|text=ﬡ ﬣ ﬥ ﬨ ﬦ}}}} (mnemonic word {{GHGheb|text=אֲהַלְתֶּם}} {{GHGpron|ʾ<sup>a</sup>haltèm}}). In some MSS. other letters suitable for the purpose are also employed in this way, as {{GHGheb|text=ד}}, {{GHGheb|text=כ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=ר}}; cf. Strack in the {{GHGcite|title=Theol. Lehrb.}}, 1882, No. 22; Nestle, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1906, p. 170 f.

{{GHGmargin-letter|5|e}}
Rem. 1. The forms of the letters originally represent the rude outlines of perceptible objects, the names of which, respectively, begin with the consonant represented (akrophony). Thus {{GHGterm|Yôd}}, in the earlier alphabets the rude picture of a hand, properly denotes {{GHGtranslate|hand}} (Heb. {{GHGheb|text=יָד}}), but as a letter simply the sound {{GHGheb|text=י}} (''y''), with which this word begins; {{GHGterm|ʿAyĭn}}, originally a circle, properly an {{GHGtranslate|eye}} ({{GHGheb|text=עַ֫ין}}), stands for the consonant {{GHGheb|text=ע}}. In the Phoenician alphabet, especially, the resemblance of the forms to the objects denoted by the name is still for the most part recognizable (see the Table). In some letters ({{GHGheb|text=ג}}, {{GHGheb|text=ו}}, {{GHGheb|text=ז}}, {{GHGheb|text=ט}}, {{GHGheb|text=ש}}) the similarity is still preserved in the square character.

It is another question whether the present names are all original. They may be merely due to a later, and not always accurate, interpretation of the forms. Moreover, it is possible that in the period from about 1500 to 1000 {{smaller|B.C.}} the original forms underwent considerable change.

{{GHGmargin-letter|5|f}}
The usual explanation of the present names of the letters<ref>We possess Greek transcriptions of the Hebrew names, dating from the fifth century {{smaller|B.C.}} The LXX give them (in almost the same form as Eusebius, {{GHGcite|title=Praep. Evang.}} 10. 5) in {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1}}–{{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|hidebook=1}}, as do also many Codices of the Vulgate (e.g. the Cod. Amiatinus) in {{GHGbible-ref|book=PsPs|chapter=111}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=PsPs|chapter=112|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=PsPs|chapter=119|hidebook=1}}, but with many variations from the customary forms, which rest on the traditional {{GHGterm|Jewish}} pronunciation. The forms {{GHGterm|Deleth}} (and {{GHGterm|delth}}), {{GHGterm|Zai, Sen}} (LXX also {{polytonic|χσεν}}, cf. Hebr. {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁן|translate=tooth}}) are to be noticed, amongst others, for {{GHGterm|Daleth}}, {{GHGterm|Zain}}, {{GHGterm|Šîn}}. Cf. the tables in Nöldeke, {{GHGcite|title=Beiträge zur sem. Sprachwiss.}}, p. 126 f. In his opinion (and so Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, i. 134) the form and meaning of the names point to Phoenicia as the original home of the alphabet, since {{GHGterm|alf}}, {{GHGterm|bêt}}, {{GHGterm|dalt}}, {{GHGterm|wāw}}, {{GHGterm|tāw}}, {{GHGterm|pei}} = {{GHGterm|pê}}, {{GHGterm|pî}}, mouth, and the vowel of {{polytonic|ῥῶ}} = {{GHGterm|rōš}}, head, are all Hebraeo-Phoenician.</ref> is: {{GHGheb|text=אָלֶף|translate=ox}},<section end="par5" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

52.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par5 />{{GHGheb|text=בֵּית|translate=house}}, {{GHGheb|text=גִּמֶל|translate=camel}} (according to Lidzbarski, see below, perhaps originally {{GHGheb|text=גַּרְזֶן|translate=axe}} or {{GHGtranslate|pick-axe}}), {{GHGheb|text=דָּלֶת|translate=door}} (properly {{GHGtranslate|folding door}}; according to Lidzbarski, perhaps {{GHGheb|text=דַּד|translate=the female breast}}), {{GHGheb|text=הֵא|translate=air-hole}} (?), {{GHGtranslate|lattice-window}} (?), {{GHGheb|text=וָו|translate=hook, nail}}, {{GHGheb|text=זַיִן|translate=weapon}} (according to Nestle, comparing the Greek {{polytonic|ζῆτα}}, rather {{GHGheb|text=זַיִת|translate=olive-tree}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֵית|translate=fence, barrier}} (but perhaps only differentiated from {{GHGheb|text=ה}} by the left-hand stroke), {{GHGheb|text=טֵית|translate=a winding}} (?), according to others a {{GHGtranslate|leather bottle}} or a {{GHGtranslate|snake}} (but perhaps only differentiated from {{GHGheb|text=ת}} by a circle round it), {{GHGheb|text=יוֹד|translate=hand}}, {{GHGheb|text=כַּף|translate=bent hand}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָמֶד|translate=ox-goad}}, {{GHGheb|text=מַיִם|translate=water}}, {{GHGheb|text=נוּן|translate=fish}} (Lidzbarski, ‘perhaps originally {{GHGheb|text=נָחָשׁ|translate=snake}},’ as in Ethiopic), {{GHGheb|text=סָמֶךְ|translate=prop}} (perhaps a modification of {{GHGheb|text=ז}}), {{GHGheb|text=עַיִן|translate=eye}}, {{GHGheb|text=פֵּא}} (also {{GHGheb|text=פֵּי|translate=mouth}}), {{GHGheb|text=צָדֵי|translate=fish-hook}} (?), {{GHGheb|text=קוֹף|translate=eye of a needle}}, according to others {{GHGtranslate|back of the head}} (Lidzb., ‘perhaps {{GHGheb|text=קֶשֶׁת|translate=bow}}’), {{GHGheb|text=רֵישׁ|translate=head}}, {{GHGheb|text=שִׁין|translate=tooth}}, {{GHGheb|text=תָּו|translate=sign, cross}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|5|g}}
With regard to the origin of this alphabet, it may be taken as proved that it is not earlier (or very little earlier) than the fifteenth century {{smaller|B.C.}}, since otherwise the el-Amarna tablets ({{GHGpar|2|f}}) would not have been written exclusively in cuneiform.<ref>In the excavations at Jericho in April, 1907, E. Sellin found a jar-handle with the Canaanite characters {{GHGheb|text=יה}} which he dates (probably too early) about 1500 {{smaller|B.C.}}</ref> It seems equally certain on various grounds, that it originated on Canaanitish soil. It is, however, still an open question whether the inventors of it borrowed

(''a'') From the Egyptian system—not, as was formerly supposed, by direct adoption of hieroglyphic signs (an explanation of twelve or thirteen characters was revived by J. Halévy in {{GHGcite|title=Rev. Sémit.}} 1901, p. 356 ff., 1902, p. 331 ff., and in the {{GHGcite|title=Verhandlungen des xiii. ... Orient.-Kongr. zu Hamb.}}, Leiden, 1904, p. 199 ff.; but cf. Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, i. 261 ff.), or of hieratic characters derived from them (so E. de Rougé), but by the adoption of the {{GHGterm|acrophonic}} principle (see {{GHGpar|5|e|nonumber=1}}) by which e.g. the hand, in Egyptian {{GHGpron|tot}}, represents the letter ''t'', the lion = {{GHGpron|laboi}}, the letter ''l''. This view still seems the most probable. It is now accepted by Lidzbarski (‘Der Ursprung d. nord- u. südsemit. Schrift’ in {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, i (1900), 109 ff., cf. pp. 134 and 261 ff.), though in his {{GHGcite|title=Nordsem. Epigr.}} (1898) p. 173 ff. he was still undecided.

(''b'') From the Babylonian (cuneiform) system. Wuttke’s and W. Deecke’s derivation of the old-Semitic alphabet from new-Assyrian cuneiform is impossible for chronological reasons. More recently Peters and Hommel have sought to derive it from the old-Babylonian, and Ball from the archaic Assyrian cuneiform. A vigorous discussion has been aroused by the theory of Frdr. Delitzsch (in {{GHGcite|title=Die Entstehung des ält. Schriftsystems od. der Urspr. der Keilschriftzeichen dargel.}}, Lpz. 1897; and with the same title ‘Ein Nachwort’, Lpz. 1898, preceded by a very clear outline of the theory) that the old-Semitic alphabet arose in Canaan under the influence both of the Egyptian system (whence the acrophonic principle) and of the old-Babylonian, whence the principle of the graphic representation of objects and ideas by means of simple, and mostly rectilinear, signs. He holds that the choice of the objects was probably (in about fifteen cases) influenced by the Babylonian system. The correspondence of names had all the more effect since, according to Zimmern ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1896, p. 667 ff.), out of twelve names which are certainly identical, eight appear in the same order in the Babylonian arrangement of signs. But it must first be shown that the present names of the<section end=par5 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

53.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude>
<section begin=par5/>‘Phoenician’ letters really denote the original picture. The identity of the objects may perhaps be due simply to the choice of the commonest things (animals, implements, limbs) in both systems.

The derivation of the Semitic alphabet from the signs of the Zodiac and their names, first attempted by Seyffarth in 1834, has been revived by Winckler, who refers twelve fundamental sounds to the Babylonian Zodiac. Hommel connects the original alphabet with the moon and its phases, and certain constellations; cf. Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, i. 269 ff., and in complete agreement with him, Benzinger, {{GHGcite|title=Hebr. Archäologie}}<sup>2</sup>, p. 173 ff. This theory is by no means convincing.

(''c'') From the hieroglyphic system of writing discovered in 1894 by {{nowrap|A. J. Evans}} in inscriptions in Crete (esp. at Cnossus) and elsewhere. According to Kluge (1897) and others, this represents the ‘Mycenaean script’ used about 3000–1000 {{smaller|B.C.}}, and according to Fries (‘Die neuesten Forschungen über d. Urspr. des phöniz. Alph.’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDPV.|Zeitschrift des deutschen Palästinavereins}}}} xxii. 118 ff.) really supplies the original forms of the Phoenician alphabet as brought to Palestine by the Philistines about 1100 {{smaller|B.C.}}, but ‘the Phoenician-Canaanite-Hebrews gave to the Mycenaean signs names derived from the earlier cuneiform signs’. The hypothesis of Fries is thus connected With that of Delitzsch. But although the derivation of the Phoenician forms from ‘Mycenaean’ types appears in some cases very plausible, in others there are grave difficulties, and moreover the date, 1100 {{smaller|B.C.}}, assigned for the introduction of the alphabet is clearly too late. [See Evans, {{GHGcite|title=Scripta Minoa}}, Oxf. 1909, p. 80 ff.]

(''d'') From a system, derived from Asia Minor, closely related to the Cypriote syllabary (Praetorius, {{GHGcite|title=Der Urspr. des kanaan. Alphabets}}, Berlin, 1906). On this theory the Canaanites transformed the syllabic into an apparently alphabetic writing. In reality, however, they merely retained a single sign for the various syllables, so that e.g. {{GHGheb|text=ק}} is not really ''q'', but ''qa, qe, qi'', &c. Of the five Cypriote vowels also they retained only the star (in Cypriote = ''a'') simplified into an ''ʾālef'' (see alphabetical table) to express the vowels at the beginning of syllables, and ''i'' and ''u'' as Yod and Waw. Praetorius claims to explain about half the twenty-two Canaanite letters in this way, but there are various objections to his ingenious hypothesis.

{{GHGmargin-letter|5|h}}
2. H. Müller}} of Vienna, containing the eight leading words of {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=19|verse=8 ff.}}, {{GHGpron|tôrā}}, {{GHGpron|ʿedûth}}, &c.); {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1}}–{{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|hidebook=1}} (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=2|hidebook=1}}–{{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=פ}} before {{GHGheb|text=ע}}<ref name="Böhmer">[Perhaps also originally in Ps 34.] {{GHGheb|text=פ}} before {{GHGheb|text=ע}} is probably due to a magic alphabet, see above, n. 1. According to Böhmer, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1908, p. 53 ff., the combinations {{GHGheb|text=אב}}, {{GHGheb|text=גד}}, {{GHGheb|text=הו}}, &c., were used in magical texts; {{GHGheb|text=עס}} was excluded, but by a rearrangement we get {{GHGheb|text=סף}} and {{GHGheb|text=עץ}}.</ref>, in chap. {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|hidebook=1}} every three verses with the same initial, see Löhr, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1904, p. 1 ff., in chap. {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|hidebook=1}} at any rate as many verses as letters in the alphabet); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=24|verse=1.3.5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=24|verse=10–31|hidebook=1}} (in the LXX with {{GHGheb|text=פ}} before {{GHGheb|text=ע}}<ref name="Böhmer" />); also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=1|verse=2–10}} Pastor Frohnmeyer of Württemberg (ob. 1880) detected traces of an alphabetic arrangement, but the attempt of Gunkel, Bickell, Arnold ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1901,

54.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par5" />p. 225 ff.), Happel ({{GHGcite|title=Der Ps. Nah}}, Würzb. 1900) to discover further traces, has not been successful. [Cf. Gray in {{GHGcite|title=Expositor}}, 1898, p. 207 ff.; Driver, in the Century Bible, {{GHGcite|title=Nahum}}, p. 26.]—Bickell, {{GHGcite|title=Ztschr f. Kath. Theol.}}, 1882, p. 319 ff., had already deduced from the versions the alphabetical character of {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ecclus|chapter=51|verse=13–30}}, with the omission of the {{GHGheb|text=ו}}-verse and with {{GHGheb|text=פ}}<ref>See note 3 on p. {{GHGpage|29}}.</ref> at the end. His conjectures have been brilliantly confirmed by the discovery of the Hebrew original, although the order from {{GHGheb|text=ג}} to {{GHGheb|text=ל}} is partly disturbed or obscured. If {{GHGheb|text=ו}} before {{GHGheb|text=צ}} is deleted, ten letters are in their right positions, and seven can be restored to their places with certainty. Cf. N. Schlögl, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 53, 669 ff.; C. Taylor in the appendix to Schechter and Taylor, {{GHGcite|title=The Wisdom of Ben Sira}}, Cambr. 1899, p. lxxvi ff., and in the {{GHGcite|title=Journ. of Philol.}}, xxx (1906), p. 95 ff.; {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|JQR.|Jewish Quarterly Review.}}}} 1905, p. 238 ff.; Löhr, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1905, p. 183 ff.; I. Lévy, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|REJ.|Revue des Études Juives. Paris, 1880 ff.}}}} 1907, p. 62 ff.

The sequence of the three softest labial, palatal, and dental sounds {{GHGheb|text=ב}}, {{GHGheb|text=ג}}, {{GHGheb|text=ד}}, and of the three liquids {{GHGheb|text=ל}}, {{GHGheb|text=מ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=נ‍}}, indicates an attempt at classification. At the same time other considerations also appear to have had influence. Thus it is certainly not accidental, that two letters, representing a hand (''Yôd'', ''Kaph''), as also two (if ''Qôph'' = back of the head) which represent the head, and in general several forms denoting objects naturally connected (''Mêm'' and ''Nûn'', ''ʿAyĭn'' and ''Pê''), stand next to one another.

{{GHGmargin-letter|5|i}}
The order, names, and numerical values of the letters have passed over from the Phoenicians to the Greeks, in whose alphabet the letters Α to Υ are borrowed from the Old Semitic. So also the Old Italic alphabets as well as the Roman, and consequently all alphabets derived either from this or from the Greek, are directly or indirectly dependent on the Phoenician.

{{GHGmargin-letter|5|k}}
3. ''a''. In default of special arithmetical figures, the consonants were used also as numerical signs; cf. G. Gundermann, {{GHGcite|title=Die Zahlzeichen}}, Giessen, 1899, p. 6 f., and Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Ephemeris}}, i. 106 ff. The earliest traces of this usage are, however, first found on the Maccabean coins (see above, {{GHGpar|2|d}}, end). These numerical letters were afterwards commonly employed, e.g. for marking the numbers of chapters and verses in the editions of the Bible. The units are denoted by {{GHGheb|text=א}}–{{GHGheb|text=ט}}, the tens by {{GHGheb|text=י}}–{{GHGheb|text=צ‍}}, 100–400 by {{GHGheb|text=ק}}–{{GHGheb|text=ת}}, the numbers from 500–900 by {{GHGheb|text=ת}} (=400), with the addition of the remaining hundreds, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=תק}} 500. In compound numbers the greater precedes (on the right), thus {{GHGheb|text=יא}} 11, {{GHGheb|text=קכא}} 121. But 15 is expressed by {{GHGheb|text=טו}} 9+6, not {{GHGheb|text=יה}} (which is a form of the divine name, being the first two consonants of {{GHGheb|text=יהוה}}).<ref>On the rise of this custom ({{GHGheb|text=יה}} having been originally used and afterwards {{GHGheb|text=הי}}), cf. Nestle in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1884, p. 250, where a trace of this method of writing occurring as early as Origen is noted.</ref> For a similar reason {{GHGheb|text=טז}} is also mostly written for 16, instead of {{GHGheb|text=יו}}, which in compound proper names, like {{GHGheb|text=יוֹאֵל}}, also represents the name of God, {{GHGheb|text=יהוה}}.

The thousands are sometimes denoted by the units with two dots placed above, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אׄׄ}} 1000.

{{GHGmargin-letter|5|l}}
''b''. The reckoning of the years in Jewish writings (generally {{GHGheb|text=ליצירה|translate=after the creation}}) follows either the ''full chronology'' ({{GHGheb|text=לִפְרָט גָּדוֹל}} or {{GHGheb|text=לפ׳ ג׳}}), with the addition of the thousands, or the ''abridged chronology'' ({{GHGheb|text=לפ׳ קָטוֹן}}), in which they are omitted. In the dates of the first thousand years after Christ, the Christian era is obtained by the addition of 240, in the second thousand years by the addition of 1240 (i.e. if the date falls between Jan. 1 and the Jewish new year; otherwise add 1239), the thousands of the Creation era being omitted.

{{GHGmargin-letter|5|m}}
4. Abbreviations of words are not found in the text of the O.T., but they occur on coins, and their use is extremely frequent amongst the later Jews.<ref>Cf. Jo. Buxtorf, {{GHGcite|title=De abbreviaturis Hebr.}}, Basel, 1613, &c.; Pietro Perreau.</ref><section end="par5" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

55.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par5"/>A point, or later an oblique stroke, serves as the sign of abridgement in old MSS. and editions, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=ישׂ׳}} for {{GHGheb|text=יִשְׂרָאֵל}}, {{GHGheb|text=פ׳}} for {{GHGheb|text=פְּלֹנִי|translate=aliquis|en=someone}}, {{GHGheb|text=ד׳}} for {{GHGheb|text=דָּבָר|translate=aliquid|en=something}}, {{GHGheb|text=וגו׳}} for {{GHGheb|text=וְגוֹמַר|translate=et complens|and he finishes}}, i.e. ''and so on''. Also in the middle of what is apparently a word, such strokes indicate that it is an abbreviation or a ''vox memorialis'' (cf. e.g. {{GHGpar|15|d}} {{GHGheb|text=תא״ם}}). Two such strokes are employed, from {{GHGpar|41|d}} onward, to mark the different classes of weak verbs.—Note also {{GHGheb|text=יְיָ}} or {{GHGheb|text=יָי}} (also {{GHGheb|text=ה׳}}) for {{GHGheb|text=יְהֹוָה}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|5|n}}
5. Peculiarities in the tradition of the O.T. text, which are already mentioned in the Talmud, are—(1) The 15 {{GHGterm|puncta extraordinaria}}, about which the tradition (from Siphri on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=9|verse=10}} onwards) differs considerably, even as to their number; on particular consonants, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=33.35|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=9|verse=10}}; or on whole words, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=3|verse=39}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=30|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=29|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=44|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=41|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=46|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=27|verse=13}}, —all no doubt critical marks; cf. Strack, {{GHGcite|title=Prolegomena Critica}}, p. 88 ff.; L. Blau, {{GHGcite|title=Masoretische Untersuchungen}}, Strassburg, 1891, p. 6 ff., and {{GHGcite|title=Einleitung in die hl. Schrift}}, Budapest, 1894; Königsberger, {{GHGcite|title=Jüd. Lit.-Blatt}}, 1891, nos. 29–31, and {{GHGcite|title=Aus Masorah u. Talmudkritik}}, Berlin, 1892, p. 6 ff.; Mayer-Lambert, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|REJ.|Revue des Études Juives. Paris, 1880 ff.}}}} 30 (1895), no. 59; and especially Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, p. 318 ff.; also on the ten points found in the Pentateuch, see Butin (Baltimore, 1906), who considers that they are as old as the Christian era and probably mark a letter, &c., to be deleted. (2) The {{GHGterm|literae majusculae}} (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=ב}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=1}}, {{GHGheb|text=ו}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=11|verse=42}} as the middle consonant of the Pentateuch, {{GHGheb|text=י}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=17}}), and {{GHGterm|minusculae}} (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=ה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=4}}). (3) The {{GHGterm|literae suspensae}} (Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, p. 334 ff.) {{GHGheb|text=נ‍}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=18|verse=30}} (which points to the reading {{GHGheb|text=משֶׁה}} for {{GHGheb|text=מְנַשֶּׁה}}, {{GHGheb|text=ע}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=80|verse=14}} (the middle of the Psalms<ref>According to Blau, {{GHGcite|title=Studien zum althebr. Buchwesen}}, Strassburg, 1902, p. 167, properly a large {{GHGheb|text=ע}}, called ''t<sup>e</sup>lûyā'' because ''suspended'' between the two halves of the Psalter, and then incorrectly taken for a {{GHGterm|littera suspensa}}.</ref>) and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=13.15}}. (4) The ‘mutilated’ {{GHGterm|Wāw}} in {{GHGheb|text=שלום}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=25|verse=12}}, and {{GHGheb|text=ק}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=25}} ({{GHGheb|text=בקמיהם}}), and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=7|verse=2}} ({{GHGheb|text=הפקודים}}). (5) {{GHGterm|Mêm clausum}} in {{GHGheb|text=לםרבה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=6}}, and {{GHGterm|Mêm apertum}} in {{GHGheb|text=המ‍ פרוצים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=2|verse=13}}. (6) {{GHGterm|Nûn inversum}} before {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=10|verse=35}}, and after ver. 36, as also before {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=107|verse=23–28}} and <sup>40</sup>; according to Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, p. 341 ff., a sort of bracket to indicate that the verses are out of place; cf. Krauss, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1902, p. 57 ff., who regards the inverted ''Nûns'' as an imitation of the Greek obelus.
<section end="par5"/>
<section begin="par6"/>{{GHGpar-heading|6|Pronunciation and Division of Consonants}}

P. Haupt, ‘Die Semit. Sprachlaute u. ihre Umschrift,’ in {{GHGcite|title=Beiträge zur Assyriologie u. vergleich. semit. Sprachwissenschaft}}, by Delitzsch and Haupt, i, Lpz. 1889, 249 ff.; E. Sievers, {{GHGcite|title=Metrische Studien}}, i, Lpz. 1901, p. 14 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|a}}
'''1.''' An accurate knowledge of the original phonetic value of each consonant is of the greatest importance, since very many grammatical peculiarities and changes ({{GHGpar|18}} ff.) only become intelligible from the nature and pronunciation of the sounds. This knowledge is obtained partly from the pronunciation of the kindred dialects, especially the still living Arabic, partly by observing the affinity and interchange<section end="par6"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

56.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Nahum" /></noinclude><section begin=par6/>of sounds on Hebrew itself ({{GHGpar|19}}), and partly from the tradition of the Jews.<ref>Cf. C. Meinhof, ‘Die Aussprache des Hebr.,’ in ''Neue Jahrb. f. Philol. u. Pädag.'', 1885, Bd. 132, p. 146 ff.; M. Schreiner, ‘Zur Gesch. der Ausspr. des Hebr.,’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1886, p. 213 ff.</ref>

The pronunciation of Hebrew by the modern German Jews, which partly resembles the Syriac and is generally called ‘Polish’, differs considerably from that of the Spanish and Portuguese Jews, which approaches nearer to the Arabic. The pronunciation of Hebrew by Christians follows the latter (after the example of Reuchlin), in almost all cases.

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|b}}
The oldest tradition is presented in the transcription of Hebrew names in Assyrian cuneiform; a later, but yet in its way very important system is seen in the manner in which the LXX transcribe Hebrew names with Greek letters.<ref>Cf. Frankel, ''Vorstudien zu der Septuag.'', Lpz. 1841, p. 90 ff.; C. Könneke, ‘Gymn.-Progr.,’ Stargard, 1885. On the transcription of eleven Psalms in a palimpsest fragment of the Hexapla at Milan, see Mercati, ''Atti della R. Accad.'', xxxi, Turin, 1896. [Cf. Burkitt, ''Fragments of... Aquila'', Cambr. 1897, p. 13.]</ref> As, however, corresponding signs for several sounds ({{GHGheb|text=ט}}, {{GHGheb|text=ע}}, {{GHGheb|text=צ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=ק}}, {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}}) are wanting in the Greek alphabet, only an approximate representation was possible in these cases. The same applies to the Latin transcription of Hebrew words by Jerome, according to the Jewish pronunciation of his time.<ref>Numerous examples occur in ''Hieronymi quaestiones hebraicae in libro geneseos'', edited by P. de Lagarde, Lpz. 1868; cf. the exhaustive and systematic discussion by Siegfried, ‘Die Aussprache des Hebr. bei Hieronymus,’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1884, pp. 34–83.</ref>

On the pronunciation of the modern Jews in North Africa, see Bargès in the ''Journ. Asiat.'', Nov. 1848; on that of the South Arabian Jews, J. Dérenbourg, ''Manuel du lecteur'', &c. (from a Yemen MS. of the year 1390), Paris, 1871 (extrait 6 du ''Journ. Asiat.'' 1870).

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|c}}
'''2.''' With regard to the pronunciation of the several gutturals and sibilants, and of {{GHGheb|text=ט}} and {{GHGheb|text=ק}}, it may be remarked:—

1. Among the gutturals, the glottal stop {{GHGheb|text=א}} is the lightest, corresponding to the ''spiritus lenis'' of the Greeks. It may stand either at the beginning or end of a syllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָמַר|pron=ʾāmár}}, {{GHGheb|text=יֶאְשַׁם|pron	=yäʾšám}}. Even ''before'' a vowel {{GHGheb|text=א}} is almost lost to our ear, like the ''h'' in ''hour'' and in the French ''habit, homme''. ''After'' a vowel {{GHGheb|text=א}} generally (and at the end of a word, always) coalesces with it, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קָרָא|translate=qārā}} for an original ''qārăʾ'', Arab. ''qărăʾä''; see further, {{GHGpar|23|a}}, {{GHGpar|27|g|nosign=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|d}}
{{GHGheb|text=ה}} before a vowel corresponds exactly to our ''h'' (spiritus asper); after a vowel it is ''either'' a guttural (so always at the end of a syllable which is not final, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=נֶהְפַּךְ}} ''nähpakh;'' at the end of a word the consonantal {{GHGheb|text=ה}} has a point—Mappîq—in it, see {{GHGpar|14}}), ''or'' it stands inaudible at the end of a word, generally as a mere orthographic indication of a preceding vowel, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גָּלָה|translate=gālā}}; cf. {{GHGpar|7|b|doublesign=1}} and {{GHGpar|75|a|nosign=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|e}}
{{GHGheb|text=ע}} is related to {{GHGheb|text=א}}, but is a much stronger guttural. Its strongest sound is a rattled, guttural ''g'', cf. e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עַזָּה}}, LXX {{polytonic|Γάζα}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֲמֹרָה}} {{polytonic|Γόμοῤῥα}}; elsewhere, a weaker sound of the same kind, which the LXX reproduce by a ''spiritus'' (''lenis'' or ''asper''), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עֵלִי}} {{polytonic|Ἡλί}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֲמָלֵק}} {{polytonic|Ἀμαλέκ}}.<ref>It is, however, doubtful if the LXX always consciously aimed at reproducing the actual differences of sound.</ref> In the mouth of the Arabs one hears in the former case a sort of guttural ''r'', in the latter a sound peculiar to themselves formed in the back of the throat.—It is as incorrect to omit the {{GHGheb|text=ע}}<section end=par6/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

57.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Nahum" /></noinclude><section begin="par6" />entirely, in reading and transcribing words ({{GHGheb|text=עֵלִי|translate=Eli}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֲמָלֵק|translate=Amalek}}), as to pronounce it exactly like ''g'' or like a nasal ''ng''. The stronger sound might be approximately transcribed by ''gh'' or ''<sup>r</sup>g''; but since in Hebrew the softer sound was the more common, it is sufficient to represent it by the sign ''ʿ'', as {{GHGheb|text=אַרְבַּע|pron=ʾarbaʿ}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַד|pron=ʿad}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|f}}
{{GHGheb|text=ח}} is the strongest guttural sound, a deep guttural ''ch'', as heard generally in Swiss German, somewhat as in the German ''Achat, Macht, Sache, Docht, Zucht'' (not as in ''Licht, Knecht''), and similar to the Spanish ''j''. Like {{GHGheb|text=ע}} it was, however, pronounced in many words feebly, in others strongly.

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|g}}
As regards {{GHGheb|text=ר}}, its pronunciation as a palatal (with a vibrating uvula) seems to have been the prevailing one. Hence in some respects it is also classed with the gutturals ({{GHGpar|22|q}}, r). On the ''lingual'' {{GHGheb|text=ר}}, cf. {{GHGpar|6|o|nonumber=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|h}}
2. The Hebrew language is unusually rich in sibilants. These have, at any rate in some cases, arisen from dentals which are retained as such in Aramaic and Arabic (see in the {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|Lexicon|A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament, based on the Thesaurus and Lexicon of Gesenius, by F. Brown, S. R. Driver, and C. A. Briggs, Oxford, 1906.}}}} the letters {{GHGheb|text=ז}}, {{GHGheb|text=צ}} and {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|i}}
{{GHGheb|text=שׁ}} and {{GHGheb|text=שׂ}} were originally represented (as is still the case in the unpointed texts) by only ''one'' form {{GHGheb|text=ש}}; but that the use of this one form to express two different sounds (at least in Hebrew) was due only to the poverty of the alphabet, is clear from the fact that they are differentiated in Arabic and Ethiopic (cf. Nöldeke in ''Ztschr. f. wissensch. Theol.'', 1873, p. 121; Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, i. 133). In the Masoretic punctuation they were distinguished by means of the diacritical point as {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}} (''sh'') and {{GHGheb|text=שׂ}} (''ś'').<ref>The modern Samaritans, however, in reading their Hebrew Pentateuch pronounce {{GHGheb|text=שׂ}} invariably as {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}}.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|k}}
The original difference between the sounds {{GHGheb|text=שׂ}} and {{GHGheb|text=ס}}<ref>The original value of {{GHGheb|text=ס}}, and its relation to the original value of {{GHGheb|text=שׂ}} and {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}}, is still undetermined, despite the valuable investigations of P. Haupt, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1880, p. 762 f.; D. H. Müller, ‘Zur Geschichte der semit. Zischlaute,’ in the ''Verhandlungen des Wiener Orient. Congresses'', Vienna, 1888, Semitic section, p. 229 ff.; De Lagarde, ‘Samech,’ in the ''NGGW.'' 1891, no. 5, esp. p. 173; Aug. Müller, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1891, p. 267 ff.; Nöldeke, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1893, p. 100 f.; E. Glaser, ''Zwei Wiener Publicationen über Habaschitisch-punische Dialekte in Südarabien'', Munich, 1902, pp. 19 ff.—On the phonetic value of {{GHGheb|text=צ‍}} see G. Hüsing, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|OLZ.|Orientalistische Literaturzeitung. Vienna, 1898 if.}}}} 1907, p. 467 ff.</ref> sometimes marks a distinction in meaning, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=סָכַר|translate=to close}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָׂכַר|translate=to hire}}, {{GHGheb|text=סָכַל|translate=to be foolish}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָׂכַל|translate=to be prudent, to be wise}}. Syriac always represents both sounds by {{GHGheb|text=ס}}, and in Hebrew also they are sometimes interchanged; as {{GHGheb|text=סָכַר}} for {{GHGheb|text=שָׂכַר|translate=to hire}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=4|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=שִׂכְלוּת}} for {{GHGheb|text=סִכְלוּת|translate=folly}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=1|verse=17}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|l}}
{{GHGheb|text=ז}} (transcribed {{polytonic|ζ}} by the LXX) is a soft whizzing ''s'', the French and English ''z'', altogether different from the German ''z'' (''ts'').

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|m}}
3. {{GHGheb|text=ט}}, {{GHGheb|text=ק‍}}, and probably {{GHGheb|text=צ}} are pronounced with a strong articulation and with a compression of the larynx. The first two are thus essentially different from {{GHGheb|text=ת}} and {{GHGheb|text=ך}}, which correspond to our ''t'' and ''k'' and also are often aspirated (see below, {{GHGpar|6|n|nonumber=1}}). {{GHGheb|text=צ}} is distinguished from every other ''s'' by its peculiar articulation, and in no way corresponds to the German ''z'' or ''ts''; we transcribe it by ''ṣ''; cf. G. Hüsing, ‘Zum Lautwerte des {{GHGheb|text=צ}},’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|OLZ.|Orientalistische Literaturzeitung. Vienna, 1898 if.}}}} x. 467 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|n}}
'''3'''. Six consonants, the weak and middle hard Palatals, Dentals, and Labials

{{center|{{GHGheb|text=ב ג ד כ‍ פ ת}} {{GHGheb|text=(בְּגַדְכְּפַת)}}}}

have a twofold pronunciation, (1) a harder sound, as mutes, like<section end="par6" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

58.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TomyDuby" /></noinclude><section begin="par6" />''k'', ''p'', ''t'', or initial ''b'', ''g'' (hard), ''d''; and (2) a softer sound as ''spirantes''.<ref>So at any rate at the time when the present punctuation arose.</ref> The harder sound is the original. It is retained at the beginning of syllables, when there is no vowel immediately preceding to influence the pronunciation, and is denoted by a point, {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}} ({{GHGpar|13}}), placed in the consonants, viz. {{GHGheb|text=בּ|translate=b}}, {{GHGheb|text=גּ|pron=g}}, {{GHGheb|text=דּ|pron=d}}, {{GHGheb|text=כּ‍|pron=k}}, {{GHGheb|text=פּ|pron=p}}, {{GHGheb|text=תּ|pron=t}}. The weaker pronunciation appears as soon as a vowel sound immediately precedes. It is occasionally denoted, esp. in mss., by {{GHGterm|Rāphè}} ({{GHGpar|14|e}}), but in printed texts usually by the mere absence of the {{GHGterm|Dageš}}. In the case of {{GHGheb|text=ב}}, {{GHGheb|text=כ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=פ}}, {{GHGheb|text=ת}}, the two sounds are clearly distinguishable even to our ear as ''b'' and ''v'', ''k'' and German (weak) ''ch'', ''p'' and ''ph'', ''t'' and ''th'' (in ''thin''). The Greeks too express this twofold pronunciation by special characters: {{GHGheb|text=כּ}} {{polytonic|κ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כ‍}} {{polytonic|χ}}; {{GHGheb|text=פּ}} {{polytonic|π}}, {{GHGheb|text=פ}} {{polytonic|φ}}; {{GHGheb|text=תּ}} {{polytonic|τ}}, {{GHGheb|text=ת}} {{polytonic|θ}}. In the same way {{GHGheb|text=ג}} should be pronounced like the North German ''g'' in ''Tage'', ''Wagen'', and {{GHGheb|text=ד}} like ''th'' in ''the'', as distinguished from {{GHGheb|text=גּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=דּ}}.

For more precise information on the cases in which the one or the other pronunciation takes place, see {{GHGpar|21}}. The modern Jews pronounce the aspirated {{GHGheb|text=ב}} as ''v'', the aspirated {{GHGheb|text=ת}} as ''s'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רַב|pron=rav}} (or even ''raf''), {{GHGheb|text=בַּיִת|pron=bais}}. The customary transcription (used also in this Grammar) of the spirants {{GHGheb|text=ב}}, {{GHGheb|text=כ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=ת}} by ''bh'', ''kh'', ''th'' is only an unsatisfactory makeshift, since it may lead (esp. in the case of ''bh'' and ''kh'') to an erroneous conception of the sounds as real aspirates, ''b–h'', ''k–h''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|o}}
'''4.''' According to their special character the consonants are divided into—

|

| {{GHGheb|text=א ה ע ח}};
|

|

| {{GHGheb|text=ג כ‍ ק}};
|

| {{GHGheb|text=ד ט ת}};
|

| {{GHGheb|text=ב פ}};
|

In the case of {{GHGheb|text=ר}} its hardest pronunciation as a ''palatal'' (see above, {{GHGpar|6|g|nonumber=1}}, end) is to be distinguished from its more unusual sound as a lingual, pronounced in the front of the mouth.

On the twofold pronunciation of ''r'' in Tiberias, cf. Delitzsch, ''Physiol. und Musik'', Lpz. 1868, p. 10 ff.; Baer and Struck, ''Dikduke ha-t<sup>e</sup>amim'', Lpz. 1879, p. 5, note ''a'', and § 7 of the Hebrew text, as well as p. 82.

{{GHGmargin-letter|6|p}}
In accordance with E. Sievers, {{GHGcite|title=Metrische Studien}}, i. 14, the following scheme of the Hebrew phonetic system is substituted for the table formerly given in this grammar:—

i. Throat sounds (Gutturals): {{GHGheb|text=ח ע ה א}}.

<references/></noinclude>

59.text:
