Sibilants: | {{center|...}} | {{center|{{GHGheb|text=ז}}}} | {{center|{{GHGheb|text=שׁ שׂ ס}}}} | {{center|{{GHGheb|text=צ‍}}}} | | |- | 3. Sonants: | {{center|...}} | {{center|{{GHGheb|text=ו י}}}} | {{center|{{GHGheb|text=ר ל}}}} | {{center|{{GHGheb|text=נ‍ מ‍}}}} | | |}
{{GHGmargin-letter|6|q}} Rem. 1. The meaning of the letters at the top is, w. = weak, m. = middle hard, e. = emphatic. Consonants which are produced by the same organ of speech are called ''homorganic'' (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=ג}} and {{GHGheb|text=כ‍}} as palatals), consonants whose sound is of the same nature ''homogeneous'' (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=י}} as semi-vowels). On their homorganic character and homogeneity depends the possibility of interchange, whether within Hebrew itself or with the kindred dialects. In such cases the soft sound generally interchanges with the soft, the hard with the hard, &c. (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=ד}} = {{GHGheb|text=ז}}, {{GHGheb|text=ת}} = {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}}, {{GHGheb|text=ט}} = {{GHGheb|text=צ‍}}). Further transitions are not, however, excluded, as e.g. the interchange of {{GHGheb|text=ת}} and {{GHGheb|text=ק}} ({{GHGheb|text=ת}} = {{GHGheb|text=כ}} = {{GHGheb|text=ק}}). Here it is of importance to observe whether the change takes place in an initial, medial, or final letter; since e.g. the change in a letter when medial does not always prove the possibility of the change when initial. That in certain cases the character of the consonantal sound also influences the preceding or following vowel will be noticed in the accidence as the instances occur. {{GHGmargin-letter|6|r}} Rem. 2. Very probably in course of time certain nicer distinctions of pronunciation became more and more neglected and finally were lost. Thus e.g. the stronger {{GHGheb|text=ע}} ''rg'', which was known to the LXX (see above, {{GHGpar|6|e|nonumber=1}}), became in many cases altogether lost to the later Jews; by the Samaritans and Galileans {{GHGheb|text=ע}} and {{GHGheb|text=ח}} were pronounced merely as {{GHGheb|text=א}}, and so in Ethiopic, {{GHGheb|text=ע}} like {{GHGheb|text=א}}, {{GHGheb|text=ח}} like ''h'', {{GHGheb|text=ש}} like ''s''. {{GHGmargin-letter|6|s}} Rem. 3. The consonants which it is usual to describe especially as ''weak'', are those which readily coalesce with a preceding vowel to form a long vowel, viz. {{GHGheb|text=א}}, {{GHGheb|text=ו}}, {{GHGheb|text=י}} (as to {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, cf. {{GHGpar|23|k}}), or those which are most frequently affected by the changes described in {{GHGpar|19|b}}–l, as again {{GHGheb|text=א}}, {{GHGheb|text=ו}}, {{GHGheb|text=י}}, and {{GHGheb|text=ן}}, and in certain cases {{GHGheb|text=ה}} and {{GHGheb|text=ל}}; finally the gutturals and {{GHGheb|text=ר}} for the reason given in {{GHGpar|22|b}} and {{GHGpar|22|q|nonumber=1}}.
{{GHGpar-heading|7|The Vowels in General, Vowel Letters and Vowel Signs}} {{GHGmargin-letter|7|a}} '''1.''' The original vowels in Hebrew, as in the other Semitic tongues, are ''a'', ''i'', ''u''. ''E'' and ''o'' always arise from an obscuring or contraction of these three pure sounds, viz. ''ĕ'' by modification from ''ĭ'' or ''ă''; short ''ŏ'' from ''ŭ''; ''ê'' by contraction from ''ai'' (properly ''ay''); and ''ô'' sometimes by modification (obscuring) from ''â'', sometimes by contraction from ''au'' (properly ''aw'').In proper names the LXX often use the diphthongs {{polytonic|αἰ}} and {{polytonic|αὐ}} where the Hebrew form has ''ê'' or ''ô''. It is, however, very doubtful whether the αἰ and αὐ of the LXX really represent the true pronunciation of Hebrew of that time; see the instructive statistics given by Kittel in Haupt’s {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|SBOT.|Sacred Books of the Old Testament, ed. by P. Haupt. Lpz. and Baltimore, 1893 ff.}}}}, on {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=1|verse=2}}, 20. In Arabic writing there are vowel signs only for ''a'', ''i'', ''u''; the combined sounds ''ay'' and ''aw'' are therefore retained uncontracted and pronounced as diphthongs (''ai'' and ''au''), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹט}} Arab. ''sauṭ'', and {{GHGheb|text=עֵינַ֫יִם}} Arab. ''‛ainain''. It was

60.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TomyDuby" /></noinclude><section begin="par7" />only in later Arabic that they became in pronunciation ''ê'' and ''ô'', at least after weaker or softer consonants; cf. {{GHGheb|text=בֵּין}} Arab. ''bain, bên'', {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם}} Arab. ''yaum, yôm''. The same contraction appears also in other languages, e.g. in Greek and Latin ({{polytonic|θαῦμα}}, Ionic {{polytonic|θῶμα}}; ''plaustrum = polostrum''), in the French pronunciation of ''ai'' and ''au'', and likewise in the German popular dialects (''Oge'' for ''Auge'', &c.). Similarly, the obscuring of the vowels plays a part in various languages (cf. e.g. the ''a'' in modern Persian, Swedish, English, &c.).<ref>In Sanskrit, in the Old Persian cuneiform, and in Ethiopic, short ''a'' alone of all the vowels is not represented, but the consonant by itself is pronounced with short ''a''.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|7|b}}
'''2.''' The partial expression of the vowels by certain consonants ({{GHGheb|text=ה}}, {{GHGheb|text=ו}}, {{GHGheb|text=י}}; {{GHGheb|text=א}}), which sufficed during the lifetime of the language, and for a still longer period afterwards (cf. {{GHGpar|1|k}}), must in the main have passed through the following stages<ref>Cf. especially Stade, ''Lehrb. der hebr. Gr.'', p. 34 ff.</ref>:—

(''a'') The need of a written indication of the vowel first made itself felt in cases where, after the rejection of a consonant, or of an entire syllable, a long vowel formed the final sound of the word. The first step in such a case was to retain the original final consonant, at least as a vowel letter, i.e. merely as an indication of a final vowel. In point of fact we find even in the Old Testament, as already in the ''Mêšaʿ'' inscription, a {{GHGheb|text=ה}} employed in this way (see below) as an indication of a final ''o''. From this it was only a step to the employment of the same consonant to indicate also other vowels when final (thus, e.g. in the inflection of the verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}, the vowels ''ā'',<ref>According to Stade, the employment of {{GHGheb|text=ה}} for ''ā'' probably took place first in the case of the locative accusatives which originally ended in {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}, as {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫רְצָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָדִ֫ימָה}}.</ref> ''ē'', ''è''). After the employment of {{GHGheb|text=ו}} as a vowel letter for ''ô'' and ''û'', and of {{GHGheb|text=י}} for ''ê'' and ''î'', had been established (see below, e) these consonants were also employed—although not consistently—for the same vowels at the end of a word.

{{GHGmargin-letter|7|c}}
According to {{GHGpar|91|b}} and d, the suffix of the 3rd sing. masc. in the noun (as in the verb) was originally pronounced {{GHGheb|text=הוּ}}. But in the places where this {{GHGheb|text=הוּ}} with a preceding ''a'' is contracted into ''ô'' (after the rejection of the {{GHGheb|text=ה}}), we find the {{GHGheb|text=ה}} still frequently retained as a vowel letter, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עִירֹה}}, {{GHGheb|text=סוּתֹה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=11}}, cf. {{GHGpar|91|e}}; so throughout the Mêšaʿ inscription {{GHGheb|text=אַרְצֹה}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֵּיתֹה}} (also {{GHGheb|text=בֵּתֹה}}), {{GHGheb|text=בְּנֹה}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֹּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֹה}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִלְתַּֽחֲמֹה}}; on the other hand already in the Siloam inscription {{GHGheb|text=רֵעוֹ}}.<ref>The form {{GHGheb|text=רעו}} contradicts the view of Oort, ''Theol. Tijds.'', 1902, p. 374, that the above instances from the Mêšaʿ-inscription are to be read ''benhu, bahu, lahu'', which were afterwards vocalized as ''beno, bo, lo''.</ref> {{GHGheb|text=ימה}} Mêšaʿ, l. 8 = {{GHGheb|text=יָמָיו|translate=his days}} is unusual, as also {{GHGheb|text=רשה}} l. 20 if it is for {{GHGheb|text=ראשיו|translate=his chiefs}}. The verbal forms with {{GHGheb|text=ה}} suffixed are to be read {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּחְלְפֵהֻ}} (l. 6), {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֶסְחָבֵהֻ}} (l. 12f.) and {{GHGheb|text=וַיְגָֽרְשֵׁהֻ}} (l. 19).

{{GHGmargin-letter|7|d}}
As an example of the original consonant being retained, we might also include the {{GHGheb|text=י}} of the constr. state plur. masc. if its ''ê'' (according to {{GHGpar|89|d}}) is<section end="par7" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

61.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TomyDuby" /></noinclude><section begin="par7" />contracted from an original ''ay''. Against this, however, it may be urged that the Phoenician inscriptions do not usually express this ''ê'', nor any other final vowel.<ref>Thus there occurs, e.g. in Melit. 1, l. 3 {{GHGheb|text=שנבן}} = {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי בְנֵי|translate=the two sons}}; elsewhere {{GHGheb|text=כ‍}} for {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} (but {{GHGheb|text=כי}} in the Mêšaʿ) and Siloam inscrr.), {{GHGheb|text=ז}} for {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}} (the latter in the Siloam inscr.), {{GHGheb|text=בנת}} = {{GHGheb|text=בָּנִתִי}} (so Mêšaʿ) or {{GHGheb|text=בָּנִיתִי}}, &c. Cf. on the other hand in Mêšaʿ, {{GHGheb|text=אנכ‍}} = {{GHGheb|text=אנכי}} (unless it was actually pronounced ''ʾanôkh'' by the Moabites!). As final ''ā'' is represented by {{GHGheb|text=ה}} and {{GHGheb|text=א}} and final ''î'' by {{GHGheb|text=י}}, so final ''û'' is almost everywhere expressed by {{GHGheb|text=ו}} in Mêšaʿ, and always in the Siloam inscription. It is indeed not impossible that Hebrew orthography also once passed through a period in which the final vowels were left always or sometimes undenoted, and that not a few strange forms in the present text of the Bible are to be explained from the fact that subsequently the vowel letters (especially {{GHGheb|text=ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=י}}) were not added in all cases. So Chwolson, ‘Die Quiescentia {{GHGheb|text=הוי}} in der althebr. Orthogr.,’ in ''Travaux du Congrès... des Orientalistes'', Petersb. 1876; cf. numerous instances in Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, p. 146 ff.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|7|e}}
(''b'') The employment of {{GHGheb|text=ו}} to denote ''ô'', ''û'', and of {{GHGheb|text=י}} to denote ''ê'', ''î'', may have resulted from those cases in which a {{GHGheb|text=ו}} with a preceding ''a'' was contracted into ''au'' and further to ''ô'', or with a preceding ''u'' coalesced into ''û'', and where {{GHGheb|text=י}} with ''a'' has been contracted into ''ai'' and further to ''ê'', or with a preceding ''i'' into ''î'' (cf. § 24). In this case the previously existing consonants were retained as vowel letters and were further applied at the end of the word to denote the respective long vowels. Finally {{GHGheb|text=א}} also will in the first instance have established itself as a vowel letter only where a consonantal {{GHGheb|text=א}} with a preceding ''a'' had coalesced into ''â'' or ''ā''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|7|f}}
The orthography of the Siloam inscription corresponds almost exactly with the above assumptions. Here (as in the Mêšaʿ inscr.) we find all the long vowels, which have not arisen from original diphthongs, ''without'' vowel letters, thus {{GHGheb|text=אִשׁ}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֹצְבִם}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִימִן}} (or {{GHGheb|text=מִיָּמִן}}); {{GHGheb|text=אַמֹּת}}, {{GHGheb|text=קֹל}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשׁ}}, {{GHGheb|text=צֻר}}. On the other hand {{GHGheb|text=מוֹצָא}} (from ''mauṣaʾ''), {{GHGheb|text=עוֹד}} (from ''ʿaud''); {{GHGheb|text=מימן}} also, if it is to be read {{GHGheb|text=מִימִן}}, is an instance of the retention of a {{GHGheb|text=י}} which has coalesced with ''i'' into ''î''. Instances of the retention of an originally consonantal {{GHGheb|text=א}} as a vowel letter are {{GHGheb|text=מָאתַ֫יִם}}, {{GHGheb|text=מוֹצָא}}, and {{GHGheb|text=קָרָא}}, as also {{GHGheb|text=רֹאשׁ}}. Otherwise final ''ā'' is always represented by {{GHGheb|text=ה}}: {{GHGheb|text=אַמָּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=זרה}}, {{GHGheb|text=נקבה}}. To this {{GHGheb|text=יֹם}} alone would form an exception (cf. however the note on {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם}}, § 96), instead of {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם}} (Arab. ''yaum'') ''day'', which one would expect. If the reading be correct, this is to be regarded as an argument that a consciousness of the origin of many long vowels was lost at an early period, so that (at least in the middle of the word) the vowel letters were omitted in places where they should stand, according to what has been stated above, and added where there was no case of contraction. This view is in a great measure confirmed by the orthography of the Mêšaʿ inscription. There we find, as might be expected, {{GHGheb|text=דיבן}} (= ''Daibōn'', as the Δαιβών of the LXX proves), {{GHGheb|text=חוֹרֹנָן}} (''ô'' from ''au''), and {{GHGheb|text=בֵּיתֹה}} (''ê'' from ''ai''), but also even {{GHGheb|text=הֽשִׁעַנִי}}<ref>{{GHGheb|text=השעני}} is the more strange since the name of king {{GHGheb|text=הוֹשֵׁעָ}} is represented as ''A-u siʾ'' in cuneiform as late as 728 {{smaller|B.C.}}</ref> instead of {{GHGheb|text=הֽוֹשִׁעַנִי}} (from ''hauš-''), {{GHGheb|text=ואשב}} = {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאוֹשִׁיב}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֵּת}} four times, {{GHGheb|text=בֵּתֹה}} once, for {{GHGheb|text=בֵּית}} and {{GHGheb|text=בֵּיתֹה}} (from ''bait''); {{GHGheb|text=ללה}} = {{GHGheb|text=לַיְלָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=אן}} = {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִן}} or {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}}.

62.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par7" />{{GHGmargin-letter|7|g}}
(''c'') In the present state of Old Testament vocalization as it appears in the Masoretic text, the striving after a certain uniformity cannot be mistaken, in spite of the inconsistencies which have crept in. Thus the final long vowel is, with very few exceptions (cf. {{GHGpar|9|d}}, and the very doubtful cases in {{GHGpar|8|k}}), indicated by a vowel letter—and almost always by the same letter in certain nominal and verbal endings. In many cases the use of {{GHGheb|text=ו}} to mark an ''ô'' or ''û'', arising from contraction, and of {{GHGheb|text=י}} for ''ê'' or ''î'', is by far the more common, while we seldom find an originally consonantal {{GHGheb|text=א}} rejected, and the simple phonetic principle taking the place of the historical orthography. On the other hand the number of exceptions is very great. In many cases (as e.g. in the plural endings {{GHGheb|text=־ִים}} and {{GHGheb|text=וֹת}}) the vowel letters are habitually employed to express long vowels which do not arise through contraction, and we even find short vowels indicated. The conclusion is, that if there ever was a period of Hebrew writing when the application of fixed laws to all cases was intended, either these laws were not consistently carried out in the further transmission of the text, or errors and confusion afterwards crept into it. Moreover much remained uncertain even in texts which were plentifully provided with vowel letters. For, although in most cases the context was a guide to the correct reading, yet there were also cases where, of the many possible ways of pronouncing a word, more than one appeared admissible.<ref>Thus e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קטל}} can be read ''qāṭal, qāṭāl, qāṭôl, q<sup>e</sup>ṭōl, qôṭēl, qiṭṭēl, qaṭṭēl, quṭṭal, qèṭel'', and several of these forms have also different senses.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|7|h}}
'''3.''' When the language had died out, the ambiguity of such a writing must have been found continually more troublesome; and as there was thus a danger that the correct pronunciation might be finally lost, the vowel signs or vowel points were invented in order to fix it. By means of these points everything hitherto left uncertain was most accurately settled. It is true that there is no historical account of the date of this vocalization of the O.T. text, yet we may at least infer, from a comparison of other historical facts, that it was gradually developed by Jewish grammarians in the sixth and seventh centuries {{smaller|A.D.}} under the influence of different Schools, traces of which have been preserved to the present time in various differences of tradition.<ref>The most important of these differences are, (''a'') those between the Orientals, i.e. the scholars of the Babylonian Schools, and the Occidentals, i.e. the scholars of Palestine (Tiberias, &c.); cf. Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, p. 197 ff.; (''b'') amongst the Occidentals, between Ben-Naphtali and Ben-Asher, who flourished in the first half of the tenth century at Tiberias; cf. Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, p. 241 ff. Both sets of variants are given by Baer in the appendices to his critical editions. Our printed editions present uniformly the text of Ben-Asher, with the exception of a few isolated readings of Ben-Naphtali, and of numerous later corruptions.</ref> They mainly followed, though with independent regard to<section end="par7" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

{{GHGmargin-letter|7|i}} '''4.''' To complete the historical vocalization of the consonantal text a phonetic system was devised, so exact as to show all vowel-changes occasioned by lengthening of words, by the tone, by gutturals, &c., which in other languages are seldom indicated in writing. The pronunciation followed is in the main that of the Palestinian Jews of about the sixth century {{smaller|A.D.}}, as observed in the solemn reading of the sacred writings in synagogue and school, but based on a much older tradition. That the real pronunciation of early Hebrew is consistently preserved by this tradition, has recently been seriously questioned on good grounds, especially in view of the transcription of proper names in the LXX. Nevertheless in many cases, internal reasons, as well as the analogy of the kindred languages, testify in a high degree to the faithfulness of the tradition. At the same recension of the text, or soon after, the various other signs for reading ({{GHGpar|11|doublesign=1}}–{{GHGpar|14|nosign=1}}, {{GHGpar|16|nosign=1}}) were added, and the accents ({{GHGpar|15}}).

64.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par8" />{{center|Preliminary Remark.}}

The next two sections (§§ 8 and 9) have been severely criticized (Philippi, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ThLZ.|Theologische Literaturzeitung, ed. by E. Schürer. Lpz. 1876 ff.}}}} 1897, no. 2) for assigning a definite quantity to each of the several vowels, whereas in reality {{GHGheb|text=־ֶ}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ׄ}} are merely signs for ''ä'', ''e'', ''o'': ‘whether these are long or short is not shown by the signs themselves but must be inferred from the rules for the pause which marks the breaks in continuous narrative, or from other circumstances.’ But in the twenty-fourth and subsequent German editions of this Grammar, in the last note on {{GHGpar|8|a}} [English ed. p. 38, note 4], it was stated: ‘it must be mentioned that the Masoretes are not concerned with any distinction between long and short vowels, or in general with any question of quantity. Their efforts are directed to fixing the received pronunciation as faithfully as possible, by means of writing. For a long time only {{GHGheb|text=שִבְעָה מְלָכִים|translate=seven kings}} were reckoned (''vox memor.'' in Elias Levita {{GHGheb|text=וַיּאֹמֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ}}), Šureq and Qibbuṣ being counted as one vowel. The division of the vowels in respect of quantity is a later attempt at a scientific conception of the phonetic system, which was not invented but only represented by the Masoretes (Qimchi; {{GHGcite|title=Mikhlol}}, ed. Rittenb. 136 ''a'', distinguishes the five long as ''mothers'' from their five daughters).’

I have therefore long shared the opinion that ‘the vowel-system represented by the ordinary punctuation (of Tiberias) was primarily intended to mark only differences of quality’ (Sievers, {{GHGcite|title=Metrische Studien}}, i. 17). There is, however, of course a further question how far these ‘later’ grammarians were mistaken in assigning a particular quantity to the vowels represented by particular signs. In Philippi’s opinion they were mistaken (excluding of course ''î'', ''ê'', ''ô'' when written {{GHGterm|plene}}) in a very great number of cases, since not only does {{GHGheb|text=־ָ}} stand, according to circumstances, for ''{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-macr}}'' or ''{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-brev}}'', and {{GHGheb|text=־ֶ}} for ''{{GHGtranslit|a-dier-macr}}'' or ''{{GHGtranslit|a-dier-brev}}'', but also {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ}} for ''ē'' or ''ĕ'', and {{GHGheb|text=־ׄ}} for ''ō'' or ''ŏ'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כָּבֵד}} and {{GHGheb|text=קָטֹן}}, out of pause ''k{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-macr}}bĕ́d'', ''q{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-macr}}ṭŏ́n'' (form {{GHGheb|text=קָטַל}}), but in pause ''k{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-macr}}bḗd'', ''q{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-macr}}ṭṓn''.

I readily admit, with regard to {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} and ''S<sup>e</sup>gol'', that the account formerly given in {{GHGpar|8|f}}. was open to misconstruction. With regard to {{GHGterm|Ṣere}} and {{GHGterm|Ḥolem}}, however, I can only follow Philippi so long as his view does not conflict with the (to me inviolable) law of a long vowel in an open syllable before the tone and (except Pathaḥ) in a final syllable with the tone. To me {{GHGheb|text=כָּבֵד}} = ''k{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-macr}}bĕ́d'', &c., is as impossible as e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עֵנָב}} = ''ʿĕnab'' or {{GHGheb|text=בֹּרַךְ}} = ''bŏrakh'', in spite of the analogy cited by Sievers (p. 18, note 1) that ‘in old German e.g. original ''ĭ'' and ''ŭ'' often pass into ''ĕ'' and ''ŏ'' dialectically, while remaining in a closed syllable.

{{GHGmargin-letter|8|a}}

For {{GHGterm|Qameṣ ḥaṭuph}}, in the previous German edition expressed by ''{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-brev}}'', we have, after careful consideration, returned to ''ŏ'' The use of the same sign {{GHGheb|text=־ָ}} for ''{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-macr}}'' (''{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-circ}}'') and ''{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-brev}}'', shows that the Massoretes did not intend to draw a sharp distinction between them. We must not, however, regard the Jewish grammarians as making a merely idle distinction between {{GHGterm|Qāmeṣ rāḥāb}}, or broad Qameṣ, and ''Qāmeṣ hatûph'', or light Qameṣ. It is quite impossible that in the living language an ''ā'' lengthened from ''ă'', as in ''dābār'', should have been indistinguishable from e.g. the last vowel in {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּשָׁב}} or the first in {{GHGheb|text=קָֽדָשִׁים}}.—The notation ''â, ê, ô'' expresses here the vowels essentially long, either naturally or by contraction; the notation ''ā, ē, ō'' those lengthened only by the tone, and therefore changeable; ''ă, ĕ, ŏ'' the short vowels. 65.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par8" />Also 3. {{GHGheb|text=־ֶ}} {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>gôl}}, an open ''e'', ''è'' (''{{GHGtranslit|a-dier-macr}}'' or ''{{GHGtranslit|a-dier-brev}}''), as a modification of ''ă'',<ref>These ''S<sup>e</sup>gôls'', modified from ''ă'', are very frequent in the language. The Babylonian punctuation (see {{GHGpar|8|g}}, note 3) has only one sign for it and tone-bearing Pathah.; see also Gaster, ‘''Die Unterschiedslosigkeit zwischen Pathach u. Segol,''’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1894, p. 60 ff.</ref> either in an untoned closed syllable, as in the first syllable of {{GHGheb|text=יֶדְכֶם|pron=yädkhèm}} (your hand) from ''yădkhèm''—or in a tone-syllable as in {{GHGheb|text=פֶּ֫סַח|pron=pĕsaḥ}}; cf. {{GHGtranslate|πάσχα|lang=grc|en=Passover, Pesakh}}, and on the really monosyllabic character of such formations, see {{GHGpar|28|e}}. But {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>gôl}} in an open tone-syllable with a following {{GHGheb|text=י}}, as in {{GHGheb|text=גְּלֶ֫ינָה|pron=g<sup>e</sup>lènā}} (cf. {{GHGpar|75|f}}), {{GHGheb|text=יָדֶ֫יךָ|pron=yādèkhā}} (cf. {{GHGpar|91|i}}), is due to contraction from ''ay''.

{{center|''Second Class. I- and E-sounds.''}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|8|b}}
{| align="center"
| ''I''
| 1. {{GHGheb|text=־ִי|translate=Ḥîrĕq}} with ''yod'', almost always ''î'', as {{GHGheb|text=צַדִּיק|translate=ṣaddîq}} (righteous).

2. {{GHGheb|text=־ִ}} either ''î'' (see below, {{GHGpar|8|i|nonumber=1}}), as {{GHGheb|text=צַדִּקִים|translate=ṣaddîqîm}}, only orthographically different from {{GHGheb|text=צדיקים}} ({{GHGheb|text=צדיקם}}),—or ''ĭ'', as {{GHGheb|text=צִדְקוֹ|pron=ṣĭdqô}} (his righteousness).
|-
| ''E''
| 3. {{GHGheb|text=־ֵי|pron=Ṣerî}} or {{GHGterm|Ṣērê}} with ''yod=ê'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בֵּיתוֹ|pron=bêthô}} (his house).

{{GHGheb|text=־ֵ}} either ''ê'', but rarely (see below, {{GHGpar|8|i|nonumber=1}}), or ''ē'' as {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁם|pron=šēm}} (name).

{{GHGterm|Ṣere}} can only be ''ĕ'', in my opinion, in few cases, such as those mentioned in {{GHGpar|29|f}}.

4. {{GHGheb|text=־ֶ}} {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>gôl}}, ''{{GHGtranslit|a-dier-brev}}'', a modification of ''ĭ'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=חֶפְצִי|pron=ḥäfṣî}} (ground-form ''ḥĭfṣ''); {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁן־|pron=šän}} (ground-form ''šĭn'').
|}

{{center|''Third Class. U- and O-sounds.''}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|8|c}}
{| align="center"
| ''U''
| 1. {{GHGheb|text=וּ|translate=Šûrĕq}}, usually ''û'', {{GHGheb|text=מוּת|pron=mûth}} (to die), rarely ''ŭ''.

2. {{GHGheb|text=־ֻ|translate=Qibbûṣ}}, either ''ŭ'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=סֻלָּם|pron=sŭllām}} (ladder): or ''û'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קֻ֫מוּ|pron=qūmū}} (rise up), instead of the usual {{GHGheb|text=ק֫וּמוּ}}.
|-
| ''O''
| 3. {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} and {{GHGheb|text=־ֹ|pron=Ḥōlĕm, ô}} and ''ō'', {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל|pron=qôl}} (voice), {{GHGheb|text=רֹב|pron=rōbh}} (multitude). Often also a defective {{GHGheb|text=־ֹ}} for ''ô''; rarely {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} for ''ō''.

On the question whether {{GHGheb|text=־ֹ}} under some circumstances represents ''ŏ'', see {{GHGpar|93|r}}.

4. {{GHGheb|text=־ָ}} On ''Qāmĕṣ ḥāṭûph=ŏ'', generally modified from ''ŭ'', as {{GHGheb|text=חָק־|pron=ḥŏq}} (statute), see above, {{GHGpar|8|a|nonumber=1}}.
|}
<section end="par8" /><noinclude>

66.text:
{{GHGcorrected}}
{{GHGmargin-letter|8|d}} The names of the vowels are mostly taken from the form and action of the mouth in producing the various sounds, as {{GHGheb|text=פַּ֫תַח|translate=opening}}; {{GHGheb|text=צֵ֫רֵי|translate=a wide parting}} (of the mouth), also {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫בֶר}} (={{GHGpron|ĭ}}) {{GHGtranslate|breaking}}, {{GHGtranslate|parting}} (cf. the Arab, {{GHGpron|kasr}}); {{GHGheb|text=חִ֫ירֶק}} (also {{GHGheb|text=חִרֶק}}) {{GHGtranslate|narrow opening}}; {{GHGheb|text=ח֫וֹלֶם|translate=closing}}, according to others {{GHGtranslate|fullness}}, i.e. of the mouth (also {{GHGheb|text=מְלֹא פּוּם}}On the erroneous use of the term {{GHGpron|melo pum}}, only in Germany, for {{GHGterm|šûreq}} (hence also pronounced {{GHGpron|melu pum}} to indicate {{GHGpron|û}}), see {{nowrap|E. Nestle}}, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1904, p. 597 ff.; Bacher, ibid., p. 799 ff., Melopum; Simonsen, ibid., p. 807 ff. {{GHGtranslate|fullness of the mouth}}). {{GHGheb|text=קָ֫מֶץ}}The usual spelling {{GHGheb|text=קָמֶץ}} and {{GHGheb|text=פַּתַח}} takes the words certainly rightly as Hebrew substantives; according to De Lagarde ({{GHGcite|title=Gött. gel. Anz.}} 1886, p. 873, and so previously Luzzatto), {{GHGheb|text=קָמֵץ}} and {{GHGheb|text=פָתַח}} are rather Aram. participles, like {{GHGterm|Dageš}}, &c., and consequently to be transliterated {{GHGpron|Qâmeṣ}} and {{GHGpron|Pâthaḥ}}. also denotes a slighter, as {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּרֶק}} and {{GHGheb|text=קִבּוּץ}} (also {{GHGheb|text=קבוץ פּוּם}}) a firmer, compression or contraction of the mouth. {{GHGterm|Segôl}} ({{GHGheb|text=סְגוֹל|translate=bunch of grapes}}) takes its name from its form. So {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלֹשׁ נְקֻדּוֹת}} ({{GHGtranslate|three points}}) is another name for Qibbûṣ. {{GHGmargin-letter|8|e}} Moreover the names were mostly so formed (but only later), that the sound of each vowel is heard in the first syllable ({{GHGheb|text=קָמֶץ}} for {{GHGheb|text=קֹמֶץ}}, {{GHGheb|text=פַּתַח}} for {{GHGheb|text=פֶּתַח}}, {{GHGheb|text=צֵרִי}} for {{GHGheb|text=צְרִי}}); in order to carry this out consistently some even write {{GHGpron|Sägôl}}, {{GHGpron|Qomeṣ-ḥatûf}}, {{GHGpron|Qübbûṣ}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|8|f}} '''2.''' As the above examples show, the vowel sign stands regularly ''under'' the consonant, ''after'' which it is to be pronounced, {{GHGheb|text=רָ|pron=rā}}, {{GHGheb|text=רַ|pron=ră}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֵ|pron=rē}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֻ|pron=rŭ}}, &c. The {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} called {{GHGterm|furtivum|en=furtive, stolen}} ({{GHGpar|22|f}}) alone forms an exception to this rule, being pronounced before the consonant, {{GHGheb|text=רוּחַ}} {{GHGpron|rûaḥ}} (wind, spirit). The {{GHGpron|Ḥōlĕm}} (without {{GHGpron|wāw}}) stands on the left above the consonant; {{GHGheb|text=רֹ|pron=rō}} (but {{GHGheb|text=לֹ|pron=lō}}). If {{GHGheb|text=א}}, as a vowel letter, follows a consonant which is to be pronounced with {{GHGpron|ō}}, the point is placed over its right arm, thus {{GHGheb|text=בֹא}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֹאשׁ}}; but e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בֹאָם}}, since {{GHGheb|text=א}} here begins a syllable. {{GHGmargin-letter|8|g}} No dot is used for the Ḥolem when {{GHGpron|ō}} (of course without {{GHGterm|wāw}}) is pronounced after {{GHGpron|śîn}} or before {{GHGpron|šîn}}. Hence {{GHGheb|text=שׂנֵא|translate=śônē}} (hating), {{GHGheb|text=נְשׂא|pron=neśō}} (to bear), {{GHGheb|text=משֶׁה|translate=môšè}} (not {{GHGheb|text=מֹשֶׁה}}); but {{GHGheb|text=שֹׁמֵר|translate=šômēr}} (a watchman). When {{GHGpron|ō}} precedes the {{GHGpron|śîn}}, the dot is placed over its right arm, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יִרְפּשֹׁ|translate=yirpōś}} (he treads with the feet), {{GHGheb|text=הַנּֽשְֹׁאִים|pront=hannôśeʾîm}} (those who carry). In the sign {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}}, the {{GHGheb|text=ו}} may also be a consonant. The {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} is then either to be read {{GHGpron|ōw}} (necessarily so when a consonant otherwise without a vowel precedes, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לֹוֶה|translate=lôwè}}, lending) or {{GHGpron|wō}}, when a vowel already precedes the {{GHGheb|text=ו}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עָוֹן|pron=ʿāwôn}} (iniquity) for {{GHGheb|text=עָווֹן}}. In more exact printing, a distinction is at least made between {{GHGheb|text=וֹ|translate=wo}} and {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} (i.e. either {{GHGpron|ô}} or, when another vowel follows the {{GHGterm|wāw}}, {{GHGpron|ôw}}Since 1846 we have become acquainted with a system of vocalization different in many respects from the common method. The vowel signs, all except {{GHGheb|text=וּ}}, are there placed ''above'' the consonants, and differ almost throughout in form, and some even as regards the sound which they denote: {Babylonian â/ā mark} = {{GHGpron|â}}, {{GHGpron|ā}}, {Babylonian ă/è mark} = tone-bearing {{GHGpron|ă}} and {{GHGpron|è}}, {Babylonian ê/ē mark} = {{GHGpron|ê}}, {{GHGpron|ē}}, {Babylonian î mark} = {{GHGpron|î}}, {Babylonian ô/ō mark} = {{GHGpron|ô}}, {{GHGpron|ō}}, {Babylonian û mark} = {{GHGpron|û}}. In an unsharpened syllable {Babylonian toneless ă/è mark} = toneless {{GHGpron|ă}} and {{GHGpron|è}}, and also Ḥaṭeph Pathaḥ; {Babylonian toneless ĕ mark} = toneless {{GHGpron|ĕ}} and Ḥaṭeph Seghôl; {Babylonian ĭ mark} = {{GHGpron|ĭ}}, {Babylonian ŭ mark} = {{GHGpron|ŭ}}, {Babylonian ŏ mark} = {{GHGpron|ŏ}}, and Ḥaṭeph Qameṣ. Lastly in toneless syllables before Dageš, {Babylonian ă mark} = {{GHGpron|ă}}, {Babylonian ĕ mark} = {{GHGpron|ĕ}}, {Babylonian i mark} = {{GHGpron|i}}, {Babylonian ŭ mark} = {{GHGpron|ŭ}}, {Babylonian {{GHGtranslit|a-ring-brev}} mark} = {{GHGpron|{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-brev}}}}. Šewâ is {Babylonian Šewâ mark}. The accents differ less and stand in some cases under the line of the consonants. Besides this complicated system of the Codex Babylonicus (see below) and other MSS., there is a simpler one, used in Targums. It is still uncertain whether the latter is the foundation of the former (as Merx, {{GHGcite|title=Chrest. Targ.}} xi, and Bacher, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1895, p. 15 ff.), or is a later development of it among the Jews of South Arabia (as Praetorius, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1899, p. 181 ff.). For the older literature on this {{GHGterm|Babylonian punctuation}} ({{GHGheb|text=נִקּוּד בַּבְלִי}}), as it is called, see A. Harkavy and H. L. Strack, {{GHGcite|title=Katalog der hebr. Bibelhandschr. der Kaiserl. öffentl. Bibliothek zu St. Petersb.}}, St. Petersb. and Lpz., 1875, parts i and ii, p. 223 ff. A more thorough study of the system was made possible by H. Strack’s facsimile edition of the {{GHGcite|title=Prophetarum posteriorum codex Babylonicus Petropolitanus}} (St. Petersb., 1876, la. fol.) of the year 916, which Firkowitsch discovered in 1839, in the synagogue at Tschufutkale in the Crimea. The MS. has been shown by Ginsburg ({{GHGcite|title=Recueil des travaux rédigés en mémoire... de Chwolson}}, Berlin, 1899, p. 149, and {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, pp. 216 ff., 475 f.) to contain a recension of the Biblical text partly Babylonian and partly Palestinian; cf. also Barnstein, {{GHGcite|title=The Targum of Onkelos to Genesis}}, London, 1896, p. 6 f. Strack edited a fragment of it in {{GHGcite|title=Hosea et Joel prophetae ad fidem cod. Babylon. Petrop.}}, St. Petersb. 1875. Cf. also the publication by A. Merx, quoted above, {{GHGpar|7|h}}, and his {{GHGcite|title=Chrestomathia Targumica}}, Berlin, 1888; G. Margoliouth, in the {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|PSBA.|Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archæology. London, 1879 ff.}}}} xv. 4, and M. Gaster, ibid.; P. Kahle, {{GHGcite|title=Der masoret. Text des A.T. nach d. Überlief. der babyl. Juden}}, Lpz. 1902, with the valuable review by Rahlfs in {{GHGcite|title=GGA}}. 1903, no. 5; Nestle, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1905, p. 719 (Babylonian {Babylonian ă/è mark} = {{GHGheb|text=ע}}. According to the opinion formerly prevailing, this Babylonian punctuation exhibits the system which was developed in the Eastern schools, corresponding to and contemporaneous with the Western or Tiberian system, although a higher degree of originality, or approximation to the original of both systems of punctuation, was generally conceded to the latter. Recently, however, Wickes, {{GHGcite|title=Accents of the Twenty-one Books}}, Oxford, 1887, p. 142 ff, has endeavoured to show, from the accents, that the ‘Babylonian’ punctuation may certainly be ''an'' Oriental, but is by no means ''the'' Oriental system. It is rather to be regarded, according to him, as a later and not altogether successful attempt to modify, and thus to simplify, the system common to all the Schools in the East and West. Strack, {{GHGcite|title=Wiss. Jahresb. der {{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1879, p. 124, established the probability that the vowels of the superlinear punctuation arose under ''Arab'' influence from the vowel letters {{GHGheb|text=יוא}} (so previously Pinsker and Graetz), while the Tiberian system shows ''Syrian'' influence.
A third, widely different system (Palestinian), probably the basis of the other two, is described by A. Neubauer, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|JQR.|Jewish Quarterly Review.}}}} vii. 1895, p. 361 ff., and Friedländer, ibid., p. 564 ff., and {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|PSBA.|Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archæology. London, 1879 ff.}}}} 1896, p. 86 ff.; C. Levias, {{GHGcite|title=Journ. of Sem. Lang. and Lit.}}, xv. p. 157 ff.; and esp. P. Kahle, ‘Beitr. zu der Gesch. der hebr. Punktation,’ and in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1901, p. 273 ff. and in {{GHGcite|title=Der masoret. Text des A.T.}} (see above), chiefly dealing with the Berlin MS. Or. qu. 680, which contains a number of variants on the biblical text, and frequently agrees with the transcriptions of the LXX and Jerome.). {{nop}}

67.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par8" />{{GHGmargin-letter|8|h}}
'''3.''' The vowels of the first class are, with the exception of {{GHGheb|text=־ֶי}} in the middle and {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ָא}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ֶה}} at the end of the word ({{GHGpar|9|a}}–{{GHGpar|9|d|nonumber=1}}, {{GHGpar|9|f|nonumber=1}}), represented ''only'' by vowel signs, but the long vowels of the I- and U-class largely by vowel letters. The vowel sound to which the letter<!-- Most of this page's text appears in the long footnote on the previous page. --><section end="par8" /><noinclude>
<references/>
<!--continuation - Footnote is contained on previous page--></noinclude>

68.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par8" />points is determined more precisely by the vowel sign standing before, above, or within it. Thus—

:{{GHGheb|text=י}} may be combined with {{GHGterm|Ṣērê}}, {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}}, {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>gôl}} ({{GHGheb|text=־ִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ֵי}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ֶי}}).
:{{GHGheb|text=ו}} with {{GHGterm|Šûrĕq}} and ''Ḥōlĕm'' ({{GHGheb|text=וּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}}).<ref>After the example of the Jewish grammarians the expression, ‘the vowel letter rests ({{GHGterm|quiesces}}) in the vowel-sign,’ has become customary. On the other hand, the vowel letters are also called by the grammarians, {{GHGterm|matres lectionres}} or {{GHGterm|supports}} ({{GHGterm|fulcra}}).</ref>

<small>
In Arabic the long {{GHGpron|a}} also is regularly expressed by a vowel letter, viz. {{GHGpron|ʾAlĕph}} ({{GHGheb|text=־ָא}}), so that in that language three vowel letters correspond to the three vowel classes. In Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=א}} is rarely used as a vowel letter; see {{GHGpar|9|b}} and {{GHGpar|23|g}}.
</small>

{{GHGmargin-letter|8|i}}
'''4.''' The omission of the vowel letters when writing {{GHGpron|î}}, {{GHGpron|û}}, {{GHGpron|ê}}, {{GHGpron|ô}} is called {{GHGterm|scriptio defectiva}} in contrast to {{GHGterm|scriptio plena}}. {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל}}, {{GHGheb|text=קוּם}} are written {{GHGterm|plene}}, {{GHGheb|text=קֹלֹת}}, {{GHGheb|text=קֻם}} {{GHGterm|defective}}.

<small>
Cf. Bardowitz, {{GHGcite|title=Studien zur Gesch. der Orthogr. im Althebr.}}, 1894; Lidzbarski, {{GHGcite|title=Ephem.}}, i. 182, 275; Marmorstein, ‘Midrasch der vollen u. defekt. Schreibung,’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1907, p. 33 ff.
</small>

{{GHGmargin-letter|8|k}}
So far as the choice of the full or defective mode of writing is concerned, there are certainly some cases in which only the one or the other is admissible, Thus the full form is necessary at the end of the word, for {{GHGpron|û}}, {{GHGpron|ô}}, {{GHGpron|ō}}, {{GHGpron|î}}, {{GHGpron|ê}}, {{GHGpron|ē}}, as well as for {{GHGpron|è}} in {{GHGheb|text=חֹזֶה}} &c. ({{GHGpar|9|f}}), also generally with {{GHGpron|â}}, {{GHGpron|ā}} (cf. however {{GHGpar|9|d}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קָֽטְלוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫לְתִּי}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָדִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכֵי}}. (But the Masora requires in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=26|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=44|verse=8|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=6|verse=21}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=32|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=גּוֹיֵ}} instead of {{GHGheb|text=גּוֹיֵי}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=2|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=גּוֹיִ}} [perhaps an error due to the following {{GHGheb|text=י}}] for {{GHGheb|text=גּוֹיִי}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=31}} {{GHGheb|text=וְקוֹיֵ}} [followed by {{GHGheb|text=י}}] for {{GHGheb|text=וְקוֹיֵי}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=38|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּלוֹיֵ}} for {{GHGheb|text=בְּלוֹיֵי}}.) On the other hand the defective writing is common when the letter, which would have to be employed as a vowel letter, immediately precedes as a strong consonant, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גּוֹיִם}} (''nations'') for {{GHGheb|text=גּוֹיִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִצְוֹת}} (''commandments'') for {{GHGheb|text=מִצְווֹת}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|8|l}}
{{smaller block/s}}
That much is here arbitrary (see {{GHGpar|7|g}}), follows from the fact that sometimes the same word is written very differently, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הֲקִימוֹתִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=60}}: {{GHGheb|text=הֲקִמֹתִי}} and also {{GHGheb|text=הֲקִמוֹתִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=23|verse=4}}; cf. {{GHGpar|25|b}}. Only it may be observed,

(''a'') That the scriptio plena in two successive syllables was generally avoided; cf. e.g. {{GHGheb|text=נָבִיא}} but {{GHGheb|text=נְבִאִים}}; {{GHGheb|text=צַדִּיק}}, but {{GHGheb|text=צַדִּקִים}}; {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל}}, {{GHGheb|text=קֹלוֹת}}; {{GHGheb|text=יְהוֹשֻׁעַ}}; {{GHGheb|text=מְצָאֻ֫הוּ}}.

(''b'') That in the later Books of the O.T. (and regularly in post-biblical Hebrew) the full form, in the earlier the defective, is more usual.
{{smaller block/e}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|8|m}}
'''5.''' In the cognate dialects, when a vowel precedes a vowel-letter which is not kindred (heterogeneous), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=־ָו}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ֵו}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ִיו}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ַי}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ָי}}, a diphthong ({{GHGpron|au}}, {{GHGpron|ai}})<ref>Cf. T. C. Foote, {{GHGcite|title=The diphthong ''ai'' in Hebrew}} (Johns Hopkins Univ. Circulars, June, 1903, p. 70 ff.).</ref> is formed if the heterogeneous vowel be {{GHGpron|a}}. This is also to be regarded as the Old Hebrew pronunciation, since it<section end="par8" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

69.text:
agrees with the vocalic character of {{GHGheb|text=ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=י}} ({{GHGpar|5|b}}, note 2). Thus such words as {{GHGheb|text=וָו}}, {{GHGheb|text=חַי}}, {{GHGheb|text=גּוֹי}}, {{GHGheb|text=עָשׂוּי}}, {{GHGheb|text=גֵּו}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫יִת}} are not to be pronounced according to the usual Jewish customIn MSS. {{GHGheb|text=ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=י}}, in such combinations as {{GHGheb|text=גֵּוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=חַיּ}}, are even marked with Mappîq ({{GHGpar|14|a}}). as {{GHGpron|vāv}}, {{GHGpron|ḥay}}, {{GHGpron|gôy}}, {{GHGpron|ʿāsûy}}, {{GHGpron|gēv}}, {{GHGpron|bayith}} (or even as {{GHGpron|vaf}}, &c.; cf. modern Greek {{GHGpron|av af}}, {{GHGpron|ev ef}} for αὐ, εὐ), but with the Italian Jews more like {{GHGpron|wāu}}, {{GHGpron|ḥai}}, &c. The sound of {{GHGheb|text=־ָיו}} is the same as {{GHGheb|text=־ָו}}, i.e. almost like {{GHGpron|āu}}, so that {{GHGheb|text=־ָו}} is often written defectively for {{GHGheb|text=־ָיו}}.
{{GHGpar-heading|9|Character of the several Vowels}} {{GHGmargin-letter|9|a}} Numerous as are the vowel signs in Hebrew writing, they are yet not fully adequate to express all the various modifications of the vowel sounds, especially with respect to length and shortness. To understand this better a short explanation of the character and value of the several vowels is required, especially in regard to their length and shortness as well as to their changeableness ({{GHGpar|25|doublesign=1}}, {{GHGpar|27|nosign=1}}). I. ''First Class. A-sound.'' '''1.''' {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} ({{GHGheb|text=־ָ}}), when it represents a long {{GHGpron|a}}, is, by nature and origin, of two kinds:— (1) The essentially long {{GHGpron|â}} (in Arabic regularly written {{GHGheb|text=־ָא}}), which is not readily shortened and never wholly dropped ({{GHGpar|25|c}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כְּתָב}} {{GHGpron|kethâbh}} (writing); very seldom with a following {{GHGheb|text=א}}, as {{GHGheb|text=רָאשׁ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=1.4}}, (see the examples in {{GHGpar|72|p}}).Of a different kind are the cases in which {{GHGheb|text=א}} has lost its consonantal sound by coalescing with a preceding {{GHGpron|a}}, {{GHGpar|23|a}}–{{GHGpar|23|d|nonumber=1}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|9|b}} The writing of {{GHGheb|text=קָאם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=10|verse=14}} for {{GHGheb|text=קָם}} would only be justifiable, if the {{GHGpron|ā}} of this form were to be explained as a contraction of {{GHGpron|ăă}} cf. however {{GHGpar|72|a}}; {{GHGheb|text=דָּאג}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=13|verse=16}} for {{GHGheb|text=דָּגּ}} ({{GHGpron|dāg}}) is certainly incorrect.—The rarity of the {{GHGpron|â}} in Hebrew arises from the fact that it has for the most part become an obtuse {{GHGpron|ô}}; see below, {{GHGpar|9|q|nonumber=1}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|9|c}} (2) {{GHGpron|ā}}, lengthened only by position (i.e. tone-long or at all events lengthened under the influence of the tone, according to the laws for the formation of syllables, {{GHGpar|27|e}}–{{GHGpar|27|h|nonumber=1}}), either in the tone-syllable itself (or in the secondary tone-syllable indicated by {{GHGterm|Mèthĕg}}, see below), or just before or after it. This sound is invariably lengthened from an original {{GHGpron|ă}},In Arabic this {{GHGpron|ă}} is always retained in an open syllable. and is found in open syllables, i.e. syllables ending in a vowel ({{GHGpar|26|b}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לְךָ}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטַל}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָקוּם}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָסִיר}} (Arab. {{GHGpron|lăkă}}, {{GHGpron|qătălă}}, {{GHGpron|yăqûmŭ}}, {{GHGpron|ʾăsîrŭ}}), as well as in closed syllables, i.e. those ending in

70.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par9" />a consonant, as {{GHGheb|text=יָד}}, {{GHGheb|text=כּוֹכָב}} (vulgar Arab. {{GHGpron|yăd}}, {{GHGpron|kaukăb}}). In a closed syllable, however, it can only stand when this has the tone, {{GHGheb|text=דָּבָ֫ר}}, {{GHGheb|text=עוֹלָ֫ם}}; whereas in an open syllable it is especially frequent ''before'' the tone, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=דָּבָ֫ר}}, {{GHGheb|text=זָקֵ֫ן}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָכֶ֫ם}}. Where the tone is moved forward or weakened (as happens most commonly in what is called the construct state of nouns, cf. {{GHGpar|89|a}}) the original short {{GHGpron|ă}} ({{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}}) is retained in a closed syllable, while in an open syllable it becomes {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wa}} ({{GHGpar|27|i}}): {{GHGheb|text=חָכָם}}, constr. state {{GHGheb|text=חֲכָם}} ({{GHGpron|ḥ<sup>a</sup>khăm}}); {{GHGheb|text=דָּבָר}}, {{GHGheb|text=דְּבַר}} ({{GHGpron|d<sup>e</sup>bhăr}}); {{GHGheb|text=קָטַל}}, {{GHGheb|text=קְטָלָם}}. For examples of the retention, in the secondary tone-syllable, of {{GHGpron|ā}} lengthened from {{GHGpron|ă}}, see {{GHGpar|93|xx}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|9|d}}
In some terminations of the verb ({{GHGheb|text=תָּ}} in the 2nd sing. masc. perf., {{GHGheb|text=ןָ}} in the 2nd pl. fem. of the imperat., as well as in the 3rd and 2nd pl. fem. of the imperf.), in {{GHGheb|text=אַתָּ|translate=thou}} (masc.) and in the suffixes {{GHGheb|text=ךָ}} and {{GHGheb|text=הָ}}, the final {{GHGpron|ā}} can stand even without a vowel letter. A {{GHGheb|text=ה}} is, however, in these cases (except with {{GHGheb|text=הָ}}) frequently added as a vowel letter.

<small>
On {{GHGheb|text=־ָ}} for {{GHGpron|ŏ}} see below, {{GHGpar|9|f|nonumber=1}}.
</small>

{{GHGmargin-letter|9|e}}
'''2.''' {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}}, or short ''ă'', stands in Hebrew almost exclusively in a closed syllable with or without the tone ({{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫ל}}, {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתֶּ֫ם}}). In places where it now appears to stand in an open syllable the syllable was originally closed, and a helping vowel ({{GHGpron|ă}}, {{GHGpron|ĭ}}) has been inserted after the second radical merely to make the pronunciation easier, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫חַל}} (ground-form {{GHGpron|naḥl}}), {{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫יִת}} (Arab. {{GHGpron|bait}}), see {{GHGpar|28|d}}, and with regard to two cases of a different kind, {{GHGpar|25|g}}, {{GHGpar|25|h|nonumber=1}}. Otherwise {{GHGpron|ă}} in an open syllable has almost without exception passed into ''ā'' ({{GHGheb|text=־ָ}}), see above, {{GHGpar|9|c|nonumber=1}}.

<small>
On the very frequent attenuation of ''ă'' to ''ĭ'', cf. below, {{GHGpar|9|h|nonumber=1}}. On the rare, and only apparent union of Pathaḥ with {{GHGheb|text=א}} ({{GHGheb|text=־ַא}}), see {{GHGpar|23|d}}, end. On ''ă'' as a helping-vowel, {{GHGpar|22|f}} ({{GHGterm|Pathaḥ furtivum}}), and {{GHGpar|28|e}}.
</small>

{{GHGmargin-letter|9|f}}
'''3.''' S<sup>e</sup>gôl ({{GHGpron|ĕ}}, {{GHGpron|è}} [{{GHGpron|{{GHGtranslit|a-dier-macr}}}}]) by origin belongs sometimes to the second, but most frequently to the first vowel class ({{GHGpar|27|o}}, {{GHGpar|27|p|nonumber=1}}, {{GHGpar|27|u|nonumber=1}}). It belongs to the first class when it is a modification of {{GHGpron|a}} (as the Germ. {{lang|de|''Bad''}}, pl. {{lang|de|''Bäder''}}; Eng. ''man'', pl. ''men''), either in a toneless syllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יֶדְכֶם}} (for {{GHGpron|yadkhèm}}), or with the tone, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫רֶץ}} from ''ʾarṣ'', {{GHGheb|text=קֶ֫רֶן}} Arab. ''qărn'', {{GHGheb|text=קֶ֫מַח}} Arab. ''qămḥ''. This {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>gôl}} is often retained even in the strongest tone-syllable, at the end of a sentence or of an important clause (in {{GHGterm|pause}}), as {{GHGheb|text=מֶ֑לֶךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=צֶֽדֶק}} (''m{{GHGtranslit|a-di-ma-ac}}l{{GHGtranslit|a-dier-brev}}kh'', ''s{{GHGtranslit|a-di-ma-ac}}d{{GHGtranslit|a-dier-brev}}q''). As a rule, however, in such cases the {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} which underlies the {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>gôl}} is lengthened into {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קָ֑מַח}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָֽרֶן}}. A {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>gôl}} apparently lengthened from {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wa}}, but in reality traceable to an original {{GHGpron|ă}}, stands in pausal forms, as {{GHGheb|text=פֶּֽרִי}} (ground-form {{GHGpron|păry}}), {{GHGheb|text=יֶֽהִי}} ({{GHGpron|yăhy}}), &c. On the cases where a {{GHGheb|text=י}} (originally consonantal) follows this S<sup>e</sup>gôl, see {{GHGpar|75|f}}, and {{GHGpar|91|k}}.
<section end="par9" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

71.text:
II. ''Second Class. I- and E-sounds.''
{{GHGmargin-letter|9|g}} '''4.''' The long {{GHGpron|î}} is frequently even in the consonantal writing indicated by {{GHGheb|text=י}} (a ''fully'' written {{GHGterm|Ḥireq}} {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}}); but a naturally long {{GHGpron|î}} can be also written ''defectively'' ({{GHGpar|8|i}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=צַדִּיק}} ({{GHGtranslate|righteous}}), plur. {{GHGheb|text=צַדִּקִים|pron=ṣaddîqîm}}; {{GHGheb|text=יִירָא}} ({{GHGtranslate|he fears}}), plur. {{GHGheb|text=יִֽרְאוּ}}. Whether a ''defectively'' written {{GHGterm|Ḥireq}} is long may be best known from the origin of the form; often also from the nature of the syllable ({{GHGpar|26}}), or as in {{GHGheb|text=יִֽרְאוּ}}. from the {{GHGterm|Metheg}} attached to it ({{GHGpar|16|f}}).{{GHGcritic|In all appearances of this form in the Qoren Bible, it is {{GHGheb|text=יִֽירְאוּ}}.|Amire80}} {{GHGmargin-letter|9|h}} '''5.''' The {{GHGterm|short Ḥireq}} (alwaysAt least according to the Masoretic orthography; cf. Wellhausen, {{GHGcite|title=Text der Bb. Sam.}}, p. 18, Rem. written ''defectively'') is especially frequent in sharpened syllables ({{GHGheb|text=קִטֵּל}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִמִּי}}) and in toneless closed syllables ({{GHGheb|text=מִזְמוֹר|translate=psalm}}); cf. however {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּשְׁבְּ}} in a closed tone-syllable, and even {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּ֫פֶן}}, with a helping Segôl, for {{GHGpron|wayyiphn}}. It has arisen very frequently by attenuation from {{GHGpron|ă}}, as in {{GHGheb|text=דִּבְרֵי}} from original {{GHGpron|dăbărê}}, {{GHGheb|text=צִדְקִי}} (ground-form {{GHGpron|ṣădq}}),Jerome (cf. Siegfried, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1884, p. 77) in these cases often gives {{GHGpron|ă}} for {{GHGpron|ĭ}}. or else it is the original {{GHGpron|ĭ}}, which in the tone-syllable had become {{GHGpron|ē}}, as in {{GHGheb|text=אֹֽיִבְךָ}} ({{GHGtranslate|thy enemy}}) from {{GHGheb|text=אֹיֵב}} (ground-form {{GHGpron|ʾâyĭb}}).Cf. the remarks of I. Guidi, ‘''La pronuncia del ṣērē'',’ in the {{GHGcite|title=Verhandl. des Hamburger Orient.-Kongr.}} of 1902, Leiden, 1904, p. 208 ff., on Italian {{GHGpron|e}} for Latin {{GHGpron|i}}, as in {{GHGpron|fede}} = {{GHGpron|fĭdem}}, {{GHGpron|pece}} = {{GHGpron|pĭcem}}. It is sometimes a simple helping vowel, as in {{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫יִת}}, {{GHGpar|28|e}}. The earlier grammarians call every {{GHGterm|Ḥireq}} written ''fully'', {{GHGterm|Ḥireq magnum}}; every one written ''defectively'', {{GHGterm|Ḥireq parvum}},—a misleading distinction, so far as quantity is concerned. {{GHGmargin-letter|9|i}} '''6.''' The longest {{GHGpron|ê}} {{GHGheb|text=־ֵי}} (more rarely defective {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עֵנֵי}} for {{GHGheb|text=עֵינֵי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=8}}; at the end of a word also {{GHGheb|text=־ה}}) is as a rule contracted from {{GHGheb|text=־ַי|pron=ay}} ({{GHGpron|ai}}), {{GHGpar|7|a}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הֵיכָל}} ({{GHGtranslate|palace}}), Arab. and Syriac {{GHGpron|haikal}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|9|k}} '''7.''' The {{GHGterm|Ṣere}} without Yôdh mostly represents the tone-long {{GHGpron|ē}}, which, like the tone-long {{GHGpron|ā}} (see {{GHGpar|9|c|nonumber=1}}), is very rarely retained except {{GHGpron|in}} and ''before'' the tone-syllable, and is always lengthened from an original {{GHGpron|ĭ}}. It stands in an open syllable with or before the tone, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=סֵ֫פֶר}} (ground-form {{GHGpron|sĭphr}}) {{GHGtranslate|book}}, {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁנָ֫ה}} (Arab. {{GHGpron|sĭnăt}}) {{GHGtranslate|sleep}}, or with Metheg (see {{GHGpar|16|d}}, {{GHGpar|16|f|nonumber=1}}) in the secondary tone-syllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שְׁאֵֽלָתִי|translate=my request}}, {{GHGheb|text=נֵֽלְכָה|translate=let us go}}. On the other hand in a closed syllable it is almost always with the tone, as {{GHGheb|text=בֵּן|translate=son}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִלֵּם|translate=dumb}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|9|l}} Exceptions: (''a'') {{GHGpron|ē}} is sometimes retained in a toneless closed syllable, in monosyllabic words before Maqqeph, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עֵֽץ־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=35|verse=18}}, as well as in the examples of {{GHGterm|nāsôg ʾāḥôr}} mentioned in {{GHGpar|29|f}} (on the quantity cf. {{GHGpar|8|b}} 3 end); (''b'') in a toneless open final syllable, Ṣere likewise occurs in examples of the {{GHGterm|nāsôg ʾāḥôr}}, as {{GHGheb|text=יֵ֫צֵא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=29}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=39}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|9|m}} '''8.''' The Segôl of the I(E)-class is most frequently an {{GHGpron|ĕ}} modified from original {{GHGpron|ĭ}}, either replacing a tone-long {{GHGpron|ē}} which has lost the tone, e.g.

72.text:
{{GHGheb|text=תֶּן־}} from {{GHGheb|text=תֵּן}} ({{GHGtranslate|give}}), {{GHGheb|text=יֹֽצֶרְךָ}} ({{GHGtranslate|thy creator}}) from {{GHGheb|text=יֹצֵר}}, or in the case discussed in {{GHGpar|93|o}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֶלְקִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֶזְרִי}} from the ground-forms {{GHGpron|ḥilq}}, {{GHGpron|ʿizr}}; cf. also {{GHGpar|64|f}}. {{GHGterm|Segôl}} appears as a simple helping-vowel in cases such as {{GHGheb|text=סֵ֫פֶר}} for {{GHGpron|siphr}}, {{GHGheb|text=יִ֫גֶל}} for {{GHGpron|yigl}} ({{GHGpar|28|e}}).
III. ''Third Class. U- and O-sounds.''
{{GHGmargin-letter|9|n}} '''9.''' For the U-sound there is— (1) the {{GHGterm|long}} {{GHGpron|û}}, either ({{GHGpron|a}}) written fully, {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} {{GHGterm|Šureq}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גְּבוּל}} ({{GHGtranslate|boundary}}), or (''b'') defectively written {{GHGheb|text=־ֻ}} {{GHGterm|Qibbûṣ}} {{GHGheb|text=גְּבֻלוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=יְמֻתוּן}}; (2) the short {{GHGpron|ŭ}}, mostly represented by {{GHGterm|Qibbûṣ}}, in a toneless closed syllable and especially common in a sharpened syllable, in e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שֻׁלְחָן}} ({{GHGtranslate|table}}), {{GHGheb|text=סֻכָּה}} ({{GHGtranslate|booth}}). {{GHGmargin-letter|9|o}} {{Smaller block/s}} Sometimes also {{GHGpron|ŭ}} in a sharpened syllable is written {{GHGheb|text=וּ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הוּכָּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=102|verse=5}}, {{GHGheb|text=יוּלָּ֑ד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=7}}, {{GHGheb|text=כּוּלָּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer.|chapter=31|verse=34}}, {{GHGheb|text=מְשׂוּכָּתוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=5}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֲרוּמִּים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=25}} for {{GHGheb|text=הֻכָּה}}, &c. For this {{GHGpron|u}} the LXX write {{GHGpron|o}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עֲדֻלָּם}} {{lang|grc|Ὀδολλάμ}}, from which, however, it only follows, that this {{GHGpron|ŭ}} was pronounced somewhat indistinctly. The LXX also express the sharp {{GHGterm|Ḥireq}} by {{lang|grc|ε}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אִמֵּר}}={{lang|grc|Ἐμμήρ}}. The pronunciation of the {{GHGterm|Qibbûṣ}} like the German {{GHGpron|ü}}, which was formerly common, is incorrect, although the occasional pronunciation of the U-sounds as {{GHGpron|ü}} in the time of the punctators is attested, at least as regards PalestineCf. Delitzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Physiologie u. Musik}}, Lpz. 1868, p. 15 f.; cf. the Turkish {{GHGpron|bülbül}} for the Persian {{GHGpron|bulbul}}, and the pronunciation of the Arabic {{GHGpron|dunyā}} in Syria as {{GHGpron|dünyā}}. {{Smaller block/e}} {{GHGmargin-letter|9|p}} '''10.''' The O-sound bears the same relation to U as the E does to I in the second class. It has four varieties:— (1) The {{GHGpron|ô}} which is contracted from {{GHGpron|aw}} (={{GHGpron|au}}), {{GHGpar|7|a}}, and accordingly is mostly written fully; {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} ({{GHGterm|Holem plenum}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹט}} ({{GHGtranslate|a whip}}), Arab. {{GHGpron|sauṭ}}, {{GHGheb|text=עוֹלָה}} ({{GHGtranslate|iniquity}}) from {{GHGheb|text=עַוְלָה}}. More rarely {{GHGterm|defectively}}, as {{GHGheb|text=שֹֽׁרְךָ}} ({{GHGtranslate|thine ox}}) from {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹר}} Arab. {{GHGpron|ṯaur}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|9|q}} (2) The long {{GHGpron|ô}} which arose in Hebrew at an early period, by a general process of obscuring, out of an original {{GHGpron|â}},Cf. above, ''b'', end. On Jerome’s transliteration of {{GHGpron|o}} for {{GHGpron|ā}}, see {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1884, p. 75. while the latter has been retained in Arabic and Aramaic. It is usually written {{GHGterm|fully}} in the tone-syllable, {{GHGterm|defectively}} in the toneless, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קֹטֵל}} Arab. {{GHGpron|qâtĭl}}. Aram. {{GHGpron|qâṭēl}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֱלוֹהַּ}} Arab. {{GHGpron|ʾĭlâh}}, Aram. {{GHGpron|ʾĕlâh}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהִים}}; {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹק}} ({{GHGtranslate|leg}}), Arab. {{GHGpron|sâq}}; {{GHGheb|text=גִּבּוֹר}} ({{GHGtranslate|hero}}), Arab. {{GHGpron|găbbâr}}; {{GHGheb|text=חוֹתָם}} ({{GHGtranslate|seal}}), Arab. {{GHGpron|ḫâtăm}}; {{GHGheb|text=רִמּוֹן}} ({{GHGtranslate|pomegranate}}), Arab. {{GHGpron|rŭmmân}}; {{GHGheb|text=שִׁלְטוֹן}} ({{GHGtranslate|dominion}}), Aram. {{GHGheb|text=שֻׁלְטָן}} and {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלְטָן}} Arab. {{GHGpron|sŭlṭân}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלוֹם}} ({{GHGtranslate|peace}}), Aram. {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלָם}}, Arab. {{GHGpron|sălâm}}. Sometimes the form in {{GHGpron|â}} also occurs side by side with that in {{GHGpron|ô}} as {{GHGheb|text=שִׁרְיָן}} and {{GHGheb|text=שִׁרְיוֹן}} ({{GHGtranslate|coat of mail}}; see however {{GHGpar|29|u}}). Cf. also {{GHGpar|68|b}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|9|r}} (3) The tone-long {{GHGpron|ō}} which is lengthened from an original {{GHGpron|ŭ}}, or from an {{GHGpron|ŏ}} arising from {{GHGpron|ŭ}}, by the tone, or in general according to the

73.text:
laws for the formation of syllables. It occurs not only in the tone-syllable, but also in an open syllable before the tone, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קֹדֶשׁ}} (ground-form {{GHGpron|qŭdš}}) {{GHGtranslate|sanctuary}}; {{GHGheb|text=בֹּרַךְ}} for {{GHGpron|burrakh}}, {{GHGheb|text=יִלְקֹטוּן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=28}}, as well as (with {{GHGterm|Metheg}}) in the secondary tone-syllable; {{GHGheb|text=אֹֽהָלִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=פֹּֽעֲלוֹ}}. But the original {{GHGpron|ŏ}} ({{GHGpron|ŭ}}) is retained in a toneless closed syllable, whereas in a toneless open syllable it is weakened to {{GHGterm|Šewâ}}. Cf. {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל|translate=all}}, but {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־}} ({{GHGpron|kŏl}}), {{GHGheb|text=כֻּלָּם}} ({{GHGpron|kŭllām}}); {{GHGheb|text=יִקְטֹל}}, {{GHGheb|text=יִקְטָלְךָ}} and {{GHGheb|text=יִקְטְלוּ}}, where original {{GHGpron|ŭ}} is weakened to {{GHGterm|Šewâ}}: {{GHGpron|yiqṭelû}}, Arab. {{GHGpron|yaqtŭlû}}. This tone-long {{GHGpron|ō}} is only as an exception written fully. {{GHGmargin-letter|9|s}} (4) {{GHGheb|text=־ָ}} {{GHGterm|Qameṣ-ḥaṭuph}} represents {{GHGpron|ŏ}} (properly {{GHGpron|{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-brev}}}}, cf. {{GHGpar|8|a}}, note 2) modified from {{GHGpron|ŭ}} and is therefore classed here. It stands in the same relation to {{GHGterm|Ḥolem}} as the {{GHGterm|Segôl}} of the second class to {{GHGpron|Sere}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־|pron=kŏl}}, {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּ֫קָם|pron=wayyāqŏm}}. On the distinction between this and {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}}, see below, {{GHGpar|9|u|nonumber=1}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|9|t}} '''11.''' The following table gives a summary of the gradation of the three vowel-classes according to the quantity of the vowels:—

''On the distinction between Qameṣ and Qameṣ-ḥaṭuph''.These statements, in order to be fully understood, must be studied in connexion with the theory of syllables ({{GHGpar|26}}) and {{GHGterm|Metheg}} ({{GHGpar|16|c}}–{{GHGpar|16|i|nonumber=1}}). According to {{GHGpar|8|a}}, long {{GHGpron|ā}} or {{GHGpron|{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-macr}}}} ({{GHGterm|Qameṣ}}) and short {{GHGpron|ŏ}} or {{GHGpron|{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-brev}}}} ({{GHGterm|Qameṣ-ḥaṭuph}}) are in manuscripts and printed texts generally expressed by the same sign ( {{GHGheb|text=ָ}} ), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קָם|pron=qām}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־|pron=kŏl}}. The beginner who does not yet know the grammatical
{{Smaller block/e}}

74.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" />{{Smaller block/s}}</noinclude><section begin="par9" />
origin of the words in question (which is of course the surest guide), may depend meanwhile on the following principal rules:—
{{Smaller block/e}}

'''1.''' ''The sign {{GHGheb|text=־ָ}}<ref>In the Babylonian punctuation ({{GHGpar|8|g}}, note) {{GHGpron|ā}} and {{GHGpron|ŏ}} are carefully distinguished. So also in many MSS with the ordinary punctuation and in Baer’s editions of the text since 1880, in which {{GHGheb|text=־ֳ}} is used for {{GHGpron|ŏ}} as well as for {{GHGpron|<sup>ŏ</sup>}}. Cf. Baer-Delitzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Liber Jobi}}, p. 43. But the identity of the two signs is certainly original, and the use of {{GHGheb|text=־ֳ}} for {{GHGpron|ŏ}} is misleading.</ref> is'' {{GHGpron|ŏ}} ''in a toneless closed syllable'', since such a syllable can have only a short vowel ({{GHGpar|26|o}}). The above case occurs—

(''a'') When {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} follows as a syllable-divider, as in {{GHGheb|text=חָכְמָ֫ה}} {{GHGpron|ḥŏkh-m{{GHGtranslit|a-macr-acut}}}} (wisdom), {{GHGheb|text=אָכְלָ֫ה}} {{GHGpron|{{GHGaleph}}ŏkh-l{{GHGtranslit|a-macr-acut}}}} (food). With {{GHGterm|Metheg}} {{GHGheb|text=־ָ}} is {{GHGpron|ā}} ({{GHGpron|{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-macr}}}}) and according to the usual view stands in an open syllable with a following {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָֽכְלָה}} {{GHGpron|{{GHGaleph}}ā-kh<sup>e</sup>l{{GHGtranslit|a-macr-acut}}}} (she ate); but cf. {{GHGpar|16|i}}.

(b) When a closed syllable is formed by {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=חָנֵּ֫נִי|pron=ḥŏnnēnî}} (have mercy upon me); but {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽתִּ֫ים}} (with {{GHGterm|Metheg}}, {{GHGpar|16|f}} ζ) {{GHGpron|bâttîm}}.

(c) When the syllable in question loses the tone on account of a following {{GHGterm|Maqqēph}} ({{GHGpar|16|a}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־הָֽאָדָם}} {{GHGpron|kŏl-hā-{{GHGaleph}}ād{{GHGtranslit|a-macr-acut}}m}} (all men).

<small>
In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=35|verse=10}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=19|verse=7}} {{GHGterm|Maqqēph}} with {{GHGheb|text=כָּל}} is replaced by a conjunctive accent ({{GHGterm|Mer<sup>e</sup>kha}}); so by {{GHGterm|Darga}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=5}} with {{GHGheb|text=סְעָד}}, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=37|verse=8}} with {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּקְרָם}} (so Baer after Qimḥi; ed. Mant., Ginsburg, Kittel {{GHGheb|text=ויקרַם}}).
</small>

(''d'') In a closed final syllable without the tone, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּ֫קָם}} {{GHGpron|wayy{{GHGtranslit|a-macr-acut}}qŏm}} (and he stood up).—In the cases where {{GHGpron|â}} or {{GHGpron|ā}} in the final syllable has become toneless through {{GHGterm|Maqqēph}} ({{GHGpar|16|a}}) and yet remains, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כְּתָֽב־הַדָּת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=4|verse=8}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָֽׁת־לִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=25}}, it has a {{GHGterm|Metheg}} in correct manuscripts and printed texts.

In cases like {{GHGheb|text=הָ֫לְאָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מָּה}} {{GHGpron|l{{GHGtranslit|a-macr-acut}}mmā}}, the tone shows that {{GHGheb|text=־ָ}} is to be read as {{GHGpron|ā}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|9|v}}
{{Smaller block/s}}
'''2.''' The cases in which {{GHGheb|text=־ָ}} appears to stand in an open syllable and yet is to be read as {{GHGpron|ŏ}} require special consideration. This is the case, (''a'') when {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph-Qameṣ}} follows, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=פָּֽעֳלוֹ|translate=his work}}, or simple vocal {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=דָּֽרְבָן|translate=ox goad}}; {{GHGheb|text=בְּעָֽבְרוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=4|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָֽׁמְרָה}} (so ed. Mant., Ginsb.) ''preserve'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=86|verse=2}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=16|verse=1|hidebook=1}} and the cases mentioned in {{GHGpar|48|i}}, n., and {{GHGpar|61|f}}, n.; other examples are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ob|chapter=1|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=15}}); {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph-Pathaḥ}} follows in {{GHGheb|text=לִמְשָֽׁחֲךָ}} (so Ginsburg; Baer {{GHGheb|text=לִמְשָֽׁחֳךָ}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=1}}, {{GHGheb|text=לַֽהֲרָֽגֲךָ}} 24:11, and {{GHGheb|text=יִֽפְגָֽשֲׁךָ}} (so Baer, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=18}}, others {{GHGheb|text=יִפְגָּֽשְׁךָ}}); (''b'') before another {{GHGterm|Qameṣ-ḥaṭuph}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=פָּֽעָלְךָ֫|translate=thy work}}; on {{GHGheb|text=אָֽרָה־לִּי}} and {{GHGheb|text=קָֽבָה־לִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=7}}, see {{GHGpar|67|o}}; (''c'') in the two plural forms {{GHGheb|text=קָֽדָשִׁים|translate=sanctuaries}} and {{GHGheb|text=שָֽׁרָשִׁים|translate=roots}} (also written {{GHGheb|text=קֳד׳}} and {{GHGheb|text=שֳׁר׳}}). In all these cases the Jewish grammarians regard the {{GHGterm|Metheg}} accompanying the {{GHGheb|text=־ָ}} as indicating a Qāmeṣ raḥabh (broad Qameṣ) and therefore read the {{GHGheb|text=־ָ}} as {{GHGpron|ā}}; thus {{GHGpron|pā-<sup>o</sup>lô}}, {{GHGpron|dā-r<sup>e</sup>bān}}, {{GHGpron|pā-ŏl<sup>e</sup>khā}}, {{GHGpron|qā-dāšîm}}. But neither the origin of these forms, nor the analogous formations in Hebrew and in the cognate languages, nor the transcription of proper names in the
<section end="par9" /><noinclude>{{Smaller block/e}}
<references/></noinclude>

75.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" />{{Smaller block/s}}</noinclude><section begin="par9" />
LXX, allows us to regard this view as correct. It is just possible that Qameṣ is here used loosely for ''{{GHGtranslit|a-ring-macr}}'', as the equivalent of ''ō'', on the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=פֹּֽעֲלוֹ}} &c., {{GHGpar|93|q}}. As a matter of fact, however, we ought no doubt to divide and read {{GHGpron|pŏʿ<sup>o</sup>-lô}} (for {{GHGpron|pŏʿ-lô}}), {{GHGpron|pŏʿŏ-l<sup>e</sup>khā}}, {{GHGpron|qŏdā-ším}}.—Quite as inconceivable is it for {{GHGterm|Metheg}} to be a sign of the lengthening into ''ā'' in {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽחֳרִי־אָֽף}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=11|verse=8}}), although it is so in {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽאֳנִי}} ''bā-ʾ<sup>o</sup>nî'' (in the navy), since here the ''ā'' of the article appears under the {{GHGheb|text=ב}}.
{{Smaller block/e}}

<section end="par9" />
<section begin="par10" />{{GHGpar-heading|10|The Half Vowels and the Syllable Divider ({{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}})}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|10|a}}
'''1'''. Besides the full vowels, Hebrew has also a series of vowel sounds which may be called {{GHGterm|half vowels}} (Sievers, {{GHGcite|title=Murmelvokale}}). The punctuation makes use of these to represent extremely slight sounds which are to be regarded as remains of fuller and more distinct vowels from an earlier period of the language. They generally take the place of vowels {{GHGterm|originally short}} standing in {{GHGterm|open syllables}}. Such short vowels, though preserved in the kindred languages, are not tolerated by the present system of pointing in Hebrew, but either undergo a lengthening or are weakened to Š<sup>e</sup>wâ. Under some circumstances, however, the original short vowel may reappear.

{{GHGmargin-letter|10|b}}
To these belongs first of all the sign {{GHGheb|text=־ְ}}, which indicates an extremely short, slight, and (as regards pronunciation) indeterminate vowel sound, something like an obscure half ''ĕ'' (''<u><sup>e</sup></u>''). It is called {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}},<ref>On {{GHGheb|text=שְׁוָא}}, the older and certainly the only correct form (as in Ben Asher), see Bather, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1895, p. 18, note 3, who compares Šewayya, the name of the Syriac accentual sign of similar form {{GHGheb|text=־֔}} (=Hebr. Zaqeph). The form {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבָא}}, customary in Spain since the time of Menaḥem b. Sarûq, is due to a supposed connexion with Aram. {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבָת|translate=rest}}, and hence would originally have denoted only {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ quiescens}}, like the Arabic ''sukūn'' (rest). The derivation from {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁבָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=שִׁיבָה}} (stem {{GHGheb|text=יָשַׁב}}, Levias, {{GHGcite|title=American Journ. of Philol.}}, xvi. 28 ff.) seems impossible.</ref> which may be either {{GHGterm|simple Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} ({{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ simplex}}) as distinguished from the compound (see {{GHGpar|10|f|nonumber=1}}), or {{GHGterm|vocal Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} ({{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}) as distinguished from {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ quiescens}}, which is silent and stands as a mere syllable divider (see {{GHGpar|10|i|nonumber=1}}) under the consonant which closes the syllable.

{{GHGmargin-letter|10|c}}
The vocal {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} stands under a consonant which is closely united, as a kind of grace-note, with the following syllable, either (''a'') at the beginning of the word, as {{GHGheb|text=קְטֹל}} ''q<sup>e</sup>ṭōl'' (to kill), {{GHGheb|text=מְמַלֵּא}} ''m<sup>e</sup>mallē'' (filling), or (''b'') in the middle of the word, as {{GHGheb|text=קֽוֹטְלָה}} ''qô-ṭ<sup>e</sup>lā'', {{GHGheb|text=יִקְטְלוּ}} ''yiq-ṭ<sup>e</sup>lû''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|10|d}}
In former editions of this Grammar {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} was distinguished as ''medium'' when it followed a short vowel and therefore stood in a supposed ‘loosely closed’ or ‘wavering’ syllable, as in {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכֵי}}, {{GHGheb|text=בִּנְפֹל}}. According to Sievers, {{GHGcite|title=Metrische Studien}}, i. 22, this distinction must now be abandoned. These syllables are really closed, and the original vowel is not merely shortened, but entirely elided. The fact that a following B<sup>e</sup>gadk<sup>e</sup>phath letter ({{GHGpar|6|n}}) remains spirant instead of taking {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}}, is explained by Sievers on the ‘supposition that the change from hard to spirant is elder than the elision<section end="par10" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

76.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par10" />of the vowel, and that the prehistoric {{GHGpron|malakai}} became {{GHGpron|malakhai}} before being shortened to {{GHGpron|malkhē’}}. In cases like {{GHGheb|text=כִּסְאוֹ}} (from {{GHGheb|text=כִּסֵּא}}), {{GHGheb|text=יִקְחוּ}} (from {{GHGheb|text=יִקַּח}}) the dropping of the {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}} shows that the original vowel is completely lost.

{{GHGmargin-letter|10|e}}
The sound ''ĕ'' has been adopted as the normal transcription of simple {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}, although it is certain that it often became assimilated in sound to other vowels. The LXX express it by {{polytonic|ε}}, or even by {{polytonic|η}}, {{GHGheb|text=כְּרוּבִים}} {{polytonic|χερουβίμ}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַלְלוּ־יָהּ}} {{polytonic|ἀλληλούια}}, more frequently by {{polytonic|α}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמוּאֵל}}, {{polytonic|Σαμουήλ}}, but very frequently by assimilating its indeterminate sound to the following principal vowel, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=סְדֹם}} {{polytonic|Σόδομα}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלֹמֹה}} {{polytonic|Σολομών}} (as well as {{polytonic|Σαλωμών}}), {{GHGheb|text=צְבָאוֹת}} {{polytonic|Σαβαώθ}}, {{GHGheb|text=נְתַנְאֵל}} {{polytonic|Ναθαναήλ}}.<ref>The same occurs frequently also in the Greek and Latin transcriptions of Phoenician words, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מְלָכָא|pron=Malaga}}, {{GHGheb|text=גְּבוּלִים|pron=gubulim}} (Schröder, {{GHGcite|title=Die phöniz. Spr.}}, p. 139 ff.). Cf. the Latin augment in ''momordi, pupugi'', with the Greek in {{polytonic|τέτυφα}}, {{polytonic|τετυμμένος}}, and the old form ''memordi''.</ref> A similar account of the pronunciation of {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} is given by Jewish grammarians of the Middle Ages.<ref>See especially ''Yehuda Ḥayyûǵ'', pp. 4 f. and 130 f. in Nutt’s edition (Lond. 1870), corresponding to p. 200 of the edition by Dukes (Stuttg. 1844); Ibn Ezra’s {{GHGcite|title=Ṣaḥoth}}, p. 3; Gesenius, {{GHGcite|title=Lehrgebäude der hebr. Sprache}}, p. 68. The {{GHGcite|title=Manuel du lecteur}}, mentioned above, {{GHGpar|6|b}}, also contains express rules for the various ways of pronouncing {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}: so too the {{GHGcite|title=Dikduke ha-ṭ<sup>e</sup>eamim}}, ed. by Baer and Strack, Lpz. 1879, p. 12 ff. Cf. also Schreiner, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} vi. 236 ff.</ref>

How the {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} sound has arisen through the vanishing of a full vowel is seen, e.g. in {{GHGheb|text=בְּרָכָה}} from {{GHGpron|bărăkă}}, as the word is still pronounced in Arabic. In that language the full short vowel regularly corresponds to the Hebrew {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|10|f}}
'''2'''. Connected with the {{GHGterm|simple Š<sup>e</sup>wâ môbile}} is the {{GHGterm|compound Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} or {{GHGterm|Ḥâṭēph}} (''correptum''), i.e. a {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} the pronunciation of which is more accurately fixed by the addition of a short vowel. There are three {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}-sounds determined in this way, corresponding to the three vowel classes ({{GHGpar|7|a}}):—

(  {{GHGheb|text=־ֲ}}) {{GHGterm|Ḥâṭēph-Páthăḥ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=חֲמוֹר}} {{GHGpron|ḥ<sup>a</sup>môr}}, ass.

(  {{GHGheb|text=־ֱ}}) {{GHGterm|Ḥâṭēph-S<sup>e</sup>gôl}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֱמֹר}} {{GHGpron|ʾ<sup>e</sup>mōr}}, to say.

(  {{GHGheb|text=־ֳ}}) {{GHGterm|Ḥâṭēph-Qāmĕṣ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=חֳלִי}}, {{GHGpron|ḥ<sup>o</sup>lî}}, sickness.

These {{GHGterm|Ḥâṭēphs}}, or at least the first two, stand especially under the four guttural letters ({{GHGpar|22|l}}), instead of a {{GHGterm|simple Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}, since these letters by their nature require a more definite vowel than the indeterminate {{GHGterm|simple Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}. Accordingly a guttural at the beginning of a syllable, where the {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} is necessarily vocal, can never have a mere {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ simplex}}.

On {{GHGheb|text=־ֲ}} the shorter Ḥaṭef as compared with {{GHGheb|text=־ֱ}} cf. {{GHGpar|27|v}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|10|g}}
Rem. A. Only {{GHGheb|text=־ֲ}} and {{GHGheb|text=־ֳ}} occur under letters which are not gutturals. {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph-Pathaḥ}} is found instead of {{GHGterm|simple Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} (especially {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}), chiefly (''a'') under strengthened consonants, since this strengthening (commonly called doubling) causes a more distinct pronunciation of the {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}, {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבֲּלֵי|translate=branches}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=4|verse=12}}. According to the rule given by Ben-Asher (which, however, appears to be unknown to good early MSS. and is therefore rejected by Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, p. 466; cf. Foote, ''Johns Hopkins Univ. Circulars'', June 1903,<section end="par10" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>
