{{GHGmargin-letter|10|h}}
'''B'''. The {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph-Qameṣ}} is less restricted to the gutturals than the first two, and stands more frequently for a simple {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}} when an original O-sound requires to be partly preserved, e.g. at the beginning, in {{GHGheb|text=רֳאִי}} (ground-form {{GHGpron|rŏʾy}}) {{GHGtranslate|vision}} (cf. {{GHGpar|93|z}}); {{GHGheb|text=כֳּנַנְיָהוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=31|verse=12}}, &c., {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} (''K<sup>e</sup>eth.'' {{GHGheb|text=כונ״}}); {{GHGheb|text=עַמֳּנִיּוֹת|translate=Ammonitish women}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=11|verse=1}} (sing. {{GHGheb|text=עַמּוֹנִית}}); {{GHGheb|text=יִרְדֳּפֶ֑ךָ}} for the usual {{GHGheb|text=יִרְדְּפֶ֑ךָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=35|verse=6}}, from {{GHGheb|text=יִרְדֹּף}}; {{GHGheb|text=תִקֳּבֶ֫נּוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=31|verse=33}}, and elsewhere before suffixes, cf. {{GHGpar|60|a}}; {{GHGheb|text=קָדְקֳדוֹ|translate=his pate}} (from {{GHGheb|text=קָדְקֹד}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=7|verse=17}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=אֶשְׁקֳטָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=18|verse=4}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}. Further, like {{GHGheb|text=־ֲ}}, it stands under consonants, which ought to have {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}, as in {{GHGheb|text=לֻֽקֳחָה}} (for {{GHGheb|text=לֻקְּחָה}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=23}}. In this example, as in {{GHGheb|text=וּֽסֳעָ֫דָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=וּֽסֳאָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=18}}; and {{GHGheb|text=וּֽצֳעָ֫קִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=20}}, the {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph-Qameṣ}} is no doubt due to the influence of the<section end="par10" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

78.text:
following guttural as well as of the preceding U-sound. (Elsewhere indeed after {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} in similar cases {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph-Pathaḥ}} is preferred, see above, {{GHGpar|78|b}}; but with {{GHGheb|text=לֻקֳחָה}} cf. also {{GHGheb|text=סֻבֳּלוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=10|verse=27|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, where the U-sound must necessarily be admitted to have an influence on the {{GHGterm|Šewâ}} immediately following.) In {{GHGheb|text=וּֽטֳהָר־}} (''û-ṭohŏr'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=17|verse=9}} it is also influenced by the following O-sound. In {{GHGheb|text=קָֽסֳמִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=8}} {{GHGterm|Qerê}}, the original form is {{GHGheb|text=קְסֹם}}, where again the ''ō'' represents an ''ŏ''. It is only through the influence of a following guttural that we can explain the forms {{GHGheb|text=נִקְרֳאָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=2|verse=14}}; {{GHGheb|text=נִֽבֳהָל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=28|verse=22}}; {{GHGheb|text=נִסְרֳחָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֶפְשֳׂעה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=27|verse=4}}; {{GHGheb|text=וָאֶֽשְׁמֳעָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=8|verse=13}}; {{GHGheb|text=שִֽׁמֳעָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=39|verse=13}}; {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽסֳעָרָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=1}} (Baer’s ed. also in ver. 11); {{GHGheb|text=הַקֳּהָתִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=34|verse=12}} (ed. Mant., Opitius, &c. {{GHGheb|text=הַקְּ׳}}). Finally in most of the examples which have been adduced, the influence of an emphatic sound ({{GHGheb|text=ק}}, {{GHGheb|text=ט}}, cf. also {{GHGheb|text=אֲלַקֳּטָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=2|verse=2}}, 7), or of a sibilant is also to be taken into account. {{GHGmargin-letter|10|i}} '''3'''. The sign of the {{GHGterm|simple Šewâ}} {{GHGheb|text=־ְ}} serves also as a mere syllable divider. In this case it is disregarded in pronunciation and is called {{GHGterm|Šewâ quiescens}}. In the middle of a word it stands under every consonant which closes a syllable; at the end of words on the other hand it is omitted except in ''final'' {{GHGheb|text=ך}} (to distinguish it better from final {{GHGheb|text=ן}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מֶלֶךְ|translate=king}}, and in the less frequent case, where a word ends with a mute after another vowelless consonant as in {{GHGheb|text=נֵרְדְּ|translate=nard}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַתְּ|translate=thou fem.}} (for ’''ant''), {{GHGheb|text=קָטַלְתְּ|translate=thou}} fem. ''hast killed'', {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּשְׁקְ|translate=and he watered}}, {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּשְׁבְּ|translate=and he took captive}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַל־תֵּשְׁתְּ|translate=drink thou not}}; but {{GHGheb|text=וַיַרְא}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֵטְא}}.On {{GHGheb|text=־ִיתְ}} as an ending of the 2nd sing. fem. perf. Qal of verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}, see {{GHGpar|75|m}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|10|k}} However, in the examples where a mute closes the syllable, the final {{GHGterm|Šewâ}} comes somewhat nearer to a vocal {{GHGterm|Šewâ}}, especially as in almost all the cases a weakening of a final vowel has taken place, viz. {{GHGheb|text=אַתְּ}} ''ʾatte'' from {{GHGheb|text=אַתִּי}} ''ʾattî (ʾanti)'', {{GHGheb|text=קָטַלְתְּ}} from {{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫לְתִּי}} (cf. in this form, the 2nd sing. fem. perf. Qal, even {{GHGheb|text=בָּאתְ}}, after a vowel, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=4|verse=10}}, &c., according to the readings of Baer), {{GHGheb|text=יִשְׁבְּ}} ''yišbe'' from {{GHGheb|text=יִשְׁבֶּה}}, &c. The Arabic actually has a short vowel in analogous forms. In {{GHGheb|text=נֵרְדְּ}} borrowed from the Indian, as also in {{GHGheb|text=קשְׁטְ}} (''qōšṭ'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=22|verse=21}}; and in {{GHGheb|text=אַל־תּוֹסְףְּ|translate=ne addas|en=do not add}} (for which we should expect {{GHGheb|text=תּ֫וֹסֶף}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=30|verse=6}} the final mute of itself attracts a slight vowel sound. {{GHGmargin-letter|10|l}} Rem. The proper distinction between ''simple Šewâ mobile'' and ''quiescens'' depends on a correct understanding of the formation of syllables ({{GHGpar|26}}). The beginner may observe for the present, that
  1. {{GHGterm|Šewâ}} is always ''mobile''
    1. at the beginning of a word (except in {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתַּים}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּי}} {{GHGpar|97|b}}, note);
    2. under a consonant with {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גִּדְּפוּ}} ''gid-dephû'';
    3. after another {{GHGterm|Šewâ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יִקְטְלוּ}} ''yiqṭelû'' (except at the end of the word, see above, {{GHGpar|10|i|nonumber=1}}).
  2. {{GHGterm|Šewâ}} is ''quiescens''
    1. at the end of a word, also in the {{GHGheb|text=ךְ}};
    2. before another {{GHGterm|Šewâ}}.
{{GHGpar-heading|11|Other Signs which affect the Reading}} Very closely connected with the vowel points are the ''reading-signs'', which were probably introduced at the same time. Besides the diacritical point over {{GHGheb|text=שׂ}} and {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}}, a point is placed ''within'' a consonant

79.text:
to show that it has a stronger sound. On the other hand a horizontal stroke ({{GHGterm|Rāphè}}) ''over'' a consonant is a sign that it has ''not'' the stronger sound. According to the different purposes for which it is used the point is either
  1. {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}, a sign of strengthening ({{GHGpar|12}}); or
  2. {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}}, a sign of the harder pronunciation of certain consonants ({{GHGpar|13}}); or
  3. {{GHGterm|Mappîq}}, a sign to bring out the full consonantal value of letters which otherwise serve as vowel letters ({{GHGpar|7|b}}), especially in the case of {{GHGheb|text=ה}} at the end of the word ({{GHGpar|14|a}}).
The {{GHGterm|Rāphè}}, which excludes the insertion of any of these points, has almost entirely gone out of use in our printed texts ({{GHGpar|14|e}}).
{{GHGpar-heading|12|Dageš in general,Oort, {{GHGcite|title=Theol. Tijdschr.}} 1902, p. 376, maintains that ‘the Masoretes recognized no distinction between {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}} and {{GHGterm|forte}}. They used a {{GHGterm|Dageš}} where they considered that a letter had the sharp, not the soft or aspirated sound.’ This may be true; but the old-established distinction between the two kinds of {{GHGterm|Dageš}} is essential for the right understanding of the grammatical forms. and Dageš forte in particular}} Cf. Graetz, ‘Die mannigfache Anwendung u. Bedeut. des Dagesch,’ in {{GHGcite|title=Monatsschr. für Gesch. u. Wiss. d. Judent.}}, 1887, pp. 425 ff. and 473 ff. {{GHGmargin-letter|12|a}} '''1'''. {{GHGterm|Dageš}}, a point standing in the middle of a consonant,{{GHGterm|Wāw}} with {{GHGterm|Dageš}} ({{GHGheb|text=וּ}}) cannot in our printed texts be distinguished from a {{GHGterm|wāw}} pointed as {{GHGterm|Šûrĕq}} ({{GHGheb|text=וּ}}); in the latter case the point should stand higher up. The {{GHGheb|text=וּ|pron=û}} is, however, easily to be recognized since it cannot take a vowel before or under it. denotes, according to {{GHGpar|11}},
  1. the ''strengthening''Stade, {{GHGcite|title=Lehrb. der hebr. Gr.}}, Lpz. 1879, pp. 44, 103, rightly insists on the expression ''strengthened pronunciation'' instead of the older term ''doubling'', since the consonant in question is only written once. The common expression arises from the fact that in transcription a ''strengthened'' consonant can only be indicated by writing it as double. of a consonant ({{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קִטֵּל|pron=qiṭṭēl}} ({{GHGpar|20}}); or
  2. the ''harder'' pronunciation of the letters {{GHGheb|text=בְּגַדְכְּפַת}} ({{GHGterm|Dageš lene}}).
For a variety of the latter, now rarely used in our printed texts, see {{GHGpar|13|c}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|12|b}} The root {{GHGheb|text=דגשׁ}} in Syriac means {{GHGtranslate|to pierce through, to bore through}} (with sharp iron); hence the name {{GHGterm|Dageš}} is commonly explained, solely with reference to its form, by ''puncture, point''. But the names of all similar signs are derived rather from their grammatical significance. Accordingly {{GHGheb|text=דגשׁ}} may in the Masora have the sense: {{GHGtranslate|acuere}} ({{GHGtranslate|literam}}), i.e. to {{GHGtranslate|sharpen}} a letter, as well as to ''harden'' it, i.e. to pronounce it as hard and without aspiration. {{GHGheb|text=דָּגֵשׁ|translate=acuens (literam)}} would then be a sign of sharpening and hardening (like {{GHGterm|Mappîq}} {{GHGheb|text=מַפִּיק|translate=proferens|en=bringing out}}, as {{GHGtranslate|signum prolationis}}), for which purposes a ''prick'' of the ''pen'', or ''puncture'', was selected. The opposite of {{GHGterm|Dageš}} is {{GHGheb|text=רָפֶה|translate=soft}}, {{GHGpar|14|e}}, and {{GHGpar|22|n}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|12|c}} '''2'''. In grammar {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}, the ''sign of strengthening'', is the more important. It may be compared to the ''sicilicus'' of the Latins (''Lucul̂us'' for ''Lucullus'') or to the stroke over ''m̄'' and ''n̄''. In the unpointed text it is omitted, like the vowels and other reading signs. For the different kinds of {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}, see {{GHGpar|20}}.

80.text:
{{GHGpar-heading|13|Dageš lene}} {{center|Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, p. 114 ff.: Dagesh and Raphe.}} {{GHGmargin-letter|13|a}} '''1'''. {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}}, the sign of {{GHGterm|hardening}}, is in ordinary printed texts placed only within the {{GHGheb|text=בְּגַדְכְּפַת}} letters ({{GHGpar|6|n}}) as a sign that they should be pronounced with their original hard sound (without aspiration), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מֶלֶךְ|pron=mèlĕkh}}, but {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכּוֹ|pron=mal-kô}}; {{GHGheb|text=תָּפַר|pron=tāphár}}, but {{GHGheb|text=יִתְפֹּר|pron=yith-pōr}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁתָה|pron=šāthā}}, but {{GHGheb|text=יִשְׁתֶּה|pron=yiš-tè}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|13|b}} '''2'''. The cases in which a {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}} is to be inserted are stated in {{GHGpar|21}}. It occurs almost exclusively at the beginning of words and syllables. In the middle of the word it can easily be distinguished from {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}, since the latter always has a vowel before it, whereas {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}} never has; accordingly the {{GHGterm|Dageš}} in {{GHGheb|text=אַפִּי|pron=ʾappî}}, {{GHGheb|text=רַבִּים|pron=rabbîm}} must be {{GHGterm|forte}}, but in {{GHGheb|text=יִגְדַּל|pron=yigdal}} it is {{GHGterm|lene}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|13|c}} A variety of the {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}} is used in many manuscripts, as well as in Baer’s editions, though others (including Ginsburg in the first two cases, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, pp. 121, 130, 603, 662) reject it together with the Ḥaṭefs discussed in {{GHGpar|10|g}}. It is inserted in consonants other than the {{GHGterm|Begadkephath}} to call attention expressly to the beginning of a new syllable:
  1. when the same consonant precedes in close connexion, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בְּכָל־לִּבִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=9|verse=2}}, where, owing to the {{GHGterm|Dageš}}, the coalescing of the two {{GHGterm|Lameds}} is avoided;
  2. in cases like {{GHGheb|text=מַחְסִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=62|verse=8}} = ''maḥ-sî'' (not ''măḥa-sî'');
  3. according to some (including Baer; not in ed. Mant.) in {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} in the combination {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ לֹּא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=5}}, or {{GHGheb|text=לֹא לּוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=1|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=6|hidebook=1}} &c. (so always also in Ginsburg’s text, except in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=9}}); see also {{GHGpar|20|e}} and {{GHGpar|20|g|nonumber=1}}.
—Delitzsch appropriately gives the name of {{GHGterm|Dageš orthophonicum}} to this variety of {{GHGterm|Dageš}} ({{GHGcite|title=Bibl. Kommentar}}, 1874, on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=94|verse=12}}); cf. moreover Delitzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Luth. Ztschr.}}, 1863, p. 413; also his {{GHGcite|title=Complutensische Varianten zu dem Alttest. Texte}}, Lpz. 1878, p. 12. {{GHGmargin-letter|13|d}} '''3.''' When {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}} is placed in a {{GHGterm|Begadkephath}}, the strengthening necessarily excludes its aspiration, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַפִּי}}, from {{GHGheb|text=אַנְפִּי}}.
{{GHGpar-heading|14|Mappîq and Rāphè}} {{GHGmargin-letter|14|a}} '''1'''. {{GHGterm|Mappîq}}, llke {{GHGterm|Dageš}}, also a point ''within'' the consonant, serves in the letters {{GHGheb|text=א ה ו י}} as a sign that they are to be regarded as full consonants and not as vowel letters. In most editions of the text it is only used in the consonantal {{GHGheb|text=ה}} at the end of words (since {{GHGheb|text=ה}} can never be a vowel letter in the middle of a word), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גָּבַהּ|pron=gābháh}} (to be high), {{GHGheb|text=אַרְצָהּ|pron=ʾarṣāh}} (her land) which has a consonantal ending (shortened from ''-hā''), different from {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫רְצָה|pron=ʾárṣā}} (to the earth) which has a vowel ending. {{GHGmargin-letter|14|b}} Rem. 1. Without doubt such a ''Hē'' was distinctly aspirated like the Arabic ''Hā'' at the end of a syllable. There are, however, cases in which this {{GHGheb|text=ה}} has lost its consonantal character (the Mappîq of course disappearing too), so that it remains only as a vowel letter; cf. {{GHGpar|91|e}} on the 3rd fem. sing. {{GHGmargin-letter|14|c}}The name {{GHGheb|text=מַפִּיק}} means ''proferens'', i.e. a sign which brings out the sound of the letter distinctly, as a consonant. The same sign was selected for this

81.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par14 />and for {{GHGterm|Dageš}}, since both are intended to indicate a hard, i.e. a strong, sound. Hence {{GHGterm|Rāphè}} (see {{GHGpar|14|e|nonumber=1}}) is the opposite of both.

{{GHGmargin-letter|14|d}}
2. In MSS. Mappîq is also found with {{GHGheb|text=א}}, {{GHGheb|text=ו}}, {{GHGheb|text=י}}, to mark them expressly as consonants, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גּוֹיִ}} (''gôy''), {{GHGheb|text=קָוִ}} (''qāw'', ''qāu''), for which {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} is also used, as {{GHGheb|text=עֵשָׂוְ}}, &c. For the various statements of the Masora (where these points are treated as {{GHGterm|Dageš}}), see Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=The Massorah, letter}} {{GHGheb|text=א}}, § 5 (also {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, pp. 557, 609, 637, 770), and ‘The Dageshed Alephs in the Karlsruhe MS.’ (where these points are extremely frequent), in the {{GHGcite|title=Verhandlungen des Berliner Orientalisten-Kongresses}}, Berlin, i. 1881, p. 136 ff. The great differences in the statements found in the Masora point to different schools, one of which appears to have intended that every audible {{GHGheb|text=א}} should be pointed. In the printed editions the point occurs only four times with {{GHGheb|text=א}} ({{GHGheb|text=אׄ}} or {{GHGheb|text=אּ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=23|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=8|verse=18}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=33|verse=21}} ({{GHGheb|text=רֻאּוּ}}; where the point can be taken only as an orthophonetic sign, not with König as {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}). Cf. Delitzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Hiob}}, 2nd ed., p. 439 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|14|e}}
'''2.''' {{GHGterm|Rāphè}} ({{GHGheb|text=רָפֶה}} i.e. weak, soft), a horizontal stroke over the letter, is the opposite of both kinds of {{GHGterm|Dageš}} and {{GHGterm|Mappîq}}, but especially of {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}}. In exact manuscripts every {{GHGheb|text=בגדכפת}} letter has either {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}} or {{GHGterm|Rāphè}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מֶלֶךְֿ|pron=mèlĕkh}}, {{GHGheb|text=תָּפַֿר}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָׁתָֿה}}. In modern editions (except Ginsburg’s 1st ed.) {{GHGterm|Rāphè}} is used only when the absence of a {{GHGterm|Dageš}} or {{GHGterm|Mappîq}} requires to be expressly pointed out.<section end=par14 />

<section begin=par15 /><section begin=par13 />{{GHGpar-heading|15|The Accents}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|15|a}}On the ordinary accents (see below, {{GHGpar|15|e|nonumber=1}}), cf. W. Heidenheim, {{GHGheb|text=מִשְׁפְּטֵי הַטְּעָמִים}} [''The Laws of the Accents''], Rödelheim, 1808 (a compilation from older Jewish writers on the accents, with a commentary); W. Wickes (see also below), {{GHGheb|text=טעמי כ״א ספרים}} [''The Accents of the Twenty-one Books''], Oxford, 1887, an exhaustive investigation in English; J. M. Japhet, {{GHGcite|title=Die Accente der hl. Schrift}} (exclusive of the books {{GHGheb|text=אׄמׄתׄ}}), ed. by Heinemann, Frankf. a. M. 1896; Prätorius, {{GHGcite|title=Die Herkunft der hebr. Accente}}, Berlin, 1901, and (in answer to Gregory’s criticism in the {{GHGcite|title=TLZ.}} 1901, no. 22) {{GHGcite|title=Die Uebernahme der früh-mittelgriech. Neumen durch die Juden}}, Berlin, 1902; P. Kahle, ‘Zur Gesch. der hebr. Accente,’ {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 55 (1901), 167 ff. (1, on the earliest Jewish lists of accents; 2, on the mutual relation of the various systems of accentuation; on p. 179 ff. he deals with the accents of the 3rd system, see above, {{GHGpar|8|g}}, note); Margolis, art. ‘Accents,’ in the {{GHGcite|title=Jewish Encycl.}}, i (1901), 149 ff.; J. Adams, {{GHGcite|title=Sermons in Accents}}, London, 1906.—On the accents of the Books {{GHGheb|text=תא״ם}} (see below, {{GHGpar|15|h|nonumber=1}}), S. Baer, {{GHGheb|text=תורת אמת}} [{{GHGcite|title=Accentual Laws of the Books}} {{GHGheb|text=אמ״ת}}], Rödelheim, 1852, and his appendix to Delitzsch’s {{GHGcite|title=Psalmencommentar}}, vol. ii, Lpz. 1860, and in the 5th ed., 1894 (an epitome is given in Baer-Delitzsch’s {{GHGcite|title=Liber Psalmorum hebr.}}, Lpz. 1861, 1874, 1880); cf. also Delitzsch’s most instructive ‘Accentuologischer Commentar’ on Psalms 1–3, in his {{GHGcite|title=Psalmencommentar}} of 1874, as well as the numerous contributions to the accentual criticism of the text, &c., in the editions of Beer and Delitzsch, and in the commentaries of the latter; W. Wickes, {{GHGheb|text=טעמי אמ״ת}} [{{GHGcite|title=Accents of the Poet. Books}}], Oxford, 1881; Mitchell, in the {{GHGcite|title=Journal of Bibl. Lit.}}, 1891, p. 144 ff.; Beer and Strack, {{GHGcite|title=Dikduke ha-ṭ<sup>e</sup>amim}}, p. 17 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|15|b}}
'''1'''. As Prätorius (see above) has convincingly shown, the majority of the Hebrew accents, especially, according to Kahle (see above), the ‘Conjunctivi’, were adopted by the Jews from the neums and punctuation-marks found in Greek gospel-books, and, like these, their primary purpose was to regulate minutely the public reading of the sacred<section end=par15 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

82.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par15" />text. The complete transformation and amplification of the system (in three different forms, see {{GHGpar|8|g}}, note), which soon caused the Jews to forget its real origin, is clearly connected with the gradual change from the speaking voice in public reading to chanting or singing. The accents then served as a kind of musical notes.<ref>On the attempts of Christian scholars of the sixteenth century to express the Hebrew accents by musical notes, cf. Ortenberg, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}}. 1889, p. 534.</ref> Their value as such has, however, with the exception of a few traces, become lost in transmission. On the other hand, according to their original design they have also a twofold use which is still of the greatest importance for grammar (and syntax), viz. their value (''a'') as ''marking the tone'', (''b'') as ''marks of punctuation'' to indicate the logical (syntactical) relation of single words to their immediate surroundings, and thus to the whole sentence.<ref>At the same time it must not be forgotten that the value of the accent as a mark of punctuation is always relative; thus, e.g. ''ʾAthnâḥ'' as regards the logical structure of the sentence may at one time indicate a very important break (as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=4}}); at another, one which is almost imperceptible (as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=1}}).</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|15|c}}
'''2.''' As a mark of the tone the accent stands almost invariably (but see below, {{GHGpar|15|e|nonumber=1}}) with the syllable which has the principal tone in the word. This is usually the ultima, less frequently the penultima. Amongst the Jewish grammarians a word which has the tone on the ultima is called {{GHGterm|Milraʿ}} (Aram. {{GHGheb|text=מִלְרַע}} i.e. accented below<ref>‘Above’ in this sense means what comes before, ‘below’ is what comes after; cf. Bacher, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}}. 1907, p. 285 f.</ref>), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫ל|pron=qāṭál}}; a word which has the tone on the penultima is {{GHGterm|Milʿêl}} (Aram. {{GHGheb|text=מִלְעֵיל}}, accented ''above''), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מֶ֫לֶךְ|pron=mèlĕkh}}. Besides this, in many cases a ''secondary tone'' is indicated in the word by {{GHGterm|Mèthĕg}} (cf. {{GHGpar|16}}). Examples such as {{GHGheb|text=נַ֣עַמְדָה יָ֑חַד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=50|verse=8}} (cf. 40:18, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=2|verse=16}}) are regarded by the Jewish grammarians as even ''proparoxytone''.<ref>Cf. Delitzsch on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=18}}.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|15|d}}'''3.''' As marks of interpunctuation the accents are subdivided into those which ''separate'' (''Distinctivi'' or ''Domini'') and those which ''connect'' (''Conjunctivi'' or ''Servi''). Further a twofold system of accentuation is to be noted: (''a'') the common system found in twenty-one of the Books (the {{GHGheb|text=כ״א}} i.e. twenty-one), and (''b'') that used in the first three Books of the ''Hagiographa'', viz. Psalms, Proverbs, and Job, for which the ''vox memor.'' is {{GHGheb|text=אֱמֶת}}, from the initial consonants of the names, {{GHGheb|text=תְּהִלִּים}} Psalms, {{GHGheb|text=מִשְׁלֵי}} Proverbs, {{GHGheb|text=אִיּוֹב}} Job, or more correctly, according to their original sequence, {{GHGheb|text=תא״ם}} ({{GHGheb|text=תְּאֹם|translate=twin}}), so that {{GHGheb|text=טַֽעֲמֵי תא״ם}} means the accents (sing. {{GHGheb|text=טַעַם}}) of these three Books. The latter system is not only richer and more complicated in itself, but also musically more significant than the ordinary accentuation.
<section end="par15" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

83.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par15" />{{GHGmargin-letter|15|e}}
{{center|I. ''The Common Accents.''}}

Preliminary remark. The accents which are marked as {{GHGterm|prepositive}} stand to the right over or under the initial consonant of the word; those marked as {{GHGterm|postpositive}}, to the left over or under the last consonant. Consequently in both cases the tone-syllable must be ascertained independently of the accent (but cf. below, {{GHGpar|15|l|nonumber=1}}).

{{center|{{GHGmargin-letter|15|f}}A. Disjunctive Accents (''Distinctivi'' or ''Domini'').}}<ref>All the disjunctives occur in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=39|verse=2}}.—The earlier Jewish accentuologists already distinguish between {{GHGheb|text=מְלָכִים|translate=Reges|en=kings}} and {{GHGheb|text=מְשָֽׁרְתִים|translate=servi|en=servants}}. The division of the disjunctive accents into Imperatores, Reges, Duces, Comites, which became common amongst Christian grammarians, originated in the {{GHGcite|title=Scrutinium S. S. ex accentibus}} of Sam. Bohlius, Rostock, 1636, and, as the source of manifold confusion, had better be given up. The order of the accents in respect to their disjunctive power is shown in general by the above classification, following Wickes. In respect to the height of tone (in chanting) 1, 2, 5, 4, 8, which were ''low'' and long sustained notes, are to be distinguished from the ''high'' notes (7, 3<sup>a</sup>, 6, 13, 9), and the highest (3<sup>b</sup>, 11, 12, 10); cf. Wickes, {{GHGheb|text=ט׳ כ״א}} p. 12 ff.—The name {{GHGheb|text=טְעָמִים}} (later=''accents'' in general) was originally restricted to the disjunctives, see Kahle, 1. c., p. 169.</ref>

1. ( {{GHGheb|text=־ֽ}} ) {{GHGheb|text=סִלּוּק}} Sillûq (''end'') always with the tone-syllable of the last word before Sôph pāsûq ({{GHGheb|text=׃}}), the verse-divider, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הָאָֽרֶץ׃}}.

2. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֑}} ) {{GHGheb|text=אַתְנָח}} ʾAthnâḥ or {{GHGheb|text=אַתְנָֽחְתָּא}} ʾAthnaḥtā (''rest''), the principal divider within the verse.

3 ''a''. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֒}} ) {{GHGheb|text=סְגֽוֹלְתָּא}} S<sup>e</sup>gôltā, ''postpositive'', marks the fourth or fifth subordinate division, counting backwards from ʾAthnâḥ (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=7.28}}).

3 ''b''. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֓ ׀}} ) {{GHGheb|text=שַׁלְשֶׁלֶת}} Šalšèleth (i.e. ''chain''), as disjunctive, or Great Šalšèleth, distinguished by the following stroke<ref>This stroke is commonly confused with ''Paseq'', which has the same form. But Pâsēq (= ''restraining, dividing'', also incorrectly called P<sup>e</sup>sîq) is neither an independent accent, nor a constituent part of other accents, but is used as a mark for various purposes; see the Masoretic lists at the end of Baer’s editions, and Wickes, {{GHGcite|title=Accents of the Twenty-one Books}}, p. 120 ff., where Pâsēq is divided into {{GHGterm|distinctivum}}, {{GHGterm|emphaticum}}, {{GHGterm|homonymicum}}, and {{GHGterm|euphonicum}}. The conjecture of Olshausen (''Lehrb.'', p. 86 f.), that Pâsēq served also to point out marginal glosses subsequently interpolated into the text, has been further developed by E. von Ortenberg, ‘Die Bedeutung des Paseq für Quellenscheidung in den BB. d. A.T.,’ in {{GHGcite|title=Progr. des Domgymn. zu Verden}}, 1887, and in the article, ‘Paseq u. Legarmeh,’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1887, p. 301 ff. (but see Wickes, ibid. 1888, p. 149 ff.; also E. König, in the {{GHGcite|title=Ztschr. f. kirchl. Wiss. u. kirchl. Leben}}, 1889, parts 5 and 6; Maas, in {{GHGcite|title=Hebraica}}, v. 121 ff., viii. 89 ff.). Prätorius, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1899, p 683 ff., pointed out that ''Paseq'' (which is pre-masoretic and quite distinct from L<sup>e</sup>garmēh) besides being a divider (used especially for the sake of greater clearness) also served as a sign of abbreviation. For further treatment of {{GHGterm|Paseq}} see H. Grimme, ‘Pasekstudien,’ in the {{GHGcite|title=Bibl. Ztschr.}}, i. 337 ff., ii. 28 ff., and {{GHGcite|title=Psalmenprobleme}}, &c., Freiburg (Switzerland), 1902, p. 173, where it is argued that {{GHGterm|Paseq}} indicates variants in a difficult sentence; J. Kennedy, {{GHGcite|title=The Note-line in the Heb. Scriptures}}, Edinb. 1903, with an index of all the occurrences of {{GHGterm|Paseq}}, p. 117 ff. According to Kennedy the ‘note-line’, of which he distinguishes sixteen different kinds, is intended to draw attention to some peculiarity in the text; it existed long before the Masoretes, and was no longer understood by them. See, however, the reviews of E. König, {{GHGcite|title=Theol. stud. u. Krit.}}, 1904, p. 448 ff., G. Beer, {{GHGcite|title=TLZ}}. 1905, no. 3, and esp. A. Klostermann, {{GHGcite|title=Theol. Lit.-blatt}}, 1904, no. 13, with whom Ginsburg agrees ({{GHGcite|title=Verhandlungen des Hamb. Or.-kongresses von 1902}}, Leiden, 1904, p. 210 ff.) in showing that the tradition with regard to the 479 or 480 uses of {{GHGterm|Paseq}} is by no means uniform. The purpose of {{GHGterm|Paseq}} is clearly recognizable in the five old rules:
# as a divider between identical letters at the end and beginning of two words;
# between identical or very similar words;
# between words which are absolutely contradictory (as ''God'' and ''evil-doer'');
# between words which are liable to be wrongly connected;
# and lastly, between heterogeneous terms, as ‘Eleazar the High Priest, and Joshua’. 
But the assumption of a far-reaching critical importance in {{GHGterm|Paseq}} is at least doubtful.—Cf. also the important article by H. Fuchs, ‘Pesiq ein Glossenzeichen,’ in the {{GHGcite|title=Vierteljahrsschrift f. Bibelkunde}}, Aug. 1908, p. 1 ff. and p. 97 ff.</ref> from the conjunctive in the poetic accentuation, is used for<section end="par15" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

15. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֤}} ) {{GHGheb|text=מְהֻפָּךְ}} M<sup>e</sup>huppākh or {{GHGheb|text=מַהְפָּךְ}} Mahpākh.

16 ''a''. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֥}} ) {{GHGheb|text=מֵירְכָא}} or {{GHGheb|text=מֵֽארְכָא}} Mêr<sup>e</sup>khā, and

16 ''b''. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֦}} ) {{GHGheb|text=מ׳ כְפוּלָה}} Mêr<sup>e</sup>khā kh<sup>e</sup>phûl̄â or Double Mêr<sup>e</sup>khā.

18. ( {{GHGheb|text=̀־ָ}} ) {{GHGheb|text=אַזְלָא}} ʾAzlā, when associated with Gèreš (see above) also called Qadmā.

[21. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֖}} ) {{GHGheb|text=מְאַיְּלָא}} M<sup>e</sup>ʾayy<sup>e</sup>lā or {{GHGheb|text=מָֽאיְלָא}} Mây<sup>e</sup>lā, a variety of Ṭiphḥa, serves to mark the secondary tone in words which have Sillûq or ʾAthnâḥ, or which are united by Maqqēph with a word so accentuated, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וַיֵּצֵ֖א־נֹ֑חַ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=18}}.]


{{center|II. ''The Accents of the Books'' {{GHGheb|text=תא״ם}}.}}

{{center|{{GHGmargin-letter|15|h}} A. Distinctivi.}}

1. ( {{GHGheb|text=־ֽ}} ) Sillûq (see above, I, 1).

2. ( {{GHGheb|text= ־֫־֥ }} ) {{GHGheb|text=עוֹלֶה וְיוֹרֵד}} ʿÔlè w<sup>e</sup>yôrēd,<ref>Wrongly called also Mêr<sup>e</sup>khā m<sup>e</sup>huppākh (''Mêr<sup>e</sup>kha mahpakhatum''), although the accent underneath is in no way connected with Mêr<sup>e</sup>khā; cf. Wickes, l. c., p. 14.</ref> a stronger divider than

3. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֑}} ) ʾAthnâḥ (see above, I, 2). In shorter verses ʾAthnâh suffices as principal distinctive; in longer verses ''ʿÔlè w<sup>e</sup>yôrēd'' serves as such, and is then mostly followed by ʾAthnâḥ as the principal disjunctive of the second half of the verse.

4. ( {{GHGheb|text= ־ֹ}} ) R<sup>e</sup>bhi<sup>a</sup>ʿ gādôl (Great R<sup>e</sup>bhi<sup>a</sup>ʿ).

5. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֜֗}} ) R<sup>e</sup>bhi<sup>a</sup>ʿ mugrāš, i.e. R<sup>e</sup>bhi<sup>a</sup>ʿ with Gèreš on the same word.

6. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֓}} ) Great Šalšèleth (see above, I. 3 ''b'').

7. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֮}} ) {{GHGheb|text=צִנּוֹר}} Ṣinnôr (Zarqā), as {{GHGterm|postpositive}}, is easily distinguished from {{GHGheb|text=צִנּוֹרִית}} Ṣinnôrîth similarly placed, which is not an independent accent, but stands only over an open syllable before a consonant which has Mêr<sup>e</sup>khā or Mahpākh.

8. ( {{GHGheb|text=־ׄ}} ) R<sup>e</sup>bhi<sup>a</sup>ʿ qāṭôn (Little R<sup>e</sup>bhi<sup>a</sup>ʿ) immediately before ʿÔlè w<sup>e</sup>yôrēd.

9. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֭}} ) {{GHGheb|text=דְּחִי}} D<sup>e</sup>ḥî or Ṭiphḥā, {{GHGterm|prepositive}}, to the right underneath the initial consonant, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַ֭גּוֹי}} (consequently it does not mark the tone-syllable).

<references/></noinclude>

86.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par15" />10. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֡}} ) Pâzēr (see above, I, 11 ''a'').

11 ''a''. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֤ ׀}} ) M<sup>e</sup>huppākh l<sup>e</sup>garmēh, i.e. Mahpākh with a following stroke.

11 ''b''. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֨ ׀}} ) ʿAzlā l<sup>e</sup>garmēh, i.e. ʿAzlā with a following stroke.

{{GHGmargin-letter|15|i}}
{{center|B. Conjunctivi.}}

12. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֥}} ) Mêr<sup>e</sup>khā (see above, I. 16 ''a'').

13. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֧}} ) Mûnaḥ (see above, I. 14).

14. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֬}} ) {{GHGheb|text=עִלּוּי}} ʿIllûy or Mûnaḥ superior.

15. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֖}} ) {{GHGheb|text=טַרְחָא}} Ṭarḥā (under the tone-syllable, and thus easily distinguished from No. 9).

16. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֪}} ) Galgal or Yèraḥ (see above, I. 20).

17. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֤}} ) M<sup>e</sup>huppākh or Mahpākh (see above, I. 15).

18. ( {{GHGheb|text=̀־}} ) ʾAzlā (see above, I. 18).

19. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֓}} ) Šalšèleth q<sup>e</sup>ṭannā (Little Šalšèleth). The last three are distinguished from the disjunctives of the same name by the absence of the stroke.

[20. ( {{GHGheb|text=־֮}} ) Ṣinnôrîth, see above under No. 7.]

{{center|Remarks on the Accents

I. ''As Signs of the Tone.''}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|15|k}}
1. As in Greek and English (cf. {{polytonic|εἰμί}} and {{polytonic|εἶμι}}, ''cómpact'' and ''compáct'') so also in Hebrew, words which are written with the same consonants are occasionally distinguished by the position of the tone, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בָּנ֫וּ|pron=banú}} (they built), {{GHGheb|text=בָּ֫נוּ|pron=bánu}} (in us); {{GHGheb|text=קָ֫מָה|pron=qáma}} (she stood up), {{GHGheb|text=קָמָ֫ה|pron=qamá}} (standing up, {{GHGterm|fem.}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|15|l}}
2. As a rule the accent stands on the tone-syllable, and properly on its initial consonant. In the case of prepositives and postpositives alone (see above, {{GHGpar|15|e|nonumber=1}}) the tone-syllable must be ascertained independently of the accent. In many MSS. as well as in Baer’s editions of the text, the postpositive sign in foretoned words stands also over the tone-syllable after the analogy of Pašṭā (see above, I. 8 ''a'', note); e.g. {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֮רֶם֮ יִשְׁכָּ֒בוּ֒}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=4}}; so the prepositive sign in cases like {{GHGheb|text=וַ֠יְהִ֠י}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=13}}.

{{center|II. ''As Signs of Punctuation.''}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|15|m}}
3. In respect to this use of the accents, every verse is regarded as a period which closes with Sillûq, or in the figurative language of the grammarians, as a province (''ditio'') which is governed by the great distinctive at the end. According as the verse is long or short, i.e. the province great or small, there are several subordinate ''Domini'' of different grades, as governors of greater and smaller divisions. When possible, the subdivisions themselves are also split up into parts according to the law of dichotomy (see Wickes, {{GHGcite|title=The Accents of the Twenty-one Books}}, p. 29 ff).—When two or more ''equivalent'' accents (Zâqēph, R<sup>e</sup>bhi<sup>a</sup>ʿ) occur consecutively, the accent which precedes marks a greater division than the one which follows; cf. e.g. the Zâqēph, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=20}}<sup>''a''</sup>.

{{GHGmargin-letter|15|n}}
4. In general a conjunctive (''Servus'') unites only such words as are closely connected in sense, e.g. a noun with a following genitive or a noun with an
<section end="par15" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

87.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="2" user="Amire80" />{{GHGcorrected}}</noinclude><section begin="par15" />adjective. For the closest connexion between two or more words {{GHGterm|Maqqēph}} is added ({{GHGpar|16|a}}). 

{{GHGmargin-letter|15|o}}
5. The consecution of the several accents (especially the correspondence of disjunctives with their proper conjunctives) conforms in the most minute details to strict rules, for a further investigation of which we must refer to the above-mentioned works. Here, to avoid misunderstanding, we shall only notice further the rule that in the accentuation of the books {{GHGheb|text=תא״ם}}, the {{GHGterm|R<sup>e</sup>bhi<sup>a</sup>ʿ mugrāš}} before {{GHGterm|Sillûq}}, and the {{GHGterm|D<sup>e</sup>ḥi}} before {{GHGterm|ʾAthnâḥ}}, must be changed into conjunctives, unless at least two toneless syllables precede the principal disjunctive. For this purpose Š<sup>e</sup>wâ ''mobile'' after Qameṣ, Ṣere, or Ḥolem (with Metheg<ref>{{GHGcritic|Should be spelled Mèthĕg.|Amire80}}</ref>) is to be regarded as forming a syllable. After ʿOlè w<sup>e</sup>yôrēd the ʾAthnâḥ does not necessarily act as pausal (cf. Delitzsch on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=45|verse=6}}). The condition of our ordinary texts is corrupt, and the system of accents can only be studied in correct editions [see Wickes' two treatises].

{{GHGmargin-letter|15|p}}
6. A double accentuation occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=22}}, from {{GHGheb|text=וישכב}} onward (where the later accentuation, intended for public reading, aims at uniting<!-- vv and v will be fixed to proper links when GHGbible-ref will be properly rewritten in Lua. --> vv. 22 and 23 into ''one'', so as to pass rapidly over the unpleasant statement in v. 22); and in the Decalogue, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=2 ff.}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=5|verse=6 ff.}}. Here also the later (mainly superlinear) accentuation which closes the first verse with {{GHGheb|text=עבדים}} (instead of {{GHGheb|text=פני}}) is adopted simply for the purposes of public reading, in order to reduce the original twelve verses (with sublinear accentuation) to ten, the number of the Commandments. Thus {{GHGheb|text=עֲבָדִים}} at the end of v. 2 has Silluq<ref>{{GHGcritic|Should be spelled Sillûq.|Amire80}}</ref> (to close the verse) in the lower accentuation, but in the upper, which unites vv. 2-6 (the actual words of God) into a single period, only R<sup>e</sup>bhi<sup>a</sup>ʿ. Again {{GHGheb|text=פני}}, regarded as closing v. 3, is pointed {{GHGheb|text=פָּנָֽי}} (pausal Qameṣ with Silluq<ref>{{GHGcritic|Should be spelled Sillûq.|Amire80}}</ref>), but in the upper accentuation it is {{GHGheb|text=פָּנַ֗י}} with Pathaḥ because not in pause. (Originally there may have been a third accentuation requiring {{GHGheb|text=עֲבָדִ֑ים}} and {{GHGheb|text=פָּנָֽי}}, and thus representing vv. 2 and 3 as the first commandment.) Further the upper accentuation unites vv. 8-11 into one period, while in vv. 12-15 the lower accentuation combines commandments 5-8 into one verse. Cf. Geiger, {{GHGcite|title=Urschrift u. Übersetsungen der Bibel}}, p. 373 ; Japhet, {{GHGcite|title=op. cit.}}, p. 158, and esp. K. J. Grimm, {{GHGcite|title=Johns Hopkins Univ. Circ.}} xix (May, 1900), no. 145. {{:Gesenius' Hebrew Grammar/Additions and Corrections/63}}
<section end="par15" />
<section begin="par16" />{{GHGpar-heading|16|Of Maqqēph and Mèthĕg}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|16|a}}
These are both closely connected with the accents.

1. Maqqēph ({{GHGheb|text=מַקֵּף}} i.e. {{GHGterm|binder}}) is a small horizontal stroke between the upper part of two words which so connects them that in respect of tone and pointing they are regarded as one, and therefore have only one accent. Two, three, or even four words may be connected in this way, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־אָדָ֫ם|translate=every man}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־כָּל־עֵ֫שֶׂב|translate=every herb}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=29}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ|translate=all that he had}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=5}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|16|b}}
Certain monosyllabic prepositions and conjunctions, such as {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־|translate=to}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַד־|translate=until}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַל־|translate=upon}}, {{GHGheb|text=עִם־|translate=with}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַל־|translate=ne|en=do not}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִם־|translate=if}}, {{GHGtranslate|whether}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִן־|translate=from}}, {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־|translate=lest}}, are almost always found with a following Maqqēph, provided they have not become independent forms by being combined with prefixes, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מֵעַל}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֵעִם}}, in which case Maqqēph as a rule does not follow. Occasionally Maqqēph is replaced by a conjunctive accent (see above, {{GHGpar|9|u}}, 1 c), as, according to the Masora, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=27|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=25|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=29|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=9|verse=4}} in the case of {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֥ל כָּל־}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=47|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=60|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=3|verse=12}} in the case of {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}} the objective particle. Longer words are, however, {{Hyphenated word start|con|connected}}<section end="par16" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

88.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par16" />{{Hyphenated word end|nected|connected}} by Maqqēph with a following monosyllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הִתְהַלֶּךְ־נֹֽחַ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=9}}, {{GHGheb|text=וַֽיְהִי־כֵֽן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=7}}; or two words of more than one syllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעָֽה־עָשָׂר|translate=seventeen}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=11}}. Cf. the Greek proclitics {{polytonic|ἐν}}, {{polytonic|ἐκ}}, {{polytonic|εἰς}}, {{polytonic|εἰ}}, {{polytonic|ὡς}}, {{polytonic|οὐ}}, which are {{GHGterm|atonic}}, and lean on the following word. 

{{GHGmargin-letter|16|c}}
2. Mèthĕg<ref group="critic">{{GHGcritic|No breve on the last e is probably a printing error.|Amire80}}</ref> ({{GHGheb|text=מֶ֫תֶג}} i.e. {{GHGtranslate|a bridle}}), a small perpendicular stroke under the consonant to the left of the vowel, indicates most frequently the secondary stress or counter-tone, as opposed to the principal tone marked by the accents. It serves, however, in other cases to point out that the vowel should not be hastily passed over in pronunciation, but should be allowed its full sound. Hence other names of {{GHGterm|Mèthĕg}} are Maʾ<sup>a</sup>rîkh, i.e. {{GHGtranslate|lengthener}}, and {{GHGterm|Gaʿyā}}, i.e. {{GHGtranslate|raising}} of the voice, which is {{GHGterm|Great Gaʿyā}} with long vowels, otherwise {{GHGterm|Little Gaʿyā}}.<ref>Cf. as the source of this account of {{GHGterm|Mèthĕg}}, the exhaustive treatment by {{nowrap|S. Baer}}, ‘Mèthĕg-Setzung nach ihren überlieferten Gesetzen,’ in {{nowrap|A. Merx's}} {{GHGcite|title=Archiv für die wissenschaftl. Erforschung des A. Test.}}, Heft i, Halle, 1867, p. 56 ff., and Heft ii. 1868, p. 194 ff.; Baer and Strack, {{GHGcite|title=Dikduke ha-ṭ<sup>e</sup>amim}}, p. 30 ff.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|16|d}}
It is divided into: 1. The {{GHGterm|light Mèthĕg}}. This is subdivided again into (α) the ordinary {{GHGtranslate|Mèthĕg}} of the counter-tone, as a rule in the second (open) syllable before the tone, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאָדָ֫ם}} (cf. also such cases as {{GHGheb|text=מֶֽלֶךְ־צֹר}}); but also in the third when the second is closed, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאַרְבָּעִ֫ים}} (also in such cases as {{GHGheb|text=עֶֽבֶד־הַמֶּלֶךְ}}), and when the third is not suitable for it, even in the fourth (open) syllable before the tone. This Mèthĕg may be repeated in the fourth syllable before the tone, when it already stands in the second, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שָֽׁבֻעֹ֥תֵיכֶ֫ם}}. Finally it is always added to the vowel of an open ultima, which is joined by Maqqēph to a word beginning with a toneless syllable and so without Mèthĕg (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בְּנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵל}}, on the other hand {{GHGheb|text=רִשְׁפֵי־קָ֑שֶׁת}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־אֶֽהְיֶה}}), or to a word beginning with Š<sup>e</sup>wâ before the tone-syllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־לְךָ֫}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלֹמֹֽה־בְנִ֫י}} &c.; the object being to prevent the Š<sup>e</sup>wâ from becoming ''quiescent''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|16|e}}
The ordinary {{GHGterm|light Mèthĕg}} is omitted with a movable {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} {{GHGterm|copulative}}, consequently we do not find {{GHGheb|text=וּֽבָנִים}}, &c. (nor even {{GHGheb|text=וּֽבְנֵי}}, &c., contrary to ''b'', α; but {{GHGheb|text=וּֽזֲהַב}}<ref group="critic">{{GHGcritic|{{GHGheb|text=וּֽזֲהַ֛ב}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=12}} in Qoren Tanakh.|Amire80}}</ref>, &c., according to ''b'', δ, cf. {{GHGpar|10|g}} ''b'').

{{GHGmargin-letter|16|f}}
(b) The {{GHGterm|firm}} or {{GHGterm|indispensable Mèthĕg}}. (α) With all long vowels (except in certain cases, {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} {{GHGterm|copulative}}, see above), which are followed by a {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}} preceding the tone-syllable; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יִֽרְאוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=יִֽשְׁנוּ}} &c. (β) To emphasize a long vowel in a closed syllable immediately before Maqqēph, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שָֽׁת־לִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=25}} (not {{GHGpron|šŏth-li}}); hence also with {{GHGheb|text=כֹּֽל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=138|verse=2}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽת־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=26}} (for {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}}; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=מֵאֵֽת־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=15|verse=18}}, &c.). (γ) With Ṣere, which has become toneless through retraction of the tone, in order to prevent its being pronounced as S<sup>e</sup>gôl<ref group="critic">{{GHGcritic|Spelled S<sup>e</sup>ghôl, possibly a typo.|Amire80}}</ref>, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֹ֫הֵֽב דָּ֑עַת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=1}} (not {{GHGpron|ʾohĕbh}}). (δ) With all vowels before composite Š<sup>e</sup>wâ, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יַֽעֲמֹד}}, {{GHGheb|text=צֹֽעֲקִים}}, &c. (except when the following consonant is strengthened, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יִקְּֽבֶ֫נּוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=62|verse=2}}, because the strengthening by {{GHGterm|Dageš}} excludes the retarding of the vowel by {{GHGterm|Mèthĕg}}); so in the cases discussed in {{GHGpar|28|c}}, where a short vowel has taken the place of a Ḥaṭeph, as {{GHGheb|text=יַֽעַמְדוּ}}, &c. (ε) In the preformative syllable of all forms of {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה|translate=to be}}, and {{GHGheb|text=חָיָה|translate=to live}}, when {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ quiescens}} stands under the {{GHGheb|text=ה}} or {{GHGheb|text=ח}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יִֽהְיֶה}}, {{GHGheb|text=תִּֽחְיֶה}} ({{GHGpron|yih-yè}}, {{GHGpron|tiḥ-yè}}), &c., cf.<section end="par16" /><noinclude>
<references />
<references group="critic"/></noinclude>

89.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" />{{GHGcorrected}}</noinclude>
<section begin="par16" />{{GHGpar|63|q}}. (ζ) With the Qameṣ of the plural forms of {{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫יִת|translate=house}} (thus {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽתִּ֫ים}} {{GHGpron|bâttím}}, cf. {{GHGpar|96}} under {{GHGheb|text=בַּיִת}}), and with {{GHGheb|text=אָֽנָּ֫ה}}<ref>The common form is {{GHGheb|text=אָֽנָּ֫א}} with an accent on both syllables, in which case, according to Qimḥi, the tone is always to be placed on the former. For the above mode of writing and position of the tone cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=38|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=1|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=4|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=116|verse=4}}. {{:Gesenius' Hebrew Grammar/Additions and Corrections/65}}</ref> {{GHGtranslate|prithee!}} to guard against the pronunciation {{GHGpron|bŏttím}}, {{GHGpron|ŏnnā}}.—Every kind of light Mèthĕg may in certain circumstances be changed into a conjunctive accent, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בָּ֣תִּים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=34|verse=11}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|16|g}}
2. The grave {{GHGterm|Mèthĕg}} ({{GHGterm|Gaʿyā}} in the more limited sense) is especially employed in the following cases in order more distinctly to emphasize a short vowel or an initial Š<sup>e</sup>wâ: (''a'') with the Pathaḥ of the article or of the prefixes {{GHGheb|text=ב}}, {{GHGheb|text=כ}}, {{GHGheb|text=ל}}, when followed by ({{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} under a consonant without ({{GHGterm|Dageš}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַֽמְסִלָּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לַֽמְסִלָּה}} &c., but not before {{GHGheb|text=יְ}} (before which {{GHGheb|text=וַ}} also remains without {{GHGterm|Mèthĕg}}, with the exception of {{GHGheb|text=וַֽיְהִי}} and {{GHGheb|text=וַֽיְחִי}} when they are followed by {{GHGterm|Maqqēph}}, or accented with {{GHGterm|Pašṭā}}), nor before the tone-syllable of a word, and neither ''before'' nor ''after'' the common {{GHGterm|Mèthĕg}}; likewise not in words which are connected by a conjunctive accent with the following word; (''b'') with the interrogative {{GHGheb|text=הַ}} with {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} (except when it precedes {{GHGheb|text=יְ}}, {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}} or the tone-syllable of the word), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַֽאֵלֵךְ}}. When a Š<sup>e</sup>wâ follows the {{GHGheb|text=הַ}} and after the Š<sup>e</sup>wâ there is an untoned syllable, Baer places the {{GHGterm|Mèthĕg}} to the right of the {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} , e.g. {{GHGheb|text=ה{{מתג}}{{מפריד תווים}}{{פתח}}בְרָכָה}}<ref group="critic">{{GHGcritic-tech|The Mèthĕg is supposed to appear to the right of Pathaḥ, but it is possible that it its correct display is not supported on your system.|Amire80}}</ref> {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=38}} (but ed. Mant. and Ginsb. {{GHGheb|text=הַֽב׳}}); (''c'') with the Pathaḥ or S<sup>e</sup>gôl<ref group="critic">{{GHGcritic|The original printing S<sup>e</sup>gol is probably a printing error.|Amire80}}</ref> of the article before a guttural (which cannot take Dageš), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַֽחַיִּים}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽהָרִים}}.—The {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ-Gaʿyā}} ({{GHGvowel-holder|{{שווא}}{{מתג}}}}) is especially important in the accentuation of the {{GHGheb|text=תא״ם}}, for purposes of musical recitation; it stands chiefly in words whose principal tone is marked by a disjunctive without a preceding conjunctive, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וְֽהָיָ֗ה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=1|verse=3}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|16|h}}
3. The {{GHGterm|euphonic Gaʿyā}}, to ensure the distinct pronunciation of those consonants which in consequence of the loss of the tone, or because they close a syllable, might easily be neglected, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּשָּ֫בַֽע לוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=9}}; {{GHGheb|text=פַּדֶּ֫נָֽה אֲרָם}} (here to avoid a hiatus) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, or in such cases as {{GHGheb|text=רֽוּחַֽ־אֵל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=33|verse=4}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=תַּֽדְשֵׁא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=11}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|16|i}}
{{GHGterm|Mèthĕg}} (especially in the cases mentioned in 1, ''b'', ''a'') is a guide to correct pronunciation, since it distinguishes ā from ŏ (except in the case noted in {{GHGpar|9|v}}, ''b'') and î from ĭ; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָֽכְלָ֫ה}} {{GHGpron|ʾā-kh<sup>e</sup>lā}} (she has eaten), but {{GHGheb|text=אָכְלָ֫ה}} {{GHGpron|ʾŏkhlā}} (food), since the {{GHGheb|text=־ָ}} stands here in a toneless closed syllable, and must therefore be a short vowel; thus also {{GHGheb|text=יִֽרְא֫וּ}} {{GHGpron|yî-r<sup>e</sup>ʾû}} (they fear), but {{GHGheb|text=יִרְא֫וּ}} {{GHGpron|yirʾû}} (they see), {{GHGheb|text=יִֽשְׁנ֫וּ}} (they sleep), but {{GHGheb|text=יִשְׁנ֫וּ}} (they repeat). The Jewish grammarians, however, do not consider the syllables lengthened by Mèthĕg as open. They regard the Š<sup>e</sup>wâ as {{GHGterm|quiescent}} in cases like {{GHGheb|text=אָֽכְלָה}} and belonging to the preceding vowel; cf. Baer, {{GHGcite|title=Thorat ʾEmeth}}, p. 9, and in Merx's {{GHGcite|title=Archiv}}, i. p. 60, Rem. I, and especially {{GHGcite|title=Dikduke ha-ṭ<sup>e</sup>amim}}, p. 13.
<section end="par16" />
<section begin="par17" />{{GHGpar-heading|17|Of the Q<sup>e</sup>rê and K<sup>e</sup>thîbh. Masora marginalis and finalis}}

On Q<sup>e</sup>rê and K<sup>e</sup>thîbh see Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Intr.}}, p. 183 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|17|a}}
1. The margin of Biblical MSS. and editions exhibits variants of an early date ({{GHGpar|3|c}}), called {{GHGheb|text=קְרֵי}}<ref>On the necessity of the punctuation {{GHGheb|text=קְרֵי}} as passive participle {{nowrap|1=( = {{GHGterm|legendum|lang=la}})}} instead of {{GHGheb|text=קְרִי}} Q<sup>e</sup>ri, which was formerly common but is properly a past tense ({{GHGterm|lectum est|lang=la}}), see Kautzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Bibl.-Aram.}}, p. 81, note.</ref> {{GHGtranslate|to be read}}, since, according to
<section end="par17" /><noinclude>
<references />
<references group="critic" /></noinclude>

90.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par17 />the opinion of the Jewish critics, they are to be preferred to the {{GHGheb|text=כְּתִיב}}, i.e. what is written in the text, and are actually to be read 
instead of it. 

On this account the vowels of the marginal reading (the Q<sup>e</sup>rê) are placed under the consonants of the text, and in order to understand both readings properly, the vowels in the text must be applied to the 
marginal reading, while for the reading of the text (the K<sup>e</sup>thîbh) its own vowels are to be used. Thus in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=42|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲנַוְּ}} occurs in the text, in the margin {{GHGheb|text=אנחנו קרי}}. Read {{GHGheb|text=אֲנוּ|translate=we}} (or according to Jewish tradition {{GHGheb|text=אָנוּ}}) in the text, in the margin {{GHGheb|text=אֲנַ֫חְנוּ}}. A small circle or asterisk in the text always refers to the marginal reading. 

{{GHGmargin-letter|17|b}}
2. Words or consonants which are to be passed over in reading, and are therefore left unpointed, are called {{GHGheb|text=כְּתִיב וְלֹא קְרֵי}} ({{GHGtranslate|scriptum et non legendum|en=written and not to be read}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=את}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=38|verse=16}}, {{GHGheb|text=אם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=39|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGheb|text=ידרך}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=3|hidebook=1}}. Conversely, words not contained in the text, but required by the Masora (as indicated by the insertion of their vowels), are called {{GHGheb|text=קְרֵי וְלֹא כְּתִיב}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=8|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=31|verse=38}}. See further Strack, {{GHGcite|title=Prolegomena Critica}}, p. 85; {{GHGcite|title=Dikduke ha-ṭ<sup>e</sup>amim}}, §§ 62, 64; Blau, {{GHGcite|title=Masoretische Untersuchungen}}, p. 49 ff. 

{{GHGmargin-letter|17|c}}
3. In the case of some very common words, which are ''always'' to be read otherwise than according to the K<sup>e</sup>thîbh, it has not been considered necessary to place the Q<sup>e</sup>rê in the margin, but its vowels are simply attached to the word in the text. This {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê perpetuum|en=pereptual Qere}} occurs in the Pentateuch in {{GHGheb|text=הִוא}} (Q<sup>e</sup>rê {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}}) wherever {{GHGheb|text=הוא}} stands for the feminine ({{GHGpar|32|l}}), and in {{GHGheb|text=נַֽעֲרָ}} (K<sup>e</sup>thîbh {{GHGheb|text=נער}}, Q<sup>e</sup>rê {{GHGheb|text=נַֽעֲרָה}}) always, except in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=22|verse=19}} (but the Sam. text always has {{GHGheb|text=היא}}, {{GHGheb|text=נערה}}). The ordinary explanation of this supposed archaism, on the analogy of Greek {{polytonic|ὁ παῖς}} and {{polytonic|ἡ παῖς}}, our ''child'', is inadequate, since there is no trace elsewhere of this epicene use; {{GHGheb|text=נער}} for {{GHGheb|text=נערה}} is rather a survival of a system of orthography in which a final vowel was written defectively, as in {{GHGheb|text=קָטַלְתָּ}}; cf. {{GHGpar|2|n}}.—Other instances are: {{GHGheb|text=יִשָּׂשכָר}} ({{nowrap|Q. {{GHGheb|text=יִשָּׂכָר}}}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=18}} &c., see the {{GHGcite|title=Lexicon}}, and Baer and Delitzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Genesis}}, p. 84, and below, note to {{GHGpar|47|b}}; {{GHGheb|text=יְרֽוּשָׁלַ͏ִם}} ({{nowrap|Q. {{GHGheb|text=יְרֽוּשָׁלַ֫יִם}}}}), properly {{GHGheb|text=יְרֽוּשָׁלֵם}}; {{GHGheb|text=יְהֹוָה}} ({{nowrap|Q. {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנָי|translate=the Lord}}}}), or (after 
{{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנָי}}) {{GHGheb|text=יֱהֹוִה}}; ({{nowrap|Q. {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהִים}}}}) properly {{GHGheb|text=יַהְוֶה}} {{GHGpron|Yahwè}} (cf. {{GHGpar|102|m}}, and {{GHGpar|135|q}}, note); on {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵים}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּים}} for {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּי}}, see {{GHGpar|97|d}}, end.

{{GHGmargin-letter|17|d}}
4. The masoretic apparatus accompanying the biblical text is divided into (a) {{GHGterm|Masora marginalis|en=marginal Masora}}, consisting of (α) {{GHGterm|Masora (marginalis) magna|en=greater marginal Masora}} on the upper and lower margins of MSS.; (β) {{GHGterm|Masora (marginalis) parva|en=lesser marginal Masora}} between and on the right and left of the columns;<section end=par17 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

91.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Nostro Fidelis" /></noinclude><section begin="par17" />(''b'') ''Massora finalis'' at the end of the several books, counting Samuel, Kings, Minor Prophets, Ezra-Nehemiah, Chronicles, each as one book. On all three varieties see especially Ginsburg, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}, p. 423 ff., and the appendices containing (p. 983 ff.) the masoretic treatise from the St. Petersburg MS. of {{smaller|A.D.}} 1009, and (p. 1000 ff.) specimens of the ''Masora parva'' and ''magna'' on two chapters.

{{GHGmargin-letter|17|e}}
In nearly all printed editions only the ''Masora finalis'' is found, indicating the number of verses, the middle point of the book, &c., and a scanty selection from the ''Masora parva''. The following alphabetical list of technical expressions (some of them Aramaic) and abbreviations, may suffice with the help of the lexicon to elucidate the subject. Further details will be found in the appendix to Teile’s edition of the Hebrew O.T., p. 1222 ff.

{{GHGheb|text=אוֹת|translate=letter}}. {{GHGheb|text=אֶלָּא|translate=nisi, except|en=if not, except}}. {{GHGheb|text=אֶמְצַע|translate=middle}}. {{GHGheb|text=אס״ף}}={{GHGheb|text=אַתְנַח סוֹף פָּסוּק}} in the formula {{GHGheb|text=בְּלֹא אס״ף|translate=without ˒Athnaḥ ''or'' Soph-pasuq}} i.e. ''although no ˒Athnaḥ or Soph-pasuq is written''.

{{GHGheb|text=בְּ|translate=with}}, before names of vowels or accents, as {{GHGheb|text=קָ֫מֶץ בְּזָקֵף|translate=Qameṣ with Zaqeph}} used instead of Pathaḥ ({{GHGpar|29|i}}). –{{GHGheb|text=ב׳}} as a numeral=''two'', as in {{GHGheb|text=ב׳ טְעָמִים|translate=two accents}}. {{GHGheb|text=במקצת}}, see {{GHGheb|text=מִקְצָת}}. {{GHGheb|text=בנ״א}} = {{GHGheb|text=בְּנוּסְחָא אַֽחֲרֵינָא}} (Aramaic) {{GHGtranslate|in another copy}}; pl. {{GHGheb|text=בְּנוּסְחָן אַֽחֲרֵינָן}}. –{{GHGheb|text=בס״א}}={{GHGheb|text=בִּסְפָרִים אֲחֵרִים|translate=in other books}}. {{GHGheb|text=בָּתַר}} (Aram.) {{GHGtranslate|after}}.

{{GHGheb|text=דָּגּוּשׁ}} fem. {{GHGheb|text=דְּגוּשָׁה|translate=marked with Dageš}} (or ''Mappiq''). {{GHGheb|text=דַּף|translate=leaf, page}}.

{{GHGheb|text=זְעֵיר}} fem. {{GHGheb|text=זְעֵירָא}} (Aram.) {{GHGtranslate|small}}.

{{GHGheb|text=חוֹל|translate=profane, not sacred}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנַי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=2}} because not referring to God. {{GHGheb|text=חוּץ|translate=except}}. {{GHGheb|text=חָסֵר}} written ''defectively'', also ''wanting'' as {{GHGheb|text=ח׳ א׳|translate=˒aleph is omitted}}.

{{GHGheb|text=טַ֫עַם|translate=accent}} (see {{GHGheb|text=ב}}); {{GHGheb|text=טָעַם}} in Hiphil {{GHGtranslate|to chant an accent}}.

{{GHGheb|text=יַתִּיר|translate=superfluous}}.

{{GHGheb|text=כַּאן|translate=here}}. {{GHGheb|text=כְּלָל}} (Aram.) {{GHGtranslate|total}}, as adv. {{GHGtranslate|in general}}.

{{GHGheb|text=ל׳}}={{GHGheb|text=לֵית}} (Aram., from {{GHGheb|text=לָא אִית|translate=non est}})=the form ''is not'' found elsewhere.

{{GHGheb|text=מְדוּיָּק|translate=accurately corrected}}. {{GHGheb|text=מָלֵא|translate=full}} i.e. written {{GHGterm|plene}}. {{GHGheb|text=מִלְּמַ֫טָּה|translate=below}} = {{GHGheb|text=מִלְּרַע}} ({{GHGpar|15|c}}). {{GHGheb|text=מִלְמַ֫עְלָה}} = {{GHGheb|text=מִלְעֵיל}} ({{GHGpar|15|c}}). {{GHGheb|text=מְנוּזָּרוֹת|translate=separated}}, the name of the strangely formed Nûns before {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=107|verse=23}} ff. ({{GHGpar|5|n}}). {{GHGheb|text=מִקְרָא|translate=that which is read}}, the name for all the O.T. scriptures. {{GHGheb|text=מִקְצָת|translate=part}}.

{{GHGheb|text=נָח}} fem. {{GHGheb|text=נָחָה|translate=quiescent}}, i.e. not sounded. {{GHGheb|text=נֶעְלָם|translate=concealed}}, i.e. only retained orthographically. {{GHGheb|text=נִקּוּד|translate=a point}}. {{GHGheb|text=נָקוּד|translate=pointed}}.

{{GHGheb|text=ס״א}} see {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}. {{GHGheb|text=סִימָן}} {{polytonic|σημεῖον}}, {{GHGtranslate|sign}}, esp. ''a mnemonic word'' or, frequently, ''sentence''. {{GHGheb|text=סך׳}} = {{GHGheb|text=סְכוּם|translate=total}}. {{GHGheb|text=ס״ף}} = {{GHGheb|text=סוֹף פָּסוּק}} ({{GHGpar|15|f}}).

{{GHGheb|text=עַמּוּד|translate=column}} of a page.

{{GHGheb|text=פָּסוּק}} a masoretic ''verse''. {{GHGheb|text=פִּסְקָא|translate=a space}}, esp. in the phrase {{GHGheb|text=פ׳ בְאֶמְצַע פָּסוּק|translate=a space within a verse}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=22}}; cf. H. Grätz, {{GHGcite|title=Monatschrift für Gesch. u. Wiss. des Judentums}}, 1878, p. 481 ff., and H. Strack, ibid. 1879, p. 26 ff.

{{GHGheb|text=ק׳}}={{GHGheb|text=קְרֵי}}, see above, ''c''. {{GHGheb|text=קודם}} properly {{GHGheb|text=קֳדָם|translate=before}}. {{GHGheb|text=קָמוּץ}} fem. {{GHGheb|text=קְמוּצָה|translate=pointed with Qameṣ}}. {{GHGheb|text=קוֹרֵא|translate=reader}} of the sacred text.

{{GHGheb|text=רַבְּתָא}}, {{GHGheb|text=רַבְּתָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=רַבָּתִי}} (Aram., all fem. sing.) {{GHGtranslate|large}}.

{{GHGheb|text=תֵּיבָה|translate=word}} (consisting of more than one letter). {{GHGheb|text=תְּלוּיָה|translate=suspensa|en=suspended letter}} ({{GHGpar|5|n}}, 3). {{GHGheb|text=תְּרֵי}} (Aram.) {{GHGtranslate|two}}.<section end="par17" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

92.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Nahum" /></noinclude><section begin="par18" />{{center|CHAPTER II

PECULIARITIES AND CHANGES OF LETTERS: THE SYLLABLE AND THE TONE}}

<!-- section begins above -->{{GHGpar-heading|18|}}

The changes which take place in the forms of the various parts of speech, depend partly on the peculiar nature of certain classes of letters and the manner in which they affect the formation of syllables, partly on certain laws of the language in regard to syllables and the tone.
<section end="par18" />
<section begin="par19" />{{GHGpar-heading|19|Changes of Consonants}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|19|a}}
The changes which take place among consonants, owing to the formation of words, inflexion, euphony, or to influences connected with the progress of the language, are ''commutation'', ''assimilation'', ''rejection'', ''addition'', ''transposition'', ''softening''.

'''1.''' ''Commutation''<ref>Cf. Barth, {{GHGcite|title=Etymologische Forschungen}}, Lpz. 1893, p. 15 ff. (‘Lautverschiebungen’).</ref> may take place between consonants which are either ''homorganic'' or ''homogeneous'' (cf. {{GHGpar|6|q}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עָלַץ}}, {{GHGheb|text=עָלַס}}, {{GHGheb|text=עָלַז|translate=to exult}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָאָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָהָה}}, Aram. {{GHGheb|text=לְעָא|translate=to be weary}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָחַץ}} and {{GHGheb|text=נָחַץ|translate=to press}}, {{GHGheb|text=סָגַר}} and {{GHGheb|text=סָכַר|translate=to close}}, {{GHGheb|text=מָלַט}} and {{GHGheb|text=פָּלַט|translate=to escape}}. In process of time, and partly under the influence of Aramaic, the harder and rougher sounds especially were changed into the softer, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=צָחַק}} into {{GHGheb|text=שָׂחַק|translate=to laugh}}, {{GHGheb|text=גָּעַל}} into {{GHGheb|text=גָּאַל|translate=to reject}}, and the sibilants into the corresponding mutes: {{GHGheb|text=ז}} into {{GHGheb|text=ד}}, {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}} into {{GHGheb|text=ת}}, {{GHGheb|text=צ}} into {{GHGheb|text=ט}}. In many cases these mutes may be regarded as a return to an earlier stage of the pronunciation.

The interchange of consonants, however, belongs rather to the lexicographical treatment of stems<ref>See in the {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|Lexicon|A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament, based on the Thesaurus and Lexicon of Gesenius, by F. Brown, S. R. Driver, and C. A. Briggs, Oxford, 1906.}}}}, the preliminary remarks on the several consonants.</ref> than to grammatical inflexion. To the latter belong the interchange (''a'') of {{GHGheb|text=ת}} and {{GHGheb|text=ט}} in {{GHGterm|Hithpaʿēl}} ({{GHGpar|54|b}}); (''b'') of {{GHGheb|text=ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=י}} in verbs ''primae Yôd'' ({{GHGpar|69}}), {{GHGheb|text=יָלַד}} for {{GHGheb|text=וָלַד}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|19|b}}
'''2.''' ''Assimilation'' usually takes place when one consonant which closes a syllable passes over into another beginning the next syllable, and forms with it a strengthened letter, as ''illustris'' for ''inlustris'', ''affero'' for ''adfero'', {{polytonic|συλλαμβάνω}} for {{polytonic|συνλαμβάνω}}. In Hebrew this occurs,
{{nop}}<section end="par19" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

93.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Nahum" /></noinclude><section begin="par19" />{{GHGmargin-letter|19|c}}
(''a'') most frequently with {{GHGheb|text=נ‍}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מִשָּׁם}} (for ''min-šām'') ''from there'', {{GHGheb|text=מִזֶּה}} (for ''min-zè'') ''from this'', {{GHGheb|text=יִתֵּן}} (for ''yintēn'') ''he gives''. {{GHGheb|text=נ‍}} is ''not'' assimilated after the prefix {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לִנְגֹּף}}, nor as a rule before gutturals (except sometimes before {{GHGheb|text=ח}}), nor when it is the third consonant of the stem, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שָׁכַ֫נְתָּ}} (cf. however {{GHGheb|text=נָתַ֫תָּ}} for ''nāthántā'') except when another ''Nun'' follows, cf. {{GHGpar|44|o}}; nor in some isolated cases, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=58|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, all in the principal pause; on {{GHGheb|text=הִנְדֹּף}} and {{GHGheb|text=תִּנְדֹּף}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=68|verse=3}}, see {{GHGpar|51|k}}, and {{GHGpar|66|f}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|19|d}}
(''b'') Less frequently and only in special cases with {{GHGheb|text=ל}}, {{GHGheb|text=ת}}, {{GHGheb|text=ד}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יִקָּח}} (for ''yilqaḥ'') ''he takes''; {{GHGheb|text=מִדַּבֵּר}} for ''mithdabbēr''; {{GHGheb|text=יִטַּמָּא}} for ''yithṭammā''; {{GHGheb|text=תִּכּוֹנֵן}} for ''tithkônēn''; {{GHGheb|text=תִּנַּשֵּׂא}} for {{GHGheb|text=תִּתְנַשֵּׂא}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַחַ֫ת}} for ''ʾaḥadt''; but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=19}} for {{GHGheb|text=לָלַת}} read probably {{GHGheb|text=לָלֶ֫דֶת}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|19|e}}
(''c'') In isolated cases with {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, {{GHGheb|text=ו}}, {{GHGheb|text=י}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָֽנָּא|translate=prithee!}} if from {{GHGheb|text=אָהּ נָא}}; {{GHGheb|text=ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=י}} mostly before sibilants in the verbal forms enumerated in {{GHGpar|71}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|19|f}}
In all these cases, instead of the assimilated letter, a {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}} appears in the following consonant. {{GHGterm|Dageš}}, however, is omitted when the strengthened consonant would stand at the end of a word, since the strengthening would then be less audible ({{GHGpar|20|l}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַף|translate=nose}} (from ''ʾanp''), {{GHGheb|text=תֵּת|translate=to give}} (from ''tint'').

<!-- begin smaller font -->
The cases are less frequent where a weak letter is lost in pronunciation,<ref>Such a suppression of a letter is sometimes inaccurately called ‘backward assimilation’.</ref> and in place of it the preceding stronger sound is sharpened, i.e. takes {{GHGterm|Dageš}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קְטָלַ֫תּוּ}} from {{GHGheb|text=קְטָלַ֫תְהוּ}} ({{GHGpar|59|g}}). {{GHGheb|text=אֶסַּק}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֶסְלַק}} ({{GHGpar|66|e}}) is an Aramaism.
<!-- end smaller font -->

{{GHGmargin-letter|19|g}}
'''3.''' Complete ''rejection'' takes place only in the case of weaker consonants, especially the sonants {{GHGheb|text=נ}} and {{GHGheb|text=ל}}, the gutturals {{GHGheb|text=א}} and {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, and the two half vowels {{GHGheb|text=ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=י}}. Such rejection takes place,

{{GHGmargin-letter|19|h}}
(''a'') at the beginning of a word (''aphaeresis''), when these weak consonants ({{GHGheb|text=א}}, {{GHGheb|text=י}}, {{GHGheb|text=ל}}, {{GHGheb|text=נ‍}}) are not supported by a full vowel, but have only Š<sup>e</sup>wâ, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫חְנוּ|translate=we}}, also {{GHGheb|text=אֲנַ֫חְנוּ}}; {{GHGheb|text=דַּע}} for {{GHGheb|text=וְדַע}}; {{GHGheb|text=קַח}} for {{GHGheb|text=לְקַח}}; {{GHGheb|text=גַּשׁ}} for {{GHGheb|text=נְגַשׁ}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִי}} for {{GHGheb|text=נְהִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=2|verse=10}}.

<!-- begin smaller font -->
{{GHGmargin-letter|19|i}}
Aphaeresis of a weak consonant with a full vowel is supposed to occur in {{GHGheb|text=רַד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=11}} for {{GHGheb|text=יָרַד}}; in {{GHGheb|text=תַּ֫תָּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=22|verse=41}} for {{GHGheb|text=נָתַ֫תָּה}}; in {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹב}} for {{GHGheb|text=יָשׁוֹב}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Je|chapter=42|verse=10}}; on {{GHGheb|text=קָח}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=17|verse=5}} for {{GHGheb|text=לָקַח}}, and on {{GHGheb|text=קָחָם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=11|verse=3}} for {{GHGheb|text=לְקָחָם}}, see {{GHGpar|66|g}}, end. In reality, however, all these forms are to be regarded merely as old textual errors.
<!-- end smaller font -->

{{GHGmargin-letter|19|k}}
(''b'') In the middle of a word (''syncope''), when Š<sup>e</sup>wâ precedes the weak consonant<ref>Syncope of a strong consonant ({{GHGheb|text=ע}}) occurs in {{GHGheb|text=בִּי|translate=prithee!}} if this stands for {{GHGheb|text=בְּעִי}} (see {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|Lexicon|A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament, based on the Thesaurus and Lexicon of Gesenius, by F. Brown, S. R. Driver, and C. A. Briggs, Oxford, 1906.}}}}), also in {{GHGheb|text=ונשׁקה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=8|verse=8}}, {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}} for {{GHGheb|text=וְנִשְׁקְעָה}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=וְשָֽׁקְעָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=5|hidebook=1}}), and in {{GHGheb|text=בָּלָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=19|verse=3}} for {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽעֲלָה}} (as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=29|hidebook=1}}). Probably, however, {{GHGheb|text=ונשׁקה}} and {{GHGheb|text=בלה}} are only clerical errors, as is undoubtedly {{GHGheb|text=כָאֹר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=8|verse=8}} for {{GHGheb|text=כַיְאֹר}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=5|hidebook=1}}).</ref>; thus in the case of {{GHGheb|text=א}} (see further {{GHGpar|23|b}}''–f'', and<section end="par19" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

94.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Nahum" /></noinclude><section begin="par19" />{{GHGpar|68|b}}–{{GHGpar|68|k|nonumber=1}}), e.g. in {{GHGheb|text=מוּם}} for {{GHGheb|text=מְאוּם}}. As a rule in such cases, however, the {{GHGheb|text=א}} is orthographically retained, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לִקְרַאת}} for {{GHGheb|text=לְקִרְאַת}}. Syncope occurs frequently in the case of {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לַמֶּ֫לֶךְ}} for {{GHGheb|text=לְהַמֶּ֫לֶךְ}} ({{GHGpar|23|k}} and {{GHGpar|35|n}}), {{GHGheb|text=יַקְטִיל}} for {{GHGheb|text=יְהַקְטִיל}} ({{GHGpar|53|a}}).

Syncope of {{GHGheb|text=א}} with Š<sup>e</sup>wâ occurs in such cases as {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽאדֹנָי}} for {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽאֲדֹנָי}} (cf. {{GHGpar|102|m}}); {{GHGheb|text=וַאעְשִׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=11|verse=5}}.<ref>Frensdorff, ''Ochla Wʾochla'', p. 97 f., gives a list of forty-eight words with quiescent {{GHGheb|text=א}}.</ref> On the cases in which {{GHGheb|text=א}} is wholly omitted after the article, see {{GHGpar|35|d}}.

Finally, the elision of {{GHGheb|text=ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=י}} in verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} ({{GHGpar|75|h}}) is an instance of syncope.—On the syncope of {{GHGheb|text=ה}} between two vowels, see {{GHGpar|23|k}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|19|l}}
(''c'') At the end of a word (''apocope''), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גִּלֹה}} pr. name of a city (cf. {{GHGheb|text=גִּֽילֹנִי}} Gilonite); {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּרְא}}, where {{GHGheb|text=א}} though really rejected is orthographically retained, &c. On the apocope of {{GHGheb|text=ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=י}} in verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}, see {{GHGpar|24|g}}, and {{GHGpar|75|a}}.

<!-- begin smaller font -->
Bolder changes (especially by violent apocope), took place in earlier periods of the language, notably the weakening of the feminine ending {{GHGheb|text=־ַת|pron=ăth}} to {{GHGheb|text=־ָה|pron=ā}}, see {{GHGpar|44|a}}, and {{GHGpar|80|f}}.
<!-- end smaller font -->

{{GHGmargin-letter|19|m}}
'''4.''' To avoid harshness in pronunciation a helping sound, Aleph prosthetic<ref>This awkward term is at any rate as suitable as the name ''Alef protheticum'' proposed by Nestle, ''Marginalien u. Materialien'', Tübingen, 1893, p. 67 ff.</ref> with its vowel, is prefixed to some words, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֶזְרוֹעַ}} and {{GHGheb|text=זְרוֹעַ|translate=arm}} (cf. {{polytonic|χθές}}, {{polytonic|ἐχθές}}; ''spiritus'', French ''esprit'').—A prosthetic {{GHGheb|text=ע}} occurs probably in {{GHGheb|text=עַקְרָב|translate=scorpion}}; cf. Arab. ''ʿuṣfûr'' bird (stem ''ṣafara'').

{{GHGmargin-letter|19|n}}
'''5.''' ''Transposition''<ref>Cf. Barth, ''Etymologische Studien'', Lpz. 1893, p. 1 ff.; Königsberger, in ''Zeitschrift f. wissenschaftliche Theologie'', 1894, p. 451 ff.</ref> occurs only seldom in the grammar, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הִשְׁתַּמֵּר}} for {{GHGheb|text=הִתְשַׁמֵּר}} ({{GHGpar|54|b}}) for the sake of euphony; it is more frequent in the lexicon ({{GHGheb|text=כֶּ֫בֶשׂ}} and {{GHGheb|text=כֶּ֫שֶׂב|translate=lamb}}, {{GHGheb|text=שִׂמְלָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=שַׂלְמָה|translate=garment}}), but is mostly confined to sibilants and sonants.

{{GHGmargin-letter|19|o}}
'''6.''' ''Softening'' occurs e.g. in {{GHGheb|text=כּוֹכָב|translate=star}}, from ''kaukabh=kawkabh'' for ''kabhkabh'' (cf. Syriac ''raurab=rabrab''); {{GHGheb|text=טֽוֹטָפוֹת|translate=phylacteries}} for ''ṭaphṭāphôth''; according to the common opinion, also in {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ|translate=man}} from ''ʾinš'', cf. however {{GHGpar|96}}.
<section end="par19" />
<section begin="par20" />{{GHGpar-heading|20|The Strengthening (Sharpening) of Consonants}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|20|a}}
'''1.''' The strengthening of a consonant, indicated by {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}, is necessary and essential ({{GHGterm|Dageš necessarium}})

(''a'') when the same consonant would be written twice in succession<section end="par20" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

95.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Dovi" /></noinclude><section begin="par20" />without an intermediate vowel or {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}; thus we have {{GHGheb|text=נָתַ֫נּוּ}} for {{GHGheb|text=נָתַ֫נְנוּ|pron=nāthăn-nû}} and {{GHGheb|text=שַׁ֫תִּי}} for {{GHGheb|text=שַׁ֫תְתִּי}}.

(''b'') in cases of assimilation ({{GHGpar|19|b}}–{{GHGpar|19|f|nonumber=1}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יִתֵּן}} for ''yintēn''.

In both these cases the {{GHGterm|Dageš}} is called ''compensativum''.

(''c'') When it is characteristic of a grammatical form, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לָמַד|translate=he has learned}}, {{GHGheb|text=לִמַּד|translate=he has taught}} ({{GHGterm|Dageš characteristicum}}). In a wider sense this includes the cases in which a consonant is sharpened by Dageš forte, to preserve a preceding short vowel (which in an open syllable would have to be lengthened by {{GHGpar|26|e}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גְּמַלִּים|translate=camels}} for ''g<sup>e</sup>mālîm''; cf. {{GHGpar|93|ee}} and {{GHGpar|93|kk|nonumber=1|nosign=1}}, {{GHGpar|93|pp}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|20|b}}
This coalescing of two consonants as indicated above does not take place when the first has a vowel or {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}. In the latter case, according to the correct Masora, a {{GHGterm|compound Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} should be used, preceded by {{GHGterm|Methĕg}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הֽוֹלֲלִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=קִֽלֲלַת}}, &c. (cf. {{GHGpar|10|g|doublesign=1}}, {{GHGpar|16|f|nosign=1}}). This pointing is not used before the suffix {{GHGheb|text=ךָ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=תְּבָֽרֶכְךָ֫}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=4}}, but the first {{GHGheb|text=כ‍}} has a {{GHGterm|vocal Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, otherwise the second {{GHGheb|text=כ‍}} would have {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}}. Also when the former of the two consonants has been already strengthened by {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}, it can only have a {{GHGterm|vocal Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, and any further contraction is therefore impossible. This applies also to cases where {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}} has been omitted (see below, {{GHGpar|20|m|nonumber=1}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַֽלֲלוּ}} properly {{GHGheb|text=הַלְּלוּ}}=''hal-l<sup>e</sup>lû''. The form {{GHGheb|text=חַֽנְנֵ֫נִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=9|verse=14}} (not {{GHGheb|text=חָנְנֵ֫נִי}}) might be explained as imperat. Piʿēl={{GHGheb|text=חַנְּנֵ֫נִי}}; if it were imperat. {{GHGterm|Qal}} the non-contraction of the monosyllabic root would be as strange as it is in {{GHGheb|text=שָׁדְדוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=28}}, and in the imperf. {{GHGheb|text=יְשָׁדְדֵם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=5|verse=6}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|20|c}}
'''2.''' A consonant is sometimes strengthened merely for the sake of ''euphony'' ({{GHGterm|Dageš euphonicum}}), and the strengthening is then not so essential. This occurs<ref>Cf. Baer, ‘''De primarum vocabulorum literarum dagessatione'',’ in his ''Liber Proverbiorum'', Lpz. 1880. pp. vii–xv; F. Prätorius, ‘Über den Ursprung des Dag. f. conjunctivum,’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1883, p. 17 ff. (ascribed to an original assimilation of {{GHGheb|text=ת}} or {{GHGheb|text=נ‍}}).</ref>—
