The forms enclosed in parentheses are the less common. A table of these pronouns with their shortened forms (''pronominal suffixes'') is given in Paradigm A at the end of this Grammar. {{center|Remarks. ''First Person.''}} {{GHGmargin-letter|32|c}} 1. The form {{GHGheb|text=אָֽנֹכִי}} is less frequent than {{GHGheb|text=אֲנִי}}.On the prevalence of {{GHGheb|text=אָנֹכִי}} in the earlier Books compare the statistics collected by Giesebrecht in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1881, p. 251 ff., partly contested by Driver in the {{GHGcite|title=Journal of Philology}}, 1882, vol. xi. p. 222 ff. (but cf. his ''Introduction'', ed. 6, p. 135, line 1 f.), but thoroughly established by König in {{GHGcite|title=Theol. Stud. u. Krit.}}, 1893, pp. 464 ff. and 478, and in his {{GHGcite|title=Einleitung in das A.T.}}, p. 168, &c. In some of the latest books {{GHGheb|text=אנכי}} is not found at all, and hardly at all in the Talmud. [For details see the {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|Lexicon|A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament, based on the Thesaurus and Lexicon of Gesenius, by F. Brown, S. R. Driver, and C. A. Briggs, Oxford, 1906.}}}}, s. v. {{GHGheb|text=אֲנֹי}} and {{GHGheb|text=אָנֹכִי}}.] The former occurs in

130.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="46.39.50.179" /></noinclude><section begin="par32" />Phoenician, Moabite, and Assyrian, but in no other of the kindred dialects;<ref>In Phoenician and Moabite (inscription of Mêšaʿ, line 1) it is written {{GHGheb|text=אנך}}, without the final {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}}. In Punic it was pronounced ''anec'' (Plaut. ''Poen.'' 5, 1, 8) or ''anech'' (5, 2, 35). Cf. Schröder, ''Phöniz. Sprache'', p. 143. In Assyrian the corresponding form is ''anaku'', in old Egyptian ''anek'', Coptic ''anok, nok''.</ref> from the latter the suffixes are derived (§ 33). The ''ô'' most probably results from an obscuring of an original ''â'' (cf. Aram. {{GHGheb|text=אֲנָא}}, Arab. ''’ána''). The pausal form {{GHGheb|text=אָ֫נִי}} occurs not only with small disjunctive accents, but even with conjunctives; so always in {{GHGheb|text=חַי אָ֫נִי|translate=as I live!}} also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=18}} with Munaḥ, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=125}} with Merkha (which, however, has been altered from D<sup>e</sup>ḥî), and twice in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=1|verse=6}}. In all these cases there is manifestly a disagreement between the vocalization already established and the special laws regulating the system of accentuation.

{{GHGmargin-letter|32|d}}
2. The formation of the plural, in this and the other persons, exhibits a certain analogy with that of the noun, while at the same time (like the pronouns of other languages) it is characterized by many differences and peculiarities. The short form {{GHGheb|text=(אָנוּ) אנו}} from which the suffix is derived occurs only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=42|verse=6}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}}. The form {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫חְנוּ}} (cf. {{GHGpar|19|h}}) only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=7.8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=32|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|verse=42}}; {{GHGheb|text=נָחְ֑נוּ}} in {{GHGterm|pause}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=11}}; in Arabic ''năḥnu'' is the regular form. In the Mišna {{GHGheb|text=(אָנוּ) אנו}} has altogether supplanted the longer forms.

{{GHGmargin-letter|32|e}}
3. The pronoun of the 1st person only is, as a rule in languages, of the ''common gender'', because the person who is present and speaking needs no further indication of gender, as does the 2nd person, who is addressed (in Greek, Latin, English, &c., this distinction is also lacking), and still more the 3rd person who is absent.

{{center|II. ''Second Person.''}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|32|f}}
4. The forms of the 2nd person {{GHGheb|text=אַתָּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַתְּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַתֶּם}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַתֵּ֫נָה}}, &c., are contracted from ''’antā'', &c. The kindred languages have retained the ''n'' before the {{GHGheb|text=ת}}, e.g. Arab. ''’ántā'', fem. ''’ánti'', thou; pl. ''’ántum'', fem. ''’antúnna'', ye. In Syriac {{GHGheb|text=אַנת}}, fem. {{GHGheb|text=אַנתי}} are written, but both are pronounced ''’at''. In Western Aramaic {{GHGheb|text=אַנְתְּ}} is usual for both genders.

{{GHGmargin-letter|32|g}}
{{GHGheb|text=אַתָּ}} (without {{GHGheb|text=ה}}) occurs five times, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=6|verse=4}}, always as {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}}, with {{GHGheb|text=אַתָּה}} as {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}. In three places {{GHGheb|text=אַתְּ}} appears as a masculine, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=5|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=28|verse=14}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|32|h}}
The feminine form was originally {{GHGheb|text=אַתִּי}} as in Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic. This form is found seven times as {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=17|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=14|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=16.23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=8|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=36|verse=13}}) and appears also in the corresponding personal ending of verbs (see {{GHGpar|44|f}}), especially, and necessarily, before suffixes, as {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתִּ֫ינִי}}, {{GHGpar|59|a}} [c]; cf. also ''î'' as the ending of the 2nd fem. sing. of the imperative and imperfect. The final ''î'' was, however, gradually dropped in pronunciation, just as in Syriac (see above, f) it was eventually only written, not pronounced. The {{GHGheb|text=י}} therefore finally disappeared (cf. {{GHGpar|10|k}}), and hence the Masoretes, even in these seven passages, have pointed the word in the text as {{GHGheb|text=אַתְּי}} to indicate the {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} {{GHGheb|text=אַתְּ}} (see § 17). The same final {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}} appears in the rare (Aramaic) forms of the suffix {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ֫ כִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יְכִי}} (§§ 58, 91).

{{GHGmargin-letter|32|i}}
5. The plurals {{GHGheb|text=אַתֶּם}} (with the second vowel assimilated to the fem. form) and {{GHGheb|text=(אַתֶּן) אַתֵּן}}, with the tone on the ultima, only partially correspond to the assumed ground-forms ''ʾantumū'', fem. ''ʾantinnā'', Arab. ''ʾ{{GHGtranslit|a-brev-acut}}ntŭm'' (Aram. {{GHGheb|text=אַתּוּן}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַנְתּוּן}}) and ''ʾăntú̆nna'' (Aram. {{GHGheb|text=אַתֵּין}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַנְתֵּין}}). The form {{GHGheb|text=אַתֵּן}} is found only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=34|verse=31}} (so Qimḥi expressly, others {{GHGheb|text=אַתֶּן}}); {{GHGheb|text=אַתֵּ֫נָה}} (for which some MSS. have<section end="par32" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

131.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par32 />{{GHGheb|text=אַתֵּ֫נָּה}}) only four times, viz. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=11.20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=34|verse=17|hidebook=1}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=20|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=אַתֶּם}} (before a {{GHGheb|text=מ‍}}) is even used as feminine.

{{center|III. ''Third Person.''}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|32|k}}
6. (''a'') In {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}} and {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}} (''hû'' and ''hî'') the {{GHGheb|text=א}} (corresponding to the ''ʾElif of prolongation'' in Arabic, cf. {{GHGpar|23|i}}) might be regarded only as an orthographic addition closing the final long vowel, as in {{GHGheb|text=לוּא}}, {{GHGheb|text=נָקִיא}}, &c. The {{GHGheb|text=א}} is, however, always written in the case of the separate pronouns,<ref>In the inscription of King Mêšaʿ (see {{GHGpar|2|d}}), lines 6 and 27, we find {{GHGheb|text=הא}} for {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}}, and in the inscription of ʾEšmunʿazar, line 22, for {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}}, but in the Zenjirli inscriptions (see {{GHGpar|1|m}}) both {{GHGheb|text=הא}} and {{GHGheb|text=הו}} occur (Hadad i, l. 29).</ref> and only as a toneless suffix ({{GHGpar|33|a}}) does {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}} appear as {{GHGheb|text=הוּ}}, while {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}} becomes {{GHGheb|text=הָ}}. In Arabic (as in Syriac) they are written {{GHGheb|text=הו}} and {{GHGheb|text=הי}} but pronounced ''húwă'' and ''hı́yă'', and in Vulgar Arabic even ''húwwa'' and ''hı́yya''. This Arabic pronunciation alone would not indeed be decisive, since the vowel complement might have arisen from the more consonantal pronunciation of the {{GHGheb|text=ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=י}}; but the Ethiopic ''weʾ<sup>e</sup>tû'' (''=huʾa-tû'') for {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}}, ''yeʾ<sup>e</sup>tî'' (''=hiʾa-tî'') for {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}} (cf. also the Assyrian ''ya-u-a'' for {{GHGheb|text=יֵהוּא}}) show that the {{GHGheb|text=א}} was original and indicated an original vocalic termination of the two words. According to Philippi ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xxviii. 175 and xxix. 371 ff.) {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}} arose from a primitive Semitic ''ha-va'', {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}} from ''ha-ya''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|32|l}}
(''b'') The form {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}} also stands in the consonantal text ({{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}}) of the Pentateuch<ref>Also in twelve places in the Babylonian Codex (Prophets) of 916 {{smaller|A.D.}}; cf. Baer, ''Ezechiel'', p. 108 f.; Buhl, ''Canon and Text of the O.T.'' (Edinb. 1892), p. 240.</ref> (with the exception of eleven places) for the ''fem''. {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}}. In all such cases the Masora, by the punctuation {{GHGheb|text=הִוא}}, has indicated the {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}} ({{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} perpetuum, see § 17). The old explanation regarded this phenomenon as an archaism which was incorrectly removed by the Masoretes. This assumption is, however, clearly untenable, if we consider (1) that no other Semitic language is without the quite indispensable distinction of gender in the separate pronoun of the 3rd pers.; (2) that this distinction does occur eleven times in the Pentateuch, and that in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=5|verse=13.14}} {{GHGheb|text=הִוא}} and {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}} are found close to one another; (3) that outside the Pentateuch the distinction is found in the oldest documents, so that the {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}} cannot be regarded as having been subsequently adopted from the Aramaic; (4) that those parts of the book of Joshua which certainly formed a constituent part of the original sources of the Pentateuch, know nothing of this epicene use of {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}}. Consequently there only remains the hypothesis, that the writing of {{GHGheb|text=הוא}} for {{GHGheb|text=היא}} rests on an orthographical peculiarity which in some recension of the Pentateuch-text was almost consistently followed, but was afterwards very properly rejected by the Masoretes. The orthography was, however, peculiar to the Pentateuch-text alone, since it is unnecessary to follow the Masora in writing {{GHGheb|text=חִיא}} for {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=17|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=11}}, or {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}} for {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=5|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=29|verse=16}}. The Samaritan recension of the Pentateuch has the correct form in the {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}} throughout. Levy’s explanation of this strange practice of the Masoretes is evidently right, viz. that originally {{GHGheb|text=הא}} was written for both forms (see k, note), and was almost everywhere, irrespective of gender, expanded into {{GHGheb|text=הוא}}. On the whole question see Driver, ''Leviticus'' (in Haupt’s Bible), p. 25 f. In the text Driver always reads {{GHGheb|text=הא}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|32|m}}
7. The plural forms {{GHGheb|text=(הֵ֫מָּה) הֵם}} and {{GHGheb|text=הֵ֫נָּה}} (after ''prefixes'' {{GHGheb|text=הֵן}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֶן}}) are of doubtful origin, but {{GHGheb|text=הֵם}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֵמָּה}} have probably been assimilated to {{GHGheb|text=הֵ֫נָּה}} which goes back to a form ''hı́nnā''. In Western Aram. {{GHGheb|text=הִמּוֹן}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִמּוֹ}} ({{GHGheb|text=הִנּוּן}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִנּוּן}}), Syr. ''henûn''<section end=par32 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

132.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par32 />(''ʾenûn''), Arab. ''húmû'' (archaic form of ''hum''), and Ethiop. ''hômû'', an ''ô'' or ''ô'' is appended, which in Hebrew seems to reappear in the poetical suffixes {{GHGheb|text=־מוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ָ֫ מוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ֫ מוֹ}} ({{GHGpar|91|l}}, 3).

{{GHGmargin-letter|32|n}}
In some passages {{GHGheb|text=הֵ֫מָּה}} stands for the feminine ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=5|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=6|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=22}}; cf. the use of the suffix of the 3rd masc. for the 3rd fem., {{GHGpar|135|o}} and {{GHGpar|145|t}}). For the quite anomalous {{GHGheb|text=עַד־הֵם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=18}} read {{GHGheb|text=עָֽדֵיהֶם}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=32|verse=12}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|32|o}}
8. The pronouns of the 3rd person may refer to ''things'' as well as persons. On their meaning as ''demonstratives'' see {{GHGpar|136}}.<section end=par32 />

<section begin=par33 />{{GHGpar-heading|33|Pronominal Suffixes}}

Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Semit. Sprachwiss.}}, p. 100 f.; {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, i. 306 ff. J. Barth, ‘Beiträge zur Suffixlehre des Nerdsemit.,’ in the {{GHGcite|title=Amer. Journ. of Sem. Lang.}}, 1901, p. 193 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|33|a}}
'''1.''' The independent principal forms of the personal pronoun (the ''separate pronoun''), given in the preceding section, express only the nominative.<ref>On apparent exceptions see {{GHGpar|135|d}}.</ref> The accusative and genitive are expressed by forms, usually shorter, joined to the end of verbs, nouns, and particles (''pronominal suffixes'' or simply ''suffixes''); e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הוּ}} (toneless) and {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} (from ''āhû'') ''eum'' and ''eius'', {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתִּ֫יהוּ|translate=I have killed him}} (also {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתִּיו}}), {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתָּ֫הוּ}} or (with ''āhû'' contracted into ''ô'') {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתּ֫וֹ|translate=thou hast killed him}}; {{GHGheb|text=אוֹר֫וֹ}} (also {{GHGheb|text=אוֹרֵ֫הוּ}}) ''lux eius''.

The same method is employed in all the other Semitic languages, as well as in the Egyptian, Persian, Finnish, Tartar, and others; in Greek, Latin, and German we find only slight traces of the kind, e.g. German, ''er gab’s'' for ''er gab es''; Greek, πατήρ μου for πατὴρ ἐμοῦ; Latin, ''eccum, eccos'', &c., in Plautus and Terence for ''ecce eum, ecce eos''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|33|b}}
'''2.''' The case which these suffixes represent is—

(''a'') When joined to verbs, the accusative (cf., however, {{GHGpar|117|x}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתִּ֫יהוּ}} I have killed ''him''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|33|c}}
(''b'') When affixed to substantives, the genitive (like πατήρ μου, ''pater eius''). They then serve as ''possessive pronouns'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָבִי}} (''ʾābh-î'') ''my father'', {{GHGheb|text=סוּסוֹ|translate=his horse}}, which may be either ''equus eius'' or ''equus suus''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|33|d}}
(''c'') When joined to particles, either the genitive or accusative, according as the particles originally expressed the idea of a noun or a verb, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בֵּינִי}}, literally ''interstitium mei'', ''between me'' (cf. ''mea causa''); but {{GHGheb|text=הִנְנִי|translate=behold me}}, ''ecce me''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|33|e}}
(''d'') Where, according to the Indo-Germanic case-system, the dative or ablative of the pronoun is required, the suffixes in Hebrew are joined to prepositions expressing those cases ({{GHGheb|text=לְ}} sign of the dative, {{GHGheb|text=בְּ|translate=in}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִן|translate=from}}, § 102), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ|translate=to him}} (''e''i) and ''to himself'' (''sibi''), {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹ|translate=in him}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִנִּי}} (usually {{GHGheb|text=מִמֶּ֫נִּי}}) ''from me''.
<section end=par33 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

133.text:
{{GHGmargin-letter|33|f}} '''3.''' The suffixes of the 2nd person ({{GHGheb|text=־ְךָ}}, &c.) are all formed with a ''k''-sound, not, like the ''separate'' pronouns of the 2nd person, with a ''t''-sound. So in all the Semitic languages, in Ethiopic even in the verbal form (''qatalka'', ''thou hast killed''=Hebr. {{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫לְתָּ}}). {{GHGmargin-letter|33|g}} '''4.''' The ''suffix of the verb'' (the accusative) and the ''suffix of the noun'' (the genitive) coincide in most forms, but some differ, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=־נִי|translate=me}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ִי|translate=my}}. Paradigm A at the end of the Grammar gives a table of all the forms of the ''separate pronoun'' and the ''suffixes''; a fuller treatment of the {{GHGterm|verbal suffix}} and the mode of attaching it to the verb will be found in {{GHGpar|58|ff}}., of the ''noun-suffix'' in {{GHGpar|91}}, of the prepositions with suffixes in {{GHGpar|103}}, of adverbs with suffixes {{GHGpar|100|o}}.
{{GHGpar-heading|34|The Demonstrative Pronoun}} {{GHGmargin-letter|34|a}}
{| |rowspan=2| Sing. ''this'' |m. | {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}}In many languages the demonstratives begin with a ''d''-sound (hence called the ''demonstrative sound'') which, however, sometimes interchanges with a sibilant. Cf. Aram. {{GHGheb|text=דֵּן}}, {{GHGheb|text=דֵּךְ}} {{GHGterm|masc.}}, {{GHGheb|text=דָּא}}, {{GHGheb|text=דָּךְ}} {{GHGterm|fem.}} (this); Sansk. ''sa, sā, tat''; Gothic ''sa, sô, thata''; Germ. ''da, der, die, das''; and Eng. ''the, this, that'', &c. Cf. J. Barth, ‘''Zum semit. Demonstr''. ''ḏ'',’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 59, 159 ff., and 633 ff.; {{GHGcite|title=Sprachwiss. Untersuchungen zum Semit.}}, Lpz. 1907, p. 30 ff. [See the {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|Lexicon|A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament, based on the Thesaurus and Lexicon of Gesenius, by F. Brown, S. R. Driver, and C. A. Briggs, Oxford, 1906.}}}}, s. v. {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}}, and Aram. {{GHGheb|text=דא}}, {{GHGheb|text=די}}.] | Plur. com. ''these'' | {{GHGheb|text=אֵ֫לֶּה}} (rarely {{GHGheb|text=אֵל}}) |- | f. | {{GHGheb|text=זֹאת}} ({{GHGheb|text=זֹה}}, {{GHGheb|text=זוֹ}})That {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}} may stand for the feminine, cannot be proved either from {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=28}} or from the certainly corrupt passage in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=17}}. | | |}
{{GHGmargin-letter|34|b}} Rem. 1. The feminine form {{GHGheb|text=זֹאת}} has undoubtedly arisen from {{GHGheb|text=זָאת}}, by obscuring of an original ''â'' to ''ô'' (for {{GHGheb|text=זָא}} = {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}} cf. the Arab. ''hâ-ḏâ'', ''this'', masc.; for {{GHGheb|text=ת}} as the feminine ending, § 80), and the forms {{GHGheb|text=זֹה}}, {{GHGheb|text=זוֹ}}, both of which are rare,{{GHGheb|text=זֹה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=19}}, and in seven other places; {{GHGheb|text=זוֹ}} only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hos|chapter=7|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=132|verse=12}}. are shortened from {{GHGheb|text=זֹאת}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=132|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=זוֹ}} is used as a ''relative'', cf. {{GHGheb|text=זוּ}} below. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=26|verse=6}}, {{GHGterm|Kethîbh}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַזּאֹתָה}} (with the article and the demonstrative termination {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}) is found for {{GHGheb|text=זֹאת}}. The forms {{GHGheb|text=אֵלֶּה}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֵל}} are the plurals of {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}} and {{GHGheb|text=זֹאת}} by usage, though not etymologically. The form {{GHGheb|text=אֵל}} occurs only in the Pentateuch (but not in the Samaritan text), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=8.25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=3.4|hidebook=1}}, &c. (8 times), always with the article, {{GHGheb|text=הָאֵל}} [as well as {{GHGheb|text=אֵלֶּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָאֵלֶּה}} frequently], and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=20|verse=8}} without the article [cf. Driver on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=42}}].According to Kuenen (cf. above, {{GHGpar|2|n}}) and Driver, on Lev {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=18|verse=27|hidebook=1}} in Haupt’s Bible, this {{GHGheb|text=אֵל}} is due to an error of the punctuators. It goes back to a time when the vowel of the second syllable was not yet indicated by a vowel letter, and later copyists wrongly omitted the addition of the {{GHGheb|text=ה}}. In Phoenician also it was written {{GHGheb|text=אל}}, but pronounced ''ily'' according to Plautus, ''Poen'', v, 1, 9. Both the singular and the plural may refer to things as well as persons. {{GHGmargin-letter|34|c}} 2. In combination with prepositions to denote the oblique case we find {{GHGheb|text=לָזֶה|translate=to this}} (cf. for {{GHGheb|text=לָ}}, {{GHGpar|102|g}}), {{GHGheb|text=לְזֹאת}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָזֹאת|translate=to this}} (fem.), {{GHGheb|text=לְאֵ֫לֶּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָאֵ֫לֶּה|translate=to these}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־זֶה|translate=hunc}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־זֹאת|translate=hanc}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־אֵ֫לֶּה|translate=hos}}, also without {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}}, even ''before'' the verb {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=75|verse=8}}, &c. Note also {{GHGheb|text=מְחִיר זֶה|translate=pretium huius}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=21|verse=2}}), &c.

134.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Dovi" /></noinclude><section begin="par34" />{{GHGmargin-letter|34|d}}
2. The secondary form {{GHGheb|text=זוּ}} occurs only in poetic style, and mostly for the relative, like our ''that'' for ''who'' [see {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|Lexicon|A Hebrew and English Lexicon of the Old Testament, based on the Thesaurus and Lexicon of Gesenius, by F. Brown, S. R. Driver, and C. A. Briggs, Oxford, 1906.}}}}, s. v.]. Like {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} ({{GHGpar|36}}), it serves for all numbers and genders.

{{GHGmargin-letter|34|e}}
Rem. 1. This pronoun takes the article ({{GHGheb|text=הַזֶּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַזֹּאת}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָאֵ֫לֶּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָאֵל}}) according to the same rule as adjectives, see {{GHGpar|126|u}}; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הָאִישׁ הַזֶּה|translate=this man}}, but {{GHGheb|text=זֶה הָאִישׁ|translate=this is the man}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|34|f}}
2. Rarer secondary forms, with strengthened demonstrative force, are {{GHGheb|text=הַלָּזֶה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=65}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=19|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=הַלֵּ֫זוּ}} {{GHGterm|fem.}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=36|verse=35}}; and shortened {{GHGheb|text=הַלָּז}}, sometimes {{GHGterm|masc.}}, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=23|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=8|verse=16}}, sometimes {{GHGterm|fem.}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=25}}: cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=1}} [and {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=19|hidebook=1}} LXX; see Commentaries and Kittel].

{{GHGmargin-letter|34|g}}
3. The personal pronouns of the 3rd person also often have a demonstrative sense, see {{GHGpar|136}}.
<section end="par34" />
<section begin="par35" />{{GHGpar-heading|35|The Article}}

J. Barth, ‘Der heb. u. der aram. Artikel,’ in {{GHGcite|title=Sprachwiss. Untersuch. zum Semit.}}, Lpz. 1907, p. 47 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|a}}
1. The article, which is by nature a kind of demonstrative pronoun, never appears in Hebrew as an independent word, but always in closest connexion with the word which is defined by it. It usually takes the form {{GHGheb|text=הַ{{זונג}}ּ}}, with ''ă'' and a strengthening of the next consonant, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַשֶּׁ֫מֶשׁ|translate=the sun}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַיְאֹר|translate=the river}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַֽלְוִיִּם|translate=the Levites}} (according to {{GHGpar|20|m}} for {{GHGheb|text=הַיְּאֹר}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַלְּוִיִּם}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|b}}
Rem. With regard to the {{GHGterm|Dageš}} in {{GHGheb|text=יְ}} after the article, the rule is, that it is inserted when a {{GHGheb|text=ה}} or {{GHGheb|text=ע}} follows the {{GHGheb|text=יְ}} e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַיְּהוּדִים|translate=the Jews}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַיְּעֵפִים|translate=the weary}} ({{GHGheb|text=כַּיְעֵנִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|verse=3}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} is an exception), but {{GHGheb|text=הַיְאוֹר}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַיְלָדִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַיְסוֹד}}, &c. {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}} also stands after the article in the prefix {{GHGheb|text=מְ‍}} in certain nouns and in the participles {{GHGterm|Piʿēl}} and {{GHGterm|Puʿal}} (see {{GHGpar|52|c}}) before {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, {{GHGheb|text=ע}} and {{GHGheb|text=ר}}, except when the guttural (or {{GHGheb|text=ר}}) has under it a short vowel in a sharpened syllable; thus {{GHGheb|text=הַמְּהוּמָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=22|verse=5}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַמְּעָרָה|translate=the cave}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּמְּרֵעִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=37|verse=1}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=40}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=4|verse=41}}); but {{GHGheb|text=הַֽמְהַלֵּךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=3}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=4|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=23|verse=12}}; before {{GHGheb|text=עַ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=103|verse=4}}); {{GHGheb|text=הַֽמְעֻשָּׁקָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=23|verse=12}}; {{GHGheb|text=הַֽמְרַגְּלִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=6|verse=22}}. Before letters other than gutturals this {{GHGheb|text=מְ}} remains without Dageš, according to {{GHGpar|20|m}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|c}}
'''2.''' When the article stands before a guttural, which (according to {{GHGpar|22|b}}) cannot properly be strengthened, the following cases arise, according to the character of the guttural (cf. {{GHGpar|27|q}}).

(1) In the case of the weakest guttural, {{GHGheb|text=א}}, and also with {{GHGheb|text=ר}} ({{GHGpar|22|c}} and q), the strengthening is altogether omitted. Consequently, the {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} of the article (since it stands in an open syllable) is always lengthened to {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}}; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הָאָב|translate=the father}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאַחֵר|translate=the other}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָאֵם|translate=the mother}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָאִישׁ|translate=the man}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָאוֹר|translate=the light}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאֱלֹהִים}} {{polytonic|ὁ θεός}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָרֶ֫גֶל|translate=the foot}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָרֹאשׁ|translate=the head}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָֽרָשָׁע|translate=the wicked}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|d}}
So also {{GHGheb|text=הָֽשְׁפוֹת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=3|verse=13}}, because syncopated from {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאַשְׁפּוֹת}} (cf. verse 14 and Baer on the passage); {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאזִקִּים}} (as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=41}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=23|verse=33}}, with the {{GHGheb|text=א}}<section end="par35" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

135.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par35" />orthographically retained), for {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאֲז׳}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=40|verse=4}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽאז׳}} verse 1); {{GHGheb|text=הָֽסוּרִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=4|verse=14}} for {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאֲס׳}}; {{GHGheb|text=הָֽרַמִּים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=22|verse=5}} for {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאֲר׳}}(cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=8|verse=28}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|e}}
(2) In the case of the other gutturals either the virtual strengthening takes place ({{GHGpar|22|c}})—especially with the stronger sounds {{GHGheb|text=ח}} and {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, less often with {{GHGheb|text=ע}}—or the strengthening is wholly omitted. In the former case, the {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} of the article remains, because the syllable is still regarded as closed; in the second ''c''ase, the {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} is either modified to {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>ghôl}} or fully lengthened to {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}}. That is to say:—

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|f}}
''A''. When the guttural has any other vowel than ''ā'' ({{GHGheb|text=־ָ}}) or ''ŏ'' ({{GHGheb|text=־ֳ}}), then

(1) before the stronger sounds {{GHGheb|text=ה}} and {{GHGheb|text=ה}} the article regularly remains {{GHGheb|text=הַ}}; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַהוּא|translate=that}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַחֹ֫דֶשׁ|translate=the month}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַחַ֫יִל|translate=the force}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַחָכְמָה|translate=the wisdom}}. Before {{GHGheb|text=ח}}, ''ā'' occurs only in {{GHGheb|text=הָחַי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=19}} [not elsewhere], {{GHGheb|text=הָֽחֲרִיטִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=22}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָֽחַמָּנִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=17|verse=8}} [not elsewhere]; before {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, always in {{GHGheb|text=הָהֵ֫מָּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָהֵם}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|g}}
(2) before {{GHGheb|text=ע}} the {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} is generally lengthened to {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הָעַ֫יִן|translate=the eye}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָעִיר|translate=the city}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָעֶ֫בֶד|translate=the servant}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=הָֽעֲבָדִים}}; {{GHGheb|text=לָֽעֲגָלִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=12|verse=32}}; also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=הָֽעַרְקִי}} is the better reading. Exceptions are {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽעוֹפֶ֫רֶת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=10}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַֽעִוְרִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=5|verse=6.8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=18}}, {{GHGheb|text=כַּעֶ֫בֶד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=24|verse=2}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַעֹֽרְכִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=65|verse=11}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּע֫שֶׁק}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=22|verse=7}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַעֹֽזְבִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=13}} and {{GHGheb|text=הַעֹזֶ֫בֶת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=17}}, {{GHGheb|text=לַֽעֵינַיִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=11|verse=7}}; but {{GHGheb|text=לָֽעֵינ׳}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=10|verse=26}}. Cf. Baer on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=18}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|h}}
''B''. When the guttural has ''ā'' ({{GHGheb|text=־ָ}}) then

(1) immediately before a tone-bearing {{GHGheb|text=הָ}} or {{GHGheb|text=עָ}} the article is always {{GHGheb|text=הָ}}, otherwise it is {{GHGheb|text=הֶ}}; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הָעָם|translate=the people}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָהָר|translate=the mountain}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָעָ֑יִן}} (in {{GHGterm|pause}}) ''the eye'', {{GHGheb|text=הָהָ֫רָה|translate=towards the mountain}}; but (according to {{GHGpar|22|c}}) {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽהָרִ֫ים|translate=the mountains}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽעָוֹן|translate=the iniquity}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|i}}
(2) before {{GHGheb|text=חָ}} the article is invariably {{GHGheb|text=הֶ}} without regard to the tone; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽחָכָם|translate=the wise man}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֶחָ֫ג|translate=the festival}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|k}}
''C''. When the guttural has {{GHGvowel-holder|ֳ}} the article is {{GHGheb|text=הֶ}} before {{GHGheb|text=חֳ}} e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽחֳדָשִׁים|translate=the months}}; {{GHGheb|text=בֶּֽחֳרָבוֹת|translate=in the waste places}} (without the article {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽחֳ׳}} ''bŏḥ<sup>o</sup>rābhôth'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=33|verse=27}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽחֳרֵבוֹת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=36|verse=35.38}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=27|verse=4}}; but {{GHGheb|text=הָ}} before {{GHGheb|text=עֳ}}, as {{GHGheb|text=הָֽעֳמָרִים|translate=the sheaves}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=2|verse=15}}.

The gender and number of the noun have no influence on the form of the article.

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|l}}
Rem. 1. The original form of the Hebrew (and the Phoenician) article {{GHGheb|text=הַ}} is generally considered to have been {{GHGheb|text=הַל}}, the {{GHGheb|text=ל}} of which (owing to the proclitic nature of the article) has been invariably assimilated to the following consonant, as in {{GHGheb|text=יִקַּח}} from ''yilqaḥ'', {{GHGpar|19|d}}. This view was supported by the form of the Arabic article {{GHGheb|text=אַל}} (pronounced ''hal'' by some modern Beduin), the {{GHGheb|text=ל}} of which is also assimilated at least before all letters like ''s'' and ''t'' and before ''l'', ''n'', and ''r'', e.g. ''ʾal-Qurʾân'' but ''ʾas-s{{GHGtranslit|a-brev-acut}}nă'' (Beduin ''has-sana'')=Hebr. {{GHGheb|text=הַשָּׁנָה|translate=the year}}.<section end="par35" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

136.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par35" />But Barth ({{GHGcite|title=Amer. Journ. of Sem. Laug.}}, 1896, p. 7 ff.), following Hupfeld and Stade, has shown that the Hebrew article is to be connected rather with the original Semitic demonstrative ''hā'',<ref>An original form ''han'', proposed by Ungnad, ‘Der hebr. Art.,’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|OLZ.|Orientalistische Literaturzeitung. Vienna, 1898 if.}}}} x (1907), col. 210 f., and {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1908, p. 80 ff., is open to grave objections.</ref> cf. Arab. ''hāḏa'', Aram. ''hādēn'', &c. The sharpening of the following consonant is to be explained exactly like the sharpening after {{GHGheb|text=וַ}} consecutive ({{GHGpar|49|f}}; cf. also cases like {{GHGheb|text=בַּמָּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=כַּמָּה}}, &c., {{GHGpar|102|k}}), from the close connexion of the ''ha'' with the following word, and the sharpening necessarily involved the shortening of the vowel.<ref>In the Liḥyanitic inscriptions collected by Euting (ed. by {{Nowrap|D. H. Müller}} in {{GHGcite|title=Epigraphische Denkmäler aus Arabien}}, Wien, 1889) the article is {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, and also in a North Arabian dialect, according to {{Nowrap|E. Littmann}}, {{GHGcite|title=Safa-inschriften}}, p. 2, Rem., and p. 34.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|m}}
The Arabic article is supposed to occur in the Old Testament in {{GHGheb|text=אַלְמֻגִּים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=10|verse=11.12}} (also {{GHGheb|text=אַלְגּוּמִּים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=2|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=9|verse=10.11|hidebook=1}}), ''sandal-wood'' (?), and in {{GHGheb|text=אֶלְגָּבִישׁ|translate=hail, ice}}={{GHGheb|text=גָבִישׁ}} (Arab. ''ǵibs'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=11.13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=38|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, but this explanation can hardly be correct. On the other hand, in the proper name {{GHGheb|text=אַלְמוֹדָד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=26}} the first syllable is probably {{GHGheb|text=אֵל|translate=God}}, as suggested by D. H. Müller (see Lexicon, s. v.) and Nöldeke, ''Sitzungsber. der Berl. Akad.'', 1882, p. 1186. {{GHGheb|text=אַלְקוּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=30|verse=31}}, commonly explained as=Arab. ''al-qaum'', the militia, is also quite uncertain.

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|n}}
2. When the prefixes {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}} ({{GHGpar|102}}) come before the article, the {{GHGheb|text=ה}} is elided, and its vowel is thrown back to the prefix, in the place of the Š<sup>e</sup>wâ ({{GHGpar|19|k}}, and {{GHGpar|23|k}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בָּשָּׁמַ֫יִם|translate=in the heaven}} for {{GHGheb|text=בְּהַשָּׁמַ֫יִם}} (so {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=36|verse=6}}); {{GHGheb|text=לָעָם}} for {{GHGheb|text=לְהָעָם|translate=to the people}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֶּֽהָרִים|translate=on the mountains}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֶּֽחֳדָשִׁים|translate=in the months}}; also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=2}}, read {{GHGheb|text=כֶּֽעָפָר}} instead of the impossible {{GHGheb|text=כֵּֽעָפָר}}. Exceptions to this rule occur almost exclusively in the later Books: {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=40|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=47|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=8|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=8|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=9|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=12|verse=38|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=10|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=25|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=29|verse=27|hidebook=1}}; cf., however, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=13|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=21|verse=20}}. Elsewhere, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=12}}, the Masora requires the elision in the {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}. A distinction in meaning is observed between {{GHGheb|text=כְּהַיּוֹם|translate=about this time}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=13}}, &c.) and {{GHGheb|text=כַּיּוֹם|translate=first of all}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=31}}, &c.). After the copula {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} (''and'') elision of the {{GHGheb|text=ה}} does not take place, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וְהָעָם}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|35|o}}
3. The words {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫רֶץ|translate=earth}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַר|translate=mountain}}, {{GHGheb|text=חַג|translate=feast}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַם|translate=people}}, {{GHGheb|text=פַּר|translate=bull}}, always appear after the article with a long vowel (as in {{GHGterm|pause}}); {{GHGheb|text=הָאָ֫רֶץ}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָהָר}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֶחָג}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָעָם}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַפָּר}}; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=אֲרוֹן|translate=ark}} (so in the absol. st. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=12|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=24|verse=8}}, but to be read {{GHGheb|text=אָרוֹן}}), with the article always {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאָרוֹן}}.
<section end="par35" />
<section begin="par36" />{{GHGpar-heading|36|The Relative Pronoun}}

The relative pronoun (cf. {{GHGpar|138}}) is usually the indeclinable {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} (''who, which'', &c.), originally a demonstrative pronoun; see further {{GHGpar|138}} and {{GHGpar|155|nosign=1}}. In the later books, especially Eccles. and the late Psalms, also Lam. (4 times), Jon. ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=1|verse=7|hidebook=1}}), Chron. (twice), Ezra (once),—and always in the Canticle (cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=7|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=8|verse=26|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=11}}), {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ{{זונג}}ּ}} is used instead; more rarely {{GHGheb|text=שַׁ{{זונג}}ּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=1|verse=7}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=29}}?); once {{GHGheb|text=שָׁ}} before {{GHGheb|text=א}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=17}} (elsewhere {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ}} before a guttural), before {{GHGheb|text=ה}} even {{GHGheb|text=שְׁ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=18}}, and according to some (e.g. Qimḥi) also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=2|verse=22}}.<ref>The full form {{GHGheb|text=אשר}} does not occur in Phoenician, but only {{GHGheb|text=אש}} (={{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁ{{זונג}}ּ}}?), pronounced ''asse, esse'' (also ''as, es, is, ys, us''), or—especially in the later Punic and in the ''Poenulus'' of Plautus—{{GHGheb|text=ש}} (''sa, si, sy, su''). Also in New Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ{{זונג}}ּ}} has become the common form. Cf. Schröder, ''Phön. Sprache'', p. 162 ff. and below, {{GHGpar|155}}; also Bergsträsser, ‘Das hebr. Präfix {{GHGheb|text=ש}},’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1909, p. 40 ff.</ref> [See Lexicon, s. v.]<section end="par36" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

137.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par37" />{{GHGpar-heading|37|The Interrogative and Indefinite Pronouns}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|37|a}}
'''1.''' The interrogative pronoun is {{GHGheb|text=מִי|translate=who?}} (of persons, even before plurals, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=60|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=18|verse=35}}, and sometimes also of things {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=1|verse=5}}; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=בַּת־מִי|translate=whose daughter?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=23}}; {{GHGheb|text=לְמִי|translate=to whom?}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־מִי|translate=whom?}})—{{GHGheb|text=מָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=מַה}} (see b) ''what?'' (of things).—{{GHGheb|text=אֵי־זֶה|translate=which? what?}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|37|b}}
The form {{GHGheb|text=מַה{{זונג}}ּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=מַ‍{{זונג}}ּ}}, &c. (followed by ''Dageš forte conjunct.'': even in {{GHGheb|text=יְ}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=1}}, &c., against {{GHGpar|20|m}}) may be explained (like the art. {{GHGheb|text=הַ{{זונג}}ּ}} {{GHGpar|35|l}}, and {{GHGheb|text=וַ{{זונג}}ּ}} in the ''imperf. consec.'') from the rapid utterance of the interrogative in connexion with the following word. Most probably, however, the {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}} is rather due to the assimilation of an originally audible {{GHGheb|text=ה}} ({{GHGheb|text=מַהּ}}, as ''Olshausen''), which goes back through the intermediate forms ''math, mat'' to an original ''mant'': so W. Wright, {{GHGcite|title=Comparative Grammar}}, Cambridge, 1890, p. 124, partly following Böttcher, {{GHGcite|title=Hebräische Grammatik}}, § 261. A ground-form ''mant'' would most easily explain {{GHGheb|text=מָן}} (''what?''), used in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=15}} in explanation of {{GHGheb|text=מָן|translate=manna}}, while {{GHGheb|text=מַן}} is the regular Aramaic for ''who''. Socin calls attention to the Arabic ''mah'' (in pause with an audible ''h'': ''Mufaṣṣal'', 193, 8). Observe further that—

{{GHGmargin-letter|37|c}}
(''a'') In the closest connexion, by means of {{GHGterm|Maqqeph}}, {{GHGheb|text=מַה־}} takes a following {{GHGterm|Dageš}} ({{GHGpar|20|d}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מַה־לָּךְ|translate=what is it to thee?}} and even in ''one'' word, as {{GHGheb|text=מַלָּכֶם|translate=what is it to you?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=15}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=4|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=1|verse=13}}, and even before a guttural, {{GHGheb|text=מהם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=8|verse=6}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|37|d}}
(''b'') Before gutturals in close connexion, by means of {{GHGterm|Maqqeph}} or (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=1}}) a conjunctive accent, either {{GHGheb|text=מַה}} is used with a virtual strengthening of the guttural ({{GHGpar|22|c}}), so especially before {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, and, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=21}}, before {{GHGheb|text=ח}}—or the doubling is wholly omitted. In the latter case either (cf. {{GHGpar|35|e}}–k) ''ă'' is fully lengthened to ''Qames'' (so always before the {{GHGheb|text=ה}} of the article, except in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=2|verse=12}}; also before {{GHGheb|text=הֵ֫מָּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֵ֫נָּה}}, and so {{GHGheb|text=ה}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=18}}), {{GHGheb|text=א}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=8|verse=14}}), {{GHGheb|text=ע}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=8|verse=13}}), or modified to {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>ghôl}}, especially before {{GHGheb|text=עָ}}, {{GHGheb|text=חָ}}, and generally before {{GHGheb|text=הָ}}. The omission of the strengthening also takes place as a rule with {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, {{GHGheb|text=ח}}, {{GHGheb|text=ע}}, when they have not {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}}, and then the form is either {{GHGheb|text=מָה}} or {{GHGheb|text=מֶה}}, the latter especially before {{GHGheb|text=ח}} or {{GHGheb|text=ע}}, if {{GHGterm|Maqqeph}} follows.

{{GHGmargin-letter|37|e}}
The longer forms {{GHGheb|text=מָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=מֶה}} are also used ({{GHGheb|text=מֶה}} even before letters which are not gutturals) when not connected by {{GHGterm|Maqqeph}} but only by a ''conjunctive accent''. As a rule {{GHGheb|text=מָה}} is then used, but sometimes {{GHGheb|text=מֶה}} when at a greater distance from the principal tone of the sentence, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=4|verse=3}}. (On {{GHGheb|text=מֶה}} in the combinations {{GHGheb|text=כַּמֶּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּמֶּה}}, and even {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מֶה}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=8}}, cf. {{GHGpar|102|k}} and l.)

{{GHGmargin-letter|37|f}}
(''c'') In the principal pause {{GHGheb|text=מָה}} is used without exception; also as a rule with the smaller ''disjunctives'', and almost always before gutturals ({{GHGheb|text=מֶה}} only in very few cases). On the other hand, {{GHGheb|text=מֶה}} more often stands before letters which are not gutturals, when at a greater distance from the principal tone of the sentence, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=1|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hag|chapter=1|verse=9}} (see Köhler on the passage), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=10|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=21}}; cf., however, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=31|verse=2}}, and Delitzsch on the passage.

{{GHGmargin-letter|37|g}}
'''2.''' On {{GHGheb|text=מִי}} and {{GHGheb|text=מָה}} as indefinite pronouns in the sense of ''quicunque, quodcunque'', and as relatives, ''is qui, id quod'', &c., see {{GHGpar|137|c}}.<section end="par37" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

138.text:
{{center|'''CHAPTER II''' THE VERB}} {{GHGpar-heading|38|General View}} {{GHGmargin-letter|38|a}} Verbal stems are either original or derived. They are usually divided into— (''a'') Verbal stems proper (''primitive verbs''), which exhibit the stem without any addition, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מָלַךְ|translate=he has reigned}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|38|b}} (''b'') {{GHGterm|Verbal derivatives}}, i.e. ''secondary'' verbal stems, derived from the pure stem (letter ''a''), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קִדַּשׁ|translate=to sanctify}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִתְקַדֵּשׁ|translate=to sanctify oneself}}, from {{GHGheb|text=קָדַשׁ|translate=to be holy}}. These are usually called ''conjugations'' (§ 39). {{GHGmargin-letter|38|c}} (''c'') ''Denominatives'',Cf. W. J. Gerber, ''Die hebr. Verbs denom., insbes. im theol. Sprachgebr. des A.T.'', Lpz. 1896. i.e. verbs derived from nouns (like the Latin ''causari, praedari'', and Eng. to ''skin, to stone''), or even from particles (see d, end) either in a primitive or derivative form, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָהַל}}, {{GHGterm|Qal}} and {{GHGterm|Piʿēl}}, ''to pitch a tent'', from {{GHGheb|text=אֹ֫הֶל|translate=tent}}; {{GHGheb|text=הִשְׁרִישׁ}} and {{GHGheb|text=שֹׁרֵשׁ|translate=to take root}}, and {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁרֵשׁ|translate=to root out}}, from {{GHGheb|text=שֹׁרֶשׁ|translate=root}} ({{GHGpar|52|h}}). {{GHGmargin-letter|38|d}} This does not exclude the possibility that, for nouns, from which denominative verbs are derived, the corresponding (original) verbal stem may still be found either in Hebrew or in the dialects. The meaning, however, is sufficient to show that the denominatives have come from the noun, not from the verbal stem, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לְבֵנָה|translate=a brick}} (verbal stem {{GHGheb|text=לבן|translate=to be white}}), denomin. {{GHGheb|text=לָבַן|translate=to make bricks}}; {{GHGheb|text=דָּג|translate=a fish}} (verbal stem {{GHGheb|text=דָּגָה|translate=to be prolific}}), denomin. {{GHGheb|text=דּוּג|translate=to fish}}; {{GHGheb|text=חָרַף|translate=to winter}} (from {{GHGheb|text=חֹ֫רֶף|translate=autumn, winter}}, stem {{GHGheb|text=חָרַף|translate=to pluck}}); {{GHGheb|text=קוּץ|translate=to pass the summer}} (from {{GHGheb|text=קַ֫יִץ|translate=summer}}, stem {{GHGheb|text=קִיץ|translate=to be hot}}). On ‘Semitic verbs derived from particles’ see P. Haupt in the {{GHGcite|title=Amer. Journ. of Sem. Lang.}}, xxii (1906), 257 ff.
{{GHGpar-heading|39|Ground-form and Derived Stems}}
{{center|Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Sem. Sprachwiss}}., p. 119 ff.; {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, p. 504 ff.}}
{{GHGmargin-letter|39|a}} '''1.''' The 3rd sing. masc. of the {{GHGterm|Perfect}} in the form of the pure stem (i.e. in {{GHGterm|Qal}}, see e) is generally regarded, lexicographically and grammatically, as the ground-form of the verb ({{GHGpar|30|a}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קָטַל|translate=he has killed}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּבֵד|translate=he was heavy}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטֹן|translate=he was little}}.For the sake of brevity, however, the meaning in Hebrew-English Lexicons is usually given in the Infinitive, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לָמַד|translate=to learn}}, properly ''he has learnt''. From this form the other

139.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par39 />persons of the {{GHGterm|Perfect}} are derived, and the {{GHGterm|Participle}} also is connected with it. {{GHGheb|text=קְטֹל}} or {{GHGheb|text=קְטַל}}, like the Imperative and Infinitive construct in sound, may also be regarded as an alternative ground-form, with which the Imperfect (see § 47) is connected.

{{GHGmargin-letter|39|b}}
In verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} (i.e. with {{GHGheb|text=ו}} for their second radical) the stem-form, given both in Lexicon and Grammar, is not the 3rd sing. masc. Perfect (consisting of two consonants), but the form with medial {{GHGheb|text=ו}}, which appears in the Imperative and Infinitive; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּב|translate=to return}} (3rd pers. perf. {{GHGheb|text=שָׁב}}): the same is the case in most stems with medial {{GHGheb|text=י}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=דִּין|translate=to judge}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|39|c}}
'''2.''' From the pure stem, or {{GHGterm|Qal}}, the derivative stems are formed according to an unvarying analogy, in which the idea of the stem assumes the most varied shades of meaning, according to the changes in its form (intensive, frequentative, privative, causative, reflexive, reciprocal; some of them with corresponding passive forms), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לָמַד|translate=to learn}}, {{GHGheb|text=לִמַּד|translate=to teach}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁכַב|translate=to lie}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִשְׁכִּיב|translate=to lay}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁפַט|translate=to judge}}, {{GHGheb|text=נִשְׁפַּט|translate=to contend}}. In other languages such formations are regarded as new or ''derivative'' verbs, e.g. Germ. ''fallen'' (to fall), ''fällen'' (to fell); ''trinken'' (to drink), ''tränken'' (to drench); Lat. ''lactere'' (to suck, Germ. ''saugen''), ''lactare'' (to suckle, Germ. ''säugen''); ''iacĕre'' (to throw), ''iacēre'' (to lie down); γίνομαι, γεννάω. In Hebrew, however, these formations are incomparably more regular and systematic than (e.g.) in Greek, Latin, or English; and, since the time of Reuchlin, they have usually been called ''conjugations'' of the primitive form (among the Jewish grammarians {{GHGheb|text=בִּנְיָנִים}}, i.e. ''formations'', or more correctly ''species''), and are always treated together in the grammar and lexicon.<ref>The term ''Conjugation'' thus has an entirely different meaning in Hebrew and Greek or Latin grammar.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|39|d}}
'''3.''' The changes in the primitive form consist either in internal modification by means of vowel-change and strengthening of the middle consonant ({{GHGheb|text=קִטֵּל}}, {{GHGheb|text=קֻטַּל}}; {{GHGheb|text=קוֹטֵל}}, {{GHGheb|text=קוֹטַל}}; cf. ''to lie, to lay''; ''to fall, to fell''), or in the repetition of one or two of the stem-consonants ({{GHGheb|text=קִטְלַל}}, {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְטַל}}), or finally in the introduction of formative additions ({{GHGheb|text=נִקְטַל}}), which may also be accompanied by internal change ({{GHGheb|text=הִקְטִיל}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִתְקַטֵּל}}). Cf. {{GHGpar|31|b}}.

In Aramaic the formation of the conjugations is effected more by formative additions than by vowel-change. The vocalic distinctions have mostly become obsolete, so that, e.g. the reflexives with the prefix {{GHGheb|text=הִתְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִתְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְ}} have entirely usurped the place of the passives. On the other hand, Arabic has preserved great wealth in both methods of formation, while Hebrew in this, as in other respects, holds the middle place ({{GHGpar|1|m}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|39|e}}
'''4.''' Grammarians differ as to the ''number'' and ''arrangement'' of these conjugations. The common practice, however, of calling them by the<section end=par39 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

140.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par39 />old grammatical terms, prevents any misunderstanding. The simple form is called {{GHGterm|Qal}} ({{GHGheb|text=קַל|translate=light}}, because it has no formative additions); the others ({{GHGheb|text=כְּבֵדִים|translate=heavy}}, being weighted, as it were, with the strengthening of consonants or with formative additions) take their names from the paradigm of {{GHGheb|text=פָּעַל|translate=he has done}},<ref>This paradigm was borrowed from the Arabic grammarians, and, according to Bacher, probably first adopted throughout by Abulwalîd. It was, however, unsuitable on account of the guttural, and was, therefore, usually exchanged in later times for {{GHGheb|text=פָּקַד}}, after the example of Moses Qimḥi. This verb has the advantage, that all its conjugations are actually found in the Old Testament. On the other hand, it has the disadvantage of indistinctness in the pronunciation of some of its forms, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=פָּקַדְתָּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=פְּקַדְתֶּם}}. The paradigm of {{GHGheb|text=קָטַל}}, commonly used since the time of Danz, avoids this defect, and is especially adapted for the comparative treatment of the Semitic dialects, inasmuch as it is found with slight change (Arab. and Ethiop. {{GHGheb|text=קתל}}) in all of them. It is true that in Hebrew it occurs only three times in {{GHGterm|Qal}}, and even then only in poetic style ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=24|verse=14|hidebook=1}}); yet it is worth retaining as a model which has been sanctioned by usage. More serious is the defect, that a number of forms of the paradigm of {{GHGheb|text=קטל}} leave the beginner in doubt as to whether or not there should be a {{GHGterm|Dageš}} in the {{GHGterm|B<sup>e</sup>gadk<sup>e</sup>phath}} letters, and consequently as to the correct division of the syllables.</ref> which was used in the earliest Jewish grammatical works. Several of these have passives which are distinguished from their actives by more obscure vowels. The common conjugations (including {{GHGterm|Qal}} and the passives) are the seven following, but very few verbs exhibit them all:

{{GHGmargin-letter|39|g}}
There are besides several less frequent conjugations, some of which, however, are more common in the kindred languages, and even in Hebrew (in the weak verb) regularly take the place of the usual conjugations (§ 55).

In Arabic there is a greater variety of conjugations, and their arrangement is more appropriate. According to the Arabic method, the Hebrew conjugations would stand thus: 1. {{GHGterm|Qal}}; 2. {{GHGterm|Piʿēl}} and {{GHGterm|Puʿal}}; 3. ''Pôʿēl'' and ''Pôʿal'' (see {{GHGpar|55|b}}); 4. {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} and {{GHGterm|Hophʿal}}; 5. {{GHGterm|Hithpaʿēl}} and {{GHGterm|Hothpaʿal}}; 6. ''Hithpô‛ēl'' (see {{GHGpar|55|b}}); 7. {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}}; 8. {{GHGterm|Hithpaʿēl}} (see {{GHGpar|54|l}}); 9. ''Piʿlēl'' (see {{GHGpar|55|d}}). A more satisfactory division would be into three classes: (1) The intensive {{GHGterm|Piʿēl}} with the derived and analogous forms {{GHGterm|Puʿal}} and {{GHGterm|Hithpaʿēl}}. (2) The causative {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} with its passive {{GHGterm|Hophʿal}}, and the analogous forms (''Šaphʿēl'' and ''Tiphʿēl''). (3) The reflexive or passive {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}}.<section end=par39 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

141.text:
{{GHGpar-heading|40|Tenses. Moods. Flexion}} A. Ungnad, ‘Die gegenseitigen Beziehungen der Verbalformen im Grundstamm des semit. Verbs,’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 59 (1905), 766 ff., and his ‘Zum hebr. Verbalsystem’, in {{GHGcite|title=Beiträge zur Assyriologie}} ed. by Fr. Delitzsch and P. Haupt, 1907, p. 55 ff. {{GHGmargin-letter|40|a}} '''1.''' While the Hebrew verb, owing to these derivative forms or conjugations, possesses a certain richness and copiousness, it is, on the other hand, poor in the matter of ''tenses'' and ''moods''. The verb has only two ''tense''-forms ({{GHGterm|Perfect}} and {{GHGterm|Imperfect}}, see the note on {{GHGpar|47|a}}), besides an {{GHGterm|Imperative}} (but only in the active), two ''Infinitives'' and a {{GHGterm|Participle}}. All relations of time, absolute and relative, are expressed either by these forms (hence a certain diversity in their meaning, {{GHGpar|106|ff}}.) or by syntactical combinations. Of moods properly so called (besides the {{GHGterm|Imperfect Indicative}} and {{GHGterm|Imperative}}), only the {{GHGterm|Jussive}} and {{GHGterm|Optative}}are sometimes indicated by express modifications of the Imperfect-form (§ 48). {{GHGmargin-letter|40|b}} '''2.''' The ''inflexion'' of the ''Perfect, Imperfect'', and {{GHGterm|Imperative}} as to persons, differs from that of the Western languages in having, to a great extent, distinct forms for the two genders, which correspond to the different forms of the ''personal pronoun. It is from the union of the pronoun with the verbal stem that the personal inflexions of these tenses arise''. {{GHGmargin-letter|40|c}} The following table will serve for the beginner as a provisional scheme of the formative syllables (''afformatives'' and ''preformatives'') of the two ''tenses''. The three stem-consonants of the strong verb are denoted by dots. Cf. {{GHGpar|44|ff}}. and the Paradigms.

142.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude>
<section begin="par41" />{{GHGpar-heading|41|Variations from the Ordinary Form of the Strong Verb.}}
{{GHGmargin-letter|41|a}}
The same laws which are normally exhibited in stems with strong (unchangeable) consonants, hold good for all other verbs. Deviations from the model of the strong verb are only modifications due to the special character or weakness of certain consonants, viz.:—

(''a'') When one of the stem-consonants (or ''radicals'') is a guttural. In this case, however, the variations only occur in the vocalization (according to {{GHGpar|22}}), not in the consonants. The {{GHGterm|guttural verbs}} ({{GHGpar|62}}–{{GHGpar|65|nosign=1}}) are, therefore, only a variety of the ''strong verb''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|41|b}}
(''b'') When a stem-consonant ({{GHGterm|radical}}) disappears by assimilation ({{GHGpar|19|b}}–{{GHGpar|19|f|nonumber=1}}), or when the stem originally, consisted of only two consonants ({{GHGterm|verbs}} {{GHGheb|text=פ״ן}}, {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}}, and {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}}, as {{GHGheb|text=נָגַשׁ}}, {{GHGheb|text=קַל}}, {{GHGheb|text=קוּם}}, {{GHGpar|66|doublesign=1}}, {{GHGpar|67|nosign=1}}, {{GHGpar|72|nosign=1}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|41|c}}
(''c'') When one of the stem-consonants ({{GHGterm|radicals}}) is a weak letter. In this case, through aphaeresis, elision, &c., of the weak consonant, various important deviations from the regular form occur. Cf. {{GHGpar|68}} ff. for these verbs, such as {{GHGheb|text=יָשַׁב}}, {{GHGheb|text=מָצָא}}, {{GHGheb|text=גָּלָה}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|41|d}}
Taking the old paradigm {{GHGheb|text=פָּעַל}} as a model, it is usual, following the example of the Jewish grammarians, to call the first radical of any stem {{GHGheb|text=פ}}, the second {{GHGheb|text=ע}}, and the third {{GHGheb|text=ל}}. Hence the expressions, {{GHGterm|verb}} {{GHGheb|text=פ״א}} for a verb whose first radical is {{GHGheb|text=א}} ({{GHGterm|primae radicalis}} [{{GHGterm|sc. literae}}] {{GHGheb|text=א}}); {{GHGheb|text=ע״ו}} for {{GHGterm|mediae radicalis}} {{GHGheb|text=ו}}; {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}} for a verb whose second radical is repeated to form a third.
<section end="par41" />
<section begin="par42" />{{center|{{larger|'''I. The Strong Verb.'''}}}}

<!-- section begins above -->{{GHGpar-heading|42|}}

As the formation of the strong verb is the model also for the weak verb, a statement of the general formative laws should precede the treatment of special cases.

Paradigm B, together with the Table of the personal preformatives and afformatives given in {{GHGpar|40|c}}, offers a complete survey of the normal forms. A full explanation of them is given in the following sections (§§ 43–55), where each point is elucidated on its first occurrence; thus e.g. the inflexion of the Perfect, the Imperfect and its modifications, will be found under Qal, &c.
<section end="par42" />
<section begin="par43" />{{center|{{larger|A. The Pure Stem, or Qal.}}}}

<!-- section begins above -->{{GHGpar-heading|43|Its Form and Meaning}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|43|a}}
The common form of the 3rd sing. masc. of the {{GHGterm|Perfect Qal}} is {{GHGheb|text=קָטַל}}, with ''ă'' ({{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}}) in the second syllable, especially in {{GHGterm|transitive}} verbs (but see {{GHGpar|44|c}}). There is also a form with ''ē'' ({{GHGterm|Ṣere}}, originally ''ĭ''), and another with ''ō'' ({{GHGterm|Ḥolem}}, originally ''ŭ'') in the second syllable, both of which, however, have almost always an {{GHGterm|intransitive}}<ref>But cf. such instances as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=48|verse=5}}. In Arabic also, transitive verbs are found with middle ''ĭ'', corresponding to Hebrew verbs with ''ē'' in the second syllable. Hence P. Haupt ({{GHGcite|title=Proc. Amer. Or. Soc.}}, 1894, p. ci f.) prefers to distinguish them as {{GHGterm|verba voluntaria}} (actions which depend on the will of the subject) and {{GHGterm|involuntaria}} (actions or states independent of the will of the subject).</ref> meaning,
<section end="par43" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

143.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par43 />and serve to express states and qualities, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כָּבֵד|translate=to be heavy}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטֹן|translate=to be small}}.

In Paradigm B a verb ''middle a'', a verb ''middle ē'', and a verb ''middle ō'' are accordingly given side by side. The second example {{GHGheb|text=כָּבֵד}} is chosen as showing, at the same time, when the {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}} is to be inserted or omitted.

{{GHGmargin-letter|43|b}}
Rem. 1. The vowel of the second syllable is the principal vowel, and hence on it depends the distinction between the transitive and intransitive meaning. The {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} of the first syllable is lengthened from an original ''ă'' (cf. Arabic ''qătălă''), but it can be retained in Hebrew only immediately before the tone, or at the most (with an open ultima) in the counter-tone with {{GHGterm|Metheg}}; otherwise, like all the pretonic vowels (''ā'', ''ē''), it becomes {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתֶּ֫ם}} 2nd ''plur. masc.'' In the Aramaic dialects the vowel of the first syllable is always reduced to Š<sup>e</sup>wâ, as {{GHGheb|text=קְטַל}}=Hebr. {{GHGheb|text=קָטַל}}. The intransitive forms in Arabic are ''qătĭlă'', ''qătŭlă''; in Hebrew (after the rejection of the final vowel) ''ĭ'' being in the tone-syllable has been regularly lengthened to ''ē'', and ''ŭ'' to ''ō''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|43|c}}
2. Examples of ''denominatives'' in {{GHGterm|Qal}} are: {{GHGheb|text=חָמַר|translate=to cover with pitch}}, from {{GHGheb|text=חֵמָר|translate=pitch}} ; {{GHGheb|text=מָלַח|translate=to salt}}, from {{GHGheb|text=מֶ֫לַח|translate=salt}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁבַר}} (usually ''Hiph.'') ''to buy'' or ''sell corn'', from {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫בֶר|translate=corn}}; see above, {{GHGpar|38|c}}.<section end=par43 />
<section begin=par44 />{{GHGpar-heading|44|Flexion of the Perfect of Qal||<ref>Cf. Nöldeke, ‘Die Endungen des Perfects’ (''Untersuchungen zur semit''. Gramm. ii.), in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} vol. 38, p. 407 ff., and more fully in {{GHGcite|title=Beiträge zur sem. Sprachwiss.}}, Strassb. 1904, p. 15 ff.</ref>}}
{{GHGmargin-letter|44|a}}
'''1.''' The formation of the persons of the Perfect is effected by the addition of certain forms of the personal pronoun, and marks of the 3rd fem. sing. and 3rd pl. (as ''afformatives'') to the ''end'' of the verbal-stem, which contains the idea of a predicate, and may be regarded, in meaning if not in form, as a {{GHGterm|Participle}} or {{GHGterm|verbal adjective}}. For the 3rd ''pers. sing. masc. Perfect'', the pronominal or subject idea inherent in the finite verb is sufficient: thus, {{GHGheb|text=קָטַל|translate=he has killed}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫לְ־תָּ|translate=thou hast killed}} (as it were, ''killing thou'', or ''a killer thou''), ''a killer wast thou''={{GHGheb|text=קטל אַתָּה}}; {{GHGheb|text=יָרֵא|translate=he was fearing}}, {{GHGheb|text=ירֵא־תֶם|translate=ye were fearing}}={{GHGheb|text=יִרא אַתֶּם}}. The ending of the 1st pers. plur. ({{GHGheb|text=־נוּ}}) is also certainly connected with the termination of {{GHGheb|text=אֲנַ֫חְנוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אנו|translate=we}} ({{GHGpar|32|b}}, d). The afformative of the 1st pers. sing. ({{GHGheb|text=תִּי}}) is to be referred, by an interchange of {{GHGheb|text=כ‍}} and {{GHGheb|text=ת}} (cf. {{GHGpar|33|f}}), to that form of the pronoun which also underlies {{GHGheb|text=אָֽנֹכִי}}, I.<ref>According to Nöldeke, ''l.c.'', p. 419, the original Semitic termination of the 1st sing. Perf. was most probably ''kû''; cf. the Ethiopic ''qatalku'', Arabic ''qataltu''.</ref> In the ''third'' person {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} (originally {{GHGheb|text=־ַת}}, cf. below, f) is the mark of the feminine, as in a great number of nouns ({{GHGpar|80|c}}), and {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} is the termination of the plural; cf., for the latter, the termination of the 3rd and 2nd pers. plur. Imperf. ''ûna'' in Arabic and ''û'' (often also {{GHGheb|text=וּן}})<section end=par44 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

144.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="2607:FB92:1F05:CB5D:2813:F9D2:CF1E:C285" /></noinclude><section begin="par44" />in Hebrew, also ''ûna'' (in the construct state ''û'') as the plural termination of masc. nouns in literary Arabic.

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|b}}
'''2.''' The characteristic {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} of the second syllable becomes {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} before an afformative beginning with a vowel, where it would otherwise stand in an open syllable (as {{GHGheb|text=קָֽטְלָ֫ה}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָֽטְל֫וּ}}; but in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=קָטָ֫לָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטָ֫לוּ}}). Before an afformative beginning with a consonant the {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} remains, whether in the tone-syllable ({{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫לְתָּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫לְתְּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫לְתִּי}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫לְנוּ}}; in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=קָטָ֫לְתָּ}} &c.) or ''before'' it. In the latter case, however, the {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} of the first syllable, being no longer a pretonic vowel, becomes vocal {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}; as {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתֶּ֫ם}}, {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתֶּ֫ן}}; cf. {{GHGpar|27|i}} and {{GHGpar|43|b}}. On the retention of ''ā'' with {{GHGterm|Metheg}} of the counter-tone in the ''Perf. consecutive'', cf. {{GHGpar|49|i}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|c}}
Rem. 1. Verbs ''middle ē'' in Hebrew (as in Ethiopic, but not in Arabic or Aramaic) generally change the ''E''-sound in their inflexion into {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} (frequently so even in the 3rd sing. masc. Perf.). This tendency to assimilate to the more common verbs ''middle a'' may also be explained from the laws of vocalization of the tone-bearing closed penultima, which does not readily admit of {{GHGterm|Ṣere}}, and never of {{GHGterm|Ḥireq}}, of which the {{GHGterm|Ṣere}} is a lengthening (cf. {{GHGpar|26|p}}). On the other hand, {{GHGterm|Ṣere}} is retained in an open syllable; regularly so in the weak stems {{GHGheb|text=ל״א}} ({{GHGpar|74|g}}), before suffixes ({{GHGpar|59|i}}), and in the pausal forms of the strong stem in an open tone-syllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=דָּבֵ֫קָה|translate=it cleaveth}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=10}} (not {{GHGheb|text=דָּבָ֫קָה}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=15}}; even (contrary to {{GHGpar|29|q}}) in a ''closed'' pausal syllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שָׁכֵן}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=12}} (out of pause {{GHGheb|text=שָׁכַן}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=16}}); but {{GHGheb|text=קָמַ֑ל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=33|verse=9}}, &c., according to {{GHGpar|29|q}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|d}}
2. In some weak stems ''middle a'', the {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} under the second radical sometimes, in a closed toneless syllable, becomes {{GHGheb|text=־ִ}}, and, in one example, {{GHGheb|text=־ֶ}}. Thus from {{GHGheb|text=יָרַשׁ}}: {{GHGheb|text=וִיֽרִשְׁתָּהּ|translate=and thou shalt possess it}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=17|verse=14}}; {{GHGheb|text=וִיֽרִשְׁתָּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=19|verse=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=וִיֽרִשְׁתֶּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=1}}, and frequently; from {{GHGheb|text=יָלַד|translate=to bring forth, to beget}}; {{GHGheb|text=יְלִדְתִּ֫יךָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=7}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=15|verse=10|hidebook=1}}); from {{GHGheb|text=פּוּשׁ}}; {{GHGheb|text=וּפִשְׁתֶּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=3|verse=20}}; from {{GHGheb|text=שָׁאַל}}; {{GHGheb|text=שְׁאלְתִּיו|translate=I have asked him}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=20}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=6}}), and three times {{GHGheb|text=שְׁאֶלְתֶּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=12|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=29}}. Qimḥi already suggests the explanation, that the ''ĭ'' (''ĕ'') of these forms of {{GHGheb|text=שׁאל}} and {{GHGheb|text=ירשׁ}} is the original vowel, since along with {{GHGheb|text=שָׁאַל}} and {{GHGheb|text=יָרַשׁ}} are also found {{GHGheb|text=שָׁאֵל}} and {{GHGheb|text=יָרֵשׁ}} (see the Lexicon). The possibility of this explanation cannot be denied (especially in the case of {{GHGheb|text=יָרַשׁ}}, see {{GHGpar|69|s}}); the ''ĭ'' in these forms might, however, equally well have arisen from an attenuation of ''ă'' ({{GHGpar|27|s}}), such as must in any case be assumed in the other instances. Moreover, it is worthy of notice that in all the above cases the ''ĭ'' is favoured by the character of the following consonant (a sibilant or dental), and in most of them also by the tendency towards assimilation of the vowels (cf. {{GHGpar|54|k}} and {{GHGpar|64|f}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|e}}
3. In verbs ''middle ō'', the {{GHGterm|Ḥolem}} is retained in the tone-syllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָגֹ֫רְתָּ|translate=thou didst tremble}}; {{GHGheb|text=יָכֹ֫לוּ}} in {{GHGterm|pause}} for {{GHGheb|text=יָֽכְלוּ|translate=they were able}}; but in a toneless closed syllable the original short vowel appears in the form of a ''Qameṣ haṭuph''; {{GHGheb|text=יְכָלְתִּ֫יו|translate=I have prevailed against him}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=13|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=וְיָֽכָלְתָּ֫}} (see {{GHGpar|49|h}}) ''then shalt thou be able'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=23}}; in a toneless open syllable it becomes vocal {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָכִֽלָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָכְֽלוּ}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|f}}
4. Rarer forms<ref>Many of these forms, which are uncommon in Hebrew, are usual in the other Semitic dialects, and may, therefore, be called Aramaisms (Syriasms) or Arabisms. They must not, however, be regarded as cases of borrowing, but as a return to original forms.</ref> are: ''Sing''. 3rd ''fem''. in {{GHGheb|text=־ַת}} (as in Arabic, Ethiopic, and<section end="par44" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

145.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par44 />Aramaic), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָֽזְלַת|translate=it is gone}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=36}}; {{GHGheb|text=וְנִשְׁכַּ֫חַת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=23|verse=15}} (in the Aramaic form, for {{GHGheb|text=וְנִשְׁכְּחָה}}); from a verb {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְשָׁבַת}}, cf. {{GHGpar|72|o}}. This original feminine ending ''-ath'' is regularly retained before suffixes, see {{GHGpar|59|a}}; and similarly in stems {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}, either in the form ''āth'' (which is frequent also in stems {{GHGheb|text=ל״א}} {{GHGpar|74|g}}), or with the {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} weakened to {{GHGterm|vocal Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} before the pleonastic ending {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גָּֽלְתָה}} {{GHGpar|75|i}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=31|verse=5}} the Aramaic form {{GHGheb|text=גָּֽבְהָא}} occurs instead of {{GHGheb|text=גָּֽבְהָה}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|g}}
2nd {{GHGterm|masc.}} {{GHGheb|text=תָּה}} for {{GHGheb|text=תָּ}} (differing only orthographically), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בָּגַ֫דְתָּה|translate=thou hast dealt treacherously}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=2|verse=14}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=12}} ({{GHGheb|text=נָתַ֫תָּה}} which is twice as common as {{GHGheb|text=נָתַ֫תָּ}}, cf. {{GHGpar|66|h}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=56|verse=9}} (so also in ''Hiphʿil''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=60|verse=4}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|h}}
2nd {{GHGterm|fem.}} has sometimes a Yodh at the end, as in {{GHGheb|text=הָלָ֑כְתְּי|translate=thou wentest}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=31|verse=21}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=33|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=4.5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=19|hidebook=1}} (but read the ptcp. {{GHGheb|text=שֹׁמַ֫עַת}}, with the LXX, instead of the 2nd fem.),{{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=46|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, and so commonly in Jeremiah, and Ez ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, &c.); see also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=4|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=3.4}}. {{GHGheb|text=הָלַ֫כְתִּי}}, &c., is really intended, for the vowel signs in the text belong to the marginal reading {{GHGheb|text=הָלַכְתְּ}} (without {{GHGheb|text=י}})<ref>Where the Masora apparently regards the {{GHGheb|text=תִּי}} as the termination of the 2nd ''sing. fem.'', e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=20}} (twice), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=4|verse=13}}, it has rather taken the form as 1st ''pers. sing.'' (cf. Stade, ''Gramm.'', p. 253); so in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5|verse=7}}, where {{GHGheb|text=קַ֫מְתִּי}}, on account of verse 12, must either have originally been intended as 2nd ''sing. fem.'', or is due to an erroneous pronunciation of the form {{GHGheb|text=קמת}} as {{GHGheb|text=קַ֫מְתִּ}} instead of 3rd ''sing. fem.'' {{GHGheb|text=קָ֫מַת}} (as LXX).</ref> as in the corresponding pronoun {{GHGheb|text=אַתְּי}} ({{GHGheb|text=אַתִּי}}) {{GHGpar|32|h}}. The ordinary form has rejected the final ''i'', but it regularly reappears when pronominal suffixes are added ({{GHGpar|59|a}}, c).

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|i}}
1st ''pers. comm.'' sometimes without Yodh, as {{GHGheb|text=יָדַ֫עְתִּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=140|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=42|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=48}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=59}} (all in K<sup>e</sup>thîbh), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=16|verse=2}}, without a Q<sup>e</sup>rê; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=18|verse=20}} also {{GHGheb|text=אָמַ֫רְתִּ}} is really intended, as appears from {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=36|verse=5}}. The Q<sup>e</sup>rê requires the ordinary form, to which the vowels of the text properly belong, whilst the K<sup>e</sup>thîbh is probably to be regarded as the remains of an earlier orthography, which omitted vowel-letters even at the end of the word.

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|k}}
{{GHGheb|text=תֶן}} as the termination of the 2nd ''plur. m.'' for {{GHGheb|text=תֶם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=33|verse=26}}, might just possibly be due to the following {{GHGheb|text=ת}} (cf., for an analogous case, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=3|verse=12}}, {{GHGpar|87|e}}), but is probably a copyist’s error. Plur. 2nd {{GHGterm|fem.}} in {{GHGheb|text=-תֶּ֫נָה}} (according to others {{GHGheb|text=-תֶּ֫נָּה}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=3}}, but the reading is very doubtful; since {{GHGheb|text=ה}} follows, it is perhaps merely due to dittography; cf., however, {{GHGheb|text=אַתֵּ֫נָה}} {{GHGpar|32|i}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|l}}
3rd ''plur. comm.'' has three times the very strange termination {{GHGheb|text=וּן}}<ref>That these examples can hardly be referred to a primitive Semitic ending ''ûn'' in the 3rd plur. Perf., has been shown by Nöldeke in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} vol. 38, p. 409 ff.; cf. also {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} vol. 32, p. 757 f., where G. Hoffmann proves that the terminations in ''Nûn'' of the 3rd plur. in Aramaic, formerly adduced by us, are secondary forms. [See also Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Heb. Tenses}}<sup>3</sup>, p. 6 ''note''.]</ref>; {{GHGheb|text=יָֽדְעוּן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=8|verse=3.16}} (both before {{GHGheb|text=א}}, and hence, no doubt, if the text is correct, to avoid a hiatus), and in the still more doubtful form {{GHGheb|text=צָקוּן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=26|verse=16}}; on {{GHGheb|text=וּן}} in the Imperf. see {{GHGpar|47|m}}; on the affixed {{GHGheb|text=א}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=10|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=12}}, see {{GHGpar|23|i}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|m}}
It is very doubtful whether, as in most Semitic languages (see {{GHGpar|47|c}}, note), the 3rd.''fem. plur.'' in Hebrew was originally distinguished from the 3rd ''masc''.<section end=par44 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

146.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par44/>''plur.'' by the termination {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}, as in Biblical Aramaic. Nöldeke ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A.
