(''a'') Which have adopted the vowels of verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}, e.g. {{GHGterm|perfect Qal}} {{GHGheb|text=כָּלִ֫אתִי|translate=I have refrained}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=101}}; {{GHGterm|participle}} {{GHGheb|text=חוֹטֶא}} ({{GHGheb|text=חֹטֶא}}) ''sinning'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=2|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=8|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=9|verse=2.18|hidebook=1}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=65|verse=20}}; {{GHGheb|text=מוֹצֶא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=7|verse=26}}; {{GHGheb|text=נשֶׁא|translate=lending}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=22|verse=2}}; ''Piʿēl perfect'' {{GHGheb|text=מִלָּא|translate=he has filled}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=34}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=9|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=2}} (where, however, the {{GHGterm|perfect Niph.}} is perhaps intended), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=89|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=143|verse=3|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=רִפִּ֫אתִו|translate=I heal}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=21}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=9}}; {{GHGterm|imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יְגַמֶּא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=39|verse=24}}; ''Niphʿal perfect'' {{GHGheb|text=נִפְלְאַ֫תָה}} (like {{GHGheb|text=נִגְלְתֶה}}) ''it was wonderful'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=26}}; ''Hiphʿîl perfect'' {{GHGheb|text=הִפְלָא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=59}}; {{GHGheb|text=תֶחְבְּאַ֫תָה}} (not {{GHGheb|text=־אָ֫תָה}}, cf. above, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=26}}) ''she hid'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=6|verse=17}}. On the other hand, forms like {{GHGheb|text=חֹטִאים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=33}}, {{GHGheb|text=קֹרִאים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=99|verse=6}}, {{GHGheb|text=נִרְפּאוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=47|verse=8}}, {{GHGheb|text=תְּדַכּאוּנַ֫נִי}}, according to the correct reading, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=2}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=39}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲחַטֶּ֫נָה}}), and {{GHGheb|text=יְראוּ|translate=imperative plur. masc.}} from {{GHGheb|text=יָרֵא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=24|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=12|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=34|verse=10}}, are due to the elision of the {{GHGheb|text=א}}, see {{GHGpar|74|i}}. On {{GHGheb|text=יִנָּשׂוּא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=5}} and {{GHGheb|text=נָשׂוּא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=20}}, see {{GHGpar|23|i}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|75|pp}}
(''b'') Forms in {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, but keeping their {{GHGheb|text=ל״א}} vowels, e.g. {{GHGterm|imperfect Qal}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶרְפָּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=22}}; {{GHGterm|imperative}} {{GHGheb|text=רְפָה|translate=heal thou}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=60|verse=4}}; ''Niphʿal;'' {{GHGheb|text=נֶחְבָּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=10}} (which must evidently be a {{GHGterm|perfect}}; read with Ewald the {{GHGterm|infinitive absolute}} {{GHGheb|text=נֶחְבֹּה}} as in verse 23), and {{GHGheb|text=הֵחָבֵה|translate=to hide oneself}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=25}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=19|verse=11}}; ''Piʿēl imperfect'' {{GHGheb|text=יְמַלֵּה|translate=he will fill}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=8|verse=21}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|75|qq}}
(''c'') Forms entirely of a {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} character, e.g. {{GHGterm|perfect Qal}} {{GHGheb|text=וְצֶמִת|translate=and when thou art athirst}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=2|verse=9}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=8}}; {{GHGheb|text=כָּלוּ|translate=they shut up}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=10}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=33|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=מָלוּ|translate=they are full}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=28|verse=16}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=39|verse=26|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGterm|infinitive}} {{GHGheb|text=חֲטוֹ}} (see above, n) ''to sin'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=6}} (on {{GHGheb|text=מְלֹאת}} see above, {{GHGpar|74|h}}); ''imperative sing. fem.'' {{GHGheb|text=חֲבִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=26|verse=20}}; {{GHGterm|imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יִכְלֶה}} (for {{GHGheb|text=יִכְלָא}}) ''he will keep back'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=6}}; {{GHGheb|text=תִּרְפֶּ֫ינָה|translate=they heal}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=18}}; {{GHGterm|participle}} {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹוטֶה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=12|verse=18}}; {{GHGterm|fem.}} {{GHGheb|text=יׄצָא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=10|verse=5}}; ''plur.'' {{GHGheb|text=צֹבֶ֫יהָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=7}}; {{GHGterm|participle passive}} {{GHGheb|text=נָשׂוּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=1}}; {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}} {{GHGheb|text=נִרְפָּ֫תָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=9}}; {{GHGheb|text=נִבֵּ֫יתָ|translate=thou hast prophesied}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=26|verse=9}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=18|verse=3}}); {{GHGterm|imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיֵּרָֽפוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=22}} ({{GHGterm|infinitive}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=19|verse=11}}); ''Piʿēl imperfect'' {{GHGheb|text=וַיְרַפּוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=8|verse=11}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=39}}; ''Hiphʿîl participle'' {{GHGheb|text=מַקְנֶה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=8|verse=3}}; ''Hithpa‛el'' {{GHGheb|text=הִתְנַבִּ֫יתָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=6}}; {{GHGterm|infinitive}} {{GHGheb|text=הִתְנַבּוֹת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=13}}. For the {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}} {{GHGheb|text=להשות}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=19|verse=25}}, Jablonski and others require as {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} the form {{GHGheb|text=לְהַשְׁאוֹת}} (so {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=26}}); the {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}} would have to be read {{GHGheb|text=לַהְשׁוֹת}}, with elision of the {{GHGheb|text=א}} and retraction of the vowel.

{{GHGmargin-letter|75|rr}}
22. On the other hand, there are forms of verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}, which wholly or in part follow the analogy of verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״א}}, e.g. in their consonants {{GHGheb|text=אָתָא|translate=he comes}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=12}}; {{GHGheb|text=בָּרָא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=17}} (''textus receptus'' {{GHGheb|text=בָּרָה}}); {{GHGheb|text=וְרָצִ֫אתִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=43|verse=27}}; {{GHGheb|text=יִשְׂגֶּא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=8|verse=11}}; {{GHGheb|text=יִשְׁנֶא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|verse=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=וַיֶּֽחֶלֶא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=16|verse=12}}; {{GHGheb|text=תִּקְרֶ֫אנָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=1|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=10|verse=19}}; {{GHGheb|text=תְּלֻאִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=66}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=11|verse=7}}); {{GHGheb|text=נִקְרֹא}} (''infin. absol. Niphʿal'' beside {{GHGheb|text=נִקְרֵ֫יתִי}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=6}}; {{GHGheb|text=שִׁנָּא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=25|verse=29}}; {{GHGheb|text=מְרַפֵּא}}<section end=par75 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

241.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par75 />{{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=38|verse=4}}; {{GHGheb|text=יְשֻׁנֶּא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=8|verse=1}}: in their vowels, {{GHGheb|text=אָתָ֫נוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=22}}; {{GHGheb|text=יִקְרָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=10|verse=14}}; {{GHGheb|text=תִּכְלָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=17|verse=14}}: in both, {{GHGheb|text=יִקְרָא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=1}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=51|verse=19}}; {{GHGheb|text=תְּלָאוּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=21|verse=12}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}; {{GHGheb|text=לִירוֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=26|verse=15}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=ויראו המוראים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=11|verse=24}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}}); {{GHGheb|text=מֹֽרְאָה}} (''participle fem. Qal'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=3|verse=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=יַפְרִיא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=13|verse=15}}; {{GHGheb|text=מְסֻלָּאִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|verse=2}}.—For {{GHGheb|text=פֹּרֹאות}} (so Baer, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=17|verse=6}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=31|verse=8|hidebook=1}}), which can only be intended for {{GHGheb|text=פֹּֽרְאוֹת|translate=participle fem. plur.}} from {{GHGheb|text=פָּרָא}}={{GHGheb|text=פָּרָה}}, read {{GHGheb|text=פֹּארוֹת|translate=branches}}, according to {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=31|verse=5}}, &c.<section end=par75 />

<section begin=par76 />{{GHGpar-heading|76|Verbs Doubly Weak}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|76|a}}
'''1.''' In a tolerably large number of verbs two radicals are weak letters, and are consequently affected by one or other of the anomalies already described. In cases where two anomalies might occur, usage must teach whether one, or both, or neither of them, takes effect.

{{GHGmargin-letter|76|b}}
Thus e.g. from {{GHGheb|text=נָדַד|translate=to flee}}, the {{GHGterm|imperfect}} is {{GHGheb|text=יִדּוֹד}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=3|verse=7}} and {{GHGheb|text=יִדַּד}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=40}} (on the analogy of verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״ן}}); {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} {{GHGheb|text=הֵנֵד}} (like a verb {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}}), but the {{GHGterm|imperfect Hophʿal}} again {{GHGheb|text=יֻדַּד}} (as {{GHGheb|text=פ״ן}}).

'''2.''' The following are examples of difficult forms, which are derived from doubly weak verbs:

{{GHGmargin-letter|76|c}}
(''a'') Verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״ן}} and {{GHGheb|text=ל״א}} (cf. § 66 and § 74), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=נָשָׂא|translate=to bear}}, imperative {{GHGheb|text=שָׂא}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=10|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=נְשָׂא}}, of which {{GHGheb|text=נְסָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=4|verse=7}} is probably only an orthographic variation); {{GHGterm|infinitive construct}} {{GHGheb|text=שְׂאֵת}} (for {{GHGheb|text=שָׂ֫אֶת}}; see the analogous noun-formations in {{GHGpar|93|t}}), also {{GHGheb|text=נְשׂא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=18|verse=3|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=נְשׂוֹא}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=89|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=שׂוֹא}} (perhaps only a scribal error); after the ''prefix'' {{GHGheb|text=ל}} always {{GHGheb|text=לָשֵׂאת}} (otherwise the contracted form only occurs in {{GHGheb|text=מִשֵּׂתוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=17}}, with rejection of the {{GHGheb|text=א}}); {{GHGterm|imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=תִּשֶּׂ֫נָה}} for {{GHGheb|text=תִּשֶּׂ֫אנָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=14}}; wholly irregular are {{GHGheb|text=תִּשְּׂאֶ֫ינָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=49}} (so Baer after Qimḥi; ''textus receptus'', and also the Mantua ed., and Ginsburg, {{GHGheb|text=תִּשֶּׂ֫אינָה}}) and {{GHGheb|text=נִשֵּׂאת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=43}} as ''infinitive absolute Niphʿal'' (on the analogy of the ''infinitive construct Qal''?); but most probably {{GHGheb|text=נִשּׂא}} is to be read, with Driver.

{{GHGmargin-letter|76|d}}
(''b'') Verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״ן}} and {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} (cf. § 66 and § 75), as {{GHGheb|text=נָטָה|translate=to bow, to incline}}, {{GHGheb|text=נָכָה|translate=to smite}}. Hence {{GHGterm|imperfect Qal}} {{GHGheb|text=יִטֶּה}}, ''apocopated'' {{GHGheb|text=וַיֵּט}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=25}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיֶּט־}}) ''and he bowed''; {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּז}} (so, probably, also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=63|verse=3}} for {{GHGheb|text=וְיֵּז}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=33}} ''and he sprinkled'' (from {{GHGheb|text=נָזָה}}); {{GHGterm|perfect Hiphʿîl}} {{GHGheb|text=הִכָּה|translate=he smote}}, imperfect {{GHGheb|text=יַכֶּה}}, ''apocopated'' {{GHGheb|text=יַךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּךְ}} (even with ''Athnaḥ'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=15|verse=16}}; but also ten times {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּכֶּה}}), {{GHGheb|text=וַנַּךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=33}}; so also {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּז}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=8|verse=11.30}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַל־תַּט}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=141|verse=4}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=11}}); {{GHGterm|imperative}} {{GHGheb|text=הַכֵּה}}, ''apocopated'' {{GHGheb|text=הַךְ|translate=smite thou}} (like {{GHGheb|text=הַט|translate=incline}}, with {{GHGheb|text=הַטֵּה}}), {{GHGterm|infinitive}} {{GHGheb|text=הַכּוֹת}}, {{GHGterm|participle}} {{GHGheb|text=מַכֶּה}}; {{GHGterm|Hophʿal}} {{GHGheb|text=הֻכֶּה}}, {{GHGterm|participle}} {{GHGheb|text=מֻכֶּה}}.

(''c'') Verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״א}} and {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} (cf.§ 68 and § 75), as {{GHGheb|text=אָבָה|translate=to be willing}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָפָה|translate=to bake}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָתָה|translate=to come}}. E.g. {{GHGterm|imperfect Qal}} {{GHGheb|text=יֹאבֶה}}, {{GHGheb|text=יֹאפֶה}}, ''plur.'' {{GHGheb|text=יֹאפוּ}}; {{GHGheb|text=וַיֵּתֵא}} (cf. {{GHGpar|68|h}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=21}} for {{GHGheb|text=וַיֵּאתֶה}} (={{GHGheb|text=וַיּאֱֽתֶה}}); {{GHGterm|imperfect apocopated}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּאת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=25}} for {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּאְתְּ}}; {{GHGterm|imperative}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵתָ֫יוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=56|verse=9.12|hidebook=1}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=אֵפוּ|translate=bake ye}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=23}}) for {{GHGheb|text=אֱתוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֱתָ֫יוּ}} ({{GHGpar|23|h}}; {{GHGpar|75|u}}); ''Hiphʿîl perfect'' {{GHGheb|text=הֵתָ֫יוּ}} for {{GHGheb|text=הֵאתָ֫יוּ}} ({{GHGheb|text=הֶֽאֱתָ֫יוּ}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=14}}; {{GHGterm|imperfect apocopated}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיֹּ֫אֶל|translate=and he adjured}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=24}}, properly {{GHGheb|text=יַֽאֲלֶה}} ({{GHGheb|text=יַאְלֶה}}) from {{GHGheb|text=אָלָה}}, whence {{GHGheb|text=יָאלֶה}}, and, with the obscuring to ''ô'', {{GHGheb|text=יֹאלָה}}; instead of the simple ''apocope'' ({{GHGheb|text=וַיּאֹל}}) the {{GHGheb|text=א}} which had already become<section end=par76 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

242.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par76 />quiescent, is made audible again by the helping {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>ghôl}} (unless perhaps there is a confusion with the ''imperfect consecutive Hiphʿîl'' of {{GHGheb|text=יאל}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|76|e}}
(''d'') Verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״י}} and {{GHGheb|text=ל״א}} (cf. § 69, § 70, and § 74), as {{GHGheb|text=יָצָא|translate=to go forth, imperative}} {{GHGheb|text=צֵא|translate=go forth}}, with {{GHGheb|text=־ָה|translate=paragogic}} {{GHGheb|text=צֵ֫אָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=29}} in principal pause for {{GHGheb|text=צְאָה}}; 2nd ''fem. plur.'' {{GHGheb|text=צְאֶ֫נָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=3|verse=11}}; {{GHGterm|infinitive}} {{GHGheb|text=צֵאת}}; {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} {{GHGheb|text=הוֹצִיא|translate=to bring forth}}.—{{GHGheb|text=יָרֵא|translate=to fear, imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יִירָא}} and {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּירָא}} (or {{GHGheb|text=וַיּרָא}}), {{GHGterm|imperative}} {{GHGheb|text=יְרָא}}; {{GHGterm|imperfect Niphʿal}} {{GHGheb|text=יִוָּרֵא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=130|verse=4}}, {{GHGterm|participle}} {{GHGheb|text=נוֹרָא}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|76|f}}
(''e'') Verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״י}} and {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} (cf. § 69, § 70, and § 75), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָדָה|translate=to throw}}, Hiphʿîl ''to confess, to praise'', and {{GHGheb|text=יָרָה|translate=to throw}} (both properly verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״ו}}), and {{GHGheb|text=יָפָה|translate=to be beautiful}}. {{GHGterm|Infinitive}} {{GHGheb|text=יָרֹה}}, {{GHGheb|text=יְרוֹת}}; {{GHGterm|imperative}} {{GHGheb|text=יְרֵה}}; {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּיף}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=31|verse=7}} (cf. also {{GHGheb|text=וַתִּ֫יפִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=13|hidebook=1}}); with ''suffixes'' {{GHGheb|text=וַנִּירָם|translate=we have shot at them}} (from {{GHGheb|text=יָרָה}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=30}}; perhaps, however, it should be read with the LXX {{GHGheb|text=וְנִינָם|translate=and their race}} (also in the very corrupt passage {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=74|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=נִינָם}} is probably a ''substantive'', and not the {{GHGterm|imperfect Qal}} with ''suffix'' from {{GHGheb|text=יָנָה}}); ''Piʿēl;'' {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּדּוּ}} for {{GHGheb|text=וַיְיַדּוּ}}, ({{GHGpar|69|u}}). {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} {{GHGheb|text=הוֹדָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=הוֹרָה}}; {{GHGterm|infinitive}} {{GHGheb|text=הוֹדֹת}} (as {{GHGterm|infinitive absolute}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=7|verse=3}}); {{GHGterm|imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יוֹרֶה}}, cf. {{GHGheb|text=אַל־תֹּנוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=3}}; ''apocopated'' {{GHGheb|text=וַיּוֹר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=13|verse=17}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|76|g}}
(''f'') Verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=ל״א}}, particularly {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹא|translate=to come}}. {{GHGterm|Perfect}} {{GHGheb|text=בָּא}}, {{GHGheb|text=בָּ֫אתָ}}, {{GHGheb|text=בָּ֫את}} or {{GHGheb|text=בָּאתְ}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=4|verse=10}}; cf. {{GHGpar|75|m}}), once {{GHGheb|text=בָּ֫נוּ}} for {{GHGheb|text=בָּ֫אנוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=8}}; for {{GHGheb|text=בֹּאוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=27|verse=18}}, which is apparently the {{GHGterm|perfect}}, read {{GHGheb|text=יָבֹ֫אוּ}}. In the {{GHGterm|imperfect Qal}} the separating vowel occurs ({{GHGheb|text=תְּבֹאָ֫ינָה}} instead of the more common {{GHGheb|text=תָּבֹ֫אנָה}}, cf. also {{GHGheb|text=תָּבֹ֫אןָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=38}}) only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=9|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=45|verse=16}}, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=7}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|76|h}}
For {{GHGheb|text=וַתָּבֹאת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=34}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} (the {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}} {{GHGheb|text=ותבאתי}} evidently combines the two readings {{GHGheb|text=וּבָאתְ}} and {{GHGheb|text=וַתָּבֹאִי}}; cf. Nestle, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} xiv. 319), read {{GHGheb|text=וַתָּבֹ֫אִי}}; on the impossible forms {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=16}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=21}} cf. {{GHGpar|48|d}}.—In the {{GHGterm|perfect Hiphʿîl}} {{GHGheb|text=הֵבִיא}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֵבֵ֫אתָ}} and (only before a suffix) {{GHGheb|text=הֲבִיאֹתָ}}; the latter form is also certainly intended in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=31}}, where the Masora requires {{GHGheb|text=וְהֵֽבֵיאתִ֫י}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=19|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=43|verse=23}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=25|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=3|verse=4}}. Before suffixes the ''ē'' of the first syllable in the 3rd ''sing.'' always becomes {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph-S<sup>e</sup>ghôl}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הֱבִֽיאֲךָ}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֱבִיאַ֫נִי}}; elsewhere invariably {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph-Pathaḥ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הֲבֵאתָ֫נוּ}} or {{GHGheb|text=הֲבִֽיאֹתָ֫נוּ}}. On the other hand, ''ē'' is retained in the secondary tone in the {{GHGterm|perfect consecutive}} when without suffixes, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וְהֵֽבֵאתָ֫}}. Cf. moreover, {{GHGheb|text=וַֽהֲקֵאֹתוֹ}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַֽהֲקֵאֹתוֹ}} in Opitius and Hahn is altogether incorrect), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=25|verse=16}}, from {{GHGheb|text=קִיא}}; but {{GHGheb|text=קְיוּ|translate=spue ye}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=25|verse=27}} (perhaps only a mistake for {{GHGheb|text=קִיאוּ}}), is not to be referred to {{GHGheb|text=קִיא}} but to a secondary stem {{GHGheb|text=קָיָה}}. In the {{GHGterm|imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=וַתָּקִא}} is found once, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=18|verse=25}}, besides {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּקֵא}} (analogous to {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּבֵא}}).—On {{GHGheb|text=אָבִי}} (for {{GHGheb|text=אָבִיא}}), {{GHGheb|text=מֵבִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָנִי}}, see {{GHGpar|74|k}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|76|i}}
(''g'') The form {{GHGheb|text=חָיַי|translate=to live}}, in the {{GHGterm|perfect Qal}}, besides the ordinary development to {{GHGheb|text=חָיָה}} ({{GHGterm|fem.}} {{GHGheb|text=חָֽיְתָה}}), is also treated as a verb {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}}, and then becomes {{GHGheb|text=חַי}} in the 3rd ''pers. perfect'', in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=חָי}}, and with {{GHGterm|wāw consecutive}} {{GHGheb|text=וָחַי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=22}}, and frequently. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=25|verse=36}} the contracted form {{GHGheb|text=וְחֵי}} is perhaps {{GHGterm|st. constr.}} of {{GHGheb|text=חַי|translate=life}}, but in any case read {{GHGheb|text=וָחַי|translate=perfect consecutive}} as in verse 35. The form {{GHGheb|text=וָחָ֫יָה}} occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=1|verse=16}} in {{GHGterm|pause}} for {{GHGheb|text=וָחַ֫יָּה}} (3rd {{GHGterm|fem.}}) with {{GHGterm|Dageš}} omitted in the {{GHGheb|text=י}} on account of the pausal lengthening of ''ă'' to ''ā''.<section end=par76 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

243.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par77"/>{{GHGpar-heading|77|Relation of the Weak Verbs to one another}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|77|a}}
The close relation which exists between some classes of the weak verbs (e.g. between {{GHGheb|text=פ״ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=פ״י}}, {{GHGheb|text=ל״א}} and {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}, {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}} and {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}} and {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}) appears not only in their similarity or identity of inflexion, or their mutual interchange of certain forms, but especially from the fact that frequently the same root (''radix bilittera'', see {{GHGpar|30|g}}) recurs in various weak stems of similar meaning. The meaning accordingly is inherent in the two constant root-consonants, while the third ''consonant̤'', which is weak (and the particular class of weak verbs with it), does not establish any difference in the meaning. Thus from the root {{GHGheb|text=דךְ}} there occur with the same meaning {{GHGheb|text=דָּכַךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=דּוּךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=דָּכָא|translate=to strike, to crush}}; and from the root {{GHGheb|text=נד}} there are {{GHGheb|text=נוּד}}, {{GHGheb|text=נָדַד}}, {{GHGheb|text=נָדָה|translate=to flee}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|77|b}}
In this manner the following classes are related in form and meaning:

1. Verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}} in which the first and third consonants are the same in both, as being essential to the meaning; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מוּךְ}} and {{GHGheb|text=מָכַךְ|translate=to become poor}}; {{GHGheb|text=מוּשׁ}} and {{GHGheb|text=מָשַׁשׁ|translate=to feel}}; {{GHGheb|text=נוּד}} and {{GHGheb|text=נָדַד|translate=to flee}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|77|c}}
2. Verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״י}} and {{GHGheb|text=פ״ן}}; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָצַב}} and {{GHGheb|text=נָצַב|translate=to place}}, {{GHGheb|text=נָקַשׁ}} and {{GHGheb|text=יָקשׁ}} (''yāqōs̆'') ''to lay snares''. Moreover, stems belonging to the classes mentioned in 1 (especially {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}}) are frequently related also to verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״י}} and {{GHGheb|text=פ״ן}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גּוּר}} and {{GHGheb|text=יָגֹר|translate=to fear}}; {{GHGheb|text=טוֹב}} and {{GHGheb|text=יָטַב|translate=to be good}}; {{GHGheb|text=נָפַח}} and {{GHGheb|text=פּוּחַ|translate=to blow}}; {{GHGheb|text=נָפַץ}} and {{GHGheb|text=פּוּץ|translate=to dash to pieces}}. Verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״א}} are less frequently connected with these classes, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָדַשׁ}} and {{GHGheb|text=דּוּשׁ|translate=to thresh}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|77|d}}
3. Verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״א}} and {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} (in which the first two consonants form the real body of the stem) are sometimes related to each other, and sometimes to the above classes. To each other, in {{GHGheb|text=דָּכָא}} and {{GHGheb|text=דָּכָה|translate=to crush}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָרָא}} and {{GHGheb|text=קָרָה|translate=to meet}} (cf. {{GHGpar|75|nn}}); to verbs of the other classes, in {{GHGheb|text=מָצָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=מָצַץ|translate=to suck}}, {{GHGheb|text=דָּחָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=דּוּחַ|translate=to thrust}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|77|e}}
4. Verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}} and {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}, on which cf. Grimm, ''Journal of Bibl. Lit.'', 1903, p. 196; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָנָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=אָנַן|translate=to sigh}}, {{GHGheb|text=דָּמָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=דָּמַם|translate=to be quiet}}, {{GHGheb|text=חָנָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=חָנַן|translate=to incline}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּלָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=כָּלַל|translate=to end}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָלָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=קָלַל|translate=to despise}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָׁגָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=שָׁגַג|translate=to err}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָׁחָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=שָׁחַח|translate=to bend down}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָׁסָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=שָׁסַס|translate=to plunder}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|77|f}}
5. Verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=ע״ה}}; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מוּל}} and {{GHGheb|text=מָהַל}} (New Hebrew; in O.T. only {{GHGheb|text=מָהוּל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=22}}) ''to circumcise'', {{GHGheb|text=מוּר}} and {{GHGheb|text=מָהַר|translate=to exchange}}, {{GHGheb|text=נוּר}} (in {{GHGheb|text=מְנוֹרָה|translate=a light}}) and {{GHGheb|text=נָהַר|translate=to shine}}; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=לְהָטִים|translate=secret arts}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=7|verse=11}} with {{GHGheb|text=לָט|translate=secret}}, from {{GHGheb|text=לוּט}}.
<section end="par77"/>
<section begin="par78"/>{{GHGpar-heading|78|Verba Defectiva}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|78|a}}
It often happens, when two kindred weak verbs are in use with the same meaning, that both are ''defective'', i.e. do not occur in all the forms. Since, however, those tenses and forms which are not in use in the one verb are generally supplied by the other, they mutually complete one another, and thus form together, as it were, an entire<section end="par78"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

244.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par78 />verb, as in Greek {{polytonic|ἔρχομαι}}, aor. {{polytonic|ἦλθον}}, fut. {{polytonic|ἐλεύσομαι}}, and in Latin ''fero, tuli, latum, ferre'', &c., but with this difference, that in Hebrew the roots of these verbs are almost always closely related.

{{GHGmargin-letter|78|b}}
The most common verbs of this kind are—

{{GHGheb|text=בּשׁ|translate=to be ashamed}}. {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} {{GHGheb|text=הֵבִישׁ}} (inferred from {{GHGheb|text=הֱבִישׁ֫וֹתָ}}), but also {{GHGheb|text=הֹבִישׁ}}, {{GHGheb|text=הוֹבִישׁ}} as if from {{GHGheb|text=יבשׁ}}, on the analogy of verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״ו}}; also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=5}} the {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} requires {{GHGheb|text=הֹבִישׁ}}, where the {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}} has {{GHGheb|text=הִבְאִישׁ}} from {{GHGheb|text=בָּאַשׁ}}.

{{GHGheb|text=טוֹב|translate=to be good}}. {{GHGterm|Perfect}} {{GHGheb|text=טוֹב}}; but {{GHGterm|imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יִיטַב}}. and {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} {{GHGheb|text=הֵיטִיב}} from {{GHGheb|text=יָטַב}} (but cf. {{GHGheb|text=הֱטִיבֹ֫תָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=10|verse=30}}).

{{GHGheb|text=יָגׄר|translate=to be afraid}}. {{GHGterm|Imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יָגוּר}} (from {{GHGheb|text=גּוּר}}).

{{GHGheb|text=יָקַץ|translate=to awake}}, only in the ''imperf.'' {{GHGheb|text=יִיקַץ}}; for the {{GHGterm|perfect}}, the {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} {{GHGheb|text=הֵקִיץ}} is used (from {{GHGheb|text=קוּץ}}).

{{GHGheb|text=נָפַץ|translate=to break in pieces}}. {{GHGterm|Imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יָפוּץ}} (from {{GHGheb|text=פּוּץ}}). {{GHGterm|Imperative}} {{GHGheb|text=פּוּץ}}. {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}} {{GHGheb|text=נָפוֹץ}}. {{GHGterm|Piʿēl}} {{GHGheb|text=נִפֵּץ}} (from {{GHGheb|text=נָפַץ}}). ''Pôlēl'' {{GHGheb|text=פּוֹצֵץ}} (from {{GHGheb|text=פּוּץ}}). {{GHGterm|reflexive}} {{GHGheb|text=הִתְפּוֹצֵץ}}. {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} {{GHGheb|text=הֵפִיץ}}. Also {{GHGheb|text=פִּצְפֵּץ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=12}}.

{{GHGheb|text=נָצַב}} ({{GHGterm|Qal}} in post-biblical Hebrew, in Aramaic and Arabic) ''to place'', whence (possibly) {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}} {{GHGheb|text=נִצַּב}} and ''Hiph‛î''l {{GHGheb|text=הִצִיב}} (see above, § 71); but {{GHGterm|Hithpaʿēl}} {{GHGheb|text=הִתְיַצֵּב}}.

{{GHGheb|text=שָׁתָה|translate=to drink}}, used in {{GHGterm|Qal}}; but in ''Hiph.'' {{GHGheb|text=הִשְׁקָה|translate=to give to drink}}, from a {{GHGterm|Qal}} {{GHGheb|text=שָׁקָה}} which is not used in Hebrew.

On {{GHGheb|text=הָלַךְ}} ({{GHGheb|text=יָלַךְ}}) ''to go'', see above, {{GHGpar|69|x}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|78|c}}
Rem. 1. To the same category belong also, to a certain extent, those cases where the ''tenses'' or ''moods'' not in use in one conjugation, are supplied by forms having the same meaning in other conjugations of the same verb. Thus:

{{GHGheb|text=יָסַף|translate=to add}}. The {{GHGterm|infinitive}} (but cf. {{GHGpar|69|h}}, note) and {{GHGterm|imperfect}}, unused in {{GHGterm|Qal}}, are supplied by the {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} {{GHGheb|text=הוֹסִיף}}, {{GHGheb|text=יוֹסִיף}} (on {{GHGheb|text=יוֹסֵף}} as {{GHGterm|imperfect indicative}}, see {{GHGpar|109|d}}, cf. also {{GHGpar|109|i}}).

{{GHGheb|text=כָּשַׁל|translate=to stumble}}. {{GHGterm|Perfect}} from {{GHGterm|Qal}}, {{GHGterm|imperfect}} from {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}}.

{{GHGheb|text=נגשׁ|translate=to approach}}, unused in ''perf. Qal'', instead of which {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}} {{GHGheb|text=נִגַּשׁ}} is used; but {{GHGterm|imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יִגַּשׁ}}, {{GHGterm|imperative}} {{GHGheb|text=גַּשׁ}}, and {{GHGterm|infinitive}} {{GHGheb|text=גֶּ֫שֶׁת}} from {{GHGterm|Qal}} only are in use.

{{GHGheb|text=נָחָה|translate=to lead}}. {{GHGterm|Perfect}} usually {{GHGheb|text=נָחָה}} in {{GHGterm|Qal}}, so {{GHGterm|imperative}} {{GHGheb|text=נְחֵה}}, but {{GHGterm|imperfect}} and {{GHGterm|infinitive}} always in {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}}.

{{GHGheb|text=נתך|translate=to be poured out}}. {{GHGterm|Perfect Niphʿal}} {{GHGheb|text=נִתַּךְ}} with {{GHGterm|imperfect Qal}} {{GHGheb|text=יִתַּךְ}}, but the {{GHGterm|perfect Qal}} and {{GHGterm|imperfect Niphʿal}} are not in use.

2. The early grammarians often speak of ''mixed forms'' (''formae mixtae''), i.e. forms which unite the supposed character and meaning of two different tenses, genders, or conjugations. Most of the examples adduced are at once set aside by accurate grammatical analysis; some others appear to have arisen from misapprehension and inaccuracy, especially from erroneous views of unusual {{GHGterm|plene}} forms. Others, again, are either merely wrong readings or represent an intentional conflation of two different readings.<section end=par78 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

245.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Inkbug" /></noinclude>
<section begin=par79/>{{center|'''CHAPTER III'''

THE NOUN}}

<!-- section begins above -->{{GHGpar-heading|79|General View}}

For the literature, see De Lagarde, {{GHGcite|title=Uebersicht über die im Aram., Arab. und Hebr. übliche Bildung der Nomina}}, Göttingen, 1889; Index and Additions, 1891; J. Barth, {{GHGcite|title=Die Nominalbildung in den semitischen Sprachen}}, first half, {{GHGcite|title=Simple nouns}}, Leipzig, 1889; second half, {{GHGcite|title=Nouns with external additions}}, 1891; second edition, with indices of words and subjects, 1894; E. König, {{GHGcite|title=Historisch-kritisches Lehrgebäude}}, &''c''., ii. 1, Leipzig, 1895, see above, {{GHGpar|3|f}}.—Of these three important works the first two especially have given rise to various articles. In support of De Lagarde: Hommel in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xliv, p. 535 ff. (against De Lagarde and Hommel: Barth, ''ibid.'', p. 679 ff.), and dealing with the Index, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xlv, p. 340 ff.—Against Barth (though with many points of agreement): Philippi in the {{GHGcite|title=Zeitschrift für Völkerpsychologie}}, 1890, p. 344 ff. (answered by Barth in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xliv, p. 692 ff.), and {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xlvi, p. 149 ff. (answered again by Barth, ''ibid.'', xlviii, p. 10 ff.), also in the {{GHGcite|title=Beiträge zur Assyriologie}}, ii (1892), p. 359 ff. ‘Die semitische Verbal- und Nominalbildung,’ and lastly, in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xlix, p. 187 ff.—Cf. also A. Müller, ‘Semitische Nomina. Bemerkungen zu de Lagarde und Barth,’ {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xlv, p. 221 ff.—The main points at issue in the works of De Lagarde and Barth are indicated below, {{GHGpar|83|d}}.—Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Semit. Sprachwiss.}}, p. 104 ff.; {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, p. 329 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|79|a}}
'''1.''' Since, according to {{GHGpar|30|a}}, most word-stems are developed into verbal stems as well as into noun-stems, it has become customary (especially in the Lexicon) to refer the noun to the most simple ground-form of the verbal formation, viz. the 3rd {{GHGterm|pers. sing. perfect Qal|en=person singular perfect Qal}}, and, as it were, to derive it from that form. This is usual, not only in those noun-stems which can be directly connected with a corresponding verbal stem ({{GHGterm|Nomina verbalia}} or ''derivativa'', {{GHGpar|83}} ff.), but also with {{GHGterm|Nomina primitiva}}, i.e. those of which no verbal stem is now found in Hebrew (see {{GHGpar|82}}), as well as finally with {{GHGterm|Nomina denominativa}}, which have evidently been derived from other nouns ({{GHGpar|86}}).

The adjective agrees in form entirely with the substantive. On the formation of adjectival ideas by giving to abstracts a concrete sense, see {{GHGpar|83|c}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|79|b}}
'''2.''' A special inflexion of the noun to express the various cases does not exist in Hebrew; only a few ancient and almost extinct traces of case-endings have survived ({{GHGpar|90}}). The syntactical relation of a noun can therefore in general only be inferred from its position in the sentence, or from its being joined to prepositions. In either case, the form of the noun undergoes no change (except for the {{GHGterm|construct}}
<section end=par79/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

246.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par79 />''state'', {{GHGpar|89}}), and the representation of case-relations belongs therefore almost exclusively to the syntax ({{GHGpar|117}} ff.). The comparative and superlative of adjectives also can be expressed only by a syntactical combination ({{GHGpar|133}}). On the other hand, several changes in the forms of nouns are occasioned by the additions of the plural, dual, and feminine terminations, as well as of the pronominal suffixes, and also by the close connexion of two nouns, by means of the {{GHGterm|construct state}}.<ref>To speak of these changes as a declension of the Hebrew noun, as is usually done, is accordingly incorrect.</ref><section end=par79 />

<section begin=par80 />{{GHGpar-heading|80|The Indication of Gender in Nouns}}

Brockelmann; {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, p. 404 ff.; ‘Ueber die Femininendung ''at'', ''ah'', ''ā''’ in {{GHGcite|title=Semit. Sprachwiss.}}, p. 106 f.; {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, pp. 105, 405 ff.; ‘Die Femininendung ''T'' im Semit.’ ({{GHGcite|title=Sitzung d. orient.-sprachwiss. Sektion d. schlesischen Gesellschaft}}, Feb. 26, 1903); against him J. Barth, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1903, p. 628 ff.; Brockelmann’s reply, ''ibid.'', p. 795 ff.; and Barth again, ''ibid.'', p. 798 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|80|a}}
'''1.''' The Hebrew, like all Semitic languages, recognizes only two genders in the noun, a ''masculine'' and a ''feminine''. Inanimate objects and abstract ideas, which other languages sometimes indicate by the ''neuter'', are regarded in Hebrew either as masculine or feminine, more often the latter (see the Syntax, {{GHGpar|122|q}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|80|b}}
'''2.''' The ''masculine'', as being the more common and important gender, has no special indication.

Feminine nouns are also without an indication of gender when the meaning of the word naturally denotes a feminine, as {{GHGheb|text=אֵם|translate=mother}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָתוֹן|translate=a she-ass}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֵז|translate=a she-goat}}, {{GHGheb|text=רָחֵל|translate=an ewe}} (cf. {{GHGpar|122|b}}). As a rule, however, the ''feminine'' had originally the ending {{GHGheb|text=־ַת}}, as in the 3rd ''sing. perfect'' of verbs ({{GHGpar|44|a}}). This {{GHGheb|text=־ַת}}, however, is regularly retained in Hebrew only in close connexion with a following genitive or suffix (cf. {{GHGpar|89|e}} and {{GHGpar|91|o}}), except where the form has arisen through the addition of a simple {{GHGheb|text=ת}}<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=1|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=מָשְׁחַת}} (so e.g. ed. Mant.) would stand for {{GHGheb|text=מָשְׁחֶ֫תֶת}}, the ptcp. fem. Hophʿal; but {{GHGheb|text=מָשְׁחָת}} (so Baer and Ginsb.) is also supported by good authority.</ref> (see below, d). Otherwise, the feminine ending of the independent form (the {{GHGterm|absolute state}}, {{GHGpar|89|a}}) is—

{{GHGmargin-letter|80|c}}
(''a'') Most commonly a tone-bearing {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=סוּס|translate=equus|en=horse}}, {{GHGheb|text=סוּסָה|translate=equa|en=mare}}. Of nouns ending in {{GHGheb|text=־ִ}}, like {{GHGheb|text=עִבְרִי}}, the feminine (by {{GHGpar|24|b}}) is {{GHGheb|text=עִבְרִיָּה}}, cf. {{GHGpar|86|h}}. As in the 3rd ''sing. fem. perfect'' ({{GHGheb|text=קָֽטְלָה}}, &c.), this {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} seems to have arisen by the rejection of the final {{GHGheb|text=ת}}, and the lengthening of the ''ă'' in the open syllable, whereupon the {{GHGheb|text=ה}} was added as an orthographic indication of the final long vowel: cf. the exactly similar origin of such forms as {{GHGheb|text=גָּלָה}} for {{GHGheb|text=גָּלַי}}, {{GHGpar|75|c}}. It must, however, be<section end=par80 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

247.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par80 />noticed that in Arabic (see m and note) the pausal form of ''at'' is ''ah'', of which a trace may be preserved in the Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|80|d}}
(''b'') Simple {{GHGheb|text=ת}} with nouns ending in a vowel, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יְהוּדִי|translate=Jew}}, {{GHGheb|text=יְהוּדִית|translate=Jewess}}. The same ending {{GHGheb|text=ת}} is very frequently added to stems ending in a consonant, but only (except before suffixes) by means of a helping vowel, which, as a rule, is {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>ghôl}}, but after gutturals {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קֹטֵל}}, {{GHGterm|fem.}} {{GHGheb|text=קֹטֶ֫לֶת|translate=killing}}; before suffixes, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קֹֽטַלְתִּי}}, according to the rule given in {{GHGpar|69|c}}, cf. also {{GHGpar|84|s|a}}; {{GHGheb|text=מוֹדַע|translate=an acquaintance, fem.}} {{GHGheb|text=מוֹדַ֫עַת}}. The forms which arise in this way follow in every respect the analogy of the {{GHGterm|segholate}} forms ({{GHGpar|94|f}}). The forms which have been developed by means of a helping vowel are retained even in the connective form ({{GHGterm|construct state}}); except {{GHGheb|text=וְיֹלַדְתְּ}} (for {{GHGheb|text=יֹלֶ֫דֶת}}, which is used elsewhere) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=5.7}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=23}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=13|hidebook=1}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}, also {{GHGheb|text=מְשָׁרַת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=15}}, ''participle fem. Piʿēl'', properly ''m<sup>e</sup>šāratt'' = {{GHGheb|text=מְשָׁרֶ֫תֶת}}; also {{GHGheb|text=מְבַעִתֶּ֫ךְ}} (''participle fem. Piʿēl'' with suffix) arises from the form {{GHGheb|text=מְבַעַ֫תְּ}} which was developed into {{GHGheb|text=מְבַעֶ֫תֶת}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|80|e}}
Rem. 1. The fem. form in {{GHGheb|text=־ֶ֫־ֶת}} is in general less frequent, and occurs almost exclusively when the form in {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} is also in use. It is only in the participles and infinitives that it is the commoner, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קֹטֶ֫לֶת}} more common than {{GHGheb|text=קֹֽטְלָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֶ֫דֶת}} than {{GHGheb|text=לֵדָ֫ה}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|80|f}}
2. ''Rarer'' feminine endings are—(''a'') {{GHGheb|text=־ַת}} with the tone, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽרְקַ֫ת|translate=emerald}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=28|verse=13}} (also {{GHGheb|text=בָּרֶ֫קֶת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=17}}); {{GHGheb|text=שִׁפְעַ֫ת|translate=a company}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=17}}, unless the reading is wrong; more frequently in proper names, especially of places among the Canaanites or Phoenicians (in whose language {{GHGheb|text=־ַת}} was the usual fem. ending, {{GHGpar|2|d}}) and other neighbouring tribes,<ref>In the list of Palestinian towns taken by Pharaoh Shoshenq, the feminine town-names all end in ''t''. Cf. also the Mêšaʿ inscription, line 3, {{GHGheb|text=הבמת זאת|translate=this high place}}; line 26, {{GHGheb|text=המסלת|translate=the highway}} [see also Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Tenses}}, § 181, ''note''].</ref> e.g. {{GHGheb|text=צָֽרְפַ֫ת|translate=Zarephath}}, {{GHGheb|text=גִּבְעַ֫ת|translate=Gibeath}}, {{GHGheb|text=קִרְיַ֫ת|translate=Kiriath}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֵילַ֫ת}} Greek {{GHGtranslate|Ailana}} in Idumea; {{GHGheb|text=אֲחֻזַּת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=26}}: on the reading {{GHGheb|text=גָּלְיַת}} cf. g. Cf., moreover, {{GHGheb|text=נְגִּינַת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=61|verse=1}} (prob. originally {{GHGheb|text=נְגִינֹת}}); {{GHGheb|text=חַיַּת}} (LXX {{GHGheb|text=חַיּוֹת}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=74|verse=19a|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=פּוּגַת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=2|verse=18}}; [{{GHGheb|text=רַבַּת|translate=much}}, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=65|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=120|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=123|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=129|verse=1.2|hidebook=1}}, is a form borrowed from the Aramaic (Syriac ''rabbath'') in which the original ''t'' of the {{GHGterm|fem.}} is often retained to form ''adverbs'', see Wright, {{GHGcite|title=Comparative Grammar}}, p. 135.]

{{GHGmargin-letter|80|g}}
(''b'') {{GHGheb|text=־ָת}}, which likewise occurs in some names of places, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽעֲלָת}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֶלְקָת}}, as well as in the {{GHGterm|masc.}} proper name {{GHGheb|text=גָּלְיָת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=4}}, &c. (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=21|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, ed. Mant. has {{GHGheb|text=גָּלְיַת}}), and in the {{GHGterm|fem.}} proper name {{GHGheb|text=שִׁמְעָת}}; otherwise, almost only in poetry, viz. {{GHGheb|text=זִמְרָת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=12|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=118|verse=14}} (really for {{GHGheb|text=זִמְרָתִי|translate=my song}}; the absorption of the ''î'', however, can scarcely have ‘taken place in the Aramaic manner’, as suggested by Duhm on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=12|verse=2}}, nor is it due merely to the following {{GHGterm|Yôdh}}, but is intended ‘to facilitate the absorption of {{GHGheb|text=יָהּ}}’; so Geiger, ''Urschrift'', p. 277 f.); {{GHGheb|text=נַֽחֲלָת|translate=heritage}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=16|verse=6}} (either again for {{GHGheb|text=נַֽחֲלָתִי|translate=heritage}}, or for {{GHGheb|text=נַֽחֲלָ֫תָה}}, cf. {{GHGpar|90|g}}, as probably also {{GHGheb|text=עֶזְרָת|translate=help}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=60|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=108|verse=13|hidebook=1}} for {{GHGheb|text=עֶזְרָ֫תָה}}). These forms are possibly<section end=par80 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

248.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par80" />survivals from a period when even final vowels were not supported by a vowel-letter. Cf. also {{GHGheb|text=פֹּרָת|translate=fecunda}} ({{GHGtranslate|a fruitful tree}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=22}}; {{GHGheb|text=יִתְרָת|translate=abundance}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=48|verse=36}} (before {{GHGheb|text=ע}}; but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=15|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=יִתְרָה}}); {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנָת|translate=sleep}} (for {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁנָה}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=132|verse=4}}; and (unless the {{GHGheb|text=ת}} is radical) in prose {{GHGheb|text=קָאָת|translate=pelican}} (which reading is also preferable, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=34|verse=11}}, to the form {{GHGheb|text=קָאַת}}), also {{GHGheb|text=מָֽחֳרָת|translate=the morrow}}, but in {{GHGterm|construct state}} always {{GHGheb|text=ממחרַת}}.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=27}} also, where the Masora (see Baer on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=5|verse=11}}) for some unknown reason requires {{GHGheb|text=ממחרָת}}, read with ed. Mant., [[Author:Daniel Ernst Jablonsky|Jablonski]], Opitius, and Ginsburg, {{GHGheb|text=ממחרַת}}.</ref>—{{GHGheb|text=תְּהִלָּת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=45|verse=25}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} is no doubt intended to indicate the reading {{GHGheb|text=תְּהִלָּתִי}}, parallel to {{GHGheb|text=מְשׂוֹשִׂי}}; cf. above, on {{GHGheb|text=זִמְרָת}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|80|h}}
(''c'') {{GHGheb|text=־ָא}}, the Aramaic orthography for {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}, chiefly in the later writers; {{GHGheb|text=זָרָא|translate=loathing}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=20}}; {{GHGheb|text=חָגָּא|translate=a terror}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=19|verse=17}}; {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁנָא|translate=sleep}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=127|verse=2}}; {{GHGheb|text=לְבִיָּא|translate=a lioness}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=19|verse=2}} (unless {{GHGheb|text=לָבִיא}} is intended); {{GHGheb|text=מַטָּרָא|translate=a mark}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|verse=12}}; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=דָּשָׁא|translate=threshing}} ({{GHGterm|participle Qal}} from {{GHGheb|text=דּוּשׁ}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=50|verse=11}}; {{GHGheb|text=מָרָא|translate=bitter}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=20}}. On the other hand, according to the western Masora, {{GHGheb|text=קָרְחָה|translate=baldness}} is to be read in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=27|verse=31}}; see Baer on the passage.

{{GHGmargin-letter|80|i}}
(''d'') {{GHGheb|text=־ֶה}}, an obtuse form of {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} ({{GHGpar|27|u}}), only in {{GHGheb|text=הַזּוּרֶ֫ה}} for {{GHGheb|text=הַזּוּרָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=59|verse=5}} (unless it is again a {{GHGterm|forma mixta}} combining the {{GHGterm|active ptcp. masc.}} {{GHGheb|text=הַזּוֹרֶה}} and the {{GHGterm|passive ptcp. fem.}} {{GHGheb|text=הַזּוּרָה}}); cf. {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫נֶה}} for {{GHGheb|text=לָנָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=5|verse=4}}; {{GHGheb|text=אָ֫נֶה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=36.42}} ({{GHGpar|90|i}}, and {{GHGpar|48|d}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|80|k}}
(''e'') {{GHGheb|text=־֫ ־ָה}} without the tone, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רָחָ֫מָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=14|verse=17}} [{{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=11|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=רָחָם}}]; {{GHGheb|text=תַּנּוּר בֹּעֵ֫רָה|translate=an oven heated}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=7|verse=4}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez.|chapter=40|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=15|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=16|verse=18|hidebook=1}}. In all those examples the usual tone-bearing {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} is perhaps intended, but the Punctuators, who considered the feminine ending inappropriate, produced a kind of {{GHGterm|locative}} form (see {{GHGpar|90|c}}) by the retraction of the tone. [In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=16|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=24|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=21|verse=31}} (note in each case the following {{GHGheb|text=ה}}), and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=42|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=7|verse=4}}, the text is probably in error.]

{{GHGmargin-letter|80|l}}
(''f'') {{GHGheb|text=־ַי}}, as an old feminine termination, preserved also in Syriac ({{GHGpron|ai}}; see examples in Nöldeke’s {{GHGcite|title=Syrische Gram}}, § 83), in Arabic and (contracted to ''ê'') in Ethiopic, very probably occurs in the proper name {{GHGheb|text=שָׂרַי|translate=Sarai}}, cf. Nöldeke, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xl. 183, and xlii. 484; also {{GHGheb|text=עֶשְׂרֵה|translate=ten}} ({{GHGterm|fem.}}) undoubtedly arises from an original {{GHGpron|ʿesray}}; so Wright, {{GHGcite|title=Comparative Grammar}}, p. 138; König, {{GHGcite|title=Lehrgebäude}}, ii. 427.

{{GHGmargin-letter|80|m}}
3. It is wholly incorrect to regard the {{GHGterm|vowel}}-ending {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}<ref>In this ending the {{GHGheb|text=ה|translate=h}} can only be considered consonantal in the sense that the {{GHGheb|text=ת}} was originally aspirated, and afterwards ‘the mute {{GHGheb|text=ת}} was dropped before ''h'', just as the old Persian {{GHGpron|mithra}} became in modern Persian {{GHGpron|mihrʾ}}; so Socin, who also points to the Arabic pausal form in {{GHGpron|ah}}, and observes that among some of the modern Beduin an ''h'' is still heard as a fem. ending, cf. Socin, {{GHGcite|title=Diwan aus Centralarabien}}, iii. 98, ed. by H. Stumme, Lpz. 1901. In Hebrew this consonantal termination was entirely abandoned, at any rate in later times.</ref> as the original termination of the feminine, and the {{GHGpron|consonantal}} ending {{GHGheb|text=־ַת}} as derived from it. The Ethiopic still has the {{GHGheb|text=ת}} throughout, so too the Assyrian ({{GHGpron|at}}, {{GHGpron|it}}); in Phoenician also the feminines end for the most part in {{GHGheb|text=ת}}, which is pronounced {{GHGpron|at}} in the words found in Greek and Latin authors; less frequently in {{GHGheb|text=א}} (see Gesenius, {{GHGcite|title=Monumm. Phoen.}}, pp. 439, 440; Schröder, {{GHGcite|title=Phön. Sprache}}, p. 169 ff.). The ancient Arabic has the obtuse ending ({{GHGpron|ah}}) almost exclusively in {{GHGterm|pause}}; in modern Arabic the relation between the two endings is very much as in Hebrew.<section end="par80" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

249.text:
{{GHGpar-heading|81|Derivation of Nouns}}
Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, p. 329 ff.
{{GHGmargin-letter|81|a}} Nouns are by their derivation either ''primitive'', i.e. cannot be referred to any verbal stem at present extant (see {{GHGpar|82}}), such as {{GHGheb|text=אָב|translate=father}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֵם|translate=mother}} (but see both words in the Lexicon; according to Stade and others {{GHGheb|text=אָב}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֵם}}, &c., are children’s words and terms of endearment, and so really primitive nouns), or ''derivative'', i.e. either ''Derivativa verbalia'' ({{GHGpar|83|doublesign=1}}–{{GHGpar|85|nosign=1}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רָם|translate=high}}, {{GHGheb|text=רָמָה|translate=high place}}, {{GHGheb|text=מָרוֹם|translate=height}}, from {{GHGheb|text=רוּם|translate=to be high}}, or less frequently ''Derivativa denominativa'' ({{GHGpar|86}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מַרְגְּלוֹת|translate=the place at the feet}}, from {{GHGheb|text=רֶ֫גֶל|translate=foot}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|81|b}} Rem. 1. The earlier grammarians consider the verb alone as stem, and therefore ''all'' nouns as verbals, dividing them into (''a'') ''Formae nudae'', i.e. such as have only the ''three'' (or ''two'') radicals, and (''b'') ''Formae auctae'', such as have formative letters or syllables added at the beginning or end, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מַמְלָכָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכוּת}}. The formative letters used for this purpose are {{nowrap|{{GHGheb|text=ה א מ נ ת י ו}}}} ({{GHGheb|text=הֶֽאֱמַנְתִּיו}}),From this ''vox memorialis'' the {{GHGterm|nomina aucta}} are also called by the older grammarians {{GHGterm|nomina heemantica}}. and the treatment of nouns formerly followed this order. {{GHGmargin-letter|81|c}} According to the view of ''roots'' and ''stems'' presented in {{GHGpar|30|d}}, nouns (other than ''denominatives'') are derived not from the verbal stem, but either from the (abstract) root or from the still undefined stem. In the following pages, however, the arrangement according to the verbal stem is retained as being simpler for the beginner. Cf. {{GHGpar|79|a}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|81|d}} 2. ''Compound'' nouns as ''appellatives'' are very rare in Hebrew, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בְּלִיַּ֫עַל|translate=worthlessness, baseness}}. On the other hand, they very frequently occur as proper names, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גַּבְרִיאֵל}} (''man of God''), {{GHGheb|text=יְהֽוֹיָקִים}} (''Yahwe raises up''), {{GHGheb|text=יְהֽוֹנָתָן}} (''Yahwe gave''), &c.G. Rammelt (''Über die zusammengesetzten Nomina im Hebr.'', Halle, 1883, and Leipzig, 1884) recognizes as appellatives only {{GHGheb|text=צְפַרְדֵּעַ}} (cf. below, {{GHGpar|85|w}}) and {{GHGheb|text=צַלְמָ֫וֶת}} (the latter certainly incorrectly [see, however, Nöldeke, ''ZATW''. 1897, p. 183 ff.]). In p. 8 ff. the author gives a list of ‘logical compounds’, i.e. new terms formed by composition with the negatives {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּלִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִבְּלִי}}.
{{GHGpar-heading|82|Primitive Nouns}} The number of ''primitive'' nouns in the sense used in {{GHGpar|81}} is small, since nouns, which in other languages are represented as independent noun-stems, can easily be traced back in Hebrew to the verbal idea, e.g. names of animals and natural objects, as {{GHGheb|text=שָׂעִיר|translate=he-goat}} (prop. ''shaggy'', from {{GHGheb|text=שָׂעַר}}), {{GHGheb|text=שְׂעֹרָה|translate=barley}} (prop. ''prickly'', also from {{GHGheb|text=שָׂעַר}}), {{GHGheb|text=חֲסִידָה|translate=stork}} (prop. ''pia'', sc. ''avis''), {{GHGheb|text=זָהָב|translate=gold}} (from {{GHGheb|text=זָהַב}}={{GHGheb|text=צָהַב|translate=to shine, to be yellow}}). Thus there remain only a few nouns, e.g. several names of members of the body in men or beasts, to which a corresponding verbal stem cannot be assigned at all, or at any rate only indirectly (from other Semitic dialects), as {{GHGheb|text=קֶ֫רֶן|translate=horn}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַ֫יִן|translate=eye}}.

250.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par83 />{{GHGpar-heading|83|Verbal Nouns in General}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|83|a}}
'''1.''' In Hebrew, as in Greek and Latin, the {{GHGterm|verbal nouns}} are connected in form and meaning primarily with certain forms of the verb, especially the participles and infinitives, which are themselves, even in their ordinary form, frequently used precisely like nouns, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֹיֵב|translate=enemy}}, {{GHGheb|text=דַּ֫עַת|translate=to know, knowledge}}. Still oftener, however, certain forms of the infinitive and participle, which are seldom or never found as such in the strong verb, though in use in the weak verb and in the kindred dialects, came to be commonly used for the verbal noun; e.g. the participial form {{GHGheb|text=קָטֵל}}, the infinitives of the (Aramaic) form {{GHGheb|text=מִקְטַל}} (as a ''noun'' also {{GHGheb|text=מִקְטָל}}), further {{GHGheb|text=קְטֹ֫לֶת}}, {{GHGheb|text=קִטְלָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטְלָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=קֻטְלָה}} ({{GHGpar|45|d}}), &c. Others (as the Arabic shows) are properly intensive forms of the participle.

{{GHGmargin-letter|83|b}}
'''2.''' As regards their meaning, it follows from the nature of the case that nouns which have the form of the infinitive regularly denote the ''action'' or ''state'', with other closely related ideas, and are therefore mostly ''abstract''; while the participial nouns, on the contrary, denote for the most part the ''subject'' of the action or state, and are therefore ''concrete''. Moreover, it is to be noticed, that a particular meaning is attached to many of the special forms of derivative nouns, although it does not appear equally in them all.

{{GHGmargin-letter|83|c}}
Rem. It need not appear strange, when we consider the analogy of other languages, that a noun which in form is properly ''abstract'' afterwards acquired a ''concrete'' sense, and vice versa. So in English, we say ''his acquaintance'', for the ''persons'' with whom he is ''acquainted''; the ''Godhead'' for ''God'' himself; in Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=מוֹדַע|translate=acquaintance}} and ''an acquaintance''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|83|d}}
The inner connexion in thought between Semitic noun-forms and the corresponding verbal forms is investigated in the works of De Lagarde and Barth (see the titles at the head of {{GHGpar|79}}) on very different lines, but with many points of agreement. De Lagarde starts from the fact that language consists of sentences. A sentence which consists of only ''one'' word is called a verb, and anything which serves as a complement to it is a noun. The oldest form of the sentence is the imperative. Closely related to it are three kinds of sentences of the nature of verbal forms, differing according as the property of the particular object of sense is to be represented as invariable (form ''qatula''), or as liable to change (form ''qatila''), or, finally, as a circumstance which takes place before our eyes (form ''qatala''). Like the imperative, these three forms of sentences have also been transformed into nouns, by means of certain phonetic changes,—especially by the omission of the final vowels and the addition of different terminations to the last consonant of the stem. But just as the forms of the verbal sentence undergo numerous modifications (in the tenses, moods, and conjugations), so also do the nouns, sometimes by assimilation of the unessential to the characteristic vowel (''qutul, qitil''), sometimes by the lengthening of the characteristic vowel (''qatûl, qatîl, qatâl''), or else through the displacement of the accent and the consequent reduction of the noun to a monosyllabic form (''qatl, qutl, qitl''), or, finally, by their being formed from the derived stems (or conjugations), e.g. ''qattal, qattâl; qutil, qittâl'', &c. Further modifications arise from the use of the various imperfect<section end=par83 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

251.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par83 />and infinitive forms, and also from the employment of the prefix ''m''. Lastly, {{GHGterm|denominalia}} are formed from {{GHGterm|deverbalia}} by appending certain suffixes.

De Lagarde does not, however, claim to be able to show in the case of each particular noun the sense it conveyed in primitive times; the origin of a number of nouns can now no longer be detected. In those, however, which are clearly derived from verbs, the original meaning is chiefly determined by the characteristic vowel.

Barth’s system is based on the thesis that ‘all Semitic nouns, adjectives, and participles are derived from either the perfect or the imperfect stem’. Thus, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קָטוֹל}} is the infinitive of the perfect stem, {{GHGheb|text=קְטֹל}} the infinitive of the imperfect stem, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁכַב}} infinitive of {{GHGheb|text=יִשְׁכַּב}}, &c. In dissyllabic noun-forms the second vowel is always alone characteristic and essential, the first vowel unessential, and therefore variable. Further modifications of the simple form are effected by strengthening (sharpening) the second or third consonant, by lengthening the characteristic vowel (instead of which, however, the feminine termination may also be used), or by ‘metaplasm’, i.e. by the use of noun-forms derived from one of the two intransitive stems for the other, e.g. {{GHGpron|qutl}} for {{GHGpron|qitl}}, and vice versa.

In nouns of the perfect stem, the vowels ''i'' and ''u'' indicate intransitive formations, the vowel ''a'' a transitive sense. In nouns of the imperfect stem on the contrary, ''u'' and ''i'', being characteristic vowels, indicate a transitive and ''a'' an intransitive sense: for {{GHGpron|yaqtŭlŭ}} is imperfect of the transitive perfect {{GHGpron|qatala}}, and {{GHGpron|yaqtŭlŭ}} imperfect of the intransitive perfects {{GHGpron|qatila}} and {{GHGpron|qatula}}, &c. This explains how nouns, apparently identical in form, may yet in sense belong to different classes: a {{GHGpron|qutl}}-form from a ''u''-imperfect has a transitive meaning, but the same form from a ''u''-perfect has an intransitive meaning. This double system of perfect and imperfect forms runs through the whole scheme of noun-formation, not only the forms connected with the conjugations, but also the forms with prefixes and suffixes.

Against the whole theory it has been urged that it postulates for the development of the language a much too abstract mechanism, and further, that the meanings of words as we find them may in many cases be due to a modification of the original sense. But though many of the details (e.g. the alleged unessential character of the vowel of the first syllable) remain doubtful, yet the agreement between the characteristic vowel of certain noun formations and that of the perfect or imperfect stem, is supported by such a number of incontestable instances, that there can be no doubt as to a systematic, intimate connexion between the two. At the same time it must be admitted that De Lagarde has put forward many important and suggestive points, and both scholars agree in laying stress on ''one'' characteristic vowel as indicative of the meaning.<section end=par83 />

<section begin=par84a />{{GHGpar-heading|84|Nouns derived from the Simple Stem|a}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|84|a|a}}
''Preliminary remark''.—From the statement made above, {{GHGpar|83|d}}, it follows that an external similarity between forms is no proof of their similar origin, and, vice versa, external difference does not exclude the possibility of their being closely related both in origin and meaning.

{{center|I. ''Nouns with One Vowel, originally Short.''}}

R. Růzička, ‘Beiträge zur Erklärung der nomina segolata,’ in {{GHGcite|title=Sitz.-ber. d. böhmischen Ges. d. Wiss.}}, Prag, 1904.

1. Nouns with one of the three short vowels after the first radical: {{GHGterm|present}} ground-form {{GHGpron|qăṭl}}, {{GHGpron|qĭṭl}}, {{GHGpron|qŭṭl}}.

The supposition of {{GHGterm|monosyllabic}} ground-forms appeared to be required by the character of forms now existing in Hebrew, as well as in Arabic, &c. But there are strong reasons for believing that at least a large proportion of these forms go back to original dissyllabic bases with a short vowel in each syllable. When formative additions were made, the vowel of the 2nd syllable<section end=par84a /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

252.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par84a/>was dropped, i.e. before case-endings in Assyrian and early Arabic, and before pronominal suffixes in Hebrew. From the forms thus produced, the bases {{GHGpron|qăṭl}}, {{GHGpron|qĭṭl}}, {{GHGpron|qŭṭl}} have been assumed, although they never appear in Hebrew except in the singular and then in connexion with suffixes.

In support of this view of a large number of original dissyllabic bases, we must not, however, appeal to the S<sup>e</sup>ghôl or Pathaḥ under the 2nd consonant of the existing developed forms, {{GHGheb|text=סֵ֫פֶר}}, {{GHGheb|text=זֶ֫רַע}}, &c. These are in no sense survivals or modifications of an original full vowel in the 2nd syllable, but are mere helping-vowels ({{GHGpar|28|e}}) to make the monosyllabic forms pronounceable,<ref>According to Delitzsch ({{GHGcite|title=Assyr. Gram.}}, p. 157 f.) the same is true in Assyrian of the corresponding {{GHGpron|qaṭl}}-forms. Without case-endings they are {{GHGpron|kalab}}, {{GHGpron|šamas}}, {{GHGpron|aban}} (= {{GHGheb|text=כֶּ֫לֶב}}, {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫מֶשׁ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫בֶן}}), with case-endings {{GHGpron|kalbu}}, {{GHGpron|šamsu}}, {{GHGpron|abnu}}. On the other hand, acc. to Sievers, {{GHGcite|title=Metrik}}, i. 261, Hebrew ground-forms probably have a twofold origin: they are shortened according to Hebrew rules partly from old absolute forms like {{GHGpron|kálbu}}, {{GHGpron|sífru}}, {{GHGpron|qúdšu}}, and partly from old construct-forms like the Assyrian types {{GHGpron|kalab}}, {{GHGpron|sifir}}, {{GHGpron|quduš}}.</ref> and consequently disappear when no longer needed. Under certain circumstances even (e.g. in {{GHGheb|text=קשְׁטְ}}) they are not used at all. Actual proofs of such original toneless full vowels in the 2nd syllable of existing Segholates are—

1. Forms like Arab. {{GHGpron|málik}}, for which rarely {{GHGpron|malk}}, corresponding to the Hebrew ground-form; cf. De Lagarde, {{GHGcite|title=Uebersicht}}, p. 72 ff.

2. In Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=גֶּ֫דֶר}}, {{GHGheb|text=יֶ֫רֶךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כֶּ֫בֶד}}, {{GHGheb|text=כֶּ֫תֶף}}, the connective forms of {{GHGheb|text=גָּדֵר}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָרֵךְ}}, &c., which latter can only come from ground-forms {{GHGpron|gădĭr}}, {{GHGpron|yărĭk}}, {{GHGpron|kăbĭd}}, {{GHGpron|kătĭp}}.

3. The forms treated under {{GHGpar|84|e|a}}, which are in many ways related to the Segholates proper, in so far as they are to be referred to original dissyllabic bases.

4. The plurals of Hebrew Segholates, since, with very rare exceptions, they take {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} under the 2nd radical before the termination {{GHGheb|text=־ִים}}, fem. {{GHGheb|text=־וֹת}}, of the {{GHGterm|absolute state}}, as {{GHGheb|text=מְלָכִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=מְלָכוֹת}}, {{GHGheb|text=סְפָרִים}}, &c. This {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} (see note 1 on {{GHGpar|26|e}}) can only be due to a lengthening of an original short vowel in the 2nd syllable, and hence it would seem as though the vowel were always ''ă''. This is impossible from what has been said, especially under 1 and 2. Hence the explanation of the consistent occurrence of {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} in the plurals of ''all'' Segholates can only be that the regularly formed plurals (i.e. from singulars with original ''ă'' in the 2nd syllable) became the models for all the others, and ultimately even for some really monosyllabic forms.<ref>On the other hand, Ungnad, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZA.|Zeitschrift für Assyriologie und verwandte Gebiete, ed. by C. Bezold. Lpz. 18S6 ff.}}}} 1903, p. 333 ff., rejecting all previous explanations, maintains that the ''a'' in ''m<sup>e</sup>lākhîm, m<sup>e</sup>lākhôth'' is inserted merely to facilitate the pronunciation. From ''qaṭlîm'' arose ''qaṭ<sup>a</sup>lim'', then ''qaṭalîm'' and finally ''q<sup>e</sup>ṭālîm''. See, however, Nöldeke, ‘Zur semit. Pluralendung,’ {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZA.|Zeitschrift für Assyriologie und verwandte Gebiete, ed. by C. Bezold. Lpz. 18S6 ff.}}}} 1904, p. 68 ff., who points out that the Semitic nouns ''faʿl, fiʿl, fuʿl'' with their corresponding feminines ''faʿla'', &c., on assuming the plural termination commonly take an ''a'' before the 3rd radical, but that no satisfactory account can be given for it. M. Margolis, ‘The plural of Segolates’ (''Proc. of the Philol. Assoc. of the Pacific Coast'', San Francisco, 1903, p. 4 ff.), and S. Brooks, ''Vestiges of the broken plural in Hebrew'', Dublin, 1883, explain m<sup>e</sup>lākhîm as a ''pluralis fractus''.</ref>

(''a'') From the strong stem the above three ground-forms are further developed to {{GHGheb|text=קֶ֫טֶל}},<ref>It is worthy of notice that St. Jerome also (cf. Siegfried, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} iv. 76) frequently represents the vowel of the first syllable by ''a'', e.g. ''gader, aben, ader, areb'', for {{GHGheb|text=גֶּדֶר}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶבֶן}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶדֶר}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֶרֶב}}, but ''cedem, secel, deber'', &c., for {{GHGheb|text=קֶדֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁקֶל}}, {{GHGheb|text=דֶּבֶר}}, &c.</ref> {{GHGheb|text=קֵ֫טֶל}}, {{GHGheb|text=קֹ֫טֶל}} (cf. {{GHGpar|27|r}} and in {{GHGpar|93}} the explanations of Paradigm I, ''a–c''); without a helping vowel ({{GHGpar|28|d}}) {{GHGheb|text=קשְׁטְ|translate=truth}}. If the second<section end=par84a/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

253.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par84a" />or third radical be a guttural, a helping {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} takes the place of the helping {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>ghôl}}, according to {{GHGpar|22|d}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=זֶ֫רַע|translate=seed}}, {{GHGheb|text=נֵ֫צַח|translate=eternity}}, {{GHGheb|text=פֹּ֫עַל|translate=work}}; but with middle {{GHGheb|text=ה}} or {{GHGheb|text=ח}}, note {{GHGheb|text=לֶ֫חֶם|translate=bread}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֶ֫חֶם}} (as well as {{GHGheb|text=רַ֫חַם}}) ''womb'', {{GHGheb|text=אֹ֫הֶל|translate=tent}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֹּ֫הֶן|translate=thumb}}; so with final {{GHGheb|text=א}}, {{GHGheb|text=פֶּ֫רֶא|translate=a wild ass}}, &c.; with a middle guttural also the modification of the principal vowel ''ă'' to ''è'' does not occur, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רַ֫הַב}}, {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫עַר}}, {{GHGheb|text=לַ֫חַץ}} (exceptions, again, {{GHGheb|text=לֶ֫חֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֶ֫חֶם}}). On the inflexion, cf. {{GHGpar|93}}, Paradigm I, {{GHGpar|93|a|nonumber=1}}–{{GHGpar|93|f|nonumber=1}}, and the explanations. In {{GHGheb|text=חֵטְא|translate=sin}}, the {{GHGheb|text=א}} has wholly lost its consonantal value.

{{GHGmargin-letter|84|b|a}}
Examples of feminines: {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכָּה}} (directly from the ground-form {{GHGpron|malk}}, {{GHGtranslate|king}}), {{GHGheb|text=סִתְרָה|translate=a covering}} (also {{GHGheb|text=סֵ֫תֶר}}), {{GHGheb|text=אָכְלָה|translate=food}} (also {{GHGheb|text=אֹ֫כֶל}}); with a middle guttural {{GHGheb|text=נַֽעֲרָה|translate=girl}}, {{GHGheb|text=טָֽהֳרָה|translate=purity}} (also {{GHGheb|text=טֹ֫הַר}}). Cf. {{GHGpar|94}}, Paradigm I.

{{GHGmargin-letter|84|c|a}}
(''b'') From weak stems: (α) from stems {{GHGheb|text=ע״ן}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַף|translate=nose}} (from {{GHGpron|ʾănp}}, hence with formative additions, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַפִּי}} for {{GHGpron|ʾanpî}}, ''my nose''); {{GHGheb|text=עֵז|translate=a she-goat}} (ground-form {{GHGpron|ʿĭnz}}); fem. {{GHGheb|text=חִטָּה|translate=wheat}}; (β) from stems {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}} ({{GHGpar|93}}, Paradigm I, {{GHGpar|93|l|nonumber=1}}–{{GHGpar|93|n|nonumber=1}}); {{GHGheb|text=פַּת|translate=a morsel}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַם|translate=people}} (so, when in close connexion with the next word; unconnected {{GHGheb|text=עָם}}; with article {{GHGheb|text=הָעָם}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָעָם}}, &c.); {{GHGheb|text=רַב}} in the sense of {{GHGtranslate|much}}, but {{GHGheb|text=רָב|translate=great, numerous}} (in close connexion also {{GHGheb|text=רַב}}); {{GHGheb|text=רָע|translate=evil}}, with the article in close connexion {{GHGheb|text=הָרַע}}, unconnected {{GHGheb|text=הָרָע}}; with the ''ă'' always lengthened to ''ā'', {{GHGheb|text=יָם|translate=sea}}; fem. {{GHGheb|text=חַיָּה|translate=life}}, and with attenuation of the ''ă'' to ''ĭ'', {{GHGheb|text=מִדָּה|translate=measure}}; from the ground-form {{GHGpron|qĭṭl}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֵם|translate=mother}}; fem. {{GHGheb|text=גִּזָּה|translate=a shearing}}; from the ground-form {{GHGpron|qŭṭl}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֹק|translate=statute}}, fem. {{GHGheb|text=חֻקָּה}}. (γ) from stems {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} (Paradigm I, {{GHGpar|93|g|nonumber=1}} and {{GHGpar|93|i|nonumber=1}}); {{GHGheb|text=מָ֫וֶת|translate=death}} (from {{GHGpron|má-ut}}, the ''u'' passing into the corresponding consonant, as in {{GHGheb|text=תָּ֫וֶךְ|translate=middle}}) or contracted {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם|translate=day}}, {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹט|translate=whip}}, {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹר|translate=a bull}}; fem. {{GHGheb|text=עַוְלָה|translate=perverseness}} (also contracted {{GHGheb|text=עוֹלָה}}); from the ground-form {{GHGpron|qŭṭl}}, {{GHGheb|text=צוּר|translate=a rock}}; fem. {{GHGheb|text=סוּפָה|translate=a storm}}. (δ) from stems {{GHGheb|text=ע״י}} (Paradigm I, {{GHGpar|93|h|nonumber=1}}); {{GHGheb|text=זַ֫יִת|translate=an olive-tree}} (with a helping {{GHGterm|Ḥireq}} instead of a helping {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>ghôl}}) from {{GHGpron|zá-it}}, the ''i'' passing into the corresponding consonant; or contracted {{GHGheb|text=חֵיק|translate=bosom}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֵיל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=18|verse=17}} (elsewhere {{GHGheb|text=חַ֫יִל}}) {{GHGpron|host}}; fem. {{GHGheb|text=שֵׂיבָה|translate=grey hair}}; from the ground-form {{GHGpron|qĭṭl}}, {{GHGheb|text=דִּין|translate=judgement}}; fem. {{GHGheb|text=בִּינָה|translate=understanding}}. (ε) from stems {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} (Paradigm I, {{GHGpar|93|k|nonumber=1}}); partly forms such as {{GHGheb|text=בֶּ֫כֶה|translate=weeping}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֶ֫גֶה|translate=murmuring}}, {{GHGheb|text=נֶ֫דֶה|translate=a present}}, {{GHGheb|text=קֶ֫צֶה|translate=the end}}, partly such as {{GHGheb|text=בְּכִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֲרִי|translate=a lion}} (ground-form {{GHGpron|băky}}, {{GHGpron|ʾăry}}); cf. also the forms from stems originally {{GHGheb|text=ל״ו}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָׂ֫חוּ|translate=swimming}} (ground-form {{GHGpron|săḥw}}); fem. {{GHGheb|text=שַׁלְוָה|translate=rest}}, {{GHGheb|text=גַּֽאֲוָה|translate=exaltation}}; from stems {{GHGheb|text=ל״י}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַלְיה|translate=a fat tail}}, and with attenuation of ''ă'' to ''ĭ'' {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְיָה|translate=captivity}}, also {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבִית}}, formed no doubt directly from the masc. {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבִי}} with the fem. termination {{GHGheb|text=ת}}; from the ground-form {{GHGpron|qĭṭl}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֲצִי}} (from {{GHGpron|ḥĭṣy}}); fem. {{GHGheb|text=חֶדְוָה|translate=joy}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֶרְוָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=עֶרְוָה|translate=nakedness}}; from the ground-form {{GHGpron|qŭṭl}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֹּ֫הוּ}} (from {{GHGpron|bŏhw}}) {{GHGtranslate|waste}}, {{GHGheb|text=תֹּ֫הוּ|translate=emptiness}}; {{GHGheb|text=דְּלִי}}, for {{GHGheb|text=דֳּלִי}}, {{GHGtranslate|bucket}}; fem. {{GHGheb|text=אֳנִיָּה|translate=a ship}} (directly from {{GHGheb|text=אֳנִי|translate=a fleet}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|84|d|a}}
The masculines as well as the feminines of these {{GHGterm|segholate}} forms may have either an ''abstract'' or a ''concrete'' meaning. In the form {{GHGheb|text=קֹ֫טֶל}} the {{GHGterm|passive}} or at any rate the ''abstract'' meaning is by far the more common (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=נֹ֫עַר|translate=youthfulness}}, abstract of {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫עַר|translate=boy}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֹ֫כֶל|translate=food}}, &c.).<ref>M. Lambert also ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|REJ.|Revue des Études Juives. Paris, 1880 ff.}}}} 1896, p. 18 ff.), from statistics of the Segholates, arrives at the conclusion that the {{GHGpron|qaṭl}}-form is especially used for concretes (in nouns without gutturals he reckons twenty concretes as against two abstracts), and the ''qiṭl''-form, and less strictly the ''quṭl'', for abstracts.</ref>
<section end="par84a" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

254.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par84a/>{{GHGmargin-letter|84|e|a}}
2. Nouns with one of the three short vowels under the second radical (present ground-form {{GHGpron|q<sup>e</sup>ṭăl}}, {{GHGpron|q<sup>e</sup>ṭŭl}}, {{GHGpron|q<sup>e</sup>ṭŭl}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=דְּבַשׁ|translate=honey}}, {{GHGheb|text=דְּוַי|translate=sickness}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֲתַת|translate=terror}}; and so always with middle {{GHGheb|text=א}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּאֵר|translate=a well}}, {{GHGheb|text=זְאֵב|translate=a wolf}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּאֹשׁ|translate=stench}}. In reality these forms, like the segholates mentioned in No. 1 (see above, {{GHGpar|84|a|a}}), are, probably, for the most part to be referred to original {{GHGterm|dissyllabic}} forms, but the tone has been shifted from its original place (the penultima) on to the ultima. Thus ''dibáš'' (originally ''dı́baš'') as ground-form of {{GHGheb|text=דְּבַשׁ}} is supported both by the Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=דִּבְשִׁי}} (with suffix of the first person), and by the Arabic {{GHGpron|dibs}}, the principal form; {{GHGpron|biʾír}} (according to Philippi with assimilation of the vowel of the second syllable to that of the first) as ground-form of {{GHGheb|text=בְּאֵר}} is attested by the Arabic {{GHGpron|biʾr}}; for {{GHGheb|text=בְּאשׁ}} (Arabic {{GHGpron|buʾs}}) similarly a ground-form {{GHGpron|buʾúš}} may be inferred, just as a ground-form {{GHGpron|qŭṭŭl}} underlies the infinitives of the form {{GHGheb|text=קְטֹל}}.<ref>On this theory cf. Stade, {{GHGcite|title=Hebräische Grammatik}}, § 199 ''b''; De Lagarde, {{GHGcite|title=Übersicht}}, p. 57 f.; A. Müller, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xlv, p. 226, and especially Philippi, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xlix, p. 208.</ref>

{{center|II. ''Nouns with an original Short Vowel in both Syllables.''}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|84|f|a}}
3. The ground-form {{GHGpron|qăṭăl}}, fem. {{GHGpron|qăṭălăt}}, developed in Hebrew to {{GHGheb|text=קָטָל}} ({{GHGpar|93}}, Paradigm II, {{GHGpar|93|a|nonumber=1}}, {{GHGpar|93|b|nonumber=1}}) and {{GHGheb|text=קְטָלָה}} ({{GHGpar|94|doublesign=1}}, {{GHGpar|95|nosign=1}}, Paradigm II, {{GHGpar|95|a|nonumber=1}}, {{GHGpar|95|b|nonumber=1}}), mostly forms intransitive adjectives, as {{GHGheb|text=חָכָם|translate=wise}}, {{GHGheb|text=חָדָשׁ|translate=new}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָשָׁר|translate=upright}}; but also substantives, as {{GHGheb|text=דָּבָר|translate=a word}}, and even abstracts, as {{GHGheb|text=אָשָׁם|translate=guilt}}, {{GHGheb|text=רָעָב|translate=hunger}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָׂבָע|translate=satiety}}; in the fem. frequently abstract, as {{GHGheb|text=צְדָקָה}}<ref>In St. Jerome’s time these forms were still pronounced {{GHGpron|ṣadaca}} ({{GHGheb|text=צְדָקָה}}), {{GHGpron|ṣaaca}} ({{GHGheb|text=צְעָקָה}}), {{GHGpron|nabala}} ({{GHGheb|text=נְבָלָה}}), &c., see Siegfried, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} iv. 79.
