''manubria''); {{GHGheb|text=פַּ֫עַם|translate=foot}}, {{GHGheb|text=פְּעָמוֹת|translate=artificial feet}} (of the ark), {{GHGheb|text=קַרְנַ֫יִם|translate=horns}}, {{GHGheb|text=קְרָנוֹת|translate=horns}} (of the altar); {{GHGheb|text=עֵינַ֫יִם|translate=eyes}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֲיָנוֹת|translate=fountains}}; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=אֲרָיִים|translate=lions}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֲרָיוֹת}} the ''figures of lions'' on Solomon’s throne, {{GHGheb|text=תָּמָר|translate=palm}}, {{GHGheb|text=תִּֽמֹרָה|translate=a palm-like column}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=תִּֽמֹרִים}} and {{GHGheb|text=תִּֽמֹרוֹת}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|87|p}}
'''4.''' A considerable number of masculines form their plural in {{GHGheb|text=וֹת}}, while many feminines have a plural in {{GHGheb|text=־ִים}}. The gender of the singular, however, is as a rule retained in the plural.<section end=par87 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

268.text:
Undoubted instances of masculines with (masculine) plural in {{GHGheb|text=־וֹת}} are: {{GHGheb|text=אָב|translate=father}}, {{GHGheb|text=אוֹצָר|translate=treasure}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֹּאר}} and {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹר|translate=cistern}}, {{GHGheb|text=זָנָב|translate=tail}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֲלוֹם|translate=dream}}, {{GHGheb|text=כִּםֵּא|translate=throne}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֵב}} and {{GHGheb|text=לֵבָב|translate=heart}}, {{GHGheb|text=לוּחַ|translate=tablet}}, {{GHGheb|text=לַ֫יִל}} and {{GHGheb|text=לַ֫יְלָה|translate=night}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִזְבֵּחַ|translate=altar}}, {{GHGheb|text=מָקוֹם|translate=place}}, {{GHGheb|text=נֹאד|translate=skin-bottle}}, {{GHGheb|text=נֵר|translate=lamp}}, {{GHGheb|text=עוֹר|translate=skin}}, {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל|translate=voice}}, {{GHGheb|text=שֻׁלְחָן|translate=table}}, {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁם|translate=name}}, {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹפָר|translate=trumpet}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|87|q}} Feminines ending in {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} which take in the plural the termination {{GHGheb|text=־ִים}} are {{GHGheb|text=אֵלָה|translate=terebinth}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֵימָה|translate=terror}} (but also {{GHGheb|text=אֵימוֹת}}), {{GHGheb|text=דְּבֵלָה|translate=a cake}} of figs, {{GHGheb|text=חִטָּה|translate=wheat}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְבֵנָה|translate=a brick}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִלָּה}} (only in poetry) ''a word'', {{GHGheb|text=סְאָה|translate=seā}}, ''a dry measure'', {{GHGheb|text=שְׂעוֹרָה|translate=barley}}, and the following names of animals {{GHGheb|text=דְּבוֹרָה|translate=a bee}} and {{GHGheb|text=יוֹנָה|translate=a dove}}; also, for {{GHGheb|text=בֵּיצִים}} fem. ''eggs'', a singular {{GHGheb|text=בֵּיצָה}} is to be assumed. {{GHGheb|text=אֲלֻמָּה|translate=sheaf}} and {{GHGheb|text=שָׁנָה|translate=year}} (see above, n) take both {{GHGheb|text=־ִים}} and {{GHGheb|text=וֹת}}; cf. finally {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבֹּ֫לֶת|translate=an ear of corn}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבֳּלִים}}, and without the fem. termination in the singular {{GHGheb|text=פִּילֶ֫גֶשׁ|translate=concubine}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=פִּֽילַגְשִׁים}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|87|r}} '''5.''' A strict distinction in gender between the two plural endings is found, in fact, only in adjectives and participles, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=טוֹבִים|translate=boni}}, {{GHGheb|text=טוֹבוֹת|translate=bonae}}, {{GHGheb|text=קֹֽטְלִים}} musc., {{GHGheb|text=קֹֽטְלוֹת}} fem. So also in substantives of the same stem, where there is an express distinction of sex, as {{GHGheb|text=בָּנִים|translate=filii}}, {{GHGheb|text=בָּנוֹת|translate=filiae}}; {{GHGheb|text=מְלָכִים|translate=reges}}, {{GHGheb|text=מְלָכוֹת|translate=reginae}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|87|s}} Rem. 1. In some few words there is added to the plural ending {{GHGheb|text=וֹת}} a second (masculine) plural termination (in the form of the ''constr. st''. {{GHGheb|text=־ֵי}}, cf. {{GHGpar|89|c}}), or a dual ending {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יִם}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בָּמָה|translate=a high place}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=בָּמוֹת}}, ''constr. st''. {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽמוֹתֵי}} (also {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽמֳתֵי}} ''bāmothê'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=8}}, &c., sometimes as ''Qerē'' to the Kethîbh {{GHGheb|text=במותי}}; see {{GHGpar|95|o}}); {{GHGheb|text=מֵרַאֲשֹׁתֵי שָׁאוּל}} ''from Saul’s head'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=12}}; {{GHGheb|text=חוֹמָה|translate=wall}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=חוֹמוֹת|translate=moenia}}, whence dual {{GHGheb|text=חוֹמֹתַ֫יִם|translate=double walls}}. This double indication of the plural appears also in the connexion of suffixes with the plural ending {{GHGheb|text=וֹת}} ({{GHGpar|91|m}}). {{GHGmargin-letter|87|t}} 2. Some nouns are only used in the singular (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָדָם|translate=man}}, and collectively ''men''); a number of other nouns only in the plural, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מְתִים|translate=men}} (the old ''sing''. {{GHGheb|text=מְתוּ}} is only preserved in proper names, see {{GHGpar|90|o}}; in Eth. the ''sing.'' is ''mĕt'', man); some of these have, moreover, a singular meaning ({{GHGpar|124|a}}), as {{GHGheb|text=פָּנִים|translate=face}}. In such cases, however, the same form can also express plurality, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=פָּנִים}} means also ''faces'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=1|verse=6}}; cf. {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהִים|translate=God}}, and also ''gods'' (the ''sing.'' {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהַּ}}, a later formation from it, occurs only ten times, except in Job forty-one and in Daniel four times).
{{GHGpar-heading|88|Of the Dual}}
Cf. the literature on the Semitic dual in Grünert, ''Die Begriffs-Präponderanz und die Duale a potiori im Altarab''. (Wien, 1886), p. 21; Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, p. 455 ff.
{{GHGmargin-letter|88|a}} '''1.''' The ''dual'' is a further indication of number, which originated in early times. In Hebrew, however, it is almost exclusively used to denote those objects which naturally occur in pairs (see e). The dual termination is never found in adjectives, verbs, or pronouns. In the noun it is indicated in both genders by the termination {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יִם}}

269.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="2" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par88" />appended to the ground-form,<ref>On dual endings appended to the plural see {{GHGpar|87|s}} and {{GHGpar|95|o}} at the beginning.</ref> e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָדַ֫יִם|translate=both hands}}, {{GHGheb|text=יוֹמַ֫יִם|translate=two days}}. In the feminine the dual termination is always added to the old ending ''ath'' (instead of {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}), but necessarily with ''ā'' (since it is in an open syllable before the tone), thus {{GHGheb|text=־ָתַ֫יִם}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שָׂפָה|translate=lip}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׂפָתַ֫יִם|translate=both lips}}. From a feminine with the ending {{GHGheb|text=־֫ ־ֶת}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=נְח֫שֶׁת}} (from ''n<sup>e</sup>ḥušt'') the dual is formed like {{GHGheb|text=נְחֻשְׁתַּ֫יִם|translate=double fetters}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|88|b}}
With nouns which in the singular have not a feminine ending, the dual termination is likewise really added to the ground-form; but the latter generally undergoes certain changes in consequence of the shifting of the tone, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כָּנָף|translate=wing}} (ground-form ''kănăph''), dual {{GHGheb|text=כְּנָפַ֫יִם}}, the first ''ă'' becoming {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, since it no longer stands before the tone, and the second ''ă'' being lengthened before the new tone-syllable. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=16|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=23}}b the form {{GHGheb|text=כִּכְּרַ֫יִם}} (which should be {{GHGheb|text=כִּכָּרַ֫יִם}}) evidently merely points to the ''constr. st''. {{GHGheb|text=כִּכְּרֵי}}, which would be expected before {{GHGheb|text=כֶּ֫סֶף}}; cf. {{GHGheb|text=כִּכָּרָ֑יִם}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=23}} a, and on the syntax see {{GHGpar|131|d}}. In the segholate forms ({{GHGpar|84|a|a}}) the dual ending is mostly added to the ground-form, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רֶ֫גֶל|translate=foot}} (ground-form ''răgl''), dual {{GHGheb|text=רַגְלַ֫יִם}}; cf., however, {{GHGheb|text=קְרָנַ֫יִם}} (only in the book of Daniel), as well as {{GHGheb|text=קַרְנַ֫יִם}} from {{GHGheb|text=קֶ֫רֶן|translate=horn}}, and {{GHGheb|text=לְחָיַ֫יִם}} from {{GHGheb|text=לְחִי|translate=cheek}} (as if from the plurals {{GHGheb|text=קְרָנוֹת}}, {{GHGheb|text=לִחָיִם}}).—A feminine dual of an adjective used substantivally occurs in {{GHGheb|text=עֲצַלְתַּ֫יִם|translate=a sluggish pair}} (of hands) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=10|verse=18}} from the sing. {{GHGheb|text=עָצֵל}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|88|c}}
Rem. 1. Certain place-names were formerly reckoned as dual-forms (so in earlier editions of this Grammar, and still in König’s {{GHGcite|title=Lehrgebäude}}, ii. 437), viz.— (''a'') those in {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יִן}} and {{GHGheb|text=־ָן}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=דֹּתַ֫יִן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=17a}} (locative {{GHGheb|text=דֹּתָ֑יְּנָה}}, but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=17b|hidebook=completely}} {{GHGheb|text=דֹּתָ֑ן}}), and {{GHGheb|text=דֹּתָן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=13}}; {{GHGheb|text=קַרְתָּן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=21|verse=32}}, identical with {{GHGheb|text=קִרְיָתַ֫יִם}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=6|verse=61}} (cf. also the Moabite names of towns in the Mêša‛ inscription, line 10 {{GHGheb|text=קריתן}} = Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=קִרְיָתַ֫יִם}}; line 30 {{GHGheb|text=בת דבלתן}} = {{GHGheb|text=בֵּית דִּבְלָתַ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=48|verse=22}}; lines 31, 32 {{GHGheb|text=חורנן}}={{GHGheb|text=חֹרוֹנַ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=15|verse=5}}, &c.); (''b'') in {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=34}} {{GHGheb|text=הָֽעֵינָם}} ( = {{GHGheb|text=עֵינַ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=21}}). The view that {{GHGheb|text=־ָן}} and {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}} arise from a contraction of the dual terminations {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יִן}} (as in Western Aramaic, cf. also nom. ''âni'', accus. ''aini'', of the dual in Arabic) and {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יִם}} seemed to be supported by the Mêša‛; inscription, where we find (line 20) {{GHGheb|text=מאתן|translate=two hundred}} = {{GHGheb|text=מָאתַ֫יִן}}, Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=מָאתַ֫יִם}}. But in many of these supposed duals either a dual sense cannot be detected at all, or it does not agree at any rate with the nature of the Semitic dual, as found elsewhere. Hence it can hardly be doubted that {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יִן}} and {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ יִם}} in these place-names only arise from a subsequent expansion of the terminations {{GHGheb|text=־ָן}} and {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}}: so Wellhausen, ''Jahrbücher für Deutsche Theologie'', xxi. 433; Philippi, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xxxii. 65 f.; Barth, {{GHGcite|title=Nominalbildung}}, p. 319, note 5; Strack, ''Kommentar zur Genesis'', p. 135. The strongest argument in favour of this opinion is that we have a clear case of such an expansion in the ''Q<sup>e</sup>rê perpetuum'' ({{GHGpar|17|c}}) {{GHGheb|text=יְרֽוּשָׁלַ֫יִם}} for {{GHGheb|text=יְרֽוּשָׂלֵם}} (so, according to Strack, even in old MSS. of the ''Mišna''; cf. ''Urusalim'' in the Tel-el-Amarna tablets, and the Aramaic form {{GHGheb|text=יְרֽוּשְׁלֵם}}): similarly in<section end="par88" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

270.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par88" />the Aramaic {{GHGheb|text=שָֽׁמְרַ֫יִן}} = {{GHGheb|text=שָֽׁמְרָן}} for the Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=שֹֽׁמְרוֹן|translate=Samaria}}.—We may add to this list {{GHGheb|text=אֶפְרַ֫יִם}}, {{GHGheb|text=נַֽהְַרַ֫יִם|translate=the river country}} (in the Tel-el-Amarna letters ''nârima, na’rima''), {{GHGheb|text=מִצְרַ֫יִם|translate=Egypt}}, Phoenician {{GHGheb|text=מצרם}}; also the words denoting time, {{GHGheb|text=צָֽהֳרַ֫יִם|translate=midday}} (Mêša‛ inscription, line 15 {{GHGheb|text=צהרם}}), and perhaps {{GHGheb|text=עַרְבַּ֫יִם|translate=in the evening}}, if the regular expression {{GHGheb|text=בֵּין־הָֽעַרְבַּ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, &c., is only due to mistaking {{GHGheb|text=עַרְבַּ֫יִם}} for a dual: LXX πρὸς ἑσπέραν, τὸ δειλινόν, ὀψέ and only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=23|verse=5}} ἀνὰ μέσον τῶν ἑσπερινῶν. The Arabs also say ''el ‛išâ’ân'', ''the two evenings'', cf. Kuhn’s ''Literaturblatt'', iii. 48.

Instead of the supposed dual {{GHGheb|text=יָדַי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=18}} read {{GHGheb|text=יָדַ֫יִם}}. On {{GHGheb|text=חַלּוֹנַי}} (generally taken to be ''a double window'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=14}}, see above, {{GHGpar|87|g}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|88|d}}
2. Only apparently dual-forms (but really plural) are the words {{GHGheb|text=מַ֫יִם|translate=water}} and {{GHGheb|text=שָׁמַ֫יִם|translate=heaven}}. According to P. Haupt in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|SBOT.|Sacred Books of the Old Testament, ed. by P. Haupt. Lpz. and Baltimore, 1893 ff.}}}} (critical notes on Isaiah, p. 157, line 18 ff.), they are to be derived from the old plural forms (found in Assyrian) ''mâmi'', ''šamâmi'', whence the Hebr. {{GHGheb|text=מים}}, {{GHGheb|text=שמים}} arose by inversion of the ''i mâmi, mâimi, maim''. It is simpler, however, to suppose that the primitive singulars ''may'' and ''šamay'', when they took the plural of extension ({{GHGpar|124|b}}), kept the tone on the ''ay'', thus causing the ''îm'' (which otherwise always has the tone, {{GHGpar|87|a}}) to be shortened to ''im''. Cf. the analogous formations, Arab. ''tarḍaina'', ''2nd fem. sing. imperf''. of a verb {{GHGheb|text=ל״י}}, for ''tarḍay'' + ''îna'', corresponding to ''taqtulîna'' in the strong verb; also bibl.-Aram. {{GHGheb|text=בָּנַיִ֫ן}} the ''abs. st. plur''. of the ''ptcp. Qal'' of {{GHGheb|text=(ל״י) בְּנָה}}, which otherwise always ends in ''în'' with the tone, e.g. in the ''ptcp. Qal'' of the strong verb, {{GHGheb|text=דָּֽבְחִין|translate=sacrificing}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|88|e}}
'''2.''' The use of the dual in Hebrew is confined, except in the numerals 2, 12, 200, &c. (see {{GHGpar|97}}), practically to those objects which are by nature or art always found in ''pairs'', especially to the double members of the body (but not necessarily so, cf. {{GHGheb|text=זְרֹעִים}} and {{GHGheb|text=זְרֹעוֹת|translate=arms}}, never in the dual), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָדַ֫יִם|translate=both hands}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָזְנַ֫יִם|translate=both ears}}, {{GHGheb|text=שִׁנַּ֫יִם|translate=teeth}} (of both rows), also {{GHGheb|text=נַֽעֲלַ֫יִם|translate=a pair of sandals}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֹֽאזְנַ֫יִם|translate=a pair of scales}}, Lat. ''bilanx'', &c.; or things which are at least thought of as forming a pair, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יוֹמַ֫יִם|translate=two}} (successive) ''days'', Lat. ''biduum''; {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבֻעַיִ֫ם|translate=two weeks}}; {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנָתַ֫יִם|translate=two years}} (in succession), Lat. ''biennium''; {{GHGheb|text=אַמָּתַ֫יִם|translate=two cubits}}.<ref>But for {{GHGheb|text=דְּרָכַ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=28|verse=6.18}} (which the Masora takes as two roads leading from the cross-ways) {{GHGheb|text=דְּרָכִים}} is to be read.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|88|f}}
In the former case the dual may be used for a plural, either indefinite or defined by a numeral, where it is thought of in a double arrangement, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַרְבַּע רַגְלָ֑יִם|translate=four feet}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=11|verse=23}}; {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁשׁ כְּנָפַ֫יִם|translate=six wings}} (i.e. three pairs), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=1|verse=6}}; even {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעָה עֵינַ֫יִם|translate=seven eyes}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=3|verse=9}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־בִּרְכַּ֫יִם|translate=all knees}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=7|verse=17}}; {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־יָדַ֫יִם|translate=all hands}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=21|verse=12}}; {{GHGheb|text=מְצִלְתַּ֫יִם|translate=cymbals}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=3|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=שְׁפַתַּ֫יִם|translate=double-hooks}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=40|verse=43}}.—To express a certain emphasis the numeral ''two'' is used with the dual, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=3|verse=12}}.—See some other remarks on the use of the dual in {{GHGpar|87|o}} and s.

{{GHGmargin-letter|88|g}}
It is not impossible that Hebrew at an earlier period made a more extensive and freer use of the dual, and that the restrictions and limitations of its use, mentioned above, belong to a relatively later phase of development. The<section end="par88" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

271.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="68.173.104.173" /></noinclude><section begin="par88"/>Arabic literary language forms the dual in the noun, pronoun, and verb, almost as extensively as the Sanskrit or Greek; but in modern Arabic it has almost entirely disappeared in the verb, pronoun, and adjective. The Syriac has preserved it only in a few stereotyped forms, with which such duals as the Latin ''duo, ambo, octo'' may be compared. In the same way, the dual of the Sanskrit is lost in the modern Indian languages, and its full use in Old Slavonic has been restricted later, e.g. in Bohemian, just as in Hebrew, to ''pairs'', such as hands, feet, eyes, ears. On the Germanic dual, see Grimm’s ''Gramm.'', 2nd ed., i. p. 814.
<section end="par88"/>
<section begin="par89"/>{{GHGpar-heading|89|The Genitive and the Construct State}}

Philippi, ''Wesen und Ursprung des Stat. Constr. im Hebr''...., Weimar, 1871, p. 98 ff: on which cf. Nöldeke in the ''Gött. Gel. Anzeigen'', 1871, p. 23.—Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, p. 459 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|89|a}}
'''1.''' The Hebrew language no longer makes a living use of ''case-endings'',<ref>On some remains of obsolete case-endings see § 90.</ref> but either has no external indication of case (this is so for the ''nominative'', generally also for the ''accusative'') or expresses the relation by means of prepositions (§ 119), while the ''genitive'' is mostly indicated by a close connexion (or interdependence) of the ''Nomen regens'' and the ''Nomen rectum''. That is to say, the noun which as genitive serves to define more particularly an immediately preceding ''Nomen regens'', remains entirely unchanged in its form. The close combination, however, of the governing with the governed noun causes the tone first of all to be forced on to the latter,<ref>The same phenomenon of the tone may also be easily seen in other languages, when two words are closely connected in a similar way. Observe, for example, in German the natural stress on the last word in ‘''der Thron des Königs''’; though here the other order of the words (inadmissible in Hebrew) ‘''des Königs Thron''’ exhibits the same peculiarity.</ref> and the consequently weakened tone of the former word then usually involves further changes in it. These changes to some extent affect the consonants, but more especially the vocalization, since vowels which had been lengthened by their position ''in'' or ''before'' the tone-syllable necessarily become shortened, or are reduced to {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} (cf. {{GHGpar|9|a}}, c, k; {{GHGpar|27|e}}–m); e.g. {{GHGheb|text=דָּבָר|translate=word}}, {{GHGheb|text=דְּבַר אֱלֹהִים|translate=word of God}} (a sort of compound, as with us in inverted order, ''God’s-word, housetop, landlord''); {{GHGheb|text=יָד|translate=hand}}, {{GHGheb|text=יַד הַמֶּ֫לֶךְ |translate=the hand of the king}}; {{GHGheb|text=דְּבָרִים|translate=words}}, {{GHGheb|text=דִּבְרֵי הָעָם|translate=the words of the people}}. Thus in Hebrew only the noun which stands ''before a genitive'' suffers a change, and in grammatical language is said to be dependent, or in the {{GHGterm|construct state}}, while a noun which has not a genitive after it is said to be in the {{GHGterm|absolute state}}. It is sufficiently evident from the above that the {{GHGterm|construct state}} is not strictly to be regarded as a ''syntactical'' and ''logical'' phenomenon, but rather as simply ''phonetic'' and ''rhythmical'', depending on the circumstances of the tone.<section end="par89"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

272.text:
{{GHGmargin-letter|89|b}} Very frequently such interdependent words are also united by {{GHGterm|Maqqeph}} ({{GHGpar|16|a}}); this, however, is not necessary, but depends on the accentuation in the particular case. On the wider uses of the ''constr. st''. see the Syntax, § 130. {{GHGmargin-letter|89|c}} '''2.''' The ''vowel'' changes which are occasioned in many nouns by the {{GHGterm|construct state}} are more fully described in §§ 92–5. But besides these, the ''terminations'' of the noun in the construct state sometimes assume a special form. Thus: (''a'') In the {{GHGterm|construct state}}, plural and dual, the termination is {{GHGheb|text=־ֵי}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=סוּסִים|translate=horses}}, {{GHGheb|text=סוּסֵי פַרְעֹה|translate=the horses of Pharaoh}}; {{GHGheb|text=עֵינַ֫יִם|translate=eyes}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֵינֵי הַפֶּ֫לֶךְ|translate=the eyes of the king}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|89|d}} Rem. The {{GHGheb|text=־ֵי}} of the dual has evidently arisen from {{GHGheb|text=־ַי}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=יָ֫דַיִם}}), but the origin of the termination {{GHGheb|text=־ֵי}} in the ''constr. st''. plur. is disputed. The Syriac ''constr. st''. in ''ay'' and the form of the plural noun before suffixes ({{GHGheb|text=סוּסַי}}, {{GHGheb|text=סוּסַ֫יִךְ}}, &c., {{GHGpar|91|h}}) would point to a contraction of an original {{GHGheb|text=־ַי}}, as in the dual. But whether this ''ay'' was only transferred from the dual to the plural (so Olshausen, and Nöldeke, ''Beitr. zur sem. Sprachwiss.'', Strassb. 1904, p. 48 ff.), or is to be regarded as the ''abstract, collective'' termination, as in {{GHGheb|text=אִשֶּׁה}} (see f) and {{GHGheb|text=חוֹרַי}} (so Philippi, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ThLZ.|Theologische Literaturzeitung, ed. by E. Schürer. Lpz. 1876 ff.}}}} 1890, col. 419; Barth, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1904, p. 431 ff.), must be left undecided. {{GHGmargin-letter|89|e}} (''b'') The original {{GHGheb|text=־ַת}} is regularly retained as the feminine termination in the {{GHGterm|construct state}} sing. of those nouns which in the ''absolute'' state end in {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכָּה|translate=queen}}, {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכַּת שְׁבָא|translate=the queen of Sheba}}. But the feminine endings {{GHGheb|text=־֫ ־ֶת}}, {{GHGheb|text=־֫ ־ַת}}, and also the plural {{GHGheb|text=־וֹת}}, remain unchanged in the {{GHGterm|construct state}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|89|f}} (''c'') Nouns in {{GHGheb|text=־ֶה}} (cf. {{GHGpar|75|e}}) from verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} (§ 93, Paradigm III ''c'') form their ''constr. st''. in {{GHGheb|text=־ֵה}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רֹאֶה|translate=seer}}, constr. {{GHGheb|text=רֹאֵה}}. If this {{GHGheb|text=־ֵה}} is due to contraction of the original {{GHGheb|text=־ַי}}, with {{GHGheb|text=ה}} added as a vowel letter, we may compare {{GHGheb|text=דַּי}}, constr. {{GHGheb|text=דֵּי|translate=sufficiency}}; {{GHGheb|text=חַי}}, constr. {{GHGheb|text=חֵי|translate=life}}; {{GHGheb|text=(גַּי) גַּיְא}}, constr. {{GHGheb|text=(גֵּי) גֵּיא|translate=valley}}. On the terminations {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} and {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}} in the ''constr. st''. see § 90.
{{GHGpar-heading|90|Real and Supposed Remains of Early Case-endings. {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} local, {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} in compound proper names, {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}} and {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} in the Construct State}}
K. U. Nylander, ''Om Kasusändelserna i Hebräiskan'', Upsala, 1882; J. Barth, ‘Die Casusreste im Hebr.,’ {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} liii. 593 ff.
{{GHGmargin-letter|90|a}} '''1.''' As the Assyrian and old Arabic distinguish three cases by special endings, so also in the Hebrew noun there are three endings which, in the main, correspond to those of the Arabic. It is, however, a question whether they are all to be regarded as real remnants of former case-endings, or are in some instances to be explained {{hws|other|otherwise}}

273.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="65.78.5.191" /></noinclude><section begin="par90" />{{hwe|wise|otherwise}}. It can hardly be doubted (but cf. h, Rem.) that the (locative) termination {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} is a survival of the old accusative termination ''a'', and that {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} in certain compound proper names is the old sign of the nominative. The explanation of the ''î'' as an old genitive sign, which, as being no longer understood in Hebrew, was used for quite different purposes, and the view that {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} is a form of the nominative termination {{GHGheb|text=וּ}}, are open to grave doubts.

{{GHGmargin-letter|90|b}}
In Assyrian the rule is that ''u'' marks the nominative, ''i'' the genitive, and ''a'' the accusative,<ref>This rule is almost always observed in the Tell-el-Amarna letters (see {{GHGpar|2|f}}); cf. the instances cited by Barth, l. c., p. 595, from Winckler’s edition.</ref> ‘in spite of the many and various exceptions to this rule which occur’ (Delitzsch, ''Assyrische Gramm.'', § 66). Similarly, the Arabic case-endings in the fully declined nouns (''Triptotes'') are: -''u'' for the nominative, -''i'' for the genitive, and -''a'' for the accusative; in the ''Diptotes'' the ending -''a'' represents the genitive also. In modern Arabic these endings have almost entirely disappeared, and if they are now and then used, as among the Beduin, it is done without regularity, and one is interchanged with another (Wallin, in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} v, p. 9, xii, p. 874; Wetzstein, ''ibid.'', xxii, p. 113 f., and especially Spitta, ''Gramm. des Arab. Vulgärdialekts von Ägypten'', Lpz. 1880, p. 147 ff.). Even as early as the Sinaitic inscriptions, their regular use is not maintained (Beer,''Studia Asiatica'', iii. 1840, p. xviii; Tuch, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} iii. 139 f.). Ethiopic has preserved only the -''a'' (in proper names -''hâ''), which is, however, still used for the whole range of the accusative, and also (the distinction of case being lost) as a termination of the ''constr. st''. to connect it with a following genitive.

{{GHGmargin-letter|90|c}}
'''2.''' As remarked above, under ''a'', the ''accusative'' form is preserved in Hebrew most certainly and clearly in the (usually toneless) ending {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}, originally ''ă'', as in the old Arabic accusative. This is appended to the substantive:

(''a'') Most commonly to express ''direction towards'' an object, or ''motion to a placer'',<ref>On this meaning of the accusative see the Syntax, {{GHGpar|118|d}}, and cf. the Latin accusative of motion to a place, as in ''Romam profectus est, domum reverti, rus ire''.</ref> e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָ֫מָּה|translate=seaward, westward}}, {{GHGheb|text=קֵ֫דְמָה|translate=eastward}}, {{GHGheb|text=צָפ֫וֹנָה|translate=northward}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַשּׁ֫וּרָה|translate=to Assyria}}, {{GHGheb|text=בָּבֶ֫לָה|translate=to Babylon}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֶ֫רָה}} (from {{GHGheb|text=הַר}}) ''to the mountain'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=10}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫רְצָה|translate=to the earth}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫יְתָה|translate=to the house}}, {{GHGheb|text=תִּרְצָ֫תָה|translate=to Tirzah}} ({{GHGheb|text=תִּרְצָה}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=14|verse=17}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=עַזָּ֫תָה|translate=to Gaza}} ({{GHGheb|text=עַזָּה}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=1}}; with the article {{GHGheb|text=הָהָ֫רָה|translate=to the mountain}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַבַּ֫יְתָה|translate=into the house}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַחַ֫דְרָה|translate=into the chamber}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=15}}; {{GHGheb|text=הָאֹ֫הֱלָה}}<ref>{{GHGheb|text=הָאֹֽהֱלָ֫ה}} in Baer’s text, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=6}}, is an error, according to his preface to Isaiah, p. v.</ref> ''into the tent'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=6}}, &c.; similarly with adverbs, as {{GHGheb|text=שָׁ֫מָּה|translate=thither}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָ֫נָת|translate=whither?}}; even with the ''constr. st''. before a genitive {{GHGheb|text=בֵּ֫יתָה יוֹסֵף}} ''into Joseph’s house'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=17.24}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫רְצָה הַנֶּ֫גֶב|translate=toward the land of the south}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫רְצָה מִצְרַ֫יִם|translate=to the land of Egypt}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=4|verse=20}}; {{GHGheb|text=מִדְבַּ֫רָה דַמֶּ֫שֶׂק|translate=to the wilderness of Damascus}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=19|verse=15}}; {{GHGheb|text=מִזְרְחָ֫ה שֶׁ֫מֶשׁ|translate=toward the sun-rising}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=41}}; and even with the plural {{GHGheb|text=כַּשְׂדִּימָה|translate=into Chaldea}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=11|verse=24}}; {{GHGheb|text=הָשָּׁמַ֫יִמָה|translate=towards the heavens}}.
<section end="par90" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

274.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par90 />Rem. The above examples are mostly rendered definite by the article, or by a following genitive of definition, or are proper names. But cases like {{GHGheb|text=יָ֫מָּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֶ֫רָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫יְתָה}} show that the locative form ''of itself'' possessed a defining power.

{{GHGmargin-letter|90|d}}
(''b'') In a somewhat weakened sense, indicating the place ''where'' something is or happens (cf. {{GHGpar|118|d}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מַֽחֲנָ֑יְמָה|translate=in Maḥanaim}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=4|verse=14}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁ֫מָּה|translate=there}} (usually ''thither'', see c), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=18|verse=2}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=23|verse=8}}, and the expression ''to offer a sacrifice'' {{GHGheb|text=הַמִּזְבֵּ֫חָה}}, properly ''towards the altar'' for ''on the altar''. On the other hand, {{GHGheb|text=בָּבֶ֫לָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=29|verse=15}}, and {{GHGheb|text=זְבֻ֫לָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=3|verse=11}}, are to be regarded as ordinary accusatives of direction, ''to Babylon, into the habitation''; also expressions like {{GHGheb|text=פְּאַת צָפ֫וֹנָה|translate=the quarter towards the north}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=5}} (at the beginning of the verse, {{GHGheb|text=גְּבוּל קֵ֫דְמָה|translate=the border toward the east}}), cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=18|verse=15.20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=26|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=23|verse=8}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|90|e}}
(''c'') The original force of the ending {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} is also disregarded when it is added to a substantive with a preposition prefixed (cf. also {{GHGheb|text=עַד־אָ֫נָה|translate=how long?}}), and this not only after {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}} or {{GHGheb|text=עַד־}} (which are easily explained), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עְלָה|translate=upwards}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫טָּה|translate=downwards}}, {{GHGheb|text=לִשְׁא֫וֹלָה|translate=to Sheol}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=9|verse=18}}; {{GHGheb|text=עַד־אֲפֵ֫קָה|translate=unto Aphek}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=13|verse=4}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־הַצָּפ֫וֹנָה|translate=toward the north}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=8|verse=14}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=20|verse=16}}; but also after {{GHGheb|text=ב}}, and even after {{GHGheb|text=מִן}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בַּנֶּ֫גְבָּה|translate=in the south}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=21}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=15.19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=31|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=52|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=מִבָּבֶ֫לָה|translate=from Babylon}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=27|verse=16}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=1|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=10|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=21|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=6}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|90|f}}
Rem. Old locative forms (or original accusatives) are, according to the Masora, still to be found in

(''a'') {{GHGheb|text=לַ֫יְלָה}}, in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫יְלָה}}, the usual word in prose for ''night'', which is always construed as masculine. The nominative of this supposed old accusative<ref>Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Sem. Sprachwiss}}., p. 113, also takes it as such, ''láylā'' being properly ''at night'', then ''night'' simply. Barth, however (''Sprachwiss. Abhandlungen'', p. 16, note 1), refers it to an original {{GHGheb|text=לַיְלֶה}}, like {{GHGheb|text=אָנָה}} from {{GHGheb|text=אָנֶ֫ה}}.</ref> appeared to be preserved in the form {{GHGheb|text=לַ֫יִל}}, only used in poetry, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=16|verse=3}}, ''constr. st''. {{GHGheb|text=לֵיל}} (even used for the ''absol. st''. in pause {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=11}}). Most probably, however, {{GHGheb|text=לַיְלָה}} is to be referred, with Nöldeke and others, to a reduplicated form {{GHGheb|text=לילי}}; cf. especially the western Aramaic {{GHGheb|text=לֵילְיָא}}, Syr. ''lilya'', &c.—Another instance is {{GHGheb|text=מְא֫וּמָה|translate=something}}, probably from {{GHGheb|text=מְאוּם}}, {{GHGheb|text=מוּם|translate=spot, point}}, generally with a negative=''nothing''. Similarly {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫רְצָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=23}} and (in pause) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=13}}, {{GHGheb|text=סוּפָ֫תָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=8|verse=7}}, and the place-name {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫הְצָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=6|verse=63}}, might be explained as accusatives. Elsewhere, however, the toneless {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} can be regarded only as a meaningless appendage, or at the most as expressing poetic emphasis; thus {{GHGheb|text=אָ֫רְצָה}} (in {{GHGterm|pause}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=37|verse=12}}; {{GHGheb|text=הַמָּ֫וְתָה|translate=death}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=116|verse=15}}; {{GHGheb|text=נֶגְדָּה־נָּא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=116|verse=14.18}}; {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫חְלָה|translate=stream}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=124|verse=4}}; {{GHGheb|text=הַחַשְׁמַ֫לָה|translate=amber}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=8|verse=2}} [in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=1|verse=4|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=הַחַשְׁמַל}}, cf. {{GHGpar|80|k}}], &c. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=הַיָּ֫מָּה}} is probably only a scribal error (dittography). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=18}} instead of the quite unsuitable poetic word {{GHGheb|text=הַחַ֫רְסָה}} (towards the sun??) read as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=15|verse=1|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=הַחַ֫דְרָה|translate=to the bride-chamber}}.
<section end=par90 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

275.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="65.78.5.191" /></noinclude><section begin="par90" />{{GHGmargin-letter|90|g}}
(''b'') In the termination {{GHGheb|text=־ָ֫ תָה}} often used in poetry with feminines, viz. {{GHGheb|text=אֵימָ֫תָה|translate=terror}} (={{GHGheb|text=אֵימָה}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=16}}; {{GHGheb|text=עֶזְרָ֫תָה|translate=help}} (={{GHGheb|text=עֶזְרָה}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=44|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=63|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=94|verse=17|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=יְשׁוּעָ֫תָה|translate=salvation}} (={{GHGheb|text=יְשׁוּעָה}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=3|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=80|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=2|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=עַוְ֫לָתָה|translate=unrighteousness}} (={{GHGheb|text=עַוְלָה}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=28|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=10|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=125|verse=3}}; {{GHGheb|text=עֹלָ֫תָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=92|verse=16}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=16}}; {{GHGheb|text=צָרָ֫תָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=120|verse=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=עֵיפָ֫תָה|translate=darkness}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=22}}; {{GHGheb|text=הַמְזִמָּ֫תָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=11|verse=15}} is corrupt, see the LXX and Commentaries. These cases are not to be taken as double feminine endings, since the loss of the tone on the final syllable could then hardly be explained, but they are further instances of an old accusative of direction or intention. In examples like {{GHGheb|text=עֶזְרָ֫תָה|translate=for help}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=44|verse=27}}) this is still quite apparent, but elsewhere it has become meaningless and is used merely for the sake of poetical emphasis.<ref>The form clings also to a few place-names, as {{GHGheb|text=גֻּדְגֹּ֫דָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=10|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלִ֫שָׁה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=42}}; {{GHGheb|text=קְהֵלָ֫תָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=33|verse=22}} f.; {{GHGheb|text=יָטְבָּ֫תָה}} verse 33 f.; {{GHGheb|text=תִּמְנָ֫תָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=19|verse=43}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=אֶפְרָ֫תָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=5|verse=1}}, &c.]</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|90|h}}
This termination {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} usually has reference to ''place'' (hence called {{GHGheb|text=־ָה|translate=locale}}<ref>Cf. Sarauw, ‘''Der hebr. Lokativ'',’ {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZA.|Zeitschrift für Assyriologie und verwandte Gebiete, ed. by C. Bezold. Lpz. 18S6 ff.}}}} 1907, p. 183 ff. He derives the {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} from the adverbs {{GHGheb|text=שָׁ֫מָּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָ֫נָה}} and holds that it has nothing whatever to do with the old accusative.</ref>); sometimes, however, its use is extended to time, as in {{GHGheb|text=מִיָּמִים יָמִ֫ימָה|translate=from year to year}}. Its use in {{GHGheb|text=חָלִ֫ילָה}} properly ''ad profanum!=absit!'' is peculiar.

{{GHGmargin-letter|90|i}}
As the termination {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} is almost always toneless (except in {{GHGheb|text=מִזְרְחָה|translate=constr. st.}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=41}}; {{GHGheb|text=גִּתָּה}} and {{GHGheb|text=עִתָּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=19|verse=13}}) it generally, as the above examples show, exercises no influence whatever upon the vowels of the word; in the ''constr. st.'' {{GHGheb|text=מִדְבַּ֫רָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=18|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=19|verse=15}}, and in the proper names {{GHGheb|text=גַּ֫תָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=40}}, {{GHGheb|text=דַּ֫נָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=6}} (so Baer; ed. Mant. and Ginsb. {{GHGheb|text=דַּ֫נָה}}), {{GHGheb|text=צְפַ֫תָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=14|verse=9}}, {{GHGheb|text=צָֽרְפַ֫תָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=17|verse=9}}, {{GHGheb|text=צָֽרְתַ֫נָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=4|verse=12}}, an ''ă'' is retained even in an open tone-syllable (cf., however, {{GHGheb|text=הֶ֫רָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=10}}, {{GHGheb|text=פַּדֶּ֫נָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=2}} from {{GHGheb|text=פַּדַּן}}, with modification of the ''a'' to ''è''; also {{GHGheb|text=כַּרְמֶ֫לָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=5}} from {{GHGheb|text=כַּרְמֶל}}). In segholate forms, as a general rule, the {{GHGheb|text=־ָה|translate=local}} is joined to the already developed form of the ''absol. st.'', except that the helping-vowel before {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} naturally becomes {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫יְתָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָאֹ֫הֱלָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=6}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=הַיַּֽ֫עֲרָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=17|verse=15}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַשַֹּֽׁ֫עֲרָה}}<ref>So Qimḥi, and the Mant. ed. (Baer {{GHGheb|text=הַשַֹּׁ֫עְרָה}}), i.e. locative from {{GHGheb|text=שַׂ֫עַר}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=20}}). The reading {{GHGheb|text=הַשַּֽׂעֲרָה}} (Opit., Ginsb.) implies a feminine in {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}}.</ref> {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=20|verse=16}}, &c., but also {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫חְלָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=34|verse=5}} (''constr. st.''; likewise to be read in the ''absolute'' in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=47|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=48|verse=28|hidebook=1}}) and {{GHGheb|text=שָֽׁעְרָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=6}} (with ''Silluq''); cf. {{GHGheb|text=נֶ֫גְבָּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=47|verse=19}} and {{GHGheb|text=גֹּ֫רְנָה}} (Baer, incorrectly, {{GHGheb|text=גֹּֽרְנָ֫ה}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=4|verse=12}} (both in {{GHGterm|pause}}).—In the case of feminines ending in {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} the {{GHGheb|text=־ָה|translate=local}} is added to the original feminine ending {{GHGheb|text=־ָת}} ({{GHGpar|80|b}}), the ''ă'' of which (since it then stands in an open tone-syllable) is lengthened to ''ā'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=תִּרְצָ֫תָה}}.—Moreover the termination {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} is even weakened to {{GHGheb|text=־ֶה}} in {{GHGheb|text=נֹ֫בֶה|translate=to Nob}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=21|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=22|verse=9|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=אָ֫נֶה|translate=whither}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=36.42}} and {{GHGheb|text=דְּדָ֫נֶה|translate=to Dedan}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=25|verse=13}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|90|k}}
'''3.''' Of the three other terminations {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} may still be regarded as a survival of the old nominative ending. It occurs only in the middle<section end="par90" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

276.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par90 />of a few (often undoubtedly very old) proper names,<ref>Cf. the list in L. Kaila, ''Zur Syntax des in verbaler Abhängigkeit stehenden Nomens im alttest. Hebr.'', Helsingfors, 1906, p. 54.</ref> viz. {{GHGheb|text=אֲחוּמַי}} (if compounded of {{GHGheb|text=אחו}} and {{GHGheb|text=מי}}), {{GHGheb|text=חֲמוּטַל}} (for which in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=52|verse=1}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}} {{GHGheb|text=חֲמִיטַל}}), {{GHGheb|text=מְתֽוּשָׁאֵל}} and {{GHGheb|text=מְתוּשֶׁ֫לַח}} (otherwise in Hebrew only in the plur. {{GHGheb|text=מְתִים|translate=men}}; to {{GHGheb|text=מְתוּ}} corresponds most probably {{GHGheb|text=בְּתוּ}} in {{GHGheb|text=בְּתוּאֵל}}), {{GHGheb|text=פְּנוּאֵל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=31}} (but in ver. 32 {{GHGheb|text=פְּנִיאֵל}}) ''face of God'' (otherwise only in the plur. {{GHGheb|text=פָּנִים|translate=constr. st.}} {{GHGheb|text=פְּנֵי}}).<ref>The name {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמוּאֵל}} formerly regarded as a compound of {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמוּ}}={{GHGheb|text=שֵׁם|translate=name}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֵל}}, is better explained with Prätorius, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1903, p. 777, as a name of affection, for {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמוּעַ אֵל}}={{GHGheb|text=יִשְׁמָעֵאל}} [but see Driver on {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=20}}]; similarly, according to Prätorius, {{GHGheb|text=פְּתוּאֵל}}={{GHGheb|text=פְּתוּחַ אֵל}} and many others.</ref>—{{GHGheb|text=גַּשְׁמוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=6|verse=6}} (elsewhere {{GHGheb|text=גֶּ֫שֶׁם}}), is the name of an Arab, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=6|verse=1|hidebook=1}}. On the other hand the terminations {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}} and {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} are most probably to be regarded (with Barth, l. c., p. 597) as having originated on Hebrew soil in order to emphasize the ''constr. st.'', on the analogy of the ''constr. st.'' of terms expressing relationship.

In view of the analogies in other languages (see b) there is nothing impossible in the view formerly taken here that the ''litterae compaginis'' {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}} and {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} are obsolete (and hence no longer understood) case-endings, ''î'' being the old genitive and ''ô'' for the nominative sign ''u''. Barth objects that the ''î'' and ''ô'' almost invariably have the tone, whereas the accusative {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} is toneless, and that they are long, where the Arab. ''ĭ'' and ''ŭ'' are short. Both these objections, however, lose their force if we consider the special laws of the tone and syllable in Hebrew. The language does not admit a final ''ĭ'' or ''ŭ'', and the necessarily lengthened vowel might easily attract the tone to itself. On the other hand a strong argument for Barth’s theory is the fact that these ''litterae compaginis'' are almost exclusively used to emphasize the close connexion of one noun with another; hence especially in the ''constr. st.'' Consequently it seems in the highest degree probable that all these uses are based upon forms in which the ''constr. st.'' is expressly emphasized by a special termination, i.e. the ''constr. st.'' of terms of relationship, {{GHGheb|text=אֲבִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֲחִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֲמִי}} from {{GHGheb|text=אָב|translate=father}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָח|translate=brother}}, {{GHGheb|text=חָם|translate=father-in-law}} (cf. § 96). The instances given under ''l'' and ''m'' followed this analogy.

Like ''î'', {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} is also used only to emphasize the ''constr. st.'' (see o), and must therefore have a similar origin, but its exact explanation is difficult. According to Barth, this {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}} corresponds to a primitive Semitic ''â'' (cf. {{GHGpar|9|q}}) and is traceable to ''ʾabâ, ʾaḥâ'', the accusatives of terms of relationship in the ''constr. st.'', which have ''â'' only before a genitive. Against this explanation it may be objected that there is no trace of the supposed Hebrew accusatives {{GHGheb|text=אֲבוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֲחוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֲמוֹ}}, and only of the analogous {{GHGheb|text=בְּנוֹ}}. It is also remarkable that so archaic a form should have been preserved (except in {{GHGheb|text=בְּנוֹ}}) only in two words and those in quite late passages. However we have no better explanation to offer in place of Barth’s.

Finally we cannot deny the possibility, in some cases, of Barth’s explanation of the {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} in compound proper names like {{GHGheb|text=בְתוּאֵל}}, &c. (see above), as due to the analogy of terms of relationship with nominative in {{GHGheb|text=וּ}}. But this in no way militates against the view expressed above, that in some very old names, like {{GHGheb|text=פְּנוּאֵל}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּתוּאֵל}}, &c., the original common nominative sign has simply been preserved.
<section end=par90 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

277.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par90 />The instances found are:

{{GHGmargin-letter|90|l}}
(''a'') Of the ending {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}}: {{GHGheb|text=בְּנִי אֲתֹנוֹ}} ''his ass’s colt'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=11}}; {{GHGheb|text=עֹֽזְבִי הַצֹּאן|translate=that leaveth the flock}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=11|verse=17}} (cf. the preceding {{GHGheb|text=רֹעִי הָֽאֱלִיל}}); {{GHGheb|text=שֹֽׁכְנִי סְנֶה|translate=the dweller in the bush}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=16}} (on {{GHGheb|text=שֹֽׁבְנִי}} cf. below Jer 49<sup>16''a''</sup>, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ob|chapter=1|verse=3}}); appended to the feminine {{GHGheb|text=גְּנֻבְֽתִי יוֹם וּגְּנֻבְֽתִי לְ֫יְלְה|translate=whether stolen by day or stolen by night}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=39}} (in prose, but in very emphatic speech); {{GHGheb|text=מְלֵֽאֲתִי מִשְׁפָּט|translate=plena iustitiae|en=full of judgment}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=21}}; {{GHGheb|text=רַבָּ֫תִי עָם|translate=full of people}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=1}} (on the retraction of the tone before a following tone-syllable, cf. {{GHGpar|29|e}}; in the same verse the second {{GHGheb|text=רבתי}} and {{GHGheb|text=שָׂרָ֫תִי}}, see below, follow the example of {{GHGheb|text=רַבָּ֫תִי}}, although no tone-syllable follows; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=10|verse=11}} below); {{GHGheb|text=עַל־דִּבְרָתִי מַלְכִּי־צֶ֫דֶק|translate=after the order of Melchizedek}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=110|verse=4}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=113|verse=9}}, Jer 49<sup>16''b''</sup>. To the same category belong the rather numerous cases, in which a preposition is inserted between the {{GHGterm|construct state}} and its genitive (cf. {{GHGpar|130|a}}), without actually abolishing the dependent relation, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רַבָּ֫תִי בַגּוֹיִם|translate=she that was great among the nations}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָׂרָ֫תִי בַמְּדִינוֹת|translate=princess among the provinces}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֹהַ֫בְתִּי לָדוּשׁ|translate=that loveth to tread}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=10|verse=11}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=16}}a, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ob|chapter=1|verse=3}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=נֶאְדָּרִי}} can only be so explained if it is a vocative referring to {{GHGheb|text=יהוה}}, but perhaps we should read {{GHGheb|text=נֶאְדָּרָה}} as predicate to {{GHGheb|text=יְמִֽינְךָ}}.

Further, the ''Ḥireq compaginis'' is found with certain particles which are really also nouns in the ''constr. st.'', as {{GHGheb|text=זֽוּלָתִי}} (={{GHGheb|text=זוּלָת}}) ''except'', {{GHGheb|text=מִנִּי}} (poetical for {{GHGheb|text=מִן}}) ''from'', {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְתִּי|translate=not}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַפְסִי|translate=not}} (thrice in the formula {{GHGheb|text=אֲנִי וְאַפְסִי עוֹד|translate=I am, and there is none else beside me}}; but many take the {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}} as a suffix here), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=8.10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=2|verse=15}}. [The above are all the cases in which this {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}} is attached to independent words in the O.T.; it occurs, however, besides] in compound proper names (again attached to the ''constr. st.''), as {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכִּי־צֶ֫דֶק}} (''king of righteousness''), {{GHGheb|text=גַּבְרִיאֵל}} (''man of God''), {{GHGheb|text=חַנִּיאֵל}} (''favour of God''), and others (cf. also the Punic name ''Hannibal'', i.e. {{GHGheb|text=חַנִּיבַ֫עַל|translate=favour of Baʿal}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|90|m}}
Otherwise than in the ''constr. st.'' the ''Ḥireg compaginis'' is only found in participial forms, evidently with the object of giving them more dignity, just as in the case of the construct forms in ''î''. We must distinguish, however, between passages in which the participle nevertheless does stand in close connexion, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=16}} ({{GHGheb|text=חֹֽצְבִי}} and {{GHGheb|text=חֹֽקְקִי}}, also in impassioned speech), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=7|verse=14}} (probably influenced by {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=16}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=101|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=113|verse=7|hidebook=1}}; and passages in which the ''î'' added to the participle with the article merely serves as an ornamental device of poetic style, e.g. in the late Psalms, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=113|verse=5.6.7.9|hidebook=1}} (on verse 8 see n), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=114|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=123|verse=1|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|90|n}}
In ''K<sup>e</sup>thibh'' the termination ''î'' also occurs four times in {{GHGheb|text=יושבתי}}, i.e. {{GHGheb|text=יוֹשַׁבְתִּי}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=23|hidebook=1}} (before {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=27|verse=3}} (before {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|verse=21}} (before {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}). Perhaps {{GHGheb|text=ישַׁבְתִּי}} and {{GHGheb|text=שֹׁכַנְתִּי}} are ''formae mixtae'', combining the readings {{GHGheb|text=ישֶׁ֫בֶת}}, &c. and {{GHGheb|text=יָשַׁבְתְּ}} (''2nd fem. perf.''), &c., but {{GHGheb|text=מְקֻנַּנְתִּי}} may be merely assimilated to {{GHGheb|text=ישַׁבְתִּי}} which immediately precedes it. The following are simply textual errors: {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=ההלכתי}} {{GHGterm|Keth.}}, due to the preceding {{GHGheb|text=אתי}}, and to be read {{GHGheb|text=הַֽהֹלֶ֫כֶת}} as in the ''Qere''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=30|verse=8}} (read {{GHGheb|text=הַֽרֲרֵי}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=113|verse=8|hidebook=1}} (read {{GHGheb|text=לְהֽוֹשִׁיבוֹ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=116|verse=1|hidebook=1}} (read {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל תח׳}}, as in five other places). On {{GHGheb|text=בְּרִיתִי}}, thrice, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=42}}, cf. {{GHGpar|128|d}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|90|o}} (''b'') Of the ending {{GHGheb|text=וֹ}}Cf. Kaila, l. c., p. 59 ff. (always with the tone): in prose only in the Pentateuch, but in elevated style, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=24}} {{GHGheb|text=חַיְתוֹ־אֶרֶץ|translate=the beast of the earth}} (={{GHGheb|text=חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ}} ver. 25); similarly in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=50|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=79|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=11.20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=56|verse=9}} (twice), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=2|verse=14}}; otherwise only in {{GHGheb|text=בְּנוֹ צִפֹּר|translate=son of Zippor}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=18}}; {{GHGheb|text=בְּנוֹ בְעֹר|translate=son of Beor}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=24|verse=3.15}}; and {{GHGheb|text=מַעְיְנוֹ מַ֫יִם|translate=a fountain of waters}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=114|verse=8}}.
{{GHGpar-heading|91|The Noun with Pronominal Suffixes}} W. Diehl, ''Das Pronomen pers. suffixum 2 u. 3 pers. plur. des Hebr.'', Giessen, 1895; A. Ungnad, ‘Das Nomen mit Suffixen im Semit.,’ ''Vienna Oriental Journal'', xx, p. 167 ff. {{GHGmargin-letter|91|a}} With regard to the connexion of the noun with pronominal suffixes, which then stand in a genitive relation ({{GHGpar|33|c}}) and are, therefore, necessarily appended to the {{GHGterm|construct state}} of the noun, we shall first consider, as in the verb (§ 57 ff.), the forms of the suffixes themselves, and then the various changes in the form of the noun to which they are attached. The nouns are also tabulated in the Paradigms of the flexion of the noun in § 92 ff. Cf. also Paradigm A in the Appendix. We are here primarily concerned with the different forms of the suffixes when added to the singular, plural, and dual. {{GHGmargin-letter|91|b}} '''1.''' {{GHGmargin-letter|91|c}} Rem. 1. There is less variety of forms in these than in the verbal suffixes; the particular forms are used as follows:— (''a'') Those without a connecting vowel (on the derivation of these ‘connecting vowels’ from original stem-vowels, see note on {{GHGpar|58|f}}) are generally joined to nouns of a peculiar form (see § 96), the ''constr. st.'' of which ends in a vowel, as {{GHGheb|text=אָבִ֫יךָ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָבִ֫יהוּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=אָבִיו}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָבִ֫יהָ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָבִ֫ינוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֲבִיכֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֲבִיכֶן}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֲבִיהֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֲבִיהֶן}}, sometimes also to segholate forms ending in ''î'' from {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} stems (see {{GHGpar|93|x}}, y), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=פְּרִיהֶם|translate=the fruit of them}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=14}} (also {{GHGheb|text=פִּרְיָם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=30}}, &c.), {{GHGheb|text=פּרִיהֶן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=29|verse=28}} (also {{GHGheb|text=פִּרְיָן}} verse 5); cf., moreover, {{GHGheb|text=חֶלְבְּהֶן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=8|verse=16.25}} and similar examples with {{GHGheb|text=הֶן}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=הֵן}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=53|hidebook=1}}.Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=15|verse=10}} read (according to {{GHGpar|61|h}}, end) {{GHGheb|text=כֻּלְּהֶם קִלְּלוּנִי}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=7|verse=6}} probably {{GHGheb|text=אַפְּהֶם}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֹֽפֵהֶם}}. Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=10|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nah|chapter=2|verse=8}}, &c., the {{GHGterm|Keth.}} perhaps intends the singular, {{GHGheb|text=לְמִֽינְהֶם}}, &c., but the Masora requires the plural with defective ''ê''. {{GHGmargin-letter|91|d}} (''b'') The forms with connecting vowels ({{GHGpar|58|f}}) are joined to nouns ending in a consonant. The connecting vowel is regularly ''a'' in the ''3rd sing. fem.'' {{GHGheb|text=־ָהּ}} (for ''aha'') and ''3rd plur.'' {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ָ֫ מוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ָן}}, also in the ''3rd sing. masc.'' {{GHGheb|text=(הֹ) וֹ}}, since the ''ô'' is contracted from ''a[h]û'', and in the pausal form of the ''2nd masc.'' {{GHGheb|text=־ֶ֫ ךָ}} (a modification of original {{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ ךָ}}). The forms with ''ē'' in the above-mentioned persons are common only with nouns in {{GHGheb|text=־ֶה}} (from stems {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}), ''constr. st.'' {{GHGheb|text=־ֵה}} (cf. {{GHGpar|89|f}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שָׂדֵ֫הוּ}} (from ''sadaihû'') ''his field''; {{GHGheb|text=עָלֶ֫הָ|translate=its leaf}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=30}}; {{GHGheb|text=מַרְאֶ֫הָ|translate=the appearance thereof}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=13|verse=4}} (from ''mar’aihā''; on the {{GHGterm|Seghôl}} see k); but {{GHGheb|text=שָׂדָהּ|translate=her field}}. The orthographic retention of the {{GHGheb|text=י}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מַֽעֲשֶׂ֫יךָ}}, {{GHGheb|text=מַֽעֲשָׂיו}}, gives to many forms the appearance of plurals; see the instances in {{GHGpar|93|ss}}. Apart from these {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} forms the connecting vowel ''ē'' in the 3rd pers. occurs only in isolated cases; {{GHGheb|text=אוֹרֵ֫הוּ|translate=his light}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=25|verse=3}}; {{GHGheb|text=לְמִינֵ֫הוּ|translate=after its kind}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=12.25}} [+ 12 times]; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=1|verse=13}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=24}} read {{GHGheb|text=פִּֽילַגְשׁוֹ}} as in vv. 2, 25. On the other hand {{GHGheb|text=־ֵךְ}} in the ''2nd sing. fem.'' and {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ֫ נוּ}} in the ''1st plur.'' are by far the more common forms, while {{GHGheb|text=־ָךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ָ֫ נוּ}} are of rare occurrence; see e.—Instead of {{GHGheb|text=־ְךָ}} ({{GHGheb|text=־ְכָה}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=13|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=29|verse=25}}, &c., cf. {{GHGheb|text=בְּכָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְכָה}} {{GHGpar|103|g}}), {{GHGheb|text=־ְכֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ְכֶן}} (with {{GHGterm|Šewâ mobile}}), if the last consonant of the noun is a guttural, the forms are {{GHGheb|text=־ֲךָ}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ֲכֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ֲכֶן}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רֽוּחֲךָ|translate=thy spirit}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֹּרַֽאֲךָ|translate=thy creator}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=43|verse=1}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֵיֽעֲכֶם|translate=your friend}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=27}} (on such cases as {{GHGheb|text=בְּחֶוֹכְכֶם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hag|chapter=2|verse=5}}, see {{GHGpar|10|g}}).—With ''Nun energicum'' (cf. {{GHGpar|58|i}}, and on {{GHGheb|text=עוֹנֶ֑ךָּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=1}}, &c., cf. {{GHGpar|61|h}}) {{GHGheb|text=דֶַיּ֑ךָּ}} occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=25|verse=16}}, in principal pause. 2. Rare or incorrect forms are— {{GHGmargin-letter|91|e}} ''Sing.'' 1st pers. {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ֫ נִי}} in {{GHGheb|text=בְּשׁוּבֵ֫נִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=47|verse=7}} (certainly only a scribal error, caused by {{GHGheb|text=וַיְשִׁבֵ֫נִי}} in verse 6).

''m''. in pause {{GHGheb|text=־ֶ֫ כָה}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כַּפֶּֽכָה}} (''thy hand''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=5}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=24|verse=10}}; once {{GHGheb|text=חֹנָ֑ךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=53|verse=6}} (cf. the analogous cases in the verbal suffix {{GHGpar|75|ll}}); {{GHGterm|fem.}} {{GHGheb|text=־ֵיךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=5|verse=12}} (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=53|hidebook=1}} also for {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבִיתַ֫יִךְ}} probably {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבִיתֵיךְ}} is intended), {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ֫ כִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=11|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=103|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=116|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=135|verse=9|hidebook=1}} (corresponding to the Aramaic suffix of the ''2nd fem. sing.''; on the wholly abnormal {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ֫ כֵה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=2|verse=14}}, cf. ''l''), {{GHGheb|text=לֵכִי}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=2|verse=13}}. Also {{GHGheb|text=־ָ֫ ךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=25|verse=4|hidebook=1}}.

3rd pers. {{GHGheb|text=־ֹה}} (cf. {{GHGpar|7|c}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָֽהֳלֹה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=21|hidebook=1}} (always with {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} {{GHGheb|text=אָֽהֳלוֹ}}); {{GHGheb|text=נֻחֹה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=10|verse=36}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֵחֹה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=34|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=בֻּלֹּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=2|verse=1}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}; {{GHGheb|text=קִצֹּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=19|verse=23}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}, for which {{GHGheb|text=קִצּוֹ}} is read in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=24}}; {{GHGheb|text=עִירֹה}} and {{GHGheb|text=סוּתֹה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=11}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=22|verse=26}} ({{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} {{GHGheb|text=עִירוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=סוּתוֹ}}); {{GHGheb|text=סֻבֹּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=10|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=27|verse=5|hidebook=1}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}; {{GHGheb|text=הֲמוֹנֹה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=31|verse=18}}, &c., {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}; {{GHGheb|text=תְּבוּאָתֹה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=48|verse=18}} [altogether fourteen times in the Pentateuch, and some forty times in other books: see Driver, ''Samuel'', p. xxxv, and on {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=21|verse=1|hidebook=1}}].

''3rd fem.'' {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} for {{GHGheb|text=־ָהּ}} (with the softening of the ''Mappiq'', cf. {{GHGpar|23|k}}, and the analogous cases in {{GHGpar|58|g}}) occurs repeatedly before ''B<sup>e</sup>ghadhk<sup>e</sup>phath'' and other soft consonants, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=18}} (before {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, if the text is right), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=13|verse=4}} (before {{GHGheb|text=ל}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=15|verse=28.31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=9}} (unless {{GHGheb|text=אָכְלָה}}, the infin. with fem. termination, is intended; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁתֹה}} follows), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=44}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=24|verse=6|hidebook=1}} (before {{GHGheb|text=ב}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=8|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=12|verse=28}} (before {{GHGheb|text=א}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=3|verse=9}} (before {{GHGheb|text=וּ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=48|verse=14}} (before {{GHGheb|text=פ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=47|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=22}} twice (before {{GHGheb|text=ת}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=17}} (before {{GHGheb|text=ה}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=32|verse=42}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=1|verse=11}} (before {{GHGheb|text=ן}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=6|verse=2}} (before {{GHGheb|text=ע}}); even in {{GHGterm|pause}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=12|verse=4}}<sup> ''a''</sup> and <sup>5 b</sup>; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=23|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=21|verse=22}}, also with Zaqeph, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=6|verse=6}} (probably), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=44|verse=19|hidebook=1}}; on {{GHGheb|text=הָשַּׁמָּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=34}}, &c., see {{GHGpar|67|y}}. Cf. also {{GHGheb|text=־ָא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=36|verse=5}}.—Sometimes the Masora appears (but this is very doubtful) to regard the {{GHGheb|text=־ָהּ}} with feminines as a shortening of {{GHGheb|text=־ָתָהּ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=נִצָּהּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=10}} for {{GHGheb|text=נִצָּ֫תָהּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=פִּנָּהּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=7|verse=8}} for {{GHGheb|text=פִּנָּ֫תָהּ}}; also {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}} for {{GHGheb|text=־ָחָם}} in {{GHGheb|text=כִּתְבוּנָם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=13|verse=2}}, and {{GHGheb|text=עָרְמָם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=13}}. The examples, however, are for the most part uncertain, e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=4}} the reading is simply to be emended to {{GHGheb|text=בִּכּוּרָה}}, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=4|verse=2}} to {{GHGheb|text=גֻּלָּה}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=9}} to {{GHGheb|text=מִדָּה}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=5|verse=14}} to {{GHGheb|text=פֶּחָה}}. [See also, after prepositions, {{GHGpar|103|g}}.]

{{GHGmargin-letter|91|f}}
''Plur.'' 1st pers. {{GHGheb|text=־ָ֫ נוּ}}, in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=קִימָ֫נוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=20}} (where, however, {{GHGheb|text=קָמֵ֫נוּ}} is certainly to be read); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=2}} [{{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=10}}, cf. {{GHGpar|61|c}}, h], and so always {{GHGheb|text=כֻּלָּ֫נוּ|translate=all of us}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=11}}, &c [cf. {{GHGheb|text=בָּנוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָנוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִתָּנוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=עִמָּנוּ}}].

2nd pers. {{GHGterm|fem.}} {{GHGheb|text=כֶ֫נָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=48.49}}.

3rd pers. {{GHGterm|masc.}} {{GHGheb|text=־ָ֫ מוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=17|verse=10}} (on {{GHGheb|text=מוֹ}} in {{GHGheb|text=פִּ֫ימוֹ}} in the same verse, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=58|verse=7}} see .l); {{GHGheb|text=־ָ֑ הַם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=23|verse=6}}, according to Sievers probably to call attention to the reading {{GHGheb|text=כלהם}}. {{GHGterm|fem.}} {{GHGheb|text=־ָ֫ הְנָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=7|verse=37}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=53}} (in {{GHGterm|pause}}); {{GHGheb|text=־ֶ֫ נָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=21}}; {{GHGheb|text=־ֶ֫ נָּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=41}}; {{GHGheb|text=־ָ֫ נָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=19}}; elsewhere generally in {{GHGterm|pause}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=36|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=8|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=31|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=39|verse=2}}); finally {{GHGheb|text=הֵן}} as suffix to a noun, only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=17}}.

For examples of singulars with plural suffixes see l.

{{GHGmargin-letter|91|g}}
'''2.''' In the ''plural masc.'' and in the ''dual'' the suffixes are to be regarded primarily as affixed to the original ending of the {{GHGterm|construct state}} ({{GHGheb|text=־ַ֫ י}}, cf. {{GHGpar|89|d}}). This ending, however, has been preserved unchanged only in the ''2nd fem.'' In most cases it is contracted to {{GHGheb|text=־ֵי}}, as in the ''constr. st.'' without suffixes (so throughout the plur. and in the poetical suffix {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ֫ יהוּ}} of the ''3rd sing. masc.''); in the ''2nd masc.'' and ''3rd fem. sing.'' it is {{GHGheb|text=־ֶי}} (cf. k). On the ''1st pers.'' and ''3rd masc. sing.'' see i.—Thus there arise the following<section end=par91 /><noinclude>

{{GHGmargin-letter|91|i}} Thus the original {{GHGheb|text=־ַי}} is (''a'') contracted in the ''3rd sing. masc.'' {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ֫ יהוּ}} and throughout the ''plural'', as {{GHGheb|text=סוּסֵ֫יהוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=סוּסֵ֫ינוּ}}, &c.; (''b'') retained unchanged in the ''1st sing.'' {{GHGheb|text=סוּסַי}}, the real suffix-ending {{GHGheb|text=י}} (see b) being united with the final {{GHGterm|Yôdh}} of the ending {{GHGheb|text=־ַי}}; and in the ''2nd fem. sing.'' {{GHGheb|text=סוּסַ֫יִךְ}}, with a ''helping''-{{GHGterm|Ḥireq}} after the {{GHGterm|Yôdh}}. On the other hand (''c'') the {{GHGterm|Yôdh}} of {{GHGheb|text=־ַי}} is lost in pronunciation and the ''ă'' lengthened to ''ā'' in the ''3rd masc. sing.'' {{GHGheb|text=סוּסָיו}}, i.e. ''sûsāw'' (pronounced ''susā-u'').In the papyrus of the decalogue from the Fayyûm, line 16, {{GHGheb|text=ויקדשיו}} occurs for {{GHGheb|text=ויקדשהו}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=11}}. Gall, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1903, p. 349, takes this as an indication that the traditional forms of the noun-suffix {{GHGheb|text=יו}} or {{GHGheb|text=ו}} represent ''aiŭ'' or ''eŭ''. P. Haupt aptly compares the Greek use of the ''iota subscript'' (ᾷ). The ''2nd masc. sing.'' {{GHGheb|text=סוּםֶ֫יךָ}} and the ''3rd fem. sing.'' {{GHGheb|text=סוּסֶ֫יהָ}} were formerly also explained here as having really lost the {{GHGheb|text=י}}, and modified the ''a'' of ''sûsakā, sûsahā'' to {{GHGterm|Seghôl}}; but cf. the view now given in ''g'' and ''k''. {{GHGmargin-letter|91|k}} Rem. 1. As {{GHGheb|text=סוּסֵ֫ינוּ}} represents ''sûsai-nû'', so {{GHGheb|text=סוּסֶ֫יךָ}} and {{GHGheb|text=סוּסֶ֫יהָ}} represent ''sûsai-kā, sûsai-hā'', and the use of {{GHGterm|Seghôl}} instead of the more regular {{GHGterm|Ṣere}} is to be explained from the character of the following syllable,—so P. Haupt who points to {{GHGheb|text=יִקְטְלֶ֫הָ}} as compared with {{GHGheb|text=יִקְטְלֵ֫הוּ}}. In support of the view formerly adopted by us that the {{GHGheb|text=י}} is only orthographically retained, too much stress must not be laid on the fact that it is sometimes omitted,So in the Mêša‛ inscription, l. 22 {{GHGheb|text=מגדלתה|translate=its towers}} (along with {{GHGheb|text=שעריה|translate=its gates}}). Can it have been the rule to omit {{GHGheb|text=י}} after the termination ''ôth''? Cf. below, n. thereby causing confusion in an unpointed text with the singular noun. A number of the examples which follow may be due to an erroneous assumption that the noun is a plural, where in reality it is a singular, and others may be incorrect readings. Cf. {{GHGheb|text=דְרָכֶ֫ךָ|translate=thy ways}} (probably {{GHGheb|text=דַּרְכְּךָ}} is intended), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=1|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=37}}; for other examples, see {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=21|verse=11}} ff. ({{GHGheb|text=מִגְרָשֶׁ֫הָ}}; but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=6|verse=40}} ff. always {{GHGheb|text=־ֶ֫ יהָ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=58|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=41.43.98}} (probably, however, in all these cases the ''sing.'' is intended); {{GHGheb|text=אֱסָרֶ֫הָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=30|verse=8}} (cf. v. 5); {{GHGheb|text=מַכֹּתֶ֫הָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=19|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=17|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=מְבִיאֶ֫ה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=11|verse=6}}. For the orthographic omission of {{GHGheb|text=י}} before suffixes cf. {{GHGheb|text=רֵעִ֫הוּ}} for {{GHGheb|text=רֵעֵ֫יהוּ|translate=his friends}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=30|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=29|verse=18}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=42|verse=10}} (but it is possible to explain it here as a ''collective'' singular); {{GHGheb|text=עֲוֹנֵ֫נוּ|translate=our iniquities}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=64|verse=5.6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=14|verse=7}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=10|verse=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=לְוִיֵּ֫נוּ}} from {{GHGheb|text=לְוִיִּם}} which is always written defectively); {{GHGheb|text=נִסְכֵּכֶם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=29|verse=33}}; {{GHGheb|text=רָעֹֽתֵכֶם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=44|verse=9}}; {{GHGheb|text=יְדֵכֶם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=134|verse=2}}; {{GHGheb|text=לְמִֽינֵהֶם|translate=after their kinds}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=21}} (but see c), cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=4|hidebook=1}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=2|verse=8}}. The
