''with suff.'' | {{GHGheb|text=צִדְקוֹתַי}} | | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנוֹתַי}} | {{GHGheb|text=יֽוֹנְקוֹתַי}} | {{GHGheb|text=גֻּלְגְּלוֹתַי}} |- | ''Dual absolute'' | [{{GHGheb|text=נְחֻשְׁתַּ֫יִם}}] | | {{GHGheb|text=שְׂפָתַ֫יִם}} | | |- | | (''fetters of brass'') | | (''lips'') | | |- | Dual ''construct'' | | | {{GHGheb|text=שִׂפְתֵי}} | | |}
{{center|{{Small-caps|Remarks.}}}} {{GHGmargin-letter|95|d}} 1. Paradigm '''I''': feminines of segholate forms. (''a'') The locative of this class has the form {{GHGheb|text=גִּבְעָ֫תָה|translate=towards Gibeah}} (masc. {{GHGheb|text=גֶּ֫בַע}}). In some cases, especially with an initial guttural, there is no means of deciding whether the form in question is to be referred to a ''qăṭl'' or a ''qĭṭl'' base, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=חֶזְקָה|translate=strength}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=חֶרְפָּה}} under ''b''). A ''dual'' of this form occurs in {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעָתַ֫יִם|translate=seven times}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫בַע|translate=seven}}, fem.). Analogous to masculine forms like {{GHGheb|text=דְּבַשׁ}} ({{GHGpar|93|s}}) is {{GHGheb|text=הֲדַסָּה|translate=myrtle}}.—From masculines of the form {{GHGheb|text=פְּרִי}} ({{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}, cf. {{GHGpar|93|I}}, k) arise feminines sometimes like {{GHGheb|text=גַּֽאֲוָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=שַׁלְוָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַלְיָה}} (see above, {{GHGpar|94|b}}), sometimes like {{GHGheb|text=בְּכִית}} ({{GHGpar|94|f}}); occasionally the final {{GHGheb|text=ת}} is retained before the plural ending, as if it belonged to the stem (cf. {{GHGpar|87|k}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=חֲנִיתוֹת|translate=spears}}. Forms like {{GHGheb|text=גְּדִיָּה}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=אֳנִיָּה}}, a ''qŭṭl'' form) are derived directly from the masculine forms {{GHGheb|text=גְּדִי|translate=kid}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֳנִי}}, ''a fleet''.—(''b'') From a stem {{GHGheb|text=ע״ן}}, {{GHGheb|text=חִטָּה|translate=wheat}} (for {{GHGheb|text=חִנְטָה}}), ''plur.'' {{GHGheb|text=חִטִּים}}.—(''c'') From {{GHGheb|text=עָרְלָה|translate=foreskin}}, the ''plur. absol.'' is {{GHGheb|text=עֲרָלוֹת}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=פְּעָלִים}}, § 93, Paradigm '''I''', ''f''), {{GHGterm|constr.}} {{GHGheb|text=עָרְלוֹת}}.—(''d'') Example of a feminine segholate form from a stem {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}} (ground-form ''qŭṭl'', like {{GHGheb|text=חַיָּה}} of the form ''qăṭl,'', {{GHGheb|text=זִטָּה}} of the form ''qĭṭl''), with ''ŏ'' for ''ŭ'', {{GHGheb|text=חָגָּא|translate=terror}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=19|verse=17}} (Aramaic orthography for {{GHGheb|text=חָגָּה}}). {{GHGmargin-letter|95|e}} (''e'') To the list of segholate forms with {{GHGheb|text=ת}} fem. belong also the infinitives of verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״ו}} and {{GHGheb|text=פ״ן}}, which have rejected the weak consonant at the beginning, as {{GHGheb|text=שֶ֫בֶת}} (from {{GHGheb|text=יָשַׁב}}), {{GHGheb|text=דַּ֫עַת}} (from {{GHGheb|text=יָדַע}}), {{GHGheb|text=גֶּ֫שֶׁת}} (from {{GHGheb|text=נָגַשׁ}}), as well as {{GHGheb|text=קַ֫חַת}} (from {{GHGheb|text=לָקַח}}); cf. {{GHGpar|69|m}} and {{GHGpar|66|b}} and g. The infinitives of verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״ו}} are, however, also found in the form {{GHGheb|text=דֵּעָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֵדָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=צֵאָה}}, and of the same origin also are {{GHGheb|text=עֵדָה|translate=congregation}} (from {{GHGheb|text=יָעַד}}), {{GHGheb|text=עֵצָה|translate=counsel}} (from {{GHGheb|text=יָעַץ}}), {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁנָה|translate=sleep}} (from {{GHGheb|text=יָשֵׁן}}), {{GHGterm|constr.}} {{GHGheb|text=עֲדַת}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנַת}}, while in the {{GHGterm|constr.}} forms {{GHGheb|text=זֵעַת|translate=sweat}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=19}} (from {{GHGheb|text=יָזַע|translate=to flow}}), and {{GHGheb|text=צֵאַת|translate=excrement}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=4|verse=12}}, the Ṣere has remained firm. {{GHGmargin-letter|95|f}} From a stem {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹשׁ|translate=to be ashamed}}) is {{GHGheb|text=בּ֫שֶׁת|translate=shame}}, with ''suffix'' {{GHGheb|text=בָּשְׁתִּי}}.

303.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par95 />From a stem {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} ({{GHGheb|text=דָּלָה}}, cf., however, Barth, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1887, p. 607, who assumes a stem {{GHGheb|text=ידל}}) the masculine {{GHGheb|text=דַּל}} appears to have been formed after the rejection of the final {{GHGterm|Yôdh}}, and afterwards the feminine {{GHGheb|text=דֶּ֫לֶת|translate=door}}; but in the ''plural'' {{GHGheb|text=דְּלָתוֹת}}, {{GHGterm|constr.}} {{GHGheb|text=דַּלְתוֹת}}, the {{GHGheb|text=ת}} of the termination is retained (see above, d, {{GHGheb|text=חֲנִיתוֹת}}). In a similar way {{GHGheb|text=רְפָתִים|translate=stalls}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=3|verse=17}}, has arisen, if it is from the stem {{GHGheb|text=רפה}}, and {{GHGheb|text=שֹׁקֶת|translate=trough}} (from {{GHGheb|text=שָׁקָה}}), of which the masc. must have been {{GHGheb|text=שֹׁק}} = {{GHGheb|text=שֳׁקִי}}; on the other hand, the ''plur. constr.'' {{GHGheb|text=שִֽׁקֲתוֹת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=38}} (again retaining the feminine {{GHGheb|text=ת}} as an apparent radical) can only be an abnormal formation from the ''singular'' {{GHGheb|text=שֹׁ֫קֶת}}, not from a kindred form {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫קֶת}} or {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁ֫קֶת}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|g}}
2. Paradigm II: ground-form ''qăṭălăt'', &c., cf. {{GHGpar|94|c}}, Paradigm II, ''a'' and ''b''. Analogous to the masculine forms like {{GHGheb|text=קָטָן}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=קְטַנִּים}}, we find {{GHGheb|text=קְטַנָּה|translate=parva}}, &c.—The {{GHGterm|constr.}} forms, like {{GHGheb|text=צִדְקַת}} (''ṣidh<sup>e</sup>qăth''), are distinguished by the vocal {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} ({{GHGpar|10|d}}) from the segholate forms, like {{GHGheb|text=כִּבְשַּׂת}} (''kibh-săth''). Consequently the ''constr. st.'' {{GHGheb|text=בִּרְכַּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=4}}, &c. (from {{GHGheb|text=בְּרָכָה|translate=blessing}}), and {{GHGheb|text=חֶרְדַּת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=15}}, &c. (from {{GHGheb|text=חֲרָדָה|translate=a trembling}}), are abnormal.—Under the influence of a guttural (see Paradigm ''b'') the original ''ă'' is retained in the first syllable in the ''constr. st.'' (cf. also {{GHGheb|text=אֲדָמָה|translate=earth}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַדְמַת}}); in other cases it is modified to {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>ghôl}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עֲגָלָה|translate=wagon}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֶגְלָתוֹ}}. Frequently from an ''absol. st.'' in {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}} the {{GHGterm|constr.}} is formed with the termination {{GHGheb|text=ת}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עֲטָרָה|translate=crown}}, constr. {{GHGheb|text=עֲטֶ֫רֶת}} (from {{GHGheb|text=עֲטַרְתְּ}}); along with {{GHGheb|text=עֲצָרָה|translate=assembly}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֲצֶ֫רֶת}} is found usually, even in the ''absol. st.''; {{GHGheb|text=יְבֶ֫מֶת}} (from {{GHGheb|text=יָבָם|translate=levir}}) before suffixes is pointed as in {{GHGheb|text=יְבִמְתִּי}}, and thus entirely agrees with {{GHGheb|text=גְּבֶ֫רֶת}} (Paradigm I ''e''). From a stem {{GHGheb|text=(אָמַן) ל״ן}} is formed {{GHGheb|text=אֱמֶת|translate=truth}} (from ''ʾaɨmant'', and this no doubt for an original ''ʾămint'', {{GHGpar|69|c}}) before suffixes {{GHGheb|text=אֲמִתִּי}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|h}}
From the masc. form {{GHGheb|text=קָטֵל}} (''qăṭĭl'') are formed, according to rule, {{GHGheb|text=גְּדֵרָה|translate=wall}}, {{GHGheb|text=נְבֵלָה|translate=corpse}}, constr. {{GHGheb|text=נִבְלַת}}; {{GHGheb|text=בְּהֵמָה|translate=cattle}}, constr. {{GHGheb|text=בֶּֽהֱמַת}} (for {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽהֲמַת}}), with suffix {{GHGheb|text=בְּהֶמְתְּךָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=19|verse=19}}. More frequently, however, the ''ē'' of the second syllable is retained before the termination ''ath'' of the ''constr. st.''; thus from {{GHGheb|text=נְבֵלָה}} once {{GHGheb|text=נְבֵֽלָתִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=26|verse=19}}, and always {{GHGheb|text=בְּרֵכַת|translate=pool}}, {{GHGheb|text=גְּזֵלַת|translate=prey}}, {{GHGheb|text=טְמֵאַת|translate=unclean}}, {{GHGheb|text=מְלֵֽאֲתִי|translate=full}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=21}} (with ''Ḥireq compaginis'', see {{GHGpar|90|l}}), {{GHGheb|text=מְרֵֽרָתִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=13}}; {{GHGheb|text=שְׁאֵֽלָתִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=27}}, &c. (with elision of the {{GHGheb|text=א}}, {{GHGheb|text=שֵֽׁלָתֵךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=17}}), also {{GHGheb|text=שֶֽׁאֱלָתִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=8}}. Cf. the analogous forms of the ''constr. st.'' {{GHGheb|text=מַגֵּפַת|translate=plague}}, {{GHGheb|text=תַּרְדֵּמַת|translate=deep sleep}}, from {{GHGheb|text=מַגֵּפָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=תַּרְדֵּמָה}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|i}}
As dual we find {{GHGheb|text=יַרְכָתַ֫יִם|translate=sides}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=יַרְכָתוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=13}}, from the obsolete {{GHGheb|text=יְרֵכָה}}, feminine of {{GHGheb|text=יָרֵךְ}}); the ''constr. st.'' {{GHGheb|text=יַרְכְּתֵי}} is perhaps to be referred to a segholate form ({{GHGheb|text=יַרְכָּה}}, cf. {{GHGheb|text=יֶ֫רֶךְ}} as ''constr. st.'' of {{GHGheb|text=יָרֵךְ}}), unless the closed syllable be due to the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=בִּרְכַּת}} and {{GHGheb|text=חֶרְדַּת}} (see g).

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|k}}
In the forms with simple {{GHGheb|text=ת}} feminine the ground-form ''qăṭĭlt'' is developed ({{GHGpar|69|c}}) to ''q<sup>e</sup>ṭalt'', and this again regularly to {{GHGheb|text=קְטֶ֫לֶת}}. Thus the feminine of {{GHGheb|text=הָבֵר|translate=companion}} is {{GHGheb|text=חֲבֶ֫רֶת}} (with suffix {{GHGheb|text=חֲבֶרְתָּהּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=2|verse=14}}, cf. {{GHGheb|text=שְׁכֶנְתָּהּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=22}}), of {{GHGheb|text=גָּדֵר}} fem. {{GHGheb|text=גְּדֶ֫רֶת}} besides {{GHGheb|text=גְּדֵרָה}}.—Of {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} stems the segholate forms {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫חַת|translate=rest}} and {{GHGheb|text=שַׁ֫חַת|translate=pit}} (from {{GHGheb|text=נוּחַ}}, {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּחַ}}) belong to this class; Böttcher (''Gram.'' i. 411) rightly distinguished the latter from {{GHGheb|text=שַׁ֫חַת|translate=corruption}} (stem {{GHGheb|text=שָׁחַת}}); in the same way also {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫חַת|translate=rest}} is distinct from {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫חַת|translate=a lighting down}} (stem {{GHGheb|text=נָחַת}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|l}}
The feminines of the form ''qăṭĭl'' from stems {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}}, as {{GHGheb|text=מֵתָה|translate=mortua}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֵדָה}} fem.<section end=par95 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

304.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="ShakespeareFan00" /></noinclude><section begin="par95" />''witness'' (from {{GHGheb|text=מוּת}}, {{GHGheb|text=עוּד}}), have likewise an unchangeable vowel in the first syllable. Cf., on the other hand, the forms from {{GHGheb|text=פ״י}} stems mentioned above, under e, such as {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁנָה|translate=sleep}}, constr. st. {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנַת}} ; moreover, {{GHGheb|text=חֵמָה|translate=anger}}, constr. st. {{GHGheb|text=חֲמַת}} (but {{GHGheb|text=חֵ֫מֶת|translate=a leathern bottle}}, in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=חֶ֑מֶת}} [so Baer, Ginsb., but Kittel {{GHGheb|text=חֵ׳}}] {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=15}}, ''constr. st.'' {{GHGheb|text=חֵ֫מַת מַ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=14}}, perhaps from a stem {{GHGheb|text=חמת}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|m}}
The feminines of the form ''qăṭŭl'', like {{GHGheb|text=עֲמֻקָּה}} (masc. {{GHGheb|text=עָמֹק}}), maintain the original ''ŭ'' by sharpening the following consonant (cf. {{GHGpar|93|kk}}); on the other hand, by appending the fem. {{GHGheb|text=ת}}, segholate forms arise like {{GHGheb|text=נְח֫שֶׁת}}, before suff. {{GHGheb|text=נְחֻשְׁתָּם}}, &c. Dual {{GHGheb|text=נְהֻשְׁתַּ֫יִם}} (see Paradigm II ''a''); but cf. {{GHGheb|text=נְחָשְׁתִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|verse=7}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|n}}
A few (aramaising) feminines from {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} stems (Paradigm II, ''c'') are found with the ending ''ăth;'', due to the rejection of the final {{GHGterm|Wāw}} or {{GHGterm|Yôdh}} and contraction of the preceding ''ă'' with the ''ă'' of the termination ''ăth''; thus {{GHGheb|text=מְנָת|translate=portion}} (for ''mănăyăth'' or ''mănăwăth''), {{GHGheb|text=קְצָת}} end (also {{GHGheb|text=קָצֶה}} and {{GHGheb|text=קָצָה}}), plur. {{GHGheb|text=מְנָיוֹת}} (''constr. st.'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=12|verse=47}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=13|verse=10|hidebook=1}}) and {{GHGheb|text=מְנָאוֹת}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=12|verse=44}}); {{GHGheb|text=קְצָוֹת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=38|verse=5}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=37|verse=8|hidebook=1}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=39|verse=4|hidebook=1}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}; on {{GHGheb|text=נֵּֽאָיֹת|translate=valleys}}, see {{GHGpar|93|v}}.—{{GHGheb|text=אוֹת|translate=sign}} (stem {{GHGheb|text=אוה}}) is obscured from {{GHGheb|text=אָת}}, and this is contracted from ''ʾâyăth'' = ''ʾăwăyăth''; plur. {{GHGheb|text=אֹתוֹת}}, with the double feminine ending; cf. above, f, and {{GHGpar|87|k}}.—The retention of the ''ā'' in the first syllable in {{GHGheb|text=אָֽלָתִי}}, &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=41}}, &c., is abnormal.

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|o}}
3. Paradigm III, cf. the various forms in {{GHGpar|94|d}} and f–h. The ''dual'' {{GHGheb|text=הֽוֹמֹתַ֫יִם|translate=two walls}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=11}}, &c., taken directly from the plur. {{GHGheb|text=חוֹמוֹת}}, for {{GHGheb|text=חֽוֹמָתַ֫יִם}}, is abnormal (cf. {{GHGpar|87|s}}, and the proper name {{GHGheb|text=גְּדֵֽרֹתַיִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=36}}).—Among the forms resembling participles {{GHGterm|Qal}} of verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}}, such as {{GHGheb|text=זָרָה}} (masc. {{GHGheb|text=זָר}} from ''zâĭr'', hence with unchangeable ''â''), must be reckoned also {{GHGheb|text=בָּמָה|translate=high place}} (from {{GHGheb|text=בּוּם}}), which has for its ''constr. st. plur.'' the pleonastic form {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽמוֹתֵי}}, or written defectively {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽמֹתֵי}} (see {{GHGpar|87|s}}); for this the Masora everywhere requires {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽמֳתֵי}}, which is to be read ''bām<sup>o</sup>thê'' (not ''bŏm<sup>o</sup>thê''), with an anomalous shortening of the ''ô'' to {{GHGheb|text=־ֳ}}; but with suffixes {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽמוֹתַי}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|p}}
In a wider sense the feminines of the form {{GHGheb|text=קַטָּל}} ({{GHGpar|84|e|b}}) belong to this class, in so far as they shorten the ''â'' of the second syllable before the termination {{GHGheb|text=ת}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=דַּלֶּ֫קֶת|translate=inflammation}} (from ''dallăqt''), with suff. {{GHGheb|text=צַדֶּקְתֵּךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=52}}; {{GHGheb|text=טַבַּ֫עַת|translate=signet}}; also fem. of the forms {{GHGheb|text=קִטַּל}} and {{GHGheb|text=קִטֵּל}} ({{GHGpar|84|c|b}} and d), as {{GHGheb|text=אִוֶּ֫לֶת|translate=folly}} (for ''ʾiwwălt''), and of all the forms which have a changeable vowel in the second syllable, and are formed with the prefix {{GHGheb|text=מ‍}} ({{GHGpar|85|g}}–k), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מַמְלָכָה|translate=kingdom}}, {{GHGterm|constr.}} always {{GHGheb|text=מַמְלֶ֫כֶת}}; {{GHGheb|text=מַזְמֵרָה}} (not used in the sing.) ''pruning-hook'', plur. {{GHGheb|text=מַזְמֵרוֹת}}; {{GHGheb|text=מַשְׂכֹּ֫רֶת}}; ''reward'', with suff. {{GHGheb|text=מַשְׂכֻּרְתִּי}}; cf. also the examples given in {{GHGpar|85|g}} and p, like {{GHGheb|text=מוֹלֶ֫דֶת|translate=birth}} (but from {{GHGheb|text=ל״א}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֽוֹצָאָה|translate=outgoing}}), {{GHGheb|text=תּוֹלֶ֫דֶת|translate=generation}}, {{GHGheb|text=תּֽוֹעֵבָה|translate=abomination}}, constr. {{GHGheb|text=תּֽוֹעֲבַת}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|q}}
Sometimes the plural of these forms is to be traced to a secondary form, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אִגֶּ֫רֶת|translate=a letter}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=אִגְּרוֹת}} (as if from {{GHGheb|text=אִגְּרָה}}); also {{GHGheb|text=יֽוֹנְקוֹת}}, which is merely formed on the analogy of the other plur. fem. of participles {{GHGterm|Qal}}, is to be referred to a sing. {{GHGheb|text=יוֹנְקָה}}. Cf., moreover, {{GHGheb|text=מַֽחֲרֶ֫שֶׁת|translate=ploughshare}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=מַֽחֲרֵשׁוֹת}} (as if from {{GHGheb|text=מַֽהֲרֵשָׁה}})<ref>{{GHGheb|text=עַשְׁתֹּ֫רֶת|translate=Astarte}} (plur. {{GHGheb|text=עַשְׁתָּרוֹת}}), which was formerly included among these examples, is most probably due to an intentional alteration of the original {{GHGheb|text=עַשְׁתֶּ֫רֶת}}, like {{GHGheb|text=מֹ֫לֶךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=18|verse=21}}, &c. (for {{GHGheb|text=מֶ֫לֶךְ}}), with the vowels of {{GHGheb|text=בּ֫שֶׁת}} shame, the latter word being substituted in reading for the name of the goddess.</ref>; on the other hand, {{GHGheb|text=כֹּֽתָרוֹת|translate=capitals}} (of columns), and {{GHGheb|text=תּֽוֹכָחוֹת|translate=reproofs}}, are the regular plurals of {{GHGheb|text=כֹּתֶ֫רֶת}} and {{GHGheb|text=תּוֹכַ֫חַת}}.
<section end="par95" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

305.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par95 />{{GHGmargin-letter|95|r}}
In {{GHGheb|text=כֻּתּ֫נֶת|translate=coat}} the original ''ŭ'' of the first syllable is maintained by the sharpening of the following consonant (cf. Arab. {{GHGpron|qŭṭŭn}}), with suff. {{GHGheb|text=כֻּתָּנְתִּי}}, the {{GHGpron|constr. st.}}, however, is {{GHGheb|text=כְּתֹ֫נֶת}} (as also in the {{GHGpron|absol. st.}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=39}}); plur. {{GHGheb|text=כֻּתֳּנוֹת}}, {{GHGterm|constr.}} {{GHGheb|text=כָּתְנוֹת}}.—The form {{GHGheb|text=גֻּלְגֹּ֫לֶת}} given in Paradigm III, ''b'' is a {{GHGpron|Pŭlpŭl}}-form of the stem {{GHGheb|text=גָּלַל}}, cf. {{GHGheb|text=קָדְקֹד}}, {{GHGpar|84|p|b}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|s}}
4. To the fourth class, for which no Paradigm is required, belong all the numerous forms which in classical Hebrew have unchangeable vowels throughout, the originally short vowel of the first syllable having become {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, owing to the tone being thrown forward. Of the forms mentioned in {{GHGpar|84|doublesign=1}} and {{GHGpar|85|nosign=1}} those from {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}} stems especially belong to this class, as {{GHGheb|text=מְגִלָּה|translate=scroll}}, {{GHGheb|text=תְּהִלָּה|translate=praise}}, {{GHGheb|text=תְּפִלָּה|translate=prayer}} ({{GHGpar|85|i}} and {{GHGpar|85|q|nonumber=1}}), as well as the feminine of the participle {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} of verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מְאִירָה|translate=enlightening}} (from {{GHGheb|text=מֵאִיר}}), and generally the feminines of {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} stems which are compounded with the {{GHGterm|preformative}} {{GHGheb|text=מ‍}}, as {{GHGheb|text=מְנוּחָה|translate=rest}} (from {{GHGheb|text=מָנוֹחַ}}), see {{GHGpar|85|l}}; from {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} stems perhaps also {{GHGheb|text=תְּעָלָה|translate=conduit}} (''constr. st.'' {{GHGheb|text=תְּעָלַת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=3}}, &c.) and {{GHGheb|text=תְּלָאָה|translate=travail}}. Thus all these forms coincide externally with those which already, in the masculine form, have unchangeable vowels throughout (see the list of them in {{GHGpar|93|ww}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|t}}
5. The feminine ending {{GHGheb|text=־ִית}} (apart from {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}-forms like {{GHGheb|text=בְּכִית}}, {{GHGpar|94|f}}) arises from the addition of the feminine {{GHGheb|text=ת}} to the ending {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}}, which is employed to form adjectives, &c., see {{GHGpar|86|d}}, {{GHGpar|86|h|nonumber=1}}, and {{GHGpar|86|k|nonumber=1}}. The ending {{GHGheb|text=וּת}}, mentioned there, is attached, in segholate forms, sometimes to the ground-form, as {{GHGheb|text=עַשְׁתּוּת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=5}} (v.l. {{GHGheb|text=עַשְׁתּוֹת}}), sometimes to forms with a loosely-closed syllable, as {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכוּת|translate=kingdom}}; from {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} stems we find forms sometimes like {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבוּת|translate=captivity}} (according to others from the stem {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּב}}, like {{GHGheb|text=לְזוּת|translate=perverseness}} from {{GHGheb|text=לוּז}}), sometimes like {{GHGheb|text=בָּכוּת|translate=weeping}}, {{GHGheb|text=גָּלוּת|translate=exile}}, {{GHGheb|text=חָזוּת|translate=vision}}; the latter retain the ''ā'' of the first syllable even in the ''constr. st.'' and before ''suffixes''. From a ''qăṭĭl''-form is formed {{GHGheb|text=כְּבֵדוּת|translate=heaviness}}; from a ''qăṭîl''-form {{GHGheb|text=פְּקִדוּת}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|95|u}}
In the plural of these forms different methods of treatment may be distinguished. In some cases the whole ending {{GHGheb|text=וּת}} is retained, as if belonging to the stem (cf. above, f), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַלְמְנוּתַ֫יִךְ}} from {{GHGheb|text=אַלְמָנוּת}}, in others this ending is resolved, as in {{GHGheb|text=מַלְכֻיּוֹת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=8|verse=22}} (no doubt for ''măl<sup>e</sup>khuwwôth''), and {{GHGheb|text=עֵֽדְוֺת}} ''ʿēdh<sup>e</sup>wōth'', from {{GHGheb|text=עֵדוּת|translate=testimony}}, but only with suffixes, {{GHGheb|text=עֵֽדְוֺתֶ֫יךָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=14}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=עֵֽדְוֺתָיו}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=3}}, &c.<section end=par95 />

<section begin=par96 />{{GHGpar-heading|96|Nouns of Peculiar Formation}}

In the following Paradigms,<ref>The only omissions from these Paradigms are {{GHGheb|text=אֶחָד}}, {{GHGheb|text=חָם}}, and {{GHGheb|text=חָמוֹת}} (on which see the remarks), and all forms which are not found in the O.T.</ref> pp. {{GHGpage|282}} to {{GHGpage|284}}, a number of frequently used nouns are arranged, whose flexion presents more or less striking peculiarities. These peculiarities, however, are almost always subordinate to the usual phonetic laws, and the usual designation of the nouns as ''irregular'' is, therefore, not justified, when once the ground-forms are properly recognized on which the present forms are based.<section end=par96 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

{{center|{{Small-caps|Remarks.}}}} {{GHGheb|text=אָב|translate=father}}; the {{GHGterm|constr.}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲבִי}}, like {{GHGheb|text=אֲחִי}} and {{GHGheb|text=בְּנִי}} (which occurs once), belongs to the connective forms discussed in {{GHGpar|90|k}}, which serve as the model for the ''Ḥireq compaginis''. However, {{GHGheb|text=אַב}} also occurs in compound proper names, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַבְשָׁלוֹם}}, beside {{GHGheb|text=אֲבִֽישָׁלוֹם}}, &c.; also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=4 f.}} {{GHGheb|text=אַב־הֲמוֹן}} for the purpose of explaining the name {{GHGheb|text=אב[ר]הם}}. On the plur. {{GHGheb|text=אָבוֹת}} see {{GHGpar|87|p}}. {{GHGheb|text=אָח|translate=brother}}. The plur. {{GHGterm|absol.}} {{GHGheb|text=אַחִים}} has ''Dageš forte implicitum'' ({{GHGpar|22|c}}); {{GHGheb|text=אֶחָיו}} stands for {{GHGheb|text=אַחָיו}} according to the phonetic law stated in {{GHGpar|27|q}}, and so also {{GHGheb|text=אֶחָֽי}} in {{GHGterm|pause}} for {{GHGheb|text=אַחָֽי}}. The sharpening of the {{GHGheb|text=ח}} merely serves to keep the preceding {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} short, as in {{GHGheb|text=גְּמַלִּים}}, &c. ({{GHGpar|93|ee}}). {{GHGheb|text=אֶחָד|translate=one}} (for {{GHGheb|text=אַחָד}}, likewise with ''Dageš forte implicitum'', {{GHGpar|22|c}}, cf. {{GHGpar|27|q}}), {{GHGterm|constr.}} and otherwise in close connexion, {{GHGheb|text=אַחַד}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=48|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=17|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=27|verse=12}},

to occur. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=52}} {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲיוֹתֵךְ}} occurs (for {{GHGheb|text=אַחְיֹתַ֫יִךְ}}). In the forms {{GHGheb|text=אֲחוֹתַי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=13}} {{GHGterm|Keth.}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֲחוֹתַ֫יִךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=51.55.61}} (to be read also in verse 45 for {{GHGheb|text=אֲחוֹתֵךְ}}, which has been erroneously assimilated to the singular occurring in vv. 48, 49, 56), and {{GHGheb|text=אֲחֽוֹתֵיכֶם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=2|verse=3}} (for which, however, read {{GHGheb|text=אֲחֽוֹתְכֶם}}), the third radical has been entirely lost. {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ|translate=man}}, according to the common opinion either incorrectly lengthened for {{GHGheb|text=אֵשׁ}} (from ''ʾišš'', with assimilation of the ''Nûn'' of the ground-form ''ʾinš'', which again has been attenuated from ''ʾanš'' from the stem {{GHGheb|text=אָנַשׁ}}), or softened directly from ''ʾinš''. It is, however, probable that a separate stem ({{GHGheb|text=אישׁ|translate=to be strong}}?) is to be assumed for the singularSo already Gesenius in his {{GHGcite|title=Thes. Linguae Hebr.}}, i. 83 f., and recently again Friedr. Delitzsch, ''Prolegg.'', p. 160 ff., Praetorius in Kuhn’s ''Orient. L.-B.'', 1884, p. 196; König, ''Lehrgeb''., ii. 38; while Nöldeke ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1886, p. 739 f.), against Delitzsch, would connect both {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ}} and {{GHGheb|text=נָשִׁים}} with the stem {{GHGheb|text=אנשׁ}}.; consequently the stem {{GHGheb|text=אָנַשׁ|translate=to be sociable}},

309.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par96 />would be connected only with the plur. {{GHGheb|text=אֲנָשִׁים}} ({{GHGheb|text=אִישִׁים}} is found only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=53|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=141|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=8|verse=4}}).

{{GHGheb|text=אָמָה|translate=slave, handmaid}}; with the plur. {{GHGheb|text=אֲמָהוֹת}}, with consonantal {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, cf. in Aram. {{GHGheb|text=אֲבָהָן|translate=fathers}}, and similarly in Phoen. {{GHGheb|text=דלהת}} from {{GHGheb|text=דלת}}, also Arab. ''ʾabahât'' (fathers), ''ʾummahât'' (mothers), with an artificial expansion into a triliteral stem.

{{GHGheb|text=אִשָּׂה|translate=woman}}, probably for {{GHGheb|text=אִנְשָׁה}}; from {{GHGheb|text=אָנַשׁ}} i.e. not (as Aram. {{GHGheb|text=אִתְּתָא}} shows) {{GHGheb|text=אָנַשׁ|translate=to be sociable}} (see above, on {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ}}) but {{GHGheb|text=אָנַשׁ|translate=to be weak}} (Arab. ''ʾănŭṯă''). So De Lagarde, {{GHGcite|title=Uebersicht}}, p. 68; König, {{GHGcite|title=Lehrgeb.}}, ii. 159 f. The form {{GHGheb|text=אֵ֫שֶׁת}} (for ''ʾišt'', with {{GHGheb|text=ת}} fem., from ''ʾišš'', after rejection of the doubling and lengthening of the ''ĭ'' to ''ē'') occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=21|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=58|verse=9}}, even in ''absol. st.'' [cf., however, below, {{GHGpar|130}}. 4, 5].—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=128|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶשְׁתְּךָ}} is found for {{GHGheb|text=אִשְׁתְּךָ}}. Instead of the plur. {{GHGheb|text=נָשִׁים}}, we find in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=44}} {{GHGheb|text=אִשֹּׁת}}.<ref>Friedr. Delitzsch (in his Babylonian glosses to Baer’s text of Ezekiel, p. xi) on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=44}} remarks that in Assyro-Babylonian the plur. of ''aššatu'' (woman) is ''aššâti'', corresponding, therefore, to {{GHGheb|text=אִשּׁוֹת}}, not to the ordinary plur. {{GHGheb|text=נָשִׁים}}. The ''a'' of {{GHGheb|text=נָשִׁים}} (instead of ''i'' as in Arab. or ''e'' as in Syr.) is to be explained with Barth (''Orient. Studien zu Ehren Th. Nöldekes'', Giessen, 1906, p. 792) from the natural connexion of the ideas ''‘men’'' and ''‘women’'', {{GHGheb|text=נָשִׁים}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֲנָשִׁים}}.</ref>

{{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫יִת|translate=house}}, locative {{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫יְתָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַבַּ֫יְתָה}}, in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=בָּ֫יְתָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַבָּ֫יְתָה}}, {{GHGterm|constr.}} {{GHGheb|text=בֵּ֫יתָה}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽתִּים}} (but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=6|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=28|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=בָּתִּים}} without {{GHGterm|Metheg}}), pronounced ''bâttîm''. The explanation of the Dageš in the {{GHGheb|text=ת}} is still a matter of dispute. The Syriac ''bâttîn'', however, shows that the {{GHGterm|Dageš}} is original, and belongs to the character of the form.<ref>This disposes of the traditional view that the {{GHGterm|Dageš}} (after a firm Metheg, see {{GHGpar|16|f}} ζ) only serves to distinguish if from {{GHGheb|text=בָּתִים|translate=passing the night}}, ptcp. Qal of {{GHGheb|text=בּוּת}}, a stem which never occurs in the O.T. According to P. Haupt the stem is {{GHGheb|text=בא|translate=to go in}}, {{GHGheb|text=ת}} therefore being the feminine termination, as in ''bint daughter'', and the original form ''baʾtu, bātu'' (''entrance'') is preserved in the plural ''bāttim'' where the ''tt'' is to be explained as due to the analogy of trisyllabic stems. In the singular ''bāt'' passed into ''bēt'' (?), and this was resolved into ''bait'', as ''Y<sup>e</sup>rūšālēm'' into ''Y<sup>e</sup>rūšālayim''.</ref> According to Wright, {{GHGcite|title=Comparative Grammar}}, p. 88, {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽתִּים}} is simply contracted from ''bai-tîm'' (as {{GHGheb|text=אָן}} from {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִן}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֵינָם}} from {{GHGheb|text=עֵינָיִם}}, &c.), and the Dageš, therefore, is ''lene''; König, ''Lehrgeb''., ii. 56, proposes the name ''Dageš forte orthoconsonanticum''; on the other hand Rahlfs, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ThLZ.|Theologische Literaturzeitung, ed. by E. Schürer. Lpz. 1876 ff.}}}} 1896, col. 587, suggests that the {{GHGheb|text=י}} is assimilated to the {{GHGheb|text=ת}}, while Philippi, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xlix, p. 206, assumes for the plural a stem distinct from that of the singular. A definite solution is at present impossible. The incorrectness of the formerly common pronunciation ''bottîm'' is sufficiently shown by the Babylonian punctuation (see {{GHGpar|8|g}}, note 3), which leaves no doubt as to the ''â''.

{{GHGheb|text=בֵּן|translate=son}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=בֵּֽן־שִׁשִּׁי}}) {{GHGterm|constr.}} usually {{GHGheb|text=בֶּן־}} (also with a conjunctive accent as an equivalent for {{GHGterm|Maqqeph}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=2}}, &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=9|verse=21}}; even with smaller disjunctives, especially in the combination {{GHGheb|text=מִבֶּן}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=30|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=27|verse=3}}, &c. [{{GHGheb|text=מִבֶּן־}} only after {{GHGheb|text=וְאִם}} and before {{GHGheb|text=חֹ֫דֶשׁ}}, also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=51|verse=12}}; see Strack on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=30|verse=14}}]), rarely {{GHGheb|text=בִּן־}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=25|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=4|verse=10}} twice, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=30|verse=1}}, and so always in the combination {{GHGheb|text=בִּן־נוּן}}, and in the proper names {{GHGheb|text=בִּנְיָמִין}} [but {{GHGheb|text=בֶּן־יִמִינִי|translate=Benjamite}}] and {{GHGheb|text=בִּן־יָקֶה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=30|verse=1}}), once {{GHGheb|text=בְּנִי}} (cf. {{GHGpar|90|l}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=11}}, and {{GHGheb|text=בְּנוֹ}} ({{GHGpar|90|o}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=24|verse=3.15|hidebook=1}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=בֵּן}}, for which {{GHGheb|text=בֶּן־}} ought to be read, is intended by the Masora for the ''absol. st.'', not the {{GHGterm|constr.}}<section end=par96 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

310.text:
{{GHGheb|text=בַּת|translate=daughter}} (from ''bant'', and this again, according to the law stated in {{GHGpar|69|c}}, for ''bint'', fem. of {{GHGheb|text=בֵּן}}), with suff. {{GHGheb|text=בִּתִּי}} for {{GHGheb|text=בִּנְתִּי}}. Plur. {{GHGheb|text=בָּנוֹת}}, from the sing. {{GHGheb|text=בָּנָה}}, comp. {{GHGheb|text=בָּנִים|translate=sons}}. {{GHGheb|text=חָם}} ''husband’s father'', only with suff. {{GHGheb|text=חָמִיךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=חָמִ֫יהָ}}; and {{GHGheb|text=חָמוֹת}} ''husband’s mother'', only with suff. {{GHGheb|text=חֲמוֹתֵךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֲמוֹתָהּ}}. Cf. {{GHGheb|text=אָב}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָח}}, and especially {{GHGheb|text=אָחוֹת}}. {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם|translate=day}} (Arab. ''yaum''),Cf. Nöldeke, ''Beitröge'', p. 58, ''yaum'', probably an extension of a biliteral word which has survived in {{GHGheb|text=יָמִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=יְמֵי}}. Barth, however, ''Orient. Studien'', p. 791 (see above on {{GHGheb|text=אִשָּׂה}}), sees in {{GHGheb|text=יָמִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=יְמֵי}}, {{GHGheb|text=יְמוֹת}} new formations in Hebrew, caused by the naturally close connexion and association of these plurals with {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנוֹת|translate=years}}, to which they became assimilated in form. The view that {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם}} is merely an incorrect obscuring of {{GHGheb|text=יָם}}, and therefore distinct from the Arab. ''yaum'', is contradicted by the invariable spelling {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם}}, &c., notwithstanding the spelling {{GHGheb|text=ובים}} (={{GHGheb|text=וּבְיֹם}} ?) in the Siloam inscription, line 3 (cf. {{GHGpar|7|f}}), and {{GHGheb|text=מִיֹּמָ֑יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=6|verse=2}}. Cf. also the note on {{GHGpar|100|g}}. dual {{GHGheb|text=יוֹמַ֫יִם}}; the plur. {{GHGheb|text=יָמִים}} is probably from a different sing. ({{GHGheb|text=יָם|translate=yām}}), {{GHGterm|constr.}} {{GHGheb|text=יְמֵי}} and (poetically) {{GHGheb|text=יְמוֹת}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=90|verse=15}}. {{GHGheb|text=כְּלִי|translate=vessel}}, in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=כֶּ֫לִי}} (with suff. {{GHGheb|text=כֶּלְיְךָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=23|verse=25}}) from {{GHGheb|text=כָּלָה|translate=to contain}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=כֵּלִים}} (as if from {{GHGheb|text=כֵּל}}, {{GHGheb|text=כֵּ֫לֶה}}; according to König, ii. 63, shortened from ''kilyîm''). {{GHGheb|text=מַ֫יִם|translate=water}}; on the plur. cf. {{GHGpar|88|d}}. {{GHGheb|text=עִיר|translate=city}}. The plur. {{GHGheb|text=עָרִים}} is scarcely syncopated from {{GHGheb|text=עֲיָרִים}}, as it is pointed in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=10|verse=4}} (no doubt erroneously, in imitation of the preceding {{GHGheb|text=עֲיָרִים|translate=ass colts}}), but from a kindred sing. {{GHGheb|text=עָר}}, which still occurs in proper names. {{GHGheb|text=פֶּה|translate=mouth}}, {{GHGterm|constr, st.}} {{GHGheb|text=פִּי}} (for original {{GHGheb|text=פֵּי}} = {{GHGheb|text=פֵּה}}?). Its origin is still disputed. According to Gesenius and König (ii. 103), {{GHGheb|text=פֶּה}} stands for {{GHGheb|text=פֵּאֶה}} (ground-form ''piʿay'') from {{GHGheb|text=פָּאָה|translate=to breathe, to blow}}; according to Olshausen, for {{GHGheb|text=פַּי}}, from a stem {{GHGheb|text=פָּיָה}} or {{GHGheb|text=פָּוָה}}. But parallel with the Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=פֶּה}} are Assyr. ''pû'', Arab. ''fû, fam, famm, fumm'', bibl. Aram. {{GHGheb|text=פֻּם}}, {{GHGheb|text=פֻּמָּא}}, Syr. ''pûm, pûmā'', so that Barth, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xli, p. 634, assumes two forms of development from the same stem ({{GHGheb|text=פמו}}), viz. ''fm'' and ''fw''. {{GHGheb|text=פִּי|translate=my mouth}}, from ''pi-y''; for {{GHGheb|text=פִּיהֶם}} we find in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=17|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=58|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=59|verse=13|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=פִּ֫ימוֹ}}. The supposed plur. {{GHGheb|text=פִּים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=13|verse=21}} is generally explained as a contraction from {{GHGheb|text=פִּיִּים}}, but the text is altogether corrupt. The plur. {{GHGheb|text=פִּיּוֹת}}, for the ''edges'' of a sword, occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=5|verse=4}}; reduplicated {{GHGheb|text=פִּֽיפִיוֹת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=149|verse=6}}. {{GHGheb|text=רֹאשׁ|translate=head}} (obscured from {{GHGheb|text=רָאשׁ}}=''răʾš''); plur. {{GHGheb|text=רָאשִׁים}} (for {{GHGheb|text=רְאָשִׁים}}, {{GHGpar|23|c}}); {{GHGheb|text=רֹאשָׁיו}} only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=15|verse=2}}. {{GHGheb|text=שֶׂה|translate=a head of small cattle}} (''sheep'' or ''goat''), ''constr. st.'' {{GHGheb|text=שֵׂה}}, with suff. {{GHGheb|text=שְׂיֵ֫הוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=34}} and {{GHGheb|text=שֵׂיוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=22|verse=1}}, according to König, ii. 131, from a ground-form ''siʾay'', but according to De Lagarde, {{GHGcite|title=Uebersicht}}, 81 f., from a stem {{GHGheb|text=ושי}} ({{GHGheb|text=שֶׂה}}=''say''=''wĭsay''). {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁם|translate=name}}, {{GHGterm|constr.}} generally {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁם}} (only six times {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁם־}}); cf. {{GHGheb|text=בֵּן}}. {{GHGheb|text=שָׁמַ֫יִם|translate=heaven}} ({{GHGpar|88|d}}).
{{GHGpar-heading|97|Numerals. (a) Cardinal Numbers}}
Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Sem. Sprachwiss}}., p. 116 ff.; {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, i. 484 ff.
{{GHGmargin-letter|97|a}} '''1.''' The formation of the cardinal numbers from 3 to 10 (on 1 and 2 see below) has this peculiarity, that numerals connected with a {{hws|mascu|masculine}}

311.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par97 />{{hwe|line|masculine}} substantive take the feminine form, and those with a feminine substantive take the masculine form. The common explanation of this strange phenomenon used to be that the primary form of the numeral was an abstract noun in the feminine (cf. {{GHGpar|122|p}}). This was originally attached in the ''constr. st.'' to the word qualified, then came to be also used in apposition to it, and finally was placed after it like an adjective. The consequence of the appositional, and finally adjectival, construction was, that for numerals connected with feminine nouns a special shorter form came to be used, whilst the original forms, with the abstract feminine ending, were used in connexion with masculine nouns, after as well as before them.

On this view the historical process would have been that originally the abstract numerals (like Latin ''trias, decas'', Greek πεντάς, δεκάς, &c.) were placed in the ''constr. st.'' before masculines and feminines alike, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שְׁל֫שֶׁת בָּנִים|translate=trias filiorum}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֲשֶׂ֫רֶת נָשִׁים|translate=decas mulierum}}. A trace of this earlier usage was seen in the examples mentioned under ''c'', like {{GHGheb|text=שְׁל֫שֶׁת נָשִׁים}}.—Further, it was possible to say {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשָׁה בָנִים|translate=trias}}, sc. ''filii'', as well as {{GHGheb|text=בָּנִים שְׁלשָׁה|translate=filii, trias}}. From this second appositional construction it was only a step to the treatment of the abstract numeral as an adjective, ''filii tres''. Similarly the subsequently shortened forms of the abstract numeral, which were used in connexion with feminines, might stand either in the ''constr. st.'' before, or in apposition before or after the word numbered, thus {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשׁ בָּנוֹת|translate=trias filiarum}}, or {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלשׁ בָּנוֹת|translate=trias}}, sc. ''filiae'', or {{GHGheb|text=בָּנוֹת שָׁלשׁ|translate=filiae, trias}}, or adjectivally ''filiae tres''.

A different and much more intelligible explanation of the striking disagreement between the gender of the numeral and that of the word numbered has recently been given by Reckendorf, ''Die syntaktischen Verhältnisse des Arabischen'', pt. ii, Leiden, 1898, p. 265 ff. He also considers that the earliest forms were abstract numerals which were placed in the ''constr. st.'' before the noun numbered, the latter depending on them in the genitive. The original form, however, of the abstract numerals from 3 to 9 is not the feminine, but the masculine, used for both genders, as it still is in the tens, 20, 30, &c. The feminine abstract numeral was first distinguished by a special form in the numbers from 13 to 19 (see further, below) when connected with masculines, and this distinction was afterwards extended to the numbers from 3 to 10. This explanation does not affect the view stated above that the appositional and adjectival use of the abstract numerals was only adopted later in addition to their use in the genitive construction.

The differentiation of the numerals (originally of common gender) into masculine and feminine forms in the second decade, was occasioned, according to Reckendorf, by the use of the abstract feminine {{GHGheb|text=עֶשְׂרֵה}} in compounds.<section end=par97 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

312.text:
So long as it was felt that {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה}} simply meant ''the three of the decade'', the gender of the noun numbered made no difference. When, however, the consciousness of this meaning became weakened and the combination of units and tens came to be felt as a copulative rather than a genitive relation, it seemed suitable to connect only feminine nouns with the feminine form {{GHGheb|text=עֶשְׂרֵה}}. New forms were therefore invented, both of the units and the tens, for use with masculine nouns. The former, however, no longer had the form of the {{GHGterm|constr.}} but of the absolute state, clearly showing that the consciousness of the original syntactical relation in {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה}}, &c., was lost. On the other hand, after the extension of these new formations to the first decade, the new feminine forms readily came to be used also in the genitive construction (and therefore in the ''constr. st.'') on the analogy of the earlier masculine forms. Of the first two numerals, {{GHGheb|text=אֶחָד}}, ''one'', with its fem. {{GHGheb|text=אַחַת}} (see § 96), may be recognized, from its form and use, as an adjective, although even so it admits of such combinations as {{GHGheb|text=אַחַד הֶֽהָרִים|translate=unus e montibus}}. The numeral two, as would be expected, appears as an abstract in the ''dual'', but, like the other numerals, can also stand in apposition to the noun numbered. In form it always agrees with the gender of its noun. Accordingly, the numerals from 1 to 10 are as follows: {{GHGmargin-letter|97|b}}
{| cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" border="0" | | colspan="2" | ''With the Masculine''. | colspan="2" | ''With the Feminine''. |- | | {{GHGterm|Absol.}} | {{GHGterm|Constr.}} | {{GHGterm|Absol.}} | {{GHGterm|Constr.}} |- | 1. | {{GHGheb|text=אֶחָד}} | {{GHGheb|text=אַחַד}} | {{GHGheb|text=אַחַת}} | {{GHGheb|text=אַחַת}} |- | 2. | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנַ֫יִם}} | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי}} |Shortened from {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנָתַ֫יִם}}, which would be the regular feminine form of {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנַ֫יִם}}. Nevertheless, the {{GHGterm|Dageš}} in {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתַּ֫יִם}}, &c. (even after {{GHGheb|text=מִן}}; {{GHGheb|text=מִֽשְׁתֵּים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=4|verse=11}}; cf., however, {{GHGheb|text=מִשְּׁתֵי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=28}}), can by no means be regarded as a {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}} arising from assimilation of the ''Nûn'', for in that case the word could only be {{GHGheb|text=שִׁתַּ֫יִם}} (cf. Arab. ''ṯintāni''). This form does occur in the Codex Babylonicus of {{smaller|A.D.}} 916, but it is only a later correction for {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתַּ֫יִם}}, while in the Berlin MS. or. qu. 680 described by Kahle (Lpz. 1902) there is no trace of the Dageš. It is rather to be read ''štáyîm, štê'' (with {{GHGterm|Dageš lene}}), cf. {{GHGheb|text=אֶשְׁתַּ֫יִם}}, representing the later Palestinian pronunciation (Philippi, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xlix, p. 206), and Arab. ''ʾiṯnătāni'' (with a kind of prosthetic {{GHGheb|text=א}}; cf. {{GHGpar|19|m}}), as a further feminine form of ''ʾiṯnāni'', ''duo''. According to Barth (''Orient. Studien... Th. Nöldeke'', ii. 792 f.) the irregularity of {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתַּ֫יִם}} (he takes the Dageš as {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}) is due to the complete assimilation of its vowels to those of the masc. {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנַ֫יִם}} where the {{GHGterm|Šewâ mobile}} is normal.{{GHGheb|text=שְׁתַּ֫יִם}} | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּי}} |- | 3. | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשָׁה}} | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁל֫שֶׁת}} | {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלשׁ}} | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשׁ}} |- | 4. | {{GHGheb|text=אַרְבָּעָה}} | {{GHGheb|text=אַרְבַּ֫עַת}} | {{GHGheb|text=אַרְבַּע}} | {{GHGheb|text=אַרְבַּע}} |- | 5. |With Dageš probably on the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=שִׁשָּׁה}}, as {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁ֫שֶׁת}} on the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=חֲמֵ֫שֶׁת}}. Cf. also J. K. Blake on {{GHGheb|text=חֲמִשָּׁה}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֲמִשִּׁים}} in{{GHGcite|title= }}{{abbr|JAOS|Journal of the American Oriental Society}}. 1905, p. 117 ff.{{GHGheb|text=חֲמִשָּׁה}} | {{GHGheb|text=חֲמֵ֫שֶׁת}} | {{GHGheb|text=חָמֵשׁ}} | {{GHGheb|text=חֲמֵשׁ}} |- | 6 | {{GHGheb|text=שִׁשָּׁה}} | {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁ֫שֶׁת}} | {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁשׁ}} | {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁשׁ}} |- | 7. | {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעָה}} | {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעַת}} | {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫בַע}} |{{GHGheb|text=שְׁבַע}} and {{GHGheb|text=תְּשַּׁע}} appear only as connective forms before {{GHGheb|text=עֶשְׂרֵה}} and {{GHGheb|text=מֵאוֹת}}.{{GHGheb|text=[שְׁבַע]}} |- | 8. | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמֹנָה}} | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמֹנַת}} | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמֹנֶה}} | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמֹנֶה}} |- | 9. | {{GHGheb|text=תִּשְׁעָה}} | {{GHGheb|text=תִּשְׁעַת}} | {{GHGheb|text=תֵּ֫שַׁע}} | [3]{{GHGheb|text=[תְּשַׁע]}} |- | 10. | {{GHGheb|text=עֲשָׂרָה}} | {{GHGheb|text=עֲשֶׂ֫רֶת}} | {{GHGheb|text=עֶ֫שֶׂר}} | {{GHGheb|text=עֶ֫שֶׂר}} |}

313.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par97 />On the connective forms {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבַע}}, {{GHGheb|text=תְּשַׁע}}, cf. the analogous forms in {{GHGpar|93|h}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|97|c}}
The other Semitic languages also exhibit the same peculiarity in the external differentiation of the numerals from 3 to 10 as regards gender. The fem. form of the numeral abstracts is only rarely found in connexion with feminine nouns,<ref>In the vulgar dialects of Arabic, and in Ethiopic, the feminine form of the numeral is by far the more common. This form appears also in Hebrew, when the number is regarded in the abstract, as in the multiplicatives (see {{GHGpar|97|h}}).</ref> e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שְׁל֫שֶׁת נָשִׁים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=7|verse=2}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}; probably also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=17|verse=11}}, where we should read with Dillmann {{GHGheb|text=שׁ׳ הַגָּפּוֹת}}. In apposition, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=3|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=4|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=36|verse=23}}. From what was said above, under ''a'', it follows that these cases are not a return to original usage, but only an intrusion of the form used before masculines into the sphere of the feminine. Conversely in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=24}} {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשׁ חֳדָשִׁים}} (but in the Samaritan {{GHGheb|text=שְׁל֫שֶׁת}}).—For {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעָה|translate=seven}}, there occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=42|verse=13}} the strange form {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעָ֫נָה}}, according to Ewald [{{GHGcite|title=Ausführl, Lehrb.}}<sup>8</sup>, {{GHGpar|269|b}}] an old feminine substantive (German ''ein Siebend'', ''a set of seven''), but more probably a scribal error.

{{GHGmargin-letter|97|d}}
'''2.''' The numerals from 11 to 19 are formed by placing the units, without the ''copula'', before the number ten (in the form {{GHGheb|text=עָשָׂר}} masc., {{GHGheb|text=עֶשְׂרֵה}} fem.), but without the two words being joined into one. As was said above, under ''a'', and as is proved by the use of {{GHGheb|text=אַחַד}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַחַת}} in the numeral 11, the feminine numerals from 13 to 19 are to be regarded as ''construct'' forms in a genitive connexion. The connective forms of the masculine abstracts, like {{GHGheb|text=שְׁל֫שֶׁת}}, &c., are not admitted in combination with {{GHGheb|text=עָשָׂר}}, since they are merely in apposition, and not in a genitive relation (see the rare exceptions at the end of ''e''). On the other hand {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי}} and {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּי}} in the numeral 12 are undoubtedly true ''constructs'', like {{GHGheb|text=אַחַד}} and the fem. numerals 13–19. But instead of {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=3|verse=12}} and four other places) and {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּי}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=4|verse=8}} and three times in Ezek.), we generally find {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵים}} and {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּים}}. Two explanations have been given of these forms: (1) that the {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}} really intends {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנַ֫יִם}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתַּ֫יִם}}, in the ''absol. st.'', which was first introduced in the case of {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנַ֫יִם}}, on the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=עֲשָׂרָה}}, &c., and then extended to {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתַּ֫יִם}}; the Masora, however, required {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּי}} (but see below), and therefore pointed {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵים}}, {{GHGheb|text=שׁתֵּים}} as a ''Q<sup>e</sup>rê perpetuum'' (see § 17).—(2) that the ''absolute'' forms {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵ֫יִם}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתַּ֫יִם}} (introduced on the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשָׁה}}, &c.) were contracted to {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵים}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּים}} to facilitate the pronunciation of the duals when closely<section end=par97 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

314.text:
connected with {{GHGheb|text=עָשָׂר}} and {{GHGheb|text=עֶשְׂרֵה}}, and that the contraction is founded on an early and correct tradition. The second explanation is supported by the large number of examples of {{GHGheb|text=שנים}} (66) and {{GHGheb|text=שתים}} (34). It would be strange if the Masora required the alteration of the far commoner forms on account of isolated instances of {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי}} and {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּי}}. As a matter of fact even in regard to the latter forms the tradition often varies between {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי}} and {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנַ֫יִם}}, &c., cf. e.g. Ginsburg on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=3|verse=12}}. We cannot therefore assume a ''Qerê perpetuum''. {{GHGmargin-letter|97|e}} Accordingly the numbers from 11 upwards are—
{| cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" border="0" | | ''Masculine''. | ''Feminine''. |- | 11. | {{GHGheb|text=אַחַד עָשָׂר}} | {{GHGheb|text=אַחַת עֶשְׂרֵה}} |- | | {{GHGheb|text=עָשָׂר}}{{GHGheb|text=עַשְׁתֵּי}}, which remained for a long time unexplained, was recognized (first by J. Oppert) in the Assyro-Babylonian inscriptions in the form ''ištin'' or ''ištên''; cf. Friedr. Delitzsch, ''Assyrische Grammatik'', p. 203, and P. Haupt, in the ''American Journal of Philology'', viii. 279. Accordingly, {{GHGheb|text=עַשְׁתֵּי עָשָׂר}} is a compound, like the Sansk. ''êkâdaçan'', ἕνδεκα, ''undecim'' (analogous to the combination of units and tens in the numerals from 12 to 19), and is used at the same time in the composition of the feminine numeral eleven. On the gradual substitution of {{GHGheb|text=עַשְׁתֵּי ע׳}} for {{GHGheb|text=אַחַד ע׳}} and {{GHGheb|text=אַחַת ׳}} see Giesebrecht in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1881, p. 226; {{GHGheb|text=עַשְׁתֵּי ע׳}} occurs only in Jer., Ez., in the prologue to Deuteronomy (1:3), in the Priestly Code, and in passages undoubtedly post-exilic, so that it may very well be a loan-word from the Babylonian. {{GHGheb|text=עַשְׁתֵּי}} | {{GHGheb|text=עַשְׁתֵּי עֶשְׂרֵה}} |- | 12. | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר}} | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה}} |- | | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי עָשָׂר}} | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּי עֶשְׂרֵה}} |- | 13. | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשָׁה עָשָׂר}} | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה}} |}
&c., on the analogy of the last. These numerals regularly have only the above form. In regard to their syntax, cf. {{GHGpar|134|f}}. Very rarely the units appear in the {{GHGterm|masc.}} in the ''constr. st.'', as {{GHGheb|text=חֲמֵ֫שֶׁת עָשָׂר|translate=fifteen}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=8|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=18}}; {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמנַת עָשָׂר|translate=eighteen}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=20|verse=25}}.—Connected by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} we find {{GHGheb|text=עֲשָׂרָה וַָֽחֲמִשָּׁה}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=45|verse=12}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|97|f}} '''3.''' The tens from 30 to 90 are expressed by the plural forms of the units (so that the plural here always stands for ''ten times'' the unit), thus, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשִׁים}} 30, {{GHGheb|text=אַרְבָּעִים}} 40, {{GHGheb|text=חֲמִשִּׁים}} 50, {{GHGheb|text=שִׁשִּׁים}} 60, {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעִים}} 70, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמֹנִים}} 80, {{GHGheb|text=תִּשְׁעִים}} 90. But ''twenty'' is expressed by {{GHGheb|text=עֶשְׂרִים}}, plur. of {{GHGheb|text=עֶ֫שֶׂר|translate=ten}}.For {{GHGheb|text=עֶשְׂרִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=תִּשְׁעִים}} (from the ''segholates'' {{GHGheb|text=עֶ֫שֶׂר}}, {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫בַע}}, {{GHGheb|text=תֵּ֫שַׁע}}), we should expect ''ʿasārîm, šebhāʿîm, tešāʿîm''. Is this very unusual deviation from the common formation (see above, {{GHGpar|93|l}}, o, r) connected with the special meaning of these plurals, or are these survivals of an older form of the plural of segholates? These numerals are all of common gender, and do not admit of the {{GHGterm|construct state}}.—In compound numerals, like 22, 23, 44, &c., the units

315.text:
may precede (''two and twenty'', as in Arabic and English), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=3|verse=39}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=26|verse=14|hidebook=1}}. Very frequently, however, the reverse order is found (''twenty and two'', as in Syriac, cf. French and English ''twenty-two''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=12|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=18|verse=5|hidebook=1}}.According to the conclusions of König ({{GHGcite|title=De Criticae Sacrae Argumento}}, p. 61, and {{GHGcite|title=Lehrgeb.}}, ii. p. 215 ff.), the smaller number more commonly precedes in Ezek. and the Priestly Code, but the larger always elsewhere. S. Herner ({{GHGcite|title=Syntax der Zahlwörter im A.T.}}, Lund, 1893, p. 71 ff.) arrives at the same conclusion by a full examination of the statistics; cf. also his remarks on König in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1896, p. 123, and König’s reply, ''ibid.'', p. 328 f. In all cases the units and tens are connected by the ''copula'', ordinarily {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, but {{GHGheb|text=וָ}}, before numerals with the tone on the penultima, {{GHGheb|text=וַ}} before {{GHGheb|text=־ֲ}}, {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} before {{GHGterm|Šewâ}} see {{GHGpar|104|d}}, e, g. {{GHGmargin-letter|97|g}} The remaining numerals are the substantives—
{| cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" border="0" | 100 | {{GHGheb|text=מֵאָה}} fem., {{GHGterm|constr.}} {{GHGheb|text=מְאַת}}. |- | 200 | {{GHGheb|text=אָמתַ֫יִם}} dual (contracted from {{GHGheb|text=מְאָתַ֫יִם}}; cf. {{GHGpar|23|c}}). |- | 300 | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשׁ מֵאוֹת}} plur. (but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=11|verse=4.9.10.15}}, {{GHGterm|Keth.}} {{GHGheb|text=הַמְּאָיוֹת}}). |- | 1000 | {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫לֶף}} masc. |- | 2000 | {{GHGheb|text=אַלְפַּ֫יִם}} dual. |- | 3000 | {{GHGheb|text=שְׁל֫שֶׁת אֲלָפִים}} plur., and so on (except {{GHGheb|text=עֲשָׂרָה אֲלָפִים}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=24|verse=14}} {{GHGterm|Keth.}}; elsewhere always {{GHGheb|text=עֲשֶׂ֫רֶת אֲלָפִים}}). |- | 10000 | {{GHGheb|text=רְבָבָה}}, in the later books the aramaisingCf. Kautzsch, ''Die Aramaismen im A.T.'' (Halle, 1902), p. 79 f. forms {{GHGheb|text=רִבּוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=רִבּוֹא}}, {{GHGheb|text=רִבּוֹת}} (properly ''multitude'', cf. μυριάς). |- | 20000 | {{GHGheb|text=רִבֹּתַ֫יִם}} dual (see below, h); but {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּי רִבּוֹת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=7|verse=70}} (also {{GHGheb|text=רִבּוֹא שְׁתֵּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=7|verse=71}}). |- | 40000 | {{GHGheb|text=אַרְבַּע רִבּוֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=7|verse=66}}. |- | 60000 | {{GHGheb|text=שֵֽׁשׁ־רִבּאֹות}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=2|verse=69}} (Baer and Ginsburg {{GHGheb|text=רִבֹּאוֹת}}, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=11|verse=12}}). {{GHGheb|text=אַלְפֵי רְבָבָה|translate=thousands of myriads}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=60}}. |}
{{GHGmargin-letter|97|h}} Rem. 1. The dual form which occurs in some of the units has the meaning of our ending -''fold'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַרְבַּעְתַּ֫יִם|translate=fourfold}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=6}}; {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעָתַ֫יִם|translate=sevenfold}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=15.24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=12|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=79|verse=12|hidebook=1}} (cf. {{GHGpar|134|r}}). The dual {{GHGheb|text=רִבֹּתַ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=68|verse=18}} (explained by {{GHGheb|text=אַלְפֵי שִׁנְאָן|translate=thousands of duplication}}) is not meant to be taken in the sense of ''two myriads'' or ''twice the number of myriads'', but in a multiplicative sense.Cf. D. H. Müller, ‘Die numeralia multiplicativa in den Amarnatafeln u. im Hebr.,’ ''Semitica'', i, Wien, 1906, p. 13 ff.—Besides the plural which denotes the tens, there are also the plurals {{GHGheb|text=אֲחָדִים|translate=some}}, also ''iidem'', and {{GHGheb|text=עֲשָׂרוֹת|translate=decades}} (not ''decem'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=21.25}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|97|i}} 2. The ''suffixes'' to numerals are, as with other nouns, properly genitives, although they are translated in English as nominatives, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלָשְׁתְּכֶּם|translate=your triad}}, i.e. ''you three'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=12|verse=4}}; {{GHGheb|text=חֲמִשָּׁיו|translate=his fifty}} (i.e. the 50 belonging to him) {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=1|verse=9–13}}, and {{GHGheb|text=חֲמִשֶּׁ֫יךָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=1|verse=10.12}}.

316.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par98 />{{GHGpar-heading|98|Numerals. (b) Ordinal Numbers}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|98|a}}
The ordinal numbers from 2 to 10 are formed from the corresponding cardinals by adding the termination {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}} ({{GHGpar|86|h}}), before which another {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}} also is generally inserted between the second and third radicals. They are as follows: {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁנִי|translate=second}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלִישִׁי}}, {{GHGheb|text=רְבִיעִי}} (like {{GHGheb|text=רֶ֫בַע}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֹ֫בַע}}, {{GHGheb|text=רִבֵּעִים}}, without the prosthetic {{GHGheb|text=א}}, which appears in {{GHGheb|text=אַרְבַּע}}, &c.), {{GHGheb|text=חֲמִישִׁי}} or {{GHGheb|text=חֲמִשִׁי}} (which, according to Strack, is always to be read for {{GHGheb|text=חֲמִשִּׁי}}), {{GHGheb|text=שִׁשִּׁי}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבִיעִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמִינִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=תְּשִׁיעִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֲשִׂירִי}}. The ordinal {{GHGtranslate|first}} is expressed by {{GHGheb|text=רִאשׁוֹן}} (cf. {{GHGpar|27|w}}), from {{GHGheb|text=רֹאשׁ|translate=head, beginning}}, with the termination {{GHGheb|text=וֹן}} ({{GHGpar|86|f}}). On the use of {{GHGheb|text=אֶחָד}} as an ordinal in numbering the days of the month, cf. {{GHGpar|134|p}}; in such cases as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, the meaning of {{GHGtranslate|first}} is derived solely from the context.

{{GHGmargin-letter|98|b}}
The feminine forms have the termination {{GHGheb|text=־ִית}}, more rarely (and only in the case of 3 and 10) {{GHGheb|text=־ִיָּה}}. They are employed also to express fractions, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=חֲמִשִׁית|translate=fifth}} or {{GHGtranslate|fifth part}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֲשִׂירִית}} and {{GHGheb|text=עֲשִֽׂירִיָּה|translate=tenth part}}. Side by side with these, in the same sense, there are also forms like {{GHGheb|text=רֹ֫בֵע}} and {{GHGheb|text=רֶֹ֫בַע|translate=a quarter}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֹ֫מֶשׁ|translate=a fifth part}}, and with the afformative {{GHGheb|text=וֹן}}, {{GHGheb|text=עִשָּׂרוֹן}} (plur. {{GHGheb|text=עֶשְׂרוֹנִים}}) {{GHGtranslate|a tenth part}}; these are to be regarded as abstracts, and are denominatives from the cardinal numbers. Cf. finally {{GHGheb|text=שָׁבוּעַ}} {{polytonic|ἑβδομάς}}, {{GHGtranslate|a week}}; {{GHGheb|text=עָשׂוֹר|translate=a decade}} (of days), and also the {{GHGtranslate|tenth day}}.

On the expression of the other relations of number, for which the Hebrew has no special forms, see the Syntax, {{GHGpar|134|q}} and r.<section end=par98 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

317.text:
{{center|'''CHAPTER IV''' THE PARTICLES}} {{GHGpar-heading|99|General View}}
Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, i. 492 f.
{{GHGmargin-letter|99|a}} '''1.''' The particles, which in general express the secondary modifications of thought in speech, the closer relation of words to one another, and the mutual connexion of sentences, are for the most part either borrowed or derived from noun-forms, sometimes also from pronouns and verbs ({{GHGpar|30|s}}). ''Primitive'' particles (apart from a few demonstrative forms, see {{GHGpar|100|i}}) can only be so called in the sense defined in {{GHGpar|81|f}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|99|b}} '''2.''' So far as the origin of the particles can be discovered with certainty, they are either (1) ''borrowed'' from other parts of speech; i.e. certain forms of the noun, pronoun, or verb, with more or less loss of their original meaning, have come to be employed as particles; cf. in the Indo-Germanic languages, e.g. the Latin ''certo, falso, partim, verum, causa'', the German ''statt, anstatt, wegen, weg'', and the English ''instead, away''; or (2) ''derived'' from other parts of speech, either (''a'') by the ''addition'' of formative syllables, as {{GHGheb|text=יוֹמִם|translate=by day}}, from {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם}} (cf., however, {{GHGpar|100|g}}); or most commonly (''b'') by ''abbreviations'' effected in various ways, the extent of their mutilation being in proportion to the frequency of their use, so that in some cases (see below) the original stem has become wholly unrecognizable. Cf. in German ''gen'', from ''gegen, Gegend; seit'', from ''Seite; weil'' (originally a particle of time, like our ''while''), from ''Weile''. Still more violent abbreviations occur in Greek, Latin, and the Romance languages, e.g. ἀπό, ''ab'', ''a''; ἐξ, ''ex, e; ad'', Fr. ''à''; ''aut'', Fr. ''ou'', Ital. ''o''; ''super'', Ital. ''su''.Even short phrases are contracted into one word: Lat. ''forsitan'', from ''fors sit an'',{{polytonic|δηλονότι}},{{polytonic|δηλαδή}}, Fr. ''peut-être'', Eng. ''prithee'' from ''I pray thee''.—In Chinese most of the particles are verbs or nouns; e.g. ''iù'' (to give), also the sign of the dative; ''ı̀'' (to make use of), ''to, for''; ''n̈i'' (the interior), ''in''. {{GHGmargin-letter|99|c}} The greatest shortening occurs in those particles which have entirely lost the character of an independent word, by being reduced to a single consonant with its vowel (generally short) or {{GHGterm|Šewâ}}. According to the laws of syllable formation in Hebrew ({{GHGpar|26|m}}),

318.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par99 />such particles cannot stand by themselves, but are united, as prefixes, with the following word (§ 102), very much like the preformatives of the imperfect (§a–d).

{{GHGmargin-letter|99|d}}
The view that this shortening of whole words to single letters has actually taken place in the gradual course of linguistic development is rendered highly probable by the fact that similar abbreviations in later Hebrew and in Aramaic, i.e. as the development of the original Semitic speech progresses, become more and more striking and frequent. Thus the Biblical Aramaic {{GHGheb|text=דִּי}} becomes at a later period {{GHGheb|text=דְּ}}; in modern Arabic, e.g. ''hallaq'' (now) is from ''halwaqt''; ''lêš'' (why?) from ''li-ayyi-šaiĭn'', &c. Cf. also the analogous cases mentioned above from the Western languages. Nevertheless, the use of the simplest particles is found already in the earliest periods of the Hebrew language, or, at any rate, in the earliest documents which have come down to us.

{{GHGmargin-letter|99|e}}
'''3.''' Less frequently particles are formed by ''composition''; as {{GHGheb|text=מַדּוּעַ|translate=wherefore?}} for {{GHGheb|text=מַה־יָּדוּעַ|translate=quid edoctus}}? (τί μαθών; ) or ''quid cognitum?''; {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְעֲדֵי}} (from {{GHGheb|text=בַּל}} and {{GHGheb|text=עֲדֵי}}) ''besides''; {{GHGheb|text=מִלְמַ֫עְלָה}} (from {{GHGheb|text=מִן}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=מַ֫עְלָה}}) ''from above, above''.

More frequent is the combination of two words into one without contraction, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲרֵי־כֵן}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַף־כִּי}}, {{GHGheb|text=כִּי־אִם}}, {{GHGheb|text=כִּֽי־עַל־כֵּן}}; cf. also the compounds of {{GHGheb|text=אֵי}} with demonstrative pronouns, as {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽי־מִוֶּה|translate=from what?}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֵי לָזֹאת|translate=wherefore?}} [R.V. ''how'']. See the lexicon under {{GHGheb|text=אֵי}}.<section end=par99 />

<section begin=par100 />{{GHGpar-heading|100|Adverbs}}

On demonstrative adverbs cf. Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, i. 323; on interrogative adverbs, ''ibid.'', i. 328; on adverbs in general, i. 492 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|a}}
'''1.''' The negative {{GHGheb|text=לֹא|translate=not}}, and a few particles of place and time, as {{GHGheb|text=שָׁם|translate=there}}, are of obscure origin.

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|b}}
'''2.''' Forms of other parts of speech, which are used adverbially without further change, are—

(''a'') Substantives with prepositions, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בִּמְאֹד}} (with might) ''very''; {{GHGheb|text=לְבַד|translate=alone}} (prop. ''in separation'', Fr. ''à part''), with suffix {{GHGheb|text=לְבַדִּי|translate=I alone}}; {{GHGheb|text=מִבַּ֫יִת|translate=from within, within}}; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=כְּאֶחָד}} (as one) ''together'', {{GHGheb|text=לְעֻמַּת}} and {{GHGheb|text=מִלְּעֻמַּת}} (originally ''in connexion with'') ''near to, corresponding to, like'', &c., cf. {{GHGpar|161|b}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|c}}
(''b'') Substantives in the accusative (the adverbial case of the Semites, {{GHGpar|118|m}}), cf. τὴν ἀρχήν, δωρεάν, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מְאֹד}} (might) ''very'', {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫פֶס}} (cessation) ''no more'', {{GHGheb|text=הַיּוֹם}} (the day) ''to-day'' (cf. {{GHGpar|126|b}}), {{GHGheb|text=מָחָר}}<ref>Generally derived from the ''ptcp. Puʿal'' {{GHGheb|text=מְאָחָר}} ''m<sup>e</sup>ʾŏḥār'' (''=m<sup>e</sup>ʾoḥḥār'') and hence to be read ''mŏḥār'' (cf. {{GHGheb|text=מָֽחֳרָת|translate=morning}}); but according to P. Haupt (notes to Esther, p. 159) from {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם אַחַר}}.</ref> ''to-morrow'', {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫חַד}} (union) ''together''. Several of these continued to be used, though rarely, as substantives, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=סָבִיב}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=סְבִיבִים}} and {{GHGheb|text=סְבִיבוֹת}}, ''circuit'', as adverb<section end=par100 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

319.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par100 />''circum, around''; others have quite ceased to be so used, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כְּבָר}} (length) ''long ago'' [Aram.: only in Ec.]; {{GHGheb|text=עוֹד}} (repetition, duration) ''again'' or ''further''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|d}}
(''c'') Adjectives, especially in the feminine (corresponding to the Indo-Germanic neuter), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רִֽאשׁוֹנָה|translate=primum, formerly}} (more frequently {{GHGheb|text=בָּרִֽאשׁוֹנָה}}, also {{GHGheb|text=לָרִאשׁוֹנָה}}); {{GHGheb|text=רַבִּה}} and {{GHGheb|text=רַבַּת}} [both rare] ''multum, much, enough''; {{GHGheb|text=נִפְלָאוֹת|translate=wonderfully}} (properly ''mirabilibus'', sc. ''modis''), {{GHGheb|text=יְהוּדִית|translate=Jewish}}, i.e. in the Jewish language.

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|e}}
(''d'') Verbs in the infinitive absolute, especially in {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}}, which are likewise to be regarded as accusatives ({{GHGpar|113|h}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַרְבֵּה}} (prop. ''a multiplying'') ''much'' [frequent], {{GHGheb|text=לְהַרְבֵּה}} [rare and late] ''in multitude''; {{GHGheb|text=הַשְׁכֵּם}} (''mane faciendo'') ''early''; {{GHGheb|text=הַֽעֲרֵב}} (''vespere faciendo'') ''in the evening''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|f}}
(''e'') Pronouns and numerals, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}} (prop. ''there=at this place'') here, {{GHGheb|text=הֵ֫נָּה|translate=here, hither}} (also of time, {{GHGheb|text=עַד־הֵ֫נָּה|translate=till now}}, cf. the late and rare {{GHGheb|text=עֲדֶן}} and {{GHGheb|text=עֲדֶ֫נָּה}}={{GHGheb|text=עַד־הֵן}}); {{GHGheb|text=אַחַת}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתַּ֫יִם}}, {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫בַע}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֵאָה|translate=once, twice, seven times, a hundred times}}; {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁנִית|translate=for the second time}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|g}}
'''3.''' Some adverbs are formed by the addition of formative syllables (most frequently {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}}) to substantives or adjectives, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָמְנָם}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֻמְנָם|translate=truly}} (from {{GHGheb|text=אֹמֶן|translate=truth}}); {{GHGheb|text=חִנָּם}} (by favour) ''gratis'' (from {{GHGheb|text=חֵן|translate=gratia}}); {{GHGheb|text=רֵיקָם|translate=in vain}}, ''frusta'', but also ''empty'', (from {{GHGheb|text=רֵיק|translate=empty, emptiness, vanum}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=21}}, parallel with the {{GHGterm|fem.}} {{GHGheb|text=מְלֵאָה|translate=full}}; {{GHGheb|text=יוֹמָם|translate=by day}} (from {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם}})<ref>Is this {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}} an instance of the locative or temporal termination (cf. especially {{GHGheb|text=צהרם}}) mentioned in {{GHGpar|88|c}}? Nöldeke, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xl. p. 721, considers {{GHGheb|text=יוֹמָם}} a secondary substantival form (used adverbially like {{GHGheb|text=לַ֫יְלָה|translate=noctu}}), corresponding to the Phoenician and Aramaic {{GHGheb|text=ימם}}, Syr. ''ʾimāmā''; cf. on the other hand, König, ii. 255, who follows Olshausen in maintaining that the ''ām'' is an adverbial termination.</ref>; with ''ô'' in the last syllable, {{GHGheb|text=פִּתְאֹם}}, for {{GHGheb|text=פִּתְעֹם}}, ''in a twinkling, suddenly'' (from {{GHGheb|text=פֶּ֫תַע|translate=a twinkling}}, the ''ô'' being probably obscured from an original ''â'').<ref>{{GHGheb|text=דּוּמָם|translate=silent}} (an adjective in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|verse=26}}; a substantive in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=19}}), which was formerly included under this head, is better taken, with Barth (''Nominal-bildung'', p. 352, Rem. 2), as a participle formed like {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹבָב}}, {{GHGheb|text=עוֹלָל}}, so that {{GHGheb|text=דּוּמָם}} (perhaps assimilated to {{GHGheb|text=דּוּמָה}}) stands for original {{GHGheb|text=דּוֹמָם}}.</ref>—Moreover, cf. {{GHGheb|text=אֲחֹֽרַנִּית|translate=backward}}, and {{GHGheb|text=קְדֹֽרַנִּית|translate=darkly attired}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=3|verse=14}}. In both these cases, the formative syllable ''an'' has been first attached to the stem, and then the feminine ending ''îth'', which is elsewhere used to form adverbs, has been added to it.

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|h}}
The termination {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}} occurs also in the formation of substantives, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אוּלָם|translate=porch}}, and hence the above adverbs may equally well be regarded as nouns used adverbially, so that {{GHGheb|text=־ָם}}, {{GHGheb|text=־ׄם}}, would correspond to {{GHGheb|text=־ָן}}, {{GHGheb|text=וֹן}} (§ 85, Nos. 53, 54), cf. {{GHGheb|text=בְּפִתְאֹם}} (with prep.) ''suddenly'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=29|verse=36}}. According to others, this ''am'' is an obsolete accusative ending, to be compared with the indeterminate accusative sing. in ''ăn'' in Arabic.<section end=par100 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

320.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="77.125.106.121" /></noinclude><section begin="par100" />{{GHGmargin-letter|100|i}}
'''4.''' A number of forms standing in very close relation to the demonstrative pronoun may be regarded as primitive adverbs, since they arise directly from a combination of demonstrative sounds. Some of these have subsequently suffered great mutilation, the extent of which, however, can now very rarely be ascertained with certainty. Such are e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָו|translate=then}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֵ֫נָּה|translate=here}} (according to Barth, ''Sprachwiss. Abhandlungen'', p. 16, formed from the two demonstrative elements ''hin'' and ''na''), {{GHGheb|text=כֵּן}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּ֫כָה|translate=thus}} (cf. {{GHGheb|text=אֵיכָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽיכָכָה}}, ''how?''), {{GHGheb|text=אַךְ|translate=only}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָכֵן|translate=truly}} (on all these adverbs, see the Lexicon), and especially the interrogative {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} (''Hē interrogativum''), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹא}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=3|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹה}}) ''nonne?'', {{GHGheb|text=הֲגַם|translate=num etiam?}} This ''Hē interrogativum'' is perhaps shortened from {{GHGheb|text=הַל}}, which is still used in Arabic, and, according to the view of a certain school of Masoretes, occurs also in Hebrew in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=6}}.<ref>The separation of the {{GHGheb|text=ה}} at the beginning of {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=6}}, expressly noticed by Qimḥi (ed. Rittenb., p. 40 b) as an unique instance, is perhaps a protestagainst admitting a particle {{GHGheb|text=הַל}}.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|k}}
The {{GHGheb|text=ה}} interrogative takes—(1) ''Ḥaṭeph-Pathaḥ'' generally before non-gutturals (even before {{GHGheb|text=ר}}), with a firm vowel, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הֲשַׂ֫מְתָּ|translate=hast thou set}}? see the interrogative clause, {{GHGpar|150|c}} ({{GHGheb|text=הַיִּיטַב}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=10|verse=19}} is an exception).

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|l}}
(2) Before a consonant with {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, usually {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} without a following {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַֽבֲרָכָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=38}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=31|hidebook=1}}; less frequently (in about ten passages), {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} with a following {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַבְּדֶרֶךְ|translate=num in via}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=20|verse=30}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַלְּבֶן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=32|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=13|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=6}}; even in {{GHGheb|text=ר}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=32}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|m}}
(3) Before gutturals, not pointed with either {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} or {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph-Qameṣ}}, it takes {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַֽאֵלֵךְ|translate=shall I go}}?, {{GHGheb|text=הַֽאַתָּה|translate=num tu}}?, {{GHGheb|text=הַאִם|translate=num si}}; {{GHGheb|text=הַֽאֶרְצֶה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=1|verse=13}}; also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=31}} read {{GHGheb|text=הַֽאַתֶּם}} (not {{GHGheb|text=הָֽא׳}}), likewise {{GHGheb|text=הַ}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=12|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=8|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=6|verse=11}}.—In {{GHGheb|text=הָאִישׁ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=22}}, the Masora intends the article; read {{GHGheb|text=הַאִישׁ}}, and cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=20|verse=19}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=21}} read {{GHGheb|text=הַֽעֹלָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=הֲיֹרֶדֶת}}; the article is a correction due to doctrinal considerations.

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|n}}
(4) The {{GHGheb|text=ה}} takes {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>ghôl}} before gutturals pointed with {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} or (as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=9}} ff.) {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph-Qameṣ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽאָמוּר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=2|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=הֶאָֽנֹכִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=4}}; {{GHGheb|text=הֶהָֽיְתָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=2}}; {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽהָשֵׁב}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=5}} (cf. the analogous instances in {{GHGpar|22|c}}, {{GHGpar|35|k}}, {{GHGpar|63|k}}). The place of this interrogative particle is always at the beginning of the clause [but see {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=13|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=15}}, where one or more words are prefixed for emphasis].

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|o}}
'''5.''' Some adverbs occur also in connexion with suffixes, thus {{GHGheb|text=יֶשְׁךָ|translate=thou art there}}, 3rd sing. masc. {{GHGheb|text=יֶשְׁנוֹ}}<ref>This form, which occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=29|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=39}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=3|verse=8}}, is textually very doubtful, and cannot be supported by the equally doubtful {{GHGheb|text=קָבְנוֹ}} (for {{GHGheb|text=קֻבֶּ֫נּוּ}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=13}}. Most probably, with Stade, ''Gramm.'', {{GHGpar|370|b}}, and P. Haupt, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|SBOT.|Sacred Books of the Old Testament, ed. by P. Haupt. Lpz. and Baltimore, 1893 ff.}}}} Numbers, p. 57, line 37, we should read {{GHGheb|text=יֵשֶׁ֫נּוּ}}.</ref> (but see note below), 2nd plur. masc. {{GHGheb|text=יֶשְׁבֶם}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֵינֶ֫נִּי|translate=I am not}}, 2nd sing. {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽינְךָ}}, fem. {{GHGheb|text=אֵינֵךְ}}, 3rd sing. {{GHGheb|text=אֵינֶ֫נּוּ}}, fem. {{GHGheb|text=אֵינֶ֫נָּה}}, 2nd plur. {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽינְכֶם}}, 3rd plur. masc. {{GHGheb|text=אֵינָם}}.—Also {{GHGheb|text=עוֹדֶ֫נִּי|translate=I am yet}} ({{GHGheb|text=עוֹדִי}} only in {{GHGheb|text=בְּעוֹדִי}} and {{GHGheb|text=מֵֽעוֹדִי}}), {{GHGheb|text=עֽוֹדְךָ}}, {{GHGheb|text=עוֹדָךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=עוֹדֵ֫ינוּ}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|verse=17}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}; {{GHGheb|text=עוֹדֶ֫ינָה}}<section end="par100" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

321.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par100 />{{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}; the oriental school [see above, p. 38, note <sup>2</sup>] recognize only the reading {{GHGheb|text=עוֹדֵ֫ינוּ}}), {{GHGheb|text=עוֹדָם}}.—{{GHGheb|text=אַיֶּ֫כָּה|translate=where art thou?}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַיּוֹ|translate=where is he?}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַיָּם|translate=where are they?}} The same applies to {{GHGheb|text=הֵן}} ({{GHGheb|text=הֶן־}}) and {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה|translate=behold!}} (prop.
