''here, here is''; see {{GHGpar|105|b}}), only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=הִנֶּה־נָּא}}; with suffixes, {{GHGheb|text=הִנְנִי}}, once {{GHGheb|text=הִנֶּ֫נִּי}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=7}} with {{GHGterm|Munaḥ}}), in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּ֫נִי|translate=behold me}} (''here am I''), {{GHGheb|text=הִנְּךָ}} ({{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=הִנֶּ֫ךָּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=8}}), {{GHGheb|text=הִנָּךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִנּוֹ}} and {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּ֫הוּ}} [both very rare], {{GHGheb|text=הִנְנוּ}} (''behold us''), and {{GHGheb|text=הִנֶּ֫נוּ}} (in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּ֫נוּ}}), {{GHGheb|text=הִנְּכֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִנָּם}}; [see more fully in the Lexicon, p. 243].

{{GHGmargin-letter|100|p}}
The usual explanation of these suffixes (especially of the forms with ''Nûn energicum'') as verbal suffixes, which ascribes some power of verbal government even to forms originally substantival (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יֶשְׁנוֹ|translate=there is, he is}}), is at least inadmissible for forms (like {{GHGheb|text=אַיּוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּעוֹדִי}}) which are evidently connected with noun-suffixes; even for the other forms it is questionable. Brockelmann suggests that the {{GHGheb|text=ן}} in connexion with these particles is a survival from {{GHGheb|text=הנה}} corresponding to the Arab. ''ʾánna'' which introduces dependent clauses.<section end=par100 />

<section begin=par101 />{{GHGpar-heading|101|Prepositions}}

{{center|Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title=Grundriss}}, i. 494 ff.}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|101|a}}
'''1.''' All words, which by usage serve as prepositions, were originally substantives, viz.:

(''a'') Substantives in the accusative and in the construct state, so that the noun governed by them is to be considered as in the genitive, and in Arabic actually has the genitive ending, cf. in German ''statt dessen, kraft dessen'', in Greek τούτου χάριν, in Latin ''huius rei causa'', or ''gratia, montis instar''.<ref>In the examples which follow, the meaning of the noun is added in parentheses, and, when it is actually in use [though it is mostly in such cases very rare], is marked with an asterisk.—On a similar use in other languages, see W. von Humboldt, ''Über die Kawisprache'', iii, p. 621.</ref> Cf. {{GHGheb|text=אַחַ֫ר}} (hinder part*) ''behind, after'' ({{GHGterm|Milʿêl}} in {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫חַר כֵּן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=14|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=21|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫חַר זֶה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=32|verse=9}}); {{GHGheb|text=אֵ֫צֶל}} (side) ''close by''; {{GHGheb|text=בֵּין}} (intermediate space*) ''between''; {{GHGheb|text=בְּעַד}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫עַד}} (distance<ref>So also J. Hoch de Long, ''Die hebr. Präpos''. {{GHGheb|text=בְּעַד}}, Lpz. 1905.</ref>) ''behind, around''; {{GHGheb|text=זוּלַת}}, or with ''Ḥireq compaginis'' {{GHGheb|text=זֽוּלָתִי}} (removal, want) ''except''; {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן}} (purpose) ''on account of''; {{GHGheb|text=מוּל}} ({{GHGheb|text=מוֹל}} only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=1}}) ''before, over against''; {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} (separation; cf. {{GHGpar|119|v}}) ''from, out of''; {{GHGheb|text=נֶ֫גֶד}} (coming in front, that which is over against) ''before, over against''; {{GHGheb|text=עַד־}} (progress, duration*) ''during, until''; {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} (height, upper part*) ''upon, over''; {{GHGheb|text=עִם־}} (connexion?) ''with''; it is doubtful whether this is to be derived from the same stem as {{GHGheb|text=עֻמַּת}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְעֻמַּת|translate=near, beside, like}}; {{GHGheb|text=תַּ֫חַת}} (under part*) ''under, instead of''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|101|b}}
(''b'') Substantives in the construct state, but to be regarded as in the genitive, since they depend on prepositions (especially the inseparable), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לִפְנֵי}} (in the face of*) ''before''; {{GHGheb|text=כְּפִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְפִי}} (according to the mouth,<section end=par101 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

322.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par101 />i.e. the command of*) ''according to''; {{GHGheb|text=בִּגְלַל}} (in the concern of) ''on account of''; {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עַן}} (for the purpose of) ''on account of''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|101|c}}
'''2.''' Substantives used adverbially very frequently become prepositions in this way, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בְּלִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=בִּבְלִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִבְּלִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְתִּי}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּאֵין}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּאֶ֫פֶס}} (with cessation) ''without'', {{GHGheb|text=בְּעוֹד}} (in the duration of) ''during''; {{GHGheb|text=בְּדֵי}}, {{GHGheb|text=כְּדֵי}} (according to the requirement of) ''for, according to''.<section end=par101 />

<section begin=par102 />{{GHGpar-heading|102|Prefixed Prepositions}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|102|a}}
'''1.''' Of the words mentioned in § 101, {{GHGheb|text=מִן־|translate=from, out of}}, frequently occurs as a prefix ({{GHGpar|99|c}}), with its ''Nûn'' assimilated to the following consonant (by means of {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מִיַּ֫עַר|translate=out of a forest}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|102|b}}
Rem. The separate {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} (always with a following {{GHGterm|Maqqeph}}) is usual (but not necessary, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=20|verse=14}} with verse 15, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=43|verse=6}}, &c.) only before the article, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מִן־הָאָ֫רֶץ}}, and sometimes occurs before the softer consonants, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מִן־אָז}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=44|verse=18}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִן־בְּנֵי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=5|verse=18}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=1|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=14|verse=30|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=7|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=10|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=7}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=23|verse=36}} before {{GHGheb|text=ר}}; also before {{GHGheb|text=ק}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=49}}), and elsewhere in the later books (as in Aramaic)<ref>König, ''Einleitung ins A.T.'', p. 393 (cf. also the almost exhaustive statistics in his {{GHGcite|title=Lehrgebäude}}, ii. 292 ff.), enumerates eight instances of {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} before a word without the article in 2 Samuel and Kings, and forty-five in Chronicles.</ref>; there is besides a poetic by-form {{GHGheb|text=מִנִּי}} (cf. {{GHGpar|90|m}}) and {{GHGheb|text=מִנֵּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=11}}. Its form is most commonly {{GHGheb|text=מִ‍·|translate=with a following Dageš}}, which may, however, be omitted in letters which have {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} (cf. {{GHGpar|20|m}}). With a following {{GHGheb|text=י}} the {{GHGheb|text=מִ‍}} is, as a rule, contracted to {{GHGheb|text=מִי}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מִידֵי}}={{GHGheb|text=מִיְּדֵי}} or {{GHGheb|text=מִֽיְדֵי}} (but cf. {{GHGheb|text=מִיְּשֵׁנֵי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=12|verse=2}}; {{GHGheb|text=מִיְּרֻשָּֽׁתְךָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=20|verse=11}}); before gutturals it becomes {{GHGheb|text=מֵ‍}} (according to {{GHGpar|22|c}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מֵֽאָדָם}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֵעָם}}; before {{GHGheb|text=ח}} the {{GHGheb|text=מִ‍}} occurs with the guttural virtually sharpened in {{GHGheb|text=מִחוּץ|translate=on the outside}}, and in {{GHGheb|text=מִחוּט}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=23}}; before {{GHGheb|text=ה}} in {{GHGheb|text=מִֽהְיוֹת}} (cf. {{GHGpar|28|b}} and {{GHGpar|63|q}}. The closed syllable here is inconsistent with the required virtual sharpening of the {{GHGheb|text=ה}}; probably {{GHGheb|text=מִֽהְיוֹת}} is merely due to the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=לִֽהְיוֹת}}); similarly {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=3}} before {{GHGheb|text=ר}}; but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=מִרְּדֹף}} is to be read, according to {{GHGpar|22|s}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|102|c}}
'''2.''' There are also three other particles, the most commonly used prepositions and the particle of comparison, which have been reduced by abbreviation ({{GHGpar|99|c}}) to a single prefixed consonant with {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} (but see below, and {{GHGpar|103|e}}), viz.:

{{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} [poet. {{GHGheb|text=בְּמוֹ}}] ''in, at, with''.

{{GHGheb|text=לְ}} [poet. {{GHGheb|text=לְמוֹ}}] ''towards'', (belonging) ''to, for'', Lat. ''ad.''

{{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}} [poet. {{GHGheb|text=כְּמוֹ}}] ''like, as, according to'' (no doubt the remnant of a substantive with the meaning of ''matter, kind, instar'').

{{GHGmargin-letter|102|d}}
With regard to the pointing it is to be observed that—

(''a'') The {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ mobile}}, with which the above prefixes are usually pronounced, has resulted from the weakening of a short vowel (an original ''ă'', according to ''f'')<ref>Jerome (see Siegfried, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} iv. 79) almost always represents {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} by ''ba.''</ref>; the short vowel is regularly retained before {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}: before {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ simplex}}<section end=par102 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

323.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="100.7.116.115" /></noinclude><section begin="par102" />in the form of an ''ĭ'', attenuated from ''ă'': before a {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph}} the prefix takes the vowel of the {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לִפְרִי|translate=for fruit}}, {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽאֲרִי|translate=as a lion}}, {{GHGheb|text=בָּֽעֳנִי}} ''bŏʿ<sup>o</sup>nî'', ''in affliction'' (sometimes with the syllable subsequently closed, cf. {{GHGpar|28|b}}, and the infinitives with {{GHGheb|text=לַ}} {{GHGpar|63|i}}): before weak consonants it follows the rule given in {{GHGpar|24|c}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לִֽיהוּדָה}} for {{GHGheb|text=לִיְ׳}}. When the prefixes {{GHGheb|text=בְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כְ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, precede {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהִים|translate=God}}, the {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} and {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph S<sup>e</sup>ghôl}} regularly coalesce in {{GHGterm|Ṣērê}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בֵּֽאלֹהִים}}, &c., for {{GHGheb|text=בֶּֽאֱל׳}}; so with suffixes {{GHGheb|text=וֵאֽלֹהָיו}}, &c. (once also in the sing. {{GHGheb|text=לֵֽאלֹהוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=1|verse=11}}); also regularly {{GHGheb|text=לֵאמֹר|translate=to say}}, for {{GHGheb|text=לֶֽאֱמֹר}}, see {{GHGpar|23|d}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|102|e}}
(''b'') When the prefixes precede the article, the {{GHGheb|text=ה}} is almost always dropped, and they take its vowel. See further in {{GHGpar|35|n}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|102|f}}
(''c'') Immediately before the tone-syllable, i.e. before monosyllables and dissyllables with the tone on the penultima (in the fore-tone), they take {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} (undoubtedly a lengthening of an original ''ă'', cf. {{GHGpar|26|e}}, {{GHGpar|28|a}}), but only in the following cases:

(''aa'') {{GHGheb|text=לָ}} before infinitives of the above-mentioned forms, as {{GHGheb|text=לָתֵת|translate=to give}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָדִין|translate=to judge}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָבֹז|translate=to plunder}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָגֹז|translate=to shear}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָחֹג|translate=to keep a festival}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָלֶ֫דֶת|translate=to bring forth}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָלֶ֫כֶת|translate=to go}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָקַ֫חַת|translate=to take}}, except when the infinitive (as a {{GHGterm|nomen regens}}) is closely connected with another word (especially its subject, {{GHGpar|115|e}}), and consequently, as being in a sort of {{GHGterm|constr. state}}, loses the principal tone, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לְצֵאת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=19|verse=1}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְשֶׁ֫בֶת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=3}}, and so always {{GHGheb|text=לְבֹא חֲמָת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=13|verse=21}}, &c. (in such cases as {{GHGheb|text=לָֽתֶת־חֶ֫רֶב}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=5|verse=21}} the ''ā'' is protected by the secondary tone; before infinitives of verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}}, the {{GHGheb|text=לָ}} is retained even in close connexion; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=21|verse=20.25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=22|verse=3|hidebook=1}});

{{GHGmargin-letter|102|g}}
(''bb'') before many pronominal forms, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בָּזֶה}} (so also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=21|verse=10}}; not {{GHGheb|text=בַּזֶּה}}), {{GHGheb|text=לָזֶה}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּזֶה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָזֹאת}} (in close connexion, however, {{GHGheb|text=לְזֹאת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=23}}; {{GHGheb|text=כְּזֹאת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=45|verse=23}}); {{GHGheb|text=כָּאֵ֫לֶּה|translate=as these}}; an especially {{GHGheb|text=בָּכֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָכֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּכֶם}} ({{GHGheb|text=כָּכֵם}}) and {{GHGheb|text=בָּהֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָהֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּהֵם}} ({{GHGheb|text=כָּהֶם}}), see {{GHGpar|103|e}};

{{GHGmargin-letter|102|h}}
(''cc'') {{GHGheb|text=לָ}} before monosyllables or fore-toned nouns in such combinations as {{GHGheb|text=פֶּה לָפֶה|translate=mouth to month}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=10|verse=21}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֵּין מַ֫יִם לָמָ֫יִם|translate=between waters and waters}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=6}}; {{GHGheb|text=לָטֹ֫רַח|translate=for a trouble}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=14}}, but always before the principal pause. The instructive example in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=17|verse=8}} also shows that the punctuation {{GHGheb|text=לָ}} is only possible with at least the lesser pause after it; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=10.13}} the {{GHGheb|text=לָ}} is twice repeated, even before the small and smallest disjunctives;

{{GHGmargin-letter|102|i}}
(''dd'') in certain standing expressions, which have become stereotyped almost as adverbs, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לָעַד|translate=to eternity}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָרֹב|translate=in multitude}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָבֶ֫טַח|translate=in security}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָנֶ֫צַח|translate=to eternity}}, but {{GHGheb|text=לְנֵ֫צַח נְצָחִים|translate=to all eternity}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=34|verse=10}}. Cf. also {{GHGheb|text=לָנֶ֫פֶשׁ|translate=for the dead}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=19|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=5|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=9|verse=10|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|102|k}}
(''d'') With the interrogative {{GHGheb|text=מָה}} they are pointed as in {{GHGheb|text=בַּמֶּה}}; in {{GHGterm|pause}} and before {{GHGheb|text=א}} as in {{GHGheb|text=בַּמָּה|translate=by what?}} (before a following relative clause, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=22}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּמֶה}}; cf. Delitzsch, ''Jesaia'', 4th ed., on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=22}}); {{GHGheb|text=כַּמָּה|translate=how much}}? but also {{GHGheb|text=כַּמֶּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=16}}, in close connexion, and at a greater distance from the {{GHGterm|pause}}. The {{GHGterm|S<sup>e</sup>ghôl}} in these forms arises from a modification of the original ''ă'', while the {{GHGheb|text=מ‍}} is sharpened in order to maintain the original ''ǎ'' of the prefixes.

{{GHGmargin-letter|102|l}}
When {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} (prop. ''la'') is united to {{GHGheb|text=מָה}}, it takes, according to {{GHGpar|49|f}}, g, the form {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מָּה}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=20}} {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מָה}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מֶה}}, all {{GHGterm|Milʿêl}}, and hence the ''ă'' in the tone is lengthened to ''ā'') ''for what? why?'' Before the gutturals {{GHGheb|text=א}}, {{GHGheb|text=ה}}, {{GHGheb|text=ע}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָמָ֫ה}} is used for euphonic reasons (exceptions {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=15|verse=18}}, before {{GHGheb|text=ה}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=22}},<section end="par102" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

324.text:
{{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=49|verse=6}}, before {{GHGheb|text=א}}); {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מָּה}}, however, remains before {{GHGheb|text=ח}}. Before letters which are not gutturals, {{GHGheb|text=לָמָ֫ה}} is found in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=42|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=43|verse=2|hidebook=1}} (immediately after a tone-syllable). {{GHGmargin-letter|102|m}} Rem. The divine name {{GHGheb|text=יְהֹוָה}}, which has not its original vowels ({{GHGheb|text=יַהְוֶה}}) but those of {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנָי}} (see {{GHGpar|17|c}}), except that the {{GHGheb|text=י}} has simple not compound {{GHGterm|Šewâ}}, takes the prefixes also, after the manner of {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנָי}}, thus {{GHGheb|text=וַֽיהוָֹה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לַֽיהוָֹה}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽיהוָֹה}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֵֽיְהֹוָה}} (since they are to be read {{GHGheb|text=וַֽאדֹנָי}}, {{GHGheb|text=לַֽאדֹנָי}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽאדֹנָי}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֵֽאֲדֹנָי}}); for the {{GHGheb|text=א}} of {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנָי}}, as of {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנִים}}, &c. (see below), {{GHGterm|quiesces}} after the prefixes {{GHGheb|text=בַּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כַּ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=לַ}}, {{GHGheb|text=וַ}}, but is ''audible'' after {{GHGheb|text=מֵ‍}} (for {{GHGheb|text=מִן}}), {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ}} (no instance in the O.T.), and {{GHGheb|text=הָ}} (in {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאֲדֹנִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=10|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=136|verse=3}}, the article, not {{GHGheb|text=הַ}} interrog., is intended; the only example with {{GHGheb|text=ה}} intertog., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=8|verse=19}}, is to be pointed {{GHGheb|text=הַֽיהוָֹה}}, i.e. {{GHGheb|text=הַֽאדֹנָי}}, not {{GHGheb|text=הַיְהֹוָה}}). Hence the rule, {{GHGheb|text=משֶׁה מוֹצִיא|translate=Moses brought out}} (i.e. {{GHGheb|text=מ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}}, {{GHGheb|text=ה}} make the {{GHGheb|text=א}} audible), {{GHGheb|text=וְכָלֵב מַכְנִיס|translate=and Caleb brought in}}, (i.e. {{GHGheb|text=ו}}, {{GHGheb|text=כ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=ל}}, {{GHGheb|text=ב}} allow it to quiesce).Another ''vox memor.'' is {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־בּוֹ נֶֽעֶלָם|translate=all is hidden in him}}.—As regards the other plural forms of {{GHGheb|text=אָדוֹן}}, elision of the {{GHGheb|text=א}} always takes place after {{GHGheb|text=בַּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=וַ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כַּ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=לַ}}, except in the form {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנֵי}}, thus {{GHGheb|text=לַֽאדֹנָיו}}, {{GHGheb|text=לַֽאדֹנֶ֫יךָ}}, &c.; but {{GHGheb|text=לַֽאֲדֹנֵי}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=לַֽאֲדֹנֵ֫ינוּ}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=לַֽאֲדֹֽנֵיהֶם}}.
{{GHGpar-heading|103|Prepositions with Pronominal Suffixes and in the Plural Form}} {{GHGmargin-letter|103|a}} '''1.''' As all prepositions were originally nouns ({{GHGpar|101}}) in the accusative, they may be united with the noun-suffixes ({{GHGpar|91|b}}–l), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֶצְלִי}} (prop. at my side) ''by me'', {{GHGheb|text=אִתִּי}} (in my proximity) ''with me'', {{GHGheb|text=תַּחְתָּם}} (in their place) ''instead of them'', like the Latin ''mea causa'', ''for my sake''. {{GHGmargin-letter|103|b}} Rem. 1. The preposition {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} (usually {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}}) ''near, with'', is distinguished from {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} (see below, and {{GHGpar|117|a}}, note 4), the sign of the definite accusative ({{GHGpar|117|a}}), in its connexion with suffixes, by a difference of pointing, the former making {{GHGheb|text=אִתִּי}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִתְּךָ}}, in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=אִתָּךְ}}, 2nd fem. {{GHGheb|text=אִתָּךְ}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=54|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=אִתֵּךְ}}), {{GHGheb|text=אִתּוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִתָּהּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִתָּ֫נוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִתְּכֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִתָּם}} (also in the later books, especially in Kings, and always in Jer. and Ezek., incorrectly {{GHGheb|text=אוֹתִי|translate=with me}}; {{GHGheb|text=מֵֽאוֹתָךְ|translate=from thee}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=20|verse=25}}; {{GHGheb|text=מֵֽאֹתוֹ|translate=from him}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָם|translate=with them}}), while the latter retains its ''ô'' (obscured from ''â'') before the light suffixes, but before grave suffixes is pointed with {{GHGterm|Seghôl}}. This Seghôl is to be explained, with Praetorius, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} Iv. 369 f., as the modification of an ''ă'' which again was shortened from original ''â'' (in ''ʾâthî'', ''ʾaîthô'', &c.) in a closed syllable (''ʾăth-hem'', &c.). The same shortening and modification of the original ''â'' takes place before words in close connexion, hence {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־כֹּל}}, &c. When not in close connexion, the toneless {{GHGheb|text=אֶת}} becomes tone-long {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֵת הַשָּׁמַ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=1}}. Hence the following forms arise:—
{| cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" border="0" | | | Sing. | | Plur. | | |- | 1. | | {{GHGheb|text=אֹתִי|translate=me}}. | | {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָ֫נוּ|translate=us}}. | |- | | ''m.'' | {{GHGheb|text=אֹֽתְךָ}}, {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָךְ}} | | {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְכֶם|translate=you}}. |- | 2. | | |  {{GHGtranslate|thee}}     | | |- | | ''f.'' | {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָךְ}} . . . . . | | . . . . . . | |- | | ''m.'' | {{GHGheb|text=אֹתוֹ|translate=him}}. | | {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָם}}, rarely {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְהֶם}} | {{GHGtranslate|them}} |- | 3. | | | | | |- | | ''f.'' | {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָהּ|translate=her}}. | | {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְהֶן}}, rarely {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָן}} | |}

325.text:
Less common are the plene, forms {{GHGheb|text=אוֹתִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֽוֹתְךָ}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=33}} {{GHGheb|text=אֹֽתְכָה|translate=before}} {{GHGheb|text=ה}}), {{GHGheb|text=אוֹתָךְ}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=29|verse=35}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָ֫כָה}}), {{GHGheb|text=אוֹתוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אוֹתָהּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אוֹתָ֫נוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אוֹתָם}}. Moreover, for {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְכֶם}} we find {{GHGheb|text=אֽוֹתְכֶם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=23|verse=15}}; for {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָם}}, five times {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְהֶם}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=20}}, &c.), and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=45}} {{GHGheb|text=אֽוֹתְהֶם}}; for {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְהֶן}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=8}}, &c. [13 times]), {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָן}} (only found in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=54}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=35|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָ֫נָה}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=34|verse=21}} {{GHGheb|text=אוֹתָ֫נָח}}), and {{GHGheb|text=אֽוֹתְהֶן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=47}}.—No instance of the 2nd fem. plur. {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְכֶן}} occurs in the O.T.; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Cant|chapter=2|verse=7}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְכֶם}} is used instead. {{GHGmargin-letter|103|c}} 2. The preposition {{GHGheb|text=עִם־|translate=with}} (with suffixes on the model of stems {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}}, {{GHGheb|text=עִמִּי}}, {{GHGheb|text=עִמְּךָ}} [{{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=עִמְּכָה}}], in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=עִמָּךְ}}; 2nd fem. {{GHGheb|text=עִמּוֹ ;עִמָּךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=עִמָּהּ}}) is united with the suffixes {{GHGheb|text=נוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כֶם}}, and {{GHGheb|text=הֶם}} by a (pretonic) {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}}, which causes the sharpening of the ''Mêm'' to be distinctly audible: {{GHGheb|text=עִמָּ֫נוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=עִמָּכֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=עִמָּהֶם}} (so in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=29|verse=16}}, both in principal pause, and often in very late passages, otherwise {{GHGheb|text=עִמָּם}} is generally used). In the first person, besides {{GHGheb|text=עִמִּי}}, we also find {{GHGheb|text=עִמָּדִי}} (probably from original {{GHGheb|text=ענדי}}; cf. Arab. ''ʿinda'', beside, with). {{GHGmargin-letter|103|d}} 3. It is but seldom that prepositions occur with verbal suffixes, as {{GHGheb|text=תַּחְתֵּ֫נִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=22|verse=37.40.48}} (for which {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=37.40.48}} {{GHGheb|text=תַּחְתַּי}}), {{GHGheb|text=תַּחְתֶּ֫נָּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=21}} and {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽעֲדֵ֫נִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=11}} (here probably for the sake of the rhyme with {{GHGheb|text=יִשׁוּפֵּ֫נִי}}).''Fînî'' and ''bînî'' (in me), in vulgar Arabic for ''fiyya'' and ''bî'', are compared by Socin. Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZA.|Zeitschrift für Assyriologie und verwandte Gebiete, ed. by C. Bezold. Lpz. 18S6 ff.}}}} xiv. 347, note 1, suggests that {{GHGheb|text=תחתני}}, {{GHGheb|text=תחתנה}}, {{GHGheb|text=בעדני}} are later formations on the model of {{GHGheb|text=מִמֶּ֫נִּי}} when its origin from the reduplication of the preposition had become obscured, but see below, m. {{GHGmargin-letter|103|e}} '''2.''' When pronominal suffixes are added to the prefixes (§ 102), there appears occasionally, especially in the case of the shorter suffixes, an endeavour to lengthen the preposition, so as to give it more strength and body. Hence to {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} is appended the syllable {{GHGheb|text=מוֹ}} (see below, k), and {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} take at least a full vowel, {{GHGheb|text=בָּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=לָ}} ({{GHGpar|102|d}}, f).—The following deviations from the analogy of the noun with suffixes are to be noticed (''a'') in the pausal forms {{GHGheb|text=בָּךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֹתְךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִתָּךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=עִמָּךְ}} (not ''bèkhā'', &c.); (''b'') in the similar forms with the suffix of the 2nd sing. fem. (not ''bēkh'', &c.) and in {{GHGheb|text=בָּ֫נוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫נוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=עִמָּ֫נוּ}}, &c. (not ''bēnû'', &c.). {{GHGmargin-letter|103|f}} (''a'') ''{{GHGheb|text=לְ}} with Pronominal Suffixes''.

''to thee''. | {{GHGheb|text=לְךָ}} ({{GHGheb|text=לְכָה}}), in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=לָךְ}} | ''to you''. | {{GHGheb|text=לָכֶם}} |- | f. | {{GHGheb|text=לָךְ}}......... | | [{{GHGheb|text=לָכֶן}}{{GHGheb|text=לָכֶן}} does not occur in the O.T., by a mere accident, no doubt; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=לָכֶ֫נָה}}.] {{GHGheb|text=לָכֶ֫נָה}} |- | 3. m. ''to him''. | {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ}} | ''to them'' | {{GHGheb|text=לָהֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָהֵ֫מָּה}} poet. {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מוֹ}} |- | | | | [53 times]The question whether {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מוֹ}} can also stand for the sing. {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ}}, which Rödiger and recently W. Diehl (''Das Pronomen pers. suff.... des Hebr.'', p. 20 f.) and P. Haupt ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|SBOT.|Sacred Books of the Old Testament, ed. by P. Haupt. Lpz. and Baltimore, 1893 ff.}}}} on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=23|verse=20}}, a contraction of ''la-humû'') have altogether denied, must be answered in the affirmative unless we conclude with Diehl and Haupt that ''all'' the instances concerned are due to corruptions of the text. It is true that in such places as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=26.27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=10}} (all ''in'' or immediately before the principal pause; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=2}} with {{GHGterm|Zaqeph qaṭon}} at least) {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מוֹ}} can be better explained as plural (in reference to collective nouns); and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=53|verse=8}} for {{GHGheb|text=נֶ֫גַע לָ֫מוֹ}} we should read with the LXX {{GHGheb|text=נִגַּע לַמָּ֫וֶת}}. On the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=44|verse=15}} its explanation as plural would be extremely forced. Even then there would remain—presuming the traditional text to be correct—{{GHGheb|text=פָּנֵ֫ימוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=11|verse=7}} and {{GHGheb|text=כַּפֵּ֫ימוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=27|verse=23}}, as well as {{GHGheb|text=עָלֵ֫ימוֹ}}, three times, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=27|verse=23|hidebook=1}} (beside {{GHGheb|text=עָלָיו}}), and especially {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=2}}. In all these places the most extreme exegetical artifices can only be avoided by simply admitting a singular suffix (={{GHGheb|text=פָּנָיו}}, {{GHGheb|text=כַּפָּיו}}, {{GHGheb|text=עָלָיו}}).—On the question of the antiquity of the suffixes in {{GHGheb|text=מוֹ}} see {{GHGpar|91|l}}. |- | f. ''to her''. | {{GHGheb|text=לָהּ}} | | {{GHGheb|text=לָהֶן}},The form {{GHGheb|text=לָהֵן}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=13}} is Aramaic (=''therefore'').{{GHGheb|text=לָהֵ֫נָּה}} |}

{{GHGmargin-letter|103|g}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}, takes suffixes in the same manner: {{GHGheb|text=בִּי}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּךָ}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=7|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=22|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=141|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּכָה}}, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=37}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=לְכָה}} [for 2nd fem. {{GHGheb|text=לָךְ}} the {{GHGterm|Kethîbh}} {{GHGheb|text=לכי}} occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=2|verse=13}}, cf. {{GHGpar|91|e}}]), {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹ}}, &c.; except that for the 3rd plur., besides {{GHGheb|text=בָּהֶם}} (especially in the later books) and {{GHGheb|text=בָּהֵ֫מָּה}} (only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=30|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=36|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=1|verse=16}}; {{GHGheb|text=לָהֵ֫מָּה}} only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=14|verse=16}}), the form {{GHGheb|text=בָּם}} is also used; and for the feminine, besides {{GHGheb|text=בָּהֵ֫נָּה}} (three times), {{GHGheb|text=בָּהֵן}} is found fifteen times, and {{GHGheb|text=בָּהֶן}} only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=31|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=38|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=42|verse=14}}.—According to the Masora, {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} is found fifteen times for {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ}} (as conversely in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=2|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ}} for {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=100|verse=3}} (and, as has been conjectured, also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=4}}); cf. Delitzsch on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=100|verse=3}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=32|verse=42}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=5|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=2|verse=14}}, the Masora requires {{GHGheb|text=לָהֿ}} instead of {{GHGheb|text=לָהּ}} (in all three places before a following tone-syllable; cf. {{GHGpar|23|k}}, and the analogous cases of the loss of {{GHGterm|Mappîq}} in {{GHGpar|58|g}}, {{GHGpar|91|e}}). {{GHGmargin-letter|103|h}} (''b'') ''{{GHGheb|text=כְּ}} with Pronominal Suffixes''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|103|k}} The syllable {{GHGheb|text=מוֹ}} (in Arabic ''mâ'' {{GHGheb|text=מָא}}=Heb. {{GHGheb|text=מָה|translate=what}}) in {{GHGheb|text=כָּמ֫וֹנִי}} (probably from {{GHGheb|text=כְּמָה אֲנִי}}, prop. ''according to what I'', for ''as I'') is, in poetry, appended to the three simple prefixes {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, even without suffixes, so that {{GHGheb|text=בְּמוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כְּמוֹ}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְמוֹ}} appear as independent words, equivalent in meaning to {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}. Poetry is here distinguished from prose by the use of longer forms; in the case of {{GHGheb|text=מִן}}, on the other hand, it prefers the shorter, which resemble the Syriac and Arabic. {{GHGmargin-letter|103|l}} The form {{GHGheb|text=כָּהֶם}}, enclosed in brackets above, occurs only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=17|verse=15}} (in {{GHGterm|pause}}), {{GHGheb|text=כָּהֵ֫מָּה}} only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=36|verse=32}} (in {{GHGterm|pause}}); {{GHGheb|text=כָּהֵן}} (Baer following Qimḥi {{GHGheb|text=כָּהֶן}}) only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=18|verse=14}}. Cf. Frensdorff, ''Massora Magna'', p. 234 ff.—For {{GHGheb|text=בָּכֶם|translate=as ye}}, Qimḥi requires {{GHGheb|text=בָּכֵם}} (invariably or only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=4}}?); in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=1|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=8|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=4|verse=2}} Baer gives {{GHGheb|text=בָּכֶם}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|103|m}} With regard to {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} with suffixes, {{GHGheb|text=מִמֶּ֫נִּי|translate=from me}} is usually explained as arising, by a reduplication of {{GHGheb|text=מִן}}, from an original {{GHGheb|text=מנמני}}, just as {{GHGheb|text=מִמֶּ֫נּוּ|translate=from him}}, from {{GHGheb|text=מנמנ-הו}}, identical in form with {{GHGheb|text=מִמֶּ֫נּוּ}}The Babylonian Masora writes {{GHGheb|text=מִמֵּ֫נוּ}} (to distinguish it from the 3rd sing.), which is justly blamed by Ibn Ezra. ''from us'', from {{GHGheb|text=מנמנ-נו}}, while {{GHGheb|text=מִמֶּ֫נָּה|translate=from her}}, goes back to {{GHGheb|text=מנמנה}}. Far simpler, however, is Mayer Lambert’s explanation ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|REJ.|Revue des Études Juives. Paris, 1880 ff.}}}} xxiii. 302 ff.), that {{GHGheb|text=מִמֶּ֫נִּי}}, &c., have arisen from {{GHGheb|text=מִנֶּנִּי}}, &c., and that the forms of the suffixes are to be explained on the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=אֵינֶ֫נִּי}}, {{GHGheb|text=עוֹדֶ֫נּוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=תַּחְתֶּ֫נָּה}}, {{GHGpar|100|o}}.—The bracketed form {{GHGheb|text=מִנֵּ֫הוּ}}, for which Baer, following Qimḥi and others, writes {{GHGheb|text=מִנֶּ֫הוּ}}, occurs only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=68|verse=24}}, and is there regarded by Delitzsch, Hupfeld, and others (following Simonis) as a substantive ({{GHGheb|text=מֵן}}=''portion''). The expression {{GHGheb|text=מִן־הוּא}} (for {{GHGheb|text=מִמֶּ֫נּוּ}}?) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=18|verse=2.7}} is very strange.—{{GHGheb|text=מֵהֵ֫מָּה}} occurs only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=12|verse=12}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=20}} {{GHGheb|text=מִנְּהֶ֑ם}}); {{GHGheb|text=מֵהֶן}} (so Baer and Ginsburg, following the best authorities, instead of the ordinary reading {{GHGheb|text=מֵהֵן}}) only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=47.52}}.

328.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par103 />{{GHGmargin-letter|103|n}}
'''3.''' Several prepositions, especially those which express relations of space and time, are (like the German ''wegen'') properly plural nouns (for the reason, see {{GHGpar|124|a}}), and are, therefore, joined with the pronominal suffixes in the form of the plural {{GHGterm|construct state}}, just like other plural nouns ({{GHGpar|91|g}}). On the other hand, the apparent connexion of {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַד־}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} with plural suffixes is explained from the ground-forms of those prepositions (from stems {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}) {{GHGheb|text=(אֲלַי) אֱלַי}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֲדַי}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֲלַי}}(contracted to {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֵי}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֲלֵי}}, &c.).<ref>The reference of these forms to original plurals has been again expressly supported by De Lagarde, {{GHGcite|title=Symmicta}}, ii. 101 ff.; {{GHGcite|title=Nachrichten der G. g. G.}}, 1881, p. 376, cf. {{GHGcite|title=Mittheilungen}}, 1884, p. 63; also {{GHGcite|title=GGA}}. 1884, p. 280 f. According to Barth, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xlii. p. 348 ff., and {{GHGcite|title=Nominalbildung}}, p. 375 ff., {{GHGheb|text=תַּחְתֶּ֫יךָ}}, &c., was only formed on the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=עָלֶ֫יךָ}}, &c., and {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲרֶ֫יךָ}} &c., only on the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=לִפְנֵי}}, &c., since the real plural forms ought to be {{GHGheb|text=תְּחָתֶ֫יךָ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֲחָרֶ֫יךָ}}, &c.; cf., however, König, {{GHGcite|title=Lehrgebäude}}, ii. 305 f.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|103|o}}
Without suffixes these prepositions are—

{{GHGheb|text=אַחַר}}, more frequently {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲרֵי}} (prop. ''hinder parts'') ''behind, after''.

{{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}},<ref>On the use of this particle see {{GHGpar|119|g}}.</ref> poet. [4 times in Job] also {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֵי}} (''region, direction''), ''towards, to, according to''.

{{GHGheb|text=בֵּין}} (''interval'') ''between''; the suffixes indicating the singular are added to the singular {{GHGheb|text=בֵּין}}, thus {{GHGheb|text=בֵּינִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֵּינְךָ}}, &c. ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=בֵּינֶ֫יךָ}}, the second {{GHGterm|Yôdh}} is, however, marked with a point as critically doubtful; {{GHGheb|text=בֵּינָיו}}, which occurs three times, is only the Masoretic {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} for {{GHGheb|text=בֵּינוֹ}}, which is found e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=36}}). On the other hand, the suffixes indicating a plural are attached to the plural forms {{GHGheb|text=בֵּינֵי}} or {{GHGheb|text=בֵּינוֹת}}.

{{GHGheb|text=סָבִיב}} (''circuit'') ''around'', as a preposition, always has the plural form, sometimes masc. {{GHGheb|text=סְבִיבֶ֫יךָ}}, &c. [10 times], but much more frequently in the few. {{GHGheb|text=סְבִיבוֹת}} (''surroundings''). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=43|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=סָבִיב אוֹתָהּ}} is a corruption of {{GHGheb|text=סְבִיבֹתֶ֫יהָ}}; [in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=6|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=סָבִיב אֶת}} also is so contrary to usage, that it must be due to some textual error].

{{GHGheb|text=עַד־}} (''continuation, duration'', from {{GHGheb|text=עָדָה}}) ''as far as, unto'', poet. {{GHGheb|text=עֲדֵי}} [12 times]. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=32|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=עָֽדֵיכֶם}}, with the ''ā'' retained in the secondary tone, is abnormal. Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=18}} for {{GHGheb|text=עַד־הֵם}} read {{GHGheb|text=עָֽדֵיהֶם}}.

{{GHGheb|text=עַל־|translate=upon, over}} (cf. the rare subst. {{GHGheb|text=עָל|translate=height}} [see Lexicon], from {{GHGheb|text=עָלָה|translate=to ascend}}), poet. {{GHGheb|text=עֲלֵי}} [40 times, and 2 {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}].

{{GHGheb|text=תַּ֫חַת|translate=under}} (prop. ''what is beneath''). On {{GHGheb|text=תַּחְתֵּ֫נִי}}, &c.; cf. above, d.<section end=par103 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

[2{{GHGheb|text=עָלֵ֫ימוֹ}}] |- | 3 | ''Pl. f.'' | {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲרֵיהֶן}} | | | {{GHGheb|text=תַּחְתֵּיהֶן}} | {{GHGheb|text=אֲלֵיהֶן}} & {{GHGheb|text=אֲלֵחֶן}} | | {{GHGheb|text=עֲלֵיהֶן}} |}
{{GHGpar-heading|104|Conjunctions}} {{GHGmargin-letter|104|a}} '''1.''' The conjunctions serve to connect sentences, and to express their relations one to another. They may be either— (''a'') Original pronouns, e.g. the demonstrative {{GHGheb|text=כִּי|translate=that, because, for}}. (''b'') Original substantives, which afterwards were reduced to the rank of pronouns, adverbs, or conjunctions; so perhaps {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} (see § 36), which is sometimes used to express the general idea of relation, sometimes as a relative pronoun (properly a demonstrative), but in many cases stands simply for {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}}; also {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} (''nothing''), ''that not''; {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־|translate=that not}} (the Greek μή of ''prohibition''), &c. To these may be added the adverbial combination of substantives with prepositions, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בְּטֶ֫רֶם}}

330.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="ShakespeareFan00" /></noinclude><section begin=par104 />(''in the not yet'') ''earlier, before'', for which {{GHGheb|text=מִטֶ֫רֶם}} is also used. On the combination of two particles to express complex ideas (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַף־כִּי}} ''added to this, that=much more''), see the Syntax, {{GHGpar|163|f}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|104|b}}
(''c'') Prepositions, which with the addition of the conjunction {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} or {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} together form one single conjunction, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן אֲשֶׁר|translate=because}}, prop. ''on account of the fact that''; {{GHGheb|text=אַחַר אֲשֶׁר}}, and more frequently {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲרֵי אֲשֶׁר}}, ''after that''; {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽאֲשֶד|translate=according as}} (with {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}}); {{GHGheb|text=עֵ֫קֶב כִּי}} and {{GHGheb|text=עֵ֫קֶב אֲשֶׁר|translate=in consequence of the fact that, for the reason that, because}}. Sometimes, however, the conjunction in such cases is omitted, and the preposition itself used as a conjunction, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} (for {{GHGheb|text=עַל־אֲשֶׁר}}) ''although'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=17}}.

So, at any rate, according to our linguistic principles. It would, however, be more correct to say, that instead of the intermediary {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} the whole of the succeeding sentence is regarded as ''one'' substantival idea, under the immediate government of the preposition. In the same way, all prepositions governing the gerund in English may be paraphrased by conjunctions with the finite verb, see §§ 114 and 115, ''passim''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|104|c}}
'''2.''' Besides those already mentioned, there are certain other small words now used as conjunctions, of which the derivation or original meaning is altogether obscure, thus {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ|translate=or}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִם־|translate=if}} (also ''or'' before the second member of a double question), {{GHGheb|text=אַף|translate=also}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְ|translate=and}}, and others.

{{GHGmargin-letter|104|d}}
Rem. The pointing of the {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} (originally {{GHGheb|text=וַ}}, as still before {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph Pathaḥ}} and—with a following {{GHGterm|Dageš forte}}—in {{GHGterm|wāw consecutive}} of the imperfect; cf. {{GHGpar|49|f}}) is in many respects analogous to that of the prefixes {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} ({{GHGpar|102|d}}–i), but as being a weak consonant, the {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}} has some further peculiarities:

(''a'') Usually it takes simple {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְ}}).

(''b'') Before words which begin with a guttural having a {{GHGterm|compound Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, it takes the vowel with which the {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} is compounded (according to {{GHGpar|28|b}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וַֽחֲכַם|translate=and be thou wise}}, {{GHGheb|text=וַֽעֲבָדִים|translate=and servants}}, {{GHGheb|text=וַֽעֱזוּז|translate=and strength}}, {{GHGheb|text=וֶֽאֱכֹל|translate=and eat thou}}, {{GHGheb|text=וָֽחֳלִי|translate=and sickness}}. On {{GHGheb|text=וֵאֽלֹהִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=וֵאֽלֹהַי}} &c., see {{GHGpar|102|d}}; on {{GHGheb|text=וַֽאדֹנַי}}, &c., see {{GHGpar|102|m}}; on such cases as {{GHGheb|text=וַעְצֹר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=2}}, cf. {{GHGpar|28|b}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|104|e}}
(''c'') Before words with simple {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} under the first consonant (except in the cases under ''f''), the {{GHGterm|Wāw}} becomes the vowel ''û'' (cf. {{GHGpar|26|a}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וּלְכֹל|translate=and to all}}, so also (except in the case under ''g'') before the cognate labials {{GHGheb|text=ב}}, {{GHGheb|text=מ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=פ}}, hence {{GHGheb|text=וּמֶ֫לֶךְ}}. On the cases in which {{GHGterm|simple Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} has become a {{GHGterm|Ḥaṭeph}} after {{GHGheb|text=וּ|translate=copulative}} (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וּֽזֲהַב}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=12}}), cf. {{GHGpar|10|g}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|104|f}}
(''d'') With a following {{GHGheb|text=יְ}} the {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} coalesces to form {{GHGheb|text=וִי}} according to {{GHGpar|24|b}}, as {{GHGheb|text=וִיהִי|translate=and let him be}}. On the peculiar punctuation of the {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}} before forms with initial {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} from {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה|translate=to be}} and {{GHGheb|text=חָיָה|translate=to live}} (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וִֽהְיִיתֶם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=8|verse=4}}, {{GHGheb|text=וֶֽחְיֵה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=7}}), cf. {{GHGpar|63|q}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|104|g}}
(''e'') Immediately before the tone-syllable it frequently takes {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}}, like {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} (see {{GHGpar|102|f}}), but in most cases only at the end of a sentence or clause (but cf. also {{GHGheb|text=וָכֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=30}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וָמֵ֖ת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=12}} (on the other hand, in verse 20<section end=par104 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

331.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Ubufox" /></noinclude><section begin=par104 />{{GHGheb|text=וּמֵ֖תִ}} is in closer logical connexion with what follows); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=וָמַ֣הְנוּ שָׁ֔ם}}, {{GHGheb|text=וָמַ֑תָנוּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=וָמָֽתְנוּ}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=וָסַֹכְתְּ}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=10|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=וָ֝רָֹע}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=וָאַ֔יִן}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=וָלֹ֔א}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=47|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=וָחָ֔י}}; cf. also (with {{GHGterm|Ṭiphḥa}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=12}}. The very frequent connexion of nouns expressing kindred ideas, by means of {{GHGheb|text=וָ}}, is due simply to considerations of rhythm, for even in such cases the {{GHGterm|Wāw}} must immediately precede the tone-syllable, which must be marked by a disjunctive accent, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=תֹּ֫הוּ וָבֹ֫הוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=2}}, {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם וָלַ֫יְלָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=22}} (see also the previous examples); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=14}} (thrice); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=25|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=זָהָב נָכֶ֫סֶף}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=96|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=כָּבוֹד וָעֹז}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=76|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=וְרֶ֫כֶב וָסוּס}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=וְשֵׁם־וְחָם וָיֶ֫פֶת}}; {{GHGheb|text=נֹחַ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=21|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=כֹּה וָכֹה ;אֱלֹהִים וָמֶ֑לֶךְ|translate=thus and thus}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=1|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ־וָאִֽישׁ}} at the end of the verse, but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=87|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ וְאִישׁ}} in spite of the {{GHGterm|D<sup>e</sup>ḥi}} with the second {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ}}, because it is closely connected with the following predicate. Also with three words {{GHGheb|text=פַּ֫חַד וָפַ֫חַת וָפָ֑ה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=24|verse=17}}. On the other hand, the rapid pronunciation {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} occurs before a conjunctive accent (and, when farther removed from the principal pause, even with the smaller disjunctives, in spite of a following tone-syllable), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=צֹאן וְעֶ֣בֶד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=6}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=40}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=7|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=21}}, and among the examples given above, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=13}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=76|verse=7}}. (Exceptions: {{GHGheb|text=וָקֵ֥דְמָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=14}}, where evidently the {{GHGheb|text=וָ}} is intended to ensure the slow and solemn recitation of the promise, but also {{GHGheb|text=וָזִ֥יף}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=55}}, {{GHGheb|text=וָעֵ֣תֶר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=19|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGheb|text=וָבֶ֥טֶן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=19|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, all immediately before the pause.) For the same rhythmical reason {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} (not {{GHGheb|text=וָ}}) is used regularly with certain monosyllables which, by their nature, lean more closely upon the following word, thus {{GHGheb|text=וְזֶה}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְאֵת}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְגַם}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא}} (to be distinguished from {{GHGheb|text=וָלֹ֔א|translate=if not}}, with {{GHGterm|Zaqeph gadol}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=17}}), and others.<section end=par104 />

<section begin=par105 />{{GHGpar-heading|105|Interjections}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|105|a}}
'''1.''' Among the interjections some (as in all languages) are simply natural sounds, or, as it were, vocal gestures, called forth involuntarily by certain impressions or sensations, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֲהָהּ}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=30|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=הָהּ}}), {{GHGheb|text=אָח|translate=ah!}} {{GHGheb|text=הֶאָח|translate=aha!}} (cf. this {{GHGheb|text=אָח}} also in {{GHGheb|text=אַחְלַי}} and {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲלֵי|translate=utinam!}}), {{GHGheb|text=אָֽנָּ֫א}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=31}}, &c. ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=50|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=אָ֣נָּ֫א}}) ''ah!'' (from {{GHGheb|text=אָהּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=נָא}}), otherwise written {{GHGheb|text=אָֽנָּ֫ה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=20|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jn|chapter=1|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=116|verse=4}}; also {{GHGheb|text=הַס}} (in pause {{GHGheb|text=הָס}}, even in the plural {{GHGheb|text=הַ֫סּוּ|translate=hold your peace!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=8|verse=11}}) {{GHGtranslate|hush!}} {{GHGheb|text=הוֹי}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=הוֹ־הוֹ}}) {{GHGtranslate|ha! woe!}} {{GHGheb|text=אוֹי}}, {{GHGheb|text=א֫וֹיָה}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=120|verse=5}}), {{GHGheb|text=אִי}} (in {{GHGheb|text=אִילוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=4|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=אִי־לָךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=10|verse=16|hidebook=1}}) {{GHGtranslate|woe!}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|105|b}}
'''2.''' Others, however, originally expressed independent ideas, and become interjections only by rapid pronunciation and by usage, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=(הֵא) הֵן}} or {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה|translate=behold!}} (prop. {{GHGtranslate|here}}); {{GHGheb|text=רְאֵה|translate=behold!}} (prop. imperative); {{GHGheb|text=הָ֫בָה}}, plur. {{GHGheb|text=הָבוּ}} (prop. {{GHGtranslate|give}}, imperative of {{GHGheb|text=יָהַב}}; as to the tone, cf. {{GHGpar|69|o}}), {{GHGtranslate|come}}, the Latin {{GHGtranslate|age|en=do (2nd sg. imp.)}}, {{GHGtranslate|agite!|en=do (2nd pl. imp.)}} {{GHGheb|text=לְכָה}} (also {{GHGheb|text=לְךָ}}), {{GHGheb|text=לְכוּ}} (prop. {{GHGtranslate|go}}, imperative of {{GHGheb|text=הָלַךְ}}) with the same meaning<ref>{{GHGheb|text=רְאֵה}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=8}}), {{GHGheb|text=הָ֫בָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=לְכָה}} are also used in connexion with the feminine and the plural, which proves that they have become quite stereotyped as interjections.</ref>; {{GHGheb|text=חָלִ֫ילָה|translate=far be it!}} (prop. ''ad profanum!'')<section end=par105 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

332.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="109.64.194.120" /></noinclude><section begin="par105" />{{GHGheb|text=בִּי}} (see the Lexicon) {{GHGtranslate|I beseech, hear me!}} {{GHGheb|text=נָא|translate=pray!}}<ref>{{GHGheb|text=נָא}} serves to express the most various shades of expression, which are discussed in the various parts of the syntax. It is used especially (''a'') after the {{GHGterm|imperative}}, either in commands or entreaty, see {{GHGpar|110|d}}; (''b'') with the {{GHGterm|imperfect}}, either in the cohortative ({{GHGpar|108|b}}) or jussive ({{GHGpar|109|b}}); (''c'') once with {{GHGterm|perfect}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=14}}; (''d'') after various particles: {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה־נָא|translate=behold now}}; particularly after the conjunctions {{GHGheb|text=אַל}} and {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}: {{GHGheb|text=אַל־נָא|translate=ne quaeso|en=please do not}} and {{GHGheb|text=אִם־נָא|translate=if now}}, {{polytonic|εἴπερ, εἴποτε}} {{GHGtranslate|if}}, in a deprecatory sense, expressive of politeness or modesty. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=12|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=נָא}} stands after a noun; but we ought certainly to read {{GHGheb|text=אַל־נָא}}.—In polite language this particle is used constantly in all these ways, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=3.4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=7.8.19|hidebook=1}}, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=50|verse=17|hidebook=1}}.</ref> used to emphasize a demand, warning, or entreaty, and always placed after the expression to which it belongs.<ref>Against the usual view which regards {{GHGheb|text=נָא}} as a hortatory particle (={{GHGtranslate|up! come!}} analogous to the original imperatives {{GHGheb|text=הָ֫בָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=לְכָה}} and the Ethiopic {{GHGpron|năʿâ}}, properly {{GHGtranslate|hither}}, also {{GHGtranslate|come!}}), P. Haupt, in the {{GHGcite|title=Johns Hopkins University Circulars}}, xiii, no. 114, p. 109, justly observes that we should then expect the particle to be {{GHGterm|prefixed}} to the imperative, &c. He proposes to describe {{GHGheb|text=נָא}} as an emphatic particle. Haupt’s suggested identification of this {{GHGheb|text=נָא}} with the Assyrian, Arabic, and Ethiopic particle ''mā'' (which is also an enclitic of emphasis), and ultimately with the interrogative ''mā'', we shall not discuss here.</ref><section end="par105" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

333.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par106" />{{center|
'''THIRD PART'''

SYNTAX<ref>Recent works on Hebrew syntax are: A. B. Davidson, {{GHGcite|title=Introductory Heb. Gram.}}, vol. ii, {{GHGcite|title=Heb. Syntax}}, Edinburgh, 1894; Ed. König. {{GHGcite|title=Hist.-compar. Syntax der hebr. Sprache}}, Lpz. 1897 (see above, {{GHGpar|3|f}}). Important contributions to Hebrew syntax are also contained in H. Reckendorf’s work {{GHGcite|title=Die syntakt. Verhältnisse des Arab.}}, 2 pts., Leiden, 1895, 1898, of which we have already made use in {{GHGpar|97|a}}. Cf. also the same author’s very instructive discussions {{GHGcite|title=Ueber syntakt. Forschung}}, Munich, 1899.</ref>

'''CHAPTER I'''

THE PARTS OF SPEECH

I. ''Syntax of the Verb.''

A. Use of the Tenses and Moods.<ref>Cf. the sketch of the tenses and moods used in Hebrew in § 40; and on the general characteristics of the perfect and imperfect see the note on {{GHGpar|47|a}}; also Driver, ''A Treatise on the Use of the Tenses in Hebrew'' (Oxford, 1874; 3rd ed. 1892); Bennett, ‘Notes on the Use of the Hebrew Tenses’ ({{GHGcite|title=Hebraica}}, 1886, vols. ii, iii). A partial modification of the accepted definition of the Semitic perfect and imperfect was proposed by J. A. Knudtzon, ''Om det saakaldte Perfektum og Imperfektum i Hebraisk'', Kristiania, 1890; of which a summary entitled ‘Vom sogenannten Perf. und Imperf. im Hebr.’ appeared in the ''Transactions of the Oriental Congress at Stockholm'', section sémitique ''b'', p. 73 ff. (Leiden, 1893). Cf. also Knudtzon’s articles, ‘Zur assyrischen und allgemein semitischen Grammatik’ in the ''Zeitschrift für Assyriologie'', especially vi. 422 ff. and vii. 33 ff.</ref>}}

<!-- section begins above -->{{GHGpar-heading|106|Use of the Perfect}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|a}}
The perfect serves to express actions, events, or states, which the speaker wishes to represent from the point of view of completion, whether they belong to a determinate past time, or extend into the present, or while still future, are pictured as in their completed state.

The definition formerly given here (‘the perfect serves to express ''completed'' actions’) applies, strictly speaking, only to some of the varieties of the perfect discussed under b–p: hence the above modification based on the arguments of Knudtzon (for the title see note 2, and cf. further {{GHGpar|107|a}}).

More particularly the uses of the perfect may be distinguished as follows:—

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|b}}
'''1.''' To represent actions, events, or states, which, after a shorter<section end="par106" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

334.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Laugh Tough" /></noinclude><section begin="par106" />or longer duration, were terminated in the past, and hence are finally concluded, viz.:

(''a'') Corresponding to the perfect proper in Latin and the English perfect definite, in assertions, negations, confirmations, interrogations, &c., e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=15}} ''then Sarah denied, saying, I laughed not'' ({{GHGheb|text=לֹא צָחַ֫קְתִּי}})......; ''and he said, Nay, but thou didst laugh'' ({{GHGheb|text=צָחָקְתְּ}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=מִי הִגִּיד לְךָ|translate=who told thee....?}} Cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=13.14.17.22|hidebook=1}}. Also pointing to some undefined time in the past, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=66|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־שָׁמַע כָּזֹאת}} ''who hath (ever yet) heard such a thing?''

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|c}}
Rem. In opposition to this express use of the perfect to emphasize the completion of an event, the imperfect is not infrequently used to emphasize that which is still future, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=1|verse=5}} ''as I was'' ({{GHGheb|text=הָיִיתִי}}) ''with Moses, so will I be'' ({{GHGheb|text=אֶֽהְיֶה}}) ''with thee;'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=1|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=38}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=46|verse=4.11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=2|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=1|verse=9}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|d}}
(''b'') As a simple ''tempus historicum'' (corresponding to the Greek aorist) in narrating past events, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=4}} ''and Abel, he also brought'' ({{GHGheb|text=הֵבִיא}}), &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=19}} ''the waters did prevail'' ({{GHGheb|text=גָּֽבְרוּ}}), &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=1}} ''there was a man'' ({{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ הָיָה}}) ''in the land of Uz'', &c.; even in relating repeated actions, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=30}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|e}}
Rem. As the above examples indicate, the perfect of ''narration'' occurs especially at the head of an entire narrative ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=1}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=2|verse=1}}) or an independent sentence (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=11.13}}), but in co-ordinate sentences, as a rule, only when the verb is separated from the copulative {{GHGheb|text=ו}} by one or more words (cf. above {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=4}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=19|hidebook=1}}). In other cases, the narrative is continued in the imperfect consecutive, according to {{GHGpar|111|a}}. The direct connexion of the narrative perfect with {{GHGheb|text=ו}} copulative (not to be confounded with the perfect consecutive proper, § 112) agrees rather with Aramaic syntax (cf. Kautzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Biblisch-Aram.}}, § 71, 1 b). On the examples (which are in many respects doubtful) in the earlier texts, see {{GHGpar|112|pp}}–uu.

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|f}}
(''c'') To represent actions, &c., which were already completed in the past, at the time when other actions or conditions took place (pluperfect),<ref>Cf. P. Haupt in the ''Notes on Esther'', 9:2.</ref> e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=3}} ''now Samuel was (long since) dead''<ref>Incorrectly, e.g. in the Vulgate, ''Samuel autem mortuus est... et Saul abstulit magos'', &c.</ref>... ''and Saul had put away'' ({{GHGheb|text=הֵסִיר}}) ''those that had familiar spirits... out of the land''. Both these statements, being as it were in parentheses, merely assign a reason for the narrative beginning at verse 6. Cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=18}}.—{{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=18}} (''for the Lord had fast closed up'', &c.); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=30|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=19.34|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=10}}; and in a negative statement, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=5}} ''for the Lord God had not'' (up to that time) ''caused it to rain'', &c. This is especially frequent, from the nature of the case, in relative, causal, and temporal clauses, when the main clause contains a tense referring to the past, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=2}} ''and he rested... from all his work which he had made'' ({{GHGheb|text=עָשָׂה}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=9}},
<section end="par106" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

335.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Laugh Tough" /></noinclude><section begin="par106" />19:27, &c.; 29:10 ''now when Jacob had seen Rachel'' ({{GHGheb|text=בַּֽאֲשֶׁר רָאָה}})..., ''Jacob went near'', &c.; so also in clauses which express the completion or incompleteness of one action, &c., on the occurrence of another, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=30|hidebook=1}}, &c.; cf. {{GHGpar|164|b}}, with the note, and c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|g}}
'''2.''' To represent actions, events, or states, which, although completed in the past, nevertheless extend their influence into the present (in English generally rendered by the present):

(''a'') Expressing facts which were accomplished long before, or conditions and attributes which were acquired long before, but of which the effects still remain in the present (present perfect), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=10|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=הִסְתִּיר פָּנָיו|translate=he hath hidden his face}} (''and still keeps it hidden''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=143|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=פֵּרַ֫שְׂתִּי|translate=I have spread forth my hands}} (''and still keep them spread forth''). This applies particularly to a large number of perfects (almost exclusively of intransitive<ref>With regard to the great but very natural preponderance of intransitive verbs (expressing an existing state), cf. the lists in Knudtzon (see above, p. 309, note 2), pp. 117 and 122 in the Danish text.</ref> verbs, denoting affections or states of the mind) which in English can be rendered only by the present, or, in the case mentioned above under ''f'', by the imperfect.<ref>Cf. ''novi, odi, memini''; οἶδα, μέμνημαι, ἔοικα, δέδορκα, κέκραγα; in the New Testament, ἤλπικα, ἡγαπηκα.</ref> Thus, {{GHGheb|text=יָדַ֫עְתִּי|translate=I know}} (prop. ''I have perceived, have experienced'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יָדַ֫עְתִּי|translate=I know not}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=9}}, &c.; on the other hand, e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=34}}, the context requires ''I knew not''; {{GHGheb|text=זָכַ֫רְנוּ|translate=we remember}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=מֵֽאֲנָה|translate=she refuseth}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=עָלַץ|translate=it exulteth}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׂמַ֫חְתִּי|translate=I rejoice}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=בִּקֵּשׁ|translate=he requireth}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=12}}; {{GHGheb|text=קִוִּ֫יתִי|translate=I wait}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=130|verse=5}} (parallel with {{GHGheb|text=הוֹחָֽ֫לְתִּי}}); {{GHGheb|text=חָפַ֫צְתִּי|translate=I delight}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=40|verse=9}} (mostly negative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=11}}, &c.); {{GHGheb|text=אָהַ֫בְתִּי|translate=I love}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=4}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׂנֵ֫אתִי|translate=I hate}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=31|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=מָאַ֫סְתִּי|translate=I despise}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=21}}; {{GHGheb|text=תִּֽעֲב֫וּנִי|translate=they abhor me}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=30|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=בָּטַ֫חְתִּי|translate=I trust}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=25|verse=2}}; {{GHGheb|text=חָסִ֫יתִי|translate=I put my trust}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=31|verse=2}}; {{GHGheb|text=צָדַ֫קְתִּי|translate=I am righteous}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=פָּקַ֫דְתִּי|translate=I have decided to requite}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=2}}.—We may further include a number of verbs which express bodily characteristics or states, such as {{GHGheb|text=גָּדַ֫לְתָּ|translate=thou art great}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=קָטֹ֫נְתִּי|translate=I am little}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=11}}; {{GHGheb|text=גָּֽבְהוּ|translate=they are high}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=55|verse=9}}; {{GHGheb|text=רָֽחֲקוּ|translate=they stand aloof}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=30|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=טֹ֫בוּ|translate=they are goodly}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=24|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=נָאווּ|translate=they are beautiful}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=52|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=זָקַ֫נְתִּי|translate=I am old}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=13}}; {{GHGheb|text=יָגַ֫עְתִּי|translate=I am weary}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=6|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׂבַ֫עְתִּי|translate=I am full}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=11}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|h}}
Rem. To the same category probably belong also the perfects after {{GHGheb|text=עַד־מָתַי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=3}} ''how long hast thou'' already ''been refusing'' (and refusest still...? which really amounts to ''how long wilt thou refuse''?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=80|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=1|verse=22}} (co-ordinate with the imperf.), and after {{GHGheb|text=עַד־אָ֫נָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=1|verse=2}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|i}}
(''b'') In direct narration to express actions which, although really only in process of accomplishment, are nevertheless meant to be repre-<section end="par106" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

336.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par106 />sented as already accomplished in the conception of the speaker, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הֲרִמֹ֫תִי|translate=I lift up}} (my hand in ratifying an oath) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=22}}; {{GHGheb|text=נִשְׁבַּ֫עְתִּי|translate=I swear}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=הַֽעִדֹ֫תִי|translate=I testify}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=8|verse=19}}; {{GHGheb|text=יָעַ֫צְתִּי|translate=I counsel}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=17|verse=11}} (but in a different context in ver. 15, ''I have counselled''); {{GHGheb|text=אָמַ֫רְתִּי}} (prop. ''I say'') ''I decide'' (''I consider as hereby settled'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=30}}; ''I declare'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=32|verse=10|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|k}}
(''c'') To express facts which have formerly taken place, and are still of constant recurrence, and hence are matters of common experience (the Greek ''gnomic aorist''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=9|verse=11}} ''for thou, Lord, hast not forsaken'' ({{GHGheb|text=לֹא־עָזַ֫בְתָּ}}) ''them that seek thee''. Cf. ver. 13, also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=10|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=40|hidebook=1}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=11}} ({{GHGheb|text=כִּבֵּס}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|l}}
Rem. In almost all the cases discussed in No. 2 (included under the English present) the imperfect can be used instead of the perfect, wherever the action or state in question is regarded, not as already completed, but as still continuing or just taking place (see {{GHGpar|107|a}}). Thus, {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יָכֹ֫לְתִּי|translate=I am not able}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=40|verse=13}} and {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אוּכַל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=35}} have practically the same meaning. Hence also it very frequently happens that the imperfect corresponds to such perfects in poetic or prophetic parallelism, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=1}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=1|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=17}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|m}}
'''3.''' To express ''future'' actions, when the speaker intends by an express assurance to represent them as finished, or as equivalent to accomplished facts:

(''a'') In contracts or other express stipulations (again corresponding to the English present, and therefore closely related to the instances noted under ''i''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=11}} ''the field I give'' ({{GHGheb|text=נָתַ֫תִּי}}) ''thee''; cf.ver. 13 and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=48|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=40|verse=4}}; in a threat, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=5|verse=6}} (unless, with Wellhausen, {{GHGheb|text=יְסִירֻ֫ךָ}} is to be read).—Especially in promises made by God, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=2}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|n}}
(''b'') To express facts which are undoubtedly imminent, and, therefore, in the imagination of the speaker, already accomplished (''perfectum confidentiae''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=17|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=הֵן גָּוַ֫עְנוּ אָבַ֫דְנוּ כֻּלָּ֫נוּ אָבָֽ֫דְנוּ|translate=behold, we perish, we are undone, we are all undone}}. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=5}} ({{GHGheb|text=נִדְמֵ֫יתִי|translate=I am undone}}<ref>Cf. the similar use of ὄλωλα (διέφθορας, ''Il.'' 15. 128) and ''perii!'' On the kindred use of the perfect in conditional sentences, cf. below, p.</ref>), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=4|verse=2}}. Even in interrogative sentences, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=17|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=9.11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=4|verse=10}} (?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=22|verse=20}}.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=14}} ''a perf. confidentiae'' (after {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אִם}}; but cf. {{GHGpar|163|d}}) appears to be used in the expression of an earnest desire that something may happen (''but have me in thy remembrance'', &c.). Neither this passage, however, nor the use of the perfect in Arabic to express a wish or imprecation, justifies us in assuming the existence of a ''precative'' perfect in Hebrew. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, also, translate ''the counsel of the wicked is far from me''. Cf. Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Tenses}}<sup>3</sup>, p. 25 f. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=43|verse=9}} either {{GHGheb|text=נִקְבְּצוּ}} is {{GHGterm|imperative}} (see {{GHGpar|51|o}}) or we must read {{GHGheb|text=יִקָּֽבְצוּ}}, corresponding to {{GHGheb|text=יֵאָֽסְפוּ}} which follows.</ref> This use of the perfect occurs most frequently in prophetic language (''perfectum propheticum''). The prophet so trans-<section end=par106 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

337.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Biolongvistul" /></noinclude><section begin="par106" />ports himself in imagination into the future that he describes the future event as if it had been already seen or heard by him, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=13}} ''therefore my people are gone into captivity'' ({{GHGheb|text=גָּלָה}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=1|hidebook=1}} ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=10|verse=28|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=11|verse=9|hidebook=1}} (after {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}}, as frequently elsewhere); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=19|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=20|verse=37}}. Not infrequently the imperfect interchanges with such perfects either in the parallel member or further on in the narrative.

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|o}}
(''c'') To express actions or facts, which are meant to be indicated as existing in the future in a completed state (''futurum exactum''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=4|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם רָחַץ|translate=when he has washed away}}=''when he shall have washed away'' (an {{GHGterm|imperfect}} follows in the co-ordinate sentence; cf. the conditional sentences in {{GHGpar|107|x}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=11}} (after {{GHGheb|text=עַד אֲשֶׁר אִם}}, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=32|verse=17}}; also {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=17|verse=13}} after {{GHGheb|text=עַד אֲשֶׁד}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=19}} after {{GHGheb|text=עַד אִם}} and elsewhere frequently after temporal conjunctions); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=5|verse=2}} ({{GHGheb|text=יָלָ֑דָה}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=וַֽאֲנִי כַּֽאֲשֶׁר שָׁכֹ֫לְתִּי שָׁכָֽלְתִּי|translate=and I}}—''if I am bereaved'' (''orbus fuero''), ''I am bereaved'', an expression of despairing resignation. Cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=23|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=4|verse=16}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|106|p}}
'''4.''' To express actions and facts, whose accomplishment in the past is to be represented, not as actual, but only as possible (generally corresponding to the Latin imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=42}} ''except the God of my father''... ''had been with me, surely now hadst thou sent me away empty'' ({{GHGheb|text=שִׁלַּחְתָּ֑נִי}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=15}} ({{GHGheb|text=שָׁלַ֫חְתִּי|translate=I had}} almost ''put forth'', &c.); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=13|verse=13}} ({{GHGheb|text=הֵכִּין}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=13|verse=19}}; so frequently after {{GHGheb|text=כִּמְעַט|translate=easily, almost}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=9}} (where {{GHGheb|text=כִּמְעַט}} is probably to be connected with the word after it), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=94|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=87|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=5|verse=14}}. Cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=10|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=בְּחָנַ֫נִי}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=12}} (''if I should think'', &c.; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=4}}); in the apodosis of a conditional sentence, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=34}}.—So also to express an unfulfilled desire, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=לוּ מַ֫תְנוּ|translate=would that we had died...!}} ({{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} with the imperfect would mean ''would that we might die!'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=30}}). Finally, also in a question indicating astonishment, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=מִי מִלֵּל|translate=who would have said...? quis dixerit?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=11}}.
<section end="par106" />
<section begin="par107" />{{GHGpar-heading|107|Use of the Imperfect||<ref>Cf. the literature cited above, p. 309, note 2.</ref>}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|a}}
The imperfect, as opposed to the perfect, represents actions, events, or states which are regarded by the speaker at any moment as still continuing, or in process of accomplishment, or even as just taking place. In the last case, its occurrence may be represented as certainly imminent, or merely as conceived in the mind of the speaker, or simply as desired, and therefore only contingent (the modal use of the imperfect).<section end="par107" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

338.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par107 />Knudtzon (see above, Rem. on {{GHGpar|106|a}}), comparing the Ass.-Bab. usage, would prefer the term ''present'' rather than imperfect, on the ground that the tense expresses what is either actually or mentally present. In any case, the essential difference between the perfect and imperfect consists, he argues, in this, that the perfect simply indicates what is actually complete, while the imperfect places the action, &c., in a more direct relation to the judgement or feeling of the speaker.

More precisely the imperfect serves—

'''1.''' In the sphere of ''past time'':

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|b}}
(''a'') To express actions, &c., which ''continued'' throughout a longer or shorter period,<ref>Cf. the ''Mêšaʿ'' inscription, l. 5, {{GHGheb|text=כי יאנף כמש בארצה|translate=for Chemosh was angry with his land}}. As Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Tenses}}, 3rd ed., § 27, 1 a, remarks, this vivid realization of the accomplishment of the action is especially frequent in poetic and prophetic style.</ref> e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=6}} ''a mist went up'' continually ({{GHGheb|text=יַֽעֲלֶה}}), 2:25, 37:7, 48:10, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=1|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=8|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=13|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, 12, 14, 15, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=9|verse=15}} f. 20 f., 23 <sup>7</sup>, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=2|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=13|verse=17|hidebook=1}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=23|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=21|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=4|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=יִמָּלֵא}}), 17:10 f., 51:2 x, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=36|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=7}}, 14, 17 ff.38 ff., 24:2, 32:4, 5 ({{GHGheb|text=אוֹדִֽיעֲךָ}}), 47:5, 68:10, 12, 104:6 ff., 106:19, 107:18, 29, 139:13, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, 15 f., 10:10 f., 15:7 f.—very frequently alternating with a perfect (especially with a frequentative perfect;
