cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=9|verse=15}}–23 and {{GHGpar|112|e}}), or when the narration is continued by means of an imperfect consecutive.<ref>According to the Masora such imperfects occur in Is 10<sup>13 ''bis''</sup> (where, however, {{GHGheb|text=וְאָסִיר}} might also mean ''I am wont to remove'', &c.), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=48|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=57|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=38}}a, also (according to {{GHGpar|49|c}}) in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=10}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=10}}. In some other cases {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} is no doubt a dogmatic emendation for {{GHGheb|text=וָ}} (''imperf. consec.'') in order to represent historical statements as promises; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=43|verse=28|hidebook=1}} [contrasted with {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=25|hidebook=1}}], {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=51|verse=2 bis|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=63|verse=3 ff.|hidebook=1}} and the note on {{GHGpar|53|p}}.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|c}}
Rem. 1. The imperfect is frequently used in this way after the particles {{GHGheb|text=אָז|translate=then}}, {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֫רֶם|translate=not yet}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּטֶ֫רֶם|translate=before}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַד־|translate=until}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=אָז יָשִֽׁיר־משֶׁה|translate=then sang Moses}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=41}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=10|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=126|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=21}}. (The {{GHGterm|perfect}} is used after {{GHGheb|text=אָז}} when stress is to be laid on the fact that the action has really taken place, and not upon its gradual accomplishment or duration in the past, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=אָז הוּחַל|translate=then began}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=22|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=89|verse=20}}.)<ref>After {{GHGheb|text=אָז|translate=then}} (to announce future events) the imperf. is naturally used in the sense of a future, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=41}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=48}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=3|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=3|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=51|verse=21}}.</ref> After {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֫רֶם}} e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֫רֶם יִשְׁכָּ֫בוּ|translate=before they lay down}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=45|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=3}}, 7, always in the sense of our ''pluperfect''. (In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=15}} instead of the perf. {{GHGheb|text=כִּלָּה}}, the imperf. should be read, as in verse 45; so also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=7}} [{{GHGheb|text=יִגָּלֶה}}] an imperf. is co-ordinated with {{GHGheb|text=ידע}}). After {{GHGheb|text=בְּטֶ֫רֶם}} (sometimes also simply {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֫רֶם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=34}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=3|verse=1}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=1|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּטֶ֫רֶם תֵּצֵא|translate=before thou camest forth}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=50|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=14}} (perhaps also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=90|verse=2}} an imperf. was intended instead of {{GHGheb|text=יֻלָּ֫דוּ}}; cf. Wellhausen on {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=2}}; but note also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=8|verse=25}}, in a similar context, ''before the mountains were settled'', {{GHGheb|text=הָטְכָּ֑עוּ}}, the predicate being separated from {{GHGheb|text=בְּטֶ֫רֶם}}, by {{GHGheb|text=הָרִים}}, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=90|verse=2}}). After {{GHGheb|text=עַד־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=10|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=17}} (''until I went''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=29|verse=34}}; on the other<section end=par107 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

339.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Laugh Tough" /></noinclude><section begin="par107" />hand, with the perf., e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=22}}. As after {{GHGheb|text=אָז}}, so also after {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֫רֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּטֶ֫רֶם}}, and {{GHGheb|text=עַד־}} the imperf. may be used, according to the context, in the sense of our ''future'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=65|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=21}}; after {{GHGheb|text=עַד־}} e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=14}}. The imperf. is used in the sense of our ''present'' after {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֫רֶם}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=7|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|d}}
2. Driver ({{GHGcite|title=Tenses}}<sup>3</sup>, p. 35 f.) rightly lays stress upon the inherent distinction between the {{GHGterm|participle}} as expressing ''mere'' duration, and the {{GHGterm|imperfect}} as expressing ''progressive'' duration (in the present, past, or future). Thus the words {{GHGheb|text=וְנָהָר יׂצֵא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=10}} represent the river of Paradise as going out of Eden in a continuous, uninterrupted stream, but {{GHGheb|text=יִפָּרֵד}}, which immediately follows, describes how the parting of its waters is always taking place afresh. In the same way {{GHGheb|text=יַֽעֲלֶה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=6}} represents new mists as constantly arising, and {{GHGheb|text=יִמָלֵא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=4}} new clouds of smoke. Also those actions, &c., which might be regarded in themselves as single or even momentary, are, as it were, broken up by the imperfect into their component parts, and so pictured as gradually completing themselves. Hence {{GHGheb|text=תִּבְלָעֵ֫מוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=12}} (after a ''perf.'' as in verse 14) represents the Egyptians, in a vivid, poetic description, as being swallowed up one after another, and {{GHGheb|text=יַבְחֵ֫נִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=7}} the leading on by stages, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|e}}
(''b'') To express actions, &c., which were ''repeated'' in the past, either at fixed intervals or occasionally (the ''modus rei repetitae''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=5}} ''thus did'' ({{GHGheb|text=יַֽעֲשֶׂה}}) ''Job continually'' (after each occasion of his sons’ festivities); 4:3 f., 22:6 f., 23:11, 29:7, 9, 12 f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=38|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=31|hidebook=1}}, 39 (''I used to bear'' the loss of it), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=1|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=19|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=7|hidebook=1}} ff. ({{GHGheb|text=יִקַּח|translate=used to take}} every time), 40:36 ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=9|verse=17}} f. 20 ff., 11:5, 9, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=21|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=13|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=27|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=5|verse=25}} (of tribute repeated year by year), 10:5, 13:33, 14:28, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=8|verse=29|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=13|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=25|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=36|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=42|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=44|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=78|verse=15.40|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=103|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=2|verse=14}}; even in a negative dependent clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=10}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|f}}
'''2.''' In the sphere of ''present time'', again

(''a'') To express actions, events, or states, which are ''continued'' for a shorter or longer time,<ref>It is not always possible to carry out with certainty the distinction between ''continued'' and ''repeated'' actions. Some of the examples given under ''f'' might equally be referred to ''g''.</ref> e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=מַה־תְּבַקֵּשׁ|translate=what seekest thou?}} 19:19 {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־אוּכַל|translate=I cannot}}; 24:50, 31:35, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=13}}. Other examples are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=31|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=11|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=2}}, and in the prophetic formula {{GHGheb|text=יֹאמַר יְהֹוָה|translate=saith the Lord}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=11.18}}, &c., cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=40|verse=1|hidebook=1}}. So especially to express facts known by experience, which occur at all times, and consequently hold good at any moment, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=15|verse=20}} ''a wise son maketh a glad father''; hence especially frequent in Job and Proverbs. In an interrogative sentence, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=17}} ''is mortal man just before God?'' In a negative sentence, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=18}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|g}}
(''b'') To express actions, &c., which may be ''repeated'' at any time, including therefore the present, or are ''customarily'' repeated on a given occasion (cf. above, e), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=44}} ''as bees do'' (are accustomed to<section end="par107" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

340.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Laugh Tough" /></noinclude><section begin="par107" />do); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=33|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=32|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=40}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=5|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=1|verse=3}}. So again (see f) especially to express facts known by experience which may at any time come into effect again, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=23|verse=8}} ''a gift blindeth'' ({{GHGheb|text=יְעַוֵּר}}), &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=3|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=1|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=2|verse=4}}, &c. Of the same kind also is the imperfect in such relative clauses (see § 155), as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=27}} ''Benjamin is'' {{GHGheb|text=זְאֵב יִטְרָף|translate=a wolf that ravineth}} (properly, is accustomed to ravin). Finally, compare also the formulae {{GHGheb|text=יֵֽאָמֵר|translate=it is}} (wont to be) ''said'' (to introduce proverbial expressions) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־יֵֽעָשֶׂה כֵן|translate=it is not}} (wont to be) ''so done'' (and hence ''may not, shall not be'', see u), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=12}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|h}}
(''c'') To express actions, &c., which although, strictly speaking, they are already finished, are regarded as still lasting on into the present time, or continuing to operate in it, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=30}} ''wherefore is it that thou dost ask'' ({{GHGheb|text=תִּשְׁאַל}}) ''after my name?'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=31|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=5|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=16|verse=9}}. In such cases, naturally, the perfect is also admissible, and is sometimes found in the same formula as the imperfect, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=7}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=2|verse=2|hidebook=1}}) {{GHGheb|text=מֵאַ֫יִן תָּבֹא|translate=whence comest thou}} (just now)? but {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=8}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=7|hidebook=1}}) {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽי־מִזֶּה בָאתְ|translate=whence camest thou?}} The imperfect represents the coming as still in its last stage, whereas the perfect represents it as an accomplished fact.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|i}}
'''3.''' In the sphere of ''future time''. To express actions, &c., which are to be represented as about to take place, and as continuing a shorter or longer time in the future, or as being repeated; thus:

(''a'') From the standpoint of the speaker’s present time, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=4|verse=1}} ''they will not believe'' ({{GHGheb|text=יַֽאֲמִ֫ינוּ}}) ''me, nor hearken'' ({{GHGheb|text=יִשְׁמְעוּ}}) ''unto my voice: for they will say'' ({{GHGheb|text=יֹֽאמְרוּ}}), &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=6|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|k}}
(''b'') In dependent clauses to represent actions, &c., which from some point of time in the past are to be represented as future, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=7}} could we in any wise know ''that he would say'' ({{GHGheb|text=יֹאמַר}})? {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר־יִמְלֹךְ|translate=qui regnaturus erat}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=13|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=4|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=2|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=78|verse=6}} ''that the generation to come might know'', {{GHGheb|text=בָּנִים יִוָּ֫לֵדוּ|translate=the children which should be born}} (''qui nascituri essent''; the imperfect here with the collateral idea of the occurrence being repeated in the future).

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|l}}
(''c'') To represent a ''futurum exactum''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=4|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=11|hidebook=1}} (co-ordinated with a perfect used in the same sense, see {{GHGpar|106|o}}); so also sometimes after the temporal particles {{GHGheb|text=עַד}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=132|verse=5}}, and {{GHGheb|text=עַד אֲשֶׁר|translate=until}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=17}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|m}}
'''4.''' Finally to the sphere of future time belong also those cases in which the (modal) imperfect serves to express actions, events, or states, the occurrence of which is to be represented as willed (or not<section end="par107" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

341.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par107" />willed), or as in some way conditional, and consequently only contingent. More particularly such imperfects serve—

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|n}}
(''a'') As an expression of will, whether it be a definite intention and arrangement, or a simple desire, viz.:

(1) Sometimes in positive sentences in place of the cohortative (cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=59|verse=17}} with verse 18; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=22|verse=50}} with {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=50}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=11}}, &c.), of the imperative ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=18|verse=3}}), or of the jussive (which, however, in most cases, does not differ from the ordinary form of the imperfect), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=תֵּֽרָאֶה|translate=let it appear}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=34|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=19|verse=2}}, 3, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=10|verse=12}} (and so frequently in verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}; cf. {{GHGpar|109|a}}, note 2); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=9|verse=5}} ({{GHGheb|text=תָּחִיל}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=61|verse=7}} ({{GHGheb|text=תּוֹסִיף}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=22|verse=17}} ({{GHGheb|text=תָּשִׁית}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=23|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=23}} (co-ordinated with the imperative), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=20|hidebook=1}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}; so probably also {{GHGheb|text=יָדִין|translate=let him judge!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=72|verse=2}}.—So also in the 1st pers., to express a wish which is asserted subsequently with reference to a fixed point of time in the past, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶגְּוַע|translate=I ought to}} [not ''should'' as A.V., R.V.] ''have'', (then, immediately after being born) ''given up the ghost''; cf. verse 19 {{GHGheb|text=אֶֽהְיֶה}} and {{GHGheb|text=אוּבָֽל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=10|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=35|verse=28}}. Even to express an obligation or necessity according to the judgement of another person, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=29}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶרְשָׁע|translate=I am to be guilty}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=4|hidebook=1}}. Cp. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=16|hidebook=1}}; in a question, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=42|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=43|verse=2|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|o}}
(2) To express the definite expectation that something will not happen. The imperfect with {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} represents a more emphatic form of prohibition than the jussive<ref>As stated in {{GHGpar|46|a}}, a prohibition cannot be expressed by {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} and the imperative.</ref> with {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} (cf. {{GHGpar|109|c}}), and corresponds to our ''thou shalt not do it!'' with the strongest expectation of obedience, while {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} with the jussive is rather a simple warning, ''do not that!'' Thus {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} with the imperfect is especially used in enforcing the divine commands, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לֹא תִגְּנׄב|translate=thou shalt not steal}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=15}}; cf. verses 3, 4, 5, 7, 10 ff. So {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} with the 3rd pers. perhaps in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=16|verse=10}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|p}}
Rem. The {{GHGterm|jussive}}, which is to be expected after {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}}, does not, as a rule (according to ''n'', and {{GHGpar|109|a}}, note 2), differ in form from the simple imperfect. That many supposed jussives are intended as simple imperfects is possible from the occurrence after {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} of what are undoubtedly imperfect forms, not only from verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}} (cf. {{GHGpar|109|a}}, note 2), but also from verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}}, to express a prohibition or negative wish, {{GHGheb|text=אַל־תַּבִּיט}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=17}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַל־תָּסוּר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=1|verse=7}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַל־נָא יַשִׂים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=25}}. Even with the 1st pers. plur. (after an imperative) {{GHGheb|text=וְאַל־נָמוּת|translate=that we die not}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=12|verse=19}}. Also to express the conviction that something cannot happen, {{GHGheb|text=אַל־יָנוּם|translate=he will not slumber}},<ref>To regard this as an optative (so Hupfeld) is from the context impossible. It is more probably a strong pregnant construction, or fusion of two sentences (such as, ''do not think he will slumber!''). Verse 4 contains the objective confirmation, by means of {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} with the imperf., of that which was previously only a subjective conviction.</ref> {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=121|verse=3}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=46|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=14|verse=10}}.<section end="par107" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

342.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par107" />{{GHGmargin-letter|107|q}}
(3) In dependent clauses after final conjunctions ({{GHGpar|165|b}}), as {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=7}} ({{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִשְׁמְעוּ|translate=that they may not understand}}); {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽעֲבוּר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, 19, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=14}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עַן אֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=17|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עַן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=51|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=78|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, and {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר יַעַ֫ן}}<ref>But {{GHGheb|text=יַעַ֫ן אֲשֶׁר}} in a causal sense (''because, since''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=2|verse=20}} (as {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=27}}) is followed by the perfect. On {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=4|verse=24}} see above, {{GHGpar|74|g}}.</ref> {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=12|verse=12}}, ''in order that''<ref>R.V. ''because he shall not see.''.]</ref>; {{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי|translate=that}}... ''not'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=14}}; also after {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־|translate=that not, lest}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, &c.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־}} occurs with the perf. in a vivid presentment of the time when the fear is realized and the remedy comes too late. (In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=6}}, since a {{GHGterm|perfect consec.}} follows, read with Driver {{GHGheb|text=יִמְצָא}}.)</ref>; cf. also the instances introduced by {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא}} in {{GHGpar|109|g}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=9|verse=6}} such an imperfect (or jussive? see the examples in {{GHGpar|109|f}}) is added to the expression of the command by an asyndeton, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=19}} to the principal clause simply by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}: ''while they sought them food'' {{GHGheb|text=וְיָשִׁ֫יבוּ אֶת־נַפְשָׁם|translate=to refresh their souls}} (cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|verse=26}}, ''it is good and let him hope'', i.e. ''that he should hope''); so after an interrogative clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=7}}. Finally also in a relative clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּדֶ֫רֶךְ־זוּ תֵלֵךְ|translate=in the way which thou shouldst go}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|r}}
(''b'') To express actions, &c., which are to be represented as possibly taking place or not taking place (sometimes corresponding to the ''potential'' of the classical languages, as also to our periphrases with ''can, may, should''<ref>By this, of course, is not meant that these finer distinctions were consciously present to the Hebrew mind. They are rather mere expedients for making intelligible to ourselves the full significance of the Semitic imperfect.</ref>). More particularly such imperfects are used—

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|s}}
(1) In a permissive sense, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=16}} ''of every tree of the garden'' ({{GHGheb|text=אָכֹל תֹּאכֵל}}) ''thou mayest freely eat'' (the opposite in verse {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=17|hidebook=completely|fullsizeverse=1}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=37|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=21|verse=3}}, 22, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=3}}. In the 1st pers. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=5|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=22|verse=18|hidebook=1}} (''I may'', or ''can, tell''); in a negative sentence, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=5|verse=5}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|t}}
(2) In interrogative sentences, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=20|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יֹאמַר|translate=quis dixerit?}} Cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=43|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=11|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹֽא־אֶרְחַץ בָּהֶם|translate=may I not wash in them?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=33|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=15|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=24|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=5|verse=5}}. So especially in a question expressing surprise after {{GHGheb|text=אֵיךְ}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=9}} ''how then can I...?'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=34|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=19|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=137|verse=4}}, and even with regard to some point of time in the past, looking forward from which an event might have been expected to take place, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=הֲיָדוֹעַ נֵדַע|translate=could we in any wise know...?}} Cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=33}} ({{GHGheb|text=יָמוּת|translate=was Abner to die as a fool}}, i.e. ''was he destined to die...?''), and so probably also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=31}} (''should he deal...?''). Very closely connected with this is the use of the imperfect—

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|u}}
(3) In a consecutive clause depending on an interrogative clause, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=11}}, ''who am I'' ({{GHGheb|text=כִּי אֵלֵךְ}}) ''that I should'' (''ought, could'') ''go?'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=8|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, similarly after {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=5|verse=2}}.<section end="par107" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

343.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par107" />{{GHGmargin-letter|107|v}}
Rem. In passages like {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=11|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=8|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=114|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, the context shows that the imperfect corresponds rather to our present. In such sentences the perfect also is naturally used in referring to completed actions, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=18|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=7|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|w}}
(4) In ''negative sentences'' to express actions, &c., which cannot or should not happen, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר לֽאֹ־יִסָּפֵד מֵרֹב|translate=which cannot be numbered for multitude}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=9|hidebook=1}} ''deeds'' ({{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁד לֹא־יֵֽעשׂוּ}}) ''that ought not to be done'' (cf. above, g); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=5|verse=5}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|107|x}}
(5) In ''conditional clauses'' (the ''modus conditionalis'' corresponding to the Latin present or imperfect conjunctive) both in the protasis and apodosis, or only in the latter, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=23|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=גַּם כִּֽי־אֵלֵךְ... לֹֽא־אִירָא רָע|translate=yea, though I walk}} (or ''had to walk'')... ''I fear'' (or ''I would fear'') ''no evil''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=20}} ''though I be righteous, mine own mouth shall condemn me''. After a perfect in the protasis, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=10}}. Very frequently also in an apodosis, the protasis to which must be supplied from the context, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=8}} ''but as for me, I would seek unto God'' (were I in thy place); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, 16, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=14|verse=14|hidebook=1 f.}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=55|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=12}}. However, some of the imperfects in these examples are probably intended as jussive forms. Cf. {{GHGpar|109|h}}.
<section end="par107" />
<section begin="par108" />{{GHGpar-heading|108|Use of the Cohortative}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|108|a}}
The cohortative, i.e. according to {{GHGpar|48|c}}, the 1st pers.<ref>For the few examples of cohortatives in the 3rd sing., see {{GHGpar|48|d}}.</ref> sing. or plur. of the imperfect lengthened by the ending {{GHGheb|text=־ָה}},<ref>But verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}, according to {{GHGpar|75|l}}, even in the cohortative, almost always have the ending {{GHGheb|text=־ֶה}}; cf. e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=20}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶרְאֶה}} after {{GHGheb|text=אַסְתִּ֫ירָה}}.</ref> represents in general an endeavour directed expressly towards a definite object. While the corresponding forms of the indicative rather express the mere announcement that an action will be undertaken, the cohortative lays stress on the determination underlying the action, and the personal interest in it.

Its uses may be divided into—

{{GHGmargin-letter|108|b}}
'''1.''' The cohortative standing alone, or co-ordinated with another cohortative, and frequently strengthened by the addition of the particle {{GHGheb|text=נָא}}:

(''a'') To express self-encouragement, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=אָסֻ֫רָה־נָּא וג׳|translate=I will turn aside now, and see...!}} So especially as the result of inward deliberation (in soliloquies), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=21|hidebook=1}} (rarely so used after {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=16}} ''let me not look''...''!'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=18|verse=18}}), and also as a more or less emphatic statement of a fixed determination, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=1}} ''I will sing''<ref>R.V. ''let me sing''.]</ref>...''!'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=31|verse=8|hidebook=1}}. Cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=46|verse=30}} ''now let me die'' (''I am willing to die''),<section end="par108" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

344.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par108 />''since I have seen thy face''; and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=31|verse=8}}. In the 1st pers. plur. the cohortative includes a summons to others to help in doing something, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=נְנַתְּקָה|translate=come! let us break asunder!}} &c., and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=3}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|108|c}}
(''b'') To express a wish, or a request for permission, that one should be allowed to do something, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶעְבְּרָה|translate=may I be allowed to pass through}} (''let me pass through'')! {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=נַעְבְּרָה־נָּא|translate=may we be allowed to pass through!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=40|verse=15}} ''let me go, I pray thee!'' &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=16|verse=9}}; so after {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=14}}; after {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=17|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=25|verse=2}} ({{GHGheb|text=אַל־אֵב֫וֹשָׁה|translate=let me not be ashamed}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=31|verse=2}}, 18, 71:1); 69:15. After {{GHGheb|text=אַל־נָא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=1|verse=14}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|108|d}}
'''2.''' The cohortative in dependence on other moods, as well as in conditional sentences: (''a'') In dependence (with {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=9|verse=15}} after {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עַן}}) on an imperative or jussive to express an intention or intended consequence, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=4}} ''bring it to me'', {{GHGheb|text=וְאֹכֵ֑לָה|translate=that I may eat}}, prop. ''then will I eat''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=56|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=25|hidebook=1}} f., 42:34, 49:1, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=6|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=39|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=20}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=19}} ''and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw nigh and come'', {{GHGheb|text=וְנֵדָֽעָה|translate=that we may know}} (''it'')! {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=27|verse=5}}. Also after negative sentences, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=30}}, 32, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=39}}, and after interrogative sentences, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=26|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=8|verse=5}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|108|e}}
(''b'') In conditional sentences (with or without {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}) to express a contingent intention, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־אֲדַבְּרָה|translate=should I determine to speak, my grief is not assuaged}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְאַחְדְּלָה|translate=and should I forbear, what am I eased?}} without {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=30|verse=26|hidebook=1}} (where, however, {{GHGheb|text=וָאיחלה}} is probably intended); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=16}} (unless {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֲח׳}} should be read), 139:8 f. After the 3rd person, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=17}} ''though it be dark'', &c. So perhaps also {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=22|verse=38}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶרְדְּפָה|translate=if I determined to pursue, then}} ..., but cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=38}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|108|f}}
(''c'') Likewise in the apodosis of conditional sentences, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=7}} f. ''if my step hath turned out of the way'' ..., {{GHGheb|text=אֶזְרְעָה|translate=then let me sow}}; cf. 16:4 f. ''I also could speak as ye do, if ...!'' So even when the condition must be supplied from the context, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=40|verse=6}} ''else would I declare and speak of them''; 51:18 ''else would I'' (''gladly'') ''give it'', i.e. if thou didst require it (cf. the precisely similar {{GHGheb|text=וְאֶשָּׂא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=55|verse=13}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=10}}. In the 1st plur. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=10}}. To the same category belong the cohortatives after the formula expressing a wish {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יִתֵּן}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יִתְּנֵ֫נִי}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=9|verse=1}} ''oh, that I had'' ..., {{GHGheb|text=וְאֶֽעֶזְבָה|translate=then}} (i.e. if I had) ''should I'' (or ''would I'') ''leave my people'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=29}}; without {{GHGterm|Wāw}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=27|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=55|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=4}} (cf. also verse 7).

{{GHGmargin-letter|108|g}}
Rem. 1. The question, whether a resolution formed under compulsion (a ''necessity'') is also expressed by the cohortative (so, according to the prevailing opinion, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=38|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵלֵ֫כָה}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, 21, 6:10, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=55|verse=3}}, 18 (?); 57:5, where, however, with Hupfeld, {{GHGheb|text=שָֽׁכְבָה}} should be read; 77:7, 88:16, and in the 1st plur. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=59|verse=10}}), is to be answered in the sense that in these examples the cohortative ''form'' is used after its meaning has become entirely lost, merely for the sake of its fuller sound, instead of the ordinary imperfect. This view is strongly<section end=par108 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

345.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="100.7.116.115" /></noinclude><section begin="par108" />supported by the rather numerous examples of cohortative forms after {{GHGterm|wāw consec.}} of the imperfect (cf. {{GHGpar|49|e}}, as also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=66|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=שָׁם נִשְׂמְחָה|translate=there did we rejoice}}<ref>Analogous to this cohortative (as equivalent to the imperfect) after {{GHGheb|text=שָׁם}} is the use of the historic imperf. after {{GHGheb|text=אָז}}, {{GHGpar|107|c}}.</ref>; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=163}} {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֲתַעֵ֑בָה}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=7|verse=7}}), which can likewise only be explained as forms chosen merely for euphony, and therefore due to considerations of rhythm.

{{GHGmargin-letter|108|h}}
2. The cohortative is strange after {{GHGheb|text=עַד־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=17}} ''until I went''... {{GHGheb|text=אָבִ֫ינָה|translate=I considered their latter end}}; possibly a pregnant construction for ‘until I made up my mind, saying, I will consider’, &c. (but {{GHGheb|text=אָבִ֫ינָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=7|verse=7}} is still dependent on the preceding {{GHGheb|text=וָ}}); {{GHGheb|text=עַד־אַרְגִּ֫יעָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=12|verse=19}} is at any rate to be explained in the same way (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=50|verse=44|hidebook=1}} we have {{GHGheb|text=כִּי־א׳}} with a similar meaning), ''as long as I'' (intentionally) ''wink with the eyelashes'' (shall wink). On the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=30}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲכַפֵּר}} is to be read, with the Samaritan, instead of {{GHGheb|text=אֲכַפְּרָה}} after {{GHGheb|text=אוּלַי}}.
<section end="par108" />
<section begin="par109" />{{GHGpar-heading|109|Use of the Jussive}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|109|a}}
As the ''cohortative'' is used in the 1st pers., so the {{GHGterm|jussive}} is especially found in the 2nd and 3rd pers. sing. and plur. to express a more or less definite desire that something should or should not happen (cf. for its form, which frequently coincides with that of the ordinary {{GHGterm|imperfect}},<ref>With regard to verbs {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}, it is true that the full form of the imperfect is frequently used with the meaning of the jussive (as also for the cohortative, see {{GHGpar|108|a}}, note 2), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַל־יִרְאֶה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=9}} (but previously {{GHGheb|text=יְקַו|translate=let it look for!}}):especially ''in'' ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=2|verse=3}}) and immediately ''before'' the principal pause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=תֵּֽרָאֶה}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=39}} {{GHGheb|text=יִהְֽיֶה}}, but previously {{GHGheb|text=יְהִי־נָא}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=תֵּֽרָאֶה}}, previously {{GHGheb|text=תִּגָּל}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=109|verse=7}}. On the attempt to distinguish such jussives from the imperfect by means of a special meaning {{GHGheb|text=־ֵה}}, see {{GHGpar|75|hh}}.</ref> {{GHGpar|48|f}}, g). More particularly its uses may be distinguished as follows:

1. The {{GHGterm|jussive}} standing alone, or co-ordinated with another jussive:

{{GHGmargin-letter|109|b}}
(''b'') In affirmative sentences to express a command, a wish (or a blessing), advice, or a request; in the last case (the optative or precative) it is frequently strengthened by the addition of {{GHGheb|text=נָא}}. Examples: {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=יְהִי אוֹר|translate=let there be light!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=6}}, 9, 11, &c. (the creative commands); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=6|verse=26}} ''the Lord lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace!'' cf. verse 25. After particles expressing a wish, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=34}} {{GHGheb|text=לוּ יְהִי}} ''I would it might be;'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=81|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־תִּשְׁמַע־לִי|translate=if thou wouldest hearken unto me!}} As a humble request, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=33}}... {{GHGheb|text=יֵֽשֶׁב־נָא עַבְדְּךָ... וְהַנַּ֫עַי יַ֫עַל|translate=let thy servant, I pray thee, abide}}, &c., ''and let the lad go up, &c.'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=4}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|109|c}}
(''b'') In negative sentences to express prohibition or dissuasion, warning, a negative wish (or imprecation), and a request. The prohibitive particle used before the jussive (according to {{GHGpar|107|o}}) is almost always {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} (in negative desires and requests frequently<section end="par109" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

346.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par109 />{{GHGheb|text=אַל־נָא}}); e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=34|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ אַל־יֵרָא|translate=neither let any man be seen!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=3|verse=7}} ''be not'' ({{GHGheb|text=אַל־תְּהִי}}) ''wise in thine own eyes!'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=31}} {{GHGheb|text=אַל־ יַֽאֲמֵן|translate=ne confidat}}. In the form of a request (prayer), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=9|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=אַל־תַּשְׁחֵת|translate=destroy not!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=27|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=69|verse=18|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|109|d}}
Rem. 1. The few examples of {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} with the jussive could at most have arisen from the attempt to moderate subsequently by means of the jussive (voluntative) form what was at first intended to be a strict command ({{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} with imperf. indic.); probably, however, they are either cases in which the defective writing has been misunderstood (as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=48|verse=14}}), or (as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=8}}) instances of the purely rhythmical jussive form treated below, under ''k''. Moreover, cf. {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יוֹסֵף}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=2|verse=2}} and from the same verb {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=12}} (unless it is to be referred to ''h'') and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=13|verse=1}}. The same form, however, appears also to stand three times for the cohortative (see below), and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=19}} for the ordinary imperfect (but see below, i). Thus it is doubtful whether an imaginary by-form of the ordinary imperf. is not intended by the Masora in all these cases, and whether consequently {{GHGheb|text=יוֹסִף}}, &c., should not be restored.—On {{GHGheb|text=לֹֽא־תָחוֹס עֵֽינְךָ}}, &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=7|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=13|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=5|verse=11}}, &c., cf. {{GHGpar|72|r}}, according to which {{GHGheb|text=תָחוּס}} should probably be read in every case.—The jussive appears in the place of the cohortative after {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=36}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְלֹֽא־נַשְׁאֵר}} co-ordinated with two cohortatives), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=17|verse=12}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=23}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}} ({{GHGheb|text=ונרא}}, i.e. {{GHGheb|text=וְנֵ֫רֶא}}, after another cohortative); also (see above) {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אֹסֵף}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=18|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=9|verse=15}}, and even without {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=5|verse=16}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|109|e}}
2. {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} with the jussive (or imperf., cf. {{GHGpar|107|p}}) is used sometimes to express the conviction that something cannot or should not happen; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=9}} (where, however, the text is very doubtful) {{GHGheb|text=וְאַל־תִּשָּׂא לָהֶם|translate=and thou canst not possibly forgive them}} [R.V. ''therefore forgive them not'']; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=34|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=41|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=50|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=121|verse=3|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=אַל־יִתֵּן}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=3|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=אַל־תִּירָא|translate=neither needest thou be afraid}}; 20:17, 40:32.

{{GHGmargin-letter|109|f}}
2. The jussive depending on other moods, or in conditional sentences:

(''a'') Depending<ref>This does not include the cases in which the jussive is not logically dependent on a preceding imperat., but is merely co-ordinated, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=27|verse=14}}, &c.</ref> (with {{GHGterm|Wāw}}) on an imperative or cohortative to express an intention or an assurance of a contingent occurrence, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=51}} ''take her and go, and let her be'' ({{GHGheb|text=וּתְהִי}} prop. ''and she will be'')...; 30:3, 31:37, 38:24, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=8|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=14|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=4|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=5|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=7|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=21|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=144|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=20|verse=22}}, Jb 14<sub>6</sub>. Also after interrogative sentences, which include a demand, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=7|verse=2}} (say) ''what is thy desire''..., {{GHGheb|text=וְתֵעָשׂ|translate=and it shall}} (i.e. in order that it may) ''be granted!'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=19|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=34}}f. Depending on a cohortative, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=20}} {{GHGheb|text=אִמָּֽלְטָה נָּא שָׁ֫פָּה|translate=oh, let me escape thither}}...{{GHGheb|text=וּתְחִי נַפְשִׁי}} ''that my soul may live;'' even after a simple imperf. (cf. below, g), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=33}} ''whosoever would, he consecrated him'' ... {{GHGheb|text=וִיהִי|translate=that he might be a priest}} (read {{GHGheb|text=כֹּהֵן}}) ''of the high places'', but probably the LXX reading {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}} is to be preferred.<section end=par109 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

347.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par109 />{{GHGmargin-letter|109|g}}
Rem. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=35|verse=21}} a negative final clause with {{GHGheb|text=וְאַל־}} is dependent on an imperative, ''forbear from'' (meddling with) ''God''... ''that he destroy thee not''. As a rule, however, negative final clauses are attached to the principal sentence by means of {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא}} and a following imperfect; so after an imperative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=14|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=44|hidebook=1}}; after a jussive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=30|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=6|verse=9}}; after a perfect consec., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=35}}, 43, 30:12, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=18|verse=5}}; after {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} with an imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=10|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=18|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=17|verse=17}} ''neither shall he multiply wives unto himself'' ({{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ}}) ''that his heart turn not away''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=21|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=11|verse=21}}; after {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} with jussive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=10|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=11|verse=43|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=16|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=25|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=37|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=38|verse=24|hidebook=1}} f.; after the asseverative {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} with the impft., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=23}}; even after a simple imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=4}} ''with nails''... ''they fasten it'' ({{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא יָפִיק}}) ''that it move not''; after a participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=7}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|109|h}}
(''b'') Frequently in conditional sentences (as in Arabic), either in the protasis or in the apodosis, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=45|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=יִתְאַו|translate=should he desire}}... ''then''...; 104:20 {{GHGheb|text=תָּ֫שֶׁת... וִיהִי|translate=if thou makest darkness, then it is night}}; so also in the protasis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=22|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=15|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=14|verse=7}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְיַ֫עַל}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=29}}; in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=7|verse=9}} ''then will it'' (not, ''then shall it'') ''become a serpent''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=9|verse=9}} after an imperat. in the protasis; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=28|hidebook=1}}. In a negative apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=12}} ({{GHGheb|text=לֹֽא־תֹסֵף}}, but see above, d). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=אַל־יֽוֹשִׁעֵךְ}} (''if the Lord do not help thee'', &c.) is to be explained as a jussive in a negative protasis.

{{GHGmargin-letter|109|i}}
Rem. Undoubtedly this use of the jussive (in conditional sentences) is based on its original ''voluntative'' meaning; let something be so and so, then this or that must happen as a consequence. Certain other examples of the {{GHGterm|jussive}}, however, show that in the consciousness of the language the ''voluntative'' has in such cases become weakened almost to a ''potential'' mood, and hence the {{GHGterm|jussive}} serves to express facts which may happen ''contingently'', or may be expected, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=19}} ({{GHGheb|text=מַה־יּׄסֵף}}, but cf. above, d); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=33}} ''there is no daysman betwixt us, that might lay'' ({{GHGheb|text=יָשֵׁת}}, hence plainly a ''subjunctive=qui ponat''; also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=נִֽיכַזֵּב|translate=that he should lie}} is probably intended as a jussive); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=5|verse=14}}; so after interrogative sentences, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=9|verse=11}} ''who is the wise man'', {{GHGheb|text=וְיָבֵן|translate=qui intelligat hoc}}?; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=14|verse=10}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|109|k}}
Moreover, in not a few cases, the jussive is used, without any collateral sense, for the ordinary imperfect form, and this occurs not alone in forms, which may arise from a misunderstanding of the defective writing, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=21}}, 36, 32:8, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=12|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=3|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=5|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=11|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=21|verse=2|hidebook=1}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} ({{GHGheb|text=מַה־יָּ֫גֶל}}, {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}} {{GHGheb|text=יָגִיל}}), 25:9, 47:4, 90:3, 91:4, 107:29, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=15|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=33|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=18|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=37|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=33|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=36|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=12|verse=6}} (verse 7 {{GHGheb|text=יָשֹׁב}}, but immediately afterwards {{GHGheb|text=תָּשׁוּב}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=8|verse=12}}, —but also in shortened forms, such as {{GHGheb|text=יְהִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=17}} (Sam; {{GHGheb|text=יִהְיֶה}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=5|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=6|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=11|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=1|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=2|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=9|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=72|verse=16}} f. (after other jussives), 104:31, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=18|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, 26, 28, 27:8, 33:21, 34:37, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=4}}. This use of the jussive can hardly be due merely to poetic licence, but is rather to be explained on rhythmical grounds. In all the above-cited examples, in fact, the jussive stands at the beginning of the sentence (and hence removed as far as possible from the principal tone), in others it is immediately before the principal pause ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=50|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=68|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=23|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=24|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=40|verse=19|hidebook=1}}), or actually ''in'' pause ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt.|chapter=32|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=9}}, 11, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|verse=50}}), and is then a simply rhythmical shortening due to the strong influence of the tone. Moreover, since the jussive in numerous cases is not distinguished in form from the imperfect ({{GHGpar|48|g}}), it is frequently doubtful which of the two the writer intended. This especially applies to those cases, in which a ''subjunctive'' is to be expressed by one or other of the forms (cf. {{GHGpar|107|k}} and m–x).<section end=par109 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

348.text:
{{GHGpar-heading|110|The Imperative}}
Mayer Lambert, ‘Sur la syntaxe de l’impératif en hébreu,’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|REJ.|Revue des Études Juives. Paris, 1880 ff.}}}} 1897, p. 106 ff.
{{GHGmargin-letter|110|a}} '''1.''' The imperative,On the close relation between the imperative and jussive (both in meaning and form), cf. § 46 and {{GHGpar|48|i}}. which, according to § 46, is restricted to the 2nd pers. sing. and plur., and to ''positive'' commands, &c., may stand either alone, or in simple co-ordination (as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=44}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=56|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=65|verse=18|hidebook=1}}) with other imperatives: (''a'') To express real commands, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=1}} ''get thee out of thy country''; or (like the jussive) mere admonitions ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=10|verse=12}}) and requests, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=3}}; on the addition of {{GHGheb|text=נָא}} see below, Rem. 1. The imperative is used in the sense of an ironical challenge (often including a threat) in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=22}} ''ask for him the kingdom also''; 22:15, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=10|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=12}} (with {{GHGheb|text=נָא}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=7|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=20|verse=39}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=3}}f., 40:10ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|verse=21}}. The imperative has a concessive sense in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=3|verse=15}} (though thou ''make thyself many'', &c.), and in the cases discussed under ''f'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=9}} f., 29:9. {{GHGmargin-letter|110|b}} (''b'') To express permission, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=23}} after previous dissuasion, (then) ''run'' (as far as I am concerned)! {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=11|hidebook=1}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|110|c}} (''c'') To express a distinct assurance (like our expression, ''thou shalt have it'')Like the threatening formulae in the Latin comic writers, e.g. ''vapula'', Ter. Phorm. v. 6, 10=''vapulare te iubeo'', Plaut. Curc. vi. 4, 12. or promise, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=65|verse=18}} ''but be ye glad'', &c. (i.e. ye will have continually occasion to be glad); and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=110|verse=2}}; in a threat, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=19}}. So especially in commands, the fulfilment of which is altogether out of the power of the person addressed, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=54|verse=14}} ''be far from anxiety'' (meaning, thou needst not fear any more); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=28}}, &c. (for other examples, such as {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=13}}, see below, f). Most clearly in the case of the {{GHGterm|imperative Niphʿal}} with a passive meaning, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=וְאַתֶּם הֵאָֽסְרוּ|translate=and ye shall be bound}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=50}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=9}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=22}}, see below, f). {{GHGmargin-letter|110|d}} Rem. 1. The particle {{GHGheb|text=נָא|translate=age!}} (§ 105) is frequently added to the imperative, as to the jussive, sometimes to soften down a command, or to make a request in a more courteous form (see above, a), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, sometimes to strengthen an exhortation uttered as a rebuke or threat ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=10|hidebook=1}}) or in ridicule ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=12}}). {{GHGmargin-letter|110|e}} 2. The imperative after the desiderative particle {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=13}} (at the end of verses 5 and 14 also read {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} for {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ}} and join it to the following imperative) is due to an anacoluthon. Instead of the imperfect which would be expected here after {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}}, the more forcible imperative is used in a new sentence. {{GHGmargin-letter|110|f}} '''2.''' The imperative in logical dependence upon a preceding imperative, jussive (or cohortative), or an interrogative sentence, serves to

349.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par110 />express the distinct assurance or promise that an action or state will ensue as the certain consequence of a previous action. So especially:

(''a'') The imperative when depending (with {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}}) upon another imperative. In this case the first imperative contains, as a rule, a condition, while the second declares the consequence which the fulfilment of the condition will involve. The imperative is used for this declaration, since the consequence is, as a matter of fact, intended or desired by the speaker (cf. ''divide et impera''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=זֹאת עֲשׂוּ וִֽחְיוּ|translate=this do, and live}}, i.e. thus shall ye continue to live. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=36|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=22|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְהִוָּֽשְׁעוּ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=6|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=4}}, 6, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=37|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=3|verse=3}}f., 4:4, 7:2, 13:20 {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=2|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=20|verse=20}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=25|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=21}} {{GHGheb|text=נָא}} is added to the first imperative. In other cases, the first imperative contains a mocking concession, the second an irrevocable denunciation, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=רֹ֫עוּ עַמִּים וָחֹ֫תּוּ}} (continue to) ''make an uproar, O ye peoples, and ye shall be broken in pieces''; cf. verse 9 ''b''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|110|g}}
Rem. 1. If a promise or threat dependent on an imperative be expressed in the 3rd pers. then the jussive is naturally used instead of the 2nd imperative {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=55|verse=2|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|110|h}}
2. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=20|verse=13}} the second imperative (containing a promise) is attached by asyndeton; elsewhere two imperatives occur side by side without the copula, where the second might be expected to be subordinated to the first, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=24}} {{GHGheb|text=הָחֵל רָשׁ}} (where {{GHGheb|text=רָשׁ}} is virtually, as it were, an object to {{GHGheb|text=הָחֵל}}) ''begin, take in possession'' for ''to take in possession'' (cf., however, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=הֽוֹאֶל־נָא וְלִין|translate=be content, I pray thee, and tarry all night}}, and on this kind of co-ordination in general, cf. {{GHGpar|120|d}}). But such imperatives as {{GHGheb|text=(לְכוּ) לֵךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=(ק֫וּמוּ) קוּם}}, when immediately preceding a second imperative, are for the most part only equivalent to interjections, ''come! up!''

{{GHGmargin-letter|110|i}}
(''b'') The imperative, when depending (with {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}}) upon a jussive (cohortative), or an interrogative sentence, frequently expresses also a consequence which is to be expected with certainty, and often a consequence which is intended, or in fact an intention; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=7}} ''and he shall pray for thee'', {{GHGheb|text=וֶחְֽיֵה|translate=and thou shalt live}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=14|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=128|verse=5}} ''the Lord bless thee ... so that'' (or ''in order that'') ''thou seest'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=4|verse=11|hidebook=1}}; after a cohortative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=45|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהוֹצֵא|translate=that thou mayest bring forth}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=12|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=12}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=35|verse=15}} (after imperative and jussive); after an interrogative sentence, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=21|verse=3}} ''wherewith shall I make atonement'', {{GHGheb|text=וּבָֽרֲכוּ|translate=that ye may bless}}, &c.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=5|verse=19}} the imperative without {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} (in 32:23 with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}) is used after a conditional clause in the sense of a definite promise.

{{GHGmargin-letter|110|k}}
Rem. The ''2nd sing. masc.'' occurs in addressing feminine persons in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=20}} ({{GHGheb|text=עֲמֹד}}, according to Qimḥi an infinitive, in which case, however, the infinitive absolute {{GHGheb|text=עָמֹד}} should be read; but probably we should simply read {{GHGheb|text=עִמְדִי}} with Moore), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=1|verse=13}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=13|verse=7}} (after {{GHGheb|text=עוּרִי}}); and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=23|verse=1}}, the ''2nd plur. masc.'' (On<section end=par110 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

350.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par110 /><section begin=par110 />the four forms of the ''2nd fem. plur. imperative'' in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=11}}, erroneously explained here in former editions, see now {{GHGpar|48|i}}). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=3|verse=15}} the interchange of masc. and fem. serves to express totality (the nation in all its aspects). Cf., moreover, {{GHGpar|145|p}} on other noticeable attempts to substitute the corresponding masculine forms for the feminine.<section end=par110 />

<section begin=par111 />{{GHGpar-heading|111|The Imperfect with Wāw Consecutive}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|a}}
'''1.''' The {{GHGterm|imperfect}} with {{GHGterm|wāw consecutive}} ({{GHGpar|49|a}}–g) serves to express actions, events, or states, which are to be regarded as the temporal or logical sequel of actions, events, or states mentioned immediately<ref>On an apparent exception (the ''imperf. consec.'' at the beginning of whole books) see {{GHGpar|49|b}} note.</ref> before. The {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} is used in this way most frequently as the ''narrative tense'', corresponding to the Greek ''aorist'' or the Latin ''historic perfect''. As a rule the narrative is introduced by a perfect, and then continued by means of imperfects with {{GHGterm|wāw consecutive}} (on this interchange of tenses cf. {{GHGpar|49|a}}, and especially {{GHGpar|112|a}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=1}} ''now the serpent was'' ({{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}}) ''more subtil... and he said'' ({{GHGheb|text=וַיֹּאמֶר}}) ''unto the woman;'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=9 ff.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=9 f.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=12 ff. 27 ff.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=5 f.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=1 f.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=1 f.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=1 ff.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=1 f.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=19 ff.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=36|verse=2 ff.|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=2|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|b}}
Rem. 1. To this class belong some of the numerous ''imperfects consec.'' after various expressions of time, whenever such expressions are equivalent in meaning to a perfect<ref>Cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=4}}, where the ''imperf. consec.'' is joined to an abrupt statement of the cause, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=36|verse=7}}, where it is joined to an abrupt statement of the place.</ref> (viz. {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה|translate=it came to pass}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=1}} ''in the year that king Uzziah died, I saw'' ({{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֶרְאֶה}}), &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=34|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=57|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=21|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=11|verse=1}}; on the use of {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}} to connect expressions of time, see below, g.—It is only in late books or passages that we find the simple {{GHGterm|perfect}} in a clause following an expression of time, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=55}} (cf. Driver on the passage), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=12|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=15|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=10|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=15|verse=19|hidebook=1}}; the {{GHGterm|Perfect}} after {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} and the subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=7|verse=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|c}}
2. The continuation of the narrative by means of the imperfect consec. may result in a series of any number of such imperfects, e.g. there are forty-nine in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn.|chapter=1}}. As soon, however, as the connecting {{GHGterm|Wāw}} becomes separated from the verb to which it belongs, by the insertion of any word, the perfect necessarily takes the place of the imperfect, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=5}} ''and God called'' ({{GHGheb|text=וַיִּקְרָא}}) ''the light Day, and the darkness he called'' ({{GHGheb|text=וְלַח֫שֶׁךְ קָרָא}}) ''Night''; verse 10, 2:20, 11:3 and frequently.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|d}}
3. Of two co-ordinate ''imperfects consecutive'' the former (as equivalent to a temporal clause) is most frequently subordinate in sense to the latter, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=8 f.}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּרְא עֵשָׂו... וַיֵּ֫לֶךְ|translate=when Esau saw that..., he went}}, &c.; so also, frequently {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּשְׁמַע}}, &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=21}}, &c. On the other hand, a second {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} is seldom used in an explanatory sense, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=10}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַתֹּ֫אמֶר|translate=for she said}}); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=7|verse=12}}. Other examples of the imperfect consecutive, which apparently represent a progress in the narrative, in reality only refer to the same time, or explain what precedes, see {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=25}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַיִּֽהְיוּ|translate=they were}}; but {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=4|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=8}} ''they are''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=36|verse=14}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַתֵּ֫לֶד}}), 36:32 ({{GHGheb|text=וַיִּמְלֹךְ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=44}}.<section end=par111 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

351.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par111" />{{GHGmargin-letter|111|e}}
4. The imperfect consecutive sometimes has such a merely ''external'' connexion with an immediately preceding perfect, that in reality it represents an antithesis to it, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=31}} ''and'' (''yet'') ''my life is preserved''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=8}} ''and yet thou chargest me''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=32|verse=3|hidebook=1}}; similarly in dependence on noun-clauses, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=30|verse=25 ff.}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|f}}
'''2.''' The introduction of independent narratives, or of a new section of the narrative, by means of an {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}}, likewise aims at a connexion, though again loose and external, with that which has been narrated previously. Such a connexion is especially often established by means of {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}} (καὶ ἐγένετο) ''and it came to pass'', after which there then follows either (most commonly) an {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=3}}, 8, 8:6, 11:2, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=13|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, &c.), or {{GHGterm|Wāw}} with the perfect (separated from it), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=30|hidebook=1}}, or even a perfect without {{GHGterm|Wāw}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=1|hidebook=1}}f., 40:1, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=41}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=10|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=8|verse=21}}, &c.), or finally a noun-clause introduced by {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|g}}
Rem. 1. This loose connexion by means of {{GHGheb|text=ויתי}}<ref>Exhaustive statistics of the use of {{GHGheb|text=ויהי}} in its many and various connexions are given by König in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1899, p. 260 ff.</ref> is especially common, when the narrative or a new section of it begins with any expression of time, see above, b; cf., in addition to the above-mentioned examples (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=1}} ''and it came to pass after these things, that God did prove Abraham''), the similar cases in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=34}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=11|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=1}}. Elsewhere the statement of time is expressed by {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} or {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}} with an infinitive ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, 29 39:13, 15:18f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=25}}) or by an independent sentence with the perfect (equivalent to a pluperfect, cf. {{GHGpar|106|f}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=30|hidebook=1}}, or by a temporal clause introduced by {{GHGheb|text=כִּי|translate=when}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=16}}, {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽאֲשֶׁר|translate=when}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֵאָזּ|translate=from the time that}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=5}}; or, finally, by a noun-clause (cf. {{GHGpar|116|u}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=13|verse=21}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי הֵם קֹֽבְרִים אִישׁ|translate=and it came to pass, as they were}} (just) ''burying a man'' (prop. they burying), ''that''...; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=35}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=11}} (the apodosis in both these cases being introduced by {{GHGheb|text=וְהִנֵּה}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=7|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=5}}, 26, 19:37 (={{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=38}}).—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=11|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=2|hidebook=1}} a noun standing absolutely follows {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}} (as the equivalent of a complete sentence; see below, h), and then an {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} follows.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|h}}
2. Closely related to the cases noticed in ''g'' are those in which the {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}}, even without a preceding {{GHGheb|text=ויחי}}, introduces the apodosis either— (''a'') to whole sentences, or (''b'') to what are equivalent to whole sentences, especially to nouns standing absolutely. As in certain cases of the {{GHGterm|perfect consecutive}} (see {{GHGpar|112|x}}), so the {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} has here acquired a sort of independent force. Cf. for (''a'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=23}} ''because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord'', {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּמְאָֽסְךָ|translate=he hath rejected thee}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=48|verse=4}}, where the causal clause precedes in the form of an infinitive with preposition), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=21}};
