for (''b'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=24}} {{GHGheb|text=וּפִֽילַגְשׁוֹ|translate=and}} (as to) ''his concubine''..., {{GHGheb|text=וַתֵּ֫לֶד|translate=she bare}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=38|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=36}}f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=4|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=41|hidebook=1}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}, 21:16, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=9|verse=20}}f., 12:17, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=25|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=6|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=28|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=33|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=44|verse=25|hidebook=1}}<ref>Cf. the ''Mêšaʿ'' inscription, l. 5 (''Omri'') ''the king of Israel'', {{GHGheb|text=ויענו|translate=he oppressed Moab}}, &c.—The peculiar imperfect consecutive in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=27}} b (in the earlier editions explained as equivalent to an object-clause) arises rather from a pregnant brevity of expression: ''I have observed and'' have come to the conclusion, ''the Lord hath blessed me'', &c.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=34}} read, with LXX, {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}} before {{GHGheb|text=כִּשְׁמֹעַ}}.</ref>—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=15|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=16|verse=14}} the preceding noun, used absolutely, is even regarded as the object of the following imperfect consecutive, and is therefore introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}}.<section end="par111" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

352.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par111 />{{GHGmargin-letter|111|i}}
'''3.''' The {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} serves, in the cases treated under ''a–h'', to represent either expressly, or at least to a great extent, a ''chronological'' succession of actions or events; elsewhere it expresses those actions, &c., which represent the logical consequence of what preceded, or a result arising from it by an inherent necessity. Thus the {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} is used—

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|k}}
(''a'') As a final summing up of the preceding narrative, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=20|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּ֫קָם הַשָּׂדֶה וג׳|translate=so}} (in this way) ''the field became'' (legally) ''the property of Abraham'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=50}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=31|verse=6|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|l}}
(''b'') To express a logical or necessary consequence of that which immediately precedes, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=2|verse=3}} ''and he still holdeth fast his integrity'', {{GHGheb|text=וַתְּסִיתֵ֫נִי וג׳|translate=so that thou thus}} (as it now appears) ''groundlessly movedst me against him''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=65|verse=9}} ''so that they are afraid'' ...; even a consequence which happens conditionally, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=וַתְּהִי|translate=so that my mother should have been}} ... Another instance of the kind perhaps (if the text be correct) is {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=38|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּ֫מָת|translate=so that he dies}} (must die).

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|m}}
Rem. Such consecutive clauses frequently occur after interrogative sentences, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=51|verse=12}} ''who art thou'' (i.e. art thou ''so helpless''), {{GHGheb|text=וַהִּֽירְאִי|translate=that thou art}} (''must needs be'') ''afraid''? {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=144|verse=3}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=8|verse=5}}, where in a very similar context {{GHGheb|text=כִּי|translate=that}} is used with the imperfect); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=19}} ({{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֶקַּח}}); 31:27 {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֲשַׁלֵּֽחֲךָ|translate=so that I might have sent thee away}}.

'''4.''' As regards the range of time it is to be carefully noticed—

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|n}}
(''a'') That the {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} may represent all varieties in the relations of tense and mood, which, according to {{GHGpar|107|a}}, follow from the idea of the imperfect;

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|o}}
(''b'') That the more precise determination of the range of time to which an {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} relates must be inferred in each case from the character of the preceding tense (or tense-equivalent), to which it is attached, in a more or less close relation, as temporal or logical sequence. Thus the {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} serves—

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|p}}
(1) To represent actions, events, or states, which are ''past'' (or were repeated in past time), when it is united with tenses, or their equivalents, which refer to an actual past.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|q}}
Cf. the examples given above, under ''a'' and ''f'', of the imperfect consecutive as an historic tense. The imperfect consecutive also frequently occurs as the continuation of a perfect (''preterite'') in a subordinate clause; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=37}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=8|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=11|verse=33|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, &c.; also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּבְחָרֶ֫ךָּ}} is the continuation of a preterite, contained, according to the sense, in the preceding {{GHGheb|text=נִֽאֱמָן}}. {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=26}}, 34 the imperfect consecutive is joined to an imperfect denoting the past in a conditional sentence. An imperfect consecutive occurs in dependence on a perfect which has the sense of a pluperfect ({{GHGpar|106|f}}), e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=6|hidebook=1}}f., 31:19, 34 (''now Rachel had taken the teraphim'', {{GHGheb|text=וַתְּשִׂמֵם|translate=and had }}<section end=par111 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

353.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par111" />''put them'', &c.); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=39|verse=1}}. Finally there are the cases in which an infinitival or participial construction representing past time, according to {{GHGpar|113|r}}, {{GHGpar|116|x}}, is taken up and continued by an imperfect consecutive.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|r}}
(2) To represent ''present'' actions, &c., in connexion with tenses, or their equivalents, which describe actions and states as being either present or lasting on into the present (continuing in their effect); so especially,

(α) In connexion with the present perfects, described in {{GHGpar|106|g}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=16|verse=9}} ''therefore my heart is glad'' ({{GHGheb|text=שָׂמַח}}) ''and my glory rejoiceth'' ({{GHGheb|text=וַיָּ֫גֶל}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=16}} (parallel with a simple imperfect). Cf. also such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=29|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיֵּ֫שֶׁב}} (prop. he sat down, ''and has been enthroned'' ever since), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=41|verse=13}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|s}}
(β) In connexion with those perfects which represent experiences frequently confirmed (see {{GHGpar|106|k}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=14|verse=2}} ''he cometh up'' ({{GHGheb|text=יָצָא}}) ''like a flower, and is cut down'' ({{GHGheb|text=וַיִּמָּל}}); ''he fleeth'' ({{GHGheb|text=וַיִּבְרַח}}) ''also as a shadow'', {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא יַֽעֲמוֹד|translate=and continueth not}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=24|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, 11, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=11|verse=2}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|t}}
(γ) In connexion with imperfects which, in one of the ways described in § 107. 2, are used in the sense of the present; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=14|verse=10}} ''but man dieth'' ({{GHGheb|text=יָמוּת}}) ''and becometh powerless'' ({{GHGheb|text=וַיֶּחֱֽלָשׁ}}), &c., i.e. remains powerless; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=8|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=1|verse=9}}f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=55|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=90|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=3|hidebook=1}} (''when thou mockest''), 12:25, 34:24, 37:8 (parallel with a simple imperfect); 39:15. In the apodosis of a conditional sentence, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=59|verse=16}}, so also after an interrogative imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=42|verse=6}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַתֶּֽהֱמִי}} for which in verse 12 and in 43:5 we have {{GHGheb|text=וּמַה־תֶּֽהֱמִי|translate=and why art thou disquieted?}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|u}}
(δ) In dependence on participles, which represent what at present continues or is being repeated, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=2}} ''behold the king weepeth'' ({{GHGheb|text=בֹּכֶה}}) ''and mourneth'' ({{GHGheb|text=וַיִּתְאַבֵּל}}) ''for Absalom''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=5|hidebook=1}}f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=1|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=34|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=20|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=22 ff.}}, but cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=קֹרֵא לֶֽאֱלוֹהַּ|translate=who called upon God}}, {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּֽעֲנֵ֫הוּ|translate=and he answered him}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|v}}
(ε) In dependence on other equivalents of the present, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=51|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=144|verse=3}} (see above, m); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=22}}. So especially as the continuation of an infinitive, which is governed by a preposition (cf. {{GHGpar|144|r}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=92|verse=8}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|w}}
(3) To represent ''future'' actions, &c., in dependence on—(α) an imperfect which refers to the future, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=49|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=94|verse=22|hidebook=1}}f.;—(β) a perfect consecutive, or those perfects which, according to {{GHGpar|106|n}}, are intended to represent future events as undoubtedly certain, and therefore as though already accomplished (''perf. propheticum''); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=15}} (parallel with a simple imperfect separated from {{GHGheb|text=ו}}); 5:16 (cf. 2:11, 17, where the same threat is expressed by the perfect consecutive); 5:25, 9:5, 10f.,<section end="par111" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

354.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="DjR" /></noinclude><section begin="par111"/>13<sup>15.17 ff.</sup>, 22:7 ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=2|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=2|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=33|verse=4}}, 6, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=7|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=64|verse=8|hidebook=1}} ff.;—(γ) a future participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=16}}.<ref>Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=29}} the imperfects consecutive are attached to the threat virtually contained in the preceding imperatives. On the other hand {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּחֵ֫לּוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=8|verse=10}} would be very remarkable as expressing a future; the text is, however, certainly corrupt, and hence the Cod. Babyl. and the Erfurt MS. 3 endeavour to remedy it by {{GHGheb|text=וְיח׳}}, and Ewald reads {{GHGheb|text=וְיָחִלוּ}}—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=28|verse=16}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=15|verse=6}}f.) {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֲחַלֶּלְךָ}} appears to announce an action irrevocably determined upon, and therefore represented as already accomplished; cf. the prophetic perfects in verse 17 ff.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|111|x}}
Rem. An imperfect consecutive in dependence on a perfect or imperfect, which represents an action occurring only conditionally, is likewise used only in a hypothetical sense, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־קָרָ֫אתִי וַיַּֽעֲנֵ֫נִי|translate=if I had called, and he had answered me, yet}} ...; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֹמַר|translate=if I should say}} (previously, in verse 8 f., hypothetical imperfects are used).—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=48|verse=18}}f. an imperfect consecutive occurs in dependence on a sentence expressing a wish introduced by {{GHGheb|text=לוּא|translate=utinam}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי|translate=and it}}, or ''so that it were'', equivalent to ''then should it be''). Cf. also the examples mentioned above, under ''l'' ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=17}}) and ''m'' ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=27}}), where the imperfect consecutive expresses facts occurring ''contingently.''
<section end="par111"/>
<section begin="par112"/>{{GHGpar-heading|112|The Perfect with Wāw Consecutive}}

G. R. Berry, ‘Waw consecutive with the perfect in Hebrew,’ in ''Bibl. Lit.'', xxii. (1903), pp. 60–69.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|a}}
'''1.''' The perfect, like the imperfect (§ 111), is used with {{GHGterm|wāw consecutive}} (cf. {{GHGpar|49|a}}; on the external differentiation of the perfect consecutive by a change in the position of the tone, see {{GHGpar|49|h}}) to express actions, events, or states, which are to be attached to what precedes, in a more or less close relation, as its ''temporal'' or ''logical'' consequence. And as, according to {{GHGpar|111|a}}, the narrative which begins with a perfect, or its equivalent, is continued in the imperfect consecutive, so, vice versa, the perfect consecutive forms the regular continuation to a preceding imperfect, or its equivalent.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|b}}
Rem. 1. This alternation of perfect and imperfect or their equivalents is a striking peculiarity of the ''consecutio temporum'' in Hebrew. It not only affords a certain compensation for the lack of forms for tenses and moods, but also gives to Hebrew style the charm of an expressive variety, an action conceived as being still in progress ({{GHGterm|imperfect}}, &c.), reaching afterwards in the {{GHGterm|perfect}} a calm and settled conclusion, in order to be again exhibited in movement in the imperfect, and vice versa.<ref>It is difficult to give a proper explanation of this phenomenon (according to {{GHGpar|49|a}}, note, to be found only in the Canaanitish group of languages), when we have given up the theory of a special {{GHGterm|wāw conversivum}} in the unscientific sense mentioned in {{GHGpar|49|b}}, note, at the end, and if we accept the fact that the {{GHGterm|perfect}} and {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} cannot possibly be used in a way which contradicts their fundamental character as described in §§ 106 and 107. In other words, even the {{GHGterm|perfect consecutive}} originally represents a finally completed action, &c., just as the {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} represents an action whichis only beginning, becoming or still continuing, and hence in any case incomplete. The simplest view is to suppose, that the use of the {{GHGterm|perfect consecutive}} originated from those cases, in which it had to express the conclusion (or final consequence) of an action which was continued (or repeated) ''in past time'' (see the examples above), and that this use was afterwards extended to other cases, in which it had to represent the temporal or logical consequence of actions, &c., still in progress, and thus in the end a regular interchange of the two tenses became recognized.</ref> The strict regularity of this<section end="par112"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

355.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="DjR" /></noinclude><section begin="par112"/>alternation belongs indeed rather to the higher style, and even then it depends upon the view and intention of the speaker, whether he wishes the action, &c., to be regarded as the logical consequence of what has preceded, or as simply co-ordinate with it, and so in the same tense.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|c}}
2. A succession of any number of other ''perfects consecutive'' may be co-ordinated with a {{GHGterm|perfect consecutive}} (cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=14|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=3}}, four perfects in each case, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=7}} five, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=6|verse=6}}f. eight). It is true, however, of the perfect (as conversely of the {{GHGterm|imperfect}}, {{GHGpar|112|c}}), that as soon as the {{GHGterm|Wāw}} is separated by any intervening word from the verb to which it belongs, an {{GHGterm|imperfect}} necessarily takes the place of the {{GHGterm|perfect}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=12}} ''when the Egyptians shall see thee, they shall say'' ({{GHGheb|text=וְאָֽמְרוּ}}), ''This is his wife: and they will kill me'' ({{GHGheb|text=וְהָֽרְנוּ אֹתִי}}) ''but thee they will save alive'' ({{GHGheb|text=וְאֹתָךְ יְהַיּוּ}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|d}}
'''2.''' The perfect consecutive, like the imperfect consecutive, always belongs to the period of time expressed by the preceding tense, or its equivalent, with which it is connected as the temporal or logical consequence. The particular cases may be classed under three heads: (''a'') the perfect consecutive in ''immediate'' dependence (see e), (''b'') in loose connexion (see x) with the preceding, and (''c'') the perfect consecutive at the beginning of the apodosis to other sentences, or their equivalents (see ff).

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|e}}
'''3.''' The perfect consecutive in immediate dependence on the preceding tense, or its equivalent, serves

(''a'') As a frequentative tense to express ''past'' actions, &c., i.e. actions repeatedly brought to a conclusion in the past, and follows tenses, or their equivalents, representing actions which have ''continued'' or been ''repeated in the past'':

(α) After a simple imperfect, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵד יַֽעֲלֶה|translate=there went up a mist}} (again and again) ''from the earth'', {{GHGheb|text=וְהִשְׁקָה|translate=and watered}} (as it were, ''and ever watered afresh''), &c. This frequentative use of the perfect consecutive is equally evident after frequentative imperfects, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=10}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה|translate=and it became}} again every time; {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}} would mean, and it became so once for all); 29:2f. (four perfects consecutive referring to actions repeated daily); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=7}}–11 {{GHGheb|text=יִקַּח|translate=he used to take}} at each new encampment ''the tent'', {{GHGheb|text=וְנָטָה|translate=and to pitch it}} again every time ''without the camp''; notice, amongst the numerous frequent. perff. consec., the imperf. in vv. 7, 8, 9, 11, always in a frequentative sense; 34:34f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=9|verse=19}}, 21 (among several simple imperfects), 10:17, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=2|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=תַּֽעֲשֶׂה}}<section end="par112"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

356.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par112"/>{{GHGtranslate|she used to make}}... {{GHGheb|text=וְהַֽעַלְתָה|translate=and brought it to him from year to year}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=27|verse=9|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְלָקַח}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=14|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=12|verse=15|hidebook=1}} (in verses 16<sup>f.</sup> imperfects occur again). So also in dependent sentences, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=4}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְיָֽלְדוּ}} as a continuation of {{GHGheb|text=יָבֹאוּ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=29}}.<ref>Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=44|verse=12}} (where Stade, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} v. 293, would read {{GHGheb|text=שֵֽׁרְתוּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּֽהְיוּ}}) the unusual tenses may have been intentionally chosen: {{GHGtranslate|because they continually ministered and so always became afresh}}...</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|f}}
(β) After an imperfect consecutive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=39|verse=3}} (Samaritan {{GHGheb|text=וקצצו}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=5|verse=7}} (? see {{GHGpar|112|rr}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=7|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=2.5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=16|verse=13|hidebook=1}} {{GHGtranslate|and he threw stones at him}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְעִפַּר|translate=and east dust}} continually; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=16|hidebook=1.31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=12|verse=11|hidebook=1 ff. 15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=37|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=5}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|g}}
Rem. The frequentative perfect consecutive is sometimes joined even with imperfects consecutive which simply express one ''single'' action or occurrence in the past; thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=40|verse=31|hidebook=1}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=1}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=14|verse=27}} (cf. verse 28); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=12|verse=10}}. For other examples of a loosely connected frequentative perfect consecutive, see below, {{GHGpar|112|dd|nonumber=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|h}}
(γ) After a perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=3}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְעָשָׂה לוֹ}}, i.e. as often as he needed a new garment)<ref>Driver, on this passage, rightly refers to {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=19}}.</ref>; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=22|verse=6}};<ref>{{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=7}} would also come under this head, if {{GHGheb|text=וְהִמְטַרְתִּ֫י}} is really intended, and the statement refers to the past; {{GHGheb|text=מָנַ֫עְתִּי}} might, however, also be a perfect expressing positive assurance ({{GHGpar|106|m}}), and the passage would then come under {{GHGpar|112|s|nonumber=1}}.</ref> in interrogative sentences, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=9}} {{GHGtranslate|who has ever}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=80|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=1.4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=4|verse=7}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|i}}
(δ) After an infinitive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=1|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=עַל־רָדְפוֹ|translate=because he did pursue his brother}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְשִׁחֵת|translate=and ''(on each occasion)'' did east off all pity}} (then an imperfect consecutive); after an infinitive absolute, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=6|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=23|verse=14}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|k}}
(ε) After a participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=3}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְקָרָא}}), &c., frequentative, as a continuation of {{GHGheb|text=עֹֽמְדִים}}, verse 2); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=17|verse=17}}.<ref>That {{GHGheb|text=וְהָֽלְכָה}}, &c., are frequentatives (''the maidservant used to go repeatedly and tell them'') may be seen from {{GHGheb|text=יֵֽלֵכוּ}} (necessarily an imperfect, since it is separated from {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} by {{GHGheb|text=הֵם}}) and {{GHGheb|text=יֽוּכְלוּ}}; on the other hand in verse 18 {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּרְא}} and {{GHGheb|text=וַיֵּֽלְכוּ}} of actions which happened only once.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|l}}
(ζ) After other equivalents of tenses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=22}} {{GHGtranslate|the priests had a portion from Pharaoh}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְאָֽכְלוּ|translate=and did eat}} (year by year), &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=4|verse=7}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|m}}
(''b'') To express ''present'' actions, &c., as the temporal or logical consequence of actions or events which continue or are repeated in the present, especially such as have, according to experience, been at all times frequently repeated, and may be repeated at any time:

(α) After a simple imperfect, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=24}} {{GHGtranslate|therefore a man leaves}} ({{GHGheb|text=יַֽעֲזֹב|translate=is accustomed to leave}}) ... {{GHGheb|text=וְדָבַק|translate=and cleaves}}, &c., here, as frequently elsewhere, clearly with the secondary idea of purpose, i.e. in order to cleave; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=11}} (if {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה}} is to be taken as a continuation<section end="par112"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

357.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="DjR" /></noinclude><section begin="par112"/>of {{GHGheb|text=יַדְלִיקֵם}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=12|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=4|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=7|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=90|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=14|verse=9}}; also in dependent clauses, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=20|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=8.11 f.}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=19}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|n}}
(β) After a participle, as the equivalent of a sentence representing a contingent action, &c., e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=מַכֵּה אִישׁ וָמֵת}} (instead of {{GHGheb|text=מַכֵּה}} there is in verse 20, &c. {{GHGheb|text=וְכִי יַכֶּה אִישׁ}}) {{GHGtranslate|if one smite a man and ''(so that)'' he die}}, &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=6|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=12}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|o}}
(γ) After an infinitive absolute, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=7|verse=9}} f. {{GHGtranslate|will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery}} (simple infinitives absolute; cf. {{GHGpar|113|ee}}), {{GHGheb|text=וּבָאתֶם|translate=and then come and stand before me... and say}}, &c.; cf. below, {{GHGpar|112|u|nonumber=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|p}}
(''c'') To express {{GHGterm|future}} actions, &c., as the temporal or logical consequence of tenses, or their equivalents, which announce or require such future actions or events. Thus—

(α) After imperfects in the sense of a simple future, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=3}} f. {{GHGheb|text=מִשָּׁם אֲחַפֵּשׂ וּלְקַחְתִּים|translate=I will search and take them out thence}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=7|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=8|verse=6}} f. (also with a change of subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=16}}, &c.); and in interrogative sentences, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=14|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=8|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=41|verse=6}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=11}}; in sentences expressing a wish, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=4}}; as well as in almost all kinds of dependent clauses. Also in conditional clauses after {{GHGheb|text=אִם־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=19|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=11}}, or {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=26}}, or {{GHGheb|text=הֵן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=1}}; in final clauses after {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עַן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=15|verse=40}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=13}}; after {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=25}}, or {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=6}}; in temporal clauses, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=16}}; and in relative clauses, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=26}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|q}}
(β) After the jussive (or an imperfect in the sense of a jussive or optative) or cohortative, with the same or a different subject, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=14}} f. {{GHGheb|text=יְהִי מְאֹרֹת... וְחָיוּ|translate=let there be lights... and let them be}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=44|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=2|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=22|verse=11}}; after a jussive expressing an imprecation, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=109|verse=10}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|r}}
(γ) After an imperative, also with the same or a different subject, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=7|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=לֵךְ וְאָֽמַרְתָּ|translate=go and tell}} (that thou mayst tell), &c., and often, {{GHGterm|perf. consec.}} after {{GHGheb|text=לֵךְ}} (as also the {{GHGterm|perf. consec.}} of {{GHGheb|text=אָמַר}} and {{GHGheb|text=דִּבֶּר}} very frequently follows other imperatives); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=43|hidebook=1}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=3}}, 18, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=48|verse=26}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|s}}
(δ) After perfects which express a definite expectation or assurance (cf. {{GHGpar|106|m}} and n), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=20}} {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה בֵּרַ֫כְתִּי אֹתוֹ וְהִפְרֵתִי אֹתוֹ|translate=behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=14|hidebook=1}}; on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=7}} see above, note 3 on h; in an interrogative sentence, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=13|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|t}}
(ε) After a participle, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=4}} {{GHGtranslate|for yet seven days}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָֽנֹכִי מַמְטִיר|translate=and I will cause it to rain}}... {{GHGheb|text=וּמָחִ֫יתִי|translate=and I will}} (i.e. in order to) {{GHGtranslate|destroy}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=21|verse=9}}; also with a different subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=43}} f. ''the''<section end="par112"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

358.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="DjR" /></noinclude><section begin="par112"/>'' maiden which cometh forth'' ({{GHGheb|text=הַיֹּצֵאת}})... {{GHGheb|text=וְאָֽמַרְתִּי אֵלֶ֫יהָ|translate=to whom I shall say}}..., {{GHGheb|text=וְאָֽמְרָה|translate=and she}} (then) ''shall say'', &c. This use of the perfect consecutive is especially frequent after a participle introduced by {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=17}} f.; with a different subject {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=20|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=6|verse=14}}; after a complete noun-clause introduced by {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} (cf. § 140), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=13}} ''behold, I come'' (i.e. if I shall come)... {{GHGheb|text=וְאָֽמַרְתִּי לָהֶם|translate=and shall say unto them}}..., {{GHGheb|text=וְאָֽמְרוּ|translate=and they}} (then) ''shall say'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=8}} ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=7|hidebook=1}} f., 39:6.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|u}}
(ζ) After an infinitive absolute, whether the infinitive absolute serves to strengthen the finite verb (see {{GHGpar|113|t}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=31|verse=5}}, or is used as an emphatic substitute for a cohortative or imperfect (§ 113 dd and ee), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=2|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=46}} f.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|v}}
(η) After an infinitive construct governed by a preposition (for this change from the infinitive construction to the finite verb, cf. {{GHGpar|114|r}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=עַד־בּוֹאִי אֵלֶ֫יךָ וְהֽוֹדַעְתִּי לְךָ|translate=till I come unto thee}} (prop. until my coming) ''and show thee'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=45|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=39|verse=27}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=37}}, 42.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|w}}
Rem. To the same class belong {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=24}}, where the idea of time precedes, ''until it be evening and'' until ''I be avenged'', &c., and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=8}}, where the idea of place precedes, in both cases governed by {{GHGheb|text=עַד־}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|x}}
'''4.''' The very frequent use of the perfect consecutive in direct dependence upon other tenses (see above, d–v) explains how it finally obtained a kind of independent force—especially for the purpose of announcing future events—and might depend loosely on sentences to which it stood only in a wider sense in the relation of a temporal or logical consequence. Thus the perfect consecutive is used—

(''a'') To announce ''future'' events, &c., in loose connexion with a further announcement, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=30}} {{GHGheb|text=וְקָמוּ}} and two co-ordinate perfects consecutive, equivalent to ''but then shall arise'', &c.; frequently so after {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} with a following substantive ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=8}}), or a participial clause (cf. the analogous instances above, under t), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=31}} ''behold, the days come'', {{GHGheb|text=וְנָֽדַעְתִּי|translate=that I will cut off}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=39|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=8|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, and very often in Jeremiah; after an expression of time, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=17|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=10|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=1|verse=4}}. Further, when joined to a statement concerning present or past facts, especially when these contain the reason for the action, &c., expressed in the perfect consecutive; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=7}} ''lo, this hath touched thy lips'', {{GHGheb|text=וְסָר|translate=therefore thine iniquity shall be taken away}}, &c. (not copulative ''and it is taken away'', since it is parallel with a simple imperfect), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=3}} (here in an adversative sense); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=8|verse=14}}. In loose connexion with a noun-clause, a long succession of perfects consecutive occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=6|verse=6}} ff. Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Amos|chapter=5|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=וּנְשָׁאתֶם}} may be an announcement ''yea, ye shall take up''; but cf. below, rr.<section end="par112"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

359.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="DjR" /></noinclude><section begin="par112"/>{{GHGmargin-letter|112|y}}
Rem. 1. Very frequently the announcement of a future event is attached by means of {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה}}<ref>On the various combinations with {{GHGheb|text=וָהָיָה}} see König’s statistics in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} xix. 272 ff.</ref> ''and it shall come to pass'' (cf. the analogous continuation in the past by means of {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}}, § 111, 2), after which the event announced (sometimes after a long parenthesis) follows in one or more (co-ordinate) perfects consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=12|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה כִי}}=''if'', as in 46:33, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=1|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=22|verse=26|hidebook=1}} and frequently), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=3}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=8|verse=9}}; or in the imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=4|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, 21 ff. (cf. 29:8); or in the jussive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=14|verse=9}}. It very rarely happens that the verb which is thus loosely added, agrees in gender and number with the following subject, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=5|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=42|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהָֽיְתָה}} (before {{GHGheb|text=הַחֶ֫רֶב}}), and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=42|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=וְיִהְיוּ}} (before {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־הָֽאֲנָשִׁים}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|z}}
2. The jussive form {{GHGheb|text=וִיהִי}} occurs (in the sense described in ''y'') instead of {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=5|verse=24}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=14|verse=15}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=14|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=4}}, although in the first three places a jussive is wholly inadmissible in the context, and even in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=4}} (where an admonition follows) {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה}} would be expected (see below, bb). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=14|verse=5}} the form is a textual error, and the pointing should simply be {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}}. In the other passages {{GHGheb|text=ויהי}} (always before an infinitive with a preposition) stands at the beginning of the sentence at an unusually long distance from the principal tone, and hence is certainly to be explained according to {{GHGpar|109|k}}, except that in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=5}}, &c., the simply rhythmical jussive form takes the place, not of the full imperfect form, but (exceptionally) of the perfect consecutive.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|aa}}
(''b'') To introduce a command or wish: {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=10|verse=19}} ''love ye therefore the stranger''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=6}} (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=14}} the precative perfect consecutive, as elsewhere the cohortative, jussive, and imperative, is strengthened by means of {{GHGheb|text=נָא}}). So, also, in loose connexion with participial and other noun-clauses (see above, x), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=45|verse=12}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=2}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=3}} f., 3:9.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=11}} the perfect consecutive ({{GHGheb|text=וּנְמַלְתֶּם|translate=and ye shall be circumcised}}, &c.) is used to explain a preceding command.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|bb}}
Rem. As in the cases mentioned above under ''y'', the connexion may be made by means of {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה}}. Thus with a following perfect consecutive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=46|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=20}}. Cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=14}}, where the real wish, at least as regards the sense, is contained in the next sentence.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|cc}}
(''c'') To introduce a question, whether in loose connexion with another interrogative sentence (see above, p), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=15}} ''art thou my brother'' (equivalent to, ''Surely thou art''), {{GHGheb|text=וַֽעֲבַדְתַּ֫נִי|translate=and shouldest thou then serve me for naught}}? or with a positive statement, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=5|verse=5}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְהִשְׁבַּתֶּם|translate=will ye then make them rest?}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=11}}, and (if it is {{GHGterm|Mil<sup>e</sup>raʿ}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=50|verse=21}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְהֶֽהֱרַשְׁתִּי}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|dd}}
(''d'') To introduce actions frequently repeated hence analogous to the numerous examples of a frequentative perfect consecutive, above, under ''e''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=3}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְעָלָה}} of annual festival journeys); 13:21 (where, however, the text appears radically corrupt); 27:9 ({{GHGheb|text=וְהִכָּה}}, i.e. every time, therefore continued by means of {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא יְחַיֶּה}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=5|verse=7}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְכִלְכְּלוּ}},<section end="par112"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

360.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="DjR" /></noinclude><section begin="par112"/>parallel with a simple imperfect); 9:25, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=25|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=12|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=8|verse=4}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=4}} f. a series of frequentative perfects consecutive is interrupted by an imperfect consecutive, while a simple imperfect (as the ''modus rei repetitae'') forms the conclusion. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=6|verse=17}} a similar perfect is expressly marked, by placing the tone on the final syllable (according to {{GHGpar|49|h}}), as parallel with the real perfects consecutive.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|ee}}
Rem. The loose connexion of ''tempora frequentativa'' by {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה}} (cf. the Rem. on y and bb) is also very common in this sense; thus with a following perfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=41}} f. (but in verse 42''<sup>a</sup>'', where the verb is separated from the {{GHGterm|Wāw}} by an insertion, we find {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יָשִׂים|translate=he used not to put them in}}, according to {{GHGpar|107|e}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=17|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=7|hidebook=1}} ff. (see above, e), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=30|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=23}} (followed by five perfects consecutive); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=5}}; with a following imperfect (as the ''modus rei repetitae''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=2|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=26}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=12|verse=5}} f. {{GHGheb|text=והיה}}, contrary to what would be expected, is continued by means of the imperfect consecutive, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=13|verse=22}} by {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא}} with the perfect (instead of the imperfect).

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|ff}}
'''5.''' Further, the perfect consecutive is very frequently employed with a certain emphasis to introduce the apodosis after sentences (or their equivalents) which contain a condition, a reason, or a statement of time. Such an apodosis, as in the cases already treated, may represent either future events, or commands and wishes, or even events which have been often repeated in the past. Thus—

(''a'') The perfect consecutive occurs in the apodosis to conditional sentences<ref>In a number of the examples of this kind the protasis is already loosely connected by means of {{GHGheb|text=והיה}}, and hence some of them had to be already mentioned above, under y, bb, ee.</ref> ({{GHGpar|159|g}}, o, s):

(α) After {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} with the imperfect, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=4}}b {{GHGheb|text=אִם־יְמִיתֻ֫נוּ וָמָֽתְנוּ|translate=if they kill us}}, (well then) ''we shall but die''; here the perfect consecutive is used obviously with greater emphasis than the imperfect ({{GHGheb|text=נִחְיֶה}}) which immediately precedes; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, 41, 32:9, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=30|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=3|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=4|verse=11}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|gg}}
(β) After {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} with the perfect (in the sense of a ''futurum exactum''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=5|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=20}}, 7<sup>4''a''</sup>, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=4|verse=4}} f.; as precative apodosis after {{GHGheb|text=אִם־נָא}} with the ''perf. preteritum'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=10}}; as a frequentative perfect consecutive, to represent past events in the apodosis after {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} with a perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=4}}; after {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} with imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=8}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|hh}}
(γ) After {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} (''in case, suppose that'') with the imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=58|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=14|verse=13}}.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=19}} a question appears to be expressed by the perfect consecutive, ''for if a man find his enemy, will he let him go well away?'' Probably, however, with Klostermann, {{GHGheb|text=וּמִי}} should be read for {{GHGheb|text=וְכִי}}.</ref> Frequentative with reference to the past, after {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} with frequentative perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=2|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=13}}f.<section end="par112"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

361.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="DjR" /></noinclude><section begin="par112"/>{{GHGmargin-letter|112|ii}}
(δ) After {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} with the imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר יִמָּצֵא אִתּוֹ... וָמֵת|translate=with whomsoever... it be found, let him die}}; with the perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=13}} ''and if a man lie not in wait'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=12}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|kk}}
(ε) Very frequently after a perfect consecutive (one or more) containing the condition, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=29}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהֽוֹרַדְתֶּם}}... {{GHGheb|text=וּלְקַחְתֶּם גַּם־אֶת־זֶה|translate=and if ye take}} (or ''shall have taken'') ''this one also... ye shall bring down'', &c.; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=38|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, 22, 47:30, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=30|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=2|verse=9}}, and probably also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=39|verse=28}}.—Also frequentative in reference to the past, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=34}} f.... {{GHGheb|text=וּבָא הָֽאֲרִי וְיָצָ֫אתִי|translate=and when there came}} (as sometimes happened) ''a lion... I went out'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=10|verse=17}} ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=9}} (the perfects consecutive being regularly continued in the apodosis by {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא}} with an imperfect<ref>In all these examples (not only in the frequentative perfects consecutive) the original idea of the perfect, which also underlies the perfect consecutive, comes out very distinctly. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=29}} (see above) implies in the mind of the speaker, If it ever shall have come to this, that ye ''have taken'' this one also, then ''ye have'' thereby brought me down to Sheol.</ref>).

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|ll}}
Rem. The perfect consecutive may be used also in the protasis to express a condition when the employment of the perfect consecutive in the apodosis has become impossible, owing to an emphatic word having to stand before it; thus in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=14|verse=14}} on account of {{GHGheb|text=הֵ֫מָּה}}; 33:4 on account of {{GHGheb|text=דָּמוֹ}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=52}} the imperfect consecutive, contrary to what might be expected, stands in the apodosis, ''and when Saul saw any... valiant man, he took him unto him'', where {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּֽאַסְפֵ֫הוּ}} suggests the special case, rather than a repeated occurrence; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=2}}. Conversely, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=16}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַיֹּאמֶֹר}} perhaps a mere mistake for {{GHGheb|text=וְאָמַר}}), 17:35 b an imperfect consecutive stands in the protasis.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|mm}}
(ζ) After various equivalents of sentences, which contain a condition; thus, after a substantive standing absolutely, or a participle (a ''casus pendens''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=וְעָרֵל זָכָר... וְנִכְרְתָה וג׳|translate=and the uncircumcised male}} (in case such an one be found), ''he shall be cut off'', &c.; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=13}}, and (after an infinitive with a preposition) {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=7|verse=14}}; in a wider sense also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=4|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=44|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=56|verse=5|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|nn}}
(''b'') The perfect consecutive serves as the apodosis to causal clauses; thus e.g. after {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן כִּי}} with the perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=16}} f.; after {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן אֲשֶׁר}} with perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=20|verse=28}}; after {{GHGheb|text=עֵ֫קֶב}} with perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=24}}; also after what are equivalent to causal clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=25|verse=11}} ({{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עַן שִׁמְךָ... וְסָֽלַחְתָּ}} ''for thy name’s sake''... ''pardon''...); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=29}} after {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן}} with an infinitive.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|oo}}
(''c'') The perfect consecutive occurs as the apodosis to temporal clauses or their equivalents, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּטֶ֫רֶם יַקְטִרוּן אֶת־הַחֵ֫לֶב נַ֫עַר הַכֹּהֵן... וּבָא}} ''before they burnt the fat, the priest’s servant came'' (used to come), &c., hence a frequentative perfect consecutive relating to the past, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=1|verse=19}}; also after participial clauses ({{GHGpar|116|w}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=13}} f. {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־אִישׁ זֹבֵחַ זֶ֫בַח... וּבָא|translate=when''(ever)'' any man offered sacrifice, then came}},<section end="par112"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

362.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="DjR" /></noinclude><section begin="par112"/>&c. (so {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=12}}), with a frequentative perfect consecutive. The perfect consecutive is very frequently used to announce future actions or events after simple expressions of time of any kind; thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=34}} (after {{GHGheb|text=בְּיוֹם}} with the infinitive), cf. also such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=6|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=23|hidebook=1}} (numerous frequentative perfects consecutive after the infinitive with a preposition; so {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=5}}, see above, ee); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=18|verse=5}}; moreover, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=17|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=10|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=26|hidebook=1}}; even after single disconnected words, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=עֶ֫רֶב וִֽידַעְתֶּם|translate=at even}} (when it becomes evening) ''then ye shall know''; cf. verse 7, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=7|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=24|verse=27}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|pp}}
'''6.''' Finally there still remains a number of passages which cannot be classed with any of those hitherto mentioned. Of these, some are due to the influence of Aramaic modes of expression, while in others the text is evidently corrupt.<ref>Mayer Lambert, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|REJ.|Revue des Études Juives. Paris, 1880 ff.}}}} xxvi. 55, is probably right in pointing some of these forms as ''infin. abs.'' instead of ''perfects''.</ref> In a few instances we can do no more than merely call attention to the incorrectness of the expression. (We are not of course concerned here with the cases—usually occurring in dependent clauses—in which a 2nd pers. ''perf.'' with Wāw copulative is simply co-ordinate with what precedes, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=6}}, and probably {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=2}}.)

(''a'') The influence of the Aramaic construction of the perfect with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} as the narrative tense, instead of the Hebrew imperfect consecutive (cf. Kautzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Bibl.-Aram.}}, {{GHGpar|71|b}}), is certainly to be traced in ''Qoheleth'', and sporadically in other very late books,<ref>In the whole of ''Qoheleth'' the imperfect consecutive occurs only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=1|verse=17|hidebook=1}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=4|verse=1.7|hidebook=1}}. Several of the perfects with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} can no doubt be explained as frequentatives, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=1|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=2|verse=5|hidebook=1.9.11.13.15}}, 5:18, compared with {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=6|verse=2|hidebook=1}}; but this is impossible in such passages as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=9|verse=14|hidebook=1}} ff. In Ezra, Driver reckons only six examples of the historical perfect with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, in Nehemiah only six, and in Esther six or seven.</ref> perhaps also in a few passages in the hooks of Kings, which are open to the suspicion of being due to later interpolation; so probably {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=12|verse=32}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהֶֽעֱמִידִ}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=11|verse=1}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}} {{GHGheb|text=וראתה}}; 14:14 {{GHGheb|text=וְלָקַח}} (in the parallel passage, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=25|verse=24}}, the word is wanting); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=23|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=וְנַשָׂא}}, &c.; verse 10 {{GHGheb|text=וְטִמֵּא}}, &c.; verse 12 {{GHGheb|text=וְהִשְׁלִיךְ}}, &c.; verse 15 {{GHGheb|text=וְשָׂרַף}}, &c.<ref>Stade in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} v. 291 ff. and in ''Ausgeäwhlte akad. Reden'', Giessen, 1899, p. 194 ff. and appendix p. 199, discusses, in connexion with {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=12|verse=12}}, a number of critically questionable perfects with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}. He considers that the whole section, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=23|verse=4}} from {{GHGheb|text=וְנָשָׂא}} to verse 5 inclusive, is to be regarded as a gloss, since the continuation of an imperfect consecutive by means of a perfect with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} never occurs in pre-exilic documents, except in places where it is due to corruption of the original text. The theory of frequentative perfects consecutive (even immediately after imperfects consecutive), which has been supported above, under f and g, by a large number of examples, is quite inconsistent with the character of the action in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=23|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהִשְׁבִּית}}, verse 8 {{GHGheb|text=וְנָתָץ}}, and verse 14 {{GHGheb|text=וְשִׁבַּר}}.</ref> Cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=37|verse=2}}, 7, 10.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|qq}}
(''b'') The text is certainly corrupt in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=6}} (read with the LXX and Vulgate<section end="par112"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

363.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par112 />{{GHGheb|text=וָאֹֽמַר}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=38|verse=28}}, where the narrative breaks off in the middle of the sentence; 40:3 ({{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה}}, &c., wanting in the LXX); also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=7|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=וְנָפַל הָאֹהֶל}} is altogether redundant; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=13}} read, with Klostermann, the ''2nd sing. masc.'' instead of {{GHGheb|text=והגדתי}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=21|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהשִׁ֫יבוּ}} is, no doubt, incorrectly repeated from verse 9, where it is an imperative.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|rr}}
Of other questionable instances, (α) the following, at any rate, may also be explained as frequentatives, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=36|verse=38}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=38|verse=28|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=39|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=5|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=11|hidebook=1}} (but even so {{GHGheb|text=וְאָֽמְרוּ}} would be expected); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=23|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=26}} (parallel with an imperfect); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=26}} (unless it is rather, ''yea, ye shall take up''; see above, x); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=26|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=8|verse=36}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|ss}}
(β) A longer or constant continuance in a past state is perhaps represented by the perfect with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} (as a variety of the frequentative perfect with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}), in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=9|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=22|verse=3|hidebook=1}}b, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=9}}. But the unusual ''perfects consec.'' in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=3}}–11, 16:2–8 (ultimately parallel with an imperf. as in 17:9, 18:20), 18:12–21, 19:11–14.22.26–29.34, are without doubt rightly explained by Bennett ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|SBOT.|Sacred Books of the Old Testament, ed. by P. Haupt. Lpz. and Baltimore, 1893 ff.}}}}, Joshua, p. 23) as originally containing the directions either of God to Joshua or of Joshua to the people; cf. the evident trace of this in 15:4b. A redactor transformed the directions into a description but left the ''perfects consec.'', which are to be explained as in ''aa''. In the same way {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=36|verse=29}} is most simply explained as repeated from 26:25.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|tt}}
(γ) The following are due to errors in the text, or to incorrect modes of expression: {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=36|verse=29}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=3|verse=23}},<ref>Or does {{GHGheb|text=ונעל}}, as a frequentative, imply fastening with several bolts? It is, at all events, to be noticed, that in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=18}} also {{GHGheb|text=ונעל}} follows an imperfect consecutive.</ref> 16:18 (read {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּֽעֲלוּ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=38|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=16|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=18|hidebook=1}} f. (read {{GHGheb|text=צָֽלְחוּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּֽעַבְרוּ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=11}} (where {{GHGheb|text=ושאלת}} is, no doubt intentionally, assimilated to the four other perfects); 13:3, 20:21; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=14|verse=7}} (where, with Stade, {{GHGheb|text=וְאֶת־הַסֶּ֫לַע תּפַשׁ}} should be read); 14:14, 18:4 (where, at any rate, {{GHGheb|text=וְשִׁבַּר}} might be taken as a frequentative, but not {{GHGheb|text=וכרת}}, &c.; evidently the perfects are co-ordinated only in form with {{GHGheb|text=הוּא הֵסִיר}}); 18:36, 21:15, 24:14, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=37|verse=15}} (where {{GHGheb|text=וְהִכּוּ}}, but not {{GHGheb|text=וְנָֽתְנוּ}}, might be frequentative); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=9|verse=7}} (omit {{GHGheb|text=וְיָֽצְאוּ}} with Stade, and read {{GHGheb|text=וְהַכּוּ}}); 20:22 ({{GHGheb|text=והשבתי}} {{GHGterm|Milʿêl}} before an imperfect consecutive); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=7|verse=4}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְאָכְלָה}} after an imperfect consecutive); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=12}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|uu}}
Finally, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=48|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=6|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=37|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=7|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}} is to be read throughout instead of {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה}}, but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהִיא}} with the LXX.<section end=par112 />

<section begin=par113 />{{center|{{Small-caps|B. The Infinitive and Participle.}}}}

<!-- section begins above -->{{GHGpar-heading|113|The Infinitive Absolute}}

Cf. the dissertation of J. Kahan, and, especially, the thorough investigation by E. Sellin, both entitled, ''Ueber die verbal-nominals Doppelnatur der hebräischen Participien und Infinitive'', &c., Lpz. 1889; F. Prätorius, ‘Ueber die sogen. Infin. absol. des Hebr.’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} 1902, pp. 546 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|a}}
'''1.''' The infinitive absolute is employed according to § 45 to emphasize the idea of the verb ''in the abstract'', i.e. it speaks of an action (or state) without any regard to the agent or to the circumstances of time and mood under which it takes place. As the ''name'' of an action the infinitive absolute, like other nouns in the stricter sense,<section end=par113 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

364.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par113 />may form part of certain combinations (as a subject, predicate, or object, or even as a genitive,<ref>The infinitive absolute can never be joined with a genitive or a pronominal suffix.</ref> see below); but such a use of the infinitive absolute (instead of the infinitive construct with or without a preposition) is, on the whole, rare, and, moreover, open to question on critical grounds. On the other hand, the infinitive absolute frequently exhibits its character as an expression of the {{GHGterm|verbal idea}} by taking an object, either in the accusative or even with a preposition.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|b}}
Examples of the use of the infinitive absolute:—

(''a'') As subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=25|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=אָכֹל דְּבַשׁ הַרְבּוֹת לֹא טוֹב|translate=it is not good to eat much honey}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=4|verse=17}}; epexegetically, after a demonstrative pronoun, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=58|verse=5}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=14|verse=12}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|c}}
(''b'') As predicate, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=17}} ''and the effect of righteousness'' (is) {{GHGheb|text=הַשְׁקֵט וָבֶ֫טַח|translate=quietness}} (prop. to ''find rest'') ''and confidence''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|d}}
(''c'') As object, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=לִמְדוּ הֵיטֵב|translate=learn to do well}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=15|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=18}}; according to the sense also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=9|verse=23}} 23:14, as well as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=5}} ({{GHGheb|text=הָסֵר}} and {{GHGheb|text=פָּרֹץ}} virtually depend on the idea of the wish contained in {{GHGheb|text=עֹשֶׂה}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=13}}, where a long series of infinitives absolute is governed by {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}}, and 59:13 (six infinitives governed by {{GHGheb|text=יְדַֽעֲנוּם}} in verse 12); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=56}} is strange since the object precedes the infinitive absolute which governs it,<ref>Perhaps {{GHGheb|text=הַצֵּג}} according to {{GHGpar|53|k}} should be explained as an infinitive construct, or should be written {{GHGheb|text=הַצִּג}}.</ref> also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=24}}, where the statement of place precedes the infinitive absolute.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=9|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=3}} the infinitive absolute as the object of the verb is placed before it for the sake of emphasis (with the verb negatived by {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=57|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=23}}), so also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|verse=45}} where it is the remoter object and co-ordinated with a substantive.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|e}}
(''d'') As genitive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּמַטְאֲטֵא הַשְׁמֵד|translate=with the besom of destruction}}; so perhaps also 4:4 {{GHGheb|text=בְּרוּחַ בָּעֵר}}; cf. further, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=1|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=21|verse=16|hidebook=1}}. The infinitive absolute is never used in immediate connexion with prepositions<ref>{{GHGheb|text=ואחרי שָׁתֹה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=9}} is impossible Hebrew, and as the LXX shows, a late addition.</ref> (which as being originally substantives govern the genitive), but always the infinitive construct; but if a second infinitive is co-ordinated by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} with such an infinitive construct, it has the form of the infinitive absolute (since it is released from the immediate government of the preposition), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=22|verse=13}} ... {{GHGheb|text=בְּתִתְּךָ לוֹ לֶחֶם וְשָׁאוֹל לוֹ בֵּֽאלֹהִים|translate=in that thou hast given him bread ... and hast enquired of God for him}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=36|verse=3}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=26}}, 33 (after {{GHGheb|text=מִן}}); after {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=7|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=44|verse=17|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|f}}
(''e'') Governing an accusative of the object, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=הָרֹג בָּקָר וְשָׁחֹם צאֹן|translate=slaying oxen and killing sheep}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=23|verse=30|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=5|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=30}}, and of the examples in ''a–d'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=56}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=58|verse=6|hidebook=1}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=25|verse=27}}, &c.; followed by a preposition, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=מָאוֹס בָּרָע וּבָחוֹר בַּטּוֹב|translate=to refuse the evil and choose the good}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=15|verse=12}} ({{GHGheb|text=הוֹכֵחַ לוֹ}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|g}}
If the object be a personal pronoun, then, since the infinitive absolute can never be united with a suffix (see the note on <sup>a</sup>), it is affixed by means of the accusative-sign {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} ({{GHGheb|text=אֹת}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=9|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=וְיָדוֹעַ אֹתִי|translate=and knoweth me}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=36|verse=3}}.<section end=par113 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

365.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par113 />{{GHGmargin-letter|113|h}}
'''2.''' Analogous to the use of the infinitive absolute as the accusative of the object, mentioned in ''d'', is its employment as a ''casus adverbialis''<ref>That this ''casus adverbialis'' also was originally regarded as an accusative, may be seen from classical Arabic, where an infinitive of this kind expressly retains the accusative ending. In Latin the ablative of the gerund corresponds in many ways to this use of the infinitive absolute.</ref> in connexion with some form of the finite verb, to describe more particularly the manner or attendant circumstances (especially those of time and place) under which an action or state has taken place, or is taking place, or will take place; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=19}} ''he shall be buried with the burial of an ass'', {{GHGheb|text=סָחוֹב וְהַשְׁלֵךְ|translate=a drawing and casting forth}}, i.e. being drawn and cast forth, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=16}} ({{GHGheb|text=הַרְחֵק|translate=a removing}}, i.e. distant; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=3|verse=16}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=30|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=6|verse=5}}, 23, 15:35 (where a subject is added subsequently; see below, gg); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=3|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=12}} ({{GHGheb|text=הָחֵל וְכַלֵּה|translate=a beginning and ending}}, i.e. from beginning to end); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=8|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=11}} ({{GHGheb|text=הַֽעֲמֵק}} and {{GHGheb|text=הַגְבֵּהַּ}}, prop. ''a making deep'' ..., and ''a making high'', i.e. whether thy request extend to the world below or to the height above); 57:17 ({{GHGheb|text=הַסְתֵּר|translate=in hiding}}, sc. my face); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=15}} ({{GHGheb|text=דֵּעָה וְהַשְׁכֵּיל|translate=with knowledge and understanding}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=3|verse=13}} ({{GHGheb|text=עָרוֹת}}, for the form cf. {{GHGpar|75|aa}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=7|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=35|verse=16}} ({{GHGheb|text=חָרֹק}}, to define more precisely {{GHGheb|text=קָֽרְעוּ}} verse 15); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=3}}.<ref>Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=21|verse=13}} for {{GHGheb|text=מָחָה וְהָפַךְ}} read with Stade and Klostermann {{GHGheb|text=מָחֹה וְהָפֹךְ}}; similarly, with Stade, {{GHGheb|text=וְקָשֹׁה}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=24}}; {{GHGheb|text=וְחָזוֹק}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=23|verse=14}}, and on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=31|verse=5}} cf. t.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|i}}
Rem. 1. To an adverbial infinitive absolute of this kind, there may further be added a ''casus adverbialis'' (the accusative of state or circumstance), or even a circumstantial clause, to define more exactly the manner in which the action is performed, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=20|verse=2}} ''and he did so'' {{GHGheb|text=הָלֹךְ עָרוֹם וְיָחֵף|translate=walking naked and barefoot}}, prop. in the condition of one naked, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=14}} ''a breaking in pieces'' (acc. to the reading {{GHGheb|text=כָּתוֹת}}; the Masora requires {{GHGheb|text=כָּתוּת}}) ''without sparing''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|k}}
2. A few infinitives of this kind, all of which are in Hiph<sup>e</sup>îl, have, through frequent use, come to be treated by the language as simple adverbs; so especially {{GHGheb|text=הַרְבֵּה}} (cf. {{GHGpar|75|ff}}) ''multum faciendo'', i.e. ''multum'', very frequently strengthened by {{GHGheb|text=מְאֹד|translate=very}} and even used without connexion with a finite verb (see the Lexicon); also {{GHGheb|text=הֵיטֵב|translate=bene faciendo}}, i.e. ''bene'', used especially to express the careful and thorough performance of an action (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=13|verse=15}}); in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=9|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=27|verse=8|hidebook=1}} it is added epexegetically to another adverbial infinitive absolute, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=4|verse=9}} it twice precedes the verb for the sake of emphasis. Finally, {{GHGheb|text=הַשְׁכֵּם|translate=mane faciendo}}, i.e. ''early in the morning'', then in general ''early'' with the additional idea of earnestness; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=16}} joined with the infinitive absolute {{GHGheb|text=וְהַֽעֲרֵב}} a denominative from {{GHGheb|text=עֶ֫רֶב|translate=evening}} (''morning and evening'', i.e. ''early and late)'', elsewhere (with the exception of {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=27|verse=14}}) always joined with the infinitive absolute of the governing verb, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=11|verse=7}} ''for I earnestly protested'' ({{GHGheb|text=הַֽעִדֹ֫תִי}}) ''unto your fathers'' ... {{GHGheb|text=הַשֵׁכֵּם וְהָעֵד|translate=rising early and protesting}}, i.e. with earnest protestation; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=25|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=26|verse=5|hidebook=1}} (where {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} should be omitted before {{GHGheb|text=ה׳}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=29|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=32|verse=33|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=16|verse=15}}.<section end=par113 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

366.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par113 />{{GHGmargin-letter|113|l}}
'''3.''' The infinitive absolute occurs most frequently in immediate connexion with the finite verb of the same stem, in order in various ways ''to define more accurately'' or ''to strengthen the idea of the verb''.<ref>Cf. A. Rieder, {{GHGcite|title=Die Verbindung des Inf. abs. mit dem Verb. fin ... im Hebr.}}, Lpz., 1872; also his {{GHGcite|title=Quae ad syntaxin Hebraicam ... planiorem faciendam ex lingua Graeca et Latina afferantur}}, Gumbinnen (Programm des Gymnasiums), 1884. G. R. Hauschild, ''Die Verbindung finiter und infiniter Verbalformen desselben Stammes in einigen Bibelsprachen'', Frankfurt a. M., 1893, discussing especially the rendering of such constructions in the Greek and Latin versions.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|m}}
These infinitives absolute joined immediately to the finite verb belong in a sense to the ''schema etymologicum'' treated in {{GHGpar|117|p}}, i.e. they are objects of the finite verb in question, except that the infinitive absolute (as a ''nomen abstractum'') lays stress rather on the actual occurrence or the energy of the action (see the examples below), while the noun proper emphasizes the result or extent of the action; cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=22|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־צָעֹק יִצְעַק אֵלַי|translate=if}} it actually happens that ''he cries to me'', with {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=34}} (as it were, ''he cried'', so that ''a great cry'' was heard).

We must further distinguish—

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|n}}
(''a'') The infinitive absolute used ''before'' the verb to ''strengthen'' the verbal idea, i.e. to emphasize in this way either the certainty (especially in the case of threats) or the forcibleness and completeness of an occurrence.
