In English, such an infinitive is mostly expressed by a corresponding adverb, but sometimes merely by putting greater stress on the verb; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=מוֹת תָּמוּת|translate=thou shalt surely die}}, cf. 18:10, 18, 22:17, 28:22, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=6}} (''cometh surely to pass''); 24:21, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=7|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=11|verse=17}}; with the infinitive strengthened by {{GHGheb|text=אַךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=28}} (but 27:30 ''and Jacob was yet scarce gone out'', &c.); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=הָעֵד הֵעִד בָּ֫נוּ|translate=he did solemnly protest unto us}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=נִשְׁאֹל נִשְׁאַל|translate=David earnestly asked leave of me}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=17|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=28}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהוֹרֵישׁ לֹא הֽוֹרִישׁוֹ|translate=and did not utterly drive them out}}; especially typical instances are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=8}} ''I will destroy it from off the face of the earth'' {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫פֶס כִּי לֹא הַשְׁמֵיד אַשְׁמִיד וג׳|translate=saving that I will not utterly destroy}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=30|verse=11}} ''and will in no wise leave thee unpunished''; cf. further {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=5}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|o}}
The infinitive absolute is used before the verb with less emphasis:

(1) Frequently at the beginning of the statement; cf. Driver on {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=6}}. However, in these cases a special emphasis on the following verb is sometimes intended; cf. above, n, on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=6}}; also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=28|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=3|hidebook=1}}. Elsewhere the infinitive absolute is evidently used only as possessing a certain fullness of sound (hence for rhythmical reasons, like some uses of the separate pronoun, {{GHGpar|135|a}}), as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, 20, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=18|hidebook=1}}.

(2) Very frequently in conditional sentences after {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}, &c. The infinitive absolute in this case emphasizes the importance of the con-<section end=par113 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

367.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par113 />dition on which some consequence depends, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=26}} ''if thou wilt diligently hearken'', &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=19|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=22|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, 11 f. 16, 22 (see above, m); 23:22, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=12|verse=25|hidebook=1}}; after {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=30}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|p}}
The infinitive absolute is used to give emphasis to an antithesis, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=24}} ''nay; but I will verily buy'' ({{GHGheb|text=קָנוֹ אֶקְנֶה}}) ''it of thee'', &c. (not receive it as a gift); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=15|verse=13}} ''no; but we will bind thee fast ... but surely we will not kill thee''; cf. further {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=30}} (thou art indeed gone=) ''though thou wouldst needs be gone'' (Vulg. ''esto''), ''because thou sore longedst'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=118|verse=13}}, 18, 126:6 (the second infinitive absolute as a supplement to the first—see below, r—comes ''after'' the verb).—Hence also, as permissive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=16}} f. {{GHGheb|text=אָכֹל תֹּאכֵל|translate=thou mayest freely eat, but}}, &c. (so that verse 16 is in antithesis to verse 17); or concessive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=30}} ''I said indeed'' ..., 14:43.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|q}}
The infinitive absolute is used to strengthen a question, and especially in impassioned or indignant questions, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=הֲמָלֹךְ תִּמְלֹךְ עָ֫לֵינוּ|translate=shalt thou indeed reign over us?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=43}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=28|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=3|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=7|verse=5}}; but cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=5}} ''must I needs bring again?''

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|r}}
(''b'') The infinitive absolute ''after the verb'', sometimes (as in ''n'') to intensify<ref>In Arabic also, the intensifying infinitive regularly stands ''after'' the verb, but in Syriac ''before'' the verb.</ref> the idea of the verb (especially after imperatives and participles, since the infinitive absolute can never precede either, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=37|verse=2|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=שִׁמְעוּ שָׁמוֹעַ|translate=hearken ye attentively}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=10}}; after participles, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=17}}, also elsewhere, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=24|verse=10|hidebook=1}} ''thou hast altogether blessed them''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=24|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=11|verse=10}}, and with the infinitive absolute strengthened by means of {{GHGheb|text=גַּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=46|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=13}}); sometimes to express the long ''continuance'' of an action; here again after an imperative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=שִׁמְעוּ שָׁמוֹעַ|translate=hear ye continually}}; after a perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=6|verse=29}}; after a participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=23|verse=17}}; after an imperfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=32}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|s}}
To this class belong especially those cases in which a second infinitive absolute is co-ordinated with the first; the latter then expresses either an accompanying or antithetical action or the aim to which the principal action is directed; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=הָֽלְכוּ הָלֹךְ וְגָעוֹ|translate=lowing as they went}} (lowing continually; so after a participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=6|verse=13}}b {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=7}} ''it went forth to and fro''<ref>Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=1|verse=14}} for the distorted form {{GHGheb|text=רצוא}} reads simply {{GHGheb|text=יָֽצְאוּ יָצוֹא}}.</ref>; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=19|verse=22}} ''smiting and'' (i.e. but also) ''healing again''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=2|verse=26}} (see above, m).

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|t}}
Rem. 1. Instead of a second infinitive absolute (see above) there is sometimes found a perfect consecutive (Jos. 6:13 a and {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=19}} [but Stade’s {{GHGheb|text=וְזָעוֹק}} is<section end=par113 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

368.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par113 />preferable], in both places as perfect frequentative; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=31|verse=5}} referring to the future, unless with Stade, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} vi. 189, we read {{GHGheb|text=וְהַצֵּיל}} and {{GHGheb|text=וְהַמְלֵיט}}), or an imperfect consecutive ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=19|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=16|verse=13}}) or participle ({{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=16|verse=5}}); cf. also u.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|u}}
2. The idea of long ''continuance'' is very frequently expressed by the verb {{GHGheb|text=הָלַךְ|translate=to go}}, along with its infinitive absolute, or even by the latter alone, and this occurs not only when it can be taken in its literal sense (''to go, to walk'', as in the examples given above, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=6|verse=9}}, 13, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=19|hidebook=1}}; cf. also, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=16}}, where both infinitives stand ''before'' the verb, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=126|verse=6}}, where {{GHGheb|text=הָלוֹךְ}} precedes), but in cases where {{GHGheb|text=הָלַךְ}} in the sense of ''to go on, to continue'', merely performs also the function of an adverb. The action itself is added in a second infinitive absolute, or sometimes (see above, t) in a participle or verbal adjective. Examples, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּשֻׁ֫בוּ הַמַּ֫יִם... הָלוֹךְ וָשׁוֹב|translate=and the waters returned... continually}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=11}}; with a participle following, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=16}} (unless we read {{GHGheb|text=וּבָכֹה}}, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=16}}); with an adjective following, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gen|chapter=26|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=5|verse=10}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=11|verse=9}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=25}}.<ref>Cf. in French, ''Le mal va toujours croissant, la maladie va toujours en augmentant et en empirant'', ‘''continually increases and becomes worse and worse''.’</ref>

On the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=41}} the participle {{GHGheb|text=הֹלֵךְ}} is used instead of the infinitive absolute. Of a different kind are the instances in which the participle {{GHGheb|text=הֹלֵךְ}} is used as predicate along with the co-ordinate adjective ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=19|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=9|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=17|verse=12}}) or participle ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=1|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=4|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=1|verse=6}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|v}}
3. The regular place of the negative is between the intensifying infinitive absolute and the finite verb,<ref>Cf. Rieder, ''Quo loco ponantur negationes'' {{GHGheb|text=לֹא|translate=et}} {{GHGheb|text=אַל}}... (''Zeitschrift für Gymn.Wesen'', 1879, p. 395 ff.).</ref> e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=5|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהַצֵּל לֹֽא־הִצַּלְתָּ|translate=neither hast thou delivered at all}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=15|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=30|verse=11|hidebook=1}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=1|verse=10}} ({{GHGheb|text=אַל}}). Exceptions are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=4}} (where the negation of the threat pronounced in 2:17 is expressed in the same form of words); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=49|verse=8}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|w}}
4. With a finite verb of one of the derived conjugations, not only the infinitive absolute of the ''same'' conjugation may be connected ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=22}} Piʿēl; 17:13, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=22|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=14|verse=3}} Niphʿal; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=15}} Puʿal; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=4|verse=18}} Hiphʿîl; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=4}} Hophʿal), but also (especially with Niphʿal, rarely with Piʿēl and Hiphʿîl; see Driver on {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=18}}) that of {{GHGterm|Qal}} as the simplest and most general representative of the verbal idea, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=18}} (with Piʿēl; but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=28|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=טֹרַף}} is a passive of Qal, {{GHGpar|52|e}}); 46:4 (with Hiphʿîl); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=19|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=23|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=2}} (with Niphʿal); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=24|verse=19}} (with Hithpoʿēl; {{GHGheb|text=רֹ֫עָה}} in the same verse must also, according to the Masora, certainly be the infinitive absolute Qal; see {{GHGpar|67|o}}), and so always {{GHGheb|text=מוֹת יוּמַת|translate=he shall surety be put to death}}. Elsewhere the infinitive absolute of a conjugation with kindred meaning is found, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=19|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=23}} Hophʿal for Niphʿal (but most probably we should read, with Driver, the ''infin. Niph.'' in both places, {{GHGheb|text=הִפָּדֵה}} and {{GHGheb|text=הֵֽחָרֵב}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=16}} (Piʿēl for Hiphʿîl, unless {{GHGheb|text=יְקַטְּרוּן}} is to be read); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=4}} (Hophʿal for Puʿal).<ref>In three passages even the infinitive absolute of another stem of like sound occurs; but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=28}} {{GHGheb|text=אָדוֹשׁ}} is no doubt a mere textual error for {{GHGheb|text=דּוֹשׁ}}, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=8|verse=13}}, according to {{GHGpar|72|aa}}, we should read {{GHGheb|text=אֹֽסְפֵם}}, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=1|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=אֹסֵף}}. Barth, ''Nom.-bildung'', {{GHGpar|49|b}}, sees in {{GHGheb|text=אַדוֹשׁ}} and {{GHGheb|text=אַסוֹף}} infinitives {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}}, exactly corresponding in form to ''ʾ<sup>a</sup>qâm''[ā] the Aram. infin. ʾAphʿēl of {{GHGheb|text=קוּם}}; but there is no more evidence for a ''Hiph.'' of {{GHGheb|text=דּוּשׁ}} in Hebrew than for a stem {{GHGheb|text=אָדַשׁ}}.</ref> Finally, the infinitive absolute may<section end=par113 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

369.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par113 />equally well be represented by a ''substantive'' of kindred stem.<ref>On these substantives (and on the use of the infinitive absolute generally as absolute object, see above, m), cf. the ''schema etymologicum'' treated in connexion with the government of the verb in {{GHGpar|117|p}}, q.</ref> In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=14}} the substantive intensifying the verb is found ''along with'' the infinitive absolute.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|x}}
5. Instead of the infinitive absolute immediately connected with the finite verb, an infinitive construct form appears (cf. {{GHGpar|73|d}}), in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=25}} ({{GHGheb|text=גַּם קֹב}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=2|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=גַּם שֹׁל}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=50|verse=34}} ({{GHGheb|text=רִיב יָרִיב}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=23|verse=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=בִּין תָּבִין}}). In the last instances the infinitive is probably assimilated to the imperfect, like the infinitive Niphʿal in the forms noticed in {{GHGpar|51|k}} and note.—Cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=24}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּבֹ֫אוּ בֹא וְהַכּוֹת}} (read so with the LXX) before {{GHGheb|text=א}}, hence, no doubt due to the dislike of a hiatus; so in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=50|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=1|verse=7}} ({{GHGheb|text=הֲבֹל}}), all in rapid style; ''after'' the verb, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=7|verse=7}}, unless {{GHGheb|text=הַֽעֲבֵיר}} is intended.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|y}}
'''4.''' Finally the infinitive absolute sometimes appears as ''a substitute for the finite verb'', either when it is sufficient simply to mention the verbal idea (see z), or when the hurried or otherwise excited style intentionally contents itself with this infinitive, in order to bring out the verbal idea in a clearer and more expressive manner (see aa).

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|z}}
(''a'') The infinitive absolute as the continuation of a preceding finite verb. In the later books especially it often happens that in a succession of several acts only the first (or sometimes more) of the verbs is inflected, while the second (or third, &c.) is added simply in the infinitive absolute. Thus after several perfects, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=9|verse=5}} (cf. verse 11) ''we have sinned ... and have transgressed thy law'', {{GHGheb|text=וִסוֹר|translate=and have turned aside}} (prop. ''a turning aside'' took place); so after a {{GHGterm|perfect}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=36|verse=7}} (?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=14|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=19|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hag|chapter=1|verse=6}} (four infinitives), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=3|verse=4}} (but read with Wellhausen, after the LXX, {{GHGheb|text=וְהַלְבִּ֫שׁוּ אֹתוֹ}}), 7:5, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=8|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=9|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=3|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=9|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, 16, 18, 12:6 ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=9|verse=8}}, 13, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=5|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=28|verse=19}};<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=7|verse=14}} a perfect appears to be continued by means of an infinitive construct; but the text is quite corrupt; Cornill reads {{GHGheb|text=תִּקְעוּ תָקוֹעַ הָכִ֫ינוּ הָכֵן}}.</ref> after the {{GHGterm|perfect consecutive}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=12|verse=10}}; after the {{GHGterm|perfect frequentative}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=9|verse=25}} (unless {{GHGheb|text=וְהִקְטִיר}} be intended); after the simple {{GHGterm|imperfect}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=25|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=30|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=32|verse=44}} (three infinitives), 36:23, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=21|verse=24}}; after a ''cohortative'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=9|verse=20}}; after the {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=43}} (as a continuation of {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּרְכֵּב}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=8|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=7|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=37|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=8|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=16|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=7|verse=3}}; with {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ|translate=or}} after the {{GHGterm|jussive}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=14|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=2|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=6|verse=9|hidebook=1}}; after the {{GHGterm|imperative}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=30}}b, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=4}}f.; after the {{GHGterm|participle}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=15}} (strengthened by {{GHGheb|text=אַף}}, and regarded, like the participle itself, as an adverbial accusative); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=8|verse=8}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|aa}}
(''b'') At the beginning of the narrative, or at least of a new section of it. The special form of the finite verb which the infinitive absolute represents must be determined from the context. The infinitive<section end=par113 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

370.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par113 />absolute is most frequently used in this way, corresponding to the infinitive of command in Greek, &c.<ref>Cf. also such infinitives in French as ''voir'' (page so and so, &c.), ''s’adresser..., se méfier des voleurs''!</ref>:—

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|bb}}
(α) For an emphatic imperative,<ref>Prätorius, ''op. cit.'', p. 547: the extraordinarily common use of the infinitive form ''qāṭōl'' in the sense of an imperative, jussive, or cohortative has long since caused it to be compared with the Arab. ''faʿāli''. It thus appears that the infin. ''qāṭōl'' in Hebrew could be used from early times as a kind of fixed, invariable word of command.</ref> e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שָׁמוֹר}} (thou shalt, ye shall), ''observe'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=5|verse=12}}; {{GHGheb|text=זָכוֹר}} (thou shalt) ''remember'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=13|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=8|hidebook=1}} (the full form occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=6|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=שָׁמוֹר תִּשְׁמְרוּן}}; 7:18 {{GHGheb|text=זָכֹר תִּזְכֹּר}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=2|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=4|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=25|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=38|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=2}}, followed by a {{GHGterm|perfect consecutive}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=1|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=31|hidebook=1}} (parallel with an {{GHGterm|imperative}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=2|verse=2}} three imperatives follow). But {{GHGheb|text=הַבֵּיט}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=142|verse=5}} may be only an incorrect spelling of {{GHGheb|text=הַבֵּט}} imperative.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=21|verse=31}}, for the infinitives construct {{GHGheb|text=הָסִיר}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָרִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַשְׁפִּיל}} (beside {{GHGheb|text=הַגְבֵּהַּ}}) read with Cornill the infinitives absolute {{GHGheb|text=הָסֵר}}, &c. The K<sup>e</sup>thîbh probably intends {{GHGheb|text=הָסֵיר}}, &c.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|cc}}
(β) For the jussive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=6|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=6|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=11|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=46}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=17|verse=12}} (''let it'' rather ''meet'').

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|dd}}
(γ) For the cohortative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=13}}b {{GHGheb|text=אָכוֹל וְשָׁתוֹ}} (the exclamation of the mocker); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=21|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=30|hidebook=1}}, 46; perhaps also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=31|verse=2}} ({{GHGheb|text=הָלוֹךְ}}).<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=18}} the infinitive construct appears to be used instead of the cohortative, but {{GHGheb|text=אוֹשִׁיעַ}} should certainly be read for {{GHGheb|text=הוֹשִׁיעַ}}. Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=30}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=18|verse=29}}), which was formerly included under this head (I will ''disguise myself and go into the battle''), read {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְחַפֵּשׂ וְאָֹבא}}.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|ee}}
(δ) For the imperfect in emphatic promises, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=43}} ye shall ''eat and leave thereof''; 19:29 ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=30}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=31|verse=10}}; also in indignant questions, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=40|verse=2}} ''shall he that cavilleth contend with the Almighty?''<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=18}} in a similar question instead of the infinitive constr. we should rather expect the infinitive absolute ({{GHGheb|text=הֶאָמֹר}}), unless with the LXX and Vulg. the participle with the article ({{GHGheb|text=הָֽאֹמֵר}}) is to be read.</ref> (on the addition of the subject cf. the Rem. below); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=1}} ''and thinkest thou to return again to me?'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=7|verse=9}} ff. (six infinitives, continued by means of the {{GHGterm|perfect consecutive}}; cf. {{GHGpar|112|o}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|113|ff}}
(ε) For any historical tense (like the Latin ''historic'' infinitive) in lively narration (or enumeration) and description, even of what is still taking place in present time, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hos|chapter=4|verse=2}} ''swearing and breaking faith, and killing, and stealing, and committing adultery'' (in these they are busied); 10:4 (after a {{GHGterm|perfect}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=59|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=8|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=14|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=35}}; cf. further {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=32|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=4|verse=2}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=12|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=15|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, and 25:4, the infinitive absolute is best rendered by the passive.<section end=par113 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

371.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par113 />{{GHGmargin-letter|113|gg}}
Rem. The subject is sometimes added to the infinitive absolute when it takes the place of the finite verb, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=6|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=15|verse=35}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=15|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=17|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=17|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=40|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=4|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=9|verse=1}}. So, probably, also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=48}}, although here {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־זָכָר}} according to {{GHGpar|121|a}} might also be taken as ''an object'' with a passive verb; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=3|verse=13}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=26}}, 33 the subject follows an infinitive absolute which is co-ordinated with an infinitive construct, see above, e.<section end=par113 />

<section begin=par114 />{{GHGpar-heading|114|The Infinitive Construct}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|a}}
'''1.''' The infinitive construct, like the infinitive absolute, may also represent a ''nomen verbale'' ({{GHGpar|45|a}}), but of a much more flexible character than the infinitive absolute (cf. {{GHGpar|113|a}}). Its close relation with nouns properly so called is especially seen in the readiness with which the infinitive construct may be used for any case whatever; thus,

(''a'') As the nominative of the subject, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָֽאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ}}, literally, ''not good is the being of man in his separation''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=17|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=25|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, 24 (but cf. 21:9 {{GHGheb|text=טוֹב לָשֶׁ֫בֶת}} in the same statement); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=9}} prop. ''there is not a coming near unto thee'', but the text is probably corrupt. With a ''feminine'' predicate, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=17}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|b}}
(''b'') As genitive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=עֵת סְפוֹד וְעֵת רְקוֹד|translate=a time of mourning and a time of dancing}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=12|verse=46}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=24|verse=14}}. This equally includes, according to {{GHGpar|101|a}}, all those cases in which the infinitive construct depends on a preposition (see below, d) [and Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Tenses}}, § 206].

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|c}}
(''c'') As accusative of the object, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אֵדַע צֵאת וָבֹא|translate=I know not the going out or the coming in}} (''I know not how to go out and come in)''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=28|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=28|hidebook=1}} (even with {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=6|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=22}} (cf. for the use of the infinitive absolute as object, {{GHGpar|113|f}}); as accusative with a verb expressing fullness, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=11|verse=9}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|d}}
'''2.''' The construction of the infinitive with prepositions (as in Greek, ἐν τῷ εἶναι, διὰ τὸ εἶναι, &c.) may usually be resolved in English into the finite verb with a conjunction, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=35|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּפִגְעוֹ־בוֹ|translate=in his meeting him}}, i.e. if (as soon as) he meets him; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=45}} ({{GHGheb|text=עַד־שׁוּב}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן מָֽאָסְכֶם|translate=because ye despise}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=35}} {{GHGheb|text=עַל־אָמְרֵךְ|translate=because thou sayest}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=1}} ''and his eyes were dim'' {{GHGheb|text=מֵרְאֹת|translate=from seeing}}, i.e. so that he could not see.

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|e}}
This use of the infinitive construct is especially frequent in connexion with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} or {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}} to express time-determinations (in English resolved into a temporal clause, as above the combination of the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן}} or {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} is resolved into a causal clause), especially after {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}} (see the<section end=par114 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

372.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par114 />examples, {{GHGpar|111|g}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=בִּֽהְיוֹתָם בְּמִצְרַ֫יִם|translate=when they were in Egypt}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=30}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי כִרְאֹת אֶת־הַנֶּ֫זֶם... וּכְשְׁמְעוֹ וג׳|translate=and it came to pass, when he saw}} (prop. in the seeing) ''the ring''..., ''and when he heard'' (prop. in his hearing), &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|f}}
But by far the most frequent is the connexion of the infinitive construct with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}.<ref>Cf. {{GHGpar|45|g}}, according to which the close union of the {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} with the first consonant of the infinitive ({{GHGheb|text=לִכְתֹּב}} with a firmly closed syllable, as opposed to {{GHGheb|text=בִּכְתֹב}}, {{GHGheb|text=כִּכְתֹב}}, &c.) seems to point to the formation of a special new verbal form. Quite distinct are the few examples where the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} serves to express time, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=63}} {{GHGheb|text=לִפְנוֹת עָ֫רֶב|translate=at the eventide}} (prop. at the time of the return of evening); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=23|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=14|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=26}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=29}} ''when Joab sent the king’s servant''.</ref> Starting from the fundamental meaning of {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, i.e. ''direction towards something'', infinitives with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} serve to express the most varied ideas of purpose or aim, and very commonly also (with a weakening or a complete disregard of the original meaning of the {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}) to introduce the object of an action, or finally even (like the infinitive absolute used adverbially, {{GHGpar|113|h}}, and the Latin gerund in ''-ndo'') to state motives or attendant circumstances. See the instances in the Remarks.

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|g}}
Rem. 1. The original meaning of the {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} is most plainly seen in those infinitives with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} which expressly state a purpose (hence as the equivalent of a final clause), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=5}} ''and the Lord came down'', {{GHGheb|text=לִרְאֹת אֶת־הָעִיר|translate=to see the city}}; also with a change of subject, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=10}} ''and thou hast taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite'' {{GHGheb|text=לִֽהְיוֹת לְךָ לְאִשָּׁה|translate=to be}} (i.e. that she may be) ''thy wife''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=38|verse=26}} ({{GHGheb|text=לָמוּת}}).—If there is a special emphasis on the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, it is placed, with its complement, before the governing verb, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=2}} with {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹא}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=15|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=25}} with {{GHGheb|text=עָלָה}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|h}}
2. Just as clearly the idea of aiming at a definite purpose or turning towards an object may be seen in the combination of the verb {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה|translate=to be}}, with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} and an infinitive. In fact {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה לַֽעֲשׂוֹת}} may mean, either (''a'') ''he was in the act of, he was about to'' (as it were, he set himself), ''he was ready, to do'' something, or (''b'') ''he'' or it ''was appointed'' or ''compelled'', &c., to do the action in question. In the latter case {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה לַֽעֲשׂוֹת}} corresponds to the Latin ''faciendum erat'', cf. also the English ''I am to go''. In both cases {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} (as elsewhere when copula) is often omitted.

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|i}}
Examples of (''a'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי הַשֶּׁ֫מֶשׁ לָבוֹא|translate=and when the sun was going down}} (just about to set); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=26|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי לִדְרשׁ אֱלֹהִים|translate=and he set himself to seek God}} (here with the secondary idea of a continuous action); with the omission of {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=38|verse=20}}, {{GHGheb|text=יְהֹוָה לְהֽוֹשִׁיעֵ֫נִי|translate=the Lord}} is ready ''to save me''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=21}} (?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=49}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=25|verse=14}} (''et foedus suum manifestaturus est eis''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=18|verse=24}} (?), 19:8 ({{GHGheb|text=לִמְצֹא|translate=consecuturus}}<section end=par114 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

373.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="DjR" /></noinclude><section begin="par114" />''est'', unless we simply read {{GHGheb|text=יִמְצָא}} with the LXX)<ref>P. Haupt ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|SBOT.|Sacred Books of the Old Testament, ed. by P. Haupt. Lpz. and Baltimore, 1893 ff.}}}}, Proverbs, p. 52, lines 10 ff.; ''Critical Notes on Esther'', p. 170, on 7:8) considers it possible that here and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=6|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=7|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=16|verse=30|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=30|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, as well as in 14:35, 17:21 before a noun, the {{GHGheb|text=ל}} is a survival of the emphatic {{GHGheb|text=ל}} with an ''imperf.'', which is especially common in Arabic. In that case {{GHGheb|text=לִמְצֹא}} must be read {{GHGheb|text=לִמְצָא}}, i.e. {{GHGheb|text=ל}}##{{GHGheb|text=יִמַצָא}}. But all the above instances can be taken as infinitives with {{GHGheb|text=ל}} without difficulty.</ref>; 20:25, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר לִֽהְיוֹת|translate=quod futurum est}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=11|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=12|verse=12|hidebook=1}} (in a negative statement); in a question, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=7|verse=8}} (''will he even''... ?). Cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=19}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|k}}
Of (''b'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי הַשַּׁ֫עַר לִסְגּוֹר|translate=and the gate was to be shut}} (had to be shut); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=109|verse=13}}.<ref>Somewhat different are the cases where {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה לְ}} with the infinitive (which is then used exactly as a substantive) implies ''to become something'', i.e. to meet with a particular fate, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=24|verse=22}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=13|hidebook=1}}) {{GHGheb|text=לְבָעֵר|translate=for wasting}}, for which elsewhere frequently {{GHGheb|text=לְשַׁמָּה}} and the like; probably also {{GHGheb|text=לְבַלּוֹת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=49|verse=15}} is to be explained in this way, the {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} being omitted.</ref> Mostly with the omission of {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=מֶה לַֽעֲשׂוֹת לָךְ וג׳|translate=what is to be done for thee?}} ({{GHGheb|text=הֲיֵשׁ לְדַבֶּר־לָךְ}}) ''wouldest thou be'' (lit. is it to be) ''spoken for to the king'', &c.? {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=13|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=לְהַכּוֹת|translate=it was to smite}} equivalent to ''thou shouldest have smitten''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=68|verse=19|hidebook=1}} (?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=30|verse=6}} (''habitandum est iis''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=9|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=10|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=22|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=8|verse=13}} (?), 11:22, 19:2, 36:19 (?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=9|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=1|verse=17}}. In a question {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=19|verse=2}}; after {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=5|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=15|verse=2|hidebook=1}}; after {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=23|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=5|verse=11}} and frequently.

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|l}}
Of the same kind also are the cases, in which the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} depends on the idea of an obligation or permission (or prohibition); especially in such forms of expression as {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=עָלַי לָ֫תֶת לְךָ וג׳}} it was ''upon me'', i.e. it would have been ''my duty to give thee'', &c.<ref>{{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=4|verse=10}} (''cui dandum erat mihi'') appears to be similar; it may, however, be better, with Wellhausen, to omit the {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}.</ref>; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=3|verse=1}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=13|verse=5}}) ''it is not for you to'' (i.e. are ye not bound to)?<ref>But in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=20}} after {{GHGheb|text=וְלָ֫נוּ|translate=and our part shall be}} the infinitive without {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} stands as the subject of the sentence.</ref> with a negative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=26|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא לְךָ וג׳|translate=it pertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the Lord, but}} only ''to the priests''; also {{GHGheb|text=אֵין לְ}} with an infinitive expresses ''it is not permitted'' (nefas est), ''may not'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=4|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אֵין לָבוֹא|translate=for none might enter}}; 8:8, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=15|verse=2}};<ref>Quite different of course are such cases as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=וְכֹחַ אַ֫יִן לְלֵדָה|translate=and there is not strength to bring forth}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=4|verse=4}}.</ref> {{GHGheb|text=אֵין לְ}} with an infinitive is used in a somewhat different sense, equivalent to ''it is not feasible, not possible'', e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=40|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=5|verse=11}}.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=אִשׁ}} (= {{GHGheb|text=יֵשׁ|translate=it is, there is}}) is used in a similar sense after {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}, the negative particle of asseveration, ''of a truth it is not'' possible ''to turn to the right hand or to the left''.</ref>—With either meaning {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} can be used instead of {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=6|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא לְהַזְכִּיר|translate=nefas est}}, ''to make mention'' of the name of the Lord: but {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=19}} ''for it was not possible to drive out'', &c., perhaps, however, the text originally stood as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=17|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יָֽכְלוּ לְה׳}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=15|verse=2}}.
{{nop}}
<section end="par114" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

374.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="DjR" /></noinclude><section begin="par114" />{{GHGmargin-letter|114|m}}
3. A further class comprises the very numerous cases, in which the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} is used as the object<ref>This view is based upon the fact, that in numerous expressions of this kind (see the examples above) the {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} may be omitted, and the infinitive consequently stand as an actual accusative of the object (see above, c). However, the connexion of the verb with the object is in the latter case closer and more emphatic (hence especially adapted to poetic or prophetic diction), than the looser addition of the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}; thus {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אָבוּ שְׁמוֹעַ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=12}} is equivalent to ''they desired not obeying'' ({{GHGheb|text=לֹא אָבוּ}} also with the infin. abs. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=24}}; cf. {{GHGpar|113|d}}); but {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אָבוּ לִשְׁמֹעַ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=20|verse=8}} rather expresses ''they could not make up their mind as to hearkening''. When connected with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, the governing verb has a more independent sense than when it directly governs the accusative of the object.</ref> of a governing verb, hence, again, for ''the direction'' which an action takes. The verbs (or conjugations) which occur most frequently in this combination with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} and an infinitive are: {{GHGheb|text=הֵחֵל}} (with an infinitive without {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=25}}, 31, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=3|verse=7}}), {{GHGheb|text=הוֹאִיל|translate=to begin}}, {{GHGheb|text=הוֹסִיף}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָסַף}} (prop. ''to add'') ''to continue'', very frequently, even in prose, with an infinitive without {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, 12, 37:5, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=27|verse=1}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=חָדַל|translate=to cease from, to desist}}; {{GHGheb|text=כִּלָּה|translate=to complete, to make an end of}}; {{GHGheb|text=תָּמַם|translate=to be finished}}; {{GHGheb|text=הִקְרִיב|translate=to come near to}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=11}}; {{GHGheb|text=מִהַר|translate=to hasten}} (with an infinitive without {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=18}}); {{GHGheb|text=אָבָה|translate=to be willing}} (with an infinitive without {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=39|verse=9}}); {{GHGheb|text=חָפֵץ|translate=to will, to desire}}; {{GHGheb|text=מֵאֵן|translate=to refuse}} (''to be unwilling''); {{GHGheb|text=בִּקֵּשׁ|translate=to seek}}; {{GHGheb|text=יָכֹל|translate=to be able}} (with an infinitive without {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=50}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=38}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=2}}); {{GHGheb|text=נָתַן}} with an accusative of the person in the sense of ''to give up to some one, to cause'', or ''permit'' him to do something, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=16|verse=11}} (with an infinitive abs. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=18}}, see {{GHGpar|113|d}}), {{GHGheb|text=יָדַע|translate=to understand}} how to do something (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=הָֽעֲתִידִם עֹיֵר}} is analogous); {{GHGheb|text=לָמַד|translate=to learn}}; {{GHGheb|text=קִוָּה|translate=to wait, expect}} (with a change of subject, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=2}} ''and he waited for it to bring forth grapes'').

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|n}}
We must further mention here a number of verbs in Hiphʿîl (partly denominatives), which express an action in some definite direction (cf. {{GHGpar|53|f}}), as {{GHGheb|text=הִגְּדִּיל|translate=to do greatly}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִשְׁפִּיל|translate=to make}} (it) ''low'', {{GHGheb|text=הִגְבִּיהַּ|translate=to make}} (it) ''high'', {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽעֱמִיק|translate=to make}} (it) ''deep'', {{GHGheb|text=הִרְחִיק|translate=to make}} (it) ''far, distant'', {{GHGheb|text=הֵימִיב|translate=to make}} (it) ''good'' (with an infinitive without {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=33|verse=3}}, but {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=17}}, in the same combination, with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}); {{GHGheb|text=הִשְׁכִּים|translate=to do}} anything ''early'' ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=127|verse=2}}, along with its opposite {{GHGheb|text=אֵחַר|translate=to do}} something ''late'', with an infinitive without {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}); {{GHGheb|text=הִרְבָּה|translate=to make}} (it) ''much'', {{GHGheb|text=הִפְלָא|translate=to make}} (it) ''wonderful'' (even with a passive infinitive {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=26|verse=15}}),<ref>In almost all these examples the principal idea is properly contained in the infinitive, whilst the governing verb strictly speaking contains only a subordinate adverbial statement, and is therefore best rendered in English by an adverb; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=20}} ''how is it that thou hast found it so quickly?'' (prop. how thou hast hastened to find!), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=27}} ''wherefore didst thou flee secretly?'' So frequently with {{GHGheb|text=הִרְבָּה}} (= ''often, abundantly''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=36|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=21|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=55|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=78|verse=38}}, &c.; with {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּב}} (= ''again''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=30|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=11|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=9|verse=14}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=1|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jn|chapter=4|verse=2}}, and the analogous instances in {{GHGpar|120|g}}; also {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=1}} ''thou hast asked a hard thing''.</ref> &c.  
{{nop}}<section end="par114" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

375.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par114" />{{GHGmargin-letter|114|o}}
4. Finally, the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} is very frequently used in a much looser connexion to state motives, attendant circumstances, or otherwise to define more exactly. In English, such infinitive constructions (like the Latin gerund in ''-do''; cf. f) must frequently be turned by ''that'' or a gerund; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=12|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=לִשְׁאֹל לָכֶם מֶלֶךְ|translate=in asking you a king}}; 14:33, 19:5, 20:36, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, 15, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=23|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=5|verse=4}}, 22, 26, 8:15, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=3}} f., 14:8, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=44|verse=7}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=63|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=78|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=101|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=103|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=14|hidebook=1}} f., 111:6, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=8|verse=34|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=18|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=13|verse=18}}. Sometimes the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} is used in this way simply by itself, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=12|verse=8}} ''as the roes upon the mountains'' {{GHGheb|text=לְמַהֵר}} (as regards hasting) ''in swiftness''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=25}} ({{GHGheb|text=לְהַלֵּל}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=לַֽחֲלוֹף}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=2|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=26|verse=2|hidebook=1}} and so very frequently the infinitive {{GHGheb|text=לֵאמֹר|translate=dicendo}} which has become stereotyped as an adverb to introduce direct narration (in the sense of ''thus, as follows'').<ref>{{GHGheb|text=לֵאמֹר}} is very often so used after {{GHGheb|text=וַיְדַבֵּר}} in the Priestly document ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, &c., and numberless times in the legal parts of Exod., Lev., and Num.)—a pleonasm which is not surprising considering the admittedly prolix and formal style of the document.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|p}}
5. In a number of instances—especially in the later books—the infin. constr. with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} appears to be attached by {{GHGterm|Wāw}} (like the infinitive absolute, {{GHGpar|113|z}}), as the continuation of a previous finite verb. In most examples of this kind it is, however, evident that the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} virtually depends on an idea of intention, effort, or being in the act of, which, according to the sense, is contained in what has preceded, whilst the copula, as sometimes also elsewhere, is used in an emphatic sense (''and that too''); thus e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=29}} (if the text be right) ''fill your hand to-day'' (sc. with an offering) ''for the Lord... and that to bring a blessing upon you'', i.e. that ye may be blessed; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=31}} (otherwise in verses 26 and 33 where the infinitive absolute is used, see {{GHGpar|113|e}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=21}},<ref>When Delitzsch on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=21}}, referring to {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=1|verse=17}}, explains the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} as an elliptical mode of expressing the ''coniugatio periphrastica'' (equivalent to ''flagitaturi sunt a deo cibum suum''), this is, in point of fact, certainly applicable to this and a few other places mentioned above; but all these passages, in which the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=וּלְ}} follows, are to be distinguished from the cases treated above under h, where the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}<!-- not a translation --> ''without Wāw'' corresponds to a Latin gerundive, or is actually used to express the ''coniugatio periphrastica''.</ref> {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=9|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=8|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=7|verse=17}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=10|verse=10 f.}} {{GHGheb|text=וּלְהַבְדִּיל}} might be regarded as an explanatory addition to the command contained in verse {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=10|verse=9b|hidebook=completely|fullsizeverse=1}} (= this prohibition of wine before the service shall ye observe, and that in order to put a difference, &c.); but probably the text has been disturbed by a redactor.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=30|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=וְלָשׁוּב}} depends on the idea of receiving favour which lies in {{GHGheb|text=לְרַֽחֲמִים}}. On the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=8|verse=12}} it is sufficient to explain ''and in order to appoint them unto him for captains of thousands'' (sc. he will take them). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=44|verse=28}} translate ''and he'' (Cyrus) ''shall perform all my pleasure, and that in saying of Jerusalem'', &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|q}}
'''3.''' The period of time to which an action or occurrence represented by the infinitive construct belongs, must sometimes be inferred from the context, or from the character of the principal tenses; cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=4}} ''these are the generations of the heaven and of the earth'', {{GHGheb|text=בְּהִבָּֽרְאָם|translate=when they were created}} (prop. in their being created); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=עַד־בֹּאִי וג׳|translate=until}}<section end="par114" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

376.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par114 />''I come unto thee, and bring forth'', &c. Cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=19}} (= ''when she should have been given''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=7|verse=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|r}}
Rem. 1. The constructions of the infinitive with a preposition, described above under d, are almost always continued in the further course of the narrative by means of the ''finite verb'', i.e. by an independent sentence, not by a co-ordinate infinitive. Such a finite verb ''we'' regard as governed by a conjunction, which corresponds to the preposition standing before the infinitive. Thus the infinitival construction (frequently even with a change of subject) is continued by a perfect (with {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=9|verse=12}} ''because they have forsaken'' ({{GHGheb|text=עַל־עָזְבָם}}) ''my law'' ... {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא שָֽׁמְעוּ|translate=and have not obeyed my voice}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=1|verse=9}}; without {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=28|verse=25}} (perf. after {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} and infin.); by a perfect with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} (cf. {{GHGpar|112|i}} and § v) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=1|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=עַל־רָדְפוֹ וג׳|translate=because he did pursue his brother with the sword}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְשִׁחֵת|translate=and did cast off}} continually ''all pity'' (a frequentative perfect; for examples of the perfect consecutive proper see {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=45}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=18|verse=32}} [{{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=36|verse=17}}], always after {{GHGheb|text=עַד־בֹּאִי|translate=until I come}}); by a simple imperfect, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=1|verse=27}} (after {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=26}} (after {{GHGheb|text=בְּיוֹם|translate=in the day}}, a temporal phrase which has here become equivalent to a preposition); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=24}} (after {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}}), 10:2, 13:9, 14:25, 45:1, 49:5, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=5|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=8|verse=21|hidebook=1}} (always after {{GHGheb|text=לְ}})<ref>The great frequency of examples of this kind, especially in the poetical books, is due to a striving after what is called ''chiasmus'' in the arrangement of the parallel members in the two halves of the verse, i.e. in the instances given, the finite verb ''at the end'' of the second (co-ordinate) clause is parallel with the infinitive ''at the beginning'' of the first. In this way the verbal form necessarily became separated from the {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, and consequently the imperfect had to be used instead of the perfect consecutive. Such a parallelism of the ''external'' and ''internal'' members of a verse is frequent also in other cases, and was evidently felt to be an elegance of elevated—poetic or prophetic—style.</ref>; by an imperfect consecutive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=18}} ''and it came to pass'', {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽהֲרִימִי קוֹלִי וָֽאֶקְרָא|translate=as I lifted up my voice and cried, that ...}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=10|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=13}} (after {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=38|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=7}}, 9 ff. (after {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=7|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=34|verse=8}} (after {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|114|s}}
2. The negation of an infinitive construct, on account of the predominance of the noun-element in its character, is effected not by the verbal negative {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}(except in the compound {{GHGheb|text=בְּלֹא}}, which has come to be used as a preposition, ''without'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=35|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=19|verse=2}}), but by {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְתִּי}}, originally a substantive (see the Lexicon), with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} prefixed (but also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=מִבִּלְתִּי}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי אֲכָל־מִמֶּ֫נּוּ|translate=not to eat of it}}; in a final sense, 4:15 ''lest any finding him should smite him''; only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=23|verse=10}} is {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} repeated before the infinitive. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=9}} (if the text be right) {{GHGheb|text=בַּל}} negatives, not the infinitive, but the predicate which is understood.<section end=par114 />

<section begin=par115 />{{GHGpar-heading|115|Construction of the Infinitive Construct with Subject and Object}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|115|a}}
'''1.''' Like the infinitive absolute (see {{GHGpar|113|a}}), the character of the infinitive construct as a {{GHGterm|verbal}} noun is shown by its power of taking the case proper to its verb, and hence in transitive verbs<ref>For examples of the accus. of the object with a pass. infin., see {{GHGpar|121|c}}.</ref> ''the accusative of the object'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=9|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּיוֹם הָקִים אֶת־הַמִּשְׁכָּן|translate=on the day the }}<section end=par115 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

377.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par115 />''tabernacle was reared up''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=19|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=לְהָמִית אֶת־דָּוִד|translate=that they should slay David}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=29|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=38|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=12|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=15|verse=4|hidebook=1}}; with a negative, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי עֲשׂוֹת אֶת־כָּל־מִצְוֹתַי|translate=so that ye will not do all my commandments}}; with the accusative of the personal pronoun, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=29|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עַן הָקִיס־אֹֽתְךָ|translate=that he may establish thee}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=24|verse=7}}; with a verbal suffix, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=לְהָרְגֵ֫נִי|translate=to kill me}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=38|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי הֲשִׁיבֵ֫נִי|translate=that he would not cause me to return}} (on the suffix, cf. c). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=6}} the object even precedes the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}; on this order cf. the note on {{GHGpar|114|r}}.—If the verb governs a double accusative, the infinitive may also take the same, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=39}} {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲרֵי הוֹדִ֫יעַ אֱלֹהִים֖ אֽוֹתְךָ אֶת־כָּל־זֹאת|translate=forasmuch as God hath showed thee all this}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=21|verse=16}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|115|b}}
Rem. 1. The object after the infinitive construct must also always be regarded as in the accusative, even when it is not expressly introduced (as inall the above examples) by the {{GHGterm|nota accusativi}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}}, and when therefore the substantive in question might easily be taken as the ''genitive of the object'' governed by the infinitive (the usual construction in Arabic), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=21|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט|translate=to do judgement}}. Against regarding it as a genitive, which is in itself possible (''the doing, the executing of judgement''), is the fact (''a'') that elsewhere the {{GHGterm|nota accusativi}} is so frequently added; (''b'') that in such a case the secondary forms of the infinitive, such as {{GHGheb|text=רְאֹה}} for ({{GHGheb|text=פָּנֶ֫יךָ}}) {{GHGheb|text=רְאֹת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=48|verse=11}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=101|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=16|verse=16}}), would be unintelligible; (''c'') that certain infinitive forms, if they were to be regarded as in the construct state, could hardly retain the pretonic Qameṣ without exception, whereas, when connected with suffixes (i.e. with real genitives; cf. {{GHGpar|33|c}}), this Qameṣ necessarily becomes {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=25}} {{GHGheb|text=לְהָמִית צַדִּיק|translate=to slay the righteous}} (never as {{GHGheb|text=לַֽהֲמִית}}; cf., on the other hand, above, {{GHGheb|text=הֲשִׁיבֵ֫נִי}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=21|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=44|verse=30}}. Similarly in such cases as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=13}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=50|verse=4}}) instead of {{GHGheb|text=לָדִין עַמִּים}} we should rather expect {{GHGheb|text=לְדִין}}, if the infinitive were regarded as in the construct state, and {{GHGheb|text=עַמִּים}} as the genitive. Hence also in cases like {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=58|verse=9}} ({{GHGheb|text=שְׁלַח}} for {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלֹחַ}}) we must assume, with Sellin, op. cit., p. 78, a merely ‘external phonetic connexion’ and not the genitive construction.

{{GHGmargin-letter|115|c}}
2. The verbal suffixes added to the infinitive are (with the exception of {{GHGheb|text=לְהֽוֹצִאֵ֫הוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=39|verse=14}}) only the suffix of the 1st pers. sing. (besides the above examples cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=5|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=27|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=12|verse=17}}, &c.) and plural; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לְהַשְׁמִידֵ֫נוּ|translate=to destroy us}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=27}} (immediately after {{GHGheb|text=לָתֵת אֹתָ֫נוּ}}, so that {{GHGheb|text=־ֵ֫ נוּ}} is doubtless a {{GHGterm|verbal}} not a ''noun''-suffix, although in form it might be either); {{GHGheb|text=לַֽהֲמִיתֵ֫נוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=23}} (after {{GHGheb|text=חָפֵץ}}). Elsewhere the pronominal object is appended either by means of the accusative sign (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּלֶ֫דֶת אֹתָם}} prop. ''in the bearing them''; {{GHGheb|text=לָדַ֫עַת אֹתִי|translate=to know me}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=24|verse=7}}) or in the form of a noun-suffix (as genitive of the object). The latter occurs almost always, whenever the context excludes the possibility of a misunderstanding; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=33}} {{GHGheb|text=לְהַכֹּתוֹ}} (prop. for his smiting) ''to smite him'', not, as the form might also mean, ''in order that he might smite''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=20|verse=35}}; with the suffix of the 3rd sing. fem. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=25}}; of the 3rd plur. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=10|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=21|verse=2}}, &c. Hence also the suffixes of the 2nd sing. with the infinitive, as {{GHGheb|text=לְהַכֹּֽתְךָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=40|verse=14}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=6|verse=13}}, and even {{GHGheb|text=גַּדֶּלְךָ|translate=to magnify thee}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=3|verse=7}}, must certainly be regarded as ''nominal'' not {{GHGterm|verbal}} suffixes. The connexion of the noun-suffix, as genitive of the object, with the infinitive,<section end=par115 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

378.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par115 />was so fully established, that it could be used not only in such strange cases, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יָכְֽלוּ דַבְּרוֹ לְשָׁלֹם|translate=they could not speak to him peaceably}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=3|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=לְשִׂטְנוֹ|translate=to be an adversary to him}}, but ultimately even in the 1st sing., as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=לְתִתִּי|translate=to give me leave}} [{{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=25|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אָבָה יַבְּמִי}} ''he will not perform the duty of a husband’s brother unto me''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=4|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי עָצְבִּי|translate=that it may not grieve me!}}]

{{GHGmargin-letter|115|d}}
3. The power of governing like a verb is also retained in those verbal nouns which, although originally secondary forms of the infinitive, have fully acquired the value of nouns, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=11|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=דֵּעָה אֶת־יְהֹוָה}} (prop. to know the Lord) ''the knowledge of the Lord''; {{GHGheb|text=לְיִרְאָה אֹתִי|translate=to fear me}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=5|verse=26|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=10|verse=12|hidebook=1}}; an accusative follows {{GHGheb|text=לְאַֽהֲבָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=10|verse=12}}, 15, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=56|verse=6}} (cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=10|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=3|verse=1}}); {{GHGheb|text=לַֽהֲנָפָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=28}}; {{GHGheb|text=בְּשִׂנְאַת יְהֹוָה אֹתָ֫נוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=27}}; after verbal nouns formed with the prefix {{GHGheb|text=מ‍}} (cf. {{GHGpar|45|e}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=10|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=13|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=17|verse=9}}. The accusative of the object likewise remains after infinitives (or their secondary forms) which have the article, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=16}}, or a suffix, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=5|verse=4}}, &c., 28:4, 6, 29:19 f., 30:15, 38:5, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=13}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|115|e}}
'''2.''' The subject of the action represented by the infinitive is mostly placed immediately<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=30}} the subject of {{GHGheb|text=כִּרְאֹת}} is wanting (but {{GHGheb|text=כְּשָׁמְעוֹ}} follows); the original reading was undoubtedly {{GHGheb|text=כִּרְאֹתוֹ}}, and the text is now in a state of confusion; verse 30''a'' should come before verse 29''b''. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=26|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=13|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=41|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=42|verse=4}} the subject, although not indicated, is easily supplied from the context. The infinitive in such cases is best rendered in English by a passive.</ref> after it, either in the ''genitive'' or ''nominative''. The subject is in the genitive ({{GHGpar|33|c}}) whenever it has the form of a noun-suffix, and also when the infinitive has the termination of the constr. st. fem. sing. (see f); probably also in many other cases, where the infinitive in form and meaning is used more like a substantive, and accordingly governs like a noun. On the other hand, the subject of the infinitive is certainly to be regarded as a nominative, when it is separated from the infinitive by any insertion, and according to certain indications (see g) very probably in ninny other instances.

{{GHGmargin-letter|115|f}}
Rem. 1. Examples of genitives of the subject after infinitives in the connective form are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּשִׂנְאַת יְהֹוָה אֹתָ֫נוּ}} prop. ''in the Lord’s hating us''; cf. 7:8, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=10|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=13|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=3|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=11}}. The subject of the infinitive is probably also to be regarded as genitive in such cases as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=17|verse=1}} ''and there was no water'' {{GHGheb|text=לִשְׁתֹּת הָעָם|translate=for the people to drink}} (prop. for the drinking of the people), and in cases like {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=16}} ({{GHGheb|text=בְּלֶ֫דֶת הָגָר}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=19|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=3}}, 4, 33:38, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=6|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=133|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=7|verse=3}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|115|g}}
2. Examples in which the subject is separated from the infinitive by an insertion, and hence must certainly be regarded as a nominative, are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=לְהִסָּ֫תֶר שָׁם פֹּֽעֲלֵי אָ֫וֶן|translate=that the workers of iniquity may hide themselves there}} (prop. for the hiding themselves there the workers of iniquity); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=35|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=19|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=76|verse=10}}, and below, i. The subject is likewise to be regarded as a ''nominative'', whenever the ''Lamedh'' is prefixed to the infinitive by means of a pretonic Qameṣ (cf. b above), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=20}} {{GHGheb|text=לָשׂוּם הַמֶּ֫לֶךְ אֶל־לְבּוֹ}},<section end=par115 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

379.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par115 /><section begin=par115 />since, if the infinitive were used as a {{GHGterm|nomen regens}}, we should rather expect {{GHGheb|text=לְשׂוּם}} according to {{GHGpar|102|f}}. That the subject of the infinitive is regarded elsewhere also as nominative is again (see above, {{GHGpar|115|b|nonumber=1}}) probable, since in such forms as {{GHGheb|text=הָנִיחַ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=25|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=3}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָמִיר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=46|verse=3}}, &c., the pretonic Qameṣ is retained without exception, whereas on the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=הֲנִיחִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=24|verse=13}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֲקִימוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=23|verse=20}}, &c., we should expect {{GHGheb|text=הֲנִיחַ}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֲמִיר}}, &c., if the infinitive were regarded as a {{GHGterm|nomen regens}}. Or was the retention of the Qameṣ (assuming the thorough correctness of the Masoretic punctuation) rendered possible even before a following genitive, because that vowel was characteristic of the form? It is at all events certain that owing to the lack of case-endings,<ref>In Arabic, where the case-endings leave no doubt as to the construction, it is equally possible to say either {{GHGpron|qatlu Zaidin}} (gen. of subj.) {{GHGpron|ʿAmran}} (acc.), literally {{GHGpron|Zaid’s killing ʿAmr}}, or {{GHGpron|qatlu ʿAmrin}} (gen. of obj.) {{GHGpron|Zaidun}} (nom. of subj.), or even {{GHGpron|el-qatlu}} (with article) {{GHGpron|Zaidun}} (nom. of subj.) {{GHGpron|ʿAmran}} (acc. of obj.).</ref> a distinction between the genitival and nominatival constructions could not have been consciously made in the case of most infinitives, e.g. in unchangeable forms like {{GHGheb|text=קְטֹל}}, {{GHGheb|text=קוּם}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|115|h}}
'''3.''' When both a {{GHGterm|subject}} and an {{GHGterm|object}} are connected with the infinitive, the rule is, that the subject should immediately follow the infinitive, and then the object. The latter, in such a case, is necessarily in the accusative, but the subject (as in {{GHGpar|115|e|nonumber=1}}) may be either in the genitive or in the nominative. The noun-suffixes again are, of course, to be regarded as genitives, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽהֲרִימִי קוֹלִי|translate=as I lifted up my voice}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=21}}, and the examples, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=5|verse=4}}, &c., enumerated above, under {{GHGpar|115|d|nonumber=1}}), and so also substantives which follow a connective form, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=27}}, &c.; see above, {{GHGpar|115|d|nonumber=1}} and {{GHGpar|115|f|nonumber=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|115|i}}
On the other hand, the subject appears necessarily to be in the nominative in such cases as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=10|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=כְּהָנִיף שֵׁ֫בֶט אֶת־מְרִימָיו|translate=as if a rod should shake them that lift it up}} (for the plur. {{GHGheb|text=מרימיו}} cf. {{GHGpar|124|k}}), not {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽהֲנִיף}}, as would be expected (see {{GHGpar|115|g|nonumber=1}} above), if {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁ֫בֶט}} were in the genitive; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=33|verse=17}}. And so probably also in other cases, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=5|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=14|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=23|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=7}}. The subject is separated from the infinitive by an insertion (and consequently must necessarily be in the nominative; see {{GHGpar|115|g|nonumber=1}} above), e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=21|verse=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|115|k}}
Rem. Less frequently the object is placed immediately after the infinitive, and then the nominative of the subject, as a subsequent complement, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=20|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=בִּשְׁלֹחַ אֹתוֹ סַֽרְגוֹן|translate=when Sargon sent him}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=14|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=56|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=25|verse=8}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=24|verse=23}} the subject follows an infinitive which has a noun-suffix in place of the object.<section end=par115 />

<section begin=par116 />{{GHGpar-heading|116|The Participles}}

Cf. Sellin (see above at the head of {{GHGpar|113}}), p. 6 ff., and Kahan, p. 11 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|a}}
'''1.''' Like the two infinitives, the participles also occupy a middle place between the noun and the verb. In form they are simple nouns,<section end=par116 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

380.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par116 />and most nearly related to the adjective; consequently they cannot in themselves be employed to represent definite relations of tense or mood. On the other hand, their verbal character is shown by their not representing, like the adjectives, a fixed and permanent quality (or state), but one which is in some way connected with an ''action'' or ''activity''. The {{GHGterm|participle active}} indicates a person or thing conceived as being in the continual uninterrupted ''exercise'' of an activity. The {{GHGterm|participle passive}}, on the other hand, indicates the person or thing in a state which has been brought about by external ''actions''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|b}}
Rem.
