That the language was fully conscious of the difference between a state implying action (or effected by external action) and mere passivity, is seen from the fact, that participles proper cannot be formed from the purely stative Qal, but only verbal adjectives of the form ''qāṭēl'' ({{GHGheb|text=מָלֵא}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּבֵד}}, &c.) or ''qāṭōl'' ({{GHGheb|text=גָּבֹהַּ}}, &c.), whereas the ''transitive'' Qal {{GHGheb|text=שָׂנֵא|translate=to hate}}, although it coincides in form with the intransitive Qal (as a verb middle ''e''), nevertheless forms a participle active {{GHGheb|text=שׂנֵא}}, and participle passive {{GHGheb|text=שָׂנוּא}} (cf. the feminine {{GHGheb|text=שְׂנוּאָה}}).—In cases where the participle proper and the verbal adjective both occur, they are by no means synonymous. When the Assyrians are called in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=לַֽעֲגֵי שָׂפָה|translate=men of stammering lips}}, a character is ascribed to them which is inseparably connected with their personality. On the other hand {{GHGheb|text=כֻּלֹּה לֹעֵג לִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=7}}, describes those about the prophet as continually engaged in casting ridicule upon him. Cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=9|verse=18}} ({{GHGheb|text=שְׁכֵחֵי}}) with 50:22 ({{GHGheb|text=שֹֽׁכְחֵי}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|c}}
On the difference between the participle as expressing ''simple'' duration and the imperfect as expressing ''progressive'' duration, cf. what has been stated above in {{GHGpar|107|d}}. Nevertheless the participle is sometimes used—especially in the later books, cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=6|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=17|verse=11}}—where we should expect the action to be divided up into its several parts, and consequently should expect the finite verb. But the substitution of the participle for the ''tempus historicum'', which becomes customary in Aramaic (cf. Kautzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Bibl.-Aram.}}, § 76. 2, d, and e), is nevertheless quite foreign to Hebrew.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|d}}
'''2.''' The period of time indicated by (''a'') a participle active, either as an attribute or predicate, must be inferred from the particular context. Thus {{GHGheb|text=מֵת}} may mean either ''moriens'' ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=11|verse=9}}), or ''mortuus'' (so commonly; with the article {{GHGheb|text=הַמֵּת}} regularly = ''the dead man''), or ''moriturus'' ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=22}}); {{GHGheb|text=בָּא|translate=coming, come}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=11}}, &c., ''venturus'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=31}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=נׄפֵל|translate=falling}}, but also ''fallen'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=3|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=5|verse=3}}, and ''ready to fall'' (threatening ruin, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=11}}). For other examples of perfect participles see {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=18|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=הַשָּׁב|translate=that was returned}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=6|verse=21}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=הַשָּׁבִים|translate=which were come again}} from the captivity); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=11|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=12|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=137|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=8|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=4}} ({{GHGheb|text=קֹרֵא}}), and see m below. For future participles see {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=1|verse=3}}, &c., probably also {{GHGheb|text=לֹֽקְחֵי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=14}}. On the ''futurum instans'' (esp. after {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}}) see p below.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|e}}
(''b'') Of the passive participles, that of {{GHGterm|Qal}} (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כָּתוּב|translate=scriptus}}) always corresponds to a Latin or Greek perfect participle passive, those of the other conjugations, especially {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}}, sometimes to<section end=par116 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

381.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par116" />a Latin gerundive (or to an adjective in ''-bilis''), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=נוֹרָא|translate=metuendus}}, ''to be feared'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=76|verse=8}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=נֶחְמָד|translate=desiderandus}} (''desiderabilis'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=19|verse=11}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=נִבְרָא|translate=creandus}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=102|verse=19}}; {{GHGheb|text=נוֹלָד}}, usually ''natus'', but also (like {{GHGheb|text=הַיּוּלָּד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=8}}) ''procreandus, nasciturus'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=22|verse=32}}; {{GHGheb|text=נַֽעֲרָץ|translate=terribilis}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=89|verse=8}}; {{GHGheb|text=נִתְעָב|translate=abominable}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=16}}; {{GHGheb|text=נֶחְשָׁב|translate=aestimandus}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=22}}; {{GHGheb|text=הַנֶּֽאֱכֶ֫לֶת|translate=that may be eaten}} (an animal) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=11|verse=47}}. In {{GHGterm|Puʿal}} {{GHGheb|text=מְהֻלָּל|translate=laudandus}}, ''worthy to be praised'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=4}}. In {{GHGterm|Hophʿal}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=21}} {{GHGheb|text=מֻשְׁלָךְ}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=11|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=הַמּֽוּמָתִים}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=12|verse=5}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} {{GHGheb|text=מוּדַ֫עַת}}.<ref>Such examples as {{GHGheb|text=נוֹרָא}}, {{GHGheb|text=נֶחְמָד}}, {{GHGheb|text=מְהֻלָּל}} show plainly the origin of this gerundive use of the participle passive. A person or thing ''feared, desired'', or ''praised'' at all times is shown thereby to be ''terrible, desirable'', or ''praiseworthy'', and therefore also ''to be feared'', &c.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|f}}
'''3.''' The participles active, in virtue of their partly verbal character, possess the power of governing like verbs, and consequently, when used in the absolute state, may take after them an object either in the accusative, or with the preposition with which the verb in question is elsewhere usually construed, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=29}} {{GHGheb|text=אֹיֵב אֶת־דָּוִד|translate=hating David}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=29}}; with the suffix of the accusative, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עשֵׂ֫נִי|translate=that made me}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=15}}; {{GHGheb|text=מִי רֹאֵ֫נוּ|translate=who seeth us?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=15}} (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=רֹאָ֫נִי}} is abnormal); {{GHGheb|text=רֹדֵם|translate=ruling them}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=68|verse=28}}, sometimes also with the article, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=33}} {{GHGheb|text=הַֽמְאַזְּרֵ֫נִי|translate=that girdeth me}} (LXX ὁ κραταιῶν με); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=8|verse=14}}–16, 13:6, 11, 20:1, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=12}} (where, however, Cheyne omits the article), 63:11, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=81|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=103|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=11|verse=6}}; followed by a preposition, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=9|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=הָֽרֹדִים בָּעָם|translate=which bare rule over the people}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=20|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=הִֽנְנִי רֹפֵא לָךְ|translate=behold, I will heat thee}}.
<ref>On the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is.|chapter=11|verse=9}} ''as the waters'' {{GHGheb|text=לַיָּם מְכַסִּים|translate=covering the sea}}, the {{GHGheb|text=ל}} serves only to introduce the object preceding the participle [cf. the Arabic parallels cited by Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Tenses}}, § 135, 7 ''Obs.'']. Cf. Hab. 2:14.</ref>

By an exhaustive examination of the statistics, Sellin (see the title at the head of § 113), p. 40 ff., shows that the participle when construed as a {{GHGterm|verb}} expresses a single and comparatively transitory act, or relates to particular cases, historical facts, and the like, while the participle construed as a ''noun'' (see g) indicates repeated, enduring, or commonly occurring acts, occupations, and thoughts.

So also the verbal adjectives of the form ''qāṭēl'' may take an accusative of the person or thing, if the finite verb from which they are derived governs an accusative, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=34|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=מָלֵא רוּחַ חָכְמָה|translate=full of the spirit of wisdom}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=5|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=חָפֵץ רֶ֫שַׁע|translate=that hath pleasure in wickedness}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|g}}
As a sort of noun the participle may, however, also exercise the same government as a noun, being in the construct state, and followed by the object of the action in the genitive (see {{GHGpar|89|a}}; and cf. {{GHGpar|128|x}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=5|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=אֹֽהֲבֵי שְׁמֶ֫ךָ|translate=that love thy name}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=19|verse=8}} f.; also when a verbal adjective, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=12}} and often {{GHGheb|text=יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים|translate=one fearing}}<section end="par116" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

382.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par116 />''God''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=15}}; with an infinitive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=127|verse=2}}; with a noun-suffix (which, according to {{GHGpar|33|c}}, also represents a genitive), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־מֹֽצְאִי|translate=whosoever findeth me}} (prop. my finder; cf. {{GHGheb|text=עשִֹׁי|translate=my maker}}); 12:3 {{GHGheb|text=מְבָֽרֲכֶ֫יךָ|translate=that bless thee}}, {{GHGheb|text=מְקַלֶּלְךָ|translate=that curseth thee}} (but read either {{GHGheb|text=מְקַלְלֶ֫יךָ}}, or {{GHGheb|text=מְבֽרֶכְךָ}} in the preceding clause); 27:29, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=63|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=49}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=33|verse=22}} read {{GHGheb|text=מְשָֽׁרְתִים אֹתִי}}.<ref>When, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=40|verse=19}}, the participle with the noun-suffix {{GHGheb|text=הָֽעשֹׁוֹ|translate=he that made him}}, also has the article (cf. {{GHGpar|127|i}}), the anomaly is difficult to understand, since a word determined by a genitive does not admit of being determined by the article.—No less remarkable is the use of the constr. st. of the participle before the accusative in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=33|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=מְשָֽׁרְתֵי אֹתִי|translate=that minister unto me}} (for which there is {{GHGheb|text=מְשָֽׁרְתַי}} in verse 21). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=13}} an accusative of the product follows the genitive of the object, {{GHGheb|text=עשֵֹׁה שַׁחַר עֵיפָה|translate=maker of the morning into darkness}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּעֵת מֽוֹלִכֵךְ}} is supposed to mean ''at the time when he led thee''; perhaps the perfect ({{GHGheb|text=הוֹל׳}}) should be read as in 6:15. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=27|verse=34}}, the ancient versions read {{GHGheb|text=נִשְׁבַּרְתְּ}} ({{GHGheb|text=ה}}){{GHGheb|text=עַתָּ|translate=now thou art broken}}, instead of the difficult {{GHGheb|text=עֵת נִשְׁבֶּ֫רֶת}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=20|verse=40}} read {{GHGheb|text=עשֶֹׁה}} before {{GHGheb|text=הֵ֫נָּה וָהֵ֫נָּה}}.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|h}}
Rem. To the class of objective genitives belong also specifications of place after the participles {{GHGheb|text=בָּא|translate=iniens}} and {{GHGheb|text=יֹצֵא|translate=egrediens}}, since the verbs {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹא}} and {{GHGheb|text=יָצָא}}, in the sense of ''ingredi, egredi'', can be directly connected with an accusative; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=10}}, 18 {{GHGheb|text=בָּאֵי שַׁ֫עַר עִירוֹ|translate=that went in at the gate of his city}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=4}}; after {{GHGheb|text=יֽׄצְאֵי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=46|verse=26|hidebook=1}}, &c.—In poetic language the participle in the construct state may be connected not only with a genitive of the object, but also with any other specifications (especially of space) which otherwise can only be made to depend on the verb in question by means of a preposition; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=38|verse=18}}, and frequently, {{GHGheb|text=יֽוֹרְדֵי־בוֹר|translate=they that go down into the pit}} (the grave); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=88|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=שֹֽׁכְבֵי קֶ֫בֶר|translate=that lie in the grave}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=24}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=7|verse=17}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=11|verse=5}}, 7, 9 ''those that came in'' (or ''went out'') ''on the sabbath'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=5|verse=18}}, &c.; instead of the construction with {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=59|verse=20}} (''those who turn from transgression''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=2|verse=8}} (cf. {{GHGpar|72|p}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|i}}
These genitives of nearer definition appear also in the form of a noun-suffix, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=40}}, 49 {{GHGheb|text=קָמַי}} (for {{GHGheb|text=קָמִים עָלַי}}) ''that rise up against me''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=44|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=שָׁבֶ֫יהָ|translate=her converts}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=53|verse=6}} ({{GHGheb|text=חֹנָךְ}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־בָּאֶ֫יהָ|translate=all that go unto her}}; the construction is especially bold in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־צֹבֶ֫יהָ וּמְצֹֽדָתָהּ|translate=all that fight against her and her stronghold}} (for {{GHGheb|text=בָּל־הַצֹּֽבְאִים עָלֶ֫יהָ וְעַל־מ׳}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=102|verse=9}} even with a participle Poʿal, {{GHGheb|text=מְהֽוֹלָלַי|translate=they that are mad against me}} (?), but read perhaps with Olshausen {{GHGheb|text=מְחֽוֹלְלַי|translate=who pierce me}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=30}} ''as a terebinth'' {{GHGheb|text=נׄבֶ֫לֶּת עָלֶ֫הָ|translate=fading as regards its leaf}}, it remains doubtful whether {{GHGheb|text=נׄבֶ֫לֶת}} is in the absolute state, and consequently {{GHGheb|text=עָלֶ֫הָ}} in the accusative, or whether it is to be regarded as construct state, and {{GHGheb|text=עָלֶ֫הָ}} as the genitive. In the latter case it would be analogous to {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=14|verse=2}} (see k).

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|k}}
'''4.''' The passive participles also may either be in the absolute state, and take the determining word in the accusative,<ref>On the proper force of this accusative when retained in the passive construction cf. below, {{GHGpar|117|cc}}, &c., and {{GHGpar|121|c}}, d. So also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=4|verse=12}} is to be understood, ''and the builders'' were {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ חַרְבּוֹ אֲסוּרִים עַל־מָתְנָיו|translate=girded every one with his sword on his side, and building}}.</ref> or may be connected<section end=par116 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

383.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par116 />with it in the construct state, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=18|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=9|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=לָבוּשׁ בַּדִּים|translate=clothed in linen}}, cf. verse 3 {{GHGheb|text=הַלָּבֻשׁ הַבַּדִּים}}; (even with a suffix {{GHGheb|text=קָרוּעַ כֻּתָּנְתּוֹ|translate=rent as regards his coat}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=32}}; with the participle following {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=7}}); but {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=9|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=לְבוּשׁ הַבַּדִּים|translate=the one clothed with linen}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=31}} {{GHGheb|text=קְרֻעֵי בְגָדִים|translate=rent in respect of clothes}}, equivalent to ''with their clothes rent'' (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=41|verse=5}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=24|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=25|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=33|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=נְשׂוּי־פֶּ֫שַׁע|translate=forgiven in respect of transgression}}, {{GHGheb|text=כְּסוּי חֲטָאָה|translate=covered in respect of sin}}); with a suffix to the noun, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=14|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=נְלוֹז דְּרָכָיו|translate=he that is perverse in his ways}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|l}}
Rem. The passive participle occurs in the construct state before a genitive of the ''cause'', e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=שְׂרֻפוֹת אֵשׁ|translate=burnt with fire}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=24}}; before a genitive denoting the ''author'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=31}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּרוּךְ יְהֹוָה|translate=blessed of the Lord}} (but {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=115|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּרוּכִים לַיהוָֹה}}, see {{GHGpar|121|f}}); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=53|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=22|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=14|verse=1}} (15:14, 25:4); hence also with noun-suffixes (which are accordingly genitive) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=9|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=קְרֻאֶ֫יהָ|translate=her invited ones}}, i.e. those invited by her; cf. 7:26, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=37|verse=22}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|m}}
'''5.''' The use of the participle as predicate is very frequent in noun-clauses (which, according to {{GHGpar|140|e}}, describe established facts and states), in which the period of time intended by the description must again (see above, d) be inferred from the context. Thus:

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|n}}
(''a'') As ''present'', in speaking of truths which hold good at all times, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=1|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=דּוֹר הֹלֵךְ וְדוֹר בָּא}} ''one generation goeth, and another generation cometh; and the earth abideth'' ({{GHGheb|text=עֹמָ֫דֶת}}) ''for ever''; cf. verse 7; also to represent incidental (continuous) occurrences which are just happening, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=8|hidebook=1}} (''I am fleeing''); 32:12, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=7}}; when the subject is introduced by the emphatic demonstrative {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה|translate=behold!}} ({{GHGpar|100|o}} and {{GHGpar|105|b}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=הִנָּךְ הָרָה|translate=behold, thou art with child}}, &c.; 27:42; frequently also in circumstantial clauses (connected by {{GHGterm|Wāw}}), cf. {{GHGpar|141|e}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=2}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|o}}
(''b'') To represent ''past'' actions or states, sometimes in independent noun-clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=וְכָל־הָעָם רֹאִים אֶת־הַקּוֹלֹת|translate=and all the people saw the thunderings}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=5}}; in negative statements, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=23}}<sup> ''a''</sup>; sometimes in relativeclauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=23}}<sup> ''b''</sup>, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=3|verse=2}} (cf. also the frequent combination of the participle with the article as the equivalent of a relative clause, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאֹמֵר|translate=which saidst}}; 12:7, 16:13, 35:1, 3, 36:35, 48:16, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=31}}, &c.); sometimes again (see n) in ''circumstantial'' clauses, especially those representing actions or states which occurred simultaneously with other past actions, &c., e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=1}} ''and the two angels came to Sodom'' {{GHGheb|text=וְלוֹט ישֵׁב|translate=and}} (i.e. ''while'') ''Lot sat'', &c.; 18:1, 8, 16, 22, 25:26, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=22|verse=9}}; also with the subject introduced by {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} 37:7, 41:17. (On {{GHGheb|text=הֹלֵךְ}} with a following adjective or participle to express an action constantly or occasionally recurring, cf. {{GHGpar|113|u}}.)

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|p}}
(''c'') To announce ''future'' actions or events, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=16}} ''at this season when the time cometh round'', {{GHGheb|text=אַתְּ חֹבֶ֫קֶת בֵּן|translate=thou shalt embrace a son}}; so after a specification of time, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hag|chapter=2|verse=6}} (but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=23|verse=15}}, where, after {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה}} we should rather expect a perfect consecutive, it is better to explain<section end=par116 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

384.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par116 />{{GHGheb|text=וְנִשְׁכַּ֫חַת}}, with Qimḥi, as the 3rd sing. fem. of the perfect; on the form, cf. {{GHGpar|44|f}}); or in relative clauses, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=5|translate=what I am doing}}, i.e. am in the act of doing; in a deliberative question, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=30}}; but especially often when the subject is introduced by {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} (especially also if the subject be attached as a suffix to {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} as {{GHGheb|text=הִנְנִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִנְּךָ}}, &c.), if it is intended to announce the event as imminent, or at least near at hand (and sure to happen), when it is called ''futurum instans'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=13|hidebook=1}} f., 48:21, 50:5, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=8|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=34|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=7|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=33|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=17|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=30|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=2|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=3|verse=8|hidebook=1}}; with a participle passive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=21}}: cf. also {{GHGpar|112|t}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|q}}
Rem. 1. As the above examples show, a noun-clause with a participle as predicate may have for its subject either a substantive or a personal pronoun; in both cases the participle, especially if there be a certain emphasis upon it, may precede the subject. Also in noun-clauses introduced by {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} the subject may be either a substantive, or (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=7}}) a separate personal pronoun, or a suffix attached to {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}}. In the same way, the subject may also be introduced by {{GHGheb|text=יֵשׁ}} (''est'', see the Lexicon) with a suffix, and in negative sentences by {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} (''non est'') with a suffix, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=36}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־יֶשְׁךָ מוֹשִׁיעַ|translate=if thou wilt save}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־אֵֽינְךָ מְשַׁלֵּחַ|translate=if thou wilt not send}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=19|verse=11}}.—In such cases as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=יָדוֹ הַנְּטוּיָה|translate=the stretched out hand is his}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַנְּטוּיָה}} is not, like {{GHGheb|text=נְטוּיָה}} in 9:11, 16, &c., the predicate (in which case the participle could not take the article), but the subject; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=45|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=66|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=20|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=7|verse=6}} (cf. {{GHGpar|126|k}}), where the participle with the article likewise refers to the present, also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=7|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=3|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=16}}, where it refers to the past. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=12|verse=8}} and 21:11 even in relative clauses after {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|r}}
2. To give express emphasis to an action continuing in the ''past'', the perfect {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} in the corresponding person is sometimes added to the participle, and similarly the imperfect {{GHGheb|text=יִֽהְיֶה}} (or the jussive {{GHGheb|text=יְהִי}}, or the imperfect consecutive) is used to emphasize an action continuing in the ''future'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=הַבָּקָר הָיוּ חֹֽרְשׁוֹת|translate=the oxen}} (cows) ''were plowing''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=9|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=6}}; the same occurs with a passive participle, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=5|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=3|verse=3}}; {{GHGheb|text=יִֽהְיֶה}} with a participle is found e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=2}}; the jussive in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=109|verse=12}};<ref>A jussive is practically to be supplied also in the formulae of blessing and cursing, {{GHGheb|text=בָּרוּךְ|translate=blessed be ...}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=26}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=אָרוּר|translate=cursed art thou}} ... 3:14, &c.</ref> and {{GHGheb|text=ויהי}} with a participle in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=1|verse=4}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|s}}
3. The ''personal pronoun'' which would be expected as the subject of a participial clause is frequently omitted, or at least (as elsewhere in noun-clauses, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=26|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=16|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=32}}) the pronoun of the 3rd pers. {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=8}} (the participle always after {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}}); cf., moreover, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=33|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=22|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=33|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=55|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=17}}, 19 ff., 25:2, 26:7.—{{GHGheb|text=הִיא}} is omitted in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=18|verse=28}}; {{GHGheb|text=הֵ֫מָּה}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=8|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=9|verse=3}}; in a relative clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=24|verse=2}}.—The personal pronoun of the 2nd pers. masc. ({{GHGheb|text=אַתָּה}}) is omitted in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=10}}; the 2nd fem. ({{GHGheb|text=אַתְּ}}) in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=16}} (where, however, for the participle {{GHGheb|text=וְנׄכַ֫חַת}} the 2nd fem. perf. {{GHGheb|text=וְוֹכַ֫חַתְּ}} is to be read); the pronoun of the 1st sing. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=1|verse=5}} (?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=9|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=2|verse=16}}; the 2nd plur. ({{GHGheb|text=אַתֶּם}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=24}} (if the text be right), 6:3, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=7}} (?). But these passages are all more or less doubtful.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|t}}
Of a different kind are the cases in which some undefined subject is to be supplied with the participle; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵלַי קֹרֵא|translate=there is one calling unto me}} (= one calleth; {{GHGpar|144|d}}); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=33|verse=4|hidebook=1}}.—So with participles in the plur., e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=5|verse=16}} ({{GHGheb|text=אֹֽמְרִים}} sc. the taskmasters); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=38|verse=23}} (in 33:5 the text is corrupt), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=7}} (?), 36:13, 37:11 (equivalent to ''sunt qui dicant'').<section end=par116 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

385.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par116" />{{GHGmargin-letter|116|u}}
4. We must mention as a special class those noun-clauses which occur at the beginning of a period, and are intended to lay stress upon the fact that the first action still continues on the occurrence of the second (always introduced by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}); e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=16}} f. {{GHGheb|text=עוֹד זֶה מְדַבֵּר וְזֶה בָא|translate=he was yet speaking, and}} (=''when'') ''another came'', &c.<ref>The independent noun-clause here lays stress upon the simultaneous occurrence (and consequently the overlapping) of the events far more forcibly than could be done by a subordinate expression of time (as e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי בְדַבְּרוֹ}}). In English it may be represented by ''scarcely had he finished speaking when''. ... As the above examples show, the apodosis also frequently consists of a noun-clause.</ref>; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=11.27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=36|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=14|verse=17}} {{GHGtranslate|she was entering the threshold of the house, when the child died}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=9|verse=20}} f.; also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=42}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=18}} f., in all which passages the apodosis is introduced by {{GHGheb|text=וְהִנֵּה}}.—On the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=14}} the noun-clause itself is introduced by {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} (as in verse 22 by {{GHGheb|text=וְהִנֵּה}}), and denotes an action only just impending.<ref>At the same time the preceding {{GHGheb|text=עוֹד|translate=still}} shows that what is announced is not merely a future event, but a future event ''contemporaneous'' with something else; the case thus entirely differs from the examples given in {{GHGpar|112|t}}, where {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} refers to the following participle, while here it belongs properlyto the apodosis, before which it is therefore generally placed; see the examples.</ref> Finally, when the whole sentence is introduced by means of {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}} (cf. {{GHGpar|111|g}}), and the apodosis by {{GHGheb|text=וְהִנֵּה}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=35}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=13|verse=21|hidebook=1}}; without {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=7|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=19|verse=37}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=38}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|v}}
{{GHGterm|Participles active}}, which are used in the sense of the perfect participle, and also {{GHGterm|participles passive}}, in accordance with their meaning, express in such noun-clauses a state still continuing on the occurrence of the principal action, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=25}} {{GHGheb|text=הִוא מוּצֵאת וְהִיא שָֽׁלְחָה|translate=she was being brought forth, when she sent}}, &c.; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=50|verse=24}}. [See further in Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Tenses}}, §§ 166–169.]

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|w}}
5. Different from the examples treated in ''u'' and ''v'' are the instances in which a participle (either alone or as the attribute of a noun) stands at the beginning of the sentence as a ''casus pendens'' (or as the subject of a ''compound noun-clause'', see {{GHGpar|143|c}}) to indicate a condition, the contingent occurrence of which involves a further consequence; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=שֹׁפֵךְ דַּם הָֽאָדָם בָּֽאָדָם דָּמוֹ יִשָּׁפֵךְ}} ''shedding man’s blood'', i.e. if any one sheddeth man’s blood, ''by man shall his blood be shed''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=75|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=17|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=18}}; so especially if {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־|translate=every}} precedes the participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=11}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=21|verse=12}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=5|verse=8}} (''whosoever smiteth''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=11|verse=6}}. The apodosis is very often introduced by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} ({{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=15}} (with a following perfect consecutive), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=35|verse=30}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=הַכֹּהֵן כָּל־אִישׁ זֹבֵחַ זֶ֫בַה וּבָא נַ֫עַר}} ''when any man offered sacrifice, the priest’s servant came'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=10}} (participle with article); 22:41 (where, however, the text is to be emended in accordance with {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=41}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=23|verse=3}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=23|verse=24}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}; 29:9.—As in the instances discussed under ''u'', such sentences are sometimes preceded by {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=11|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי כָּל־הַבָּא|translate=and it came to pass, that as many as came}}, &c. [or by {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיְה}}, frequentative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=30}}].—On the other hand, {{GHGheb|text=וְהַנִּשְׁבֶּ֫רֶת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=8|verse=22}} is a mere catchword (equivalent to ''and as for that which was broken'') to call to mind the contents of verse 8.

6. On the use of the participle after the infinitive absolute {{GHGheb|text=הָלוֹךְ}} cf. {{GHGpar|113|u}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|116|x}}
7. Almost as a rule the participial construction beginning a sentence (like the infinitival constructions according to {{GHGpar|114|r}}) is continued by means of a finite verb with or without {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, before which the English construction requires us to supply the relative pronoun implied in the participle; thus,<section end="par116" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

386.text:
continued by means of a perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=שָׂם תֵּבֵל כַּמִּדְבָּר וְעָרָיו הָרָ֑ס|translate=that made the world as a wilderness, and overthrew the cities thereof}}On the parallelism between the ''external'' and ''internal'' members, which appears here and in many other examples of this kind, see the note on {{GHGpar|114|r}}.; 43:7, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=22|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=136|verse=13}} ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=17}}; by a perfect without {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=11}}; by a simple imperfect (as the ''modus rei repetitae'' in the present), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=46|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=7|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=17}}, 19 ff., 24:21; by an imperfect without {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=19|verse=26|hidebook=1}}; by an imperfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=10}} (after several participles), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=136|verse=10|hidebook=1}}f.
{{center|C. {{Small-caps|The Government of the Verb}}.}} {{GHGpar-heading|117|The Direct Subordination of the Noun to the Verb as Accusative of the Object. The Double Accusative}}
L. Kaila, ''Zur Syntax des in verbaler Abhängigkeit stehenden Nomens im alttest. Hebr.'', Helsingfors, 1906.
{{GHGmargin-letter|117|a}} '''1.''' The simplest way in which a noun is subordinated to a verbal form is by the addition of an accusative of the object to a transitive verb.The verb in question may either have been originally transitive, or only have become transitive by a modification of its original meaning. Thus the vocalization shows that {{GHGheb|text=חָפֵץ}} (''to have pleasure'', usually with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}) ''to desire'', {{GHGheb|text=מָלֵא}} (''to be full'' of something, also transitive) ''to fill'', were originally intransitive. Cf. also such cases as {{GHGheb|text=בָּכָה|translate=to weep}} (generally with {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}} or {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}), but also ''to bewail'' with an accusative; {{GHGheb|text=יָשַׁב|translate=to dwell}} (usually with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}), but also ''to inhabit'' with an accusative (cf. further, under u).—The examples are different in which verbs of motion such as {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹא|translate=intrare}}, also ''aggredi'', {{GHGheb|text=יָצָֹא|translate=egredi}} (cf. {{GHGpar|116|h}} above), {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּב|translate=redire}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=52|verse=8}}, take an accusative of the aim of the motion, while {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹא}} according to the Old Semitic usage, even takes an accusative of the person (at least in poetry, equivalent to {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹא אֶל־}} in prose). In the absence of case-endings,On traces of these endings, especially the remains of a former accusative ending in ''a'', cf. {{GHGpar|90|c}}. this accusative can now be recognized only from the context, or by the particle {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}} ({{GHGheb|text=אֵת}}, before suffixes also {{GHGheb|text=אֹת}}, {{GHGheb|text=אוֹת}}){{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}} (toneless owing to the following Maqqeph), and {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} (with a tone-long ''ē'', {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽת־}} only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=26}}), {{GHGheb|text=אֹת}} or {{GHGheb|text=אוֹת}} before the light suffixes (on all these forms cf. {{GHGpar|103|b}}: the underlying form ''āth'' was obscured in Hebrew to ''ôth'', shortened to ''ăth'' before suffixes beginning with a consonant and then modified to {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}}, whence finally the secondary form {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} with the tone), Phoenician {{GHGheb|text=אית}} i.e. probably ''iyyāth'' (for the Phoenician form, cf. G. Hoffmann, ''Einige phönik. Inschriften'', Göttingen, 1889, p. 39 f.), Punic ''yth'' or (according to Euting) pronounced even as a mere prefixed ''t'', Arabic, before suffixes, ''’iyyâ'', Aram. {{GHGheb|text=יָת}}, {{GHGheb|text=יַת}}. It was no doubt originally a substantive, meaning ''essence, substance, self'' (like the Syriac ''yāth''; on the other hand, any connexion with the Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=אוֹת}}, Syriac ''’āiā'', Arabic ''’āyat'', ''a sign'', must, with Nöldeke, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZDMG.|Zeitschrift der deutschen morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Lpz. 1846 ff., since 1903 ed. by A. Fischer.}}}} xl. 738, be rejected), but now united in the construct state with a following noun or suffix stands for the pronoun ''ipse'', αὐτός. In common use, however (cf. Wilson, ‘The particle {{GHGheb|text=את}} in Hebrew,’ {{GHGcite|title=Hebraica}}, vi. 2, 3, and the precise statistics of the use of {{GHGheb|text=את}} on p. 140 ff.), it has so little force (like the oblique cases αὐτοῦ, αὐτῷ, αὐτόν, sometimes also ''ipsius, ipsum'', and the Germ. ''desselben'', &c.) that it merely serves to introduce a determinate object; {{GHGheb|text=אֵת הַשָּׁמַ֫יִם}} prop. αὐτὸν τὸν οὐρανόν (cf. αὐτὴν Χρυσηΐδα, Iliad i. 143) is no stronger than the simple {{GHGheb|text=הַשָּׁמַ֫יִם}} τὸν οὐρανόν. Cf., further, P. Haupt on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=18|verse=24}} in his Rainbow Bible, and also in the ''Notes on Esther'', p. 191. prefixed to it. The use of this {{GHGterm|nota accusativi}}

387.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par117" />is, however, somewhat rare in poetry, and even in prose it is not invariably necessary but is restricted to those cases in which the accusative of the object is more closely determined by being a proper name, or by having the article, or by a following determinate genitive (hence also by the suffixes), or in some other way (see below, c), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=1}} ''and she bare'' {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־קַ֫יִן|translate=Cain}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=1|hidebook=1}} ''God created'' {{GHGheb|text=אֵת הַשָּׁמַ֫יִם וְאֵת הָאָ֫רֶץ|translate=the heaven and the earth}} (but {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=4|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫רֶץ וְשָׁמַ֫יִם}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=25|hidebook=1}} ''and God made'' {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־חַיַּת הָאָ֫רֶץ|translate=the beast of the earth}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=24|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|b}}
Rem. 1. The rare occurrence of the {{GHGterm|nota accusativi}} in poetic style (e.g. it never occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=2–18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2}}, &c., though it is frequent in the late Psalms) may be explained from the fact that in this as in other respects (cf. {{GHGpar|2|q}}) poetry represents a somewhat more archaic stage of the language than prose. The need of some external means of indicating the accusative could only have been felt after the case-endings had become wholly extinct. Even then the {{GHGheb|text=את}} would probably have been used at first to indicate only an object placed ''before'' the verb (when it followed, it was already sufficiently characterized by its position as depending on the verb), or proper names.<ref>Thus, in Dt 33, {{GHGheb|text=את}} occurs only in verse 9 (twice, with an object preceding the verb), in Gn 49 in the blessing of Jacob only in verse 15 with a co-ordinate second object (consequently farther removed from the verb). Of the thirteen instances of {{GHGheb|text=את}} in the ''Mêša‛'' inscription, seven stand directly and four indirectly before proper names.</ref> Finally, however, the {{GHGterm|nota accusativi}} became so customary everywhere in prose, that even the pronominal object was expressed rather by {{GHGheb|text=את}} with suffixes than by verbal suffixes, even when none of the reasons mentioned under ''e'' can be assigned for it; cf. Giesebrecht in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1881, p. 258 ff., and the statistics of H. Petri, cited above at the head of § 58. Such examples as {{GHGheb|text=כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=22}} in the ''Priestly Code'', beside {{GHGheb|text=בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּ֫הוּ יְהֹוָה}} 7:5 in the ''Jahvist'', are especially instructive.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|c}}
2. As accusatives determined in other ways, we have in the first place to consider the collectives introduced by {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל|translate=entirety}}, without a following article or determinate genitive, inasmuch as the meaning of {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל}} includes a determinative sense, cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=21}}, 30, 8:21, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=34}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=25|verse=9}}. {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־כֹּל}} is used absolutely in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=3}}, cf. 39:23; similarly, {{GHGheb|text=מִי}} is determinate of itself, since it always denotes a person, hence {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־מִי|translate=quem?}} e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, &c., but never {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־מָה|translate=quid?}} So also the relative {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} in the sense of ''eum qui'' or ''quem'', &c., e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=3}}, or ''id quod'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=24}}, &c. Cf. also such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=19}}, where {{GHGheb|text=אֵת אֲשֶׁר}} is equivalent to ''the circumstance, that'', &c.—Elsewhere {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} stands before nouns which are determinate in sense, although the article is omitted, which according to {{GHGpar|126|h}} is very frequently the case in poetic or otherwise elevated style; thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=24|verse=14}}, 15, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=7}} (to distinguish the object from the subject); 50:4 (with the first of two accusatives, also for the sake of clearness); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=43|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=13|verse=21}} (where the {{GHGheb|text=צַדִּיקִים}} are to be regarded as a distinct class); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=25}}<section end="par117" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

388.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par117 />(unless, with Beer and others, we read {{GHGheb|text=וְאִם}} for {{GHGheb|text=וְאֶת־}}); also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=7|verse=7}} may be a quotation of an ancient maxim.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|d}}
On the other hand {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} occurs very seldom in prose before a noun actually or apparently undetermined. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=כָּנָף}} is more closely defined by means of the following relative clause; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=4|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ צַדִּיק}} refers to Ishbosheth (as if it were ''him, who was an innocent man''); in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=6|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=עֶשְׂרִים אַמָּה}} refers to the particular twenty cubits. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=28}} (otherwise in verse 29) perhaps the {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}} is used in order to avoid the combination {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹר אִישׁ}} (as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=9}} to avoid the cacophony {{GHGheb|text=נָשַׁךְ הַנָּחָשׁ אִישׁ}}?); in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=7|verse=8}} and 20:10 the accusatives are at any rate defined by the centext.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־אַהַד מֵהֶם}} probably means ''even a single one'' (and then ''ipso facto'' a definite one) ''of them'', as also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־אַחַד מֵֽהַנְּעָרִים}} may refer to some definite one of the men-servants. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=30}} we should read {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־שֶׁ֫בַע הַכְּבָשׂת}} with the Samaritan, since the seven lambs have been already mentioned; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=1}} translate with Meyer, ''Die Israeliten'', p. 79, {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־בַּת־לֵוִי|translate=the daughter of Levi}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=9}} read {{GHGheb|text=הַשֹּׁ֫הַם}} with the Samaritan; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=20|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־אִשָּׁה}} is probably a scribal error due to {{GHGheb|text=וְאֶת־אִמָּה}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=20}} read {{GHGheb|text=נַפְשִׁי}} with the LXX for {{GHGheb|text=פַּרְעשׁ אֶחָד}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=5|verse=24}} read {{GHGheb|text=הַצְּעָדָה}} as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=14|verse=15}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=16}} the {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}} is incorrectly inserted from 20:3, where it refers to the women already mentioned; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=18}} read {{GHGheb|text=הַמַּצֶּ֫בֶת}}, or omit both {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} with the LXX and Lucian; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=12|verse=31}} omit {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=23|verse=20}} probably {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־עַצְמוֹתָם}} is to be read; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=25|verse=9}} the text is corrupt. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=32}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־זָרִים}} might refer to ''the strangers in question''; but see Smend on the passage.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|e}}
3. The pronominal object ''must'' be represented by {{GHGheb|text=את}} with a suffix (instead of a verbal suffix), when (''a'') it precedes the verb, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=33}} {{GHGheb|text=אֹֽתְכָה הָרַ֫גְתִּי וְאוֹתָהּ הֶֽחֱיֵ֫יתִי|translate=I had slain thee and saved her alive}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=22|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=8|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=43|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=57|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=17}}, 22, 7:19; (''b'') when a suffix is already attached to the verb, and as a rule when a second accusative with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} follows, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=25}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהִרְאַ֫נִי אֹתוֹ|translate=and he will show me it}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=17|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=לְהָמִית אֹתִי וְאֶת־בָּנַי|translate=to kill us and our children}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=5|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=16}} (but cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=11|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=15|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, &c., and Driver on {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=5|verse=10}}); (''c'') after an infinitive absolute, see above {{GHGpar|113|a}} note; (''d'') after an infinitive construct, when it is immediately followed by the subject, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=39}}, or when the combination of a suffix with the infinitive might lead to a misunderstanding, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי הַכּֽוֹת־אֹתוֹ|translate=lest one should smite him}}, &c., where {{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי הַכּוֹתוֹ}} might also mean ''lest he should smite''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|f}}
4. The pronominal object is very frequently omitted, when it can be easily supplied from the context; so especially the neuter accusative referring to something previously mentioned (the English ''it'') after {{GHGterm|verba sentiendi}} ({{GHGheb|text=שָׁמַע}}) and ''dicendi'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=22}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּגֵּד|translate=and he told}} (it); also after {{GHGheb|text=נָתַן|translate=to give}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=41|hidebook=1}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=לָקַח|translate=to take}}, {{GHGheb|text=הֵבִיא|translate=to bring}}, {{GHGheb|text=שִׂים|translate=to lay}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=23}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=מָצָא|translate=to find}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=33}}, &c. A personal object is omitted, e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=51|hidebook=1}} (after {{GHGheb|text=לָקַח}}.—The omission of the plural object is remarkable, because it leaves an opportunity for a misunderstanding, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=שָׁמַ֫עְתּי אֹֽמְרִים}}<ref>According to the ordinary rules of syntax (cf. {{GHGpar|116|t}}) we should translate, ''I heard men who said'', &c.</ref> ''I heard'' them ''saying''; perhaps, however, we should read {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמַעְתִּים}} with the Samaritan.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|g}}
5. In common formulae the substantival object is also sometimes omitted<section end=par117 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

389.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par117 />(an elliptical expression); thus e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כָּרַת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=16}}, &c. (see the Lexicon) stands for {{GHGheb|text=כָּרַת בְּרִית}} like the English ''to close'' (sc. a bargain) with any one; {{GHGheb|text=נָטַר|translate=to keep}} (sc. {{GHGheb|text=אַף|translate=anger}}) equivalent to ''to be resentful'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=103|verse=9}}, &c.; so also {{GHGheb|text=שָׁמַר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=5}} (beside {{GHGheb|text=נָטַר}}); {{GHGheb|text=נָשָׂא}} for {{GHGheb|text=נָשָׂא קוֹל|translate=to lift up the voice}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=נָשָׂא לְ}} for {{GHGheb|text=נָשָׂא עָוֹן לְ}} ''to take away any one’s sin'' (to forgive), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=24}}, 26, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=9}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלַח|translate=to put forth}} (sc. {{GHGheb|text=יָד|translate=the hand}}) equivalent to ''to reach after something'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=6|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=17}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|h}}
6. {{GHGterm|Verba sentiendi}} may take a second object, generally in the form of a participle or adjective and necessarily indeterminate, to define more exactly the action or state in which the object is perceived, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּשְׁמַע משֶׁה אֶת־הָעָם בֹּכֶה|translate=and Moses heard the people weeping}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=אֽתְךָ רָאִ֫יתִי צַדִּיק|translate=thee have I seen righteous}}. Frequently, however, the second object is expressed by a separate clause. This is especially frequent with {{GHGheb|text=רָאָה|translate=to see}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=4}} ''and God saw the light, that it was good''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=25|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=23|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=2|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=8|verse=17|hidebook=1}}; so with {{GHGheb|text=יָדַע|translate=to know}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=17|verse=8|hidebook=1}} (with two objects); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=5|verse=17}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|i}}
7. In certain instances {{GHGheb|text=את}} serves apparently to introduce or to emphasize a nominative. This cannot be regarded as a reappearance of the original substantival meaning of the {{GHGheb|text=את}}, since all unquestionable examples of the kind belong to the later Books of the Old Testament. They are rather (apart from textual errors or other explanations) cases of virtual dependence on an implied {{GHGterm|verbum regens}} understood. The constant use of {{GHGheb|text=את}} to indicate a clause governed by the verb, necessarily led at length to the use of {{GHGheb|text=את}} generally as a defining particle irrespective of a governing verb. So in the Hebrew of the Mishna<ref>Cf. Weiss, {{GHGheb|text=משפט לשון המשנה}} (Vienna, 1867), p. 112.</ref> (see above, {{GHGpar|3|a}}) {{GHGheb|text=אֹתוֹ}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָהּ}} are prefixed even to a nominative without any special emphasis.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|k}}
Naturally the above does not apply to any of the places in which {{GHGheb|text=את}} is not the {{GHGterm|nota accusativi}}, but a preposition (on {{GHGheb|text=את|translate=with}}, cf. {{GHGpar|103|b}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=57|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=34}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְאֶת־הַדּוֹב|translate=and that, with a bear}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}} here, however, has probably been interpolated from verse 36, where it is wanting); nor the places in which the accusative is subordinate to a passive (according to {{GHGpar|121|c}}) or to a verb of wanting as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=22|verse=17}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=9|verse=32}}, see below, z. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=43|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=סָבִיב|translate=about}} governs like a verb, being followed by {{GHGheb|text=אוֹתָהּ}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|l}}
Other cases are clearly due to attraction to a following relative pronoun in the accusative ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=14|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=8|verse=17}}; but {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hag|chapter=2|verse=5}}a, to {{GHGheb|text=ממצרים}}, must be omitted, with the LXX, as a later addition), or the accusative depends on a verbal idea, virtually contained in what has gone before, and consequently present to the speaker’s mind as governing the accusative. Thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=3|verse=26}} (the verbal idea contained in {{GHGheb|text=ומשמרת}} verse 25 is ''they had to take charge of''); in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=17|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=ויהי לְ}} implies ''it was given up'' or ''they gave him''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=16|translate=see where}} is equivalent to ''search now for''; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=11|verse=25}} {{GHGheb|text=אל־ירע בעיניך}} is used in the sense of ''noli aegre ferre''<ref>So also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=13}} the Qal ({{GHGheb|text=יִיטַב}}) is, with Wellhausen, to be read instead of the {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}}.</ref>; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=36|verse=33|translate=and}} he had ''the brazier before him''; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=4|verse=3}} a verb like ''I esteem'' is mentally supplied before {{GHGheb|text=אֵת אֲשֶׁר}}. On {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=22|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=9|verse=32}}, see below, aa.—Aposiopesis occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=11|verse=2|translate=for not your children}} (do I mean); still more boldly in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=7|verse=7}}, where either {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמַעְתֶּם}} or {{GHGheb|text=(תַּֽעֲשׂוּ) תִּשְׁמְעוּ}} is to be supplied.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|m}}
Setting aside a few undoubtedly corrupt passages<ref>Thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=16}}, where {{GHGheb|text=וְאֵי}} is to be read for {{GHGheb|text=וְאֶת}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=11|verse=25}}, where at present the predicate of the relative clause is wanting; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=5}} the {{GHGheb|text=את}} is probably derived from a text which read the {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} instead of {{GHGheb|text=נָפַל}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=23|verse=33}} instead of the artificial explanation ''what a burden'' (is, do ye ask?) we should read with the LXX and Vulg. {{GHGheb|text=אַתֶּם הַמַּשָּׂא|translate=ye are the burden}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=10|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=מַרְאֵיהֶם וְאוֹתָם}} is unintelligible; in 37:19 read with Hitzig {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}} for {{GHGheb|text=את}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hag|chapter=2|verse=17}} for {{GHGheb|text=אתכם}} read with the LXX {{GHGheb|text=שֻֽׁבְכֶם}} [or {{GHGheb|text=אֵינְכֶם}}; for the {{GHGheb|text=אֶל}} cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=15|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=36|verse=9}}].</ref> there still remain the<section end=par117 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

390.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par117 />following examples, in which {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}} in the later Hebrew manner (almost in the sense of the Latin ''quod attinet ad'') introduces a noun with more or less emphasis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=3|verse=46}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=5|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=35|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=20|verse=44}}, 46, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=17|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=20|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=35|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=44|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=9|verse=19}}, 34, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=9|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=31|verse=17}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=47|verse=17}}–19 (cf. also 43:7) it is simplest to emend {{GHGheb|text=זֹאת}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}}, according to verse 20. However, even the LXX, who have ταῦτα only in verse 18, can hardly have known any other reading than {{GHGheb|text=את}}; consequently in all these passages {{GHGheb|text=את}} must be regarded as virtually dependent on some governing word, such as ''ecce'' (LXX 43:7 ἐώακας), and 47:17 ff. as equivalent to ''thou shalt have'' as a border, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|n}}
8. Another solecism of the later period is finally the introduction of the object by the preposition {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} (prop. ''in relation to, in the direction of''), as sometimes in Ethiopic<ref>Dillmann, ''Grammatik der äthiopischen Sprache'', p. 349.</ref> and very commonly in Aramaic.<ref>With regard to Biblical Aramaic, see Kautzsch’s ''Grammatik des Bibl.-Aram.'', p. 151 f. In other ways, also, a tendency may be observed in later Hebrew to make use of the looser connexion by means of prepositions instead of the closer subordination of the noun in the accusative.</ref>. Less remarkable is this looser connexion of the object with a participle, as with {{GHGheb|text=אָכַל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|verse=5}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִסֵּף}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=10|verse=25}}, {{GHGheb|text=זָקַף}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=145|verse=14}} (but cf. 146:8), {{GHGheb|text=צָרַר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=25|verse=18}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִשְׂגִּיא}} and {{GHGheb|text=שָׁטַה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=23}}; ''before'' the participle {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=11|verse=9}}.—To introduce an object ''preceding'' the finite verb {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} is employed in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=2}} (cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=11|verse=38}}); also ''after'' {{GHGheb|text=אָהֵב}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=19|verse=18}}, 34; {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽאֱרִיךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=129|verse=3}}; {{GHGheb|text=הִבְדִּיל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=8|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=25|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=הֵבִין}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=11}}; {{GHGheb|text=בֵּרַךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=29|verse=20}} (immediately before with an accusative); {{GHGheb|text=הִגְלָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=5|verse=26}}; {{GHGheb|text=דָּרַשׁ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=6|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=22|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=17|verse=13}}; {{GHGheb|text=חֶֽהֱיָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=45|verse=7}}, where, however, read {{GHGheb|text=פְּלֵיטָה}} with the LXX for {{GHGheb|text=לפליטה}} and take {{GHGheb|text=לָכֶם}} as a ''dativus commodi''; {{GHGheb|text=הִלֵּל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=16|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=5|verse=13}}; {{GHGheb|text=הָרַג}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=135|verse=11}} (verse 10 with accusative), 136:19 f.; {{GHGheb|text=חָבַשׁ}} (''to bind up'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=61|verse=1}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=34|verse=4|translate=before}} the verb); {{GHGheb|text=יָדַע}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=69|verse=6}}; {{GHGheb|text=כִּבֵּד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=86|verse=9}}; {{GHGheb|text=לָקַח}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=40|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=23|verse=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=הִמְלִיךְ}} and {{GHGheb|text=מָשַׁה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=29|verse=22}}; {{GHGheb|text=נֵהַל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=28|verse=15}}; {{GHGheb|text=סָמַךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=145|verse=14}}; {{GHGheb|text=עָזַב}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=16|verse=37}}; {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽעֱלָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=26|verse=3}}; {{GHGheb|text=פִּתַּח}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=116|verse=16}}; {{GHGheb|text=רָדַף}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=28}}; {{GHGheb|text=הִצְדִּיק}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=53|verse=11}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׂכַר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=24|verse=12}} (previously accusatives); {{GHGheb|text=שִׂים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=22|verse=7}} (but probably {{GHGheb|text=וְכֻּלְּכֶם}} is to be read); {{GHGheb|text=הֵשִׁיב}} (in the connexion, {{GHGheb|text=הֵשִׁיב דָּבָר לְ}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=10|verse=6}} (but verse 9 and {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=12|verse=9}} with an accusative); {{GHGheb|text=שִׁחֵת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=32|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=שִׁית}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=18}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלַח}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=8|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=2|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=17|verse=7|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁמַר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=29|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=5|verse=11}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|o}}
9. Sometimes the verb, on which an accusative of the object really depends, is contained only in sense in the verb which apparently governs, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲסִירָיו לֹא־פָתַח בָּֽיְתָה|translate=his prisoners he let not loose}} nor sent them back ''to their home''. On this ''constructio praegnans'' in general, see {{GHGpar|119|ff}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|p}}
'''2.''' With the proper accusatives of the object may also be classed what is called the ''internal'' or ''absolute object'' (also named ''schema etymologicum'' or ''figura etymologica''), i.e. the addition of an object in the form<section end=par117 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

391.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par117 />of a noun derived from the same stem,<ref>On a kindred use of the infinitive absolute as an ''internal object'', see above, {{GHGpar|113|w}}.</ref> e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=14|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=פָּֽחֲדוּ פַ֫חַד|translate=they feared a fear}} (i.e. they were in great fear), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=15|verse=27}}; also with the object preceding, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=חֵטְא חָֽטְאָה יְרוּשָׁלַ͏ִם|translate=Jerusalem hath sinned a sin}}; with a double accusative (see below, cc), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=12}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִֽיעָצֵךְ נָא עֵצָה|translate=let me, I pray thee, give thee counsel}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=12}}.<ref>Cf. βουλὰς βουλεύειν, Iliad x. 147.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|q}}
Rem. (''a'') Strictly speaking the only cases of this kind are those in which the verbal idea is supplemented by means of an ''indeterminate'' substantive (see the examples above). Such a substantive, except in the case of the addition of the internal object to denominative verbs (see below), is, like the infinitive absolute, never altogether without force, but rather serves like it to strengthen the verbal idea. This strengthening is implied in the indeterminateness of the internal object, analogous to such exclamations as, ''this was a man!''<ref>The Arab grammarians assign to the indeterminate eases generally an intensive sense in many instances; hence the commentators on the Qorân usually explain such cases by adding ''and what ...!'' see {{GHGpar|125|b}}.</ref> Hence it is intelligible that some intensifying attribute is very frequently (as in Greek usually) added to the internal object, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=34}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּצְעַק צְעָקָה גְדֹלָה וּמָרָה עַד־מְאֹד|translate=he cried}} (with) ''an exceeding great and bitter cry''; cf. the Greek νοσεῖν νόσον κακήν, ἐχάρησαν χαρὰν μεγάλην (Matt. 2:10); ''magnam pugnare pugnam, tutiorem vitam vivere'', &c.

Examples of an internal object ''after'' the verb, and without further addition, are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=22|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=24|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=35|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=25|verse=15}}), 26:15, 27:35, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mic|chapter=4|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=1|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=21|verse=26}}; with an intensifying attribute, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=15|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=40}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=4|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=29|verse=9}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=1|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=1|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=8|verse=2|hidebook=1}}a, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=11|verse=3}}; along with an object proper the internal object occurs with an attribute in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=15}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=4|verse=1}}.—An internal object without an attribute ''before'' the verb: {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=24|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=46|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=3|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=27|verse=12}}; with an attribute ''before'' the verb: {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=14|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=1|verse=15}} (cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=30|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=22}}). Instead of the substantive which would naturally be expected, another of kindred meaning is used in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=8|verse=2}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|r}}
(b) Only in a wider sense can the ''schema etymologicum'' be made to include cases in which the denominative verb is used in connexion with the noun from which it is derived, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=18|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=144|verse=6}}, probably also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=2|verse=4}}, or where this substantive, made determinate in some way, follows its verb, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=37}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=25|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=13|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|verse=58}},<ref>Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=13|verse=4}} ''lest I sleep the'' sleep of ''death'', {{GHGheb|text=הַמָּ֫וֶת}} is only used pregnantly for {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנַת הַמָּ֫וֶת}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=39}}), as {{GHGheb|text=צְדָקוֹת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=33|verse=15}} for {{GHGheb|text=דֶּ֫רֶךְ צְדָקוֹת}}. On the similar use of {{GHGheb|text=הֹלֵךְ תָּמִים}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=15|verse=2}}, see {{GHGpar|118|n}}.</ref> and, determinate at least in sense, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=16}}; or precedes it, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=62|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=3|verse=7}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=9}}. In both cases the substantive is used, without any special emphasis, merely for clearness or as a more convenient way of connecting the verb with other members of the sentence.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|s}}
'''3.''' Verbs which denote ''speaking'' (''crying out, weeping''), or any external act, frequently take a direct accusative of the organ or means by which the action is performed. In this case, however, the accusative must be more closely determined by an attributive adjective or a noun in the genitive. This fact shows the close relation between these accusatives and the ''internal objects'' treated under ''p'', which also,<section end=par117 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

392.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par117 />according to ''q'', mostly take an intensifying attribute. On the other hand, they must not be regarded as adverbial (instrumental) accusatives, nor are they to be classed with the second (neuter) subjects treated below in {{GHGpar|144|l}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|t}}
Examples of the accusative following the verb are {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֶזְעַק קֽוֹל־גָּדוֹל|translate=and I cried a loud voice}}, i.e. with a loud voice, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=11|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=23}} (after the proper object, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=5|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=55}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=109|verse=2}} ''they have spoken unto me'' {{GHGheb|text=לְשׁוֹן שֶׁ֫קֶר|translate=a tongue of deceit}}, i.e. with a lying tongue; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=10|verse=4}} ''he'' becometh ''poor'' {{GHGheb|text=עשֶֹׁה כַף־רְמִיְּה|translate=dealing a slack hand}}, i.e. who dealeth with a slack hand; cf. the German ''eine schöne Stimme singen'', to sing a fine voice, ''eine tüchtige Klinge schlagen'', to smite a trusty sword, ''Schlittschuhe laufen'', to run skates (i.e. to skate), and our ''to write a good hand, to play ball'', &c.—Examples of the accusative preceding are {{GHGheb|text=שִֹׂפְתֵי רְנָנוֹת יְהַלֶּל־פִּי|translate=my mouth shall praise}} with ''joyful lips'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=63|verse=6}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=12|verse=3}}, where a ''casus instrumenti'' with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} follows the accusative.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|u}}
'''4.''' Many verbs originally intransitive (sometimes even in form; see a, note 2 may be used also as transitives, in consequence of a certain modification of their original meaning, which has gradually become established by usage; cf. e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רִיב|translate=to strive}}, but also with an accusative ''causam alicuius agere'' (so even in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=17}}, &c.; elsewhere with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} of the person for whom one strives); {{GHGheb|text=יָכֹל}} absolutely ''to be able'', with an accusative ''to prevail over'' any one; {{GHGheb|text=חָפֵץ|translate=to be inclined}} and {{GHGheb|text=רָצָה|translate=to have pleasure}} (usually with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}), with an accusative to ''wish for some one'' or ''something''; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁכַב|translate=cubare}}, then in the sense of ''concumbere'', originally joined with {{GHGheb|text=עִם־|translate=cum}}, but quite early also with the accusative, equivalent to ''comprimere'' (''feminam''), &c. So in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=14}}, &c., unless in all or some of the passages the preposition {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} is intended, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אִתָּהּ}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָהּ}}; in the earlier passages {{GHGheb|text=עִם־}} is the more usual.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|v}}
Rem. 1. It is certainly difficult to decide whether some verbs, which were afterwards used absolutely or joined with prepositions, were not nevertheless originally ''transitive'', and consequently it is only the supposed original meaning, usually assigned to them in English, which causes them to appear ''intransitive''.<ref>Thus e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עָנָה|translate=to reply to}} (ἀμείβεσθαί τινα), ''to answer any one''; {{GHGheb|text=צִוָּה|translate=to command}} (iubere aliquem); {{GHGheb|text=זָכַר|translate=to remember}}; {{GHGheb|text=קִוָּה}} (also with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}) ''to wait for any one'' (to expect any one); {{GHGheb|text=בִּשַֹׂר|translate=to bring glad tidings to any one}} (see the Lexicon); {{GHGheb|text=נָאַף}} and {{GHGheb|text=נִאֵף|translate=to commit adultery}} (adulterare matronam); {{GHGheb|text=עָבַד|translate=to serve}} (colere); {{GHGheb|text=עָרַב|translate=to become surety for}} ..., and many others.</ref> In that case there is of course no syntactical peculiarity to be considered, and a list of such verbs would at the most be requisite only for practical purposes.
