{{GHGheb|text=פְּנוּ לָכֶם|translate=turn you}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=40}}; {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּבוּ לָכֶם|translate=return ye}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=5|verse=27}}; {{GHGheb|text=ק֫וּמִי לָךְ|translate=rise up}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=2|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבוּ לָכֶם|translate=abide ye}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=חֲדַל לְךָ|translate=forbear thee}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=35|verse=21}} (in the plural, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=22}}); {{GHGheb|text=הָ֫בוּ לָכֶם|translate=take you}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=18|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=20|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=16|verse=20}}, and so almost regularly {{GHGheb|text=הִשָּׁ֫מֶד לְךָ}} (see above, {{GHGpar|51|n}}) ''cave tibi!'' and {{GHGheb|text=הִשָּֽׁמְלוּ לָכֶם|translate=take heed to yourselves}}; {{GHGheb|text=דְמֵה רְךָ|translate=be thou like}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=2|verse=17}} (cf. verse 9), 8:14, is remarkable; after a perfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=17|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=22|verse=5}}; after an imperfect consecutive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=36|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=וַתִּבְטַח לְךָ|translate=and puttest thy trust}}.—In the 3rd person, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וַתֵּ֫שֶׁב לָהּ|translate=and sat her down}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=16}}, cf. 22:5, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=120|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=123|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=19}}; even after a participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=8|verse=9}}.—In the 1st person plural, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=37|verse=11}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|t}}
(3) To introduce the result after verbs of making, forming, changing, appointing ''to'' something, esteeming ''as'' something; in short, in all those cases in which, according to {{GHGpar|117|ii}}, a second ''accusative'' may also be used.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|u}}
(4) In loose connexion with some verbal idea in the sense of ''in reference to, with regard to''... ({{GHGpar|143|e}}); so after a {{GHGterm|verbum dicendi}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=13}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=10|verse=23}}, cf.<section end=par119 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

406.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="79.176.221.29" /></noinclude><section begin="par119" />{{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=36|verse=9}}; even before the verb, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=9|verse=2}}.—To the same class belongs also the ''Lamedh inscriptionis'' (untranslatable in English, and hardly more than a mere quotation-mark) which introduces the exact wording of an inscription or title; thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=1}} ''write upon it''... (the words) {{GHGheb|text=מַהֵר שָׁלָל וגו׳}} (cf. verse 3, where the {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} naturally is not used); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=37|verse=16}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|v}}
(''d'') {{GHGheb|text=מִן}}, originally (according to {{GHGpar|101|a}}) ''separation'',<ref>Cf. O. Molin, ''Om prepositionen'' min ''i Bibelhebreisken'', Upsala, 1893, and especially N. Zerweck, ''Die hebr. Praep.'' min, Leipzig, 1893, who, instead of the partitive meaning (formerly accepted by us also), more correctly takes ‘separation’ as the starting-point of its various uses.</ref> represents both the idea of ''distance, separation'' or ''remoteness from'' something, and that of ''motion away from'' something, hence also ''descent, origin from'' a place, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=1|verse=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|w}}
(1) From the idea of ''separation'' is naturally derived on the one hand the sense of (''taken'') ''from among''..., ''e numero'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=1}} ''subtil as none other of the beasts'', &c.; cf. 3:14, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5|verse=24}} (so especially after the idea of choosing ''out of''<ref>All the ''partitive'' uses of {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} also come most naturally under this idea of separation ''out of'' a larger class. Thus {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} is used in the sense of ''some, something'', and even ''one'', in such expressions as ''and he slew... also'' {{GHGheb|text=מִשָּׂרֵי יִשְּׂרָאֵל}} (''divers'') ''of the princes of Israel'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=21|verse=4}}; {{GHGheb|text=מִכָּל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=4|verse=2}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=מִדַּם הַפָּר|translate=some of the blood of the bullock}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=29|verse=12}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=27|verse=6}} ''my heart doth not reproach me'' {{GHGheb|text=מִיָּמַי|translate=for any}}, i.e. for one, ''of my days''; 38:12 {{GHGheb|text=מִיָּמֶ֫יךָ|translate=one of thy days}}, i.e. ''ever in thy life'' (this explanation is confirmed by {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=6}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=45}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=28|hidebook=1}}). In this way also, the frequently misunderstood Hebrew (and Arabic) idiom is to be explained, by which {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} before {{GHGheb|text=אֶחָד}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַחַת}} is equivalent to ''ullus''; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=4|verse=2}} ''and shall do'' {{GHGheb|text=מֵֽאַחַת מֵהֵ֫נָּה|translate=any one of these things}}; 5:13, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=15|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=18|verse=10}}; so before a ''nomen unitatis'' (see {{GHGpar|122|t}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=45}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=52}}) {{GHGheb|text=מִשַּֽׂעֲרַת רֹאשׁוֹ|translate=not one hair of his head}}.—{{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} is used in the sense of the Arabic ''min el-beyān'' or explicative ''min'' (often to be simply translated by ''namely''), e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=22}} ''of all that was'', i.e. ''so far as it was'', probably also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=2}} (=''whomsoever they chose'').</ref> a larger class, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=28}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=19|verse=5}}, &c.), and on the other hand, the sense of ''without'' (separated, free from...), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=מִקֶּ֫שֶׁת אֻסָּ֫רוּ|translate=without the bow}} (i.e. without one needing to bend a bow against them) ''they were made prisoners''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=48|verse=45}} {{GHGheb|text=מִכֹּחַ|translate=without strength}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=6|verse=6}}, as the first half-verse shows, not ''more than burnt offerings'' (as R.V.), but ''and not burnt offerings''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=3|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=52|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=26|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, also such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=15|verse=24}} ''far from the eyes'', i.e. unobserved by the congregation; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=20|verse=3}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|x}}
Here also belongs the use of {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} after the ideas of ''restraining, withholding from, refusing to'' any one, frequently in pregnant expressions, which we can render only by complete final or consecutive clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=23}} ''he hath rejected thee'' {{GHGheb|text=מִמֶּ֫לֶךְ|translate=away from}} (being) ''king'', instead of {{GHGheb|text=מִֽהְיוֹת מ׳}} (as in verse 26), ''that thou be no longer king''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=15|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=17|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=מֵעִיר|translate=so that it is no longer a city}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=17|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=28|verse=11}} ''he bindeth the streams'' {{GHGheb|text=מִבְּכִי|translate=that they trickle not}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=6|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=מִקְּבֹר|translate=that thou shouldst not bury thy dead}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=24|verse=10}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|y}}
The {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} has a still more pregnant force in those examples in which the idea of precluding from anything is only indirectly contained in the preceding verb, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=1}} ''his eyes were dim'' {{GHGheb|text=מֵֽרְאֹה|translate=away from seeing}}, i.e. ''so that he could not see''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=8}} ''Ephraim shall be broken in pieces'' {{GHGheb|text=מֵעָם|translate=that it be not a people}} (just as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=23|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=48|verse=2}}, 42, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=83|verse=5}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=54|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=2|verse=62}} (for other pregnant constructions with {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} see below, ff)<ref>On the use of {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} to express the comparative, which likewise depends on the idea of ''distance from...'', cf. below, {{GHGpar|133|a}}; on {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} as expressing the distance of time from a fixed limit, in the sense of ''after'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=20}} {{GHGheb|text=מֵהָקִיץ|translate=after awaking}} (cf. ἐξ, ἀρίστου, ''ab itinere''), or ''after the lapse of...'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=6|verse=2}}, and very frequently {{GHGheb|text=מִקֵּץ|translate=from the end of}}, i.e. ''after the lapse of...'', see the Lexicon; also for the use of {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} to represent ''resting beside'' anything, like the Latin ''prope abesse ab''...</ref>; on {{GHGheb|text=מִבְּלִי}} and {{GHGheb|text=מֵאֵין|translate=without}}, cf. {{GHGpar|152|y}}.<section end="par119" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

407.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="79.176.221.29" /></noinclude><section begin="par119" />{{GHGmargin-letter|119|z}}
(2) On the sense of ''motion away from'' anything depends the use of {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} after such ideas as ''to take away from, to beware, to be afraid of, to flee, to escape, to hide oneself from'' (cf. καλύπτω ἀπό, ''custodire ab''), sometimes again in pregnant expressions, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=33|verse=15}}. On the idea of ''starting from'' anything depends finally the very frequent ''causative'' use of {{GHGheb|text=מִן|translate=on account of, in consequence of}} (cf. our ''that comes from''...), ''prae'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מֵרֹב|translate=for multitude}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=5}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|aa}}
(''e'') {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}}.<ref>Cf. Budie, ''Die hebr. Präpos''. ''ʾAl'' ({{GHGheb|text=עַל}}), Halle, 1882.</ref> The two original local meanings of this preposition are ''upon'' (ἐπί)<ref>Since the placing ''upon'' anything is an addition to it, {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} also implies ''in addition to'' something, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=9}} (31:50); 30:40, 32:12 (probably a proverbial saying=''mother and children''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=22|verse=6}}. Also {{GHGheb|text=עַל|translate=notwithstanding}} is no doubt properly ''in addition to'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=7}} ''although thou knowest'', prop. ''in addition to thy knowing''.—From the original meaning ''upon'' is also derived that of ''on account of'' (prop. ''upon the ground of'') and ''in agreement with, according to'', since the pattern is regarded as the foundation ''upon'' which a thing stands or rests.</ref> and ''over'' (ὑπέρ, ''super'').

(1) From the original meaning ''upon'' is explained the use of {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} after ideas of ''commanding, commissioning'' ({{GHGheb|text=פָּקַד עַל־}}), &c., inasmuch as the command, obligation, &c., is ''laid upon'' the object. The construction is self-evident in the case of ''to lie, rest, lean, rely, press upon'' something; cf. also, for the last, such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, and especially {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=וְעָלַי}} prop. ''upon me'' would it have been, it would have been incumbent ''upon me'', &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|bb}}
(2) From the original meaning ''over'' is explained the use of {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} after ideas of ''covering, protecting, guarding'' {{GHGheb|text=כָּסָה עַל־}}, {{GHGheb|text=גָּנַן עַל־}}; also the combinations {{GHGheb|text=רִחַם עַל־|translate=to have compassion upon}}..., {{GHGheb|text=חוּס עַל־}}, {{GHGheb|text=חָמַל עַל־|translate=to spare}} some one, arise from the idea of a compassionate or protective ''bending over'' something. Cf. also {{GHGheb|text=נִלְחַם עַל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=17}} = ''to fight for'' some one, i.e. in his defence.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|cc}}
(3) Moreover {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} is used after verbs of ''standing'' and ''going'', to express a towering ''over'' some one or something, sometimes in phrases, in which the original local idea has altogether fallen into the background, and which are therefore to be rendered in English by means of other prepositions (''by, with, before, near''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=1}}, &c., ''Pharaoh... stood'' {{GHGheb|text=עַל־הַיְאֹר|translate=by the Nile}} (above the water level; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=1|verse=3}}), and so especially {{GHGheb|text=עָמַד עַל־}} in the pregnant sense ''to stand serving before'' some one (prop. ''over'' one who sits or reclines at table) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=4|verse=14}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=2}}, where {{GHGheb|text=מִמַּ֫עַל לְ}} is used for {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}}); {{GHGheb|text=הִתְיַצֵּב עַל־|translate=to present oneself}} by command ''before'' some one, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=6}}, &c. Cf. also {{GHGheb|text=עַל־יַד}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַל־יְדֵי}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=14}}) ''near, at (on) the side'' of some one or something.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|dd}}
(4) From the original meaning ''above'' (not, as formerly, explained, ''on to'' something, ''at'' something) there arise finally all the various constructions with {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} in the sense of ''towards, against''. The original idea (which in many of these constructions has become wholly unrecognizable) starts from the view that the assailant endeavours to take up his position ''over'' the person attacked, so as to reach him from above, or to ''over'' power him; cf. especially {{GHGheb|text=קוּם עַל־}} to rise up ''over'', i.e. ''against'' some one, then with a transference of<section end="par119" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

408.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="79.176.221.29" /></noinclude><section begin="par119" />thought applied to any kind of hostile approach, {{GHGheb|text=נִלְחַם עַל־|translate=to fight against...}}, {{GHGheb|text=חָנָה עַל־|translate=to encamp against...}}, {{GHGheb|text=נֶֽאֱסַף עַל־|translate=to be gathered together, to assemble against}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=4|verse=11}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=2}}), &c.; even after verbs which express a mental action, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=חָשַׁב רָעָה עַל־|translate=to imagine evil against}} any one, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|ee}}
'''4.''' Sometimes a preposition appears to be under the immediate government of a verb, which, by its meaning, excludes such a union. In reality the preposition is dependent on a verb (generally a verb of motion), which, for the sake of brevity, is not expressed, but in sense is contained in what is apparently the governing verb.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|ff}}
Various examples of this ''constructio praegnans'' have been already noticed above in ''x'' and ''y'' under {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}}; for {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=22|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=וּמִקַּרְנֵי רֵמִים עֲנִיתָ֫נִי|translate=and thou hast answered}} and saved ''me from the horns of the wild oxen'' (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=38|verse=17}}, which Delitzsch translates by ''thou hast loved'' and delivered ''my soul from the pit'', read {{GHGheb|text=חָשַׂ֫כְתָּ}} with the LXX); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=28|verse=12}}; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=זָנָה מִן־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=27}} ''to go a whoring from'' any one i.e. ''to be unfaithful to him''; {{GHGheb|text=רָשַׁע מִן־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=22}} = ''to depart wickedly from God''; {{GHGheb|text=חָרַשׁ מִן־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=28|verse=1}} ''to be silent from'' one (to turn away in silence); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=13}} [; so with {{GHGheb|text=מֵעַל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=30|verse=17}}, 30].

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|gg}}
Pregnant constructions wgith {{GHGheb|text=אַחֲרֵי}}: {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=24}} equivalent to {{GHGheb|text=וַיְמַלֵּא לָלֶ֫כֶת אַֽחֲרָ֑י|translate=and he made full to walk}} i.e. walked fully ''after me''; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=13|verse=7}} read with the LXX {{GHGheb|text=חָֽרְדוּ מֵאַֽחֲרֶיו|translate=they trembled}}, i.e. ''went trembling away from him''; with {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=33}} {{GHGheb|text=הָּמַהּ אֶל־|translate=to turn in astonishment to}} some one (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=13|verse=8}}); {{GHGheb|text=דְּרַשׁ אֶל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=11|verse=10}}, &c., ''to turn inquiringly to'' some one; {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽחֱרִישׁ אֶל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=1}} ''to turn in silence to'' some one; {{GHGheb|text=חָרַד אֶל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=28}} ''to turn trembling to'' some one (cf. {{GHGheb|text=חָרַד לִקְרַאת|translate=to come trembling to meet}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=21|verse=2}} [also with {{GHGheb|text=שאג}}, {{GHGheb|text=הריץ}}, {{GHGheb|text=שמת}} and other verbs, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=15|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=3|hidebook=1}}; see Lexicon]); cf. further {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=41|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=7|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=32|verse=1}}; with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=55|verse=19}} ''he hath redeemed'' and hath put ''my soul in peace'', exactly like {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=118|verse=5}}; with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=74|verse=7}} ''they have profaned'' and cast... ''even to the ground''; cf. 89:40.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|hh}}
'''5.''' In poetic parallelism the governing power of a preposition is sometimes extended to the corresponding substantive of the second member;<ref>Similarly the force of a negative is sometimes extended to the parallel member; see {{GHGpar|152|z}}.</ref> e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=48|verse=14|hidebook=1}} ''he shall perform his pleasure'' {{GHGheb|text=בְּבָבֶל|translate=on Babylon, and his arm}} shall be {{GHGheb|text=כַּשְׂדִּים}} (for {{GHGheb|text=בַּכַּשְׂדִּים}}) ''on the Chaldaeans''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=3}}; {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=22|hidebook=1}} (but probably {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} has fallen out after another {{GHGheb|text=ל}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=39|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=10}} (perhaps also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=45|verse=8}}; {{GHGheb|text=משֵׁל}} may, however, be taken here as a second accusative according to {{GHGpar|117|ii}}); {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עַן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=48|verse=9}}; {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=58|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=141|verse=9}} (unless {{GHGheb|text=וּמִמֹּֽקְשׁוֹת}} is to be read); {{GHGheb|text=עַד־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=15|verse=8}}; {{GHGheb|text=תַּ֫חַת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=61|verse=7}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|ii}}
'''6.''' Adverbs which have acquired a substantival value are sometimes governed by prepositions, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־חִנָּם|translate=in vain}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=6|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַחֲרֵי־כֵן|translate=after this}}; {{GHGheb|text=בְּכֵן}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=8|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=4|verse=16}}) ''then, on this condition''; {{GHGheb|text=לָכֵן}} and {{GHGheb|text=עַל־כֵּן|translate=therefore}}; {{GHGheb|text=עַד־כֵּן|translate=hitherto}}.<section end="par119" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

409.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par120 />{{GHGpar-heading|120|Verbal Ideas under the Government of a Verb. Co-ordination of Complementary Verbal Ideas}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|120|a}}
'''1.''' When a ''relative'' verb (incomplete in itself) receives its necessary complement in the form of a verbal idea, the latter is, as a rule, subordinated in the infinitive construct (with or without {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}), less frequently in the infinitive absolute, in a few instances in the form of a participle (or verbal adjective), or finally in the imperfect without the copula. In these combinations the principal idea is very frequently represented by the subordinate member of the sentence, whilst the governing verb rather contains a mere definition of the manner of the action; cf. d and g below, and {{GHGpar|114|n}}, note 2.

{{GHGmargin-letter|120|b}}
(''a'') On the subordination of an infinitive construct as an accusative of the object, and as the complement of relative verbal ideas, see above, {{GHGpar|114|c}}, and the numerous examples given in {{GHGpar|114|m}}; on the infinitive absolute as object, see {{GHGpar|113|d}}.—The complement in the form of a participle (as in Greek, and also frequently in Syriac) occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=33|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽהֲתִֽמְךָ שׁוֹדֵד}} (cf. for the form, {{GHGpar|67|v}}) ''when thou hast ceased as a spoiler'', i.e. to spoil; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=30}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יִצְלַח... ישֵׁב|translate=he shall never prosper, sitting}}, i.e. so as to sit, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=1|verse=6}} ''what meanest thou, sleeping?'' i.e. that thou sleepest;<ref>In {{GHGheb|text=יֹדֵעַ מְנַגֵּן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=16}}, which appears to be a case of this kind, two different readings are combined, {{GHGheb|text=יֹדֵעַ לְנַגֵּן}} and the simple {{GHGheb|text=מְנַגֵּן}}.</ref> by a verbal adjective, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=2}} ''now his eyes'' {{GHGheb|text=הֵחֵ֫לּוּ כֵהוֹת|translate=had begun being dim}}, i.e. to wax dim (unless we read {{GHGheb|text=כְּהוֹת}}={{GHGheb|text=לִכְהוֹת}}, cf. {{GHGpar|114|m}}); by a substantive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=20}} ''and Noah began'' to be ''an husbandman'' (omitting the article before {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֶמָה}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|120|c}}
(''b'') Examples of the subordination of the complementary verbal idea in the imperfect<ref>This kind of subordination is frequent in Arabic and in Syriac (cf. e.g. the Peshiṭtâ, Luke 18:13); as a rule, however, a conjunction (corresponding to our ''that'') is inserted. Cf. moreover, the Latin ''quid vis faciam?'' Terence; ''volo hoc oratori contingat'', Cicero, Brut. 84; and our ''I would it were; I thought he would go''.</ref> (in English usually rendered by ''to, in order to'' or ''that'') are—(1) with both verbs in the same person: after the perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=21}} {{GHGheb|text=יְהֹוָה חָפֵץ... יגְדִּיל|translate=it pleased the Lord... to magnify}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=30|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=32|verse=22|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יָדַ֫עְתִּי אֲכַנֶּה|translate=I know not to give flattering titles}}; after a perfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=19}} (where for {{GHGheb|text=תֵּרֵד}} we should read with the LXX {{GHGheb|text=תִּפָּקֵד}}); after an imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=88|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=102|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=24|verse=14|hidebook=1}}; after an imperf. consec., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=8}}; after a participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=11}}a.—(2) with a difference in the persons: after a perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=9|verse=6}} ''this is the thing'' {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּה יְהֹוָה תַּֽעֲשׂוּ|translate=which the Lord commanded}} (that) ''ye should do''; a negative imperfect follows {{GHGheb|text=צִוָּה}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=10}}; after the imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=1}} (<sup>5</sup>) {{GHGheb|text=כִּי לֹא תוֹסִ֫יפִי עוֹד יִקְרְאוּ־לָךְ|translate=for thou shalt no more continue}} (that) ''they call thee'', i.e. thou shalt no longer be called, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=1|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אוֹסִיף עוֹד אֲרַחֵם|translate=I will no longer continue}} (and) ''have mercy'', i.e. ''I will no more have mercy''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=52|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=23|verse=35}}.—{{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=6}} ''peradventure I shall prevail'' (that) ''we may smite thom, and'' (that) ''I may drive them out of the land'' ({{GHGheb|text=אוּכַל}} may, however, be a scribal error for {{GHGheb|text=נוּכַל}}, due to the preceding {{GHGheb|text=אוּלַי}}, and in that case the example would belong to No. 1); after a participle,<section end=par120 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

410.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par120 />{{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=21|verse=4}}.—A perfect is possibly subordinated in {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=10}}; but the explanation of {{GHGheb|text=בְּ֫אוּ}} as a relative clause is preferable.

{{GHGmargin-letter|120|d}}
'''2.''' Instead of subordination (as in the cases mentioned in ''a–c''), the ''co-ordination'' of the complementary verbal idea in the finite verb (cf. above, c) frequently occurs, either—

(''a'') With the second verb co-ordinated in a form exactly corresponding to the first (but see below, e) by means of {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַ}}, {{GHGheb|text=וָ}}).<ref>Cf. the English colloquial expression ''I will try and do it''.</ref> As a rule, here also (see above, a) the principal idea is introduced only by the second verb, while the first (especially {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּב}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָסַף}}<ref>Of a different kind are the cases in which {{GHGheb|text=יָסַף}} with a negative is co-ordinated with a verb to emphasize the non-recurrence of the action; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=25}} ''they prophesied and added not'', sc. ''to prophesy'', i.e. ''but they did so no more''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=5|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=27|verse=19}} (reading {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא יֹאסִיף}}).</ref>, {{GHGheb|text=הוֹסִיף}}) contains the definition of the manner of the action, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּ֫שָׁב וַיַּחְפֹּד|translate=and he returned and digged}}, i.e. he digged again; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=1|verse=11}}, 13; in the perfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=13}}; with {{GHGheb|text=הוֹסִיף}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=1}} ''and Abraham added and took a wife'', i.e. again took a wife; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=5}} and frequently; with {{GHGheb|text=הוֹאִיל}} in the jussive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=9}}; in the imperative (cf. {{GHGpar|110|h}}), Ju 1 <sup>6</sup> {{GHGheb|text=וְלִין הֽוֹאֶל־נָא|translate=be content, I pray thee, and tarry all night}} (cf. the English ''he was persuaded and remained'', for ''to remain''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=7|verse=29}}; with {{GHGheb|text=מִהַד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=18}}, 20, &c.; with {{GHGheb|text=חִמַּד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=2|verse=3}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|120|e}}
Rem. 1. Instead of an exact agreement between co-ordinate verbal forms, other combinations sometimes occur, viz. imperfect and perfect consecutive (cf. {{GHGpar|112|d}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=31|verse=12}} ''that they'' {{GHGheb|text=יִלְמְדוּ וְיָרְֽאוּ אֶת־יְהֹוָה|translate=may learn, and fear the Lord}}, i.e. ''to fear the Lord''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=2|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=8|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=9|verse=25}}b; perfect and imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=3}} (''O that I knew how I might find him''); perfect and imperfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=7|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=4|verse=1}}, 7; jussive and imperative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=17|verse=10}}; cf., finally, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=וְאם־יָדַ֫עְתָּ וְיֶשׁ־בָּם|translate=and if thou knowest and there are among them}}, &c., i.e. that there are among them.

{{GHGmargin-letter|120|f}}
2. Special mention must be made of the instances in which the natural complement of the first verb is suppressed, or is added immediately after in the form of an historical statement, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=25}} ''then Joseph commanded and they filled''<ref>Cf. the analogous examples in Kautzsch’s {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Bibl. Aram.}}, §102.</ref> (prop. that they should fill, and they filled...; cf. the full form of expression in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=50|verse=2}}); a further command is then added by means of {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} and the infinitive; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=36|verse=6}}; another instance of the same kind is {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=27}} ''I have divined and the Lord hath blessed me'', &c., i.e. that the Lord hath blessed me for thy sake.

{{GHGmargin-letter|120|g}}
(''b'') With the second verb (which, according to the above, represents the principal idea) attached ''without the copula''<ref>To be distinguished, of course, from the cases in which two equally important and independent verbs are used together without the copula in vigorous poetic imagery, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=8}}, &c.</ref> in the same mood, &c. In this construction (cf. {{GHGpar|110|h}}) the imperatives {{GHGheb|text=קוּם}} ({{GHGheb|text=ק֫וּמָת}}, {{GHGheb|text=ק֫וּמִי}},<section end=par120 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

411.text:
&c.) and {{GHGheb|text=לֵךְ}} ({{GHGheb|text=לְכָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְכִי}}, &c.) are exceedingly common with the sense of interjections, before verbs which express a movement or other action, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קוּם הִתְהַלֵּךְ|translate=arise, walk}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=43|hidebook=1}}; in the plural, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=14}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=19|verse=24}} {{GHGheb|text=לֶךְ־רֵד|translate=go, get thee down}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=9}}; with a following cohortative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=לְכָה נֵלֵכָ֑ה|translate=come, let us go}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=44}} and frequently.—Also with {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּב}} (a periphrasis for ''again'') in the perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=8|verse=15}}; in the imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=7|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=7|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=59|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=71|verse=20|hidebook=1}}; in the jussive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=16}}; in the cohortative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=31}}; in the imperative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=5|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=5}} ''lie down again''; {{GHGheb|text=הוֹאִיל}} (sometimes to express the idea of ''willingly'' or ''gladly'') in the perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=5|verse=11}}; in the imperative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=28}}; {{GHGheb|text=הִרְבָּה}}=''much'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=אַל־תַּרְבּוּ תְדַבְּרוּ גְּבֹהָה|translate=do not multiply}} and ''talk'', i.e. talk not so much ''arrogancy''; in the imperative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=51|verse=4}}; {{GHGheb|text=הֵחֵל}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=24}} {{GHGheb|text=הָחֵל דְשׁ|translate=begin, possess}}; {{GHGheb|text=יָכֹל}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּלֹא יֽוּכְלוּ יִגְּעוּ}}, ''without men’s being able to touch'', &c.; {{GHGheb|text=מִהַר}}=''quickly'', in the perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=106|verse=13}}; in the imperative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=48}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=6|verse=10}}.—Other examples are: {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=9|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽעֱמִיק}}=''deeply, radically''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=3|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=הִשְׁכִּים}}=''early'' (even in the participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=6|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=13|verse=3|hidebook=1}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=שָׁפֵל}}=''low'', cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=18}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=3|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=תָּמַם}}=''wholly''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=112|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=פִּוַּר}}=''plentifully''. {{GHGmargin-letter|120|h}} Rem. This co-ordination without the copula belongs (as being more vigorous and bolder) rather to poetic or otherwise elevated style (cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=52|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=1|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=9|verse=9|hidebook=1}} with {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=1}}, &c.). Asyndeton, however, is not wanting even in prose; besides the above examples (especially the imperatives of {{GHGheb|text=קוּם}} and {{GHGheb|text=הָלַךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=3|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=5}}) cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=3|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=13|verse=2}}. For special reasons the verb representing the principal idea may even come first; thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=53|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=יִרְאֶה יִשְׂבָּע|translate=he shall see, he shall be satisfied}} (sc. with the sight), for the satisfaction does not come until after the enjoyment of the sight; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=קִרְאוּ מַּלְאוּ|translate=cry, fill}}, i.e. cry with a full (loud) voice.
{{GHGpar-heading|121|Construction of Passive Verbs}}
Blake, ‘The internal passive in Semitic,’ {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|JAOS|Journal of the American Oriental Society}}}} xxii.
{{GHGmargin-letter|121|a}} '''1.''' Verbs which in the active take ''one'' accusative (either of the proper object, or of the ''internal'' object, or of some other nearer definition; cf. {{GHGpar|117|a}}, p, u) may in the passive, according to our mode of expression, be construed ''personally'', the object of the active sentence now becoming the subject, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=וַתָּ֫מָת רְחֵל וַתִּקָּבֵר|translate=and Rachel died, and was buried}}, &c. The passive, however, is also used ''impersonally'' (in the 3rd sing. masc.), either absolutely, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=21|verse=3}}f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=16|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=34}} (with a dative added, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=17|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=53|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=5|verse=5}}), or, more frequently, with the object of the active construction still subordinated in the accusative,When this is not recognizable either by the {{GHGterm|nota accusativi}}, or by its disagreement with the passive form in gender, number, and person, it naturally cannot be determined whether the construction is really impersonal. The construction itself can only be explained by supposing that while using the passive form the speaker at the same time thinks of some author or authors of the action in question, just as on the theory of the Arab grammarians a ''concealed agent'' is included in every passive. This accounts for the possibility (cf. {{GHGpar|144|g}}) of using the active without a specified subject as a periphrasis for the passive. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=42}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיֻּגַּד לְרִבְקָה אֶת־דִּבְרֵי עֵשָׂו|translate=and there were told}} (i.e. one told) ''to Rebekah the words of Esau''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=21|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=13}}.

412.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par121 />{{GHGmargin-letter|121|b}}
Other examples are: after Niph., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיִוָּלֵד לַֽחֲנוֹךְ אֶת־עִירָד|translate=and unto Enoch was born Irad}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=26|verse=60}}, and after an infinitive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=5}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=8|hidebook=1}} (after an infinitive); 29:27 (unless {{GHGheb|text=וְנִתְּנָה}} is 1st plur. cohortative); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=25|verse=28|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=6|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=7|verse=10}} (after an infinitive); 26:55 (cf. verse 53); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=20|verse=8}} (where, however, for {{GHGheb|text=יִמַּס}} the Hiph. {{GHGheb|text=יַמֵּס}} should be read, according to 1:28); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=7|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=16|verse=10}}; with the object preceding, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=13|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=19|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=29}}, Dan 9:24.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=18|verse=30}} {{GHGheb|text=יִנָּתֵן}} is to be read or {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}} is to be omitted, as in the parallel passage {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=36|verse=15}}.</ref>— Also after Puʿal, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=50|verse=20}}; ''before'' Puʿal, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=3}} ({{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁד}} equivalent to the internal object {{GHGheb|text=עֲבֹדָה}}=''which they have caused to be served by thee''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=9}}; according to the Masoretic text also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=46|verse=22}}, where, however, the Samaritan and LXX read {{GHGheb|text=יָֽלְדָת}} for {{GHGheb|text=יֻלַּד}}; the Samaritan in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=26}} and 46:27 also reads {{GHGheb|text=יָֽלְדוּ}}, and this (or {{GHGheb|text=יֻלַּד}}) should certainly be read instead of {{GHGheb|text=יֻלְדוּ}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=21|verse=22}}.—After Hoph., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=27|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=10|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=16|verse=27|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=32|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=16|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=30|verse=15}}; after the infinitive Hoph., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=4}} f., 27:7; ''before'' Hoph., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=17|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=10|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=13|verse=6}}; after the infinitive ''Hothpaʿel'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=13|verse=55}} f.

{{GHGmargin-letter|121|c}}
'''2.''' Verbs which in the active take two accusatives ({{GHGpar|117|cc}}) retain in the passive construction at least ''one'' accusative, namely that of the second or remoter object, whilst the nearer object now becomes the subject. Thus, corresponding to {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶ֫ךָּ|translate=which I will show thee}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=1}}) the passive is {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר אַתָּה מָרְאֶה}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=25|verse=40}}) ''which thou hast been shown'', i.e. which has been shown to thee; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=26|verse=30}} (but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=13|verse=49}} with an accusative of the person); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=3}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=22|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=מֻדְבָּק מַלְקוֹחָ֑י}} depends on an assumed transitive {{GHGheb|text=הִדְבִּיק}} governing two accusatives (= ''my tongue is made to cleave to my jaws''); also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=20}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֶ֫רֶב תְּאֻכְּלוּ|translate=ye shall be devoured with the sword}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֶרֶב}} is not an ''accus. instrumenti'', but most probably an accusative of the object retained from the active construction.<ref>In the active, the sentence would be ''I will cause the sword to devour you''; by the rule stated above, under ''c'', this would become in the passive, ''the sword'' (nom.) ''shall be made to devour you'' (acc.). Instead of this, the remoter object is here made the subject, and the nearer object is retained in the accusative. Otherwise, the only possible explanation would be, according to the Arabic idiom, ''to cause one to devour the sword'' (remoter object), i.e. to give him over to it. It would then be simplest to read {{GHGheb|text=תֹּֽאכְלוּ}}.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|121|d}}
Rem. 1. Examples of the retention of the second accusative are—(''a'') with {{GHGterm|verba induendi}} and ''exuendi'' ({{GHGpar|117|cc}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=80|verse=11}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּסּוּ תָרִים צִלָּתּ|translate=the mountains were covered with the shadow of it}} (the vine); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=19|verse=23}}. So also some of the examples in {{GHGpar|116|k}} of passive participles of these verbs, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=18|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=10}},<section end=par121 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

413.text:
{{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=9|verse=2}}, 3;Analogous to {{GHGheb|text=הַלָּבוּשׁ הַבַּדִּים|translate=who was clothed in linen}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=9|verse=3}}, would be {{GHGheb|text=וְהַנּוֹתָר אֶת־הֶהָמוֹן הַזֶּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=31|verse=10}}; but we must certainly read there {{GHGheb|text=וַנּוֹתֵר}} with the LXX.—Still less can {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=87|verse=3}} be so explained, {{GHGheb|text=נִכְבָּדוֹת}} being not an accusative, but the subject of a noun-clause. On the other hand, {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלוּחַ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=14|verse=6}} may be explained with Ewald in the sense of ''being charged with'' something, so that, like {{GHGheb|text=צִוָּח}}, it may be construed with an accusative. with the accusative preceding, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=4|verse=12}}.—(''b'') with {{GHGterm|verba copiae}} and ''inopiae'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=1|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=38|verse=10}} (equivalent to ''I must forego the residue of my years''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=20}}.—(''c'') an accusative of the result ({{GHGpar|117|ii}}) with the passive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=14|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=28|verse=2}}; with the accusative preceding, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=24|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=3|verse=12}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=26|verse=18}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=16|hidebook=1}}.In reality {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּרֻם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=20}}, 26 (''it became putrid'') is equivalent to a passive (''it was changed''), to which {{GHGheb|text=תּֽוֹלָעִים}} is added as an accusative of the result. Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=40|verse=17}} and 46:23, the accusative preceding {{GHGheb|text=עָשׂוּי}} (in 41:18 following it) can only be taken as the accusative of the result; some general idea, such as that of ''place'', is to be understood as the subject of {{GHGheb|text=עָשׂוּי}}.—(''d'') an accusative of the member or part specially affected by the action ({{GHGpar|117|ll}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=7}} (accusative ''before'' part. pass.); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=32}} (accusative with suffix after the part. pass.). {{GHGmargin-letter|121|e}} 2. Both accusatives are retained in an unusual manner after the passive of a {{GHGterm|verbum implendi}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=21}}; instead, however, of the ''Niph.'' {{GHGheb|text=וְיִמָּלֵא}} the {{GHGterm|Qal}} (which is sometimes used transitively elsewhere) should simply be read with the LXX; similarly in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=72|verse=19}}, although there the LXX also translate the passive. {{GHGmargin-letter|121|f}} '''3.''' The efficient cause (or personal agent) is, as a rule, attached to the passive by {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} (thus corresponding to the Greek and Latin dative), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=21}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיֵּעָ֫תֶ֫ר לוֹ יְהֹוָה|translate=the Lord let himself be intreated by him}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=10}} and the blessing {{GHGheb|text=בָּרוּךְ הוּא לַֽיהוָֹה|translate=blessed be he of the Lord}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=2|verse=20}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=17|verse=2}}b, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=13}}; also in the plural, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=21}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=115|verse=15}}).—''Before'' the verb, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=14|verse=20}} and frequently; less commonly by {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} (called {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} of origin=''coming from''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=11}}; ''before'' the verb, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=37|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=24|verse=1}}; by {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} (''instrumenti'') [rarely, König § 106], {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=6}} ({{GHGheb|text=בָּֽאָדָם|translate=by man}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=36|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=3}} b [but ?=''wherewith it was worked'' ({{GHGpar|52|e}}) ''with thee''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=21|verse=3}}, König § 106; and see {{GHGheb|text=עָבַד בְּ}} in the Lexicon], {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=14|verse=4}}, always to introduce a personal agent.—On the connexion of the passive participle with a genitive of the agent, cf. {{GHGpar|116|l}}.
{{center|''Syntax of the Noun.''}} {{GHGpar-heading|122|Indication of the Gender of the Noun}}
Cf. F. Schwabe, ''Die Genusbestimmung des Nomens im bibl. Hebr.'', Jena, 1894, and especially the thorough investigation by K. Albrecht, ‘Das Geschlecht der hebr. Hauptwörter,’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1895, p. 313 ff., and 1896, p. 61 ff. H. Rosenberg, ‘Zum Geschlecht der hebr. Hauptwörter,’ in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1905, p. 325 ff. (supplementing Albrecht’s work by a treatment of the gender of many nouns in the Mishna); and his ‘Notizen aus der tannaitischen Literatur...’ {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1908, p. 144 ff.
{{GHGmargin-letter|122|a}} '''1.''' According to {{GHGpar|80|a}}, Hebrew, like the other Semitic languages, distinguishes only a ''masculine'' and ''feminine'' gender. To indicate the

414.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par122 />latter a special feminine ending is generally used ({{GHGpar|80|b}} and {{GHGpar|87|i}}) both in the singular and plural (see, however, {{GHGpar|87|p}}), its use being most consistent in adjectives and participles; cf. {{GHGpar|87|r}}. The employment of these special endings is most natural when by means of them the feminine names of persons or animals are distinguished from the masculine of the same stem and the same formation, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָח|translate=brother}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָחוֹת|translate=sister}}; {{GHGheb|text=עֶלֶם|translate=a young man}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַלְמָה|translate=a young woman, maid}}; {{GHGheb|text=פָּר|translate=iuvencus}}, {{GHGheb|text=פָּרָה|translate=iuvenca}}; {{GHGheb|text=עֵגֶל|translate=vitulus}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֶגְלָה|translate=vitula}}. On the other hand, the feminine plays an important part in denoting the gender of whole classes of ideas (see below, p, &c.), which the Hebrew regards as feminine. The language, however, is not obliged to use the feminine ending either for the purpose of distinguishing the ''sex'' of animate objects (see b), or as an indication of the (''figurative'') gender of inanimate things which are regarded as feminine (see h).

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|b}}
'''2.''' The distinction of ''sex'' may be effected even without the feminine ending, (''a'') by the employment of words of different stems for the masculine and feminine; (''b'') by the different construction (either as masculine or feminine) of the same word (''communia''). But the distinction may also, (''c'') in the case of names of animals, be entirely neglected, all examples of a species being included under one particular gender, either masculine or feminine (''epicoena'').

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|c}}
Examples of (''a'') are: {{GHGheb|text=אָב|translate=father}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֵם|translate=mother}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִל|translate=ram}}, {{GHGheb|text=רָחֵל|translate=ewe}}; {{GHGheb|text=תַּ֫יִשׁ|translate=he-goat}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֵז|translate=she-goat}}; {{GHGheb|text=חֲמוֹר|translate=he-ass}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָתוֹן|translate=she-ass}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַרְיֵה|translate=lion}}, {{GHGheb|text=לָבִיא|translate=lioness}}. Sometimes with the feminine ending as well, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עֶ֫בֶד|translate=male slave, man-servant}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָמָה}} or {{GHGheb|text=שִׁפְחָה|translate=female slave, maid}}; {{GHGheb|text=חָתָן|translate=bridegroom}}, {{GHGheb|text=כַּלָּה|translate=bride}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|d}}
Of (''b''): {{GHGheb|text=גָּמָל|translate=camel}}. Plur. {{GHGheb|text=גְּמַלִּים}} construed as masculine, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=63}}; as feminine, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=16}}; {{GHGheb|text=בָּקָר}} collect, ''oxen'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=37}}, construed as masculine, but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=14}} as feminine. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=24}} the construction of {{GHGheb|text=פֶּ֫רֶה|translate=wild ass}}, changes directly from the masculine (intended as epicene) to the feminine.Cf. the Greek ὁ, ἡ παῖς· ὁ, ἡ βοῦς.

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|e}}
Of (''c''): analogous to the epicene nouns of other languages, many species of animals which are strong and courageous, are regarded in Hebrew as always masculine, while the weak and timid are feminine; cf. ὁ λύκος, ἡ χελιδών, and the German ''der'' Löwe, ''der'' Adler, &c., but ''die'' Katze, ''die'' Taube, &c. Similarly in Hebrew, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַלּוּף|translate=ox}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=144|verse=14}} even referring to cows when pregnant), {{GHGheb|text=דֹּב|translate=bear}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=13|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=דּוֹב שַׁכּוּל}} (''a bear that is bereaved of her whelps''; cf., however, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=11|verse=7}}), {{GHGheb|text=זְאֵב|translate=wolf}}, {{GHGheb|text=כֶּ֫לֶב|translate=dog}}, all masculine; but {{GHGheb|text=אַרְנֶ֫בֶת|translate=hare}}, {{GHGheb|text=יוָֹנָה|translate=dove}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֲסִידְה|translate=stork}}, {{GHGheb|text=דְּבוֹרָה|translate=bee}}, {{GHGheb|text=נֲמָלָה|translate=ant}}, &c., feminine.

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|f}}
Rem. 1. Masculine nouns which either have a separate feminine form or might easily form one, are but seldom used as epicene; such are, {{GHGheb|text=חֲמוֹר|translate=ass}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=27}} for {{GHGheb|text=אָתוֹן}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַיָל|translate=hart}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=42|verse=2}} for {{GHGheb|text=אַיָלָה}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=3}} ff. {{GHGheb|text=מֵת|translate=a dead body}}, refers more especially to the body of a woman; {{GHGheb|text=אָמוֹן|translate=a master workman}}, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=8|verse=30}} refers to wisdom ({{GHGheb|text=חָכְמָה}} feminine, cf. Plin. 2, 1 ''natura omnium artifex''; and our<section end=par122 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

415.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par122 />use of ''friend, teacher, servant, neighbour'', either as masculine or feminine; in German, ''Gemahl''<ref>So in early Arabic, ''ba‛l'' (lord) and ''zauǵ'' (conjux) are used both for ''maritus'' and ''uxor''; ''‛arūs'' for ''bridegroom'' and ''bride''; the later language, however, distinguishes the feminine from the masculine in all these cases generally by the ending ''a'' (''at''). In early Arabic also the feminine ending is commonly omitted in such participles as ''ḥāmil, bāṭin'' (gravida), and the like, which from the nature of the case can only be used of females. Thus also {{GHGheb|text=אֹמֵן}}, at least in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=12}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=23}}?), probably means ''nurse'' (for {{GHGheb|text=אֹמֶ֫נֶת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=4|verse=4}}, &c.), not ''nursing-father''.</ref> spouse, also for fem. ''Gemahlin'', &c.).

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|g}}
2. Of words denoting persons {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫עַר}} παῖς, according to the formerly common opinion, was in early times used as epicene (see, however, above, {{GHGpar|2|n}}). The use of the plural {{GHGheb|text=נְעָרִים}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=19}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=2|verse=21}} in the sense of ''young people'' (of both genders) does not, however, prove this. In this and in similar cases (cf. e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=27}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְהֶם}} 32:1) the masculine as ''prior gender'' includes the feminine.<ref>The Arab grammarians call this use of the masculine plural and dual (e.g. ''el-abawāni'', the two fathers, i.e. ''parentes'') ''taghlîb'' or ''the making'' (the masculine) ''prevail'' (over the feminine).—Cf. M. Grünert, ''Die Begriffs-Präponderanz und die Duale a potiori im Altarab.'', Vienna, 1886.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|h}}
'''3.''' The following classes of ideas are usually regarded as feminine,<ref>The masculine gender is attributed ‘by the Hebrews and the Semites generally to whatever is dangerous, savage, courageous, respected, great, strong, powerful ...; the feminine to whatever is motherly, productive, sustaining, nourishing, gentle, weak, ... subject, &c.’ (Albrecht, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1896, p. 120 f.).</ref> although the substantives which express them are mostly without the feminine ending:<ref>When, on the other hand, words ''with'' a feminine-ending, such as {{GHGheb|text=קֶ֫שֶׁת|translate=a bow}} (stem {{GHGheb|text=קוש}}), {{GHGheb|text=עֵת|translate=time}} (see the Lexicon), are sometimes construed as masculine, this is owing probably in some cases to a misunderstanding of the formation of the word, the {{GHGheb|text=ת}} of the feminine being regarded as a radical.</ref>

(''a'') Names of ''countries'' and ''towns'', since they are regarded as the mothers<ref>Cf. ''a city and a mother'' ({{GHGheb|text=אֵם}}) ''in Israel'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=19}}. In the same way {{GHGheb|text=אֵם}} (like μήτηρ, ''mater'') on Phoenician coins stands for ''mother-city'', μητ ρόπολις. The same figure is used in such expressions as ''sons of Zion'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=149|verse=2}}; ''sons of Babylon'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=15}}, &c., as also in speaking of the suburbs of a city as its ''daughters'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=15|verse=45}} ff., &c.—The comparison of Jerusalem to a woman is especially frequent in allegorical descriptions, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=1}}, &c.</ref> and nurses of the inhabitants; e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַשּׁוּר|translate=Assyria}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֱדֹם|translate=Idumaea}}, {{GHGheb|text=צֹר|translate=Tyre}}; cf. also such expressions as {{GHGheb|text=בַּת בָּבֶל}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּת צִיּוֹן|translate=daughter of Babylon, daughter of Zion}}, &c. On the other hand appellatives which are originally masculine, remain so when used as place-names, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=בֵּית־אֵל}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַגִּלְגָּל}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|i}}
Rem. The same proper nouns, which as names of countries are regarded as feminine, are frequently used also as names of the people, and may then, like national names in other languages, be construed as masculine (the national name almost always being used also as the personal name of the supposed ancestor of the people); thus {{GHGheb|text=יְהוּדָה}} masc. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=8}}, &c., ''Judaei''; but<section end=par122 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

416.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par122 />{{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=6}}, fem., ''Judaea''; {{GHGheb|text=אֱדֹם}} masc., ''Idumaei'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=20}}; fem., ''Idumaea'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=17}}. Nevertheless, it sometimes happens that by a very common transference of thought (just as we say ''Turkey concludes peace'') these names are construed as feminine, even when they denote not the country but the inhabitants; so {{GHGheb|text=יְהוּדָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=3}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=33|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=8|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=50|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=15}}. Hence the frequent personification of nations (as well as of countries and towns, see h, note 5) as female beings, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=50|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=54|verse=1|hidebook=1}} ff., and the use of the expressions {{GHGheb|text=בַּת בָּבֶל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=1}} ff., {{GHGheb|text=בַּת צִיּוֹן}} &c. (see above) as collective poetical personifications of the people.

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|k}}
(''b'') Appellative nouns, which denote a ''circumscribed space'', such as {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫רֶץ|translate=earth, land}}, {{GHGheb|text=תֵּבֵל|translate=world}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁאֹל|translate=the abode of the dead}}, {{GHGheb|text=כִּכָּר|translate=circle}} (of the Jordan valley), {{GHGheb|text=עִיר|translate=a town}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּאֵר|translate=a well}}, {{GHGheb|text=צָפוֹן|translate=the north}}, {{GHGheb|text=תֵּימָן|translate=the south}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|l}}
In the majority of nouns denoting place the gender is variable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֹ֫רַח}} and {{GHGheb|text=דֶּ֫רֶךְ|translate=a way}} (usually feminine; the masculine gender only begins to predominate with Ezekiel; cf. Albrecht, l. c., 1896, p. 55), {{GHGheb|text=גַּיְא}} ({{GHGheb|text=גַּי}}) ''valley'', {{GHGheb|text=גַּן|translate=garden}} (fem. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=15}}, unless {{GHGheb|text=לְעָבְדֹה}}, &c., is to be read), {{GHGheb|text=הֵיכָל|translate=palace, temple}}, {{GHGheb|text=חָעֵר|translate=court}}, {{GHGheb|text=כֶּ֫רֶם|translate=vineyard}}, {{GHGheb|text=שַׁ֫עַר|translate=door}},<ref>{{GHGheb|text=מַֽחֲנֶה|translate=camp}} is feminine only when it is a collective, denoting the persons in a camp.</ref> &c.; also {{GHGheb|text=מָקוֹם|translate=place}}, at least in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=24}} (referring to Sodom), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=9}}, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=17|verse=12}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}}, is construed as feminine. The mountains and hills commanding the surrounding country are almost without exception masculine (see Albrecht, l. c., p. 60 f.).

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|m}}
(''c'') The names of ''instruments, utensils'', and (on the same analogy) ''members'' and ''parts of the body'' in man or beast, since these are all regarded as subservient and subordinate (consequently as feminine).

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|n}}
Thus {{GHGheb|text=חֶ֫רֶב|translate=sword}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָתֵד|translate=tent-peg}}, {{GHGheb|text=כַּד|translate=bucket}}, {{GHGheb|text=כּוֹס|translate=cup}}, {{GHGheb|text=נַ֫עַל|translate=shoe}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֶ֫רֶשׂ|translate=bed}}, &c.; in other cases, as {{GHGheb|text=אֲרוֹן|translate=chest, ark}} (with the article {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאָרוֹן}}), {{GHGheb|text=תַּנּוּר|translate=oven}}, the gender is variable. (‘Instruments for binding or holding, girdles and the like, as constraining and mastering, are masculine,’ Albrecht, l. c., p. 89.)—Also {{GHGheb|text=אֹ֫זֶן|translate=ear}} (and in general, members occurring in pairs, Albrecht, l. c., p. 73 f.), {{GHGheb|text=אֶצְבַּע|translate=finger}} (and so probably {{GHGheb|text=בֹּ֫הֶן|translate=thumb, great toe}}), {{GHGheb|text=יָד}} and {{GHGheb|text=כַּף|translate=hand}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָמִין|translate=right hand}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֶ֫גֶל|translate=foot}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֶּ֫רֶךְ|translate=knee}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָרֵךְ|translate=thigh}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּתֵף|translate=shoulder}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְחִי|translate=cheek}}, {{GHGheb|text=בֶּ֫טֶן|translate=belly}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּנָף|translate=wing}}, {{GHGheb|text=קֶ֫רֶן|translate=horn}}, {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁן|translate=tooth}}; as a rule also {{GHGheb|text=זְרוֹעַ|translate=arm}} (masc. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=17|verse=5}}, &c.), {{GHGheb|text=לָשׁוֹן|translate=tongue}} (masc. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=22|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=26|verse=28}}, &c.), {{GHGheb|text=עַ֫יִן|translate=eye}} (masc. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=3|verse=9}}, &c.), {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹק|translate=thigh}} (masc. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=29|verse=27}}).<ref>{{GHGheb|text=אַף|translate=nose}}, {{GHGheb|text=גִּיד|translate=sinew}}, {{GHGheb|text=זָנָב|translate=tail}}, {{GHGheb|text=חֵךְ|translate=palate}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּבֵד|translate=liver}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֵב}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֵבָב|translate=heart}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֵעִים}}, {{GHGheb|text=רַֽחֲמִים|translate=bowels}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֵ֫צַח|translate=forehead}}, {{GHGheb|text=עוֹר|translate=skin}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֹרֶף|translate=back of the neck}}, {{GHGheb|text=פֶּה|translate=mouth}}, {{GHGheb|text=צַוָּאר|translate=neck}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֹאשׁ|translate=head}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁכֶם|translate=shoulder}}, also {{GHGheb|text=רֶ֫חֶם|translate=womb}}, except in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=17}}, are invariably construed as masculine.—{{GHGheb|text=עֶ֫צֶם|translate=bone}} is common.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|o}}
(''d'') Certain names of natural forces or substances are feminine, being probably regarded as instruments, while in the names of the heavens, the heavenly bodies and natural phenomena, the masculine generally predominates (cf. Albrecht, l. c., p. 323 ff.); thus feminine are {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫מֶשׁ|translate=sun}} (but often also {{GHGterm|masc.}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=19|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=19|hidebook=1}}); {{GHGheb|text=אֵשׁ}} (Ethiopic ''’ĕsât'')<section end=par122 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

417.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par122 />''fire'' (rarely {{GHGterm|masc.}}); {{GHGheb|text=נֹ֫גַהּ|translate=brightness}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫בֶן|translate=a stone}}, as a rule also {{GHGheb|text=רוּחַ|translate=wind, spirit}}; {{GHGheb|text=נֶ֫פֶשׁ|translate=breath, soul}}; also {{GHGheb|text=אוֹר|translate=light}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=36|verse=32}}, and others.

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|p}}
'''4.''' The following classes of ideas, which are also regarded as feminine in Hebrew (see above, h), are usually indicated by the feminine ''form'', notwithstanding their occasional transference to masculine persons (see r and s):

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|q}}
(''a'') Abstracts<ref>Cf. the list of masculine and feminine abstracts in Albrecht, l. c., 1896, p. 111 ff.</ref> (sometimes along with masculine forms from the same stem, as {{GHGheb|text=נְקָמָה|translate=vengeance}}, as well as {{GHGheb|text=נָקָם}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֶזְרָה|translate=help}}, as well as {{GHGheb|text=עֵ֫זֶר}}), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֱמוּנָה|translate=firmness, faithfulness}}, {{GHGheb|text=גְּבוּרָה|translate=strength}}, {{GHGheb|text=גְּדוּלָה|translate=greatness}}, {{GHGheb|text=מְלֵאָה|translate=fullness}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֶמְשָׁלָה|translate=dominion}}, &c. Similarly, the feminine (sing. and plur.) of adjectives and participles is used substantivally in the sense of the Latin and Greek ''neuter'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=נְכוֹנָה|translate=stedfastness}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=5|verse=10}}, {{GHGheb|text=טוֹבָה|translate=goodness}}, {{GHGheb|text=רָעָה|translate=evil}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=50|verse=20}}, {{GHGheb|text=נְקַלָּה|translate=a light thing}} (i.e. a trifling thing), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=6|verse=14}}; so especially in the plural, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גְּדֹלוֹת|translate=great things}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=12|verse=4}}; {{GHGheb|text=הַנֶּֽהֱרָסוֹת|translate=the ruined places}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=36|verse=36}}, along with {{GHGheb|text=הַנְּשַׁמָּה|translate=that which was desolate}}, {{GHGheb|text=טֹבוֹת|translate=kindnesses}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=25|verse=28}}, {{GHGheb|text=נְכֹחוֹת|translate=uprightness, honesty}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=26|verse=10}}, {{GHGheb|text=נְעִימוֹת|translate=amoena}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=16|verse=11}} (but in verse 6 in the same sense {{GHGheb|text=נְעִימִים}}), {{GHGheb|text=נִפְלָאוֹת|translate=wonderful things}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=34|verse=10}} and frequently, {{GHGheb|text=קָשׁוֹת|translate=hard things, roughly}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=7}}, 30 (but cf. also {{GHGheb|text=רֵיקִם|translate=vain things}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=12|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=28|verse=19|hidebook=1}}). Cf. moreover, the very frequent use of {{GHGheb|text=זֹאת}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}} (as well as {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}} and {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=118|verse=23}}, &c., in the sense of ''hoc, illud'' (also {{GHGheb|text=הֵ֫נָּה}} equivalent to ''illa'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=51|verse=19}}): also the use of the feminine form of the verb in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא תָקוּם וְלֹא תִֽהְיֶה|translate=it shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=7}}; so too the suffixes {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=18}}, referring back to a whole statement.<ref>While in all these instances it is simplest to speak of the ''feminine'' in Hebrew as being used ''for the neuter'' (which in Latin, Greek, and German is commonly employed for similar purposes), it must yet not be forgotten that since the language is wholly wanting in ''neuters'', the Semitic mind regarded the above-mentioned forms primarily as actual feminines. Hence the Arab commentators are accustomed to explain the feminines of adjectives and participles (which would be neuter in Latin, &c.) by supplying a feminine substantive.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|r}}
(''b'') Titles and designations of office, properly a subdivision of the abstract ideas treated above, under q, and specially noticed here only on account of their peculiar transference to concrete male persons. Thus we have {{GHGheb|text=קֹהֶ֫לֶת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=1|verse=1}}, &c. (as a title of Solomon), properly no doubt ''that which takes part in'' or ''speaks in a religious assembly'', hence LXX ἐκκλησιαστής, i.e. ''concionator, preacher''; the proper names {{GHGheb|text=סֹפֶ֫רֶת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=2|verse=55}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=7|verse=57}}, and {{GHGheb|text=פֹּכֶ֫רֶת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=2|verse=57}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=7|verse=59}}, and the foreign word {{GHGheb|text=פֶּחָה|translate=viceroy}}; in the plural {{GHGheb|text=כְּנָוֹת}} prop. ''cognomina'', then ''like-named, colleagues''; {{GHGheb|text=פְּרָעוֹת|translate=princes}} (if this be the true meaning).<ref>This use of the feminine form is far more frequent in Arabic, Ethiopic, and Aramaic; cf. e.g. in Arabic ''ḥalîfa'' (fem. from ''ḥalîf'', following after, taking the place of) in the sense of ''the'' successor or representative (of Muḥammad), and ''‛allāma'' (''great wisdom'') as a title of learned men. Analogous to this is the Latin ''magistratus, magistracy'', for ''magistrate'', and our ''his Majesty, Excellency, Highness'', &c.</ref> All these words, in accordance with their meaning, are construed as masculine (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=7|verse=27}} instead of {{GHGheb|text=אָֽמְרָה ק׳}} the words should rather be divided as {{GHGheb|text=אָמַר הַקּ׳}}; cf. 12:8).
<section end=par122 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

418.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par122" />{{GHGmargin-letter|122|s}}
Abstract ideas include also—

(''c'') ''Collectives'' in the fem. form,<ref>Cf. in Greek ἡ ἵππος, ''the cavalry'' (as well as τὸ ἱππικόν), ἡ κάμηλος, Hdt. 1, 80, &c., ''the camel corps''.</ref> generally fem. participles used substantivally, especially as the comprehensive designation of a number of ''persons'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֹֽרְחָה}} (fem. of ''travelling''), prop. ''the travelling'' (company), i.e. travelling persons (a caravan); {{GHGheb|text=גּוֹלָה}} (fem. of {{GHGheb|text=גֹּלֶה|translate=one going into exile}}) ''the company of exiles'' (also frequently used of those who had returned home again); {{GHGheb|text=יוֹשֶׁ֫בֶת}} (that which inhabits) i.e. ''the population'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=12|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=1|verse=11}} f.; {{GHGheb|text=אֹיֶ֫בֶת}} (prop. that which is hostile) ''the enemy'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=7|verse=8}}, 10 (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=4|verse=6}} f. ''the halting, cast off, driven away'', i.e. ''those who halt'', &c.); {{GHGheb|text=דַּלָּה}} (the abject) ''the poorest sort''; of living beings which are not persons, cf. {{GHGheb|text=חַיָּה}} (that which lives) in the sense of ''cattle, beasts''; {{GHGheb|text=דָּגָה|translate=a shoal of fish}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=26}} (but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=2|verse=2}} as a {{GHGterm|nomen unitatis|en=name of a unit}}, cf. t, for {{GHGheb|text=דָּג|translate=a fish}}, which in verses 1 and 11 is used as the ''nomen unitatis''). Cf., moreover, {{GHGheb|text=נְבֵלָה|translate=dead body}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=26|verse=19}}, &c. (construed as masculine), for ''a heap of dead bodies''.—On the collective poetic personification of a nation, by means of {{GHGheb|text=בַּת|translate=daughter}}, in {{GHGheb|text=בַּת בָּבֶל}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּת עַמִּי}} (equivalent to {{GHGheb|text=בְּנֵי עַמִּי}}) ''my countrymen'', see above, i.

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|t}}
(''d'') Conversely the feminine form of substantives is sometimes used (as in Arabic) as a ''nomen unitatis'', i.e. to indicate a ''single'' example of a class which is denoted by the masculine form; cf. {{GHGheb|text=אֳנִי|translate=a fleet}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=9|verse=26}}), {{GHGheb|text=אֳנִיָּה|translate=a}} single ''ship'' ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=1|verse=3}} ff.); {{GHGheb|text=צַ֫יִד|translate=hunting, game}}, {{GHGheb|text=צֵידָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=3}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}} ({{GHGheb|text=צָ֑יִד}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}) ''a piece of venison''; {{GHGheb|text=שֵׂעָר|translate=hair}} (coll.), {{GHGheb|text=שַֽׂעֲרָה|translate=a}} single ''hair'' ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=20|verse=16}}; in the plural, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=40|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=69|verse=5|hidebook=1}}); {{GHGheb|text=שִׁיר|translate=a poem}}, frequently collective, {{GHGheb|text=שִׁירָה|translate=a}} single ''song''; so probably also {{GHGheb|text=תְּאֵנָה|translate=a fig}} (the corresponding masculine ''tîn'' is collective in Arabic); {{GHGheb|text=שֽׁוֹשַׁנָּה|translate=a lily}} (also {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹשָׁן}}); {{GHGheb|text=לְבֵנָה|translate=a brick}} (Arab. ''libina'', but ''libin'' collective), &c.

(''e'') The feminine is also used for things ''without life'' (as being weaker or less important), which are named from their resemblance to ''organic'' things expressed by the corresponding masculine form; cf. {{GHGheb|text=יָרֵךְ|translate=side}} (of the body), ''thigh'', {{GHGheb|text=יְרֵכָה}} or {{GHGheb|text=יַרְכָּה|translate=back part, border}} (of a country, house, &c.); {{GHGheb|text=מֵ֫צַח|translate=forehead}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִצְחָה|translate=greaves}}. On a similar distinction between the masculine for natural, and the feminine for artificial objects, see {{GHGpar|87|o}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|122|v}}
Rem. The juxtaposition of the masculine and feminine from the same stem serves sometimes to express entirety; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=מַשְׁעֵן וּמַשְׁעֵנָה|translate=stay and staff}}, i.e. every kind of support (unless we omit verse {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=1b|hidebook=completely|fullsizeverse=1}} as a gloss and take ''staff'' as = ''staff-bearer, official''; the list of officials begins in verse 2); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=16|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=8|verse=13}}. For similar groupings in the case of persons, see {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=43|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=60|verse=4|hidebook=1}} (''sons and daughters''); 49:23, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=2|verse=8}}.
<section end="par122" />
<section begin="par123" />{{GHGpar-heading|123|The Representation of Plural Ideas by Means of Collectives, and by the Repetition of Words}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|123|a}}
Besides the plural endings treated in {{GHGpar|87|a}}–i, the language employs other means to express a plurality of living beings or things:

(''a'') Certain words employed exclusively in a collective sense, while the individual members of the class are denoted by special words ({{GHGterm|nomina unitatis}}, but not in the same sense as in {{GHGpar|122|t}}).<section end="par123" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

419.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par123 />Thus {{GHGheb|text=בָּקָר|translate=cattle, oxen}}<ref>The plural form {{GHGheb|text=בְּקָרִים}} from {{GHGheb|text=בָּקָר}} is found only in very late Hebrew, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=10|verse=37}} (where according to the Mantua edition, Ginsburg, &c., even {{GHGheb|text=צֹאנֵ֫ינוּ|translate=our sheep}}, is also to be read; Baer, however, has {{GHGheb|text=צֹאנֵ֫נוּ}}), and {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=4|verse=3}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=6|verse=12}} read, with Hitzig, {{GHGheb|text=בַּבָּקָר יָם}}.</ref> (even joined with numerals, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=37}} {{GHGheb|text=חֲמִשָּׁה בָקָר|translate=five head of cattle}}), but {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹר|translate=an ox}}; {{GHGheb|text=צֹאן|translate=small cattle}}, i.e. sheep and goats (μῆλα), cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעַת אַלְפֵי־צֹאן|translate=seven thousand sheep}}; but {{GHGheb|text=שֶׂה|translate=a single head of small cattle}} (a sheep or a goat). Other more or less common collectives are: {{GHGheb|text=זִיז}} (prop. that which prowls or roams) ''wild beasts'', {{GHGheb|text=טַף}} (perhaps prop. ''tripping'') ''a number of little children''; {{GHGheb|text=דֶּ֫שֶׁא|translate=fresh green herb}}, i.e. young plants, {{GHGheb|text=יֶ֫רֶק|translate=green}}, i.e. vegetation in general; {{GHGheb|text=עוֹף|translate=birds, fowl}}; {{GHGheb|text=רֶ֫כֶב|translate=chariots}} or ''cavalcade'', {{GHGheb|text=רִמָּה|translate=worms}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֶ֫מֶשׂ|translate=creeping things}} (of small creatures), {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫רֶץ|translate=swarming things}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|123|b}}
