3. {{GHGheb|text=עֶ֫צֶם|translate=bone}} (then metaphorically for ''substance'') expresses the idea of ''self, selfsame, very same'', in reference to ''things'' (as {{GHGheb|text=נֶ֫פֶשׁ}} to persons, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בְּעֶ֫צֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה|translate=in the selfsame day}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=13}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=10|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=24|verse=2}}; {{GHGheb|text=כְּעֶ֫צֶם הַשָּׁמַ֫יִם לָטֹהַר|translate=as it were the very heaven for clearness}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=24|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=בְּעֶ֫צֶם תֻּמּוֹ|translate=in the very fullness of his strength}} (= ''in the midst of his full strength''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=23}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|139|h}}
4. The simple plural of words denoting time sometimes includes also the idea of a ''few, some'';<ref>''Some'' in reference to persons in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=20}} is expressed by {{GHGheb|text=אֲנָשִׁים}}, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=5|verse=2}}–4 by {{GHGheb|text=יֵשׁ אֲשֶׁר|translate=sunt qui}}, with a participle following.</ref> thus {{GHGheb|text=יָמִים|translate=a few days}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=55}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=4|hidebook=1}} (here even of a longer period, = ''for some time''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=65|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=8|verse=27}} (on the other hand, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=44}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=20|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=יָמִים אֲחָדִים}}; see § 96 under {{GHGheb|text=אֶחָד}}); {{GHGheb|text=שָׁנִים|translate=some years}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=11|verse=6}}, 8.<section end=par139 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

474.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par140 />{{center|'''CHAPTER II'''

THE SENTENCE

''The Sentence in General.''}}

<!-- section begins above -->{{GHGpar-heading|140|Noun-clauses, Verbal-clauses, and the Compound Sentence}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|140|a}}
'''1.''' Every sentence, the subject and predicate of which are nouns or their equivalents (esp. participles), is called a ''noun-clause'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָהוָֹה מַלְכֵּנוּ|translate=the Lord is our king}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=33|verse=22}}; {{GHGheb|text=וְאַנְשֵׁי סְדֹם רָעִים וְחַטָּאִים|translate=now the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=13}}; {{GHGheb|text=פֶּה לָהֶם|translate=a mouth is theirs}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=115|verse=5}}; see further, § 141.

{{GHGmargin-letter|140|b}}
'''2.''' Every sentence, the subject of which is a noun (or pronoun included in a verbal-form) and its predicate a finite verb, is called a ''verbal-clause'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וַיֹּא֫מֶר אֱלֹהִים|translate=and God said}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=3}}; {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּבְדֵּל|translate=and he divided}}, 1:7; see further, § 142.

{{GHGmargin-letter|140|c}}
Rem. In the last example the pronominal subject is at least indicated by the preformative ({{GHGheb|text=י}}), and in almost all forms of the perfect by afformatives. The 3rd pers. sing. perf. however, which contains no indication of the subject, must also be regarded as a full verbal-clause.

{{GHGmargin-letter|140|d}}
'''3.''' Every sentence, the subject or predicate of which is itself a full clause, is called a ''compound sentence'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=31}} {{GHGheb|text=הָאֵל תָּמִים דַּרְכּוֹ}} ''God—his way is perfect'', equivalent to ''God’s way is perfect''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=שְׁכֶם בְּנִי חָֽשְׁקָה נַפְשׁוֹ בְּבִתְּכֶם}} ''my son Shechem—his soul longeth for your daughter''; see further, § 143.

{{GHGmargin-letter|140|e}}
'''4.''' The above distinction between different kinds of sentences—especially between noun- and verbal-clauses—is indispensable to the more delicate appreciation of Hebrew syntax (and that of the Semitic languages generally), since it is by no means merely external or formal, but involves fundamental differences of meaning. Noun-clauses with a substantive as predicate, represent something ''fixed, a state'' or in short, ''a being'' so and so; verbal-clauses on the other hand, something ''moveable'' and ''in progress'', an ''event'' or ''action''. The latter description is indeed true in a certain sense also of noun-clauses<section end=par140 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

475.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par140" />with a participial predicate, except that in their case the event or action (as distinguished from that expressed by the verbal-clause) is of a fixed and abiding character.

{{GHGmargin-letter|140|f}}
Rem. By the Arab grammarians every clause beginning with an independent subject is regarded as a noun-clause, and every clause beginning with a finite verb as verbal. If a finite verb follows the noun-subject the two together (since the verb comprises its own subject and is thus a complete verbal-clause) form a compound noun-sentence, just as when the predicate consists of an independent noun-clause. Though this definition of the different kinds of sentence, which we formerly accepted (in {{GHGpar|144|a}} of the 22nd to the 24th German editions of this Grammar), is rejected above, ''a–d'', we must, nevertheless, mention here the point in which this more complicated view of the Arab grammarians may be regarded as at least relatively correct, namely, in classifying verbal-clauses according as the subject precedes or follows the verb, a distinction which is often of great importance in Hebrew also; see further, in {{GHGpar|142|a}}.
<section end="par140" />
<section begin="par141" />{{GHGpar-heading|141|The Noun-clause}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|a}}
'''1.''' The ''subject'' of a noun-clause (see {{GHGpar|140|a}}) may be—

(''a'') A substantive, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וְנָהָר יֹצֵא מֵעֵ֫דֶן|translate=and a river went out ''(was going out)'' of Eden}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=10}}.

(''b'') A pronoun, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=אָֽנֹכִי מַמְטִיר|translate=I will cause it to rain}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=18|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהוּא כֹהֵן|translate=and he was priest}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=23|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=זֹאת}} before a feminine predicate, as {{GHGheb|text=אֵ֫לֶּה}} before a plural in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=4}}); {{GHGheb|text=מִי חָכָם|translate=who is wise?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=14|verse=10}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=5|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=וּלְנָגִיד מִמֶּ֫נּוּ|translate=and of him}} one became ''a prince'', the subject is contained in {{GHGheb|text=מִמֶּ֫נּוּ}}.<ref>For other remarkable instances of ellipse in the Chronicler, see Driver, ''Introduction'', ed. 8, p. 537, no. 27.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|b}}
'''2.''' The ''predicate'' of a noun-clause may be—

(''a'') A substantive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=14|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=בָּנִים אַתֶּם וגו׳|translate=ye are children of the Lord your God}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=13}}. Specially characteristic of the Semitic mode of expression are the cases in which both subject and predicate are substantives, thus emphasizing their identity (‘the thing is its measure, material, or equivalent’), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=41|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=הַמִּזְבֵּחַ עֵץ ... וְקִֽירֹתָיו עֵץ|translate=the altar}} (was) ''wood ..., and the walls thereof'' (were) ''wood'', i.e. of wood. Cf. below, c.

(''b'') An adjective or participle, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=וּֽזֲהַב הָאָ֫רֶץ הַהִיא טוֹב|translate=and the gold of that land is good}}; {{GHGheb|text=וְעֶפְרוֹן ישֵׁב|translate=now Ephron was sitting}}, &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=10}}.<ref>Cf. the numerous examples in {{GHGpar|116|n}}–p.</ref> Very frequently such noun-clauses, attached by {{GHGterm|Wāw}} to a verbal-clause, are used to represent a state ''contemporaneous'' with the principal action; cf. e below.

(''c'') A numeral, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר עֲבָדֶ֫יךָ|translate=the twelve}} (of us) ''are thy servants''.<section end="par141" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

476.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par141 />(''d'') A pronoun, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=12}} ({{GHGheb|text=הִיא}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=27}} ({{GHGheb|text=אֲנִי}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=65}} ({{GHGheb|text=מִי}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=9|verse=13}} ({{GHGheb|text=מָה}}).<ref>Why in these examples the pronouns, notwithstanding appearances to the contrary, are to be considered as predicates and not as subjects, may be seen from what has been remarked above, {{GHGpar|126|k}}.</ref>

(''e'') An adverb or (esp. if formed with a preposition) any specification of time, place, quality, possessor, &c., which may be regarded as the equivalent of a noun-idea, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שָׁם הַבְּדֹ֫לַח|translate=there is the bdellium}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=12}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֵי הֶ֫בֶל|translate=where is Abel?}} 4:9; {{GHGheb|text=לְעוֹלָם חַםְדּוֹ|translate=his mercy}} endureth ''for ever'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=136|verse=1}} f.; {{GHGheb|text=ע֫שֶׁר בְּבֵיתוֹ|translate=riches}} are ''in his house'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=112|verse=3}}; {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ אֲנָחְ֑נוּ|translate=we are his}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=100|verse=3}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|c}}
Rem. 1. The employment of a substantive as predicate of a noun-clause is especially frequent, either when no corresponding adjective exists (so mostly with words expressing the material; cf. {{GHGpar|128|o}}) or when the attribute is intended to receive a certain emphasis. For in all cases there is a much greater stress upon a substantival predicate,<ref>The same naturally applies to most of those cases which are not pure noun-clauses, but have the substantival predicate connected with the subject by {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=2}} ''and the earth was a waste and emptiness''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=35|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=8|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=4}}) or where a preposition precedes the substantival predicate, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=29|verse=4}} ''the voice of the Lord is with power'', i.e. ''powerful''.</ref> since it represents something as ''identical'' with the subject (see above, b [a]), than upon an adjectival or verbal predicate; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=1|verse=10}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=25|verse=10}} ''all the paths of the Lord are'' {{GHGheb|text=חֶ֫סֶד וֶֽאֱמֶת|translate=lovingkindness and truth}} (i.e. ''wholly lovingkindness'', &c.; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=10}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=38|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=10|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=19|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=23|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=88|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=3|verse=17}},<ref>{{GHGheb|text=שָׁלוֹם}} here, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=9}}, is evidently a substantive after a plural subject; on the other hand, it is doubtful whether {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלוֹם}} in such passages as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=120|verse=7}}, &c., is not rather to be regarded as an adjective.</ref> {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=26|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=2}}. Sometimes the emphasis on the predicate is obtained by the use of the plural form (according to {{GHGpar|124|e}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=110|verse=3}} ''thy people'' are {{GHGheb|text=נְדָבֹת|translate=altogether willingness}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=5|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=9|verse=23}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|d}}
Sometimes the boldness of such combinations is modified by the repetition of the subject, as ''regens'' of the predicate, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־כֹּחַ אֲבָנִים כֹּחִי|translate=is my strength the strength of stones?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=3|verse=17}}. That the language, however—especially in poetry—is not averse even to the boldest combinations in order to emphasize very strongly the unconditional relation between the subject and predicate, is shown by such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=45|verse=9}} ''myrrh and aloes and cassia'' are ''all thy garments'' (i.e. so perfumed with them that they seem to be composed of them); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=1|verse=15}} ''thine eyes'' are ''doves'', i.e. dove’s eyes (but 5:12 {{GHGheb|text=כְּיוֹנִים}});<ref>As a rule, in such comparisons {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}} (which is then to be regarded as ''nominative'') stands before the predicate, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=63|verse=2}} ''wherefore'' are ''thy garments'' {{GHGheb|text=כְּדֹרֵךְ בְּגַת|translate=like}} those of ''one that treadeth in the wine-press''? (prop. ''the like of one'' that treadeth, ''instar calcantis''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=50|verse=9}}. The comparison is then much less emphatic than in the noun-clauses cited above.</ref> {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=23|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=109|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=8|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=2|verse=13}}. In prose, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=10|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=הָעֵת גְּשָׁמִים|translate=the season}} is ''rain showers'', i.e. ''the rainy season''; with a bold enallage of the number, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=30}} {{GHGheb|text=וַֽאֲנִי מְתֵי מִסְפָּר|translate=and I}} (with my family) ''am'' persons few ''in number''. For similarly bold expressions with {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=17|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=28}}, and again with a bold enallage of the number, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=15}} ''I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame'', but in prose, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=10|verse=31}} ''and thou shalt be to us'' {{GHGheb|text=לְעֵנַ֫יִם}}.
<section end=par141 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

477.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par141 />{{GHGmargin-letter|141|e}}
'''2.''' The noun-clause connected by {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}} to a verbal-clause, or its equivalent, always describes a state ''contemporaneous'' with the principal action, or (when the predicate is a transitive participle) an action represented in constant duration (cf. {{GHGpar|107|d}}, as well as {{GHGpar|116|n}} and o), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=1}} ''and the two angels came to Sodom at even'', {{GHGheb|text=וְלוֹט ישֵׁב|translate=while Lot sat}}, &c.; 18:1, 8, 16, 22, 25:26, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=4|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=11|verse=4|hidebook=1}} (always with a participle); with an adjectival predicate, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=12}}; with a substantival predicate, 18:27; with an adverbial predicate, 9:23. Not infrequently such a ''circumstantial'' clause indicates at the same time some contradictory fact, so that {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} is equivalent to ''whereas, whilst, although'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=27|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=48|verse=14|hidebook=1}} (''although he was the younger''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=15}} ''how canst thou say, I love thee'', {{GHGheb|text=וְלִבְּךָ אֵין אִתִּי|translate=whereas thine heart is not with me}}? {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=39}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=28|verse=3}} ''whilst mischief is in their hearts''. These clauses describing a state are, however, only a subdivision of the large class of circumstantial clauses, on which see § 156.

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|f}}
'''3.''' As the examples given under ''a'' and ''b'' show, the syntactical relation existing between the subject and predicate of a noun-clause is as a rule expressed by simple juxtaposition, without a ''copula'' of any kind. To what period of time the statement applies must be inferred from the context; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=21}} {{GHGheb|text=יְהֹוָה הָֽאֱלֹהִים|translate=the Lord}} is ''the'' true ''God''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=19}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=31|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=גַּם־הוּא חָכָם|translate=yet he also is wise}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=11}}; on the other hand, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=וְלוֹט ישֵׁב|translate=and}} (=while) ''Lot was sitting''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=28|verse=15}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=אָֽנֹכִי מַמְטִיר|translate=I am raining}}, i.e. ''I will rain''. Sometimes even a jussive or optative is to be supplied as predicate, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=13}} ''upon me'' be ''thy curse''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=2}}. Cf. {{GHGpar|116|r}}, note.

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|g}}
Not infrequently, however, a connexion is established between subject and predicate (''a'') by adding the separate pronoun of the 3rd person singular or plural, expressly resuming and therefore strengthening the subject, or (''b'') (especially for the sake of a more exact specification of time) by the help of the verb {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}}. The first of these will be a ''compound'' sentence, since the predicate to the main subject consists of an independent clause.

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|h}}
Examples of (''a''): {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=26}} ''the seven good kine'' {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫בַע שָׁנִים הֵ֫נָּה|translate=they}} are ''seven years''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=24|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=5|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=זֹה מַתַּת אֱלֹהִים הִיא|translate=this}}—''it'' is ''a gift of God''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=3|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵ֫לֶּה הֵם}}; in a question, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=38}}. Sometimes {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}} is used in this way to strengthen a pronominal subject of the first or second person, and at the same time to connect it with the predicate which follows,<ref>On a similar use of the separate pronoun of the third person in Aramaic ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=2|verse=38}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=5|verse=11}}, &c.) see Kautzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Bibl. Aram.}}, § 87. 3.</ref> e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אָֽנֹכִי אָֽנֹכִי הוּא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=43|verse=25}} ''I, even I'', am ''he that blotteth out'', &c.; 51:12; {{GHGheb|text=אַתָּה הוּא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=7|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=44|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=9|verse=6}}, 7; in an interrogative sentence, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=14|verse=22}};<ref>This is of course to be distinguished from the use of {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}} (to be inferred from the context) as predicate in the sense of ὁ αὐτός; see above, {{GHGpar|135|a}}, note 1; or such cases as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=39}} ''see now'' {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אֲנִי הוּא|translate=that I, even I}}, am ''he''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=21|verse=17}}.</ref> in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}} in a {{GHGterm|verbal}}-clause strengthens {{GHGheb|text=אַתָּה}}.
<section end=par141 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

478.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par141 />{{GHGmargin-letter|141|i}}
Of (''b''): naturally this does not apply to the examples, in which {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}}, in the sense of ''to become, to fare, to exist'', still retains its full force as a verb, and where accordingly the sentence is verbal, and not a noun-clause; especially when the predicate precedes the subject. On the other hand, such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=2}} ''and the earth was'' ({{GHGheb|text=הָֽיְתָה}}) ''waste and emptiness'', can scarcely be regarded as properly verbal clauses; {{GHGheb|text=הָֽיְתָה}} is used here really only for the purpose of referring to past time a statement which, as the description of a state, might also appear in the form of a pure noun-clause; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=1}}. This is especially true of the somewhat numerous instances in which {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} occurs as a connecting word between the subject and the participial predicate; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=14}} (immediately afterwards a pure noun-clause). The imperfect of {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} announces what is future in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=33}}, &c.; cf. {{GHGpar|116|r}}. However, especially in the latter case, {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} is not wholly without verbal force, but comes very near to being a mere copula, and this use is more frequent in the later books<ref>According to Albrecht, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} viii. 252, especially in Deuteronomy and in the Priestly Code.</ref> than in the earlier.

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|k}}
Rem. On the employment of {{GHGheb|text=יֵשׁ|translate=existence}}, and {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִן|translate=non-existence}}, which were originally substantives (on their tendency to be used as verbs, equivalent to ''est'', and ''non est'', cf. {{GHGpar|100|o}}, and the ''Negative Sentences'', § 152) as a connecting link between a pronominal subject and a participial predicate (especially in conditional and interrogative sentences, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=42}}, 49, 43:4, &c.), see above, {{GHGpar|116|q}}, and the various kinds of subordinate clauses mentioned in §§ 150, 159.

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|l}}
'''4.''' The natural ''arrangement'' of words in the noun-clause, as describing a state, is ''subject—predicate''; the principal stress falls on the former since it is the object of the description. Very frequently, however (and not merely in poetry, where greater freedom is naturally allowed in the arrangement of words), the reverse order is found, i.e. ''predicate—subject''. The latter order ''must'' be used when special emphasis is laid on the predicate,<ref>For the same reason specifications of place (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=7}}) or other adverbial qualifications may stand at the beginning of the sentence.</ref> or when it consists of an interrogative word; thus with a substantival predicate, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=עָפָר אַתָּה|translate=dust thou art}}; 4:9, 12:13 (''my sister'', not my wife); 20:2, 12, 29:14, Is 6<sup>3 ''b''</sup>, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=12|hidebook=1}}; with an adjectival predicate, e.g. Is 6<sup>3 ''a''</sup>, 28:21, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=6}}; with a participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=12|hidebook=1}}; with an interrogative pronoun, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=65}};<ref>The only exceptions, according to Albrecht (see the Rem. above), are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=7}}, 8.</ref> with an adverbial interrogative, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=9}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|m}}
Rem. On the above cf. the exhaustive investigations of C. Albrecht, ‘''Die Wortstellung im hebr. Nominalsatze'',’ {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} vii. 218 ff. and viii. 249 ff.; with a complete list of the exceptions to the order ''subject—predicate'', p. 254 ff. The predicate ''must'' precede for the reasons stated (an ''adjectival predicate'' is particularly emphatic when it has the force of a comparative, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=13}}; the predicate expressed by means of a preposition precedes most frequently when it serves to convey the ideas of ''having, possessing'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, &c.; cf. also 26:20, 31:16, 43).

{{GHGmargin-letter|141|n}}
The predicate ''may'' precede: (''a'') when the subject is a pronoun, for ‘the person assumed to be generally known, does not excite the same interest as<section end=par141 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

479.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par141 />that which is stated about him;’ (''b'') ‘in order not to be a mere appendage to a subject which consists of several words,’ e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=20|verse=19}}; (''c'') in interrogative sentences (with a substantival or adjectival predicate or one compounded with a preposition), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=4}}; finally (''d'') in a relative clause, when the predicate is adverbial or compounded with a preposition, as a rule closely united (by Maqqeph) with {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר־שָׁם}}; 1:29 f. {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר־בּוֹ}}.<section end=par141 />

<section begin=par142 />{{GHGpar-heading|142|The Verbal-clause}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|142|a}}
'''1.''' By {{GHGpar|140|f}} there is an essential distinction between verbal-clauses, according as the subject stands before or after the verb. In the verbal-clause proper the principal emphasis rests upon the action which proceeds from (or is experienced by) the subject, and accordingly the verb naturally precedes (''necessarily'' so when it is in the perf. consec. or imperf. consec.). Nevertheless, the subject does sometimes precede even in the verbal-clause proper, in the continuation of the narrative, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=12}}; especially so if there is special emphasis upon it, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=13}} (it is not I who am to blame, but) ''the serpent beguiled me'', cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=5}}, &c.<ref>This of course applies also to the cases, in which the subject consists of a strongly emphasized personal pronoun, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=אַתָּה|translate=thou thyself}}; 33:3 {{GHGheb|text=הוּא|translate=he himself}}.</ref> In the great majority of instances, however, the position of the subject at the beginning of a verbal-clause is to be explained from the fact that the clause is not intended to introduce a new fact carrying on the narrative, but rather to describe a ''state''. Verbal-clauses of this kind approximate closely in character to noun-clauses, and not infrequently (viz. when the verbal form might just as well be read as a participle) it is doubtful whether the writer did not in fact intend a noun-clause.

{{GHGmargin-letter|142|b}}
The particular ''state'' represented in the verb may consist—

(''a'') Of an act completed long before, to which reference is made only because it is necessary for understanding the sequel of the principal action. If the predicate be a perfect (as it almost always is in these cases), it is generally to be rendered in English by a pluperfect; cf. the examples discussed above in {{GHGpar|106|f}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=3}}, &c.); also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=8}} (not ''Noah found grace''); 16:1, 18:17, 20:4, 24:1, 39:1 (''and Joseph'' in the meanwhile ''had been brought down to Egypt''); 41:10, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=27|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=1}}, &c.—In a wider sense this applies also to such verbal-clauses as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=6}} (see further, {{GHGpar|112|e}}), since when they serve to represent an action continuing for a long period in the past, and thus to some extent a state.

{{GHGmargin-letter|142|c}}
(''b'') Of a fact, contemporaneous with the principal events or continuing as the result of them. To the former class belong all those instances in which the predicate is combined with {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} (provided that {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}} has not, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, &c., been weakened to a mere copula, in which case the precedence of the subject is fully explained from the character of the clause as a noun-clause; cf. {{GHGpar|141|i}}, and the examples of {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}}, &c., with a participle, {{GHGpar|116|r}}); as an example of the second class, cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=אַבְרָם יָשַׁב בְּאֶֽרֶץ־כְּנָ֑עַן וגו׳|translate=Abraham}} accordingly ''continued to dwell in the land of Canaan'', but ''Lot dwelt'', &c.
<section end=par142 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

480.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par142 />{{GHGmargin-letter|142|d}}
Rem. 1. The close relation between verbal-clauses beginning with the subject and actual noun-clauses, is seen finally from the fact that the former also are somewhat frequently added with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} (or subordinated) to a preceding sentence in order to lay stress upon some accompanying circumstance; on such noun-clauses describing a ''state'' or ''circumstance'', cf. {{GHGpar|141|e}}. This is especially the case, again, when the circumstantial appendage involves an antithesis; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=18}} ''seeing that'' nevertheless ''Abraham shall surely become'', &c.; 24:56, 26:27, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=14|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=50|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=22}}, and such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=2.4}}, 29:17, where by means of {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} a new subject is introduced in express antithesis to one just mentioned. Moreover, in the examples treated above, under ''b'' and ''c'' ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=3}}, &c.), the subject is frequently introduced by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, which then corresponds to the Greek δέ, used to interpose an explanation, &c., see Winer, {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des neutest. Sprachidioms}}, § 53. 7<sup>b</sup>.

{{GHGmargin-letter|142|e}}
2. By a peculiar construction verbal-clauses may be joined by means of {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} and a following subject to participial clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=25}} {{GHGheb|text=הִיא מוּצֵאת וְהִיא שָֽׁלְחָה|translate=she was already brought forth, when she sent}}, &c.; 44:3, 4, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=18|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=8}}; for other examples, see {{GHGpar|116|u}} (where it is pointed out, note 1, that the apodosis also frequently appears in the form of a ''noun''-clause, a further proof of the close relation between verbal-clauses beginning with the subject and noun-clauses proper). Without doubt there is in all these cases a kind of inversion of the principal clause and the temporal subordinate clause; the latter for the sake of greater emphasis being raised to an independent noun-clause, while the real principal action is added as though it were an accompanying circumstance, and hence in the form of an ordinary circumstantial clause. [Cf. Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Tenses}}, § 166 ff.]

{{GHGmargin-letter|142|f}}
'''2.''' According to what has been remarked above, under ''a'', the natural ''order of words'' within the verbal sentence is: ''Verb—Subject'', or ''Verb—Subject—Object''. But as in the noun-clause ({{GHGpar|141|l}}) so also in the verbal-clause, a variation of the usual order of words frequently occurs when any member of the sentence is to be specially emphasized by priority of position.<ref>Not infrequently also the striving after ''chiasmus'' mentioned in {{GHGpar|114|r}}, note, occasions a departure from the usual arrangement of words.</ref> Thus the order may be:—

(''a'') ''Object—Verb—Subject'': {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=40}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=23|verse=19}} and frequently. Naturally the examples are far more numerous, in which the object precedes a verbal form which includes the subject in itself, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=10.14.18}}, 6:16, 8:17, 9:13, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=21|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=22|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=13|verse=5}}, &c.

(''b'') ''Verb—Object—Subject'': {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=5|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=16}} (but {{GHGheb|text=המלאך}} is probably only a subsequent addition); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=19|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=34|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=19}}, &c.

(''c'') ''Subject—Object—Verb'': {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=11|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=13|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=12|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=6|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=11|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=25}}.<ref>This sequence occurs even in prose ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, &c.); it is, however, more doubtful here than in the above prophetical and poetical passages, whether the preceding subject should not be regarded rather as the subject of a compound sentence (§ 143), the predicate of which is an independent verbal-clause; this would explain why the verbal-clause is usually separated from the subject by one of the greater disjunctives.—On the other hand, the sequence ''Subject''—''Object''—{{GHGterm|Verb}} is quite common in Aramaic (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=2|verse=7}}, 10); cf. Gesenius, ''Comm.'' on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=24}}, and Kautzsch’s {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Bibl. Aram.}}, § 84. 1 ''b''. The pure Aramaic usage of placing the ''object'' before the {{GHGterm|infinitive}} occurs in Hebrew in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=19|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=21|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=56}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=11|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=28|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=31|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=36|verse=19|hidebook=1}} (?).</ref><section end=par142 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

481.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par142 />(''d'') ''Object—Subject—Verb'' (very rarely): {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=51|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=13|verse=16}} (read {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל}}).<ref>This sequence occurs more frequently in noun-clauses with a participial predicate, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=4}}, &c., in interrogative sentences, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=7|verse=19}}; in all which cases the emphasized object is placed before the natural sequence of ''subject—predicate''. [Cf. Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Tenses}}, § 208.]</ref>

(''e'') A substantival complement of the verb {{GHGheb|text=היה}} is placed first in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=18|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=וּבֹסֵר גֹּמֵל יִֽהְיֶה נִצָּה|translate=and a ripening grape the flower becometh}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|142|g}}
Rem. Of specifications compounded with a preposition those of ''place'' stand regularly after the verb, unless they are specially emphatic as e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=5|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=9|verse=12}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=25}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּרָחֵל}} with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ|translate=pretii}} precedes for the sake of emphasis. Cf., however, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=13}} the order {{GHGterm|verb}}—specification of ''place—subject''.—The remoter object precedes for the sake of emphasis, e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=15}} (26:3), 15:3; even before the interrogative. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=37}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=15}} where the subject precedes an interrogative, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=31}} where a prepositional specification precedes). — Prepositional specifications of ''time'', such as {{GHGheb|text=בְּרֵאשִׁית}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=1}}), {{GHGheb|text=בְּיוֹם}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא}}, &c. (but not {{GHGheb|text=בָּרִֽאשֹׁנָה}}, nor the simple {{GHGheb|text=רִֽאשֹׁנָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=בַּתְּחִלָּה}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְעוֹלָם}}), stand, as a rule, before the verb, provided it be not in the perf. consec. or imperf. consec.; so also certain adverbs of time, such as {{GHGheb|text=אָז}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַתָּה}}, whilst others like {{GHGheb|text=עוֹד}}, {{GHGheb|text=תָּמִיד}} regularly follow the verb.<section end=par142 />

<section begin=par143 />{{GHGpar-heading|143|The Compound Sentence}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|143|a}}
A compound sentence ({{GHGpar|140|d}}) is formed by the juxtaposition of a subject<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=40}} a verbal-clause ({{GHGheb|text=הָיִ֫יתִי|translate=I was}}) occurs instead of the subject, and is then explained by another verbal-clause.</ref> (which always precedes, see c) and

(''a'') An independent noun-clause, which (''a'') refers to the principal subject by means of a pronoun, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=1|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=יְהֹוָה בְּסוּפָה דַרְכּוֹ}} ''the Lord—in the storm is his way''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=23|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=125|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=2|verse=14}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=23}}, where the predicate is an interrogative clause.—A personal pronoun is somewhat frequently used as the principal subject, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=59|verse=21}} {{GHGheb|text=וַֽאֲנִי זֹאת בְּרִיתִי אֹתָם|translate=and as for me, this is my covenant with them}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=28|verse=2}};<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Chr|chapter=28|verse=2}} (cf. also 22:7 {{GHGheb|text=אֲנִי הָיָה עִם־לְבָבִי}}) {{GHGheb|text=אֲנִי}} might also be taken as strengthening the pronominal suffix which follows (equivalent to ''I myself had it in my mind''), as e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=33|verse=17}} ''whereas their own way is not equal''; cf. {{GHGpar|135|f}}.</ref> with an interrogative noun-clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=19|hidebook=1}}:—or (β) is without a retrospective suffix (in which case naturally the connexion between the subject and predicate is much looser), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=23}} ''and'' as touching ''the matter which'', &c.... ''behold the Lord is between thee and me for ever''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=27|verse=2}}.
<section end=par143 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

482.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par143 />{{GHGmargin-letter|143|b}}
(''b'') An independent verbal-clause: (''a'') with a retrospective suffix,<ref>Cf. the Mêšaʿ inscription, l. 31, ''and Ḥoronain'', ''therein dwelt'', &c.</ref> e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=6}} (cf. {{GHGpar|116|w}}); 17:15 ''as for Sarai thy wife, thou shalt not call her name Sarai''; 26:15, 28:13, 34:8, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=30|verse=37}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=10|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=11|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=33|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=9|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=11|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=46|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=65|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=74|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=1|verse=17}}; with a pronoun as the principal subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=27}}; (β) without a retrospective suffix, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=19|verse=17}} ''every one'' that ''mentions it'' (Judah) ''to it'' (Egypt), ''it'' (Egypt) ''is afraid''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|143|c}}
Rem. 1. In all the above examples prominence is given to the principal subject (by its mere separation from the context by means of a greater disjunctive, as a ''casus pendens''<ref>But this term must not (any more than that formerly used ‘the subject preceding ''absolutely''’) be misunderstood to mean that the principal subject is, as it were, floating in the air, and that the whole sentence results in an anacoluthon. On the contrary, to the Semitic mind, such sentences appear quite as correctly formed as ordinary noun- and verbal-clauses.</ref>) in a manner which would be quite impossible in a simple noun or verbal-clause (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=1|verse=3}} if it were {{GHGheb|text=דֶּ֫רֶךְ יְהֹוָה בְּסוּפָה}}); cf. the French ''c’est moi qu’on a accusé''. But the statement or question contained in the clause which forms the predicate also receives greater weight. For the same purpose other members of the sentence also are sometimes placed at the beginning and resumed again by a following suffix; thus the object, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=21|hidebook=1}} (with the Samaritan and LXX read perhaps {{GHGheb|text=הֶֹֽעֱבִיד}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=29}}; a specification of place, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=22|verse=18}}, &c.; a substantive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=6|verse=23}}; cf. the examples in {{GHGpar|135|a}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=15|verse=29}} a dative is co-ordinated with the ''casus pendens'', i.e. there is a transition to a different construction.

{{GHGmargin-letter|143|d}}
2. To compound sentences belong also the numerous examples already treated in the account of the tenses, where the predicate of a ''casus pendens'' is introduced by the {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}. The isolation and prominence of the principal subject is in this case still more marked than in the instances treated above; on the ''casus pendens'' with a following imperfect consecutive (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=6|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=33|verse=24|hidebook=1}}), cf. {{GHGpar|111|h}}; with a following perfect consecutive (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=4|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=44|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=56|verse=6|hidebook=1}} f.), {{GHGpar|112|t}} and mm; on the participle as ''casus pendens'', {{GHGpar|112|oo}} and {{GHGpar|116|w}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=17}} {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}} follows with the cohortative; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=115|verse=7}}, the imperfect is separated by {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} from the {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=6}} as for ''thy hope'', it is ''the integrity of thy ways'', 36:26, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=5|verse=6}}, an incomplete noun-clause is appended by {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}. On {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}} after disconnected specifications of time, cf. {{GHGpar|112|oo}} at the end, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=34}} {{GHGheb|text=וְעַתָּה וַֽאֲנִי עַבְדֶּ֫ךָ|translate=and now}} (so far as the present is concerned) ''I will be thy servant'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=12|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=1}} (''me thou needest not fear'').

{{GHGmargin-letter|143|e}}
3. Sometimes a substantive introduced by {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} (''in respect to''; cf. {{GHGpar|119|u}}) serves the same purpose as the ''casus pendens'' beginning the sentence, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=18|verse=8}} (unless the {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} here serves to introduce the object, according to {{GHGpar|117|n}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=1}} (where, however, {{GHGheb|text=וְשָׂרִים}} should most probably be read); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=9|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=7|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=24|verse=20|hidebook=1}} ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=7|verse=21}}. On the other hand, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=16|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=17|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=89|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=91|hidebook=1}}, are very doubtful. The suggestion of P. Haupt ({{GHGcite|title=Johns Hopkins University Circulars}}, xiii. no. 114; Baltimore, 1894) also deserves attention, that in passages like {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=9|verse=4}}, and in {{GHGheb|text=לְכֹל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=27|verse=3}}, 19, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=44|verse=9}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} is not the preposition, but an emphasizing particle, answering to the Arab. ''lă, surely''; Assyrian ''lû''; with {{GHGheb|text=בֹּל}} it is equivalent to ''in short.'' Cf. also {{GHGheb|text=לְ־לְ|translate=sive—sive, et—et|en=either—or, both—and}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=17|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=1|verse=11}}, Assyrian ''lû''—''lû''.<section end=par143 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

483.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par144 />{{GHGpar-heading|144|Peculiarities in the Representation of the Subject (especially in the Verbal-clause)}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|a}}
'''1.''' According to § 40 ff. most forms of the finite verb include a specification of the subject in the form of ''personal afformatives'' (in the imperfect also in the form of preformatives). Not infrequently, however, masculine forms are used in referring to feminines, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וִֽידַעְתֶּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=49}}; {{GHGheb|text=עֲשִׂיתֶם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=8}}; in the imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=2|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=2|verse=7}}; in the imperative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=13|verse=7}} (for other examples, see {{GHGpar|110|k}}). On emphasizing the pronominal subject by the addition of the separate pronoun, see {{GHGpar|135|a}} and b.

On the masculine as ''prior gender'', cf. {{GHGpar|122|g}}; on similar anomalies in the use of the personal pronoun, {{GHGpar|135|o}}, in the connexion between substantive and adjective, {{GHGpar|132|d}}, between subject and predicate, {{GHGpar|145|p}}, t, u.

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|b}}
'''2.''' The third person singular is often used impersonally, especially in the masculine, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וַֽיְהִי|translate=and it came to pass}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה|translate=and it shall come to pass}}; {{GHGheb|text=חָרָה}} followed by {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ}}, &c., ''it became hot to him'', i.e. ''he became angry'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=6}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=וַיֵּ֫צֶר לוֹ}} lit. ''and it became strait to him, he was distressed'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=8}};<ref>In Arabic and Ethiopic the masculine is commonly used in this case, in Syriac the feminine.—The forms {{GHGheb|text=חַם|translate=hot}}, {{GHGheb|text=טוֹב|translate=good, well}}, {{GHGheb|text=מַר|translate=bitter}}, {{GHGheb|text=צַר|translate=narrow}}, {{GHGheb|text=רַע|translate=evil}} (frequently joined by {{GHGheb|text=לִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ}}, &c.), which many regard as impersonal, are no doubt to be regarded in most cases not as forms of the 3rd pers. sing. perf., but, with Hupfeld on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=7}}, as adjectives.</ref> also in the feminine, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=30|verse=6}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=10|verse=9}}) {{GHGheb|text=וַתֵּ֫צֶר לְדָוִד}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=39}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=7|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=12|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=32}} (unless {{GHGheb|text=תְּמֽוּרָתוֹ}} in verse 31 be the subject); cf. also the impersonal passives, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=6}} ({{GHGheb|text=רֻכְּכָה}}), 29:6 ({{GHGheb|text=תִּפָּקֵד}}). Somewhat different are the instances in which the 3rd singular feminine occurs as the predicate of a feminine subject which is not mentioned, but is before the mind of the speaker, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=18|verse=15|hidebook=1}} (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=24|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־אֲשֶׁר}} is used in this way with a feminine predicate, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=19|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} alone); different, too, are the instances in which the 3rd singular masculine refers to an act just mentioned, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה|translate=and this}} (the circumcision) ''shall be a token of a covenant'', &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|c}}
Rem. The expressions for natural phenomena may be either in the 3rd sing. masculine or feminine, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אוֹר|translate=it becomes light}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=29|verse=10}} (but with an explicit subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=3}}); {{GHGheb|text=וַיֵּאוֹר|translate=and it became light}}; so also {{GHGheb|text=יַחְשִׁךְ|translate=it grows dark}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=16}}; but {{GHGheb|text=וְחָֽשְׁכָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=3|verse=6}}; {{GHGheb|text=תָּעֻ֫פָה|translate=though there be darkness}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=17}}; {{GHGheb|text=תַּמְטִיר|translate=it rains}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=7}} (where, however, the context requires the reading {{GHGheb|text=אַמְטִיר}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=50|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=נִשְׂעֲרָה|translate=it is tempestuous}}.
<section end=par144 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

484.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par144 />{{GHGmargin-letter|144|d}}
'''3.''' The indefinite personal subject (our ''they, one'', the French ''on'', and the German ''man''<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=הָאִישׁ}} (prop. ''the man'') is used in exactly the same sense as our ''one''.</ref>) is expressed—

(''a'') By the 3rd person singular masculine, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קָרָא|translate=one ''(sc. any'' one who named ''it, see the Rem.)'' called ''(or'' calls)}} it, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=23}}; {{GHGheb|text=וַוִּקְרָא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=8}}, 10, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=וַיֹּא֫מֶר|translate=one said}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=48|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=4}};<ref>Elsewhere in such cases {{GHGheb|text=וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ}} usually occurs (but not in the perfect, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=22}}), so that it is doubtful whether the present reading of {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=48|verse=1}}, &c., would not be better explained according to {{GHGpar|7|d}}, note. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=48|verse=2}} for the extraordinary {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּגֵּד}} the common form {{GHGheb|text=וַיֻּגַּד}} is to be read; so in 50:26 for {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּישֶׂם}} (after a plural) either {{GHGheb|text=וַיּוּשַׂם}} or the 3rd plur.; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=21|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּקְבְּרוּ}}.</ref> other examples are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=28}} ''one put out a hand''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=38}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=וְרָפָא לוֹ|translate=and one heals them}}; 8:4 ({{GHGheb|text=יִשָּׂא}}); 46:7 ({{GHGheb|text=יִצְעַק}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=6|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=2|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=27|verse=23}}; by the 3rd singular feminine ({{GHGheb|text=יָֽלְדָה}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=26|verse=59}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|e}}
Rem. The Jewish commentators, following the Arab grammarians, usually explain these singulars by the addition of the participle (generally determinate) of the same stem, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=קָרָא הַקֹּרֵא}}. This view is supported by the fact that such a complement sometimes occurs, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=16|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=יִדְרֹךְ הַדֹּרֵךְ|translate=the treader treads out}}, for ''one treads out''; 28:4, 24 (''doth one plow continually?''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=17|verse=6}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=18|verse=32}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=22|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=17|verse=9}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=33|verse=4}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=9|verse=23}}; with an indeterminate participle (as in Arabic, e.g. ''qāla qāʾilun'', ''a sayer says'', i.e. ''some one says''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=6|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=1}}; cf. above, {{GHGpar|116|t}}, and, on the whole question, Driver on {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=4}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|f}}
(''b'') Very frequently by the 3rd plural masculine, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=2}} ''for out of that well'' {{GHGheb|text=יַשְׁקוּ|translate=they}} (i.e. people generally) ''watered the flocks''; 26:18, 35:5, 41:14, 49:31, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=38|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=12|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=18|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=2|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=2|verse=7}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|g}}
Rem. The 3rd plur. also is sometimes used to express an indefinite subject, where the context does not admit of a human agent or at least not of several, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=27}}. In such a case the 3rd plur. comes to be equivalent to a passive, as very commonly in Aramaic (see Kautzsch’s {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Bibl. Aram.}}, § 96. 1 c); e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=3}} ''wearisome nights'' {{GHGheb|text=מִנּוּ־לִי|translate=have they allotted to me}} (equivalent to ''were allotted to me''; to make ‘invisible powers’ the subject is a merely artificial device); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=18|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=26|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=32|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=63|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=22}} (in parallelism with a passive); 9:11.

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|h}}
(''c'') By the 2nd singular masculine, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=25}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹֽא־תָבוֹא שָׁ֫מָּה|translate=one will}} (or ''can'') ''not come thither'' (prop. ''thou wilt''...); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=23|verse=37}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=19|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=30|verse=28|hidebook=1}} (unless the reading should be {{GHGheb|text=תִּתָּפֵשׂ}}). Cf. also {{GHGheb|text=עַד־בֹּֽאֲךָ}} or simply {{GHGheb|text=בֹּֽאֲךָ}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=19}}, 30, 13:10 {{GHGheb|text=בֹּֽאֲבָה}}) prop. ''until thy coming'', i.e. ''until one comes''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|i}}
(''d'') By the plural of the participle, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=38|verse=23}} ''and all thy wives and thy children'' {{GHGheb|text=מֽוֹצִאִים}} (prop. ''are they bringing out''=) ''they will bring out'', &c.; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=6|verse=10}} (''for some are coming to slay thee'')<section end=par144 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

485.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par144 />and the passages discussed above, {{GHGpar|116|t}}.<ref>That this form of expression also (see g) comes to be equivalent to a passive is seen from the analogy of such Aramaic passages as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=4|verse=22}}, which exclude any idea of human agency. Cf. Kautzsch, {{GHGcite|title=Gramm. des Bibl. Aram.}}, § 76. 2 ''e'' at the end, and in post.-bibl. Hebrew, e.g. ''Pirqe Aboth'' [[:he:משנה אבות ב טז|2, 16]]; [[:he:משנה אבות ג ה|3, 5]], &c.</ref> In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=5|verse=1}} the text is corrupt.

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|k}}
(''e'') By the passive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=אָז הוּחַל לִקְרֹא|translate=then}} (''was it begun''=) ''began men to call upon'', &c. (but read {{GHGheb|text=זֶה הֵחֵל|translate=he began}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|l}}
'''4.''' A peculiar idiom, and one always confined to poetic language, is the not infrequent occurrence of two subjects in a verbal sentence,<ref>Two subjects occur in a noun-clause in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=83|verse=19}}.</ref> one of the person and the other of the thing. The latter then serves—whether it precedes or follows—to state the instrument, organ, or member by which the action in question is performed, and may be most often rendered in English by an adverb, as a nearer definition of the manner of the action. All the examples of this kind have this in common, that the subject denoting the thing takes a suffix in the same person as the personal subject.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=6|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=שְׁמִי}} is subordinated to the following passive {{GHGheb|text=נוֹדַ֫עְתִּי}} ({{GHGpar|121|b}}); in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=26}}, 33 {{GHGheb|text=יָדִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָֽדְךָ}} are subjects to the infinitive absolute {{GHGheb|text=הוֹשֵׁעַ}}, according to § 113 gg. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=69|verse=11}} read {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֲעַנֶּה}} for {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֶבְכֶּה}}.</ref> They are thus distinguished from the ''accusatives'' treated in {{GHGpar|117|s}}, with which they are often confused.

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|m}}
(''a'') Examples where the subject denoting the ''thing'' precedes, {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־יְהֹוָה אֶקְרָא קוֹלִי}} ''my voice—I cry unto the Lord'', i.e. ''I cry aloud unto the Lord'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=3|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=27|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=142|verse=2|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=פִּֽי־קָרָ֫אתִי|translate=my mouth}}—''I cried'', i.e. ''I cried aloud'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=66|verse=17}} (cf. 17:10); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=26|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=נַפְשִׁי|translate=with my soul}}, i.e. ''fervently'', and parallel with it {{GHGheb|text=אָף־רוּחִי}}; but {{GHGheb|text=נַפְשִׁי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=57|verse=5}} is rather a periphrasis for the 1st pers. ''I''.

(''b'') Where the subject denoting the ''thing'' follows, {{GHGheb|text=צַֽהֲלִי קוֹלֵךְ|translate=cry}}—''thy voice'' (i.e. aloud), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=10|verse=30}}; so also after an imperative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=17|verse=13}} ({{GHGheb|text=חַרְבֶּ֫ךָ}}) and verse 14 ({{GHGheb|text=יָֽדְךָ}}); 60:7, 108:7 ({{GHGheb|text=יְמִֽינְךָ}}); after a perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=3|verse=15}} ({{GHGheb|text=סוּסֶ֫יךָ}}); after a cohortative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=108|verse=2}} ({{GHGheb|text=אַף־כְּבוֹדִי}}). The subject denoting the ''thing'' stands between the personal subject and the predicate in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=44|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=אַתָּה יָֽדְךָ}}.<ref>In several of the above examples it might naturally be supposed that the subject denoting the thing (especially when it follows the verb) is to be explained rather as a ''casus instrumentalis'', i.e. as an accusative, analogous to the adverbial accusatives in {{GHGpar|118|q}}. But although it is true that the subject denoting the thing often defines more closely the manner in which the action is performed, and although in similar (but still different) examples, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=89|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=109|verse=30|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=16}}, {{GHGheb|text=פִּי}} occurs with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ|translate=instrumentale}}, the explanation given above must nevertheless be accepted.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|n}}
Rem. 1. Sometimes (as in other languages) an action is ascribed to a subject which can only have been performed at his direction by another<section end=par144 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

486.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par144 />person; cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=22}} (41:13), 41:14, 43:34 (''and he commanded to set before them'', &c.); 46:29, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=9}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|o}}
2. Supposed ellipses of a definite subject are due either to a misunderstanding of the passage, or to a corruption of the text. Thus in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=11}} after {{GHGheb|text=וַתָּ֫חָס}} either {{GHGheb|text=עֵינִי}} has dropped out (through confusion with {{GHGheb|text=עָלֶ֫יךָ}}) or we should read with the LXX {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאָחֻס}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=39}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַתְּכַל דָּוִד}}) the text is obviously corrupt.

{{GHGmargin-letter|144|p}}
3. In poetic (or prophetic) language<ref>In prose, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=2|verse=8}}; but {{GHGheb|text=וְהִקְרִיבָהּ}} here is hardly the original reading. Different from this is {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=7}}, where there is a transition to direct narration.</ref> there sometimes occurs (supposing the text to be correct) a more or less abrupt transition from one person to another. Thus from the 2nd to the 3rd (i.e. from an address to a statement), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=4}} (?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=31|verse=6}} (?), 42:20, 52:14, 61:7, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=2|verse=15}} (where, however, for {{GHGheb|text=יִבְגֹּד}} we should undoubtedly read {{GHGheb|text=תִּבְגּׄד}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=22|verse=9}} [and regularly after a vocative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=48|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=54|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, 11, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, 16, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=6}}f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mic|chapter=1|verse=2}} (={{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=28}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=3|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=31}}; and after {{GHGheb|text=הוֹי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=13}}]. From the 3rd to the 2nd pers., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=29}} (but read probably {{GHGheb|text=חֶמְדָּתָם}} for {{GHGheb|text=חֲמַדְתֶּם}}, which has caused the insertion of {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}), 5:8, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=29|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=7}}, cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=17}}. From the 1st to the 3rd pers., {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|verse=1}} (in a relative clause). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=28}} the 3rd pers. {{GHGheb|text=וְהוּא}} is probably employed δεικτικῶς for the 1st.<section end=par144 />

<section begin=par145 />{{GHGpar-heading|145|Agreement between the Members of a Sentence, especially between Subject and Predicate, in respect of Gender and Number}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|a}}
'''1.''' As in other languages, so also in Hebrew, the predicate in general conforms to the subject in gender and number (even when it is a pronoun, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=זֹאת בְּרִיתִי|translate=this is my covenant}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=10}}). There are, however, numerous exceptions to this fundamental rule. These are due partly to the ''constructio ad sensum'' (where attention is paid to the meaning rather than to the grammatical form; see b–l below), partly to the position of the predicate (regarded as being without gender) ''before'' the subject.

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|b}}
'''2.''' Singular nouns which include in themselves a collective idea ({{GHGpar|123|a}}), or which occasionally have a collective sense ({{GHGpar|123|b}}), may readily, in accordance with their meaning, be construed with the plural of the predicate, whether it precedes or follows. This is also the case, when the collective is itself feminine but represents, exclusively or at least generally, masculine persons.

Examples:—

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|c}}
(''a'') Of collectives proper (cf. {{GHGpar|132|g}}): (α) with the predicate preceding, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=38}} {{GHGheb|text=תָּבֹ֫אןָ הַצֹּאן}} (cf. 30:39, 31:8 and 33:13); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=22}} f. {{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫יִת}} representing persons belonging to the tribe; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=4|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=גּוֹי}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=25|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=חַ֫יִל|translate=army}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=11|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=לְאוֹם}}<section end=par145 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

487.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par145 />''the people''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=10|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־הָֽעֵדָה|translate=all the congregation}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=5}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=40}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=25|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=1|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=עַם}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=47}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=10|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=קָהָל|translate=assembly}}. Cf. also the construction of national names, as {{GHGheb|text=אֲרָם}} ({{GHGpar|122|i}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=20|verse=20}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּנֻ֫סוּ אֲרָם|translate=and the Syrians fled}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=5}}.—(β) with the predicate following, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=צֹאן וּבָקָר|translate=sheep and oxen}}, construed with the plural in the following relative clause; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=הַבָּקָר הָיוּ חֹֽרְשׁוֹת|translate=the cattle}} (cows) ''were ploughing''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=1}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=10|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫יִת}}=''family'' (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=בֵּית שֶׁ֫מֶשׁ}} on the analogy of names of countries, is used for ''the inhabitants of Bethshemesh''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=11|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=4|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=עַם}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=68|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=חַיָּה|translate=herd}} [if correct, figuratively for ''people'']; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=26|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=נְבֵלָה|translate=dead bodies}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=27|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=קָצִיר|translate=boughs}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=יִשְׂרָאֵל}}, preceded by a predicate in the singular.

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|d}}
(''b'') Of substantives occasionally used as collectives: (α) with the predicate preceding, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=24}} {{GHGheb|text=זָכָר}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=55}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=15|verse=10|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=16|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=רֹמֵס|translate=the treader down}}.—(β) with the predicate following, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=8|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=אַחֵר}}=''others''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=28|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=סָתוּם|translate=a secret}}; [{{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=9|verse=7}}, and even after {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=19}}.]

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|e}}
(''c'') Of feminines as collective terms denoting masculine persons: (α) with the predicate preceding, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=46}} {{GHGheb|text=וְיֵדְעוּ כָּל־הָאָרֶץ|translate=that all the earth may know}}, the i.e. all the inhabitants of the earth; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=9|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=66|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=96|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, 9, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=1|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=שְׁאֵרִית|translate=remnant}}; ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=33|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־הָאָ֫רֶץ}}).—(β) with the predicate following, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=57}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=10|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=48|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=מוֹלֶ֫דֶת|translate=issue}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=33}} {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־מַרְבִּית|translate=all the increase}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=30|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=פִּרְחָח|translate=rabble}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hag|chapter=2|verse=7}} read {{GHGheb|text=חֲמֻדֹת}} with the LXX.

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|f}}
Examples of predicates in the singular, notwithstanding the collective meaning of the subject, occur in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=14|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=39}}, &c.—For examples of bold enallage of the number in noun-clauses with a substantival predicate, see above, {{GHGpar|141|c}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|g}}
Rem. Not infrequently the construction begins in the singular (especially when the predicate precedes; see o below), but is carried on, after the collective subject has been mentioned, in the plural; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=1|verse=20}} {{GHGheb|text=מְאֹד וַיִּ֫רֶב הָעָם וַיַּֽעַצְמוּ|translate=and the people multiplied, and waxed very mighty}}; 33:4.

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|h}}
'''3.''' On the other hand, plurals which have a singular meaning ({{GHGpar|124|a}}) are frequently construed with the singular, especially the ''pluralis excellentiae'' or ''maiestatis'' (§ g–i; on the union of these plurals with attributes, cf. {{GHGpar|132|h}}), as {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=1}}, 3, &c. (but see the Rem.), {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנִים|translate=master}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּעָלִים|translate=master, owner}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=29}}; cf., moreover, {{GHGheb|text=פָּנִים}} with the singular, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=16}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}, {{GHGheb|text=רַֽחֲמִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=12|verse=10}}.—So feminine forms with a masculine meaning are construed with a masculine predicate, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=12|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה קֹהֶ֫לֶת חָכָם|translate=the preacher was wise}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|i}}
Rem. The construction of {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהִים|translate=God}} with the plural of the predicate may be explained (apart of course from such passages as {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=19|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=20|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, where the speakers are heathen, and {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהִים}} may, therefore, be a numerical plural) partly as an acquiescence in a polytheistic form of expression, partly from the peculiar usage of one of the early documents of the Hexateuch, called ''E'' by Wellhausen, &c., ''B'' by Dillmann; cf. his commentary on Numbers—Joshua, p. 618, and above, {{GHGpar|124|g}}, note 2. So {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=13}} (but in conversation with a heathen); 31:53, 35:7, cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=24|verse=19}}. That this construction was afterwards studiously avoided from fear of misconception, is shown by such passages as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=9|verse=18}} compared with {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=4}}, 8, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=17|verse=21}} compared with {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=7|verse=23}}. Cf. Strack’s excursus on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gen|chapter=20|verse=13}} in {{GHGcite|title=Die Genesis}}, Munich, 1905, p. 77.
<section end=par145 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

488.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par145 />{{GHGmargin-letter|145|k}}
'''4.''' Plurals of names of animals or things, and of abstracts, whether they be masculine or feminine, are frequently construed with the feminine singular of the verbal predicate<ref>Cf. in Greek the construction of the neuter plural with the singular of the predicate τὰ πρόβατα βαίνει; in Attic Greek the plural of the predicate is allowed only when the neuter denotes actual persons, as τὰ ἀνδράποδα ἔλαβον. In Arabic also the ''pluralis inhumanus'' (i.e. not denoting persons) is regularly construed with the feminine singular of the attribute or predicate, as are all the ''plurales fracti'' (properly collective forms).</ref> (on the collective sense of the feminine form, cf. {{GHGpar|122|s}}); thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=20}} {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽהֲמוֹת שָׂדֶה תַּֽעֲרֹג|translate=the beasts of the field long}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=12|verse=4}} (where the predicate precedes), cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=7}}; names of things with the predicate preceding occur in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=34|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=29|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=35}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=37|verse=31|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=2|hidebook=1}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}, 103:5 (unless {{GHGheb|text=הַֽמְחַדֵּשׁ}} is to be read for {{GHGheb|text=תִּתְחַדֵּשׁ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=14|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=27|verse=20|hidebook=1}}; with the predicate following, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=22}} ({{GHGheb|text=בָּנוֹת}}=''branches''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=21|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=15}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְעֵינָיו קָ֫מָה}}),<ref>On the possibility of explaining forms like {{GHGheb|text=קָ֫מָה}} as 3rd plural feminine, cf. above, {{GHGpar|44|m}}; but this explanation would not apply to all the cases under this head, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=37|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=103|verse=5|hidebook=1}}.</ref> {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=10|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=59|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=15}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}, 48:41, 49:24, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=15|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=20|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=10}}.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=14|verse=1}} an abstract plural {{GHGheb|text=חָכְמוֹת}} (to be read thus with 9:1, &c., instead of {{GHGheb|text=חַכְמוֹת}}) is construed with the singular; but cf. {{GHGpar|86|l}}, {{GHGpar|124|e}}, end.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|l}}
'''5.''' Moreover, the plural of persons (especially in the participle) is sometimes construed with the singular of the predicate, when instead of the whole class of individuals, each severally is to be represented as affected by the statement.
