Undoubted examples of this ''distributive'' singular are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=29}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=24|verse=9}}) {{GHGheb|text=אֹֽרֲרֶ֫יךָ אָרוּר וּמְבָֽרֲכֶ֫יךָ בָּרוּךְ|translate=those that curse thee, cursed be}} every one of them, ''and those that bless thee, blessed be'' every one of them; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=31|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=17|verse=14}} and 19:8 (in both places the Samaritan has {{GHGheb|text=אֹֽכְלוֹ}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=12}} unless {{GHGheb|text=נֽׄגְשָׂיו}} is to be regarded as a ''pluralis maiestatis'' according to {{GHGpar|124|k}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=3|verse=18.35}} (?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=18|verse=21|hidebook=1}} (?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=21|verse=27b|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=27|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=28|verse=1b|hidebook=1}}, 28:16 {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|m}}
Rem. Analogous to the examples above mentioned is the somewhat frequent<ref>In several of the above examples the text is doubtful, and hence Mayer Lambert ({{GHGcite|title={{abbr|REJ.|Revue des Études Juives. Paris, 1880 ff.}}}} xxiv. 110) rejects the theory of distributive singulars generally. [Cf. Driver, ''Jeremiah'', p. 362, on 16:7.]</ref> use of suffixes in the singular (distributively) referring to plurals; cf. the {{GHGterm|verbal}}-suffixes in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=21|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=48|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=6|verse=10}}; and the ''noun''-suffixes in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=31|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=4|verse=8}} (but since {{GHGheb|text=ו}} follows, {{GHGheb|text=נַפְשׁוֹ}} is undoubtedly a dittography for {{GHGheb|text=נָֽפֶשׁ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=14|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=5|verse=10}} (where, however, {{GHGheb|text=פִּימוֹ}} is clearly to be read with all the early versions); 62:5, 141:10 (?), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=10|verse=15}} [but LXX {{GHGheb|text=הַכְּסִיל}}]; finally, the suffixes with prepositions in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=20}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר עָֽשׂוּ־לוֹ|translate=which they made}} each one ''for himself'' (according to others, ''which they'' (''the makers'') ''made for him''); 5:26, 8:20, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=24|verse=5}}, in each case {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ}} refers to the collectives {{GHGheb|text=חַיָּה}} and {{GHGheb|text=עוֹף}}; cf. further, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=24|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=מִמֶּ֫נּוּ}} after {{GHGheb|text=צַדִּיקִים}} (but read probably {{GHGheb|text=צַדִּיק}} with the LXX, &c.). Conversely in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=1|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=עִבְרִי לָכֶם}} [cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=20}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}], but the text is undoubtedly corrupt.
<section end=par145 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

489.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par145" />{{GHGmargin-letter|145|n}}
'''6'''. Subjects in the dual are construed with the plural of the predicate, since verbs, adjectives, and pronouns, according to {{GHGpar|88|a}}, have no dual forms; thus {{GHGheb|text=עֵינַ֫יִם}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=וְעֵינֵי לֵאָה רַכּוֹת}} ''and Leah’s eyes were dull''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=14|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=7|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=38|verse=11|hidebook=1}} (on the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=15}} the predicate is in the feminine singular ''after'' the subject, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=4|verse=11}} ''before'' it; on both constructions cf. k above); so also {{GHGheb|text=אָזְנַ֫יִם|translate=ears}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=6|verse=40}}; {{GHGheb|text=יָדַ֫יִם|translate=hands}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=10|hidebook=1}} (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=17|verse=12}} even with the plural masculine {{GHGheb|text=כְּבֵדִים}}; cf. ''p''); {{GHGheb|text=שְׂפָתַ֫יִם|translate=lips}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=27|verse=4}}; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁדַ֫יִם|translate=breasts}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=9|verse=14}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|o}}
'''7.''' Variations from the fundamental rule (see above, a) very frequently occur ''when the predicate precedes the subject'' (denoting animals or things<ref>Only rarely does an uninflected predicate precede a personal subject, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=27}} (but {{GHGheb|text=הֵבִ֫יאָה}} should probably be read, as in verse 35); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=9|verse=23}} (before a plur. mass.). Such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=42|verse=15}} are to be explained according to {{GHGpar|121|a}}.</ref>). The speaker or writer begins with the most simple form of the predicate, the uninflected 3rd singular masculine, and leaves us without indication as to which of the following subjects (and so which gender or number) is to define the predicate thus left temporarily indefinite.<ref>In a certain sense this is analogous to the German ''es kommt ein Mann, eine Frau'', &c.</ref> Thus inflexions are omitted in—

(''a'') The verb, with a following singular feminine, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=וְשַׁח גַּבְהוּת הָֽאָדָם|translate=and bowed down shall be the loftiness of man}}; 9:18, 14:11, 28:18, 47:11; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=27}} (see note 1 below); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=31}}b, 22:36, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=46}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=7|verse=7}}; with a following plural masc., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=13|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=וְעָנָה אִיִּים|translate=and there shall cry wolves}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=17}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}, 20:46, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=48}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=124|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=9|verse=23}} (see note 1 below); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=יְהִי מְאֹרֹת|translate=let there be lights}}; with a following plural feminine, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=35}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=11|verse=3}}a, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=2|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=57|verse=2}}; before collectives and mixed subjects, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=43|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, &c.; before a following dual, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=44|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=7}} (where, however, with the LXX {{GHGheb|text=עֲוֹנָ֫מוֹ}} should be read).

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|p}}
Rem. 1. The instances in which a preceding predicate appears in the plural masculine before a plural (or collective singular) feminine of persons ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=21|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=11|verse=3}}b), of animals ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=39}} where however {{GHGheb|text=צאֹן}} may refer specially to male animals) or of things ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=14|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=16|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=6|verse=9}}), or before a dual ({{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=4|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=3|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=15|verse=7}}) are to be explained not on the analogy of the examples under ''o'', but from a dislike of using the 3rd plur. fem. imperf., for this is the only form concerned in the above examples (cf., however, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=3|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=תְּהִי}} instead of {{GHGheb|text=תִּֽהְיִי}}); cf. the examples of a following predicate in the 3rd plur. masc., instead of the fem., under ''t'' and ''u'', and on an analogous phenomenon in the imperative, see {{GHGpar|110|k}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|q}}
2. As in the case of verbs proper so also the verb {{GHGheb|text=הָיָה}}, when used as a copula, frequently remains uninflected before the subject; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=5|verse=23 ff.}}, 39:5,<section end="par145" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

490.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par145 />{{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=21|verse=3}} (according to the accents); 22:23, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=18|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=וּבֹסֶר גֹּמֵל יִֽהְיֶה נִצָּה|translate=and a ripening grape the flower becometh}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|r}}
(''b'') The adjective in a noun-clause, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=137}} {{GHGheb|text=יָשָׁר מִשְׁפָּטֶ֫יךָ|translate=upright are thy judgements}}; cf. verse 155.<ref>This does not include such cases as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=24|verse=7}}, 10, where {{GHGheb|text=עָרוֹם}} is rather to be explained as an accusative denoting a state, {{GHGpar|118|n}}.</ref>—On the other hand, {{GHGheb|text=רֹעֵה}} in {{GHGheb|text=רֹעֵה צֹאן עֲבָדֶ֫יךָ|translate=thy servants are shepherds}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=3}}, is either an unusual orthography or simply a misspelling for {{GHGheb|text=רֹעֵי}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|s}}
Rem. 1. As soon as a sentence which begins with an uninflected predicate is carried on after the mention of the subject, the gender and number of the subsequent (co-ordinate) predicates must coincide with those of the subject, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=1|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=יְהִי מְאֹרֹת... וְהָיוּ}} (see o above); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=9|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=14|verse=1}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=39}} (see p above).

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|t}}
2. The dislike mentioned in ''p'' above, of using the feminine form (cf., further, {{GHGpar|144|a}}, with the sections of the Grammar referred to there, and below, under ''u''), is exemplified sometimes by the fact that of several predicates only that which stands next to the feminine substantive is inflected as feminine (cf. the treatment of several attributes following a feminine substantive, {{GHGpar|132|d}}); thus in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=רָֽגְזָה}}, and afterwards {{GHGheb|text=עוֹרֵר}} (but {{GHGheb|text=עוֹרֵר}} is better taken as an infin. abs.=''excitando'', reading {{GHGheb|text=הָקֵם}} for {{GHGheb|text=הֵקִים}}); 33:9 {{GHGheb|text=אָבַל אֻמְלְלָה אֶ֫רֶץ|translate=mourneth, languisheth the land}}. Cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=19}}, and the examples ({{GHGpar|47|k}}) where only the first of several consecutive forms of the 2nd sing. fem. imperf. has the afformative ''î'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=57|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=22|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=32|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=תִּֽהְיֶה}} after {{GHGheb|text=תִּשְׁתִּי}}); on the converse sequence of genders in imperatives, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=3|verse=15}}, cf. {{GHGpar|110|k}}.—Of a different kind are instances like {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=2|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=5|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=20|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, where {{GHGheb|text=נֶ֫פֶשׁ|translate=person}} (fem.) as the narrative continues, assumes (in agreement with the context) the sense of a masculine person.

{{GHGmargin-letter|145|u}}
3. The instances in which the gender or number of the ''following'' predicate appears to differ from that of the subject are due partly to manifest errors in the text, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=9}} read with the Samaritan {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאֶחָד}} instead of {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאַחַת}}; {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה}} then follows correctly; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=20}} read with Wellhausen {{GHGheb|text=שָׁאֻל}}, according to 1:28, instead of {{GHGheb|text=שָׁאַל}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=4}} read {{GHGheb|text=וַיּֽאֹמְרוּ}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=18|verse=29}} instead of {{GHGheb|text=יִתָּכֵן}} read the plural as in verse 25; so also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=20|verse=38}} for {{GHGheb|text=יָבוֹא}},
<ref>{{GHGheb|text=יבוא}} probably an error for {{GHGheb|text=יבאו}}. The Masora on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=11|verse=34}} reckons fourteen instances of {{GHGheb|text=יָבֹא}}, where we should expect the plural.</ref> and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=20}} for {{GHGheb|text=נָּטָ֑ח}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=5|verse=10}} read {{GHGheb|text=נִכְמָר}}, and cf. in general, {{GHGpar|7|d}}, note; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=2|verse=48}} read {{GHGheb|text=יָלְֽדָה}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=48|verse=15}} also the text is certainly corrupt. Other instances are due to special reasons. The anomalies in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=14|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=1|verse=16}} (after {{GHGheb|text=רַגְלָיו}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=11|verse=4}} (after {{GHGheb|text=עֵינָיו}}), 63:4, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=5|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=10|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, 32 18:6, 26:23, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=6}} (all after {{GHGheb|text=שְׂפָתַ֫יִם}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=3|verse=2}} (after {{GHGheb|text=מִצְוֹתַי}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=102|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=22}} (after {{GHGheb|text=שָׁנוֹת}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=11|verse=41}} (read {{GHGheb|text=וְרִבּוּת}}), and perhaps {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=17}} are also to be explained (see p) from the dislike of the 3rd plur. fem. imperf.; moreover, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=44|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=26|verse=23}} the plur. masc. even of a participle occurs instead of the plur. fem.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=8}} f. {{GHGheb|text=יִהְֽיֶה}}, after a plural subject, is explained as a case of attraction to the following singular predicate.<ref>So also the pronoun {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}} emphatically resuming the subject (see {{GHGpar|141|h}}) is attracted to the predicate in number in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=13|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=אִשֵּׁי יְהֹוָה... הוּא נַֽחֲלָתוֹ|translate=the offerings of the Lord... that is his inheritance}}; in number and gender, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=25|verse=33}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=3}}.</ref>—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=רֹבֵץ}}<section end=par145 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

491.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par145 />is a substantival participle (''a lurker, a coucher''). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=24}} {{GHGheb|text=יִֽהְיֶה}} remains undefined in gender (masc.), although the noun precedes for the sake of emphasis; so also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=49}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, 32, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=9|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=15|verse=29|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=50|verse=46}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=2|verse=7}} ({{GHGheb|text=הָיָה לִי}} as if the sentence began afresh, ''and servants born in my house... there fell to my lot'' this possession also). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹֽא־נֻפַּח}} may (unless {{GHGheb|text=אֵשׁ}} is regarded as masculine, {{GHGpar|122|o}}) be taken impersonally, ''fire, without its being blown upon''.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=16|verse=8}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=3|verse=17}} the predicate in the singular is explained from the collective character of {{GHGheb|text=שְׁדֵמוֹת}} (see h above); on the other hand, the masculine form of the predicate is abnormal in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=87|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=12|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=29|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=8|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=36|verse=18|hidebook=1}}.<section end=par145 />

<section begin=par146 />{{GHGpar-heading|146|Construction of Compound Subjects}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|146|a}}
'''1.''' When the subject is composed of a nomen regens (in the construct state) with a following genitive, the predicate sometimes agrees in gender and number not with the nomen regens, but with the genitive, when this represents the principal idea of the compound subject.<ref>Sometimes, however, the attraction of the predicate to the genitive may be merely due to juxtaposition.</ref> Thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=קֶ֫שֶׁת גִּבֹּרִים הַתִּים|translate=the bow of the mighty men is broken}}, as if it were ''the mighty men with their bow are broken''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=26|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=13|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=41}} (but the text is clearly very corrupt), 17:16, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=21|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=8|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=32|verse=7|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=רֹב שָׁנִים}} equivalent to ''many years''); 38:21; with the predicate preceding, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=10|verse=9}}, unless it is to be explained according to {{GHGpar|145|k}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|146|b}}
Rem. 1. The cases in which {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל}} (''voice, sound'') with a following genitive stands at the beginning of a sentence, apparently in this construction, are really of a different kind. The {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל}} is there to be taken as an exclamation, and the supposed predicate as in apposition to the genitive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=10}} ''the voice of thy brother’s blood, which crieth'' (prop. ''as one crying'')...!=''hark! thy brother’s blood is crying'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=13|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=66|verse=6|hidebook=1}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=52|verse=8}} an independent verbal-clause follows the exclamation ''the voice of thy watchmen!''; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=22}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=2|verse=8}} an independent noun-clause; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל קֹרֵא|translate=the voice of one that crieth!}} i.e. ''hark! there is one crying'' is followed immediately by direct speech; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=6|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל|translate=hark!}} may be used disconnectedly (cf. the almost adverbial use of {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל}} in {{GHGpar|144|m}}) and {{GHGheb|text=יְהֹוָה}} be taken as the subject to {{GHGheb|text=יִקְרָא}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|146|c}}
2. When the substantive {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל}} ({{GHGheb|text=כָּל־}}) ''entirety'' is used in connexion with a genitive as subject of the sentence, the predicate usually agrees in gender and number with the genitive, since {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל}} is equivalent in sense to an attribute (''whole, all'') of the genitive; hence, e.g. with the predicate preceding, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=5|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיִּֽהְיוּ כָּל־יְמֵי אָדָם|translate=and all the days of Adam were}}, &c. (in 5:23, 9:29, {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}}; but the Samaritan reads {{GHGheb|text=ויהיו}} here also); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=20}}; with the predicate following, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=150|verse=6}}, &c. Exceptions are, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=17|verse=14}} (but cf. {{GHGpar|145|l}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=8|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=64|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=16|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=3|verse=7}}. On the other hand, in such cases as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=16}} the agreement of the<section end=par146 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

492.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par146 />predicate with {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־}} is explained from the stress laid upon the latter, {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־מְלָאכָה לֹא}} being equivalent to ''the whole of work'' (is forbidden).

{{GHGmargin-letter|146|d}}
'''2.''' When the subject of the sentence consists of several nouns connected by {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}}, usually

(''a'') The predicate ''following'' is put in the plural, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=22}} ''seed time and harvest, and cold and heat... shall not cease'' ({{GHGheb|text=לֹא יִשְׁבֹּ֫תוּ}}); after subjects of different genders it is in the masculine (as the ''prior gender'', cf. {{GHGpar|132|d}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=אַבְרָהָם וְשָׂרָה זְקֵנִים|translate=Abraham and Sarah}} were ''old''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=21}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|146|e}}
Rem. Rare exceptions are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=27|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫מֶן וּקְטֹ֫רֶת יְשַׂמַּח־לֵב|translate=ointment and perfume rejoice the heart}}, where the predicate agrees in gender with the masculine {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫מֶן}} (as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=51|verse=3}} with {{GHGheb|text=שָׂשׂוֹן}}); on the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=4}} (where {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאִשָּׁה וִֽילָדֶ֫יהָ}} are the subjects) it agrees with {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאִשָּׁה}} as being the principal person; in the compound sentence, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=4}}, it agrees with the feminine subject immediately preceding.<ref>Similarly with a mixed object, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=2}} ''he put... Leah and her children'' {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲרֹנִים|translate=after}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲרֹנִים}} agrees with the masculine immediately preceding.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|146|f}}
(''b'') The predicate ''preceding'' two or more subjects may likewise be used in the plural ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=5}}, &c.); not infrequently, however, it agrees in gender and number with the first, as being the subject nearest to it. Thus the predicate is put in the singular masculine before several masculines singular in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=9|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=29|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=32|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=50|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=5}}; before a masculine and a feminine singular, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=55|hidebook=1}} ''then said'' ({{GHGheb|text=וַיּאֹ֫מֶר}}) ''her brother and her mother''; 33:7; before a masculine singular and a plural, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּבֹא נֹחַ וּבָנָיו|translate=and Noah went in, and his sons}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=18}} (where feminines plural also follow); 44:14, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=5|verse=21}}; before collectives feminine and masculine, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=2}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|146|g}}
Similarly, the feminine singular occurs before several feminines singular, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=וַתַּ֫עַן רָחֵל וְלֵאָה|translate=then answered Rachel and Leah}}; before a feminine singular and a feminine plural, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=61}}; before a feminine singular and a masculine singular, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=12|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=וַתְּדַבֵּר מִרְיָם וְאַֽהֲרוֹן|translate=then spake Miriam and Aaron}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5|verse=1}}; before a feminine singular and a masculine plural, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=7}} (cf., on the other hand, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=75|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=נְמֹגִים אֶ֫רֶץ וְכָל־יֽשְׁבֶ֫יהָ|translate=dissolved are the earth and all the inhabitants thereof}}). The plural feminine occurs before a plural feminine and a plural masculine in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=8|verse=13}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=44|verse=25}} for {{GHGheb|text=אַתֶּם וּנְשֵׁיכֶם}} read {{GHGheb|text=אַתֶּם הַנָּשִׁים}} with the LXX, and cf. verse 19.

{{GHGmargin-letter|146|h}}
(''c'') When other predicates follow after the subjects have been mentioned, they are necessarily put in the plural; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=61|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, &c., and {{GHGpar|145|s}}.<section end=par146 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

493.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par147 />{{GHGpar-heading|147|Incomplete Sentences}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|147|a}}
'''1.''' Sentences are called ''incomplete'', in which either the subject or the predicate or beth must in some way be supplied from the context.<ref>This does not apply to such cases as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=8}}, where an infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} appears alone in answer to a question, the substance of the question being presupposed as a main clause; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=7}}, where {{GHGheb|text=הִיא}} must again be supplied after {{GHGheb|text=אִשְׁתִּי}}.</ref> Besides the instances enumerated in {{GHGpar|116|s}} (omission of the personal pronoun when subject of a participial clause) and the periphrases for negative attributes {{GHGpar|152|u}}, this description includes certain (noun-) clauses introduced by {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} (see b below), and also a number of exclamations of the most varied kinds (see c below).

Rem. Incomplete sentences are very common in Chronicles, but are mostly due to the bad condition of the text; cf. Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}<sup>6</sup>, p. 537, no. 27. Thus in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=11|verse=22}}b restore {{GHGheb|text=חָשַׁב}}, with the LXX, before {{GHGheb|text=לְהַמְלִיכוֹ}}; in 35:21 add {{GHGheb|text=בָּ֫אתִי}}, with the LXX, after {{GHGheb|text=הַיּוֹם}} and read {{GHGheb|text=פְּרָת}} for {{GHGheb|text=בֵּית}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=19|verse=6}} and 28:21 the pronoun {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}} is wanted as subject, and in 30:9 the predicate {{GHGheb|text=יִֽהְיוּ}}; cf. also the unusual expressions in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=9|verse=33}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=3|verse=3}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=15|verse=13}} (''ye were not present?''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=15|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=16|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, 12 (bis), 18:3.

{{GHGmargin-letter|147|b}}
'''2.''' The demonstrative particle {{GHGheb|text=הֵן}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה|translate=en, ecce}} may be used either absolutely (as a kind of interjection, cf. {{GHGpar|105|b}}) before complete noun-or verbal-clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהִנֵּה אָֽנֹכִי עִמָּךְ|translate=and, behold! I am with thee}}; 37:7, 48:21, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=34|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, or may take the pronoun, which would be the natural subject of a noun-clause, in the form of a suffix, see {{GHGpar|100|o}}. Whether these suffixes are to be regarded as in the accusative has been shown to be doubtful in {{GHGpar|100|p}}. However, in the case of {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} the analogy of the corresponding Arabic demonstrative particle ’''inna'' (followed by an accusative of the noun) is significant.<ref>On the same analogy any substantive following {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} would have to be regarded as originally a virtual accusative. Since, however, Hebrew does not possess case-terminations (as the Arabic does, and uses the accusative necessarily after ’''inna''), it is very doubtful whether, and how far, substantives following {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} were felt to be accusatives.</ref> If {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} with a suffix and a following adjective or participle (see the examples in {{GHGpar|116|p}} and q) forms a noun-clause, the subject proper, to which {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} with the suffix refers, must, strictly speaking, be supplied again before the predicate.<ref>That these are real noun-clauses and that the participle (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מֵת}} in {{GHGheb|text=הִנְּךָ מֵת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=8}}) cannot be taken as a second accusative (as it were ''ecce te moriturum''), is also shown by the analogy of Arabic, where after ’''inna'' with an accusative the predicate is expressly in the ''nominative''.</ref> Sometimes, however, the pronoun referring to the subject is wanting, and the simple {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} takes the place of the<section end=par147 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

494.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par147" />subject and copula (as Gn 18<sub>9</sub> {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה בָאֹ֫הֶל|translate=behold}} she is ''in the tent''; 42:28), or there is no indication whatever of the predicate, so that the sentence is limited to {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} with the suffix, as in the frequent use of {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּ֫נִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִנֶּ֫נִּי|translate=here am I}}, in answer to an address. Elsewhere a substantive follows {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} (or {{GHGheb|text=הֵן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=35}}), and {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} then includes the meaning of a demonstrative pronoun and the copula, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה הָאֵשׁ וְהָֽעֵצִים|translate=here is the fire and the wood}}, &c.; 12:19 ''behold'' thou hast ''thy wife!'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=24|verse=8}}; with reference to the past, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=7|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהִנֵּה לֶ֫קֶשׁ וג׳|translate=and lo}}, it was ''the latter growth'', &c. By a very pregnant construction the simple {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} is used as the equivalent of a sentence in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=19}}, ''lo, here am I!''

{{GHGmargin-letter|147|c}}
'''3.''' Examples of exclamations (threatening, complaining, triumphing, especially warlike or seditious) in which, owing to the excitement of the speaker, some indispensable member of the sentence is suppressed, are—(''a'') with suppression of the predicate (which has frequently to be supplied in the form of a jussive), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=7|verse=20}} ''a sword for the Lord and for Gideon!'' (verse 18 without {{GHGheb|text=חֶ֫רֶב}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=1}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=10|verse=16}} (cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=36}}) ''every man to his tents, O Israel!'' (i.e. ''let every man go to'' or ''remain in his tent''); without {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=12|verse=16}}; moreover, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=13|verse=4|hidebook=1}} (on the exclamatory {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל}} equivalent to ''hark!'' cf. {{GHGpar|146|b}}); 28:10, 29:16 ({{GHGheb|text=הַפְכְּכֶם|translate=O your perversity!}} i.e. how great it is!); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=16}} (if {{GHGheb|text=תִּפְלַצְתְּךָ}} be equivalent to ''terror be upon thee!''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=4|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=1|verse=13}} ({{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה מַתְּלָאָה|translate=behold what a weariness!}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=29}}; perhaps also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=פַּ֫חַז כַּמַּ֫יִם|translate=a bubbling over as water}} (sc. happened), unless it is better to supply a subject {{GHGheb|text=אַתָּה}} (''thou wast'').—(''b'') With suppression of the subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=20}}, cf. {{GHGpar|152|k}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=אַיֵּה|translate=where}} sc. is bread?—(''c'') With suppression of both subject and predicate, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=7|verse=18}} (see above); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=12|verse=16}} (see above); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=גַּם אֹתוֹ|translate=him also!}} explained immediately afterwards by {{GHGheb|text=הַכֻּהוּ|translate=smite him!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=5|verse=8}} ''after thee, Benjamin!'' sc. is the enemy (differently in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5|verse=14}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=6|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=90|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=עַד־מָתַי}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=74|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=עַד־מָה}}.—On {{GHGheb|text=וָלֹא|translate=and if not}} (unless {{GHGheb|text=וְלוּ}} is to be read), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=17}}, see § 158 dd.

{{GHGmargin-letter|147|d}}
Rem. 1. To the class of incomplete sentences naturally belong exclamations introduced by interjections {{GHGheb|text=אֲהָהּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אוֹי}}, {{GHGheb|text=הוֹי}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַס}};<ref>We do not consider here the cases in which these interjections (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=3|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=6|verse=10}}) stand quite disconnectedly (so always {{GHGheb|text=אָח}} and {{GHGheb|text=הֶאָח}}).</ref> cf. § 105. After the first two the object of the ''threat'' or ''imprecation'' follows regularly with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} (cf. ''vae tibi'') or {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}} or {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אוֹי לָ֫נוּ|translate=woe unto us!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=5}}; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=אֲהָהּ לַיּוֹם|translate=alas for the day!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=15}}; on the other hand, the object of ''commiseration'' (after {{GHGheb|text=הוֹי}}) follows mostly in the vocative, or rather in the accusative of exclamation (cf. ''vae te'' in Plautus); so in lamentation for the dead, {{GHGheb|text=הוֹי אָחִי|translate=alas, my brother!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=30}},<section end="par147" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

495.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par147" />{{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=18}}; {{GHGheb|text=הוֹי גּוֹי חֹטֵא|translate=ah, sinful nation!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=8.11.18.20.22|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGtranslate|ah! they that...}}).— For {{GHGheb|text=הַס}} cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=1|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=2|verse=17}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|147|e}}
2. Finally, instances of noun-clauses shortened in an unusual manner may perhaps occur in {{GHGheb|text=יְדֵיהֶם}} and {{GHGheb|text=רַגְלֵיהֶם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=115|verse=7}}, for {{GHGheb|text=יָדַ֫יִם לָהֶם|translate=they have hands}}, &c.; cf. verses 5 and 6 {{GHGheb|text=פֶּֽה־לָהֶם}}, &c. Perhaps also {{GHGheb|text=וּפִֽילַגְשׁוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=24}}, and {{GHGheb|text=וְחָלְיוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=5|verse=16}} are to be regarded in the same way, but hardly {{GHGheb|text=נְבִֽיאֲכֶם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=12|verse=6}}; cf. {{GHGpar|128|d}} above.
<section end="par147" />
<section begin="par148" />{{center|II. Special Kinds of Sentences.}}

<!-- section begins above -->{{GHGpar-heading|148|Exclamations}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|148|a}}
The originally interrogative {{GHGheb|text=מָה}} is used to introduce exclamations of wonder or indignation = ''O how!'' or ridicule, ''why! how!'' sometimes strengthened by {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}} or {{GHGheb|text=זֹאת}} according to {{GHGpar|136|c}}.—Astonishment or indignation at something which has happened is introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אֵיךְ|translate=how}} (likewise originally interrogative) with the perfect; the indignant refusal of a demand by {{GHGheb|text=אֵיךְ}} (but also by {{GHGheb|text=מָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=1}}) with the imperfect; an exclamation of lamentation by {{GHGheb|text=אֵיכָה}}, less frequently {{GHGheb|text=אֵיךְ|translate=how!}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=18}} by {{GHGheb|text=מָה}}.

Examples:—

{{GHGmargin-letter|148|b}}
{{GHGheb|text=מָה}} (or {{GHGheb|text=מַה־}} with a following ''Dagĕš'', see § 37) expressing admiration (or astonishment) before verbal-clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=20}} ({{GHGheb|text=מַה־זֶּה}}); 38:29, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=24|verse=5}} (''how goodly are...!''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=21|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=7|verse=2}}; before the predicate of noun-clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=8|verse=2}}; mockingly before the verb, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=6|verse=20}} (''how glorious was...!''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=26|verse=2}} f.; indignantly, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=מַה־וֹּאת}}; 4:10, 20:9, 31:26 ''what hast thou done!''

{{GHGheb|text=אֵיךְ}} with the perfect, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=19}}; in scornful exclamation, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=4}}, 12; in a lament (usually {{GHGheb|text=אֵיכָה}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=25}}, 27; with the imperfect, in a reproachful question, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=11|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=137|verse=4|hidebook=1}}; in a mocking imitation of lament, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=2|verse=4}}.

{{GHGheb|text=אֵיכָה}} with the perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=1}}; with the imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=2|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=4|verse=1|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|148|c}}
Rem. 1. The close relation between a question and an exclamation appears also in the interrogative personal pronoun {{GHGheb|text=מִי}} in such cases as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=7|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=מִי־אֵל כָּמ֫וֹךָ|translate=who is a God like unto thee?}} and so in general in ''rhetorical'' questions as the expression of a forcible denial; similarly in the use of an interrogative sentence to express a wish, see {{GHGpar|150|d}}, 151 a.

{{GHGmargin-letter|148|d}}
2. A weaker form of exclamation is sometimes produced by the insertion of a corroborative {{GHGheb|text=כִּי|translate=verily, surely}}, before the predicate, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=20}}; cf. 33:11, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=9}}, and the analogous cases in the apodoses of conditional sentences, § 159 ee.
<section end="par148" />
<section begin="par149" />{{GHGpar-heading|149|Sentences which express an Oath or Asseveration}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|149|a}}
The particle {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}, in the sense of ''certainly not'', and {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא}} (rarely {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=16}}) in the sense of ''certainly'', are used to introduce promises or threats confirmed by an oath (especially after such formulae as {{GHGheb|text=חַי־יְהֹוָה}},<section end="par149" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

496.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Wuschelkopf" /></noinclude><section begin="par149" />{{GHGheb|text=חֵֽי־נַפְשְׁךָ}},<ref>Also combined {{GHGheb|text=חַי־יְהֹוָה וְחֵי נַפְשְׁךָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=26|hidebook=1}} ''as the Lord liveth, and as thy soul'' (i.e. ''thou'') ''liveth!'' (Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=11|verse=11}} read {{GHGheb|text=חַי־יהוה}} instead of the impossible {{GHGheb|text=חַיֶּ֫ךְ}}). On {{GHGheb|text=חַי}} and {{GHGheb|text=חֵי}} in these noun-clauses (prop. ''living is the Lord'', &c.), cf. {{GHGpar|93|aa}}, note.</ref> {{GHGheb|text=חַי אָ֫נִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=בִּי נִשְׁבַּ֫עְתִּי}}, &c., as well as after imprecations, see below), and also simple asseverations, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=27|verse=5}} after {{GHGheb|text=חָלִ֫ילָה לִי|translate=far be it from me}}, but mostly without any introductory formula.

{{GHGmargin-letter|149|b}}
Rem. No certain explanation of these particles has yet been given. According to the usual view, phrases expressing an oath depend on the suppression of an imprecation upon oneself, e.g. ''the Lord do so unto me, if I do it'' equivalent to ''I certainly will not do it''; then naturally {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא}} properly ''if I do it not'' equivalent to ''I certainly will do it''. It is indeed difficult to understand such self-imprecations, put into the mouth of God, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=34}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=3|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=35|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=95|verse=11}}. Possibly, however, the consciousness of the real meaning of the formula was lost at an early period, and {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא}} simply came to express ''verily'', {{GHGheb|text=אִם|translate=verily not}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=22}}, where, instead of a self-imprecation, a curse is pronounced upon others, read {{GHGheb|text=לְדָוִד}} with the Lxx for {{GHGheb|text=לְאֹֽיְבֵי דָוִד}}.

Examples:—

{{GHGmargin-letter|149|c}}
(''a'') The particles {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} and {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא}} used after the utterance of an oath and after formulae of swearing, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=11|verse=11}} (see note on <sup>a</sup>) {{GHGheb|text=חַי־יְהֹוָה וְחֵי נַפְשֶׁ֫ךָ אִם־אִֽעֱשֶׂה אֶת־הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה|translate=as the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth, I will not do this thing}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=45}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=16}} (after {{GHGheb|text=חַי יְהֹוָה}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=39}} and 29:6 {{GHGheb|text=חַי־י׳}} is followed by a simple {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=2|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=3|verse=5|hidebook=1}} (after {{GHGheb|text=הִשְׁבַּ֫עְתִּי|translate=I adjure you}}); cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=29|hidebook=1}}; spoken by God, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=34}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=95|verse=11}}; similarly {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=37}} f.; spoken by God, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=24}}, where {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא}} occurs first with the perfect in the sense of a prophetic perfect, {{GHGpar|106|n}}, but in the parallel clause with the imperfect; Jer 22<sub>6</sub>; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=52}} the negative oath introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אִם־אָ֫נִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=אִם־אַתָּה}} is immediately afterwards continued by {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} with the imperfect.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=34|verse=10}} the threat introduced in verse 8 by {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא}} is, after a long parenthesis, resumed with {{GHGheb|text=הִנְנִי}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|149|d}}
(''b'') {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} and {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא}} after formulae of cursing, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=כֹּה יַֽעֲשֶׂה־לְּךָ אֱלֹהִים וְכֹה יוֹסִיף אִם־תְּכַחֵד מִמֶּ֫נִּי דָבָר וג׳|translate=God do so to thee, and more also! thou shalt not hide anything from me}}, &c.; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=22}}. On the other hand, {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} follows the curse, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=44}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=23}} (here with a perfect), and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=35}} {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אִם}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=34}} the preceding {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} is repeated before {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=13}} the purport of the asseveration is repeated (after the insertion of a conditional sentence) in the perfect consecutive.

{{GHGmargin-letter|149|e}}
(''c'') {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} and {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא}} as simple particles of asseveration, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=מָגֵן אִם־ֵי֥רָאֶה וָרֹמַח וג׳|translate=truly, there was not a shield and spear seen}}, &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=28}} (in the middle of the sentence); after {{GHGheb|text=חָלִ֫ילָה חָלִ֫ילָה|translate=absit}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=20}}; {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא}} with the imperf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=9}}, with the perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=20}}.<section end="par149" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

497.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par150" />{{GHGpar-heading|150|Interrogative Sentences}}

H. G. Mitchell, ‘The omission of the interrogative particle,’ in {{GHGcite|title=Old Test. and Sem. Studies in memory of W. R. Harper}}, Chicago, 1907, i, 113 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|a}}
'''1.''' A question need not necessarily be introduced by a special interrogative pronoun or adverb. Frequently<ref>Mitchell (op. cit.) restricts the number of instances to 39, of which he attributes 12 (or 17) to corruption of the text. Thus in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=24}} he would road, with the Samaritan, {{GHGheb|text=הַֽאַתָּה}} as in verso 21, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=הֲשָׁלֹם}}, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=29}} {{GHGheb|text=הֲשָׁלוֹם}} as in verse 32; similarly he would read the interrogative particle in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=11|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=40|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=1|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=30|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=11|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=17|verse=9|hidebook=1}}.</ref> the natural emphasis upon the words is of itself sufficient to indicate an interrogative sentence as such; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=24}} {{GHGheb|text=אַתָּה זֶה בְּנִי עֵשָׂו|translate=thou art my son Esau?}} (but cf. note <sup>1</sup> below) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=14}} ({{GHGheb|text=פָּנַי י׳}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=11|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=שָׁאוּל יִמְלֹךְ עָלֵ֫ינוּ|translate=Saul shall reign over us?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=22|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=16|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=29|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=שָׁלוֹם לַנַּ֫עַר|translate=is it well with the young man?}} (but cf. note <sup>1</sup>); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=4|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=8|verse=6}} (''should it also be marvellous in mine eyes?''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=5|verse=16}}. So especially, when the interrogative clause is connected with a preceding sentence by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jn|chapter=4|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=וַֽאֲנִי לֹא אָחוּס|translate=and I should not have pity?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=8|verse=22}} ''will they not stone us?'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=11|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=11}}, 44<sup>19 ''b''</sup>, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=25|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=45|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=20|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=9|hidebook=1}}; or when (as in some of the examples just given) it is negative (with {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} for {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹא|translate=nonne?}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=26}} (but cf. note <sup>1</sup>), {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=3|verse=38}}.
<ref>But in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=27|verse=10}} instead of {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} (which according to the usual explanation would expect a negative answer) read either {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־מִי}} ({{GHGheb|text=עַל־מִי}}) with the LXX, or better, {{GHGheb|text=אָן}} ({{GHGheb|text=אָ֫נָה}}) ''whither?'' with the Targum. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=23|verse=5}} read {{GHGheb|text=חֶפְצִי הֲלֹא}} with Wellhausen.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|b}}
Rem. The statement formerly made here that the interrogative particle is omitted especially before gutturals, cannot be maintained in view of Mitchell’s statistics (op. cit. p. 123 f.). The supposed considerations of euphony are quite disproved by the 118 cases in which {{GHGheb|text=הַ}} or {{GHGheb|text=הֶ}} occurs before a guttural.

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|c}}
'''2.''' As a rule, however, the simple question is introduced by ''He interrogative'' {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} ({{GHGheb|text=הַ}}; as to its form, cf. {{GHGpar|100|k}}–{{GHGpar|100|n|nonumber=1}}), ''ne? num?'' the disjunctive question by {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} (''num? utrum?'') in the first clause, and {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}<ref>Quite exceptional is the use of the particle {{GHGheb|text=אִין|translate=num?}} (common in Aramaic) in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=21|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=וְאִין יֶשׁ־פֹּה|translate=num est hic?}} The text is, however, undoubtedly corrupt; according to Wellhausen, ''Text der Bücher Sam.'', the LXX express the reading {{GHGheb|text=רְאֵה הֲיֵשׁ}}; but cf. the full discussion of the passage by König, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} xviii. 239 ff.—The above does not apply to interrogative sentences introduced by interrogative pronouns (§ 37) or by the interrogatives compounded with {{GHGheb|text=מָה|translate=what?}} such as {{GHGheb|text=כַּמָּה|translate=how many?}} {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מָּה|translate=why?}} (see {{GHGpar|102|k}}), {{GHGheb|text=מַדּוּעַ|translate=why?}} ({{GHGpar|99|e}}), or by {{GHGheb|text=אַיֵּה|translate=where?}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵיךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֵיכָה|translate=how?}} (§ 148), &c. On the transformation of pronouns and adverbs into interrogative words by means of a prefixed {{GHGheb|text=אֵי}}, see the Lexicon.</ref> (also {{GHGheb|text=וְאִם}}, less frequently {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ}}) ''an?'' in the second, e.g.<!-- continued on the next page --><section end="par150" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

498.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par150" /><!-- continued from the previous page -->{{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=הֲנֵלֵךְ אִם <ref>On the use of the {{GHGterm|imperfect}} in deliberative questions, see {{GHGpar|107|t}}; on the ''perfectum confidentiae'' in interrogative sentences, see {{GHGpar|106|n}}.</ref>נֶחְדָּ֑ל}} ''shall we go... or shall we forbear?'' Cf. also {{GHGheb|text=אָן|translate=where? whither?}} {{GHGheb|text=אָ֫נָה|translate=whither}}, and J. Barth, {{GHGcite|title=Sprachwiss. Untersuchungen}}, i. 13 ff.

The particular uses are as follows:—

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|d}}
(''a'') The particle {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} stands primarily before the simple question, when the questioner is wholly uncertain as to the answer to be expected, and may be used either before noun-clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=הַעוֹד אֲבִיכֶם חַי הֲיֵשׁ לָכֶם אָח|translate=is your father yet alive? have ye}} another ''brother?'' for {{GHGheb|text=הֲיֵשׁ}} cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=11}}; for {{GHGheb|text=הֲכִי|translate=is it that?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=22}}; for {{GHGheb|text=הֲכִי יֶשׁ־|translate=is there yet?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=9|verse=1}} (but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=23|verse=19}} for {{GHGheb|text=הֲכִי}} read {{GHGheb|text=הִנּוֹ}} with {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=11|verse=25}}); for {{GHGheb|text=הַאֵין|translate=is there not?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=7}}, &c.; or before verbal-clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=2|verse=3}} ''hast thou considered'' ({{GHGheb|text=הֲשַׂ֫מְתָּ לִבְּךָ}}) ''my servant Job?'' In other cases {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} (= ''num?'') is used before questions, to which, from their tone and contents, a negative answer is expected, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=14|verse=14}} ''if a man die'', {{GHGheb|text=הֲיִחְֽיֶה|translate=shall he}} indeed ''live'' again? Sometimes a question is so used only as a rhetorical form instead of a negative assertion, or of a surprised or indignant refusal,<ref>Analogous to this is the use of the interrogative {{GHGheb|text=מָה}} in the sense of a reproachful remonstrance instead of a prohibition, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=8|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=מַה־תָּעִירוּ|translate=why should ye stir up?}} i.e. ''pray, stir not up''; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=1}}; see above, § 148.</ref> e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=7|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=הַֽאַתָּה תִבְנֶה־לִּי בַיִת|translate=shalt thou build me an house?}} (in the parallel passage {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=17|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אַתָּה וג׳|translate=thou shalt not}}, &c.); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=הֲשֹׁמֵר אָחִי אָנֹ֫כִי}} ''am I my brother’s keeper?'' cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=7}}, and the two passages where {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} is used before the infinitive ({{GHGterm|constr.}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=18}}, {{GHGterm|absol.}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=40|verse=2}}; on both, see § 113 ee, with the note).—On the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=16|verse=31}} for {{GHGheb|text=הֲנָקֵל}} (after {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}}) read {{GHGheb|text=הַנָּקֵל}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|e}}
Rem. 1. A few passages deserve special mention, in which the use of the interrogative is altogether different from our idiom, since it serves merely to express the conviction that the contents of the statement are well known to the hearer, and are unconditionally admitted by him. Thus, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=11}} ''surely thou hast eaten''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=36}} {{GHGheb|text=הֲכִי קָרָא}} prop. ''is it so that one names?'' &c., i.e. ''of a truth he is rightly named Jacob''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=15}} ''verily thou art my brother''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=11|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=6}}, I S 2:27 ''I did indeed'', &c.; 20:37, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=3}} ''ye know surely...''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=3|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=4}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=19}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=54|verse=2}}) a surprising communication is introduced in this way (by {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹא}}) in order to show it to be absolutely true, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=7}} a concession is expressed by {{GHGheb|text=הֲלוֹא|translate=I have, it is true}}, &c. Finally, we may include the formula of quotation {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹא הִיא כְתוּבָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=10|verse=13}} or {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹא־הֵם כְּתוּבִים}} equivalent to ''surely it is, they are'' written (the latter in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=11|verse=41}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=14|verse=29|hidebook=1}}, and very often elsewhere in the books of Kings and Chronicles), synonymous with the simple formula of assertion {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה כְתוּבָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=18}}, and {{GHGheb|text=הִנָּם כְּתוּבִים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=14|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=15|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=27|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=32|verse=32|hidebook=1}}.

Of very frequent occurrence also are questions introduced by {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מָּה}}, which really contain an affirmation and are used to state the reason for a request or warning, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=22}} ''turn thee aside... wherefore should I smite thee to the ground?'' i.e. ''otherwise I will'' (or ''must'') ''smite'', &c.; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=19|verse=17}}, and Driver on the passage; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=25|verse=16}}; also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=45}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=12}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=2|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=79|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=115|verse=2|hidebook=1}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=1|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=5|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=7|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=1|verse=10}}.<section end="par150" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

499.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par150 />{{GHGmargin-letter|150|f}}
2. The rare cases in which a ''simple'' question is introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} (as sometimes in Latin by ''an? is it?'') are really due to the suppression of the first member of a double question; thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=39|verse=13|hidebook=1}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|g}}
(''b'') Disjunctive questions are, as a rule, introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}—{{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} (''utrum—an?'') or sometimes by {{GHGheb|text=וְאִם}}<ref>{{GHGheb|text=וְאִם}} occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=27|verse=24}} after a negative statement; we should, however, with Dyserinck read {{GHGheb|text=וְאֵין}}. Not less irregular is {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹא}} instead of {{GHGheb|text=אִם לֹא}} in the second clause of {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=15}}, but the text can hardly be correct (cf. Moore, ''Judges'', New York, 1895, p. 337); in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=11}} the second {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} introduces a fresh question which is only loosely connected with the first.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=17|verse=28}} and in the third clause of {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=13}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַאִם}} is best taken with Ewald in the sense of {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹא}}, since {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} from its use in oaths (see above, {{GHGpar|149|b}}) may simply mean ''verily not''.</ref>—{{GHGheb|text=הֲ}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=4}} (even with {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} repeated after {{GHGheb|text=וְאִם}} in a question which implies disbelief, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=17}}). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=40|verse=8|hidebook=1}} f. special emphasis is given to the first member by {{GHGheb|text=הַאַף}} prop. ''is it even?'' The second member is introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ|translate=or}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=28|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=36|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=1|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ הֲ}}), in each case before {{GHGheb|text=מ‍}}, and hence no doubt for euphonic reasons, to avoid the combination {{GHGheb|text=אִם מ׳}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=18|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=2|verse=19}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|h}}
Double questions with ({{GHGheb|text=וְאִם}}) {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}—{{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} need not always be mutually exclusive; frequently the disjunctive form serves (especially in poetic parallelism; but cf. also e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=8}}) merely to repeat the same question in different words, and thus to express it more emphatically. So {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=17}} ''shall mortal man be just before God? or'' ({{GHGheb|text=אִם}}) ''shall a man be pure before his Maker?'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=5}} f., 8:3, 10:4 f., 11:2, 7, 22:3, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=10|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=5|verse=29}}. The second member may, therefore, just as well be connected by a simple {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=7|hidebook=1}} f., 38:16 f.22, 32, 39; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=8|verse=5}} after {{GHGheb|text=מָה}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=17}} f. after {{GHGheb|text=כַּמָּה}}; or even without a conjunction, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=8|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=4|hidebook=1}}; after {{GHGheb|text=מָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=144|verse=3}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|i}}
(''c'') With regard to ''indirect'' questions<ref>It should here be remarked that the distinction between direct and indirect questions cannot have been recognized by the Hebrew mind to the same extent as it is in Latin or English. In Hebrew there is no difference between the two kinds of sentence, either as regards mood (as in Latin) or in tense and position of the words (as in English). Cf. also {{GHGpar|137|c}}.</ref> after verbs of inquiring, doubting, examining,<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=6}} the {{GHGheb|text=הַ}} after {{GHGheb|text=לְהַגִּיד}} is explained from the fact that the latter, according to the context, implies ''to give information upon a question''.</ref> &c., simple questions of this kind take either {{GHGheb|text=הֲ|translate=whether}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=8|verse=8}},<ref>Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=21}} we should read {{GHGheb|text=הַֽעֹלָה}} and {{GHGheb|text=הֲיׄרֶ֫דֶת}} (''whether—whether'') instead of the article which is assumed by the Masora.</ref> or {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=1|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=7|verse=13}}; even before a noun-clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=5|verse=1}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=10}} the indirect question is introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ}}, i.e. probably ''if perchance''. In disjunctives (''whether—or'') {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}—{{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=13|verse=18}} at the end (or {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא}}—{{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=32|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=4}}), and {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}}—{{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=13|verse=18}}, which is followed by {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}—{{GHGheb|text=הֲ}}; also {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ}}—{{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=2|verse=19}}. The formula {{GHGheb|text=מִי יוֹדֵעַ אִם}} has an affirmative force, ''who knows whether... not'', like the Latin ''nescio an'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=4|verse=14}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|k}}
In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=1|verse=7}}, 8 the relative pronouns {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ·}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} owing to the following {{GHGheb|text=לְמִי}} have become also interrogative, ''for whose cause?''

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|l}}
(''d'') {{GHGheb|text=זֶה}} and {{GHGheb|text=הוּא}} (cf. {{GHGpar|136|c}}) immediately after the interrogative serve to give vividness to the question; so also {{GHGheb|text=אֵפוֹא}} (for which {{GHGheb|text=אֵפוֹ}} five times in Job) ''then, now'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=33}} {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־אֵפוֹא הוּא|translate=who then is he?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=38}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=19|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=17|verse=15}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַיֵּה אֵפוֹ}}<section end=par150 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

500.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par150 />''where then is...?'' However, {{GHGheb|text=אֵפוֹא}} may also be placed at the end of the entire question ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=1}}; also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=13|verse=10}}, since either {{GHGheb|text=אֱהִי}} is a dialectical form of {{GHGheb|text=אַיֵּה}}, or {{GHGheb|text=אַיֵּה}} should be read instead of it) or at the beginning of the question proper, after a strongly emphasized word, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=37}}.<ref>On the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=24}} and 24:25 {{GHGheb|text=אֵפוֹ}} is not prefixed to the {{GHGheb|text=מִי}}, but appended to the conditional sentence.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|m}}
(''e'') Sometimes one interrogative governs two co-ordinate clauses, the first of which should rather be subordinated to the second, so that the interrogative word strictly speaking affects only the second; thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=4}} after {{GHGheb|text=מַדּוּעַ|translate=wherefore looked I... and it brought forth?}} i.e. wherefore brought it forth, while I looked, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=50|verse=2}}; after {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=32|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=8|verse=4}}, also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=22}} (read {{GHGheb|text=הַאִישׁ}}); after {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=22|verse=20}}; after {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מָּה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=58|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=32|verse=4}}; after {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־מִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=25}}.<ref>Cf. the analogous sentences after {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן|translate=because}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=65|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=35|verse=17}}; after causal {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=23}}; after {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=12|verse=1}}; likewise after {{GHGheb|text=גַּם}} § 153 at the end; after {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=8|verse=12}}–14, 25:3, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=6|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=28}}.</ref> But {{GHGheb|text=הֲ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=4|verse=2}} and {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹא}} 4:21 are separated from the verb to which they belong by the insertion of a conditional clause.

{{GHGmargin-letter|150|n}}
'''3.''' The affirmative answer is generally expressed, as in Latin, by repeating the emphatic word in the question (or with the second person changed to the first, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=58}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=11}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=32|hidebook=1}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=21|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=37|verse=17}}. (On {{GHGheb|text=וָיֵשׁ|translate=if it be so}} in the corrected text of {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=10|verse=15}}, see § 159 dd.) As a negative answer the simple {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} is sometimes sufficient, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=22}}, &c.; cf. {{GHGpar|152|c}}; and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=20}} the simple {{GHGheb|text=אָֽיִן}} equivalent to ''no'' or ''no one''.<section end=par150 />

<section begin=par151 />{{GHGpar-heading|151|Desiderative Sentences}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|151|a}}
A wish may be expressed not only by the simple imperfect ({{GHGpar|107|n}}), cohortative (§ 108, especially with {{GHGheb|text=נָא}} {{GHGpar|108|c}}), jussive (§ 109; with {{GHGheb|text=נָא}} {{GHGpar|109|b}}), imperative ({{GHGpar|110|a}}), perfect consecutive ({{GHGpar|112|aa}}) or by a simple noun-clause ({{GHGpar|116|r}}, note, and {{GHGpar|141|g}}) but also in the following ways:—

'''1.''' By exclamations in the form of ''interrogative'' clauses:<ref>The transition from a question to a wish may be seen, e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=4}} ''who shall give us flesh to eat?'' i.e. ''O that we had flesh to eat!''</ref> especially sentences with {{GHGheb|text=מִי}} followed by the imperfect as being the mood of that which is still unfulfilled but possible, and hence also of that which is desired, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יְשִׂמֵ֫נִי שֹׁפֵט|translate=who maketh me judge?}} i.e. ''O that I were made judge!'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=23|verse=15}}. On the other hand, {{GHGheb|text=מִי}} with the perfect ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=53|verse=1}}, &c.) or participle ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=59|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=24|verse=22}}, &c.), rather expresses a rhetorical question, i.e. a denial, cf. {{GHGpar|150|d}}. Especially frequent is the use of {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יִתֵּן}} (prop. ''who gives?'') to introduce all kinds of desiderative clauses (see under b).—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=1|verse=10}} the desiderative clause proper is co-ordinated with an interrogative clause,<section end=par151 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

501.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par151 />{{GHGheb|text=מִי גַם־בָּכֶם וְיִסְגּׄר דְּלָתַ֫יִם|translate=would that one were among you and would shut the doors}}, i.e. O that one would shut the doors!

{{GHGmargin-letter|151|b}}
Rem. Sometimes the original sense of {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יִתֵּן}} is still plainly discernible, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=29}} {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יִתֵּן אֶת־הָעָם הַוֶּה בְיָדִי|translate=who gives this people into my hand?}} equivalent to, O that this people were given into my hand! cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=55|verse=7}}. In these examples, however, {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יִתֵּן}} is still equivalent to ''O had I!'' and in numerous other instances the idea of ''giving'' has entirely disappeared, {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יִתֵּן}} having become stereotyped as a more desiderative particle (''utinam''). Its construction is either—

(''a'') With the ''accusative'' (in accordance with its original meaning) of a substantive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=67}} ''would that it were even!... morning!'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=14|verse=7}} (53:7), 55:7; with an accusative and a following infinitive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=5}}; with two accusatives, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=8|verse=23}}; with the accusative of an infinitive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יִתֵּן מוּתִי אֲנִי תַחְתֶּ֫יךָ|translate=would that I had died for thee}} (for {{GHGheb|text=אֲנִי}} cf. {{GHGpar|135|f}}); of a participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=35}}; of a personal pronoun (as a suffix), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=2}} (with a following {{GHGheb|text=ךְּ}}; but {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יִתְּנֵ֫נִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=27|verse=4}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=9|verse=1}} with a following accusative is not simply equivalent to {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יִתֵּן לִי}}, but is properly ''who endows me with'', &c.; cf. {{GHGpar|117|ff}}).—With a still greater weakening of the original meaning {{GHGheb|text=מִֽי־יִתֵּן}} is used with an adjective in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=14|verse=4}} ''could a clean thing but come out of an unclean!'' i.e. ''how can a clean thing come'', &c.; similarly in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=31}} ''who can find one that hath not been satisfied!''

{{GHGmargin-letter|151|c}}
(''b'') With a following perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=3}} (cf. {{GHGpar|120|e}}); with a perfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=5|verse=26}} ''O that they had such an heart!''

{{GHGmargin-letter|151|d}}
(''c'') With a following imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=14|verse=13|hidebook=1}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=23}} the imperfect is twice added with {{GHGterm|Wāw}} (cf. a above, on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal.|chapter=1|verse=10}}).

On the cohortative in the apodosis to such desiderative clauses, cf. {{GHGpar|108|f}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|151|e}}
'''2.''' The wish may also be expressed by the particles {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=81|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=95|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=24|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=4|verse=10}}; always with a following imperfect) and {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} (for which in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=5}} we have {{GHGheb|text=אַחְלַי}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲלֵי}}, from {{GHGheb|text=אָח|translate=ah!}} and {{GHGheb|text=לַי}}={{GHGheb|text=לוּ}}; both with a following imperfect)''si, o si! utinam''.<ref>Cf. a similar transition from a conditional to a desiderative particle, in consequence of the suppression of the apodosis, in the English, ''O if I had!'' and the like; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=29}} ''if there were'' ({{GHGheb|text=לוּ יֶשׁ־}}) ''a sword in my hand now had I surely killed thee!''</ref> {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} is followed by the imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=2}}; by the jussive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=34}} (rather concessive, equivalent to ''let it be so''); by the perfect, as the expression of a wish that something might have happened in past time (cf. {{GHGpar|106|p}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=לוּ מַ֫תְנוּ|translate=would that we had died}}; 20:3 and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=7|verse=7}} (both times {{GHGheb|text=וְלוּ}}); on the other hand, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=48|verse=18}} and 63:19 (both times {{GHGheb|text=לוּא}}) to express a wish that something expected in the future may already have happened.—On {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} with the imperative (by an anacoluthon) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=13}} cf. {{GHGpar|110|e}}. On the perfect after {{GHGheb|text=בִּי אִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=20}}, cf. {{GHGpar|106|n}}, note 2.<section end=par151 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

502.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par152 />{{GHGpar-heading|152|Negative Sentences}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|a}}
'''1.''' Besides the use of rhetorical questions ({{GHGpar|150|d|doublesign=1}}, {{GHGpar|151|a|nosign=1}}), independent sentences are made negative by the adverbs {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=21}}, where instead of the {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}} {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ}} we must evidently read {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}; perhaps preserved as a substantive) = the Greek οὐ, ''not'', {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} = μή ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=24|verse=25}} as a substantive), {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} (''it is'') ''not''; {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֫רֶם|translate=not yet}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫פֶס|translate=not}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַפְסִי}} (cf. {{GHGpar|90|m}}) ''not''. The forms {{GHGheb|text=בַּל}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּלִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְתִּי|translate=not}} belong almost entirely to poetry.—With regard to {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} the main distinction is that verbal-clauses (rarely noun-clauses, see e) are regularly negatived by {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} (besides its use as negativing ''single'' words<ref>Especially in compounds, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־אֵל}} lit. ''a no-God'' (Germ. ''Ungott'')who is indeed called a god, but is not really a god, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=21}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אֱלֹהַּ}} verse 17, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=5|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=13|verse=9}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־עָם}} lit. ''a not-people'' (Germ. ''Unvolk''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=21}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא דָבָר|translate=a nothing}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=6|verse=13}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא עֵץ}} lit. ''not-wood'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=10|verse=15}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־אִישׁ}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֹֽא־אָדָם}} lit. ''not-man'', ''superhuman'' (of God), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=31|verse=8}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־עֶ֫דֶק|translate=unrighteousness}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=13}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=22|verse=29}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־סְדָרִים|translate=disorder}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=22}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֹֽא־חָמָם|translate=not-violence}}, 16:17; after {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=26|verse=2}} f.
