({{GHGheb|text=לֹא־כֹחַ}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־עֹז|translate=helplessness}}, {{GHGheb|text=לֹא חָכְמָה|translate=insipientia}}); cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=55|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּלוֹא לְשָׂבְעָה|translate=for what is unsatisfying}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=44|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=8|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=32|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=12|verse=33}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=5}} a construct state with several genitives is negatived by {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}.—Also {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} is used with an infinitive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=35|verse=23}}; with an adjective, {{GHGheb|text=לֹא חָכָם|translate=unwise}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=13|verse=13}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֹֽא־חָסִיד|translate=impius}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=43|verse=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־עָז}} and {{GHGheb|text=לֹֽא־עָצוּם|translate=not strong}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=30|verse=25}} f.; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־כֵן|translate=unsuitably}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=9}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא־טוֹב|translate=not-good}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=65|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=20|verse=25}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא טָהוֹר|translate=not-clean}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=30|verse=17}}; with a participle, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=2}} (''unsown''); (6:8, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=4|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=22|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, Zn 2:1, 3:5; the Masora, however, requires {{GHGheb|text=נֻחָ֫מָה}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=54|verse=11}}, {{GHGheb|text=נֶֽעֱזָ֫בָה}} in 62:12, {{GHGheb|text=נוֹשָׁ֫בָה}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=6|verse=8}}, {{GHGheb|text=רֻחָ֫מָה}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=1|verse=6}}, i.e. always 3rd sing. fem. perf. in pause = ''she was not comforted'', &c., and consequently not compounds, but either relative clauses or ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=54|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=1|verse=6}}, and especially 2:25) main clauses instead of proper names.—On the above compounds generally, cf. the dissertation mentioned in {{GHGpar|81|d}}, note 2; on their use in sentences expressing a state, to convey attributive ideas, see u below.</ref>), while {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} is used exclusively with noun-clauses (see the examples below).

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|b}}
The conjunctions {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־}} and {{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי|translate=that not}}, serve to negative dependent clauses. The particular uses of these particles are as follows:—

(''a'') {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} (less frequently {{GHGheb|text=לוֹא}}), like οὐ, οὐκ, is used regularly for the ''objective, unconditional'' negation, and hence is usually connected with the perfect or imperfect (as indicative); on {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} with the imperfect to express an unconditional prohibition, see {{GHGpar|107|o}}; on its use with the jussive, see {{GHGpar|109|d}}.—On {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} for {{GHGheb|text=הֲלֹא|translate=nonne}}, in interrogative sentences, cf. {{GHGpar|150|a}}. In connexion with {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־}} (= ''any''), {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} is used to express an ''absolute'' negation, ''nullus, none whatever'' (cf. the French ''ne... personne, ne... rien''), usually in the order {{GHGheb|text=לֹא... כֹּל}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא תֹֽאכְלוּ מִכֹּל עֵץ הַגָּן|translate=ye shall not eat of any tree of the garden}}; 9:11, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=7|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=8|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=13|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=32|verse=17|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=לֹא... כָּל־דָּבָר|translate=nothing at all}}; cf. the same statement in the form of a rhetorical question, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=32|verse=27}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=12|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=30|verse=30|hidebook=1}}<section end=par152 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

503.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par152" />{{GHGheb|text=לֹא... מִפְּנֵי־כֹל}} and turneth ''not'' away ''for any''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=32|verse=15}}; but cf. also the inverted order, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=בָּל־מְלָאכָה לֹא־יֵֽעָשֶׂה|translate=no manner of work shall be done}}; 12:43, 15:26, 22:21, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=16|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=33|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=11|verse=37}}. The meaning is different when {{GHGheb|text=בֹּל}} by being determinate is used in the sense of ''whole'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=כֻּלּוֹ לֹא תִרְאֶה|translate=thou shalt not see them all}}, but only a part.

Analogous to {{GHGheb|text=לֹא... כֹּל}} is the use of {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ... לֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=6}}, &c., in verbal-clauses in the sense of ''no one at all, not a single one''. On {{GHGheb|text=אֵין־כֹּל|translate=nothing at all}}, see under p.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|c}}
Rem. 1. The examples in which {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} is used absolutely as a negative answer, equivalent to ''certainly not! no!'' must be regarded as extremely short verbal-clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=2}} ({{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} according to the context for {{GHGheb|text=לֹא נָסוּר}} &c.); 23:11, 42:10, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hag|chapter=2|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=6}}, sometimes with a following {{GHGheb|text=כִּי|translate=but}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=2}} (see above); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=5|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=22}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|d}}
2. The negation of ''noun''-clauses by {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} (as opposed to the regular negationd by {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}}) always includes a certain emphasis, since the force of the negation falls rather upon a particular word (cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=36|verse=32}}), than upon the whole clause. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=34}} {{GHGheb|text=יָדֶ֫יךָ לֹֽא־אֲסוּרוֹת|translate=thy hands}} were ''not bound'', a participle is thus specially negatived by {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=74|verse=9}}, where, however, {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} is separated from the participle by {{GHGheb|text=אִתָּ֫נוּ}}, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=3}}. As a rule, noun-clauses with a pronominal subject are thus negatived by {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=35|verse=23}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=42}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=19|verse=4|hidebook=1}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=21|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=22|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=28|verse=14}}, parallel with {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}}; generally with {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} before a substantival predicate, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=4|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אִישׁ דְּבָרִים אָנֹ֫כִי|translate=I am not a man of words}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=18}}.—Noun-clauses with a substantival subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=44|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hag|chapter=1|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=22|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=18|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=36|verse=26|hidebook=1}} (with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} of the apodosis); 41:2; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=33}} even {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יֵשׁ|translate=non est}} is used instead of {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=18|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} is used before an adjectival predicate; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=26}} (where a preceding noun-clause is negatived by {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְתִּי}}) read {{GHGheb|text=לֹא טֹהָר}} with the LXX, for {{GHGheb|text=לֹא טָהוֹר}}. On {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} in circumstantial clauses to express attributive ideas, see u below.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|e}}
3. As a rule {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} stands immediately before the verb, but sometimes is separated from it (frequently to bring into special prominence another word which follows it); thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=10|verse=10}} before the object and verb; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=29}} before the subject and verb; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=8|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=34}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=49|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=103|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=23|hidebook=1}} before a complementary adjunct. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} according to the accentuation even stands at the end of the clause (''they offend him not''); but undoubtedly {{GHGheb|text=לֹא בָנָיו}} are to be taken together.—On the position of {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} with the infinitive absolute, see {{GHGpar|113|v}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|f}}
(''b'') {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} is used like μή and ''ne'' to express a ''subjective'' and ''conditional'' negation, and hence especially in connexion with the jussive ({{GHGpar|109|c}} and e) to introduce prohibitions, warnings, negative desires, and requests. On {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} with the imperfect, see {{GHGpar|107|p}}; with the cohortative, see {{GHGpar|108|c}}; on {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=6|verse=27}}, see {{GHGpar|109|h}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|g}}
Rem. 1. {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}} (like {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}, see note on <sup>a</sup> above) maybe used to form a compound word, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=12|verse=28}} {{GHGheb|text=אַל־מָוֶת|translate=not-death}} (immortality); though all the early versions read {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־מָוֶת}}. The instances in which {{GHGheb|text=אַל}} appears to stand absolutely, equivalent to ''no, certainly not'' (like μή for μὴ γένηται), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=1|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=אַל בְּנׄתַי|translate=nay, my daughters}}, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=10|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=אַל־נָא}}), are also due (see under c) to extreme shortening of a full clause (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=25}} such a clause is repeated immediately<section end="par152" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

504.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par152 />afterwards); thus in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=62|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=83|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=יְהִי}} is evidently to be supplied, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=2|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=8|verse=10}} the corresponding jussive from the preceding imperatives, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=17|verse=12}} from the preceding infinitive absolute.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|h}}
2. {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}}, like {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}, regularly stands immediately before the verb, but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=64|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=10|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=15|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=6|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=38|verse=2|hidebook=1}} before another strongly emphasized member of the sentence.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=3}} the pointing {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}} occurs twice instead of {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}}, and is thus, in the opinion of the Masoretes, equivalent to ''against'' him that ''bendeth''; but undoubtedly we should read {{GHGheb|text=אַל־}}.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|i}}
(''c'') {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} construct state (unless it be sometimes merely a contracted connective form, cf. {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵים}} for {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנַ֫יִם}} {{GHGpar|97|d}}) of {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִן|translate=non-existence}} (as also the absolute state, see below) is the negative of {{GHGheb|text=יֵשׁ|translate=existence}}; cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=29}} with {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=5|verse=5}}. As {{GHGheb|text=יֵשׁ}} (''he, she, it is, was'', &c.) includes the idea of ''being'' in all tenses, so {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִן}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} includes the idea of ''not being'' in all tenses. Hence—

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|k}}
(1) The absolute state {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִן}}, with an evident transition to the meaning of a verbal predicate, ''there does not exist'', always ''follows'' the word negatived, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=37|verse=3}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=19|verse=3}}) {{GHGheb|text=וְכֹחַ אַ֫יִן לְלֵדָה|translate=and strength does not exist to bring forth}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִן|translate=was not}} present; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=17|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־אָֽיִן|translate=or is he not}}? after {{GHGheb|text=הֲיֵשׁ|translate=is he...}}? (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=13|verse=20}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=37}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=20}} ({{GHGheb|text=אָֽיִן|translate=no}}). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=4}} and 10:14 {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִן}} is used in reference to a plural; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=59|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=7|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=13|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=25|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=וָאַ֫יִן|translate=and let there be none, let none come!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=19}}.—Cf. finally {{GHGheb|text=אִם־אַ֫יִן|translate=if it be not so}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=10}}.—Quite anomalous is {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=35|verse=15}} before a perfect as an emphatic negation; the text, however, can hardly be correct.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|l}}
(2) The construct state {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} stands in its natural position immediately before the substantive whose non-existence it predicates, or before the subject of the sentence which is to be negatived. To the former class belong also the very numerous instances in which {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} is joined to a participle, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=וְאֵין רֹאֶה וְאֵין יוֹדֵעַ וְאֵין מֵקִיץ|translate=and there was not one seeing}}, &c., i.e. ''and no man saw it, nor knew it, neither did any awake''; so especially {{GHGheb|text=וְאֵין}} with a participle in subordinate ''circumstantial'' or ''descriptive clauses'', such as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=29}} {{GHGheb|text=וְיַפְלִיט וְאֵין מַצִּיל|translate=and he shall carry it away}}, while there is none delivering, i.e. ''without any one’s delivering'' it; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=7|verse=3}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=6}} &c., {{GHGheb|text=וְאֵין מַֽחֲרִיד}} ''without any one’s making you afraid''; cf. {{GHGpar|141|e}}. {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} is used as the negation of an entire noun-clause, e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=42}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵין יְהוַֹה בִּקִרְבְּכֶם|translate=the Lord is not among you}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=29}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽין־יוֹסֵף בַּבּוֹר|translate=Joseph was not in the pit}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|m}}
(3) When the subject which is to be negatived is a personal pronoun, it is joined as a suffix to {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}}, according to {{GHGpar|100|o}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֵינֶ֫נִּי|translate=I am not, was not, shall not be}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽינְךָ}}, fem. {{GHGheb|text=אֵינֵךְ}}, ''thou art not'', &c.; {{GHGheb|text=אֵינֶ֫נּוּ}}, fem. {{GHGheb|text=אֵינֶ֫נָּה|translate=he, she is not}}, &c.; also absolutely, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=13}} ''he is'' (5:24 ''he was'') ''no'' longer ''alive''; {{GHGheb|text=אֵינָם|translate=they are not}}, &c. When the accompanying predicate is a verb, it follows again (see l) in the form of a participle, since {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} always introduces a noun-clause, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=5|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵינֶ֫נִּי נׄתֵן|translate=I will not give}}; 8:17, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=32}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|n}}
Rem. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=4|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵין אֲנִי}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֵינֶ֫נִּי}} is due to its being co-ordinate with three other (substantival) subjects; these are again expressly summed up in {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽין־אֲנַחְנוּ}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hag|chapter=2|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵין אֶתְכֶם}} the pronominal complement of {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} appears<section end=par152 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

505.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par152 />to follow with the sign of the accusative;<ref>According to De Lagarde, ''Novae psalterii graeci editionis specimen'', p. 26, {{GHGheb|text=יְשׁוּעָ֫תָה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=3|verse=3}} is also an accusative after {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}}.</ref> but most probably we should read with the LXX {{GHGheb|text=שֻֽׁבְכֶם}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֶתְכֶם}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|o}}
(4) The fact that {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} (like {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִן}}) always includes the idea of a verb (''is not, was not'', &c.) led finally to such a predominance of the verbal element, that the original character of {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} as a construct state (but cf. i above) was forgotten, and accordingly it is very frequently separated from its noun (substantive or participle); especially so by the insertion of shorter words (of the nature of enclitics), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בּוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=6}}, {{GHGheb|text=לוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=11|verse=10}}, 12, {{GHGheb|text=לָהּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=30}}, {{GHGheb|text=גַּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=14|verse=3}}, {{GHGheb|text=שָׁם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=18|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=30}}; but cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=5|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=6|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, and {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} used absolutely in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=22|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=4|verse=4}}.—Hence, finally, even the transposition of {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} and its noun became possible, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=8}} and 41:15 {{GHGheb|text=וּפֹתֵר אֵין אֹתוֹ|translate=and an interpreter there is not of it}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=21|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=30|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=5|verse=17}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְאֵין}}=''neve sint''; cf. k above, on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=9}}); 30:27.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=5|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} is placed between the subject and predicate.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|p}}
Rem. 1. Like {{GHGheb|text=לֹא... כֹּל}} or {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל... לֹא}} (see b above) so also {{GHGheb|text=אֵין כֹּל}} expresses an ''absolute'' negation, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=1|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵין כָּל־חָדָשׁ|translate=there is no new thing}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=1|verse=4}} (cf. also {{GHGheb|text=אֵין מְא֫וּמָה|translate=there is nothing}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=18|verse=43}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=5|verse=13}}); as also {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־... אֵין}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=19}}; cf. {{GHGheb|text=מְא֫וּמָה אֵין}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=6}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|q}}
2. Undoubtedly akin to {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} in origin is the negative syllable {{GHGheb|text=אִי}} occurring in the two compounds {{GHGheb|text=אִי כָבוֹד}} (as a proper name, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=21}}; Baer {{GHGheb|text=אִֽי־כָבוֹד}}) and {{GHGheb|text=אִֽי־נָקִי|translate=not innocent}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=30}}; but the proper name {{GHGheb|text=אִֽיתָמָר}} is doubtful, and the fem. {{GHGheb|text=אִיזֶ֫בֶל}} very doubtful. In Ethiopic this {{GHGheb|text=אִי}} is the most common form of negation, prefixed even to verbs.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|r}}
(''d'') {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֫רֶם|translate=not yet}}, when referring to past time is used, as a rule ({{GHGpar|107|c}}), with the imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל... טֶ֫רֶם|translate=none}}... ''yet''; see b and p above; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=45|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=3}}; with the imperfect in the sense of a present, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=הֲטֶ֫רֶם תֵּדַע|translate=knowest thou not yet?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=30}}; but cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=15}}, and {{GHGheb|text=בְּטֶ֫רֶם}} with the perfect in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=90|verse=2}} (but see {{GHGpar|107|c}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=8|verse=25}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|s}}
(''e'') {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫פֶס}} (prop. a substantive, ''cessation'') ''no longer'', including the verbal idea of ''existing'', cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=6}}, 14, 46:9; used absolutely, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=6|verse=10}} in the question {{GHGheb|text=הַאֶ֫פֶס עוֹד אִישׁ|translate=is there none left?}} &c., {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=9|verse=3}}; frequently also in the sense of ''non nisi''; with {{GHGheb|text=־ִי}} paragogic ({{GHGpar|90|m}}) {{GHGheb|text=אַפְסִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=8}}, 10, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=2|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲנִי וְאַפְסִי עוֹד|translate=I}} am, ''and there is none else''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|t}}
(''f'') {{GHGheb|text=בַּל}},<ref>Evidently from {{GHGheb|text=בָּלָה|translate=to waste away}}, from which stem also {{GHGheb|text=בְּלִי}} and {{GHGheb|text=בֶּ֫לֶת}} (whence {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְתִּי}} {{GHGpar|90|m}}), originally substantives, are formed.</ref> in poetic and prophetic style, and with a certain emphasis,={{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}, is used with the imperfect, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=26|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=33|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, 23 (immediately afterwards with a perfect); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=7|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=49|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=10|verse=30}} (but {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=21}} before the jussive,={{GHGheb|text=אַל־}}); before an adjective, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=24|verse=23}}; before a preposition, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=16|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=23|verse=7}}.

(''g'') {{GHGheb|text=בְּלִי}} with a perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=6}}; with an imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=18}}; to negative a participle, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=7|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=19|verse=4}}; to negative an adjective, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=21}}.

(''h'') {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְתִּי}} to negative an adjective, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=26}}; on {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְתִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=3}}, see x; on<section end=par152 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

506.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="BerdeGaraiko" /></noinclude><section begin="par152" />{{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי}} as the regular negative with the infinitive construct, see {{GHGpar|114|s}}; on {{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי}} as a conjunction, see x below.

On {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} as a negative particle in oaths (''verily not''), see {{GHGpar|149|c}} above.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|u}}
Rem. on {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּלִי}}. To the category of negative sentences belongs also the expression of negative attributes by means of {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּלִי|translate=not}} (both so used almost exclusively in poetic language) or {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} with a following substantive, mostly in the simplest form of circumstantial clause; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=23|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=בּ֫קֶֹר לֹא עָבוֹת|translate=a morning}} when there are ''not clouds'', i.e. ''a cloudless morning''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=26|verse=2|hidebook=1}}<sup> ''b''</sup>, 38:26 ({{GHGheb|text=לֹא־אִישׁ|translate=where no man is}}, i.e. ''uninhabited''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=2|verse=30}}, 32 {{GHGheb|text=לֹא בָנִים|translate=childless}}; so also {{GHGheb|text=בְּלִי}} e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=24|verse=10}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=88|verse=5}} ''I am as a man'' {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽין־אֱיָל|translate=there is not help}}, i.e. ''like a helpless man''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=9|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽין־קֵץ|translate=endless}}; 47:1, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=7|verse=11}}; {{GHGheb|text=אֵֽין־מִסְפָּר|translate=countless}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=6|verse=8}}, &c., but usually ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=25}}, &c.) like a proper circumstantial clause (cf. {{GHGpar|141|e}}) connected by {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְאֵֽין־מִסְפָּר}}.—Less frequently such periphrases take the form of relative clauses (cf. {{GHGpar|155|e}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=30|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא עֹזֵר לָ֫מוֹ}} they ''for whom there is no helper'', i.e. ''the helpless'' (but probably {{GHGheb|text=עֹזֵר}} is only an intrusion from 29:12, and we should read {{GHGheb|text=עֹצֵר}} ''without any one’s restraining them''; in 29:12 translate ''the fatherless and him that had none to help him''; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=72|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=וְאֵֽין־ע׳}} is used in the same sense); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=1|verse=14}}; with {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=9}} ''thy work'' is that of a man ''who hath no hands''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=9|verse=11}} ''out of the waterless pit''.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=9|verse=13}} (perhaps also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=14|verse=7}}; but see Delitzsch on the passage) a verbal-clause is used co-ordinately in this way as a periphrasis for an adjective.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|v}}
How far such compounds finally came to be regarded by the language simply as negative adjectives, may be seen partly from the fact that they (as also relative clauses analogous to the above) are frequently co-ordinated with real adjectives, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=72|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=12}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=59|verse=10}}, where {{GHGheb|text=כְּאֵֽין־עֵינַ֫יִם}} is parallel with {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽעִוְרִים}}; partly from their being introduced by the sign of the dative {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=29}} (= ''and to the powerless''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=26|verse=2}}<sup> ''a''.3</sup>, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=8|verse=10}}.

---- 

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|w}}
(''i'') {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־|translate=lest, that not}}, at the beginning of a clause expressing a fear or precaution, hence especially after such ideas as ''fearing'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=12}}, &c. (cf. δείδω μή, ''vereor ne''), ''taking heed'', frequently after {{GHGheb|text=הִשָּׁ֫מֶר}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִשָּֽׁמְרוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, &c., ''taking care'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=10|verse=23}}, &c. Not infrequently the idea on which {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־}} depends, is only virtually contained in the main clause, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=19}} ''I cannot escape to the mountain'' (because I am afraid), {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־תִּדְבָּקַנִי הָֽרָעָה|translate=lest some evil overtake me}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=11|hidebook=1}}; also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=34}} from the rhetorical question ''how shall I... ?'' we must understand ''I cannot'', governing {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן}}. This is especially the case after an appeal to do or not to do an action by which something may be prevented (in which case {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־}} is simply equivalent to the final ''ne''); cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=18}} (where {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־|translate=lest}} is separated from the verb by a strongly emphasized substantive); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=15|verse=12}} after ''swear unto me''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=24|verse=18}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=22}} ''and now, lest he put forth his hand'', &c., {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־}} is to be regarded as virtually dependent on a cohortative, which immediately afterwards (verse 23) is changed into an historic tense; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=31|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=4|hidebook=1}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=13|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=13|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=27|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=38|verse=17}}, in every case after {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אָמַ֫רְתִּי}}, {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אָמַר}}, &c.=''I thought'', &c., ''I must beware lest'', &c.

Rem. According to {{GHGpar|107|q}}, {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן־}} is naturally followed by the imperfect; for the exceptions, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=16}}, see {{GHGpar|107|q}}, note 3; cf. moreover, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=10|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=רְאוּ פֶּן־יֶשׁ־פֹּה|translate=look lest there be here}}, &c.
<section end="par152" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

507.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par152 />{{GHGmargin-letter|152|x}}
(''k'') {{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי|translate=that... not}}, with the imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=14}} (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=23|verse=14}} read the infinitive {{GHGheb|text=שׁוּב}} for {{GHGheb|text=שָׁ֫בוּ}}, in 27:8 {{GHGheb|text=יָבֹ֫אוּ}} for {{GHGheb|text=בֹּ֫אוּ}}). In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְתִּי ירָאוּ}} is a relative clause governed by {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}= ''according to'' things which ''they have not seen''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|y}}
'''2.''' Two negatives in the same sentence do not neutralize each other (as in ''nonnulli, non nemo''), but make the negation the more emphatic (like οὐκ οὐδείς, οὐκ οὐδαμῶς, ''nulli—non, nemo non''); e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=2|verse=2}} (if the text is correct) {{GHGheb|text=בְּטֶ֫רֶם לֹֽא־יָבוֹא|translate=before there shall}} (not) ''come''.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=10|verse=21}} {{GHGheb|text=אֵין־כֶּ֫סֶף}} goes with what precedes and must be emended, with the LXX and Lucian, to {{GHGheb|text=כִּי הַכֶּ֫סֶף}}.</ref> This especially applies to the compounds formed by the union of {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} or {{GHGheb|text=בְּלִי}} with {{GHGheb|text=מִן־|translate=without}} ({{GHGpar|119|y}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=9}} (6:11) {{GHGheb|text=מֵאֵין יוֹשֵׁב}} (for which in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=15}} {{GHGheb|text=מִבְּלִי ישֵׁב}}), prop. ''without no inhabitant'', i.e. ''so that no inhabitant is left there''. On the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=50|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=מֵאֵין מַ֫יִם}} the {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} is causative, ''because there is no water''; as also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=14|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=הֲמִבְּלִי אֵין־|translate=is it because there were no...?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=1|verse=3}}, 6, 16. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=מִבְּלִי אֲשֶׁר לֹא|translate=except that}} (''yet so that man cannot'', &c.).

{{GHGmargin-letter|152|z}}
'''3.''' The negative sometimes extends its influence from the first to a second negative sentence parallel with it (which may or may not have {{GHGterm|Wāw}}) ; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=3}} ''talk not so much arrogancy''; ''let'' (not) ''boasting come out of your mouth''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=43}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=19|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=22|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, 15 f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=7|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=23|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=27|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=38|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=47|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=47}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=9|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=13|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=35|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=38|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=44|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=75|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=28|verse=17}} (so {{GHGheb|text=לָ֫מָּה לֹא|translate=why... not?}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=11}} also affects the parallel clause).<section end=par152 />

<section begin=par153 />{{GHGpar-heading|153|Restrictive and Intensive Clauses}}

The particles {{GHGheb|text=אַךְ}}, {{GHGheb|text=רַק|translate=only}}, serve to introduce restrictive clauses, and {{GHGheb|text=גַּם}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַף|translate=also, besides, even}}, intensive clauses. It is to be observed that the force of these particles does not necessarily affect the word which immediately follows (as is the case with {{GHGheb|text=אַךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=15|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=רַק}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=3|verse=2}}; even {{GHGheb|text=הֲרַק אַךְ|translate=hath he indeed only?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=12|verse=2}}; {{GHGheb|text=גַּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=34}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=11}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַף}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=15|verse=17}}), but very frequently extends to the whole of the following sentence. Thus with {{GHGheb|text=אַךְ}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=17|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=17|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=14|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=6|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=רַק}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=13|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=גַּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=21|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=גַּם הִנֵּה}}), 44:10; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=22|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=9|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=17|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=20|verse=11|hidebook=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַף}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=14|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=4|hidebook=1}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=1|verse=10}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=2|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=גַּם}} is placed before two co-ordinate sentences, although, strictly speaking, it applies only to the second. Cf. the analogous examples in {{GHGpar|150|m}}.<section end=par153 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

508.text:
{{GHGpar-heading|154|Sentences connected by Wāw}} {{GHGmargin-letter|154|a}} {{GHGterm|Wāw copulativum}}For further particulars of the use of {{GHGterm|wāw copulativum}}, see Gesenius’ ''Thesaurus'', i. 393 ff. On its use in the co-ordination of similar tenses and moods (e.g. five imperfects consecutive in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=34}}, five perfects with {{GHGheb|text=וְגַם}}) as well as of dissimilar tenses and moods, the remarks made in the treatment of the tenses will suffice. With regard to the connexion of single ''nouns'' by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} (which strictly speaking is always really a contraction of so many clauses into a single sentence) the following observations may be made:—

(''a'') Contrary to English usage, which in lengthy enumerations uses the ''and'' to connect only the last member of the series, in Hebrew ''polysyndeton'' is customary, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=16}} wāw copulativum six times, 24:35 seven times, 15:19 ff. nine times, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=7|verse=24}} ten times. Sometimes, however, only the last two words are joined (so in a series of three members, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=5|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=26|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=39|hidebook=1}}, &c.; the last three out of a series of four, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=26}}); less frequently only the first two, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=45|verse=9}}; cf. {{GHGpar|132|d}}. The formula {{GHGheb|text=תְּמוֹל שִׁלְשׁוֹם|translate=yesterday}} (and) ''the day before yesterday'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=5|verse=8}}, &c., is always without the copula. On the other hand, the ''constructio asyndetos'' in a series of verbs is used as a rhetorical expedient to produce a hurried and so an impassioned description; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5|verse=27}} ''at her feet he bowed, he fell, he lay''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=10|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=14|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=45|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=28|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=2|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=5|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, &c.

(''b'') Frequently {{GHGterm|wāw copulativum}} is also ''explanatory'' (like ''isque, et—quidem'', and the German ''und zwar'', English ''to wit''), and is then called {{GHGterm|wāw explicativum}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=4}} and (i.e. ''namely'') ''of the fat thereof'' (unless it is simply copulative); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=24|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=25|verse=12|hidebook=1}} (''to wit two''); 27:14, 28:23, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=17|verse=3}} (in {{GHGheb|text=וּמַסֵּכָה}}; here as often elsewhere, to introduce an explanatory gloss, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=17|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=3|verse=15}}, and especially P. Haupt, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|SBOT.|Sacred Books of the Old Testament, ed. by P. Haupt. Lpz. and Baltimore, 1893 ff.}}}} Isaiah, p. 90, l. 21 ff.), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=34}} ''and that too with the bear''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=57|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=17|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=3|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, Ze 9:9, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=3|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=8|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=23|verse=10}} (but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=3}} the {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} before {{GHGheb|text=בְּעִירוֹ}} is to be omitted with the LXX); cf. also such combinations as {{GHGheb|text=וְעַד}}—{{GHGheb|text=מִן|translate=from... and even to...}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, 11, &c.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=11}} (see Driver on the passage), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=23}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=ו}} is equivalent to ''yea, and''; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=7}} ''even''.

{{GHGheb|text=וְ}} is used to express emphasis (=''and especially''), e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהֵֽרֹנֵךְ}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=1}}, perhaps also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=17}} ''yea'', a whole ''host''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=16|verse=14}}.—An undoubted example of what is called {{GHGterm|wāw concomitantiae}} occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=12}} ''a seething pot'' {{GHGheb|text=וְאַגְמֹן|translate=with}} burning ''rushes''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=10}} (''with your little ones''), 12:8, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=1|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=5}}. In Arabic this {{GHGterm|wāw concom.}} is followed by the accusative.

{{GHGheb|text=וְ-וְ}} is used in the sense of ''both''—''and'' in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=76|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=1|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=8|verse=13|hidebook=1}}. On {{GHGheb|text=וְ-וְ}} as meaning ''sive''—''sive'', cf. {{GHGpar|162|b}}.

(''c'') See the Lexicon on adverbs used in a copulative sense, such as {{GHGheb|text=גַּם|translate=also, moreover}}, summing up a number, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גַּם־שְׁנַ֫יִם|translate=both together}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=45}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=17|verse=15}}; {{GHGheb|text=גַּם־כֹּל|translate=all together}}; as an intensive ''and'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=30|verse=8}}; cf. also such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=12}} ''see, yea see!'' {{GHGheb|text=גַּם-גַּם}} or {{GHGheb|text=גַּם-וְגַם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=44}}=''both''—''and''; {{GHGheb|text=גַּם}} occurs three times in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=25}} and 32:20; also {{GHGheb|text=אַף}}, which is generally still more intensive, in the sense of ''also, in addition to this, even'', and belongs rather to poetry, and to the later language; frequently also equivalent to a mere ''and'', but sometimes adversative ''but now'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=44|verse=10}}, &c.; and {{GHGheb|text=אַף-אַף}} (also three times), equivalent to ''both—and''; cf. {{GHGheb|text=וְאַף גַּם|translate=and even}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=44}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַף־כִּי}} prop. ''add to this also that'', equivalent to ''not to mention'', according to the context either ''quanto magis'' or ''quanto minus''. ({{GHGheb|text=וְ}}) serves to connect two or more sentences, or single words (on its various vocalization, cf. {{GHGpar|104|d}}–g). Its use, however, is by no means restricted merely to joining sentences which

509.text:
are actually co-ordinate. Frequently the language employs merely the simple connexion by {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, even to introduce an antithesis ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=2|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=25}}, and very frequently in circumstantial noun-clauses), or when one of the two clauses is not co-ordinated, but subordinated to the other. On the use of {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} to introduce circumstantial clauses, cf. especially {{GHGpar|141|e}} and {{GHGpar|142|d}}; introducing causal clauses, {{GHGpar|158|a}}; comparative clauses, {{GHGpar|161|a}}; final clauses, {{GHGpar|165|a}}; consecutive clauses, {{GHGpar|166|a}}. On {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}, cf. {{GHGpar|143|d}}, and the sections there cited; on the use of {{GHGterm|Wāw}} in numerical sayings, cf. {{GHGpar|134|s}}. {{GHGmargin-letter|154|b}} Rem. Sometimes wāw copulativum joins a sentence apparently to what immediately precedes, but in reality to a sentence which is suppressed and which must, therefore, be supplied from the context. So especially {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} with imperatives to express inferences, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=וְשַֽׁאֲלִי|translate=ask now rather}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=18|verse=32}} ''for I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth''..., {{GHGheb|text=וָהָשִׁיבוּ|translate=wherefore turn yourselves}}. Also at the beginning of a speech in loose connexion with an act or speech of another person, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=4|verse=14}}, 41, 7:13, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=25|verse=9}}; cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=7|verse=7}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְלוּ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=4|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=7}}. Sometimes the suppression of the protasis is due to passionate excitement or haste, which does not allow time for full expression; this is especially illustrated by {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=12|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=3|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=וְלוּ}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=22|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=22}} ({{GHGheb|text=וָלָ֫מָּה}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=1|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=19|hidebook=1}} (cf. verse 2); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=6}} (at the same time a circumstantial clause ''whereas I=and yet I have'', &c.); cf. also a new clause beginning with the formula of wishing {{GHGheb|text=וּמִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=29}}; on the disconnected use of {{GHGheb|text=וָלֹא}} and {{GHGheb|text=וָיֵשׁ}} cf. § 159 dd.
{{GHGpar-heading|155|Relative Clauses}}
See V. Baumann, {{GHGcite|title=Hebräische Relativsätze}}, Leipzig, 1894 (cf. the heading of § 138 above); G. Bergsträsser, ‘Das hebr. Präfix {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}},’ ''ZATW'' 1909, p. 40 ff.In this exhaustive article the author shows that between {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}} (on the pronunciation see § 36) and {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} there is syntactically no primary difference, but only a secondary distinction which arose in the course of the development of the language, namely that {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} is preferred in combinations which are customary in the old literary language, and {{GHGheb|text=שׁ}} in those which are derived from the popular language or from Aramaic.
{{GHGmargin-letter|155|a}} '''1.''' By {{GHGpar|138|a}}, e, relative clauses are divided into two classes: those which are used for the nearer definition of a noun (substantive or pronoun), and those which are not dependent on a noun. The former may be called ''incomplete'', the latter ''complete'' relative clauses. {{GHGmargin-letter|155|b}} Complete relative clauses, as a rule (see the exceptions under n), are introduced by the originally demonstrative pronoun {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}; see further in {{GHGpar|138|e}}. Similarly, incomplete relative clauses may also be introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}, or by some other demonstrative pronoun; see further in {{GHGpar|138|a}} and g–k. Very frequently, however, especially

510.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par155 />in poetic style, the attributive relation is expressed by simple co-ordination.<ref>The old view that all these cases arise from the ''omission'' of {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} is incorrect. These co-ordinated attributive clauses are rather a mere subdivision of the various kinds of circumstantial clauses (see § 156) which may be attached to a {{GHGterm|nomen regens}}. Cf. in English ''this is the letter'' (which) ''he wrote to me''.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|c}}
The governing substantive or pronoun is frequently (in certain cases ''always'') resumed by a pronominal suffix or an adverb. The resumption may, however, be omitted, just as in relative clauses introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}, &c.; see {{GHGpar|138|f}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|d}}
In Arabic a distinction is made between relative clauses used for the nearer definition of a ''determinate'' substantive (''ṣila''), and those which are attached to an ''indeterminate'' substantive (''ṣifa''). The former must be introduced by the demonstrative pronoun ''allaḏî'', the latter are always simply co-ordinated. The same distinction was no doubt originally observed in Hebrew, since simply co-ordinated relative clauses are most commonly found after ''indeterminate'' substantives (see the examples below), and in cases like {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=49}} ({{GHGheb|text=גּוֹי אֲשֶׁר לֹֽא־תִשְׁמַע לְשֹׁנוֹ|translate=a nation whose tongue thou shalt not understand}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=66|verse=13}}, and especially {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=11}}), the addition of {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} is explained from the special stress laid on the indeterminate substantive,<ref>So Baumann, op. cit., p. 14 f., following Böttcher, ''Lehrbuch'', ii. 80.</ref> ''a nation of such a kind, thou understandest not their tongue''. On the other hand, in poetic style at least, {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} is somewhat frequently omitted even after a determinate noun, but only rarely in prose (except by the Chronicler; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=9|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=12|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=29|verse=1|hidebook=1}} (read prob. {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֶחַד}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=15|verse=11}}; after {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=29|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=18|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=30|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=31|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=1|verse=5}}, but also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=4}}; for further instances, see Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}<sup>8</sup>, p. 537, no. 30); so {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=8|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=20|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=12}} (=which way), so {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=18|verse=23}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=13|verse=23}}; after a pronominal subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=9}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=52|verse=12}} for {{GHGheb|text=עָמַד}} read {{GHGheb|text=עֹמֵד}} with the LXX.

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|e}}
'''2.''' If the nearer definition of a substantive or pronoun is effected by simple co-ordination of the relative clause, it may take the form—

(''a'') Of a noun-clause, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=21}} ''a man of the hill country of Ephraim'' {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫בַע שְׁמוֹ|translate=whose name was Sheba}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=6|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=15|hidebook=1}} ''with princes'' {{GHGheb|text=זָהָב לָהֶם|translate=that had gold}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=11|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=22|verse=11}}; when referring to a noun-suffix, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=49|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=זֶה דַרְכָּם כֵּ֫סֶל לָ֫סוֹ|translate=this is the way of them who have}} (self-)''confidence''.—On periphrases of this kind to express negative attributes, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=עַל־אֶ֫רֶץ לֹא־אִישׁ|translate=on a land}} where ''no man'' is, see {{GHGpar|152|u}}, and cf. for this very short form of the relative clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּאֶ֫רֶץ לֹא לָהֶם|translate=in a land}} that belongs ''not to them''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=17}} ({{GHGheb|text=לַשֵּׁדִים לֹא אֱלֹהַּ}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=1|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=26|verse=17}} ({{GHGheb|text=לֹא־לוֹ}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|f}}
(''b'') Of a verbal clause.

Here we must distinguish the cases in which the retrospective pronoun—

(1) Is the subject of the relative clause, and is contained in the<section end=par155 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

511.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par155 />verb; so after a determinate substantive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=34|verse=9}} ''happy is the man'' {{GHGheb|text=יֶֽחֱסֶה־בּוֹ|translate=that trusteth in him}}; Jb 3<sup>3 ''b''</sup> {{GHGheb|text=הַלַּ֫יְלָה אָמַ֫ר|translate=the night which said}}; after {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=71|verse=18}}; referring to a vocative, which is determinate in itself even without the article, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=54|verse=1}}, or to a noun-suffix (see under e), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=16|verse=4}}; after an indeterminate substantive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=12}} ''it is a fire'' (that) ''devoureth unto Abaddon''; Dt 32<sup>17 ''b''</sup>, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=55|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=56|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=68|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=78|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=30|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=28|verse=9}}; referring to the suffix in {{GHGheb|text=הִנְנִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=28|verse=16}}, prop. ''behold me, who have laid'', &c., but perhaps the participle {{GHGheb|text=יׄסֵד}} is to be read; 29:14, 38:5 (but probably again the participle {{GHGheb|text=יוֹסֵף}} should be read instead of the imperfect); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=25|verse=7}}. The relative clause is used in this way especially to supply the place of an adjective, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=זְאֵב יִטְרָ֑ף|translate=a wolf that ravineth}}, i.e. ''a ravining wolf''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=51|verse=12}}; to express a negative quality, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=4|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=עָם לֹֽא־יָבִין|translate=an undiscerning people}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|g}}
Rem. Very frequently such relative sentences are attached to substantives which have the particle of comparison {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=כְּעֶ֫בֶד יִשְׁאַף־צֵל|translate=as a servant}} that ''earnestly desireth the shadow'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=62|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=23|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=6|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=42|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=83|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=16|hidebook=1}}; so also after {{GHGheb|text=כְּמוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=58|verse=5}}; after a determinate substantive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=53|verse=7}} (but the better reading is {{GHGheb|text=כְּשֶׂה}} without the article), 61:10 f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=49|verse=13}}, 21, 125:1; see also the examples under h. Sometimes it seems simpler in such cases, to take the verb directly as predicate to the preceding substantive, and to explain {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}} (for {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽאֲשֶׁר}}; see ''Comparative Clauses'', {{GHGpar|161|b}}) as a conjunction—a view which even Hupfeld was ready to accept, at least as regards {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=90|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=125|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=53|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=61|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, but it can hardly be right.

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|h}}
(2) The cases in which the retrospective pronoun represents an accusative of the object, or would do so if not suppressed, as it usually is in such cases in relative clauses with {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}, cf. {{GHGpar|138|b}}. Examples with the retrospective pronoun are, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהִים לֹא יְדָעוּם|translate=gods whom they knew not}} (see also the end of the verse); after a substantive with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}(see above, g), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=23|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=13|verse=28}}. Without a retrospective pronoun, after a determinate substantive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=8|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=33|verse=12}} (preceded by a relative clause with {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=28|verse=1}}. Other examples of this kind, though the article is omitted according to poetic usage, are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=15|verse=7}} ({{GHGheb|text=יִתְרָה עָשָׁה}}, for which {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=48|verse=36}} {{GHGheb|text=יִתְרָת עָשָׂה}} with the substantive in the construct state governing the relative clause, see {{GHGpar|130|d}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=7|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=51|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=21}}.—Without the retrospective pronoun, after an indeterminate substantive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=רִצְפָּה בְמֶּלְקָחַ֫יִם לָקַח מֵעַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ|translate=a live coal which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=16}} (48:17, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=25|verse=12}}, all after {{GHGheb|text=בְּדֶ֫רֶךְ}}; but {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּדֶ֫רֶךְ־זוּ תֵלֵךְ}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=64|verse=2}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=10|verse=5}} (in 6:1 the same clause with {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}); moreover, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=14|verse=18}} read with the LXX {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־אֶ֫רֶץ לֹא יָדָֽעוּ|translate=into a land}} (that) ''they know not''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|i}}
(3) The cases in which the retrospective pronoun is dependent on a preposition, or its place is taken by the adverb {{GHGheb|text=שָׁם}}, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=6}} end.<section end=par155 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

512.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par155 />Thus after a determinate substantive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=צוּרִי אֶֽחֱסֶה־בּוֹ|translate=my rock in which I take refuge}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=1}}; in Jb 3<sup>3 ''a''</sup> also, the omission of the article with {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם}} is only a poetic licence. After an indeterminate substantive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=6}}, last clause but one; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=2}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|k}}
In this case also the retrospective word is not infrequently suppressed, giving rise to extremely short, bold expressions, such as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=51|verse=1}} ''look unto the rock'' {{GHGheb|text=חֻצַּבְתֶּם}} (whence) ''ye were hewn, and to the hole of the pit'' {{GHGheb|text=נֻקַּרְתֶּם}} (whence) ''ye were digged''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=27}} ''the devices'' (where-with) ''ye act violently against me''.—A retrospective adverb is suppressed in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=19}} ''where is the way'' (to the place where) ''the light dwelleth?'' cf. 38:24.

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|l}}
Rem. 1. The omission of the retrospective word occurs most frequently in relative clauses which are governed by the construct state of a preceding substantive (especially an expression of time) and hence are virtually in the genitive. In addition to the instances already given in {{GHGpar|130|d}}, cf. the following: after {{GHGheb|text=בְּיוֹם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=7|verse=35}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=56|verse=10}}; after {{GHGheb|text=מִיּוֹם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=36|verse=2}}; after simple {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=56|verse=4}} ({{GHGheb|text=יוֹם אִירָא|translate=on the day}} when ''I am afraid''); after {{GHGheb|text=בְּעֵת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=29|verse=27}} ({{GHGheb|text=בְּעֵת הֵחֵל הָֽעוֹלָה|translate=at the time}} when ''the burnt offering began''); 20:22, 24:11, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=17}}; after {{GHGheb|text=לְעֵת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=35}}; after {{GHGheb|text=עַד־עֵת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=5|verse=2}}; after {{GHGheb|text=מֵעֵת}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=4|verse=8}} ''thou hast put gladness in my heart more than'' (their gladness) ''at the time'' (when) ''their corn and their wine are increased''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|m}}
2. The agreement ({{GHGpar|138|d}}) of the retrospective pronoun with a pronominal regens in the 1st or 2nd person also takes place in a simple co-ordinated relative clause in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=14}} ''who art thou'' (that) ''criest?'' Cf., however, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=63|verse=19}} ''we are become'' as they ''over whom'' ({{GHGheb|text=בָּם}} not {{GHGheb|text=בָּ֫נוּ}}) ''thou no longer bearest rule''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|n}}
'''3.''' Occasionally—chiefly in poetic or otherwise elevated style—even ''independent'' relative clauses are simply co-ordinated with a regens, whereas we should expect them always to be preceded by a demonstrative pronoun, on the analogy of the examples in {{GHGpar|138|e}}. The suppressed pronoun would stand—

(''a'') As subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=24}} ''an abomination'' (is he) ''that chooseth you'' (but read perhaps {{GHGheb|text=לִבְחֹר}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=30|verse=13}}, cf. {{GHGpar|152|u}}.

(''b'') As object, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=2}}, with a retrospective pronoun; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=2|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=וְכִסָּה|translate=and}} him ''that covereth'' (or read {{GHGheb|text=וְכֹסֶה|translate=?}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=12}} ''I delivered... the fatherless also, and'' him ''that had none to help him''.

(''c'') In the genitive governed by a substantive (cf. {{GHGpar|130|d}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=4|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלַח־נָא בְּיַד־תִּשְׁלָֽח|translate=send, I pray thee, by the hand of}} him ''whom thou wilt send'', i.e. by the hand of some one else; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=65|verse=5}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=8|verse=32}}, verbal-clauses after {{GHGheb|text=אֵשְׁרֵי|translate=O the happiness of}} the man, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=81|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=141|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=14}}; after {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=4}}, but we must certainly read here, with the Samaritan and LXX, {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־אֲשֶׁר יֶשׁ־לוֹ}} as in verses 5 and 8; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=4}}; verbal-clauses after {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=29|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=30|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=31|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=1|verse=5}}.

(''d'') Governed by a preposition; so verbal-clauses after {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲרֵי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=8}}; after {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}} (=''to the place where''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=15|verse=12}}, but {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=23|verse=20}} before the same<section end=par155 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

513.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par155 />verb {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר}}; after {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=1|verse=4}} ({{GHGheb|text=בַּֽהֵכִין}}={{GHGheb|text=בְּהַֽה׳}}=''to the place where''); after {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=65|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=לְלוֹא שָׁאָ֫לוּ}} by them ''that asked not'' for me... {{GHGheb|text=לְלֹא בִקְשֻׁ֫נִי}} them ''that sought me not''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=3}} that which ''they have not seen'', but the text is hardly correct; after {{GHGheb|text=עַל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=136}}, cf. {{GHGpar|158|b}}; after {{GHGheb|text=עִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=16|verse=9}}.—A noun-clause follows {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=8|verse=10}}. An analogous instance in Aramaic is {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=5|verse=14}} ''to'' one ''whose name was Sheshbazzar'' [so in the papyri, see the Lexicon, p. 1116<sup>a</sup>].<section end=par155 />

<section begin=par156 />{{GHGpar-heading|156|Circumstantial Clauses}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|156|a}}
'''1.''' The statement of the particular circumstances under which a subject appears as performing some action, or under which an action (or an occurrence) is accomplished, is made especially (apart from relative clauses, see § 155) by means of noun-clauses connected by {{GHGterm|Wāw}} with a following subject (see further on this kind of ''circumstantial clause'' in {{GHGpar|141|e}}), and by verbal-clauses (see {{GHGpar|142|d}}). Very frequently, however, such statements of the particular circumstances are subordinated to the main clause by being simply attached, without {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, either as noun-clauses, sometimes extremely short (see c), or as verbal-clauses (see d–g).

{{GHGmargin-letter|156|b}}
Rem. Among relative clauses of this kind the commonest are the various noun-clauses, which are most closely subordinated to a preceding substantive without {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=12}}; also statements of weight, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=22}}; of name, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=1}} (also introduced by {{GHGheb|text=וּשְׁמוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=1}}, &c., or {{GHGheb|text=וּשְׁמָהּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, &c.); of a condition of body, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=7}}, and others.—Noun-clauses which begin with {{GHGterm|wāw}} and the ''predicate'' have a somewhat more independent character than those introduced by {{GHGterm|wāw}} and the ''subject''<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=31}} this form of sequence appears to be selected for another purpose, ''and indeed our enemies are judges'' thereof, with {{GHGterm|wāw emphatic}}; to take it as a circumstantial clause is too artificial.</ref> ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=1}}, &c.). The former, however, are also to be regarded as circumstantial clauses, in so far as they describe a ''state'' which is simultaneous with the principal action; thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=7}} ''I will not be an healer'', {{GHGheb|text=וּבְבֵיתִי אֵין לֶ֫חֶם|translate=while in my house is neither bread nor clothing}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=6}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=7|verse=7}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=16|verse=1|hidebook=1}}. Cf. also the instances in {{GHGpar|152|l}} of {{GHGheb|text=וְאֵין}} followed by a participle, as {{GHGheb|text=וְאֵין מַצִּיל}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|156|c}}
'''2.''' Characteristic examples of circumstantial ''noun''-clauses are {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=8}} ''and pitched his tent'' {{GHGheb|text=בֵּֽית־אֵל מִיָם וְהָעַי מִקֶּ֫דֶם}} with ''Bethel on the west and Ai on the east''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=14}} ''through the heart of Absalom'', {{GHGheb|text=עוֹדֶנּ֫וּ חַי}} while ''he'' was ''yet alive''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=30|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=9|verse=2}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=3|verse=8}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=3|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=14|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=23|verse=10}}; with the predicate preceding, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=32|verse=8}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=29}} a noun-clause serves to announce a state in the future.—We may also include here certain set phrases, as {{GHGheb|text=פָּנִים אֶל־פָּנִים|translate=face to face}} (prop. while ''face'' was turned ''towards face''), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=34|verse=10}},<section end=par156 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

514.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par156 />&c.;<ref>The expression {{GHGheb|text=הִתְרָאָה פָנִים|translate=to look one another in the face}} (i.e. to contend in combat) {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=14|verse=8}}, 11, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=25|verse=17}}, 21, is probably only a shortened form for {{GHGheb|text=הִתְרָאָה פָנִים אֶל־פָּנִים}}.</ref> so also ''to cast oneself down'', {{GHGheb|text=אַפַּ֫יִם אָֽרְצָה|translate=the face}} being turned ''to the earth'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=1}}, &c. (for {{GHGheb|text=אָֽרְצָה}} we find {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫רֶץ}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=23}}).<ref>That {{GHGheb|text=(אֶ֫רֶץ) אָֽרְצָה}} is really to be regarded as a virtual predicate to {{GHGheb|text=אַפַּ֫יִם}}, and not {{GHGheb|text=אַפַּ֫יִם}} as a ''casus instrumenti'', is seen from {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=23}}, where {{GHGheb|text=אַפַּ֫יִם אֶ֫רֶץ}} precedes the verb.</ref>—Cf. finally the formula {{GHGheb|text=אֵם עַל־בָּנִים|translate=mother with children}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=12}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=10|verse=14}} and {{GHGpar|119|aa}} note 2.

Rem. On circumlocutions of this kind to express negative attributes by means of short noun-clauses (complete or incomplete), cf. {{GHGpar|152|u}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|156|d}}
'''3.''' As circumstantial {{GHGterm|verbal}}-clauses,<ref>Some examples of these have been already discussed in another connexion above, {{GHGpar|120|a}}–c.</ref> we find (1) sometimes affirmative clauses (see below), but far more frequently (2) negative clauses (see f), and among these (3) a certain number of expressions which may be regarded simply as equivalent to negative adverbial ideas (see g).

Examples of (1) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=11}}<sup> ''b''</sup> woe unto them, that tarry late in the evening, {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫יִן יַדְלִיקֵם|translate=while wine inflames them}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=10|verse=24|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=31|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=7|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=4|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=5|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=21|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=62|verse=5|hidebook=1}}. The circumstantial verbal-clause is used to particularize an action which has before been expressed generally, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=48|verse=14|hidebook=1}}=''crossing his hands''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=19}}; antithetically, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=כִּחֵשׁ לוֹ|translate=wherewith however he lied unto him}}. The verbal-clause seems to assign a reason in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=7|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=מִשְׁפָּט צִוִּ֫יתָ|translate=since thou hast commanded judgement}}; a consequence in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=103|verse=5}}.<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=14}} the circumstantial verbal-clause {{GHGheb|text=שָׂם עַל־שִׁכְמָהּ}} is only due to a harmonizing transposition; read {{GHGheb|text=וְאֶת־הַיֶּ֫לֶד שׂ׳ ע׳ שׁ׳}}. According to the source used in cap. 21 Ishmael was still a young child; according to 17:25 he was about 16 or 17 years old.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|156|e}}
Rem. On the cases in which an imperfect in the sense of a final clause is subordinated to a verb of motion (generally {{GHGheb|text=קוּם}}), see {{GHGpar|120|c}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|156|f}}
Of (2), subordinate verbal-clauses with {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} (in English usually rendered by ''without'' and the gerund, if the subject be the same as in the principal clause), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=1|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יַבְדִּיל|translate=without dividing}} it ''asunder''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=34}}; {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}} with the perfect is so used in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=34|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=30|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=26}} (''without its being blown upon it''). With a different subject, equivalent to a consecutive clause in English, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=27|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹֽא־יָקֻ֫מוּ|translate=so that they shall rise up no more}}.—Moreover, verbal-clauses in the same sense (''without'' doing, &c.) are frequently connected by {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=24|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=42|verse=3|hidebook=1}}; in a concessive sense, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=33|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=44|verse=18}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|156|g}}
Of (3), cf. {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יֵדַע}} (prop. ''he knows it not'') ''unawares'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=35|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=5|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יַחְמֹל|translate=unsparingly}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=14}} (after an infinitive absolute); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=1|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=10}} (but {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא יַחְמֹל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=27|verse=22|hidebook=1}}; see f at the end); {{GHGheb|text=לֹא כִחֵ֑דוּ}} (prop. ''they hide not'') ''openly'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=9}} (but<section end=par156 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

515.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par156 />{{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא כִחֲדוּ}}); {{GHGheb|text=בְּלִי חָשָׂ֑ךְ}} (prop. ''he restrains not'') ''unceasingly'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=6}}; {{GHGheb|text=בַּל־יִמּוֹט}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=15}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=93|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=בַּל־תִּמִּוֹט}}) and {{GHGheb|text=לֹא יִמּוֹט}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=40|verse=20}} (''without tottering'') ''immovably''; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אֶמְעָ֑ד|translate=without wavering}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=26|verse=1}}.<section end=par156 />

<section begin=par157 />{{GHGpar-heading|157|Object-Clauses (Oratio Obliqua)}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|157|a}}
Clauses which depend on a transitive verb, especially on what are called {{GHGterm|verba cordis}}, i.e. verbs denoting any mental act, such as ''to see, to hear, to know, to perceive, to believe, to remember, to forget, to say, to think'', &c., may be subordinated to the governing verb without the help of a conjunction by simple juxtaposition ({{GHGpar|120|a}}), or they may be co-ordinated with it either with or without {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}} ({{GHGpar|120|d}}–h). As a rule, however, the objective clause is introduced by the conjunction {{GHGheb|text=כִּי|translate=that}}, less frequently by {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר|translate=that}}.<ref>On these clauses with {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} and generally on clauses which we should render as subordinate, cf. P. Dörwald ‘Zur hebr. Syntax’ in ''Neue Jahrbb. für Philol. und Pädag.'' 1890, p. 115 ff.</ref>

Examples:—

(''a'') Object-clauses without a conjunction.
