Besides the passages mentioned in § 120 (especially under ''e'') there are a number of examples, in which a clause depending on a {{GHGterm|verbum dicendi}} or ''sentiendi'' (the ''oratio obliqua'' of the Latin and English Grammar) is added in the form of an independent noun-clause or verbal-clause; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=אִמְרִי־נָא אֲחֹ֫תִי אָ֑תְּ|translate=say, I pray thee, thou}} art ''my sister''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=10|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=25|verse=3}}''<sup>a</sup>''<sup>.14</sup>, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=6|verse=6}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=8|verse=23}} (after {{GHGheb|text=שָׁמַע}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=9|verse=21}} (after {{GHGheb|text=יָדַע}}); verbal-clauses, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=50|verse=21}} ''thou thoughtest'' {{GHGheb|text=הֱיֽוֹת־אְהְיֶה כָמ֫וֹךָ|translate=I was surely like thyself}} [but read {{GHGheb|text=הָיוֹ}} for {{GHGheb|text=הֱיוֹת}}]; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=48}} ''what ye have seen me do''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=48|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=7|verse=2}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|157|b}}
(''b'') Object-clauses introduced by {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּרְא יְהֹוָה כִּי רַבָּה רָעַת הָֽאָדָם|translate=and the Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great}}, &c.—Direct narration also is very frequently introduced by {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} (analogous to the ὅτι ''recitativum''; frequently, indeed, with the secondary idea of a particle of asseveration, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=20|hidebook=1}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=16|hidebook=1}} f., 26:22, 29:32, 37:35, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=24}}, &c., even when the direct narration is not expressly indicated, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=31|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=51|hidebook=1}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=4}}.—On the expression of a second object by means of a clause introduced by {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}}, see {{GHGpar|117|h}}.<ref>Instead of a complete objective clause we sometimes find a kind of accusative and infinitive construction, especially after {{GHGheb|text=נָתַן}} (prop. ''to give up'') in the sense of ''to allow'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹֽא־נָתַן סִיחֹן אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל עֲבֹר בִּגְבֻלוֹ|translate=and Sihon did not suffer Israel to pass through his border}}; 20:21; followed by an infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=19}}.—Cf. also the analogous examples in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=56}} (after {{GHGheb|text=נִסָּה|translate=to venture}}; see {{GHGpar|113|d}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=20}} (after{{GHGheb|text=הָֽאֱמִין|translate=to trust}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=19|verse=4}} (after {{GHGheb|text=שָׁאַל|translate=to request}}).</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|157|c}}
(''c'') Object-clauses introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=3|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=כִּֽי־הִגִּיד לָהֶם אֲשֶׁר־הוּא יְהוּדִי|translate=for he had told them that he was a Jew}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=18|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=20|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=8|verse=12}},<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=28|verse=9}} a ''subject''-clause is thus introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} instead of the usual {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}}.</ref> even before direct narration, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=4}}. Somewhat frequently {{GHGheb|text=אֲשְׁר}} is preceded by<section end=par157 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

516.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par157 />the {{GHGterm|nota accusativi}} {{GHGheb|text=אֶת־}} (equivalent to ''the circumstance, the fact, that''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=11}}, 19, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=11|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=38|verse=3}}, but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=29|verse=15}} equivalent to ''the way in which''.<section end=par157 />

<section begin=par158 />{{GHGpar-heading|158|Causal Clauses}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|158|a}}
A complete clause, assigning the reason for statements, demands, threats, &c., sometimes follows with the simple {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=60|verse=13}} ''give us help against the adversary, and'' (for) ''vain is the help of man''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=17}} ({{GHGheb|text=וַֽאֲנִי}}), 22:12, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=23|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=12}}, perhaps also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=7|verse=10}}; or even without {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=14}}. As a rule, however, special conjunctions in various combinations are used to introduce causal clauses.

{{GHGmargin-letter|158|b}}
The most common causal conjunctions are {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן כִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=16}}, &c., and {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן אֲשֶׁר|translate=because}}, prop. ''on account of the fact that''; both, however, may also be shortened to the simple {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=20|verse=12}}, &c., or to {{GHGheb|text=כִּי|translate=because}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=14}}, 17, &c., or to {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=49|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, 27, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=42|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, 23, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=33|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=14|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=1|verse=15}}; also {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽאֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=9}}, 23. On the other hand, the simple {{GHGheb|text=יָ֫עַן}} is sometimes repeated for emphasis, {{GHGheb|text=יָ֫עַן וּבְיַ֫עַן}} (something like the German ''sintemal und alldieweil'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=43}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=10}} (without {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} 36:3); also {{GHGheb|text=עַל־אֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=3|verse=30}}, and {{GHGheb|text=עַל־כִּי}}<ref>Also {{GHGheb|text=כִּֽי־עַל־כֵּן}} prop. ''for therefore'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=33|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=26|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=10|verse=31}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=43|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=20}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}, and {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר עַל־כֵּן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=27}}, always mean ''for as much as''.</ref> {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=31|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=3|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=2|verse=14}} ''on the ground that''; {{GHGheb|text=עַל־דְּבַר אֲשֶׁר|translate=because of the circumstance that}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=23|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=עַל־כָּל־אֹדוֹת אֲשֶׁר|translate=for this very cause that}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=8}}. But just as the simple {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן}} is used for {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫עַן אֲשֶׁר}}, so also the simple {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} with the perfect stands for {{GHGheb|text=עַל־אֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=119|verse=136}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=3|verse=11}}; cf. {{GHGheb|text=עַל־בְּלִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=20}} and {{GHGheb|text=מִבְּלִי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=55}} both with the perfect, equivalent to ''because... not''.—Cf. further {{GHGheb|text=עֵ֫קֶב אֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=6}}, all with the perfect, and {{GHGheb|text=עֵ֫קֶב כִּי}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=10}} with the perfect; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=12}} with the imperfect) prop. ''in return'' for the fact ''that''; similarly again the simple {{GHGheb|text=עֵ֫קֶב}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=24}} with the perfect, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=7|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=8|verse=20|hidebook=1}} with the imperfect; finally, {{GHGheb|text=מֵֽאֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=43|verse=4}} ''arising from'' the fact ''that,= because''; {{GHGheb|text=תַּ֫חַת אֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=26|verse=21}}, &c., and {{GHGheb|text=תַּ֫חַת כִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=37}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=1|verse=29}} ''for the reason that''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|158|c}}
Rem. 1. The preposition {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} (''because of, on account of'') with the infinitive ({{GHGpar|114|e}}) is frequently used as the equivalent of a full causal clause; cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=1|verse=3}}, 6, 13, 2:1, 6. Such a construction with the infinitive may, however, according to {{GHGpar|114|r}}, be continued by means of a finite verb, in which case {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} governs the verb as a conjunction; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=1|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=עַל־הַסְגִּירָם... וְלֹא זָֽכְרוּ|translate=because they delivered up... and remembered not}}, &c.; 1:11, 2:4; without {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=14}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|158|d}}
2. The choice of tense is regulated by the general principles stated in § 106 ff., viz. the perfect (cf. especially {{GHGpar|106|f}}) refers to causes already brought fully into effect, the imperfect to those which may contingently arise; cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=7|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=8|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=33}}, where the imperfect leaves the possibility still open that the persons addressed will perhaps escape the threatened punishments by avoiding disobedience.—Cf. further, {{GHGpar|111|h}} on the imperfect consecutive, and {{GHGpar|112|nn}} on the perfect consecutive in the apodosis to causal clauses.<section end=par158 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

517.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par159 />{{GHGpar-heading|159|Conditional Sentences}}

Cf. H. Ferguson, ‘The Use of the Tenses in Conditional Sentences in Hebrew’ (''Journal of the Society of Bibl. Lit. and Exeg.'', Middletown, Conn., June and September, 1882).—P. Friedrich, ''Die hebr. Conditionalsätze'', Königsberg, 1884 (Inaug.-Diss.).—Driver, ''Use of the Tenses'', 3rd ed., p. 174 ff.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|a}}
'''1.''' The great variety of construction in conditional sentences is owing to the fact that it frequently depends on the subjective judgement of the speaker, whether he wishes a condition to be regarded as ''capable of fulfilment'' (absolutely, or at least possibly), thus including those already fulfilled, or as ''incapable of fulfilment''. On this distinction depends the choice both of the conditional particle to be used (see below), and especially (as also in Greek and Latin) of the tense. The use of the latter is naturally determined according to the general principles laid down in § 106 ff.<ref>It may, moreover, happen that a different idea is introduced in the apodosis, from that with which the protasis started—a source of many further variations.</ref> In the following sketch, for the sake of clearness, conditional sentences ''without'' conditional particles will be first discussed (under b), and afterwards sentences ''with'' these particles (under l).

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|b}}
'''2.''' The relation between condition and consequence may be expressed, as in English, by the simple juxtaposition of two clauses. At the same time, it is to be observed in general as a fundamental rule (in accordance with the original character of the two tenses), that the {{GHGterm|imperfect}}, with its equivalents (the jussive, cohortative, imperative, perfect consecutive, and participle), is used to express a condition and consequence which are regarded as being ''capable of fulfilment'' in present or future time, while the {{GHGterm|perfect}} represents a condition already fulfilled in the past, and its consequence as an accomplished fact. The other use of the perfect—to represent conditions regarded as ''impossible''—occurs only in connexion with particles.

Examples:—

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|c}}
(''a'') {{GHGterm|Imperfect}} (cf. {{GHGpar|107|x}}) in protasis and apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=22|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=28}} ff. {{GHGheb|text=יִלְקֹם֑וּן}}<ref>On the termination {{GHGheb|text=-וּן}} cf. {{GHGpar|47|m}}. In verse 28 ''b'' also {{GHGheb|text=יִשְׂבְּעוּן}} is probably to be explained from its immediately preceding the greater {{GHGterm|pause}}. These terminations in verses 28–30 and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=18}} can scarcely have any connexion with the conditional sentence, although it is strange that {{GHGheb|text=-וּן}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=32|verse=23}} appears after {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא}} in the protasis. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=32|verse=20|hidebook=1}} {{GHGheb|text=-וּן}} as before {{GHGheb|text=א}} (as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=10}} in the apodosis) is to be explained from the dislike of hiatus.</ref> {{GHGheb|text=תִּתֵּן לָתֶם}} (if) ''thou givest unto them, they gather'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=12|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=1|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=1|verse=8}}; with an interrogative imperfect in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=12}}; with the jussive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=16}}; with the cohortative, Pr. 1:23; with the perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=26|verse=10}} (''yet will he not learn righteousness''; the apodosis forcibly denies<section end=par159 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

518.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par159 />what the imperfect in the protasis had represented as still conceivable; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=8|verse=12}}); with the perfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=5}}; with the protasis suppressed, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=8}} (see {{GHGpar|107|x}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|d}}
(''b'') {{GHGterm|Jussive}} in protasis (cf. {{GHGpar|109|h}}, i) and apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=תָּֽשֶׁת־ח֫שֶׁךְ וִיהִי לָ֑יְלָה}} (if) ''thou makest darkness, it is night''; imperfect in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=104|verse=29}}<sup> ''b''</sup>; cohortative {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=1|verse=23}}. Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=7|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=יְהִי לְתַנִּין|translate=it shall become a serpent}}, is the apodosis to a suppressed protasis ''if thou cast it down''; so in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=וְיָשֹׁב}} is the apodosis to a protasis ''if thou wash'', contained in what precedes.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|e}}
(''c'') ''Cohortative'' (see {{GHGpar|108|e}}) in the protasis; perfect in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=40|verse=6}}; imperfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=אָק֫וּמָה וַיְרַבְּרוּ־בִי}} (if) ''I arise, they speak against me''; on the cohortative in the apodosis, cf. {{GHGpar|108|f}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|f}}
(''d'') {{GHGterm|Imperfect consecutive}} in the protasis ({{GHGpar|111|x}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=וָאֹֽמַד|translate=if I say}}, &c. (with a noun-clause as the apodosis); with a frequentative perfect consecutive in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=16}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|g}}
(''e'') {{GHGterm|Perfect consecutive}} in the protasis and apodosis (see the examples, {{GHGpar|112|kk}} and ll), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=וְעָוַב אָבִיו וָמֵת|translate=and should he leave his father, his father would die}}; 9:15, 44:29, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=4|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=16|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=19|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=30}}; with frequentative perfects, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=21}} (referring to the past, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=9}}); with imperfect in the apodosis (being separated from the {{GHGterm|Wāw}} by {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=24}}; introduced by an infinitive absolute, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=37}}; an interrogative clause in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=10|verse=19}}; a noun-clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=37|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=21}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|h}}
(''f'') ''A simple perfect'' (to represent actions which are to be regarded as completed) in the protasis and apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=18|verse=22}} {{GHGheb|text=מָצָא אִשָּׁה מָצָא טוֹב|translate=has one found a wife, he has found a good thing}}; an imperfect in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=19|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=10|hidebook=1}}; an imperfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=11|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=23|verse=13|hidebook=1}}<sup> ''b''</sup>, 29:11; an interrogative clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=12|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=20}} ''if I have sinned'' (prop., well, now I have sinned!) ''what can I do unto thee?'' 21:31, 35:6, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=3|verse=8}}; a noun-clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=27|verse=19}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|i}}
(''g'') ''A participle as casus pendens'' (cf. {{GHGpar|143|d}}, and the sections of the Grammar there cited, esp. {{GHGpar|116|w}}) or a complete noun-clause in the protasis; the apodosis mostly introduced by {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=23|verse=24}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}} {{GHGheb|text=יוֹלֵד חָכָם וְיִשְׂמַח בּוֹ|translate=if one begetteth a wise child, he shall have joy of him}}; with perfect frequentative in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=13}}, &c.; but also with a simple imperfect, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=12}} (cf. {{GHGpar|112|n}}); with an interrogative imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=2}}, 19; with an interrogative perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=13}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|k}}
(''h'') ''Infinitive with preposition'' (also as the equivalent of a conditional clause) in the protasis, and a perfect consecutive in the apodosis (cf. {{GHGpar|112|mm}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=7|verse=14}} ff. {{GHGheb|text=בְּהַֽעֲוֹתוֹ וֽהֹֽכַחְתִּיו וג׳|translate=if he commit iniquity, I will correct him}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=34|verse=34}} f. (with imperfect, followed by perfects frequentative in the apodosis).

Rem. On the expression of condition and consequence by means of two co-ordinate ''imperatives'', see {{GHGpar|110|f}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|l}}
'''3.''' Particles used to introduce conditional sentences are {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} (for which in the later and latest Books sometimes {{GHGheb|text=הֵן}}, see below, under w) and {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}}<ref>On {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} cf. Kohler in Geiger’s ''Zeitschr. für Wiss. und Leben'', vi (1868), p. 21 ff.</ref> ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=30}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=63|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=לוּא}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=6|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=7|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=אִלּוּ}}, from {{GHGheb|text=אִם לוּ}}) ''if'', negative {{GHGheb|text=אִם לֹא}} and {{GHGheb|text=לוּלֵא}} ({{GHGheb|text=לוּלֵי}}) ''unless''; {{GHGheb|text=כִּי|translate=supposing that}} (Lat. ''ut''), ''in case that'', sometimes used almost in the same sense as {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}. With regard to the difference between {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} ({{GHGheb|text=אִם לֹא}}) and {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} ({{GHGheb|text=לוּלֵא}}), the fundamental rule is that {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} is used if the condition be regarded either as already fulfilled, or if it, together with its consequence, be thought of as possibly (or<section end=par159 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

519.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par159" />probably) occurring in the present or future. In the former case, {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} is followed by the perfect, in the latter (corresponding to the Greek ἐὰν with the present subjunctive) by the imperfect or its equivalent (frequently in the apodosis also). On the other hand, {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} ({{GHGheb|text=לוּלֵא}}) is used when the condition is to be represented as ''not fulfilled'' in the past, or as ''not capable of fulfilment'' in the present or future, and the consequence accordingly as not having occurred or never occurring. In the former case, {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=לוּלֵא}} are necessarily followed by the perfect (mostly also in the apodosis) corresponding to the Greek εἰ with the indicative of an historic tense, and the Latin imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive. In the latter case (which is extremely rare) the perfect, or the participle, or even the imperfect, may be used.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|m}}
Rem. Since it again frequently depends on the subjective judgement of the speaker (see under a), whether a condition is to be regarded as possible or impossible, we cannot wonder that the distinction between {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} and {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} is not always consistently observed. Although naturally {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=לוּלֵא}} cannot take the place of {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} and {{GHGheb|text=אִם לֹא}} (on the strange use of {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=50|verse=15}} see below), yet conversely {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} is sometimes used where {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} would certainly be expected; cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=50|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=137|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=9|verse=12}} (cf. verse 11). These examples, indeed ({{GHGheb|text=אִם}} with the imperfect), may without difficulty be explained from the fact that the connexion of {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} with the imperfect was evidently avoided, because the imperfect by its nature indicates a still unfinished action, and consequently (as opposed to {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}}) a still open possibility. But {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} is also used for {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} in connexion with the perfect, especially when an imprecation is attached by the apodosis to the condition introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=7|verse=4}} ff. {{GHGheb|text=אִם־עָשִׂ֫יתִי זֹאת... יִֽרַדֹּף וג׳|translate=if I have done this..., let the enemy pursue my soul}}, &c., cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=9}} ff. The speaker assumes for a moment as possible and even actual, that which he really rejects as inconceivable, in order to invoke the most severe punishment on himself, if it should prove to be the case.

On the frequent addition of an infinitive absolute to the verb in clauses with {{GHGheb|text=אם}} see {{GHGpar|113|o}} above.

Examples:—

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|n}}
'''A.''' {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} 1. with {{GHGterm|perfect}} in the protasis to express conditions, &c., which have been completely fulfilled in the past or which will be completely fulfilled in the future (the perfect is here equivalent to the ''futurum exactum'', {{GHGpar|106|o}}). The apodosis<ref>We are not here concerned with the fact that the logical apodosis (the consequence of the condition) is sometimes mentioned before the condition; as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=28}}, 30, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=11|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=63|verse=6}} f., 137:6, and according to Dillmann {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=4|verse=4}}.</ref> takes—

(''a'') A {{GHGterm|perfect}} also, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=9|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־חָכַ֫מְתָּ חָכַ֫מְתָּ לָּ֑ךְ|translate=if thou art wise, thou art wise for thyself}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=15}} (see below on {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}}).

(''b'') {{GHGterm|Imperfect}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=41}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־שַׁנּוֹתִי|translate=if I whet my glittering sword}}... {{GHGheb|text=אָשִׁיב|translate=I will render vengeance}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=15}} f.30 (in both cases we should expect {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} rather than {{GHGheb|text=אִם־}}; so also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=44|verse=21}} f., with an interrogative imperfect in the apodosis); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=13}} (the apodosis is in verse 15).

(''c'') {{GHGterm|Jussive}} (or ''optative''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=9}} ff. (see m above); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=3}}.
<section end="par159" /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

520.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par159 />{{GHGmargin-letter|159|o}}
(''d'') {{GHGterm|Perfect consecutive}} (see the examples in {{GHGpar|112|gg}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־לֹא הֲבִֽיאֹתִיו וג׳|translate=if I bring him not... then I shall have sinned}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=4}}. On the other hand, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=5|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=4}} refer to actions already completed; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=9}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=9}} the perfect with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} is a perfect frequentative and refers to past time.

(''e'') {{GHGterm|Imperfect consecutive}} (see {{GHGpar|111|q}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=8|verse=4}} ''if thy children have sinned'' ({{GHGheb|text=חָֽטְאוּ}})..., {{GHGheb|text=וַיְשַׁלְּחֵם|translate=he has delivered them}}, &c.

(''f'') {{GHGterm|Imperative}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=50|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־נָא מָצָ֫אתִי חֵן בְּעֵֽינֵיכֶם דַּבְּרוּ־נָא לג׳|translate=if now I have found grace in your eyes, speak, I pray you}}, &c.; the imperative precedes in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=47|verse=16}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=4}}, 18.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|p}}
(''g'') A (complete or incomplete) noun-clause, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=14|verse=18}} (a vivid realization of the future) ''if I have gone forth into the field'' (= ''if I go'', &c.), ''then, behold, the slain with the sword!'' &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=24|verse=14}} (apodosis with {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|q}}
2. {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} with {{GHGterm|imperfect}} in the protasis, to express what is possible in the present or future, as well as (according to {{GHGpar|107|b}}) what has continued or been repeated in the past. The apodosis takes—

(''a'') The {{GHGterm|perfect}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=32|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=וְאִם־לֹא תַֽעֲשׂוּן כֵּן הִנֵּה חֲטָאתֶם|translate=but if ye will not do so, behold, ye have sinned}}; here the apodosis represents the time when the consequence has already taken place; so also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=12}}–14. On the other hand, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=29}} (as also {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=9}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=28}}) is a case of a pregnant construction, ''if these men die as all men die, then'' (it will follow from this) ''the Lord hath not sent me''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|r}}
(''b'') The {{GHGterm|imperfect}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־יֶחַיֻּ֫נוּ הִֽחְיֶה|translate=if they save us alive, we shall live}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=28|hidebook=1}}, 30, 28:20 ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=25}} (the second imperfect is equivalent to a {{GHGterm|jussive}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=10|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=2}}–4, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=50|verse=12}} (where {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} ironically represents an impossibility as possible); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=8|verse=5}} f. (with the insertion of a second condition in the form of a noun-clause); 9:3, 20, 14:7; a frequentative imperfect referring to the past, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־כֹּה יֹאמַר|translate=if}} (ever) ''he said thus''..., {{GHGheb|text=וְיָֽלְדוּ|translate=then they bare}}...; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=40|verse=37}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=42|verse=37}} the consequence (on {{GHGheb|text=תָּמִית}} cf. {{GHGpar|107|s}}) precedes the condition.

(''c'') The {{GHGterm|jussive}} (or ''optative''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=137|verse=5}}; cf. {{GHGpar|109|h}}.

(''d'') The ''cohortative'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=7}}; cf. {{GHGpar|108|f}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|s}}
(''e'') The {{GHGterm|perfect consecutive}} (see the examples in {{GHGpar|112|ff}} and gg), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־פָּקֹד יִפְקְרֵ֫נִי אָבִ֫יךָ וְאָֽמַרְתָּ|translate=if thy father miss me at all, then shalt thou say}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=41}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=20}}; with a frequentative perfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=8}} ''if he said'' (as often happened)..., ''then'', &c.

(''f'') The {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}}; so perhaps {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=59|verse=16}}, if {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּלִ֫ינוּ}} is to be explained according to {{GHGpar|111|t}}.

(''g'') The {{GHGterm|imperative}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=50}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=21}} (with {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}, but in verse 22 simply {{GHGheb|text=לֵךְ}}), 21:10, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=33|verse=5}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|t}}
(''h'') A noun-clause, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=139|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=8|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=26|hidebook=1}} f.

3. {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} with ''cohortative'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=31}}; cf. the passages in {{GHGpar|108|e}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|u}}
4. {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} with {{GHGterm|infinitive}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־אָמְרִי}} prop. ''if my saying is'' (but probably we should read {{GHGheb|text=אָמַ֫רְתִּי}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|v}}
5. {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} with a noun-clause, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=5|verse=22}} (in the apodosis a perfect with {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=46}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=15}} (imperative in the apodosis); 11:9 (imperfect in the apodosis); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=12|verse=8}} (cohortative in the apodosis); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=12|verse=12}}; especially if the subject of the conditional clause be a personal pronoun. In an affirmative sentence this pronoun is often joined to {{GHGheb|text=יֵשׁ}}, in a negative sentence to {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} (cf. on both, {{GHGpar|100|o}}), while the predicate (cf. {{GHGpar|116|q}}) is represented by a participle, usually expressing the future, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=36}} f. {{GHGheb|text=אִם־יֶשְׁךָ מוֹשִׁיעַ}}<section end=par159 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

521.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par159 />''if thou will save'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=49}} {{GHGheb|text=אִם־יֶשְׁבֶם עֹשִׂים|translate=if ye will deal}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=23|verse=23}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=42}} f. the condition is expressed in a more humble form by the addition of {{GHGheb|text=נָא}}. With {{GHGheb|text=אֵין}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=וְאִם־אֵֽינְךָ מְשַׁלֵּחַ|translate=but if thou wilt not send}}, &c.; 20:7 (with imperative in the apodosis); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=8|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=2|hidebook=1}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=19|verse=11}} (all with a participle also in the apodosis). But {{GHGheb|text=יֵשׁ}} and {{GHGheb|text=אַ֫יִן}} may also be used after {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} without a suffix; thus {{GHGheb|text=יֵשׁ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=23|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=20|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=15}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=אִם־אַ֫יִן}} (''if it be not the case'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=9|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=10}}; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=אִם־כֵּן|translate=if it be so}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=22}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|w}}
'''B.''' {{GHGheb|text=הֵן|translate=if}}, generally supposed to be originally identical with {{GHGheb|text=הֵן|translate=behold!}}<ref>There could be no doubt of their identity if {{GHGheb|text=וְהִנֵּה}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=11}}, simply meant ''if''. We must, however, keep to the meaning ''but behold''.</ref> Probably, however, {{GHGheb|text=הֵן|translate=if}}, is a pure Aramaism, and since the Aramaic word never has the meaning ''behold'', it is at least improbable that it had originally any connexion with {{GHGheb|text=הֵן}} or {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}}. Cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=8|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=25|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=54|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hag|chapter=2|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=7|verse=13}}, and frequently in Job, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, 12, 12:14, 15, 19:7, 23:8, 40:23, always with wāw apodosis following, except in 13:15, where consequently the meaning ''see'' is no doubt preferable.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|x}}
'''C.''' {{GHGheb|text=לוּ|translate=if}}, {{GHGheb|text=לוּלֵא}} ({{GHGheb|text=לוּלֵי}}) ''if not''.

1. With {{GHGterm|perfect}} in the protasis and apodosis (cf. {{GHGpar|106|p}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=8|verse=19}}; {{GHGheb|text=אִלּוּ}} is used in the same sense as {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=7|verse=4}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=6|verse=6}} (with a question in the apodosis).—With the perfect in protasis and apodosis after {{GHGheb|text=לוּלֵא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=42}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=14|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=34}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=9}}. On the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=29}} {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} with a perfect is followed by an imperfect in the apodosis, ''if they were wise, they would understand this''; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=2|verse=11}} by a perfect consecutive.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|y}}
2. With {{GHGterm|imperfect}} after {{GHGheb|text=לוּלֵא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=27}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָגוּר}} probably as the ''modus rei repetitae, were it not that I ever and again feared'', &c.; so also the imperfect after {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} with the apodosis suppressed, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=50|verse=15}} ''supposing that Joseph should hate us''; since, according to the context, the danger was real, the use of {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} here is strange; conversely in other cases, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=73|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=15}} f.30, {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} would be more natural than {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|z}}
3. A noun-clause occurs after {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=81|verse=14}}, all with imperfect in the apodosis; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=לוּ יֵשׁ}}, with cohortative in the apodosis.

'''D.''' {{GHGheb|text=כִּי|translate=supposing that, if}}:—

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|aa}}
1. {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} with {{GHGterm|perfect}} in the protasis, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=5|verse=20}} {{GHGheb|text=וְאַתְּ כִּי שָׂטִית|translate=but thou, if thou hast gone astray}}, &c.; with a frequentative perfect consecutive in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=7|verse=13}} f.; with an imperfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=29}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|bb}}
2. {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} with {{GHGterm|imperfect}} in the protasis, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=23|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=גַּם כִּֽי־אֵלֵךְ|translate=yea, though I walk}} (have to walk)..., ''I will fear no'' ({{GHGheb|text=לֹֽא־אִירָא}}) ''evil''; 37:24; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=כִּֽי־תִקְנֶה עֶ֫בֶד עִבְרִי וג׳|translate=if thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years shall he serve}} (but in verses 3–5 a series of definite conditions with definite consequences is introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}; so also the {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} in verse 7 is followed in verses 8–11 by the special cases with {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}; cf. also verse 17 ff.); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=41|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=5}}; with a perfect consecutive in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=18}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=16}}; with a noun-clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=15}}.

3. {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} with a ''noun-clause'' (and imperfect in the apodosis), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=8}}.

{{center|{{Small-caps|Remarks.}}}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|cc}}
1. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=13}} the particle {{GHGheb|text=אבי}} (Masora {{GHGheb|text=אָבִי}}, probably in the sense of ''my father'') appears exceptionally for {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}}; its meaning here is unquestionable, but<section end=par159 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

522.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par159 />its origin is obscure. Cf. the exhaustive discussion of Delitzsch and Wetzstein on {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=36}}, where this {{GHGheb|text=אבי}} appears to be used as a desiderative particle.—Sometimes when one case has been already discussed, another of the same character is added by means of {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ}} or, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=36}} {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ נוֹדַע וג׳|translate=or}} (another possible case) ''it is known that'', &c., i.e. ''but if it be known'', &c., LXX ἐὰν δέ, Vulg. ''sin autem''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=4|verse=23}}, 28, 5:1, 25:49, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=18|verse=13}}; with a following imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=14|verse=17}}f.—On the hypothetical use of {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} (which is interchangeable with {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} in other senses also) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=4|verse=22}} (in verses 3 and 27 {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=11|verse=27}} (verse 28 {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=4|verse=21}}, see the Lexicon.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|dd}}
2. The conditional sentence is frequently found in an abridged form, where the suppressed clauses can be easily supplied from the context; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=49|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=וְאִם־לֹא|translate=and if not}}, i.e. ''and if thou wilt not give it to me, then I take'' it (perfect according to {{GHGpar|106|n}}) ''by force''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=9}}. The use of {{GHGheb|text=וְיֵשׁ}} alone in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=13}} is peculiar, as also {{GHGheb|text=וָיֵשׁ}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=10|verse=15}} (where read with the LXX {{GHGheb|text=וַיֹּא֫מֶר יֵהוּא וָיֵשׁ}}) in the sense of ''if it be so''.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=וָלֹא}} alone appears to be used in the sense of ''if really ... not'', in each case with a following jussive equivalent to ''may there at least'', &c. (cf. {{GHGpar|143|d}}); but perhaps with Matthes, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1903, p. 122 ff., following Kuipers, we should read {{GHGheb|text=וְלוּ|translate=would that!}}—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=13|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=13}} the condition must be supplied from the preceding clause to complete the sentence introduced by {{GHGheb|text=כִּי עַתָּה}}, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=28}} by {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}}, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=13|verse=19}} by {{GHGheb|text=אָז}}.—The apodosis also appears sometimes in an abridged form (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=43|verse=2}}) or is entirely suppressed, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=50|verse=15|hidebook=1}} (see y above), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=32|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=27|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=5}}, where properly {{GHGheb|text=הַגֵּד}} must be supplied with {{GHGheb|text=כִּי תֵדָ֑ע}} as in verses 4 and 18; cf. {{GHGpar|167|a}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=8|verse=4}}, instead of the apodosis ''I exclaim'' which we should expect, the exclamation itself follows.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|ee}}
3. The absolute certainty with which a result is to be expected is frequently emphasized by the insertion of {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=9}}; {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אָזָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=19|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=15}}; or {{GHGheb|text=כִּי עַתָּה|translate=now verily}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=22|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=30}} after {{GHGheb|text=לוּ}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=42}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=10|hidebook=1}} after {{GHGheb|text=לוּלֵי}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=8|verse=6}} after {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}. On this ''corroborative'' {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} cf. such passages as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=20}}, &c., and {{GHGpar|148|d}}. On {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אִם}} after an oath cf. 163 d.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|ff}}
4. Sometimes the force of a hypothetical particle extends beyond the apodosis to a second conditional clause, as in the case of {{GHGheb|text=אִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=9|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, and {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=43|verse=2}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|159|gg}}
5. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=33|verse=20}} a negative statement takes the place of a condition with a negative consequence, ''for a man doth not see me and live'', instead of ''for if a man sees me, he does not live''; cf. the similar passages, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=22|verse=1}}, 4 ''thou shalt not see ... and hide thyself, instead of if thou seest ... thou shalt not hide thyself''.<section end=par159 />

<section begin=par160 />{{GHGpar-heading|160|Concessive Clauses}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|160|a}}
Besides the use of the imperative in the sense of a concession, meant either seriously ({{GHGpar|110|a}}) or mockingly ({{GHGpar|110|f}}), and of concessive circumstantial clauses ({{GHGpar|141|e}}, {{GHGpar|142|d}}, and {{GHGpar|156|f}}), concessive clauses may be introduced—

(''a'') By a simple {{GHGheb|text=אִם|translate=if}}: thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=15}} with perfect, ''if'' (=''though'') ''I had been in the right''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=18}} and 10:22 with imperfect in reference to a contingent event.

{{GHGmargin-letter|160|b}}
(''b'') By {{GHGheb|text=גַּם כִּי|translate=yea though}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=15}} with imperfect; for which we find simply {{GHGheb|text=גַּם}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=15}} with imperfect, ''yea, though these may forget, yet'' ...; on the other hand, with perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=36|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=95|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=6|verse=1}}; finally {{GHGheb|text=כִּי גַם|translate=even if, though}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=4|verse=14}}.
<section end=par160 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

523.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par160 />{{GHGmargin-letter|160|c}}
(''c'') By the preposition {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} governing a complete noun-clause, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=16|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=עַל לֹֽא־חָמָס בְּכַפָּ֑י|translate=notwithstanding}} that ''no violence is in mine hands'', or a verbal-clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=53|verse=9}}. On {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}} with the infinitive in a similar sense (equivalent to ''in addition to the fact'' that = ''notwithstanding'' that), cf. {{GHGpar|119|aa}}, note 2.<section end=par160 />

<section begin=par161 />{{GHGpar-heading|161|Comparative Clauses}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|161|a}}
'''1.''' A comparison between two facts is sometimes established by simply uniting them with {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}}, especially in gnomic poetry, when facts of a moral nature are compared with those of the physical world, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=7}} ''man is born unto trouble, and the sons of flame fly upward'', i.e. as the sparks by nature fly upward, so man, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=12|verse=11}} (in an interrogative form; in 34:3 the same comparison as a statement); 14:11 f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=17|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=25|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=26|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, 9, 14, 27:21, &c.<ref>On this {{GHGterm|wāw adaequationis}}, and in general on these proverbial comparisons, see Delitzsch, ''Das Salomonische Spruchbuch'', p. 9 f. Moreover, instead of entire clauses, the nouns alone (without predicates) are frequently grouped together, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=25|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=26|verse=21|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=27|verse=21|hidebook=1}} (called by Delitzsch, the ‘emblematic Mashal’). The expressions {{GHGheb|text=נֶחְשַׁב עִם}} prop. ''to be counted with some one'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=88|verse=5}}, and {{GHGheb|text=נִטְשַׁל עִם|translate=to be likened with some one}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=28|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=143|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, also arise from the idea of comparison implied in grouping things together. On this use of {{GHGheb|text=עִם}} cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=26}}, where ''with'' is equivalent to ''like''.</ref> Even without the connecting {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=24|verse=19}} ''drought and heat consume the snow waters'', {{GHGheb|text=שְׁאוֹל חָטָ֫אוּ}} so doth ''Sheol'' those who ''have sinned'' (cf. {{GHGpar|155|n}}); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=17|verse=11}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|161|b}}
'''2.''' The conjunction {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽאֲשֶׁר}} (cf. {{GHGpar|155|g}}; the simple {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} occurs in the same sense in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=14|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=34|verse=18|hidebook=1}}) ''as'', ''quemadmodum'', is used as a comparative conjunction ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ob|chapter=1|verse=15}}), frequently with {{GHGheb|text=כֵּן|translate=so}}, corresponding to it in the apodosis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=31|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=52|verse=14|hidebook=1}} f.. Sometimes, however, {{GHGheb|text=כֵּן}} (''so also'') occurs even after independent statements, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=55|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=3|verse=20}}.—Exact coincidence of two facts is expressed in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=5|verse=15}} by {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־עֻמַּת שָׁ·}}<ref>In spite of its form this particle has originally nothing to do with {{GHGheb|text=כֹּל}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־|translate=all}}. The expression is compounded of {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}} and {{GHGheb|text=לְעֻמַּת}}, like the Aramaic {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־קֳבֵל}} for {{GHGheb|text=כְּלָֽקֳבֵל}}; cf. M. Lambert, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|REJ.|Revue des Études Juives. Paris, 1880 ff.}}}} xxx. 47.</ref> ''in all points as''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|161|c}}
Rem. On the use of {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍|translate=as}}, with single nouns or pronouns to introduce comparisons, cf. 118 s; on the alleged use of {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}} as a conjunction (equivalent to {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽאֲשֶׁר}}), cf. {{GHGpar|155|g}}.—It is to be further remarked that {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}}—{{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}} when used in correspondence with one another, ''as—so'' (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=7|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=8|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=24|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=4|verse=9}}; also ''so—as'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=4}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=14|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=30|verse=24}} {{GHGheb|text=וּךְ}}—{{GHGheb|text=ךְּ}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=127|verse=4}} and often, {{GHGheb|text=כֵּן}}—{{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=2|verse=4}}), are not to be regarded as conjunctions, but as virtual substantives with a following genitive; {{GHGheb|text=כָּכֶם כַּגֵּר יִֽהְיֶה}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=15|verse=15}} properly means ''the like of you shall be the like of the stranger'', i.e. ''your duty shall be'' (also) ''the stranger’s duty''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=24|verse=22}}.<section end=par161 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

524.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par162 />{{GHGpar-heading|162|Disjunctive Sentences}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|162|a}}
The introduction of another possible case, excluding that which preceded, is effected by {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ}} or, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=36}}, equivalent to the Latin ''vel''; but also equivalent to ''aut'' with an exclusive antithesis, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=2|verse=16}}; so {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=27|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ}}= ''it would then happen that'', for which elsewhere {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ כִי}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|162|b}}
In the sense of ''sive—sive'' we find {{GHGheb|text=אוֹ}}—{{GHGheb|text=אוֹ}}, or {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}—{{GHGheb|text=אִם}}, or {{GHGheb|text=וְאִם}}—{{GHGheb|text=אִם}} (see the examples in the Lexicon), also {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}—{{GHGheb|text=וְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=5|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=9|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=24|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=13}} ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=32|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=76|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=34|verse=29}}, perhaps also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=21|verse=16}} (but not {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=29|verse=9}}; cf. Delitzsch on the passage), and {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}—{{GHGheb|text=לְ}} (see {{GHGpar|143|e}}); cf. also {{GHGheb|text=גַּם}}—{{GHGheb|text=גַּם}} (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=44}} {{GHGheb|text=וְגַם}}—{{GHGheb|text=גַּם}}) ''both—and''; but {{GHGheb|text=גַּם לֹא}}—{{GHGheb|text=גַּם לֹא}} (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=וְגַם לֹא}}—{{GHGheb|text=וְגַם לֹא}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=1|verse=18}} {{GHGheb|text=גַּם ... לֹא}}—{{GHGheb|text=גַּם}}) ''neither—nor''. On disjunctive questions, see {{GHGpar|150|g}}.<section end=par162 />

<section begin=par163 />{{GHGpar-heading|163|Adversative and Exceptive Clauses}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|163|a}}
'''1.''' After negative sentences (especially after prohibitions) the antithesis (''but'') is introduced by {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אִם}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=8|verse=19}} ''and they said, Nay, but we will have a king over us''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=1|verse=2}}, &c.; frequently also by {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} alone, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, or even simply connected with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=5}}, {{GHGheb|text=וְהָיָה}} as perfect consecutive; 42:10; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=5|verse=18}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|163|b}}
Rem. Sometimes the negation is only virtually contained in the preceding sentence, e.g. in the form of a rhetorical question ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=6|verse=3}} f.) or of conditions which are to be regarded as not having been fulfilled ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=18}}); {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} or {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אִם}} in such cases becomes equivalent to ''nay, rather''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|163|c}}
'''2.''' {{GHGterm|Exceptive}} clauses, depending on another sentence, are introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫פֶס כִּי|translate=except that}}, and (again after negative sentences, see a above) {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אִם}}<ref>Very probably this use of {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אִם}} arises from the original meaning ''for if, surely if'' ({{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} in an affirmative sense); so evidently in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=22|verse=22}} as a forcible resumption of the preceding {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}. Thus, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=15|verse=7}} is simply ''surely when I have been avenged of you, after that I will cease'', equivalent to, I will not cease, until I have, &c. When the exception follows, an ellipse must be assumed, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=18}} ''surely'' (or ''for'') ''when he has finished it'' (then the man will rest). It is far less natural to assume such an ellipse with {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אִם|translate=but}} (before entire clauses as before single nouns); see a above.</ref> ''unless''; especially {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אִם}} with the perfect (equivalent to ''unless previously'') after imperfects which contain a declaration, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=27}} ''I will not let thee go, except thou hast'' previously ''blessed me''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=22|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=55|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=65|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=3|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=18}}. Finally, {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְתִּי אִם|translate=unless}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=3|verse=4}} (with perfect after a rhetorical question), or simply {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְתִּי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=43|verse=3}} with a noun-clause, ''except your brother be with you''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=10|verse=4}} after a rhetorical question, with a verbal-clause.
<section end=par163 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

525.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par163 />{{GHGmargin-letter|163|d}}
Rem. The principal statement, to which {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אִם}} appends an exception, must sometimes be supplied from the context; thus, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=14}} (I desire nothing else) ''except that thou remember me'', equivalent to ''only do thou remember'', &c. (cf. 106 n, note 2; but it is probably better to read {{GHGheb|text=אַךְ}} for {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}}). Cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=6|verse=8}}, where {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אִם}}, equivalent to ''nothing but'', is used before an infinitive, and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=42|verse=8}}, equivalent to ''only'', before a noun. Similarly when {{GHGheb|text=כִּי אִם}} after an oath introduces an emphatic assurance, e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=20}} ''as the Lord liveth'' (I can do nothing else) ''except I run after him'', &c.; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=21}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ru|chapter=3|verse=12}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}, and even without the oath, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=15|verse=7}}; cf. the Rem. on ''c''.<section end=par163 />

<section begin=par164 />{{GHGpar-heading|164|Temporal Clauses}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|164|a}}
'''1.''' The relations of time existing between two different actions or events are frequently expressed without the aid of a conjunction simply by juxtaposition:—

(''a'') Actions or events are represented as wholly or in part ''simultaneous'' by connecting a noun-clause with another noun-clause or verbal-clause introduced by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} (or {{GHGheb|text=וְהִנֵּה}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=6}} ''and Noah'' was ''six hundred years old'' (prop. ''a son of six hundred years''), {{GHGheb|text=וְהַמַּבּוּל הָיָה}} and (i.e. ''when'') ''the flood was''. This is especially the case when the predicate of the noun-clause (frequently introduced by {{GHGheb|text=עוֹד|translate=still}}) is expressed by an active participle, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=16}} f. {{GHGheb|text=עוֹד זֶה מְדַבֵּר וְזֶה בָא וג׳|translate=he}} was ''yet speaking, and there came another'', &c.; see the numerous examples in {{GHGpar|111|g}} and {{GHGpar|116|u}}. Instead of a complete noun-clause there often occurs a simple ''casus pendens'' after {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־}} with a participial attribute in the sense of ''whenever any one''..., e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=זׄבֵחַ זֶ֫בַח וּבָא וג׳ כָּל־אִישׁ|translate=whenever any man offered sacrifice, then came}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=23}}, &c.; see the examples (in which the second member is generally introduced by {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}) in {{GHGpar|116|w}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|164|b}}
(''b'') Sequence is expressed by the juxtaposition

(''1'') of two imperfects consecutive, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=וַתְּכַל לְהַשְׁקֹתוֹ וַתֹּאמֶר|translate=and when she had done giving him drink, she said}}, &c.; 28:8 f., 29:31, 30:9, 32:26, &c.; cf. {{GHGpar|111|d}};

(2) of a noun-clause with a passive participle as predicate, and a verbal-clause attached by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=25}}; cf. {{GHGpar|116|v}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=29}} an imperative follows without {{GHGheb|text=וְ}};

(3) of two perfects (frequently with the secondary idea of rapid succession<ref>This secondary idea is implied here by the mere co-ordination of two independent {{GHGterm|verbal}}-clauses, just as the idea of simultaneous occurrence (according to {{GHGpar|116|u}}, note 1) is implied in the co-ordination of a ''noun''-clause with another clause. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=30}} the immediate succession is especially emphasized by {{GHGheb|text=אַךְ}} and the infinitive absolute, ''Jacob was yet scarce gone out... then Esau his brother came''; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=9|verse=24}} by {{GHGheb|text=אַךְ}} only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=48|verse=6}} by {{GHGheb|text=כֵּן}} and the addition of two more perfects without {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}.</ref> of the two actions or events in past time), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=הַשֶּׁ֫מָשׁ יָצָא... וְלוֹט בָּא וג׳|translate=the sun was just risen..., and}} (=when) ''Lot came'', &c., cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=2|verse=24}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=3}} f., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=3|verse=24}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=15|verse=14|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=20|verse=39|hidebook=1}} f.—In all these examples the subject follows immediately after the connective {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, and then the (simple) perfect. On the other hand,

(4) a perfect consecutive follows another perfect consecutive to express the contingent succession of future actions, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=44|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהִשַּׂגְתָּם וְאָֽטַרְתָּ אֲלֵהֶם}}<section end=par164 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

526.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par164 />''and when thou dost overtake them'' (as soon as thou shalt have overtaken), ''thou shalt say unto them''. Naturally, examples of this kind are very closely related to conditional sentences; see, therefore, the examples in {{GHGpar|112|kk}} and {{GHGpar|159|g}}. On the connexion of an imperfect consecutive or a perfect with detached expressions of time (as equivalent to complete clauses), cf. {{GHGpar|111|b}}; on the imperfect consecutive after {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}} and a statement of time, cf. {{GHGpar|111|g}}; on the perfect consecutive following a detached statement of time, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=6}}, cf. {{GHGpar|112|oo}}.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=29|verse=10}} an imperative with {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} follows the perfect consecutive.

{{GHGmargin-letter|164|c}}
(5) The fact that one action or event has not yet taken place on the occurrence of another, is expressed by {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֫רֶם}} (an adverb, not a conjunction) with the imperfect (according to {{GHGpar|107|c}}). The apodosis, which may consist of a subject and perfect or even of a noun-clause ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=15}}),<ref>On the perfect in the protasis, which is critically doubtful, cf. {{GHGpar|107|c}}.</ref> is then connected by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} (or {{GHGheb|text=וְהִנֵּה}}) as in the examples above, under no. 3, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=4}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=8}}) {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֫רֶם יִשְׁכָּ֫בוּ וְאַנְשֵׁי הָעִיר ... נָסַ֫בּוּ וג׳|translate=they had not yet lain down, and}} (=when) ''the men of the city'' ... ''compassed'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=25}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|164|d}}
'''2.''' Conjunctions used to introduce temporal clauses are {{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} (with perfect, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=1|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=16|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=12}}; with imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=41|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=21|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=31|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=19|hidebook=1}}) and {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}<ref>On {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} as an original demonstrative, cf. {{GHGpar|138|a}}; hence {{GHGheb|text=עַד־אֲשֶׁר נָשׁוּב}} is properly ''up to that'' (moment)—''we shall return''.</ref> ''when'' ({{GHGheb|text=כִּי}} with the imperfect also=''as often as'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=8|verse=4}}; with perfect {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=5}}); less frequently {{GHGheb|text=אִם}}<ref>Cf. the frequent use of ''wenn'' [prop. ''if''] for ''wann'' [=''when''] in German.</ref> (joined with a perfect), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=41|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=94|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=24|verse=13}}=''quotiescunque''; also in the same sense with an imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=36|verse=4}}; with a perfect, equivalent to the ''futurum exactum'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=4|verse=4}}. Other conjunctions of time are the compounds {{GHGheb|text=כְּמוֹ|translate=when}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=15}}; {{GHGheb|text=כַּֽאֲשֶׁר|translate=when, after that}}; {{GHGheb|text=עַד־אֲשֶׁר}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַד־כִּי|translate=until}} (also the simple {{GHGheb|text=עַד־}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=22}} [with the imperfect=''only when'', as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=10|verse=5}}]); 2:5, &c.; especially in the formula {{GHGheb|text=עַד־בִּלְתִּי הִשְׁאִיר לוֹ|translate=until there was none left remaining to him}} (where indeed it would be very natural to read {{GHGheb|text=הַשְׁאִיר}} the infin. constr., as elsewhere after {{GHGheb|text=בִּלְתִּי}}, {{GHGpar|114|s}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=21|verse=35}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=3|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=8|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=11|verse=8|hidebook=1}} (but {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=19}} ''while, as long as''); {{GHGheb|text=עַד אֲשֶׁר לֹא|translate=before that}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=12|verse=1}}, 2, 6 with an imperfect, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=8|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=עַד}} with a perfect; {{GHGheb|text=עַד־אִם}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַר־אֲשֶׁר אִם|translate=until the time when}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲרֵֽי־אֲשֶׁר}} (for which in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=40|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=אַחַר־אֲשֶׁר}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=25|verse=48}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=5|verse=9}} simply {{GHGheb|text=אַֽחֲרֵי}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=14|verse=43}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=41|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=42|verse=7}} simply {{GHGheb|text=אַחַר}}) ''after that''; {{GHGheb|text=מֵאָז}} (prop. ''since that time''; the dependent clause is attached to it in the same way as the attributive clause to the demonstrative {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} {{GHGpar|138|e}}) ''since'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=בְּטֶ֫רֶם}} (and simply {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֫רֶם}} {{GHGpar|107|c}}) ''before''; {{GHGheb|text=קַדְמַת}} (for {{GHGheb|text=קַדְמַת אֲשֶׁר}}) ''before'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=129|verse=6}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|164|e}}
Rem. 1. With regard to the tenses used with the above conjunctions, the rules are practically the same as those given in {{GHGpar|158|d}} for causal clauses. The perfect indicates actions completed in the past or future (in the former case corresponding to the Latin pluperfect, {{GHGpar|106|f}}, and in the latter to the<section end=par164 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

527.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par164"/>Latin ''futurum exactum'', {{GHGpar|106|o}}), the imperfect denotes actions occurring contingently in the future. On {{GHGheb|text=טֶ֫רֶם}}, {{GHGheb|text=בְּטֶ֫רֶם}}, and {{GHGheb|text=עַד}} with the imperfect as a ''tempus historicum'', cf. {{GHGpar|107|c}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|164|f}}
2. Clauses introduced by {{GHGheb|text=עַד}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַד־כִּי}} or {{GHGheb|text=עַד־אֲשֶׁר}}, sometimes express a limit which is not absolute (terminating the preceding action), but only relative, beyond which the action or state described in the principal clause still continues; thus, {{GHGheb|text=עַד}} with the imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=110|verse=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=עַד־כִּי}} with the perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=13}}, with impf. 49:10; {{GHGheb|text=עַד־אֲשֶׁר}} with the perfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=15}}; with the imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=112|verse=8}}.—Like the Arab. {{arabic|حَتَّى}}, {{GHGheb|text=עַד}} may even introduce a main clause; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=עַד־יַֽעֲבֹר}} prop. no doubt=thus it came to this—''they passed through'', i.e. so ''they passed through''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|164|g}}
3. The infinitive construct governed by a preposition ({{GHGpar|114|d}}, {{GHGpar|114|e|nonumber=1}}) is very frequently used as the equivalent of a temporal clause; the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} may usually be rendered by ''when, as'', or ''whilst''; the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}} by ''when, as soon as'' (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=10|verse=25}} followed by a noun-clause introduced by {{GHGterm|wāw apodosis}}), or, when referring to the future, by ''if''; the infinitive after {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} by ''since''. According to {{GHGpar|111|g}} such statements of time are generally preceded by {{GHGheb|text=וַיְהִי}} and the apodosis follows in the imperfect consecutive; hence in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=55}} (cf. Driver on the passage) {{GHGheb|text=וְכִרְאוֹת}} with a simple perfect following, is unusual. On the continuation of these infinitival constructions by means of the perfect consecutive, cf. {{GHGpar|112|v}}, and in general, {{GHGpar|114|r}}.—With the participle, {{GHGheb|text=כְּ‍}} appears to be used as the equivalent of a conjunction in {{GHGheb|text=כְּמֵשִׁיב|translate=as he drew back}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=29}} (unless we should read {{GHGheb|text=כְּהָשִׁיב}} [or {{GHGheb|text=כְּמוֹ הֵשִׁיב}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=15}}]), and in {{GHGheb|text=כְפֹרַ֫חַת|translate=when it budded}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=40|verse=10|hidebook=1}}.
<section end="par164"/>
<section begin="par165"/>{{GHGpar-heading|165|Final Clauses||<ref>Cf. H. G. T. Mitchell, ''Final Constructions of Biblical Hebrew'', Leipzig, 1879.</ref>}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|165|a}}
'''1.''' Like most of the dependent clauses hitherto treated, the final clause may also be joined by a simple {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}} to the main clause, unless the final clause is directly subordinated to the governing verb.

Examples of the connexion: (α) of a final imperfect (or jussive?) with a perfect by means of {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=19}}, see {{GHGpar|107|q}}; with an interrogative sentence, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=9|verse=1}}, 3, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=24}}; with an optative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=51|verse=9}}; with an imperative, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=11|verse=21}}; (β) of a cohortative with an imperative by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=16}}, or a jussive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=2|verse=5}} ({{GHGpar|108|d}}); (γ) of a jussive with an imperative by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=16|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=5|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=59|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=86|verse=17|hidebook=1}}; with a jussive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=19}}, or cohortative, {{GHGpar|109|f}}, g (cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=24|verse=21}} the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=1|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=מָה}} with the 1st plur. imperf., and {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=29|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=עִם־לְבָבִי}}, which are equivalent to cohortatives); (δ) of an imperative with a jussive, cohortative, or interrogative sentence by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}, {{GHGpar|110|i}}; (ε) of a perfect consecutive after another perfect consecutive, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=14|verse=36}}; after an imperfect, {{GHGpar|112|m}} and {{GHGpar|112|p|nonumber=1}}; similarly after a jussive, {{GHGpar|112|q}}; after an imperative, {{GHGpar|112|r}}.—On negative final clauses joined by {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא}} to the imperfect (so {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=43}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=30|verse=20|hidebook=1}}; and {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=25}} after {{GHGheb|text=אַל־נָא}} with a jussive in the main clause) see the Rem. on {{GHGpar|109|g}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=39|verse=23|hidebook=1}} the negative final clause is simply connected by {{GHGheb|text=לֹא}}.—On the use of an historical statement after verbs of command-<section end="par165"/><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

528.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par165 />ing, where we should expect a final clause (e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=13|verse=9}} ''then I commanded, and they cleansed'', equivalent to ''that they should cleanse, and they cleansed''; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=7}} a negative final clause is connected in this way by {{GHGheb|text=וְלאֹ}}), cf. {{GHGpar|120|f}}.

For examples of the direct subordination of the final imperfect (without {{GHGheb|text=וְ}}) see {{GHGpar|120|c}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|165|b}}
'''2.''' Final conjunctions are {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עַן אֲשֶׁר|translate=to the end that}}; also simply {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עַן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=25|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=4|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=51|verse=6}}, &c.; {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽעֲבוּר אֲשֶׁר}} prop. ''for the purpose that'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=10}}, and simply {{GHGheb|text=בַּֽעֲבוּר}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=20|hidebook=1}}; also the simple {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=36|verse=27}} a final clause is introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אֵת אֲשֶׁר}}, thus at the same time taking the form of an object-clause.</ref> {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=10}}, 40, 6:3, 32:46, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=3|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=8|verse=14}} f.; negatively, {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר לֹא}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=16}}; or {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ ּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=14}}; also negatively, {{GHGheb|text=עַל־דִּבְרַת שֶׁלֹּא}} ''for the matter (purpose) that'' ... ''not'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=7|verse=14}}; {{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי}} with imperfect, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=20|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=14}} ''that'' ... ''not''.—Quite exceptional is the use of {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} (if the text be right) in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=מִן־יְקוּמוּן}}, with the imperfect, equivalent to ''that'' ... ''not'' [in prose, {{GHGheb|text=מִקּוּם}}].

{{GHGmargin-letter|165|c}}
Rem. All the conjunctions here mentioned are naturally always used with the imperfect, see {{GHGpar|107|q}} (on the apparent exception in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=4|verse=24}}, see {{GHGpar|74|g}}).—On the negative conjunctions {{GHGheb|text=אַל}} and {{GHGheb|text=פֶּן|translate=that not, lest}}, see {{GHGpar|152|f}} and w. On the infinitive with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}<ref>On {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} as a supposed conjunction (equivalent to the Arabic ''li'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=6|verse=19}}, see {{GHGpar|66|i}}.</ref> (also {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עַן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, &c.) as the equivalent of a final clause ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=28|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, &c.), see {{GHGpar|114|f}}, h, p. On the continuation of such infinitival constructions by means of the finite verb, see {{GHGpar|114|r}}. On the negation of the final infinitive by {{GHGheb|text=לְבִלְתִּי}}, {{GHGpar|114|s}}. On the preposition {{GHGheb|text=מִן}} with a substantive or infinitive as the equivalent of a negative final clause ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=31|verse=29}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=23}}, &c.), see {{GHGpar|119|x}} and y.<section end=par165 />

<section begin=par166 />{{GHGpar-heading|166|Consecutive Clauses}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|166|a}}
'''1.''' Consecutive clauses are added by means of simple {{GHGterm|wāw copulative}} with the jussive,<ref>That such examples as {{GHGheb|text=וִיֽכַזֵּב}} are to be regarded as jussive is probable from the analogy of {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=14|verse=10}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=33}}.</ref> especially after negative and interrogative sentences, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=23|verse=19}} {{GHGheb|text=לֹא אִישׁ אֵל וִיֽכַזֵּב וּבֶן־אָדָם וְיִתְנֶחָ֑ם|translate=God is not a man, that he should lie, and}} (i.e. neither) ''the son of man, that he should repent''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=53|verse=2}} {{GHGheb|text=וְנֶחְמְדֵ֫הוּ}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=14|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=מִי חָכָם וְיָבֵן אֵ֫לֶּה נָבוֹן וְיֵֽדָעֵם|translate=who is wise, that he may understand these things? prudent, that he may know them?}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=5|verse=12}} {{GHGheb|text=וְלֹא}}=''so that'' ... ''not''; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=30|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} is separated from the predicate by the object. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=16|verse=10}} a negative consecutive clause comes after a cohortative, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=5}} after a perfect consecutive.—On the other hand, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=32}}, 33 the jussive in the sense of a consecutive clause is attached without {{GHGterm|Wāw}} to the preceding negative sentence (in<section end=par166 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>

529.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par166" />verse 32 a second jussive follows, likewise without {{GHGterm|Wāw}}, ''for he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him'', that ''we should come together in judgement'').
